Papers consistently place the construct under non-monotonic reasoning, and one paper uses the label non-monotonic reasoning for the capability to revise prior conclusions in light of new evidence. Another naming variation is defeasible inference. The main internal breakdown stated in the definitions is by how new information affects a conclusion, namely strengthening, weakening, or defeating it, and one paper contrasts this kind of reasoning with traditional NLI as a different type of natural language reasoning.

Space of measurement. Papers link it to no measurement instruments, one behavioral indicat

nodes.name: Deontological morality
nodes.definition: A moral framework where the morality of an action is judged based on its adherence to a set of rules or norms, such as not defecting against a cooperator.

nodes.name: Deontological reasoning
nodes.definition: A moral reasoning style that evaluates actions by adherence to moral rules, duties, rights, or principles rather than outcomes.

nodes.name: Depth
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, depth is treated as a property of model outputs: how fully and substantively a response develops its topic, rather than remaining shallow. One definition describes it as generated content that develops topics in a detailed, substantive, and non-shallow way, while another uses the variant name depth of knowledge for the degree to which a response demonstrates substantive expertise or detailed subject-matter knowledge. The shared core is detail and substance in responses, though the emphasis differs between topic development and demonstrated expertise.

Space of facets. Systematization is limited. One paper places depth alongside relevance, breadth, and novelty as parallel evaluation dimensions, while another discusses depth of knowledge together with expertise and reports that both humans and LLMs assign high weight to those attributes. The material does not describe subtypes of depth or a broader taxonomy beyond these neighboring terms.

Space of measurement. No measurement instrument is linked to depth, and no behavioral indicator is linked to it. In the uses, papers apply it directly as an evaluation criterion for generated content, f

nodes.name: Description correctness
nodes.definition: The degree to which a model's textual description of an image accurately reflects the visual content, including entities, attributes, and relationships.

nodes.name: Detoxification ability
nodes.definition: The underlying capacity of a model to effectively identify and remove toxic content across different forms and contexts without over- or under-correcting.

nodes.name: Diagram understanding ability
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage frames this as a latent ability to interpret structured information in diagrams, including their components, layout, and semantic meaning. A smaller line of work narrows it to a perceptual ability for diagrams representing physical systems, emphasizing correct interpretation of components, their properties, and their structural relationships. The main difference is scope and framing: broad diagram interpretation in most definitions, versus perception-focused understanding in a physical-science setting in a minority framing.

Space of facets. Papers use closely related labels, namely diagram understanding, diagram comprehension, and physical diagram understanding, with the last functioning as the more specific variant. One paper places physical diagram understanding inside a perception component of expert-level multi-modal reasoning, describing it as understanding the physical context in multi-modal input and handling diagrams with complex physical structures.

Space of measurement. The only linked operationalization uses 1 measurement instrument, the MMMU benchmark, and no behavioral indicators are linked. In that u

nodes.name: Dialogue understanding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. In the one definition, the construct is framed as processing conversational context and responding to dialogue-based inputs over long contexts. No competing definition or explicit disagreement appears in the papers.

Space of measurement. Operationalization is limited in the papers here: it is linked to 1 measurement instrument and 1 behavioral indicator overall, but only the instrument is explicitly recorded as measuring it. InfiniteBench is the only linked measurement instrument, with evidence coming from a table entry for a "Dialogue" task in An Evolved Universal Transformer Memory. The only linked behavioral indicator is dialogue state tracking, but that link is recorded as related rather than measured_by, so the relationships do not provide a second direct measurement route.

Links. Beyond measurement, one paper reports that dialogue state tracking is related to dialogue understanding. In A Zero-Shot Open-Vocabulary Pipeline for Dialogue Understanding, the evidence connects dialogue state tracking to understanding user needs and executing appropriate system actions in task-oriented dialogues. No causal or correlational links are recorded, and no linked co

nodes.name: Disability bias
nodes.definition: A latent tendency of LLMs to generate systematically less favorable, less accurate, or more stereotypical responses when queries reference disability, reflecting embedded ableist patterns in model behavior.

nodes.name: Disambiguation ability
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage is a latent capacity to resolve ambiguity by using context to choose among multiple plausible interpretations. Most definitions cast it as a property of the model and vary mainly in what is being disambiguated, including ambiguous questions, word senses, entity names, translations, vague instructions, and superlative readings. A smaller framing defines it as sensitivity to same-sense versus different-sense boundaries that should mirror human judgments, and some papers extend the construct to explaining word senses in context.

Space of facets. Papers use several near-synonymous labels, including ambiguity resolution, word sense understanding, disambiguation capability, ambiguity understanding, and sensitivity to sense boundaries, for overlapping phenomena. One survey organizes disambiguation work into query rewriting, long-form answer generation, and asking clarifying questions. At the same time, the same broad label spans distinct ambiguity types, from conditional question answering with possible clarifications, to same-sense versus different-sense judgments, to entity-name disambiguation and absolute versus rela

nodes.name: Discourse understanding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. A recurring framing treats discourse understanding as understanding the relations and organization that make text coherent: papers describe it as understanding how a text is organized and how its parts contribute to overall meaning and coherence, or as a latent model ability to infer and generate coherent continuations from discourse relations, with one paper noting that such relations involve "longer spans and complex reasoning." Other papers use differently scoped versions of the construct: one defines it as interpreting and reasoning over lengthy, complex narratives to answer questions that require a cohesive understanding of the whole text, while another uses a related label for comprehending and using reply dependency structure in multi-turn dialogue for semantic interpretation and information extraction. Across these definitions, the main differences are whether the construct is framed as a latent model ability or as a task, and whether it targets text organization, discourse relations across argument spans, whole-narrative reasoning, or dialogue reply structure.

Space of facets. Papers do not present a single shared breakdown of the construct, but they

nodes.name: Discrete reasoning
nodes.definition: The ability to reason over distinct, separate elements within a text, such as performing multi-step inferences over facts presented in a paragraph.

nodes.name: Disentanglement
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the cited definitions, the concept is treated as a property of internal representations: distinct, interpretable factors of variation in the data are captured by separate dimensions of the representation. The only explicit definition uses this framing, and the accompanying usage stays close to it by describing a "rich disentangled orthogonal basis" in the frequency domain, "more compact disentangled representations over LoRA," and a greater tendency to disentangle adapters for multi-adaptor fusion (FouRA: Fourier Low-Rank Adaptation). No competing framing is stated in the cited definitions.

Space of facets. The cited papers do not introduce named subtypes or a broader taxonomy for the construct. What is made explicit is its locus and unit of separation: it is a property of a model's internal representations, and what gets separated are "distinct, interpretable factors of variation"; in practice, the same idea is expressed through an orthogonal basis in the frequency domain, compact representations, and disentangling adapters.

Space of measurement. No measurement instrument is linked to it, and no behavioral indicator is linked to it. The papers theref

nodes.name: Disparity
nodes.definition: A systematic difference in model behavior across socially or factually contrastive conditions, reflecting either social bias or susceptibility to misinformation, which persists as a latent trait across evaluation instances.

nodes.name: Distraction bias
nodes.definition: A tendency for an LLM judge to be influenced by irrelevant or unimportant details in the prompt or response.

nodes.name: Distribution alignment
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the common core is distributional matching. One usage defines it as the degree to which selected training data matches representative examples from a target task so the model can learn the target distribution efficiently, while another uses the same term for a student model's ability to replicate a teacher's output probability distribution across tokens and contexts. The shared idea is alignment between distributions, but the papers differ on what is being aligned, training data to task examples versus student outputs to teacher outputs.

Space of facets. Rather than introducing named subtypes, the papers use the term at two levels. One line treats it as dataset-level alignment, where selected data should match representative examples from the target task, and another treats it as fine-grained, token-wise alignment, with dynamic emphasis of divergence or mixing for each token to better capture a teacher distribution. One paper also contrasts distribution alignment with calibration instead of treating them as the same construct.

Space of measurement. Papers do not link it to any measurement instrument or behavioral indicator. Still, the

nodes.name: Divergent thinking
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most commonly, papers treat divergent thinking as the capacity to generate multiple distinct, novel, or unconventional solution pathways from the same task or starting point, sometimes by varying in-context examples and few-shot prompts. Some definitions add that it reflects adaptability to explore new environments or constraints and to produce alternatives not previously used in the human solution space. A smaller line of work uses the label "divergent reasoning" for generating multiple plausible connections and hypotheses from limited expert knowledge, so the definitions vary between alternative solution generation for a task and extrapolation from sparse knowledge.

Space of facets. Papers often discuss it in relation to Creativity, and one formulation explicitly presents creativity as consisting of convergent thinking and divergent thinking, with the latter tied to adaptability under new environments or constraints. Related labels are also used for more specific processes: a "divergent thoughts" process is described as retrieving relevant demos and generating different few-shot prompts, while "divergent reasoning" is described as extrapolating expert tripl

nodes.name: Document understanding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most definitions treat document understanding as extracting, interpreting, and using information from documents, often to answer questions or support extraction, and often in multimodal settings with text, images, tables, figures, or layout. Some papers explicitly place it in retrieval settings, describing the need to use relevant information from a retrieved document and to reason over that document. A smaller line of work frames it more broadly as a latent capacity to understand document content, structure, context, and positional cues in complex or unstructured documents, while a minority narrows it to document-level understanding, meaning synthesis of information and relations across an entire document beyond isolated sentences; one paper instead defines document comprehension as the observable task of answering questions about a document image.

Space of facets. Across papers, the concept spans several facets: content understanding, document structure and context, layout and positional cues, multimodal elements such as text, figures, tables, and images, and, in a narrower usage, relations that span texts, paragraphs, or chapters within a document. Papers

nodes.name: Domain knowledge
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats domain knowledge as a latent understanding or repository of environment-specific or domain-specific concepts, facts, terminology, entities, and procedures that a model can access and apply within a field or task. Many definitions tie it to interpreting observations, constraints, or professional context and choosing appropriate actions or answers, for example having enough knowledge about Minecraft biomes, understanding terms such as "backlogging" and "lot-sizing," or bringing relevant background knowledge to mathematical modeling and multi-domain translation. A smaller line of work broadens the construct to professional or comprehensive knowledge across a wide spectrum of subjects, while other papers narrow it to deep domain expertise, localized Chinese knowledge, in-domain knowledge gained from fine-tuning, or the quality of a response showing expertise; the clearest differences are scope and whether the construct is framed as an internal model property or as demonstrated output quality.

Space of facets. Papers use several neighboring labels for similar territory, including domain-specific knowledge, professional kn

nodes.name: Domain specialization
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most commonly, papers use domain specialization for expert-level selectivity across domains: specific experts preferentially activate for, or are preferentially routed, tokens from particular domains, and in one formulation from distinct modalities as well. Within that prevailing framing, some authors describe it as a latent tendency of experts, while others make it explicitly degree-based, as the proportion of tokens from a domain routed to a given expert. A minority usage applies the same term more broadly to adapting a general-purpose LLM to domain-specific contextual data and domain objectives for a specific field and task.

Space of facets. The papers organize the concept at different levels. In the expert-routing usage, it is defined for a particular expert and domain pair, and one paper makes the scale explicit by stating that a value of 100% means all data from that domain is routed to that expert; another broadens the relevant categories from domains to modalities. By contrast, the broader usage treats domain specialization as a process applied to a general-purpose LLM for a domain and task, rather than as a property of an individual expert.

Space of

nodes.name: Domain-specific performance
nodes.definition: The model's effectiveness on a specific, targeted set of tasks or data distribution, as opposed to general-purpose performance.

nodes.name: Domain-specific reasoning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the shared framing is a latent ability to apply knowledge from a particular domain to interpret dialogue in context. A technical-dialogue usage casts it as interpreting utterances, diagnosing issues, and inferring likely misunderstandings, and describes it as especially needed for subtler, more context-dependent cases of misalignment. Another usage applies the same construct to emotional support dialogue, where the domain knowledge comes from psychological theories and expert-like reasoning about emotional states, causal events, and user intentions.

Space of facets. Papers do not provide a formal subtype taxonomy for this construct. Instead, they position it through nearby ideas: one paper places it alongside pragmatic reasoning when discussing subtle misalignment, while another associates it with psychological theory, expert cooperation, and dialogue analysis from multiple perspectives for extracting user-related information. The main variation across definitions is the target domain, technical troubleshooting in one usage and emotional support in another, while both treat it as a latent ability rather than an observable behavior.

Sp

nodes.name: Domain-specific robustness
nodes.definition: The model's ability to maintain performance and reliability when applied to specialized, high-stakes domains like medicine.

nodes.name: Dynamic adaptability
nodes.definition: The ability of a multi-agent system to adjust expert selection and collaboration strategies in response to evolving task demands and performance feedback over time.

nodes.name: Easy-to-hard generalization
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats easy-to-hard generalization as generalizing from easier, simpler, or smaller training cases to harder, larger, or more complex unseen cases, often with no direct supervision on the harder cases. Definitions differ on whether this is a latent model ability or a training and evaluation paradigm: some describe it as "the latent ability" to perform on more complex instances, while others describe a setup where human annotation is provided only for easier tasks, or where models are trained on SIMPLE examples and evaluated on HARD examples. A narrower formulation recasts the same pattern as transferability from simpler circuits to circuits with more components.

Space of facets. Papers use several nearby labels for overlapping uses, including simple-to-hard generalization, logical extrapolation, and transferability. The main organizing axis is task difficulty or size: one paper explicitly says simple-to-hard generalization is a type of length generalization, while another frames the phenomenon as solving problems of greater size and difficulty than those in training. Another distinction is scope, with broader formulations s

nodes.name: Editability
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the dominant framing treats editability as a capacity for successful model modification under repeated or ongoing editing while preserving what is already there. Definitions describe it as an "inherent capacity" to be modified efficiently without harming overall performance, as the ability to "edit multiple times without forgetting previous edits," and as continuous integration of a stream of factual updates while retaining previously acquired knowledge. A smaller framing shifts the emphasis from a model-level capacity to a method-level evaluation dimension, defining editing reliability as the degree to which a concept editing method consistently controls a target concept across different inputs.

Space of facets. Papers organize this concept mainly around time and retention. Some use narrower labels such as multiple edits, centered on accumulating successive updates without interference, while others use lifelong knowledge editing for continuous incorporation of a stream of factual updates. One paper instead places editing reliability within a four-dimension evaluation framework, alongside output generalization, neuron-level consistency, an

nodes.name: Editing locality
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across definitions, the prevailing usage describes editing locality as the degree to which an edit stays confined to the targeted knowledge, leaving unrelated inputs, knowledge, or tasks unchanged and minimizing unintended side effects. A smaller line of work casts it either as a latent property of an editing method, namely modifying targeted knowledge without influencing unrelated knowledge or model capabilities, or as an observable outcome, "unrelated knowledge preservation," meaning maintained performance on untargeted knowledge. One definition instead uses locality for a bounded-distance constraint on relevant tokens for prediction, so the main disagreement is between a knowledge-editing preservation notion and a token-locality notion, and within the preservation notion between a method property and observed behavior.

Space of facets. The papers mainly differentiate it by what should remain unchanged after editing: unrelated knowledge, unrelated inputs, untargeted tasks, or broader model capabilities. The naming is mostly stable, with "locality" and "editing locality" used for the same idea, while "unrelated knowledge preservation" names the observable ve

nodes.name: Effective receptive field
nodes.definition: The range of preceding tokens from which a model can effectively integrate information when processing a given token in a sequence.

nodes.name: Egocentric video understanding
nodes.definition: The latent capability to comprehend first-person videos by recognizing activities, objects, and other visual details from a self-centered viewpoint.

nodes.name: Elegance
nodes.definition: The ability of a model to capture and reproduce the aesthetic and artistic qualities of the source poetry, such as vivid imagery, concise expression, and emotional depth.

nodes.name: Embodied reasoning
nodes.definition: The latent ability of a model to understand and reason about physical environments, including objects, their relations, and dynamics, in order to inform action planning.

nodes.name: Emergent abilities
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats emergent abilities as threshold-like changes in task performance with scale: performance stays near chance or improves only slightly in smaller models, then improves sharply or discontinuously beyond a size or pretraining-compute threshold, with capabilities not seen in smaller models. A recurring alternative framing describes them more broadly as latent or qualitatively new abilities in larger, more advanced, or aligned models, including humor interpretation, creative generation, instruction following, few-shot learning, and complex reasoning, without always requiring a sharp threshold. More specialized definitions narrow the term to open-world multimodal and compositional behavior, or make emergence stricter by requiring simultaneous discontinuities across multiple tasks together with learning of underlying data-generating regularities.

Space of facets. Papers do not systematize the term in one way, and several nearby labels are used, including emergent abilities, emergent capabilities, and emergence. One line distinguishes a stricter form in which a capability must show discontinuous improvement on a required task

nodes.name: Emotion understanding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage treats emotion understanding as a latent ability to perceive, identify, infer, or interpret emotional content from visual or multimodal evidence, including emotions, sentiment, affective tone, and sometimes the atmospheric quality of a scene. A smaller line of work defines it more narrowly as recognizing a person's emotion category or emotional expressions, while another broadens it to complex, coexisting, and nuanced states that go beyond basic or discrete categories. The main variation is in the target of inference, scene atmosphere versus human emotion, and in the expected output, label prediction versus natural-language description.

Space of facets. Papers organize the construct mainly by granularity. Some use nearby labels such as emotion perception and emotional recognition for identifying and interpreting cues from multimodal inputs and predicting an emotion label, while others introduce fine-grained or nuanced emotion recognition for subtle, compound, culturally specific, or arbitrary categories beyond basic taxonomies. One paper also relates it to a coarse-grained then fine-grained classification pipeline,

nodes.name: Emotional alignment
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing framing treats emotional alignment as the degree to which an LLM's emotional responses to specific situations correspond with those of humans. A broader framing uses the same label for whether an AI's responses are affectively appropriate and supportive in emotionally sensitive conversations, including avoiding emotional destabilization and using "tone moderation and content adjustment" (EmoAgent: Assessing and Safeguarding Human-AI Interaction for Mental Health Safety). A smaller line of work shifts to "emotional calibration", defining the construct as responses tuned to a user's emotional complexity and context rather than generic or overly affirmative, and describing failures as "surface-level rather than context-specific empathy".

Space of facets. Papers do not present a settled subtype structure, but they do organize the construct around a few recurring facets: correspondence with human emotion appraisal, affective appropriateness and supportiveness in sensitive exchanges, and context-sensitive handling of nuanced, multi-layered emotions such as anger, guilt, or relational tension. The main naming variation is betwe

nodes.name: Emotional coherence
nodes.definition: The consistency of emotional expression over the course of a dialogue so that responses remain aligned with the character's emotional pattern.

nodes.name: Emotional expression
nodes.definition: The ability of a character to convey emotions vividly and appropriately within the context of an interaction, enhancing user immersion.

nodes.name: Emotional intelligence
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats emotional intelligence as a model, agent, or system ability, sometimes explicitly a latent ability, to perceive or understand human emotions and respond appropriately, usually in conversation. Some authors broaden this to managing emotions in social interactions or interpreting social situations, especially interpersonal conflict, and one definition extends the target to the emotions of oneself and others. The main variation is scope, from conversational emotion handling to broader social interaction and conflict-resolution settings.

Space of facets. One explicit decomposition treats emotional fidelity as an aspect of emotional intelligence, with emotional fidelity framed as part of a broader capability in social interaction. Elsewhere, papers organize the construct by setting rather than named subtypes, especially emotional support dialogue and interpersonal conflict resolution. One study also places emotional intelligence alongside other highly subjective tasks such as creative writing and persuasiveness.

Space of measurement. Papers link emotional intelligence to one measurement instrument: it is measured by

nodes.name: Emotional reasoning
nodes.definition: The ability to recognize and understand emotions from expressions or context and link them to behavior and decision-making.

nodes.name: Emotional resonance
nodes.definition: The capacity of generated content to evoke genuine emotional responses or reflect sincere feelings that deeply connect with human audiences.

nodes.name: Emotional stability
nodes.definition: The latent disposition of an LLM to generate responses perceived as calm, resilient to emotional influence, and low in emotional variability.

nodes.name: Emotional support
nodes.definition: The ability to provide comfort, encouragement, and understanding to a user experiencing emotional distress.

nodes.name: Emotionality
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the usage in the papers, Emotionality is framed as a latent tendency of an LLM to express emotional sensitivity and vulnerability. In Exploring the Impact of Personality Traits on LLM Bias and Toxicity, this framing is explicitly tied to generated text: both high and low Emotionality scores are described as leading to an increase in negative responses, and responses are said to "tend to be more negative" regardless of whether the score is high or low.

Space of measurement. Papers do not link Emotionality to any measurement instrument or behavioral indicator.

nodes.name: Empathic concern
nodes.definition: A component of empathy characterized by other-oriented feelings of sympathy and compassion for a person in distress.

nodes.name: Empathy
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the literature, the prevailing usage treats empathy as a capacity or tendency to understand another person's feelings and perspectives and to respond in ways that show understanding, compassion, resonance, or emotional support. This appears in formulations such as understanding users' emotions in dialogue, showing empathy toward a narrator, aligning with a user's subjective experience, and considering others' perspectives and feelings when addressing issues. A narrower line defines empathy as emotional alignment, that is, how a model's feelings change in specific situations and whether those changes match what humans would feel.

Space of facets. Papers do not use a single internal structure for the concept. One recurring account describes empathy as a complex, multidimensional construct whose facets can be treated as a trait, a state, or a social function in conversation, and it explicitly names empathic concern and personal distress as primary facets. In counseling-oriented evaluation, some authors separate a broader notion of emotional support quality from a narrower empathic understanding, defined as reflecting feelings and aligning with the user's

nodes.name: Engagement
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most papers treat engagement, or engagingness, as a response or dialogue quality, whether phrased as outputs that are interesting, captivating, likely to elicit further interaction, or judged engaging in social interaction. A smaller line of work narrows this to interactive engagement, described as a text's ability to "draw the user in" and encourage ongoing, dynamic contribution to the dialogue. Another usage shifts the construct to the discussion level, defining engagement as interest plus participation, combining reciprocity, response diversity, and discussion length, so the main difference across papers is whether engagement is located in model responses or in broader user participation.

Space of facets. Papers use several near-neighbor names, especially engagement, engagingness, and interactive engagement, for overlapping but not identical ideas. Most of these variants still center on maintaining attention or interest, and long-term dialogue work further frames engagingness as the ability to maintain an annotator's interest over time, with shared memories described as making dialogues more engaging. One paper also places engagement alongside honesty, hel

nodes.name: Episodic memory
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, episodic memory is consistently framed as access to specific past episodes rather than general knowledge. Some papers describe it at the model level as storage and retrieval of sequence-specific information, independent of generalized or natural language knowledge, while others emphasize recall of events grounded in time and space or of past user interactions and autobiographical experiences. The main variation is whether the construct is phrased as a storage and retrieval capacity or in more human-like autobiographical terms.

Space of facets. The clearest systematization is a contrast with semantic memory or generalized world knowledge: episodic memory is reserved for details of specific events, personal experiences, or sequence-specific information. Some authors also use the term for a memory mechanism, with embeddings or recurrent state described as serving as episodic memory that passes information between time steps, while others use the same term for a latent ability to recall specific experiences.

Space of measurement. In the linked operationalizations, no measurement instrument is attached to episodic memory, and no linked con

nodes.name: Epistemic uncertainty
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats epistemic uncertainty as the model's lack of knowledge about its own prediction, a reducible uncertainty that can decrease with more information or data. Several definitions stress that it reflects ambiguity or missing knowledge rather than token-level likelihood alone, and one definition describes it as model-specific uncertainty tied to lack of knowledge in the model's parameters. A smaller line narrows the term to uncertainty in model parameters or weights, modeled through a posterior distribution and expected to diminish with more data.

Space of facets. Papers systematize the concept mainly through contrasts and nearby labels. One recurring contrast separates it from lexical confidence, since next-token likelihood is described as lexical confidence rather than epistemic uncertainty, while another places it alongside knowledge-boundary language as model-specific uncertainty related to the parametric knowledge boundary. Some authors also use weight uncertainty for the parameter-focused version, so the term spans both a broad lack-of-knowledge framing and a narrower posterior-over-weights framing.

Space of meas

nodes.name: Epistemic uncertainty awareness
nodes.definition: The tendency to recognize uncertainty caused by missing information or incomplete evidence, where additional knowledge could reduce uncertainty.

nodes.name: Error detection ability
nodes.definition: The latent ability to identify incorrect or flawed reasoning steps within a chain of thought, even when the final answer may appear plausible.

nodes.name: Error propagation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats error propagation as a cascading-error pattern in which mistakes made early in a chain, step sequence, or token sequence spread to later parts of the reasoning process and can yield an incorrect final answer. Definitions largely agree on that pattern, though some phrase it as a tendency for errors to propagate and compound, while others describe it as an observable phenomenon in which early-token or early-step errors lower later accuracy. A smaller line of work applies the same idea to multi-agent communication, defining it as erroneous information from one agent spreading through the network and negatively influencing the system's final output.

Space of facets. Papers use both error propagation and error accumulation for closely related phenomena, but scope varies. Most chain-oriented accounts describe within-trace cascading at the level of reasoning steps or tokens, including a reported pattern of higher token accuracy at the beginning of the chain and lower accuracy at the end, while another account ties the effect to longer outputs that amplify compounding mistakes. A distinct multi-agent framing shift

nodes.name: Error recovery
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats error recovery as a latent ability or capability to recover from mistakes in perception, skill execution, partner actions, invalid actions, or unexpected state changes and continue toward task completion or goal progress; one paper reports that LLMs "struggle to recover from skill failures and perception grounding errors." Several definitions broaden this to handling and managing execution errors, including revising code or adjusting reasoning from execution feedback. A smaller, narrower framing specializes it to out-of-sync recovery, where the agent must notice that its belief has diverged from the true state, diagnose the mismatch, and update its understanding to resynchronize, while one paper instead casts it as observable self-correction during inference rather than a latent capability.

Space of facets. Papers use adjacent labels such as failure recovery, error tolerance, error handling, and out-of-sync recovery for overlapping formulations of the same general idea. One framing groups supporting mechanisms such as error identification, recovery loops, self-correction, and fallback strategies under error handling,

nodes.name: Ethical alignment
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats ethical alignment as a latent tendency or degree of fit between a model's responses or behaviors and ethical norms, principles, or values. Most definitions frame it through conformance, responses that follow ethical standards, societal values, or specified principles, often alongside avoidance of harmful, misleading, inappropriate, biased, or manipulative content; some narrow this to professional service contexts, while others broaden it to safety, privacy, and fairness. A smaller line of work uses nearby labels such as moral alignment or value conformity to define it instead as correspondence between an LLM's preferences or internal moral representations and aggregated human preferences, especially in moral dilemmas.

Space of facets. Papers do not present a single shared taxonomy, but they recurrently break the concept into ethical principles or value domains. One grouping describes it through safety, privacy, fairness, and harm avoidance, while another treats value issues as social bias, ethics, and toxicity; another definition adds societal values and cultural contexts to ethical norms. The naming is al

nodes.name: Ethical bias
nodes.definition: Systematic deviations in moral judgment that may be influenced by factors such as language or culture.

nodes.name: Ethical decision-making
nodes.definition: The capacity to make judgments and choices based on ethical or moral principles, particularly in social dilemmas involving shared resources.

nodes.name: Evaluation ability
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats evaluation ability as a latent capability of a model or LLM to accurately assess the quality or correctness of generated outputs. Most formulations focus on judging model responses or text, sometimes including intermediate reasoning steps or full trajectories, and they anchor accuracy against human judgments, score rubrics and reference answers, or adherence to instruction constraints. Smaller variants narrow it to fine-grained evaluation with user-defined criteria, coding-solution judgment, multimodal comparison that matches human voting, or judging that guides reranking, beam search, and refinement.

Space of facets. Papers mostly use a cluster of near-synonymous labels, including evaluation capability, judging ability, text evaluation ability, judgment capability, and judge ability, for the same underlying judging capacity. The clearest subtype is fine-grained evaluation capability, explicitly contrasted with coarse or generic preferences and tied to user-defined score rubrics and reference materials. A smaller line of work argues that reranking, beam search, and refinement are all tied to a single underlying f

nodes.name: Evaluation bias
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across these papers, the dominant framing treats evaluation bias as systematic distortion in model-based judging or assessment: a model acting as a reviewer or judge may unfairly favor or disfavor responses, and one formulation defines judge bias as the expected difference between a judge's proxy score and the ground-truth score. A parallel framing defines it more broadly as systematic deviation in estimated model capability caused by flaws in the evaluation protocol. Smaller lines of work use narrower variants, including self-favoring bias, affinity bias toward models whose predictions are functionally similar to the judge's own, bias in human or AI-generated feedback, and implicit preferences that lead judges to prioritize some criteria over explicit instructions.

Space of facets. Papers break the construct down in several ways. One account decomposes evaluation bias into original, independent, and related terms, while another describes bias in feedback through presentation-related, social-related, content-related, and cognitive-related biases. Across judge-centered work, affinity bias, self-favoring bias, and implicit bias appear as named variants, so rela

nodes.name: Evaluator self-consistency
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. The paper treats this construct, under the name "Self-alignment," as the extent to which an evaluator's internal reasoning and scoring are consistent with its own task understanding and instructions. Its usage is tied to "internal thinking": the paper says it instructs GPT to conduct internal thinking that aligns itself for better task and preference understanding, and presents this internal thinking as strengthening task understanding and instruction following.

Space of measurement. Papers do not link this construct to any measurement instrument or behavioral indicator. The material therefore does not specify a benchmark, human evaluation setup, judge-model procedure, probe, or analysis that operationalizes it.

Links. No causal, correlational, or related links are reported for this construct.

nodes.name: Event-level understanding
nodes.definition: The ability to comprehend videos at a fine-grained level by identifying, localizing, and describing individual events, as opposed to providing a single summary for the entire video.

nodes.name: Event understanding
nodes.definition: The latent ability of a model to correctly identify and interpret event types and their structures from multimodal inputs, integrating relevant textual and visual cues while ignoring irrelevant or misleading features.

nodes.name: Evidence grounding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, papers treat evidence grounding as answers being anchored in relevant evidence from the input, including visual scenes or video content, rather than unsupported claims. One framing emphasizes response-level behavior, support with "specific, relevant, and accurate references to observable content"; another, under the label credibility, emphasizes whether answers reflect a "genuine understanding" of relevant evidence instead of shortcuts or biases. As MovieCORE: COgnitive REasoning in Movies describes it, the construct appears in the ability to reference specific scenes and provide concrete examples to support assertions, while CG-Bench: Clue-grounded Question Answering Benchmark for Long Video Understanding emphasizes retrieving relevant clues.

Space of facets. Systematization is limited. The papers do not break the construct into formal subtypes, but they do separate two facets: explicit references to observable content in the response, and the underlying basis of the answer in genuine understanding of relevant evidence rather than shortcuts or biases. Terminology also varies, with one paper using evidence grounding and another discuss

nodes.name: Exaggeration
nodes.definition: The latent tendency of an LLM to amplify persona-defining semantic features beyond what is topically necessary, contributing to caricature in identity-conditioned narratives.

nodes.name: Execution feedback utilization
nodes.definition: The latent ability of a model to effectively incorporate execution outcomes from public tests to improve subsequent code generations across turns.

nodes.name: Executive function
nodes.definition: Higher-level control abilities involved in integrating contextual information and managing task demands.

nodes.name: Expert diversity
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across these papers, the prevailing usage treats the construct as expert-to-expert distinctness within an MoE model: experts have dissimilar parameters, non-overlapping capabilities or processing preferences, and distinct, non-redundant knowledge, all described as signs of functional specialization. This framing is repeatedly contrasted with overlap in expert functionalities or other forms of redundancy. A smaller line of work uses the alternative label functional similarity, defining the comparison instead by experts producing equivalent outputs for the same input, which reflects redundancy in learned representations.

Space of facets. Papers do not divide the construct into formal subtypes. Instead, they organize it through contrasts: most describe diversity through specialization, uniqueness, and complementary expert roles, while the opposing side is described as overlap, redundancy, functional equivalence, or equivalent outputs on the same input. The terminology is not fully uniform, because most papers use expert diversity for the distinctness side of the comparison, whereas a smaller line of work uses functional similarity for the equivalence and redunda

nodes.name: Expert routing recency bias
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions here, the most specific usage treats it as a routing tendency in Mixture-of-Experts systems: the router preferentially uses newly added experts or knowledge and neglects older ones. Papers using the broader label recency bias also define it more generally as attention or retrieval favoring more recent, near, or final tokens over earlier context. The main disagreement is therefore about where the bias is located, expert routing over components versus temporal preference over input positions or context.

Space of facets. The papers do not present a shared subtype scheme. Instead, they use the same label across different mechanisms: MoE routing, recent-corpus overfitting, stick-breaking attention or retrieval, single-state linear attention, and long-context attention that is "more strongly concentrated at the tail." In that sense, the term is used for different targets, newly added experts in one usage and recent or near tokens in others.

Space of measurement. No measurement instrument or behavioral indicator is linked to this construct. In the papers' descriptions, it is identified through observable patterns such as tokens being "predomi

nodes.name: Expert specialization
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most papers describe expert specialization as a division of labor inside mixture models: individual experts, adapters, or LoRA experts develop focused capabilities for particular tasks, domains, data patterns, inputs, or parts of the data distribution, instead of remaining redundant or overlapping. The recurring evidence is that an expert 'becomes adept at handling a certain type of task or data pattern', that experts are weighted differently depending on the task, and that mixture members specialize in distinct parts of the distribution. A smaller line of work uses the same term for collaboration structure, defining a specialized expert as one primarily co-activated with a small specific group of other experts, so the main disagreement is between functional task sensitivity and co-activation based specialization.

Space of facets. When papers break it down, they do so mainly through contrasts: specialization is opposed to redundant or overlapping functionality, and one paper separates shared knowledge in the backbone from specialized, task-specific residuals in experts. Another paper contrasts expert collaboration with specialization, describing collaborative

nodes.name: Expert utilization
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats this construct as the extent to which experts are actually used, rather than left underused or concentrated in a small subset. One definition emphasizes whether selected experts are leveraged effectively and whether routing is more balanced, while another, under the name expert activation, emphasizes utilization of distinct experts during optimization and inference and denser use of otherwise underused experts. The main variation is whether the focus is balanced use of selected experts or broader activation of distinct experts as a way of leveraging parameter capacity.

Space of facets. The papers do not offer a broader taxonomy, but they use closely related labels for much the same phenomenon. Expert activation is treated as near-aligned with expert utilization, and one paper explicitly frames denser activation as mitigating low expert utilization and improving use of dead experts. Beyond this terminological variation, the papers do not distinguish formal subtypes or place it under a larger named construct.

Space of measurement. Papers link it to no measurement instruments and no behavioral indicators. Instead,

nodes.name: Explanation faithfulness
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, usage splits between two closely related framings rather than converging on one. One framing, under the label causal faithfulness, treats it as how well a feature interpretation matches the feature's causal role in computation, so that features are "interpretable in a way consistent with their causal role" (Towards Principled Evaluations of Sparse Autoencoders for Interpretability and Control). Another framing treats explanation faithfulness as how accurately and reliably a textual explanation describes the behavior of a specific neural network unit, with the stated goal of evaluating "how faithfully this explanation describes the neuron" (Evaluating Neuron Explanations: A Unified Framework with Sanity Checks).

Space of facets. The main variation is in what is being evaluated and against what standard. One paper centers feature interpretations and whether they match causal role, while another centers textual explanations and whether they accurately describe a unit's behavior; the difference is between matching causal role and accurately describing behavior. In the unit-explanation framing, papers also discuss faithfulness alongside reliabil

nodes.name: Explanation quality
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats explanation quality as the quality of model-generated explanations or rationales, especially whether they are logical and appropriate for the problem being solved. One definition emphasizes clarity, relevance, logical coherence, and whether the explanation provides meaningful insights into the optimization process and results, while a closely aligned phrasing emphasizes plausibility, logic, and appropriateness for a given query or answer. A smaller framing uses the term more narrowly for the correctness and policy adherence of guardrail explanations.

Space of facets. The clearest structuring in the papers is to treat explanation quality as an overall evaluation aspect that can be set alongside modeling accuracy. Another paper uses the label rationale quality for the generated explanation behind an answer, with criteria that overlap strongly with explanation quality. Across these uses, the object being judged shifts between optimization-focused explanations, answer rationales, and guardrail explanations, and the named criteria shift between insight, plausibility, and policy adherence.

Space of measurement. Papers

nodes.name: Explicit social bias
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing framing treats explicit social bias as bias that is consciously or intentionally expressed and accessible to direct report or control. One definition ties it specifically to models making overt judgments about demographic attributes, while another states it more broadly as bias that is not automatic, relatively controllable, and captured with direct measures. The shared core is directness, reportability, and non-automatic expression, while the main difference is whether the construct is defined narrowly around overt demographic judgments by models or more broadly as a kind of explicit association or belief.

Space of facets. Papers mainly organize this construct in contrast to implicit bias. On the explicit side, authors describe fairness-related questions and tasks where models make direct judgments, and one paper refers to explicit associations as individual beliefs; on the contrasting side, the same work distinguishes implicit tasks such as image description and form completion. Beyond this explicit versus implicit split, the papers do not introduce finer subtypes.

Space of measurement. Operationally, the construct is link

nodes.name: Exploitation
nodes.definition: The process of refining and improving upon known, promising solutions by leveraging feedback and prior search experience to intensify the search in a local region.

nodes.name: Exploration ability
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats exploration ability as breadth of search: a latent ability, tendency, or process for searching broadly across a solution space and generating varied reasoning trajectories or solution paths. Many definitions stress discovering novel or effective solutions through diverse reasoning paths, multiple candidate answers, or trial-and-error alternatives. A smaller line of work uses the same term for active environment search to locate objects or information, and a few papers narrow it to search over candidate programs or puzzle states. The main disagreement is whether exploration is a latent model property or an observable search behavior, and whether the search happens in reasoning space, an embodied environment, or a program space.

Space of facets. Papers use several overlapping labels around this construct. "Self-exploration" is a narrower version centered on identifying flaws in one's reasoning and generating alternative paths without external intervention, while "parallel search" names an observable behavior in which multiple distinct solution paths or program fragments are explored within a single iteration. Sever

nodes.name: Exploration-exploitation tradeoff
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the dominant framing is a balancing ability or latent tendency between exploration and exploitation. Most definitions describe exploration as trying uncertain actions or generating novel, diverse candidates, and exploitation as selecting immediately promising options or refining known high-quality or high-potential ones. The main variation is the level of description: some papers state it as action choice, while others place it in optimization over sequences or chemical candidates.

Space of facets. Papers consistently organize the construct into two poles, exploration and exploitation. Exploration is described as trying uncertain actions, generating novel solutions, or producing diverse sequences, whereas exploitation is described as choosing promising actions or refining existing candidates; one paper says an agent "intelligently balances exploration and exploitation in the chemical space." Another paper formalizes the balance with a rationality parameter, stating that β controls the explore-exploit tradeoff.

Space of measurement. No measurement instrument is linked to this construct. Papers link it to 1 behavioral indicator, Action selection

nodes.name: Expressive power
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most definitions describe expressive power as the range or complexity of functions, tasks, or signals a model can represent, approximate, or solve. Many papers cast it as an in-principle architectural property, often in formal-language or complexity-class terms, and some explicitly separate it from learnability, the training process, or inductive bias. A recurring secondary usage narrows the construct to parameterization or adaptation capacity under efficiency constraints, especially low-rank, shared-rank, or compact updates. Smaller lines of work place the property in token representations, embeddings, prompts or control mechanisms, or in richer preference and value representations, so the main disagreement is over whether expressive power belongs to the architecture, the parameter space, or the learned representations themselves.

Space of facets. Papers use several near-synonyms for the same general construct, most often expressivity, expressiveness, representational capacity, computational power, and function approximation power. Within that cluster, one common strand organizes it through formal languages and complexity classes, asking what automata, langu

nodes.name: External validity
nodes.definition: The extent to which the model’s inferred quantities match ground truth values within a tolerance threshold.

nodes.name: Extraversion
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats extraversion as a personality trait marked by sociability, assertiveness, and an outgoing, energetic orientation. Most definitions stay at that level, while a smaller framing presents it as a fundamental Big Five trait and adds excitement-seeking and positive emotions. The definitions largely agree on the trait framing, with variation mainly in the reference model, HEXACO or Big Five, and in whether extra facets beyond sociability and assertiveness are named.

Space of facets. The papers place it within broader personality models: one line lists Extraversion as one of the six HEXACO dimensions, while others list Extraversion or Extroversion as one of the five Big Five traits. Naming is not fully uniform, since both Extraversion and Extroversion appear, but the descriptions overlap around sociability and assertiveness.

Space of measurement. No measurement instrument is linked to it, and no behavioral indicator is linked to it. One paper mentions the IPIP-NEO-120 questionnaire as quantifying behavior patterns across five dimensions including Extraversion, but no measured_by relationship is recorded for this entity.

nodes.name: Fact-checking ability
nodes.definition: The overall capacity of an LLM to correctly verify claims and produce sound justifications across diverse and complex real-world scenarios.

nodes.name: Factual grounding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the usage in the papers, factual grounding is described as alignment between a model's outputs, real-world distributions, and factual information. The same paper also ties it to producing outputs "grounded in factual information and real-world context" and to aligning models with "real-world distributions" to support such grounding (LLM Bias Detection and Mitigation through the Lens of Desired Distributions).

Space of facets. The only explicit systematization frames it through a desired-distribution contrast: one paper pairs equal distributions with social equity, and real-world distributions with factual grounding. In that formulation, the axis of distinction is the reference distribution used to frame bias.

Space of measurement. Operationalization is minimal in the linked literature. No measurement instrument is linked to factual grounding, and the only linked behavioral indicator is Information retrieval; in the recorded relationships, it appears as a claimed cause of factual grounding rather than as a direct measure.

Links. One paper claims a causal relationship from Information retrieval to factual grounding, stating that retrieval-augmented gen

nodes.name: Factual knowledge
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats factual knowledge as a latent store, or extent, of encoded world facts that a model can accurately retrieve from its parameters or pretraining when queried. Closely related labels, including factual recall, fact recall, knowledge recall, factual knowledge retrieval, and parametric knowledge retrieval, mostly preserve this retrieval-centered framing. Smaller variations narrow the construct to specific factual associations or subject-relation-object triples, or emphasize whether retrieval is independent of current context versus used within a given task or query; as one paper notes, "the correct fact was present in the pretraining data but the model hallucinated" (HALoGEN: Fantastic LLM Hallucinations and Where to Find Them).

Space of facets. Papers use several near-synonymous names for overlapping ideas: factual knowledge, factual recall, fact recall, knowledge recall, long-term knowledge recall, factual knowledge recall, factual knowledge retrieval, and parametric knowledge retrieval. The same label is not used uniformly: knowledge recall can refer to retrieving world knowledge for visual question answering, recallin

nodes.name: Factual reasoning
nodes.definition: The ability to produce responses grounded in factual knowledge and to avoid generating false claims, especially in the presence of misleading or humorous prompts.

nodes.name: Factual retention
nodes.definition: The ability of an agent to locate and retrieve specific, instruction-relevant pieces of information from within a video to complete a task, even if the information is incidental to the video's main focus.

nodes.name: Factuality
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats factuality as output correctness: generated statements, answers, rationales, summaries, or queries should be factually correct, accurate, and aligned with real-world or otherwise externally verifiable knowledge, often framed as being free from factual errors, unsupported claims, or hallucinations. Many definitions also tie it to grounding in retrieved documents, evidence, or other knowledge sources. A smaller line of work treats it as a latent ability or tendency of the model, sometimes tied to parametric knowledge or even to the hidden truth status of a statement, and some papers narrow the reference standard from world knowledge to source- or task-specific correctness, such as consistency with images, source articles, ground-truth annotations, dialogue state labels, or the user’s intended question.

Space of facets. Systematizations are mixed rather than uniform. Some papers place factuality under broader abilities, for example as part of Background Knowledge or as one dimension of instruction following, while others pair it with logical correctness as an objective criterion distinct from stylistic preferences. Seve

nodes.name: Fairness
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the literature, fairness is most commonly described as avoiding biased, stereotypical, or prejudicial outputs and treating social or demographic groups equitably. Several definitions make this more specific as prediction behavior that is independent of sensitive attributes, or as equitable error rates across groups; one paper quantifies it as the share of cases where a model shows no gender preference, saying fair models should prefer neither the masculine nor the feminine version. Smaller lines of work frame fairness as parity between model performance and users' needs across cultures, as adherence to an idealized fairness standard such as gender parity in translation, or as a moral dimension involving justice, reciprocity, and equitable treatment.

Space of facets. When papers subdivide fairness, the clearest splits are counterfactual fairness versus performance disparity, and stereotype versus bias and preference. Some authors use nearby labels for overlapping ideas, including equitability for cross-cultural parity, biasness for the presence or absence of unfair prejudice in task-oriented dialogue, and normative correctness for fairness judged agains

nodes.name: Faithful calibration
nodes.definition: The degree to which a model's linguistically expressed uncertainty aligns with its intrinsic uncertainty, reflecting a trustworthy and accurate communication of confidence.

nodes.name: Faithfulness
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most papers describe faithfulness as source- or context-groundedness in generation: outputs should be supported by the input, source document, retrieved passages, graph, image, or instruction, often framed as entailment and as avoiding hallucinated, unsupported, contradictory, or unverified content. A smaller but recurring line of work uses the term for explanation faithfulness, where an explanation should reflect the model's actual reasoning or decision process, sometimes with reliability under perturbations. Only a few definitions shift further, treating faithfulness as alignment between stated intentions and behavior in negotiations, or as sensitivity to logical changes in a conclusion; one line also separates it from external factuality by reserving faithfulness for fidelity to the provided context.

Space of facets. When papers systematize the construct, the clearest facet split is internal versus external consistency: one negotiation study checks whether agents' own acceptable offers match later behavior and whether they can predict the other party's acceptable offers. Explanation-oriented work also separates alignment with input features from alignment

nodes.name: Faithfulness to decomposition
nodes.definition: The degree to which a model's translation adheres to the specific guidance or analysis provided in a prior decomposition step, reflecting consistency between planning and execution.

nodes.name: Feasibility
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers here, the prevailing and only explicit definition treats feasibility as the extent to which a generated scientific hypothesis can be practically tested or validated through empirical methods. The usage is tied to judging generated research ideas and hypotheses, including references to hypotheses with "high feasibility and impact as judged by human experts" in HypER: Literature-grounded Hypothesis Generation and Distillation with Provenance.

Space of measurement. Operationalization is narrow: papers link feasibility to one measurement instrument, Human evaluation, and to no behavioral indicators. In these studies, human evaluators assess feasibility directly alongside other dimensions of generated ideas or content, with one paper describing evaluation of the "intrinsic quality" of generated content through novelty and feasibility, and another reporting human evaluation of novelty, relevance, and feasibility.

nodes.name: Few-shot generalization
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats few-shot generalization as a model-level capacity to generalize, learn, or adapt from only a few examples or very small amounts of task-specific data. Most definitions keep this broad, describing generalization to new tasks, unseen scenarios, or novel settings under limited data. Some authors add narrower emphases, framing it as leveraging domain-level abstractions rather than surface patterns, inferring broader rules or properties from a few in-context examples, learning effective policies from little task data, or adapting to new prediction tasks with minimal fine-tuning samples.

Space of facets. Across definitions, the term spans several settings: generalization to new tasks from a few examples, inference of general rules or relevant properties from limited in-context examples, low-data policy learning, and adaptation to novel prediction scenarios or frequency bands with minimal fine-tuning. The clearest variation is scope, with some papers using it for broad few-example generalization and others for a more task-specific form of low-data adaptation.

Space of measurement. No measurement instrument or behaviora

nodes.name: Fidelity
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats fidelity as a quality property of generated outputs, especially images: realism, high quality, clarity, and freedom from artifacts or unintended distortions. Nearby formulations call this image fidelity, visual quality, or image quality, and one paper lists it alongside Overall and Alignment as an evaluation aspect. A smaller line of work uses the same name for different reference standards: in Sparse Autoencoders for Hypothesis Generation, fidelity is how accurately a natural-language concept matches a neuron's firing behavior through precision and recall, while another paper uses fidelity for preserving the semantic information of original watermarked text, described as the similarity between transformed and original text.

Space of facets. Rather than a single shared taxonomy, papers mostly position fidelity through overlapping quality labels. Visual quality is defined as aesthetic appeal, fidelity, and clarity in one use, and elsewhere as clarity, resolution, brightness, color, and absence of artifacts; in chart generation, visual quality is also tied to readability, layout, scales, ticks, and the clari

nodes.name: Figurative language understanding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the construct is used in two distinct ways rather than one settled definition. One paper treats it as a latent interpretive ability: understanding utterances whose intended meaning diverges from the literal meaning, including irony or hyperbole, by reasoning about rhetorical strategy, and it describes this as enabling "human-compatible interpretations of non-literal utterances." Another paper uses the nearby label figurative competence for a broader, context-sensitive ability to produce and interpret figurative expressions with pragmatic appropriateness in communicative settings, and explicitly says this requires more than recognizing figurative markers in isolation.

Space of facets. The papers organize the construct around different facets. One framing centers rhetorical strategy, non-literalness, and the communicative goals of speakers and listeners; another reframes it as a usage-level, discourse-level, context-sensitive ability. The naming also varies: one paper speaks of figurative language understanding, while another uses figurative competence for the broader production-and-interpretation framing.

Space of measurement. The re

nodes.name: Financial reasoning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most definitions treat financial reasoning as a latent ability rather than a directly observed task. The broader framing is the ability to solve finance-related questions that require reasoning over financial documents or calculations, while a narrower variant specializes it as financial numerical reasoning, multi-step computations over financial data that integrate text and tables, apply domain-specific logic, and generate executable programs to derive answers. A smaller line of work instead uses a task-level framing, present value calculation, as the observable computation of the current worth of future cash flows given a discount rate, so the main difference is between a broad latent ability, a narrower numerical version of that ability, and a specific observable task.

Space of facets. The papers split the label into a broad financial reasoning usage and narrower task-focused variants, rather than a stable set of named subconstructs. One specialization describes it as requiring "multi-step problem-solving including fact extraction, logical inference, and mathematical computation," and also emphasizes text-and-table integration and program generation; anoth

nodes.name: Fine-grained perception
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats fine-grained perception as a facet or latent visual ability centered on recognizing detailed, specific, and subtle visual attributes. Definitions converge on examples such as object locations, celebrity identities, clothing styles, instance-level features, positions, counts, and spatial relationships; some papers further stress pixel-level details like color, texture, and relations among small objects. One paper instead uses the label "fine-grained visual perception" and defines it as the capacity to capture detailed visual attributes and subtle appearance cues from images.

Space of facets. Some papers place the construct inside larger perception taxonomies. It is contrasted with OCR and spatial perception in one framing, and appears alongside coarse perception, instance reasoning, and logical reasoning in another. Within the construct itself, papers emphasize detailed appearance and identity cues on the one hand, and localization, counting, and other spatially specific visual detail on the other.

Space of measurement. Operationalization is benchmark-heavy: papers link the construct to 8 measurement instr

nodes.name: Fine-grained video understanding
nodes.definition: The ability of a model to comprehend and reason about specific, detailed events and their temporal relationships within a video, as opposed to just understanding the overall gist.

nodes.name: Fine-grained visual reasoning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing framing is an ability to reason over detailed visual content rather than only coarse scene content. Papers describe it in terms of object attributes, object relationships, and other subtle or intricate image features, and one study explicitly characterizes the relevant content as "object attributes, object relationships, and intricate visual features" (Enhancing Large Vision-Language Models with Ultra-Detailed Image Caption Generation). A closely aligned wording emphasizes complex reasoning that depends on precise understanding of small or detailed visual elements.

Space of facets. Papers do not lay out formal subtypes, but they recurrently organize the construct around a few facets: detailed visual attributes, object relations, and small or subtle visual elements. The main contrast is with reasoning over only coarse scene content, so the construct is used for cases where precise local detail matters.

Space of measurement. No measurement instrument or behavioral indicator is linked to it. In the quoted usage, authors point to tasks that require fine-grained visual reasoning and to examples such as correctly identifying

nodes.name: Fine-grained visual understanding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the dominant framing is a model ability to perceive and interpret detailed local visual information, especially small, pixel-level, point-level, or region-level content, rather than only high-level objects, scenes, or whole-image summaries. Most definitions keep the scope visual and focus on recognizing or understanding fine details, though narrower versions emphasize small objects, occluded details, text-like elements, confusing concepts, or subtle motion differences. A smaller line broadens the scope to preserving detailed visual information during multimodal question answering, integrating local details with broader context, or capturing subtle semantics in both vision and language.

Space of facets. Papers use many near-equivalent labels for overlapping ideas, including perception of small visual details, granular visual recognition, detailed scene understanding, fine-grained image comprehension, region-level comprehension, and fine-grained comprehension. The recurring facets are pixel or point-level detail, specific spatial regions, object attributes and relations, varying-sized text, confusing-concept discrimination, and frame-level action

nodes.name: Flatness
nodes.definition: A property of the solution landscape where a model's parameters reside in a wide, flat region of the loss function, which is correlated with better generalization.

nodes.name: Flexibility
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Papers do not converge on a single meaning of flexibility. In $R^2$-Guard: Robust Reasoning Enabled LLM Guardrail via Knowledge-Enhanced Logical Reasoning, it is used for a guardrail model's ability to adapt to new or unseen safety categories without complete retraining, with examples that it "shows flexibility to new safety categories by simple PGM graph editing" and can adapt "by simply editing the reasoning graph." In MuseScorer: Idea Originality Scoring At Scale, the term instead refers to response diversity across semantic categories, defined as "distinct semantic category count" or "the number of categories in each participant's responses."

Space of facets. No shared subtype scheme appears across papers. The main pattern is that the same label is used for two different targets, one a model-level adaptation property tied to new safety categories and changes to a knowledge or reasoning graph, the other an output-level count of distinct semantic categories in responses. One paper also mentions Creativity Quotient (CQ) scores alongside the latter usage.

Space of measurement. No measurement instrument is linked to it and no behavioral indicator is linked to

nodes.name: Fluency
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats fluency as an output-quality construct: generated text should be grammatically correct, coherent, natural-sounding, and often smooth or readable. Most definitions locate it in the text itself, but some describe it as a latent ability of the model to produce such text, including under very long context conditioning and measurement by perplexity. A smaller set narrows or shifts the emphasis, for example to target-language idiomaticity or orthographic accuracy, to conversational smoothness, or, in one paper, to natural communication style independent of strict grammaticality or context.

Space of facets. Rather than using stable subdimensions, papers mostly introduce task-specific variants such as language fluency, utterance fluency, linguistic fluency, and, in one case, linguistic correctness, with overlapping content around grammar, coherence, naturalness, and smooth readability. The boundary with neighboring constructs varies: some definitions fold repetition avoidance into fluency, many present it beside coherence, informativeness, consistency, or naturalness, and one simplification paper explicitly notes that a text

nodes.name: Fluid intelligence
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. In the usage in the papers, fluid intelligence is treated as a latent ability for solving novel problems without relying on prior or pre-existing knowledge or memorization. The definition also specifies abstract inductive reasoning and pattern induction from examples, and frames evaluating fluid intelligence as a way to assess LLM reasoning abilities given their exposure to and memorization of large amounts of knowledge during pre-training.

Space of facets. The construct is organized mainly by contrast: it is described as solving new problems without relying on prior knowledge or memorization, and as involving abstract inductive reasoning and pattern induction from examples. A nearby construct is analogical reasoning, which one paper describes as tightly linked to fluid intelligence.

Space of measurement. It is linked to 1 measurement instrument and no behavioral indicators.
