The only linked instrument is the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus, which one paper calls the de facto standard for measuring machine fluid intelligence, so the recorded operationalization is performance on the ARC task.

Links. One paper reports that analogical reasoning is related to f

nodes.name: Forecasting ability
nodes.definition: The ability of a model to accurately predict the outcome of future events, typically measured against ground truth resolutions.

nodes.name: Forget quality
nodes.definition: The degree to which an unlearning method successfully removes the influence of specified data from a model, often measured by comparing the unlearned model's outputs to a model never trained on the data.

nodes.name: Formal linguistic competence
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the descriptions, the construct is framed as the ability to produce fluent, grammatically correct text from statistical patterns in training data, rather than from deep semantic understanding. The only explicit definition further characterizes it as surface-level "data" memory, and a quoted passage says it "mainly comes from statistical learning during training on large text corpora" (Memorization ≠ Understanding: Do Large Language Models Have the Ability of Scenario Cognition?).

Space of facets. The framing organizes the construct through a contrast between surface linguistic form and deeper meaning. It is described through fluent and grammatically correct text generation, while being set against "deep semantic understanding" and tied to surface-level "data" memory.

Space of measurement. Operationalization is benchmark-based: papers link formal linguistic competence to 3 measurement instruments and no behavioral indicators. BLiMP and SyntaxGym are the most recurrent instruments, with papers stating that they use these benchmarks to assess formal linguistic competence; another paper also includes GLUE among benchmarks that measure it. These measures f

nodes.name: Formal reasoning
nodes.definition: The latent capacity to represent and verify mathematical statements using a formal logical system, enabling computer-checked proofs and eliminating reliance on intuitive or ambiguous reasoning.

nodes.name: Format following ability
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats this construct as a model capability to make outputs match requested formatting constraints or predefined structural templates. The examples are concrete, including answers enclosed in bold, structured lists, and outputs with specified tags or sections. One definition makes the scope explicit as adherence to format constraints independent of task performance, while another emphasizes consistent conformity to a strict template such as `<rewrite> rewrite here </rewrite>`.

Space of facets. The papers use closely aligned labels, "format-instruction following" and "format adherence", and do not distinguish them as separate constructs. One paper formalizes a "format-instruction following function FC", while another places format adherence alongside reasoning and query rewriting as part of a model's "fundamental capabilities". No further subtype structure is specified in the definitions or quoted passages.

Space of measurement. The papers do not link this construct to any measurement instrument or behavioral indicator. The only explicit operational detail is a "rule-based heuristic" used to determine a format-instructi

nodes.name: Frame-semantic knowledge
nodes.definition: The latent ability of a model to understand and represent meaning through structured conceptual scenarios (frames) and their associated roles.

nodes.name: Framing divergence
nodes.definition: The latent tendency of an LLM to generate conflicting narrative interpretations of the same event when conditioned on different personas, reflecting epistemic contradictions shaped by perspective.

nodes.name: Full-stack engineering ability
nodes.definition: The ability to engineer solutions across the entire technology stack, including mobile, web, APIs, and browsers, while reasoning about complex inter-codebase interactions.

nodes.name: Functional correctness
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage treats functional correctness as whether a generated artifact does what it is intended to do under a specification or user request, typically by passing relevant test cases or functional verification. Most formulations are about generated code, smart contracts, programs, or API calls, while a smaller formulation extends it to an LLM output that correctly solves the intended problem as verified by an external solver. Papers also separate it from syntactic validity, with one quoted passage noting that better-formed outputs do not by themselves guarantee functional correctness.

Space of facets. Papers do not introduce named subtypes, but they recurrently position the construct against nearby evaluation dimensions. The clearest contrast is with syntactic correctness, and some work evaluates it alongside design quality or alongside API hallucination as a distinct target; in benchmark descriptions, test-based checking is also described as execution correctness. No linked constructs are reported as superordinate, equivalent, or contrasting constructs beyond these pairings.

Space of measurement. Operationalization is domi

nodes.name: Functional linguistic competence
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. In the defining paper, the concept is framed as a deeper form of language understanding: the model must not only parse surface text but also understand deeper meanings, including semantic integration and reasoning about roles and relationships. The same paper ties this to robust "knowledge" memory, and also notes that what counts as functional linguistic competence is still unclear and under debate.

Space of facets. The paper organizes generalized knowledge memorization into two parts: surface-level "data" memory and deeper "knowledge" memory, corresponding to formal and functional linguistic competence, respectively. Within that framing, functional linguistic competence is paired with knowledge memory and contrasted with a surface-level side of memorization.

Space of measurement. Papers link it to 6 measurement instruments and no behavioral indicators. The linked instruments are all benchmarks: ARC-Challenge, ARC-Easy, HellaSwag, PIQA, and SIQA, plus 1 other instrument. One paper says these benchmarks cover world knowledge, social reasoning, physical reasoning, and common-sense reasoning, so the operationalization centers on benchmark performance in those a

nodes.name: Functional theory of mind
nodes.definition: A behavioral marker indicating that a model produces responses consistent with understanding mental states, without implying the presence of an internal causal model or true cognitive mechanism underlying such understanding.

nodes.name: Gender bias
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across these papers, the prevailing usage treats gender bias as a latent or systematic tendency in a model's outputs, representations, or reasoning that disadvantages, misrepresents, or unfairly associates people on the basis of gender. Most definitions emphasize stereotyped or spurious associations, such as linking gender-neutral expressions, occupations, or roles to a specific gender, or depicting men with more agentic language than women. Smaller strands narrow the construct to harmful content against marginalized genders, especially within the LGBTQ+ community, or to gendered stereotypes in clinical reasoning independent of clinical relevance. One study also frames it as persisting even in non-stereotypical settings, reporting fair behavior in only 9%-41% of stereotype-free sentences.

Space of facets. Papers do not use a single subtype scheme, but they recurrently break the construct into specific manifestations: gender-occupation associations, agency versus communal language, skewed role and attribute representations, biased clinical reasoning, and harms toward marginalized genders. The broad label 'gender bias' often serves as the umbrella term, while '

nodes.name: General ability
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most commonly, papers treat general ability as broad model competence across many tasks, domains, or benchmarks, rather than performance on a narrow target task. In this prevailing usage it is the overall proficiency, knowledge, reasoning, question answering, summarization, instruction following, or general-purpose usefulness that papers want to preserve when editing, fine-tuning, unlearning, steering, safeguarding, or compressing a model. A smaller line of work makes the construct more explicitly latent, describing an unobservable ability inferred from scores, sometimes as a unidimensional trait, a capabilities set, or a first-order factor over benchmarks. Another minority usage narrows it to retained or benign performance after intervention, and one paper uses "general abilities" for newly enhanced high-level abilities such as reasoning, coding, and instruction following rather than only pre-existing competence.

Space of facets. Papers use several near-overlapping names for this construct, including general capabilities, model capability, model utility, downstream performance, and foundational capabilities, usually for the same broad competence. The facets

nodes.name: General reasoning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats general reasoning as a latent or unobservable model ability to logically process information, solve problems, and understand relationships across diverse or non-specialized domains. A narrower framing appears in one paper, where it is defined as solving individual reasoning tasks or examples without necessarily capturing the common patterns or generic facts shared across multiple examples. The main axis of disagreement is scope: a broad cross-domain capability versus an example-level ability defined in contrast to extracting shared structure across examples.

Space of facets. Papers do not present a rich internal breakdown of general reasoning. Instead, they mainly locate it by contrast: one paper separates it from abstract reasoning, stating that general reasoning focuses on each single example whereas abstract reasoning considers examples supported by a generic fact as a whole, and the same work reports a substantial discrepancy between the two performances. Other papers contrast it with specialized tasks requiring proprietary or domain-specific knowledge, and with math reasoning as a distinct task category.

Space

nodes.name: Generality
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across these papers, the prevailing usage treats generality as post-edit transfer beyond the exact edit prompt: applying newly edited knowledge to rephrased, paraphrased, or semantically equivalent queries. One paper makes this especially concrete as updating "rephrased in-scope examples," and another defines "paraphrase execution" as producing the correct edited output for a paraphrased version of the original prompt. A smaller line of work extends the same idea across languages, defining cross-lingual propagation as whether an edit made in one source language transfers to semantically equivalent queries in other target languages. The main difference across definitions is therefore the scope of transfer, within-language rephrasing versus multilingual propagation.

Space of facets. Papers organize the concept around variations of the edited query. The most common distinction is between the original prompt and rephrased or paraphrased in-scope examples, while one survey presents cross-lingual propagation as a multilingual extension of the same concern. The naming is not fully uniform: authors use "generality," "generalization," and "paraphrase execution" for cl

nodes.name: Generalization
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats generalization as transfer beyond the training setup: maintaining useful performance or learned behavior on new, unseen, or out-of-distribution data, tasks, domains, instructions, tools, users, languages, modalities, or environments. Many definitions also set it against memorization or overfitting, asking whether results reflect "genuine ability or just memorization of the training data" (DyVal: Dynamic Evaluation of Large Language Models for Reasoning Tasks). Smaller lines narrow it to particular settings, such as preserving performance across model sizes or evaluation settings after quantization, extending edited or abstention behavior to related inputs, or preserving the union of skills in merged models. Papers also vary on whether it is a latent property of a model, method, prompt, or attack, or an observed pattern of test performance or error under distribution shift.

Space of facets. Papers use several near-synonymous labels, especially generalizability, generalization ability, generalization capability, and generalization performance. The broad construct is commonly decomposed by what must transfer, across tas

nodes.name: Generalization to unseen users
nodes.definition: The model's ability to accurately estimate the preferences of new users who were not part of the training data, based on a small number of their annotations.

nodes.name: Generation diversity
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats generation diversity as variety across a model's outputs, usually the extent to which generations are distinct and non-repetitive rather than mode-collapsed, often described through varied vocabulary, unique n-grams, or multiple different responses to the same prompt. Some papers broaden this to semantic, structural, syntactic, or logical variation, and one paper explicitly adds linguistic complexity and coverage of the real data distribution. A smaller line of work uses the same label for diversity across collections of texts, across ensemble predictions, across solution or plan paths, or for balanced yes and no perspectives in summaries, so definitions differ on whether the property belongs to sampled outputs, datasets, or broader search and representation coverage.

Space of facets. Papers most often use diversity, generation diversity, response diversity, output diversity, and content diversity as neighboring labels, usually for varied and non-repetitive generations. One paper breaks generation diversity into three aspects, multiple distinct responses for a prompt, linguistically complex responses, and coverage of

nodes.name: Generative ability
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats generative ability as a latent or underlying model capacity for producing fluent, coherent, and contextually appropriate text across generation tasks or open-ended settings. Many definitions add nearby qualities such as diversity, high quality, accuracy, or task relevance. A smaller line of work defines it through the ability to produce free-form, non-multiple-choice outputs in formats such as numbers, phrases, code, JSON, or open-ended text, and a few task-specific formulations narrow or broaden the target to multimodal-conditioned text, detailed object descriptions, text adaptable into jailbreak prompts, or even prompt-satisfying content such as text or images.

Space of facets. Papers mostly use generative ability, generative capability, text generation ability, and language generation as near-equivalent labels for the same latent capacity. The distinctions that appear are mainly by setting and facet: open-ended free-form output versus general task generation, prompt-conditioned or multimodal generation, and qualities such as diversity, coherence, accuracy, and meaning. Some papers pair it with reasoning or evaluat

nodes.name: Geographic bias
nodes.definition: The tendency of models to systematically favor predictions in certain geographic regions—particularly high-density or well-represented urban centers—over others, reflecting uneven learning or data distribution.

nodes.name: Geometric inductive bias
nodes.definition: The model's inherent architectural capacity to capture spatial and geometric relationships among protein residues, such as pairwise distances and angular constraints, which are critical for accurate structure prediction.

nodes.name: Geometric reasoning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats geometric reasoning as a latent ability to understand information in geometric diagrams, symbols, and text, and then carry out multi-step, often symbolic or logical inference to solve a problem. Several definitions add spatial relationships, theorems, and spatial comprehension to this framing, and some descriptions emphasize understanding basic geometric elements and their relationships as part of the challenge. A smaller line of work narrows the concept to subskills such as geometric structure understanding or geometric relationship identification, while another definition shifts from latent ability to the observable task of geometric problem solving, receiving a diagram plus text and producing an answer, often step by step.

Space of facets. Papers use several nearby labels for overlapping parts of this space, including geometric reasoning, geometry reasoning, geometric understanding, and geometric ability. Within that broader capability, they single out geometric comprehension of points, lines, angles, and their properties, geometric structure understanding, and geometric relationship identification, the step of id

nodes.name: Geospatial reasoning
nodes.definition: The ability to interpret and reason about spatial relationships and environmental features, such as distance from epicenter and local site conditions, to infer disaster impact severity.

nodes.name: Geospatial route cognition
nodes.definition: The latent ability of LLMs to understand and reason about sequences of connected landmarks and navigational paths, enabling tasks such as route reversal without relying on global survey knowledge.

nodes.name: Global context understanding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage treats this construct as whole-context integration or understanding: the ability to use information distributed across the entire input context, sequence, or text, rather than just retrieving isolated facts. Some papers phrase this in more cognitive terms, as comprehending, synthesizing, and reasoning over distributed information, while others describe maintaining awareness of high-level information across long sequences or integrating both preceding and succeeding text into a comprehensive representation.

Space of facets. Papers use closely related labels, including global context understanding, global context awareness, and global contextual awareness, for largely the same whole-sequence idea. One paper explicitly pairs it with local precision and links it to coarse-grained compression over relevant context blocks, while another associates it with long-range dependency handling.

Space of measurement. No measurement instrument is linked to this construct, and no behavioral indicator is linked to it. Where papers describe it operationally, they do so through task demands rather than recorded instruments: one bench

nodes.name: Global reasoning
nodes.definition: The ability to perform reasoning that involves integrating information from a large number of input tokens simultaneously, rather than relying on local patterns.

nodes.name: Goal interpretation
nodes.definition: The ability of an agent to understand the overall objective of a task from a natural language description.

nodes.name: Goal misgeneralization
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. In the papers, goal misgeneralization is used in a single explicit sense: a model learns and pursues a proxy goal that is subtly different from the intended goal, which then leads to undesirable behavior in new situations. In Estimating the Probabilities of Rare Outputs in Language Models, it is also mentioned as one possible reason an outcome could occur, alongside an adversarially chosen input, which keeps the focus on a mismatch between the intended goal and the learned proxy goal.

Space of measurement. Papers do not link goal misgeneralization to any measurement instrument or behavioral indicator, and no linked constructs are reported. The papers therefore do not specify an operationalization for it.

Links. No papers report causal, correlational, or other related links involving goal misgeneralization.

nodes.name: Graceful forgetting
nodes.definition: The ability to enhance learning on a new task by selectively discarding irrelevant or outdated knowledge.

nodes.name: Grade-level adaptability
nodes.definition: The latent ability of an LLM to adjust its responses in terms of language, complexity, and content to match the cognitive and developmental stage of students at different grade levels.

nodes.name: Grammatical agency
nodes.definition: The latent tendency of an LLM to vary the distribution of syntactic agency in narrative framing, using passive or active constructions to shift attention toward or away from responsible actors based on persona role.

nodes.name: Graph reasoning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats graph reasoning as a latent ability or facet of reasoning for understanding and solving problems on graph-structured data. Definitions commonly describe inferring graph properties such as paths, connectivity, or cycles, and one definition broadens this to understanding, retaining, and manipulating relations among entities across tasks. A narrower framing places it under algorithmic reasoning, while a smaller and distinct usage applies the same name to interpreting data in graphical or chart form to answer a question.

Space of facets. Papers most often describe graph reasoning through families of graph problems. One line treats it as a specific facet of algorithmic reasoning, and one paper spells out graph reasoning tasks through graph connectivity, shortest path, and cycle detection; other definitions emphasize identifying nodes, edges, and constraints and applying appropriate graph algorithms. A smaller strand uses graph recall, described as recalling and encoding relations given earlier in text, as a simple task for studying graph reasoning ability.

Space of measurement. No measurement instrument is linked to grap

nodes.name: Graph understanding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the construct is treated as an LLM ability or degree of understanding graph-structured information. The shared core is interpreting structure and relations, but papers place that understanding in different representations: visual graph representations, textual graphs with attributes, or knowledge-graph embeddings with semantic and topological meaning. Scope also varies somewhat, because some definitions include reasoning over subgraphs or neighborhoods, while the visual-graph formulation treats reasoning as a later step after the model understands graph features.

Space of facets. Papers use closely related labels for overlapping variants, including graph comprehension, graph understanding, and graph structure understanding. The main facets are representational, moving from visual graph features and relational information, to textual attributes in real-world textual graphs, to the semantic and topological meaning of graph embeddings, with recurring attention to subgraphs and neighborhoods. One paper also explicitly separates understanding from reasoning by first teaching the model the features of a visual graph and then fine-tuning reasoning wit

nodes.name: Grokking
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, grokking is most commonly treated as an observable training phenomenon in which test-set generalization improves abruptly long after near-perfect training-set performance has already been reached through memorization. Some descriptions phrase the shift as an "abrupt change from random guessing to generalization" after the model memorized the training set, but the shared framing is delayed generalization after the training set has already been fit.

Space of facets. In the papers, grokking is positioned between memorization and generalization: models are described as first memorizing, or remaining at random guessing, and only later generalizing on the test set. One account also says it "results from the model learning very structured representations," adding a representation-level description alongside the memorization to generalization transition.

Space of measurement. No measurement instrument or behavioral indicator is linked to grokking. Instead, papers operationalize it through the described pattern of train and test performance, sudden test-set improvement long after near-perfect training performance, and one paper treats whether model

nodes.name: Grounded reasoning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, grounded reasoning is framed as reasoning or responding that is based on some form of first-hand or actual evidence rather than on abstract knowledge alone or plausible but unsupported content. In Grounded Answers for Multi-agent Decision-making Problem through Generative World Model, the emphasis is on simulated, first-hand experience within an environment's dynamics, with trial and error described as necessary to ground reasoning on complicated problems. In Re-Align: Aligning Vision Language Models via Retrieval-Augmented Direct Preference Optimization, the construct is defined as a latent capacity to base responses on actual visual evidence, with failures described as fabricated details about objects, attributes, and logical relationships in an input image. The main variation is the source of grounding, simulated environmental experience in one usage and visual evidence in the other.

Space of facets. The papers organize the construct through contrasts. One usage sets it against abstract knowledge alone and ties it to trial and error within an environment, while another contrasts it with plausible but unsupported content and with ina

nodes.name: Groundedness
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most papers treat groundedness as a property of responses or outputs that stay within provided or retrieved evidence, rather than drawing on the model's internal parametric knowledge, and that can be verified against those sources. A stricter formulation says a response is grounded only if it answers using only the attached documents and its claims can be inferred from inline citations. Smaller variations narrow the construct to arguments, defined by factual support and consistency with retrieved evidence, or broaden the evidence base to input contracts and external legal sources, while one paper shifts the locus from the output to the retrieval and reasoning process under the label factual reliability.

Space of facets. Papers do not offer a detailed subtype taxonomy, but they do separate groundedness by locus. The prevailing usage is response or output groundedness, while smaller lines of work discuss argument groundedness and a closely related process-oriented framing, factual reliability. Across these uses, authors repeatedly contrast grounded content with hallucination, contradiction, unsupported claims, and reliance on parametric knowledge, and some pape

nodes.name: Grounding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats grounding as a latent ability to connect language or high-level reasoning to concrete referents, most often fine-grained visual details or exact spatial locations in images, videos, UIs, and 3D scenes. Definitions repeatedly describe localizing regions or elements from text, producing coordinates or bounding boxes, or tying predictions to object identities, motion, interactions, and other low-level evidence; as one paper puts it, "model predictions need to be grounded in fine-grained low-level details, such as object motions and object interactions" (Look, Remember and Reason: Grounded Reasoning in Videos with Language Models). Smaller lines of work use the same term more broadly for anchoring outputs in environmental context and feedback, executable actions, structured schemas, provided evidence, or retrieved context. There is also a recurring difference between papers that frame grounding as a latent capacity and one UI-focused definition that treats it as the observable task of locating elements on a screen.

Space of facets. Papers systematize grounding mainly by setting rather than through one shared taxonomy

nodes.name: GUI understanding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats GUI understanding as a latent capability or capacity to interpret visual screen or interface information, including structure, content, layout, text, icons, and function, and to identify relevant interactive or actionable elements. Several definitions converge on comprehension from visual inputs and accurate identification of buttons, menus, text fields, or other on-screen information for action selection. A smaller line of work narrows the construct to screen reading comprehension, reading textual and symbolic screen information to answer questions, or to GUI action grounding, mapping natural-language instructions to specific executable elements or locations.

Space of facets. Papers use several neighboring labels for overlapping but not identical phenomena: GUI understanding, UI understanding, and screen understanding name the broader interpretation of interface layouts and actionable components, while screen reading comprehension and GUI action grounding denote narrower slices. Element identification and grounding are often folded into the broader construct, with papers describing the need to interpret t

nodes.name: H-creativity
nodes.definition: The quality of an idea being novel in the context of all of human history, meaning no one else has had the idea before.

nodes.name: Hallucination resistance
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed definitions, the prevailing usage treats this as a latent trait, tendency, ability, or degree by which a model avoids unsupported, false, or factually incorrect outputs. Most descriptions stay at that broad level, while some narrow the scope to specific output types: fabricated or ungrounded knowledge triples, multimodal answers, semantically plausible but factually ungrounded entity relations, citation predictions that do not correspond to real works, unsupported medical information, or molecules that follow structural rules but lack the expected activity or utility. A smaller line of work frames the same family of phenomena from the opposite side, as hallucination tendency, knowledge hallucination, factuality hallucination, or molecular hallucination, including cases where generated content is inconsistent with actual facts even when those facts are provided.

Space of facets. Papers organize the concept mainly through domain-specific variants rather than a shared abstract taxonomy. Recurring variants include knowledge hallucination in knowledge creation, factuality hallucination as entity-relation distortions, molecular hallucination as

nodes.name: Harmlessness
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most definitions treat harmlessness as a latent safety-oriented tendency or property of a model, or of its responses, to avoid generating unsafe, harmful, unethical, toxic, offensive, or dangerous content, often even under harmful or adversarial prompts. Across papers, the reference standard is broad but similar: responses should not violate ethical, legal, or social norms, and should avoid content such as illegal advice, discrimination, misinformation, hate, self-harm, or dangerous activities. Smaller strands state the construct in the inverse as harmfulness, the disposition to generate ethically problematic or privacy-revealing content, and one paper narrows harm to eating-disorder-related promotion, so the main differences are inverse wording, model versus response focus, and scope.

Space of facets. Most commonly, papers place harmlessness inside broader alignment bundles, especially with helpfulness and often honesty, sometimes under the labels 3H or HHH, and sometimes as one objective in multi-objective alignment alongside humor or other user-alignment skills. Several papers explicitly separate it from helpfulness by evaluating them on independent axes a

nodes.name: Hedonism
nodes.definition: A value orientation focused on pleasure and sensuous gratification for oneself.

nodes.name: Help-seeking
nodes.definition: The disposition of an agent to proactively seek help and engage in productive interactions with collaborators when faced with a problem.

nodes.name: Helpfulness
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats helpfulness as the quality, or latent tendency, of a model response to be useful, relevant, informative, supportive, or satisfying for a user’s query, instruction, or needs. Many definitions alternate between describing it as a property of outputs and as a model ability, disposition, or capacity, but they largely converge on assistance that meets user goals, sometimes explicitly through instruction following or direct task completion. Smaller lines define it more narrowly as completing the basic task in an instruction, serving as a direct answer, or fully understanding user intent, while a few domain-specific papers recast it as culturally aware support, advice shaped by personal or majority preferences, or tutor guidance that is constructive and appropriately toned without giving away the full answer. A minority framing shifts the reference point to the user, defining perceived helpfulness as how effectively users feel the model supported their needs and goals, and some authors use usefulness as a near-synonym for meeting user requirements or retaining task performance.

Space of facets. Papers most often

nodes.name: Heterogeneous reasoning
nodes.definition: The ability to apply different types of logical reasoning—such as temporal, causal, spatial, and numerical—within the same task or context.

nodes.name: Hierarchical concept representation
nodes.definition: The organization of knowledge in LLMs such that high-level task concepts (e.g., 'capital') are encoded in directions orthogonal to low-level, task-specific features, enabling selective attention and compositionality.

nodes.name: Hierarchical generalization
nodes.definition: The model's latent ability to use tree-based syntactic rules to correctly process language, enabling it to generalize to out-of-distribution examples with complex structures.

nodes.name: Hierarchical planning
nodes.definition: The ability to break a complex goal into ordered subgoals and execute them over multiple steps in an interactive environment.

nodes.name: Hierarchical reasoning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the shared framing is multi-step reasoning with hierarchical organization. One usage defines it as the ability to solve problems that require multiple dependent reasoning steps organized in a hierarchy or sequence, while another, under the aligned label "hierarchical thinking," defines it as a latent LLM ability to decompose complex reasoning problems into multiple levels of sub-tasks through a divide-and-conquer strategy for organized planning. As one study puts it, it is "a multi-level divide-and-conquer approach that facilitates deeper and more organized reasoning" (HyperTree Planning: Enhancing LLM Reasoning via Hierarchical Thinking), so the main difference is whether papers frame it as solving hierarchically structured problems or as a latent decomposition and planning ability of the model.

Space of facets. Papers mainly systematize the construct through two closely aligned labels, "hierarchical reasoning" and "hierarchical thinking." The fuller elaboration is the divide-and-conquer version, described as decomposing complex problems across multiple levels of sub-tasks, reducing the length of reasoning chains, and maintaining the

nodes.name: Hierarchical understanding
nodes.definition: The model's latent ability to incorporate and leverage the structural relationships between labels in a taxonomy during classification.

nodes.name: Holistic object understanding
nodes.definition: The model's comprehensive ability to not only identify and segment objects but also to generate meaningful descriptive captions, integrating visual and semantic information.

nodes.name: Holistic understanding
nodes.definition: The latent ability of a model to grasp the overall scene, context, and structure of an image, as opposed to just identifying individual objects.

nodes.name: Honesty
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats honesty as a latent model trait or disposition toward truthfulness, factual accuracy, and non-deception. Most definitions also fold in acknowledging limits, for example abstaining, saying "I don't know," declining to answer when information is insufficient, avoiding fabrication or hallucination, or matching stated confidence to accuracy. A smaller line of work narrows it to consistency with the model's internal beliefs or knowledge, and one survey uses the label "sincerity" for acting on what one believes to be true with sufficient evidence. Some authors describe honesty as a property of the model, while others describe it as the degree to which outputs are truthful and do not misrepresent facts or mislead.

Space of facets. Papers most often place honesty inside broader alignment taxonomies, especially alongside helpfulness and harmlessness as part of 3H or HHH, and one paper also lists it among five fine-grained alignment perspectives with unbiasedness and engagement. The concept is not fully stabilized against nearby terms: some papers separate honesty from truthfulness, with one defining honesty as stat

nodes.name: Honesty-Humility
nodes.definition: The latent tendency of an LLM to avoid flattery, deception, and self-serving responses, promoting truthful and ethically grounded outputs.

nodes.name: HTML understanding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage treats HTML understanding as an ability, often a latent one, to comprehend the structure and semantics of HTML documents or elements. The more common HTML-specific definitions add adjacent aspects: some include content and say this understanding informs actions, while others include the functionality of elements. A smaller framing broadens the construct to structural awareness, the ability to comprehend and use hierarchical and semantic information in document structures such as HTML tags to improve representation quality.

Space of facets. Papers mostly use HTML comprehension and HTML understanding for closely similar ideas centered on structure and semantics in HTML. A smaller line of work uses the broader label structural awareness for a wider scope, shifting from individual HTML documents and elements to hierarchical document structure and its use in representation learning. In the quoted passages, the construct is also discussed as something instruction-finetuning can improve, and as a requirement in conditional program synthesis where models must follow natural-language instructions while understanding the sem

nodes.name: Human behavior prediction ability
nodes.definition: The latent capability to infer how individuals will respond in social science experiments from their demographic attributes, experimental condition, and outcome question.

nodes.name: Human-likeness
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats human-likeness as resemblance between a model's outputs or behavior and human patterns, often explicitly contrasted with absolute task accuracy. One recurring formulation centers on response distributions, described as "comparing models and humans on their response patterns, not their absolute performance" (DevBench: A multimodal developmental benchmark for language learning); other papers use closely related language for human-like daily activities judged by naturalness, coherence, and plausibility, natural and conversational tutoring responses, realistic role-playing, learning trajectories that mirror human learners, or text with more human-like word distributions and flexible wording. A smaller line of work uses nearby labels for different targets: human-like comprehension is framed as depth, flexibility, and nuance of understanding, while perceived humanlikeness is framed as whether users experience the agent as resembling a human interlocutor.

Space of facets. Papers do not converge on a single subtype scheme, and the same label spans several facets. Some authors unpack it into naturalness, coherence, and plausi

nodes.name: Human preference alignment
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats human preference alignment as the degree to which an LLM's outputs or behaviors conform to human preferences, judgments, values, intentions, or desired objectives. Many definitions anchor those preferences in qualities such as helpfulness, harmlessness, honesty, truthfulness, coherence, appropriateness, safety, or broadly desirable assistant behavior, and several papers describe the construct as something learned from preference data, reward models, RLHF, DPO, or related optimization. A smaller line narrows the reference standard to user expectations such as conciseness and readability, to physician note preferences, to multimodal interactions, or to human or model-derived preferences rather than human preferences alone. Only a few definitions shift from a latent property to an explicitly observable tendency, such as producing higher-ranked responses, or to a continuous scalar objective over parameter space.

Space of facets. A recurring way of organizing the construct is through HHH or 3H style components: helpfulness, honesty, and harmlessness, sometimes with a broader general criterion. Nearby labels are

nodes.name: Humanistic care
nodes.definition: The tendency to communicate respectfully, empathetically, and politely while providing appropriate guidance and respecting patient wishes.

nodes.name: Humor
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, humor is consistently treated as a stylistic alignment dimension: a model's tendency or ability to produce witty, amusing, or funny responses when that style is desired. The definitions largely agree on this framing, with only a mild shift in emphasis between model-level tendency or ability and response-level quality, and one formulation also presents humor as a secondary objective in generation.

Space of facets. In these papers, humor is positioned alongside helpfulness and harmlessness as one of the pre-defined dimensions, values, or objectives used in multi-objective alignment. The recurring organization is therefore not into subtypes of humor, but into a set of preference dimensions that may need to be balanced and can be described as sometimes conflicting; one paper further frames helpfulness as the primary objective while humor is the target reward.

Space of measurement. Humor is linked to one measurement instrument, HH-RLHF, and no behavioral indicators are linked to it. Papers describe this operationalization as using a large-scale dataset, or a task based on the Anthropic-HH dataset, together with open-sourced reward models o

nodes.name: Humor understanding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats humor understanding as a latent ability to grasp why something is humorous: papers describe comprehending and interpreting humor's nuances, underlying logic, and context, and in one case cultural cues. Within that shared framing, some definitions center on contradictions and comic juxtaposition, including nonlinear narratives, while others focus on wordplay such as puns and the recognition of ambiguity, contrast, and surprise. A smaller line of work uses a narrower recognition framing, defining it as the ability to identify or detect humor in content rather than to interpret its mechanisms.

Space of facets. Papers subdivide the construct by the kind of humor to be grasped. One strand emphasizes humor through juxtaposition and contradictory narratives, another emphasizes rationales, internal humorous logic, context, and cultural nuances, and another targets puns as context-dependent humor grounded in ambiguity, contrast, and surprise. In one account, humor understanding is contrasted with pattern recognition or memorizing patterns, while the recognition-based usage blurs humor understanding with humor recog

nodes.name: Idea diversity
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats this construct as within-set diversity among a model's generated ideas: the degree to which solution ideas differ semantically from one another instead of repeating near-duplicate or similar content. The definitions align on the comparison standard, diversity is assessed across the ideas in a generated set rather than against an external reference. One paper further situates the issue as a lack of high-level diversity in model outputs, specifically in candidate plans for solving a problem in natural language.

Space of facets. The main variation is terminological rather than conceptual. One paper uses the name Idea diversity, while another uses Distinctness and describes average idea distinctness for a model in a domain; in both cases, the construct refers to diverse idea generation. The wording also shifts by setting, with one paper framing it in an idea-space for solution planning and another in generated scientific research ideas.

Space of measurement. No measurement instrument or behavioral indicator is linked to the construct. Still, the papers operationalize it through direct scoring of difference among gen

nodes.name: Imagination
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats imagination as a visual simulation or generation ability. One framing defines it as generating novel visual representations, specifically intermediate subgoal images tied to planned sub-instructions, while another defines it as mentally simulating or visualizing changes in a scene to infer missing perceptual knowledge. The shared core is producing or simulating visual representations beyond the immediately available scene, while the scope differs between action-oriented subgoal images and hypothetical scene changes used to deduce missing details.

Space of facets. The papers do not break imagination into named subtypes. Instead, the same label is used for two closely related roles: imagined subgoal images that provide "more intuitive guidance" before acting, and imagination "rooted in prior knowledge" that helps fill perceptual knowledge gaps before reasoning. In these descriptions, imagination is discussed alongside reasoning and action, rather than being equated with another construct.

Space of measurement. No measurement instrument or behavioral indicator is linked to imagination. In the descriptions, it appea

nodes.name: Impermissible information leakage
nodes.definition: The extent to which a model's outputs, even if individually permissible, reveal dangerous or undesirable knowledge that an adversary can infer.

nodes.name: Implicit personalization
nodes.definition: The latent tendency of an LLM to infer and act upon user demographic attributes based on subtle conversational cues, even when not explicitly stated, thereby tailoring responses in ways that may reflect stereotypes.

nodes.name: Implicit reasoning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. The only explicit definition treats it as a model capacity for recovering what is not said directly: inferring unstated assumptions, background knowledge, and indirect logical connections needed to interpret ambiguous or incompletely specified argumentative content. This usage is illustrated by descriptions of using different background knowledge to complement implicit information, and by the claim that a model can sometimes identify implicit logic that annotators did not realize. A separate usage overlaps it with multi-hop reasoning, describing implicit reasoning as solving multi-hop reasoning tasks in a single forward pass, without chain of thought.

Space of facets. The papers do not divide it into named subtypes. The main difference across uses is scope and framing: one centers on interpreting argumentative content and identifying logical structure from implicit information, while another frames the construct through multi-hop task solving in a single forward pass. Papers also place it alongside broader constructs rather than under a stable taxonomy, especially multi-hop reasoning, and one paper relates it to social intelligence through information reasoni

nodes.name: Implicit social bias
nodes.definition: The tendency of a model to exhibit unconscious, automatic attitudes or stereotypes that influence its decisions and behaviors without being explicitly directed to do so.

nodes.name: Impossible video understanding
nodes.definition: The observable ability of a model to detect, classify, or explain why a video depicts an impossible or counterfactual event, based on visual and temporal analysis.

nodes.name: In-context interference
nodes.definition: The latent tendency for model performance to degrade as the number of in-context demonstrations increases, due to suboptimal action selection rather than format errors.

nodes.name: In-context learning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the dominant framing is a model ability at inference or test time: the model adapts to or performs a new task by conditioning on a few demonstrations, usually input-output or input-label pairs in the prompt, without updating weights or parameters. Many definitions make the task of the model explicit, namely inferring task rules, mappings, patterns, or functions from those examples and then answering a new query. A smaller line of work broadens the context beyond labeled demonstrations to instructions, unlabeled token sequences, reference texts, optimization histories, or other contextual information, and a minority of papers use the term for an observable few-shot prompting procedure or evaluation setup rather than a latent capability.

Space of facets. Papers use nearby labels such as in-context learning ability or capability, and some neighboring terms, especially few-shot capability or adaptation, describe the same prompt-conditioned task adaptation pattern. They also carve out narrower variants such as in-context causal structure selection and multi-modal long-context learning, while one theoretical line defines in-context learnability a

nodes.name: In-context reasoning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats in-context reasoning as a model ability or capacity to reason, solve problems, and make judgments from information in the current prompt or context, often as step-by-step logical inference and, in some definitions, with retrieved knowledge and without fine-tuning. A smaller line of work uses the label knowledge-free reasoning for a narrower framing: performing inference by organizing only the knowledge given in context to derive an answer, without relying on internally stored factual knowledge, including arithmetic, symbolic, and logical operations. The main difference across definitions is scope, from broad context-based problem solving to a stricter contrast with stored factual knowledge or factual recall.

Space of facets. Papers systematize the construct only lightly. One paper treats it as covering simple reasoning examples such as Key-value retrieval and Indirect object identification, and relates Factual recall to it in the same discussion, while another describes a facet in which predicates are bound in context and structured representations are formed in activations rather than in weights. Naming a

nodes.name: In-weights learning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed papers, the prevailing usage treats in-weights learning as a parameter-based form of learning: query-response relationships, or memorized information, are encoded in the model's weights or parameters. Papers agree on that locus and often contrast it with relying on context examples at inference time, using phrases such as "query-response relationships encoded in the weights of the network." A smaller line frames it more broadly as the ability to acquire knowledge by updating parameters during training and thereby encode patterns from training data into the weights.

Space of facets. Papers mostly organize the concept through its contrast with in-context learning, pairing in-weight and in-context predictors as different predictors a model can learn and implement. Some descriptions align it with memorization, including references to memorized information in parameters and to a "memorizing" in-weight predictor. The naming varies slightly, with authors using both "in-weights learning" and "in-weight learning."

Space of measurement. No measurement instrument is linked to it, and no behavioral indicator is linked to it. The papers discuss it thr

nodes.name: Inclusivity
nodes.definition: The extent to which generated stories represent diverse sociocultural groups without overemphasizing stereotypes or narrowing representation.

nodes.name: Individuation
nodes.definition: The latent ability of an LLM to generate responses that are distinctively aligned with a specific persona, as opposed to a neutral or default narrative stance.

nodes.name: Inductive bias
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats inductive bias as a model- or training-level set of implicit assumptions, preferences, or tendencies that make some solutions or generalizations more likely than others on new or unseen tasks. Many definitions tie it to architecture or training procedure, and some make the preference concrete as simpler or sparser solutions, while others describe it as assumptions supplied by pre-training or as tendencies that shape behavior even without explicit instruction. The main variation is scope: most definitions stay broad at the level of the model or training method, whereas a smaller line of work narrows it to particular architectures or components, such as transformer architectures or positional encodings.

Space of facets. Papers systematize the construct mainly by source and by what it favors. Some write of transformer-specific, model-specific, or component-level biases, including looped-transformer biases toward simpler or sparser solutions and positional-encoding biases that facilitate counting in different task formats. Another recurring split concerns distinctiveness: one paper says common architectures and training

nodes.name: Inductive reasoning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats inductive reasoning as inferring general rules, principles, patterns, or abstractions from a small or limited set of examples or observations and then applying them to novel situations. One paper phrases this as deriving underlying principles from a handful of observations and then generalizing to novel situations (Phenomenal Yet Puzzling: Testing Inductive Reasoning Capabilities of Language Models with Hypothesis Refinement). Smaller variants make the inferred object more explicit, describing induction as first finding a latent function or hypothesis that explains training examples before predicting test outputs, or as inferring an unstated rule or concept from in-context demonstrations. A smaller line of work narrows the ability further to extracting compact human-understandable predictive rules or deriving possible game mechanisms from interaction history and environmental interaction.

Space of facets. Papers use several overlapping names around the construct, including induction, rule induction, inductive inference, compositional rule inference, concept inference, and interpretable learning. Most of these labels

nodes.name: Industrial knowledge
nodes.definition: The model's internalized knowledge specific to industrial products, manufacturing processes, and defect types, which is necessary for accurate quality inspection.

nodes.name: Information content
nodes.definition: The amount of information transferred from the training dataset into the model's weights, which the paper argues grows sublinearly with model size.

nodes.name: Information integration
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage treats information integration as a latent ability to combine and use evidence from more than one textual unit to make a relevance judgment or prediction. The shared core is integration across distributed information, but the scope varies: some papers place it in multi-hop retrieval as combining evidence across multiple passages to determine relevance, while others frame it more broadly as combining information from different parts of a linguistic context, especially across sentence and clause boundaries.

Space of facets. Papers systematize the construct mainly by scale and boundary. One line describes information as distributed across words, sentences, and discourse, and studies integration across these time scales through an "information integration window" that sentence and clause boundaries can constrain; another presents it in multi-document settings, with phrases such as "information integration across multiple passages" and multi-hop integration that involves relationships between documents.

Space of measurement. No measurement instrument is linked to this construct, and one behavioral indicator is linked:

nodes.name: Information preservation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Papers are split between two framings rather than using a single prevailing one. One paper defines it as the extent to which an encoder's embeddings retain enough content for an LLM to recover the original input or a downstream signal. Another, under the closely related name information retention, defines it as the degree to which an LLM preserves and transmits its full belief distribution across communication steps rather than discarding uncertainty through discrete token selection, and explicitly says the token sampling step "poses a potential risk of information loss" because it uses one token to represent belief over the vocabulary (Let Models Speak Ciphers: Multiagent Debate through Embeddings). The disagreement is therefore both about where the property resides, embeddings versus communication steps, and about what is preserved, recoverable content versus the model's full belief distribution and uncertainty.

Space of facets. The main pattern is terminological rather than taxonomic. Papers use both information preservation and information retention, but the associated definitions do not fully align: one centers reconstructability from embeddings, while t

nodes.name: Information retrieval ability
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most definitions treat the construct as an ability to locate, search for, retrieve, or extract relevant information from text, a long context, memory, or an external corpus. Within that broad framing, many papers focus on finding specific facts or answer spans from earlier input or cross-lingual context, while some define it at the document level as identifying relevant items from a corpus. Smaller lines of work narrow it to reasoning-intensive retrieval, where relevant documents are connected by underlying principles, algorithms, or theorems rather than simple keyword or semantic matching, or broaden it to multimodal search and retrieval using both visual and textual information; one paper further specializes it to finding inspiration papers associated with a research background.

Space of facets. Papers explicitly divide the construct into subtypes such as reasoning-intensive retrieval, multimodal retrieval capability, text retrieval capability, cross-lingual context retrieval, answer retrieval, in-context retrieval, recall capability, and information retrieval and localization. Some works also position it against neighboring constructs: one disentangles ret

nodes.name: Information-seeking ability
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing framing is a latent model capability for proactive question-asking: identifying knowledge gaps, eliciting missing details, and gathering the information needed to make more informed decisions or solve a task, especially under uncertainty and ambiguity. The papers also describe success in turn-by-turn terms, with an information-seeking expert deciding whether it already has enough information to answer confidently. A smaller usage applies the label "information seeking" to a task category, namely responding to queries that ask for factual information or explanations, so the main disagreement is between a model ability and a type of query.

Space of facets. There is little formal subdivision. Papers mostly organize the construct around question-asking ability, active information-seeking capabilities, and proactive information-seeking settings, all centered on asking effective questions to obtain missing details; one description of a successful information-seeking expert emphasizes deciding at each turn whether further questions are needed before answering. The main naming ambiguity is that the same label is also used in one

nodes.name: Informativeness
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats informativeness as the extent to which an output provides relevant, useful, sufficiently detailed information, often with an added expectation of completeness. Many definitions phrase this as adequate or engaging detail in a coherent plot, relevant and complete commentary, or summaries that capture all relevant and key details without omission, and one definition explicitly anchors the judgment in human evaluation. A smaller line of work narrows it to preserving useful non-conflicting content during revision, to reasoning steps that add new and non-redundant information, or to information-dense latent factors, synthetic samples, and even harmful responses; the main variation is the object being judged and whether novelty or non-redundancy is part of the criterion.

Space of facets. Papers do not offer a single taxonomy, but a recurring breakdown equates informativeness with relevance and completeness, and sometimes with being insightful. Other papers systematize it through novelty and concision, describing informative steps as adding new, relevant information without repetition, and informative summaries as capturing

nodes.name: Insight
nodes.definition: The ability to generate psychologically meaningful understanding or reframing that goes beyond surface-level support.

nodes.name: Insightfulness
nodes.definition: The tendency of a response to provide useful, thoughtful, or informative content beyond minimal correctness.

nodes.name: Instance-level stability
nodes.definition: The degree to which an accelerated model produces the same predictions for the same inputs as its original, unaccelerated counterpart.

nodes.name: Instance reasoning
nodes.definition: The latent ability to reason about specific instances of objects, their properties, and their relationships within an image.

nodes.name: Instruction following ability
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats this as a latent capacity or tendency to understand natural-language instructions and produce responses or actions that satisfy them. Most definitions emphasize adherence to explicit constraints, requested formats, and user intent, and, as "Evaluating Large Language Models at Evaluating Instruction Following" puts it, it is "the ability to correctly parse open-ended instructions and adhere to the specified requirements." A smaller line of work treats it more behaviorally, as the observable act of generating outputs that stay on task, follow formats, or carry out action sequences, and some papers narrow it to multimodal, multilingual, retrieval, tool-use, or rule-bound settings.

Space of facets. Papers do not settle on one subtyping scheme, but they repeatedly narrow the construct by what is being followed, for example domain guidelines, prompt or system-message constraints, and formal rules or principles. Another recurring split is scope: general versus open-ended instruction following, single-turn compliance versus maintaining constraints across turns, and text-only versus multimodal, multilingual, spoken, retri

nodes.name: Instruction understanding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats instruction understanding, often also called instruction comprehension, as a latent model ability to grasp the meaning, intent, constraints, or goals expressed in natural language instructions and to map them to appropriate actions, plans, or task execution. Most definitions place this ability in complex settings, such as constrained environments, specialized domains with intricate terminology, multi-condition questions, README-guided deployment, or embodied tasks, and one paper states that "Instruction Understanding Difficulty measures whether the model comprehends the instruction." A smaller line of work narrows the emphasis either to command-to-action mapping in embodied or tool-using contexts, or to understanding diverse phrasings and the full intent of instructions, including implicit and explicit constraints, across varied tasks.

Space of facets. The recurring facets are understanding meaning and intent, interpreting explicit or implicit constraints, handling specialized terminology, and converting directives into goals, actions, or plans. Another recurring distinction is between general instruction followi

nodes.name: Intelligence
nodes.definition: The emergent ability of a system to learn effective, generalizable representations and perform well on complex downstream tasks, hypothesized to arise from exposure to and prediction of complex data.

nodes.name: Intelligibility
nodes.definition: The latent ability of synthesized or edited speech to be accurately understood by listeners, reflecting clarity of pronunciation and word-level fidelity.

nodes.name: Intent understanding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed papers, the prevailing framing is a latent ability to recover an underlying purpose, goal, task, or information need from an utterance, prompt, or interaction sequence, often when that intent is not stated directly. Most definitions place the construct in context-sensitive inference, for example over conversational turns, GUI trajectories, vague or incomplete queries, or instructions that omit the target object or action. Smaller strands narrow the reference standard to pragmatic speaker meaning beyond literal content, to relevance to social and cultural expectations, or to recognizing malicious versus benign requests.

Space of facets. The construct appears under several neighboring names, including speaker meaning inference, intention inference, intent perception, intention awareness, and user intent understanding, and one paper says the task is sometimes called goal understanding. Across these uses, papers shift the object of inference, from another person's intentions in interaction, to intended meaning and implications, to intended task, to text-based user intentions for recommendation, or to information need in conversational search.

nodes.name: Inter-agent trust
nodes.definition: A latent positive disposition developed by an agent towards its peers based on their historical accuracy, which can increase its propensity to conform to their subsequent judgments.

nodes.name: Interactive reasoning
nodes.definition: The ability to use multi-turn dialogue to gather evidence, update hypotheses, and converge on a correct answer.

nodes.name: Interactivity
nodes.definition: The degree to which a system engages the user in its generation process, allowing them to provide feedback and influence the outcome to align with their preferences.

nodes.name: Intergroup empathy bias
nodes.definition: The latent tendency to empathize less with out-group members relative to in-group members, which is inferred from differences in predicted emotion intensity.

nodes.name: Interleaved understanding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the cited papers, the prevailing usage treats interleaved understanding as a latent ability or capacity for understanding, processing, and often reasoning over inputs that mix images and text in an interleaved sequence. Most formulations emphasize alternating or intertwined visual and textual elements within a single input, including the ability to "process interleaved image-text inputs effectively" and to integrate them into a coherent interpretation. A narrower formulation focuses on long-form content with multiple images and text, adding the need to identify relevant information while ignoring distractors. The main variation is therefore scope: general multimodal sequence comprehension versus long-form interleaved image-text comprehension with distractor filtering.

Space of facets. The terminology varies across papers, with near-overlapping labels such as interleaved understanding, interleaved multimodal comprehension, and interleaved image-text comprehension. Across these labels, recurring facets are comprehension, reasoning, and integration of alternating image-text sequences into a coherent interpretation. Some formulations also pair the construc

nodes.name: Interlocutor awareness
nodes.definition: The latent ability of an LLM to infer the identity and characteristics of its conversational partner, enabling adaptive behavior based on the interlocutor's model family, reasoning patterns, linguistic style, or alignment preferences.

nodes.name: Internal consistency
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Papers use the term in two different ways. One framing, stated in Calibrating Reasoning in Language Models with Internal Consistency, defines it as agreement between latent predictions decoded from intermediate layers and the final prediction, reflecting the stability of the model's internal reasoning process and serving as a measure of confidence. Another, in Compositional Causal Reasoning Evaluation in Language Models, defines it as giving equivalent answers to theoretically equivalent queries, regardless of correctness relative to ground truth, so the split is between layer-wise internal agreement and concordance across equivalent outputs.

Space of facets. The main contrast papers draw is with external validity. One paper treats compositional consistency as involving both agreement with ground truth, labeled external validity, and concordance among the model's own responses, labeled internal consistency. Across these uses, the same name covers both agreement among internal layer-wise predictions and equivalence among responses to theoretically equivalent queries.

Space of measurement. No measurement instrument is linked to it, and no behavioral indicator

nodes.name: Interpretability and explainability
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats this as a broad umbrella for making a model, feature, reasoning process, or prediction understandable to humans, either by exposing internal computations or by giving rationales for outputs. Most definitions emphasize concise human-understandable explanations of activations, internal states, decision factors, or predictions, and many quoted passages tie that understanding to traceability, such as linking tokens to training data, phrases to source documents, or decisions to concepts and intermediate steps. A smaller line of work narrows the term to interpretable sparse features or monosemantic latents, direct inspection or manipulation of model internals or even weights, and intrinsic interpretability through human-interpretable concepts rather than post-hoc explanation. The main difference across definitions is whether the property belongs to internal mechanisms, learned representations, or output-side justifications and evidence traces.

Space of facets. Papers often blur interpretability, explainability, and transparency, and some explicitly treat interpretability and explainability as near-equivalent. Within that u

nodes.name: Intersectional bias
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats intersectional bias as bias that arises from the interaction or interplay of multiple social or demographic attributes, rather than from a single attribute in isolation. Recurring examples are combinations such as race and gender, physical characteristics and gender, and age and socioeconomic status. The definitions largely align on this core idea, with only a minor shift between describing it as a form of social bias and as a model's tendency to exhibit such bias.

Space of facets. Papers organize the construct around combinations of attributes under study, especially race, gender, physical characteristics, age, and socioeconomic status, and they contrast this with fairness evaluation that examines only one demographic category at a time. One paper further describes it through cases where groups that share one attribute but differ on another are stereotyped differently. The papers do not introduce formal subtypes or connect it to other named constructs beyond this single-attribute versus multi-attribute distinction.

Space of measurement. Operationalization is sparse: papers link intersectional bias to one measur

nodes.name: Intrinsic bias
nodes.definition: The tendency of a large language model to favor certain types of solutions or options based on patterns in its pre-training data, limiting the diversity of its outputs.

nodes.name: Invariance
nodes.definition: The tendency for a predictor to rely on stable features that remain predictive across environments rather than environment-specific correlations.

nodes.name: Irrelevance detection ability
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. The paper frames this construct as a model-side ability to recognize when none of the available functions or tools matches the user's intent and to refuse the task in that case. In that usage, irrelevance detection centers on judging that "no suitable function exists" and "decline the task, rather than making incorrect attempts" (Robust Function-Calling for On-Device Language Model via Function Masking).

Space of measurement. No measurement instrument or behavioral indicator is linked to it. In the use, the construct is stated as a capability, but it is not tied to a named benchmark, human evaluation method, judge model, probe, or analysis.

Links. One paper reports that it is correlated with Tool use ability, describing an inverse relationship between accurate function-call execution and irrelevance detection capacity.

nodes.name: Judge sentiment bias
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definition, the construct is framed as an LLM judge's tendency to have its judgment affected by emotional expression in the content it evaluates. The paper describes this as a preference for positive or negative emotions, and its source language also states that the judge may prefer content without emotional elements.

Space of measurement. No measurement instrument is linked to this construct, and no behavioral indicator is linked to it. The papers therefore do not specify an operationalization for it.

nodes.name: Kanji-rule compatibility
nodes.definition: The model's latent understanding of which mnemonic-creation rules are semantically or visually suitable for a given kanji based on its specific structural or semantic features.

nodes.name: Keyword organization inference
nodes.definition: The latent ability of LLMs to reconstruct the correct semantic organization of keywords from disordered, unnatural inputs by leveraging contextual cues from subsequent natural language questions.

nodes.name: Knowledge
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats knowledge as a model-level latent ability to recall or retrieve factual information the model has acquired, often framed as world knowledge and as information not directly available in the input. Some authors broaden this to the model's ability to store and correctly apply factual, semantic, procedural, or conceptual information, and a smaller line defines knowledge capacity as retrieving and utilizing acquired knowledge to solve professional problems. The main difference is between a narrower recall-of-facts framing and a broader retrieve-and-apply framing, though both describe knowledge as an underlying ability of the model.

Space of facets. Papers use closely related labels such as knowledge, knowledge ability, and knowledge capacity for this family of abilities. One line of work splits evaluation into knowledge ability versus inference ability, while other work repeatedly pairs knowledge with reasoning, including benchmark setups that report separate knowledge and reasoning tasks. A separate relation connects knowledge to general ability through the claim that a single common factor can underlie reasoning-and

nodes.name: Knowledge acquisition
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage treats this as a latent ability to internalize, retrieve, and use factual or contextual knowledge, with papers describing that knowledge as coming from training data, external sources, or internal representations and being used to support decision-making. A smaller line of work instead uses neighboring labels for process views: fact learning is the encoding of factual information into model weights, knowledge internalization is absorbing tool-generated solutions into parametric knowledge so problems can be solved without tool calls, and knowledge gain is the increase in knowledge or certainty after new information, estimated through shifts in an internal knowledge distribution. One paper also describes this acquisition as data-inefficient, saying models may need hundreds to thousands of diverse representations to learn a fact.

Space of facets. The papers use several neighboring labels rather than a single uniform breakdown. One recurring split is between broad knowledge use and narrower factual storage, with one paper focusing on simple associations such as birthdays, capital cities, and concept relations, while an

nodes.name: Knowledge application
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the common framing is a latent ability or capacity to access and use knowledge during reasoning or task performance. Some authors locate that knowledge in inherent pre-trained or stored facts, others in newly learned facts or information supplied in the prompt or retrieved context, and several domain-specific formulations narrow it to applying agricultural knowledge, mathematical knowledge, or physical laws and formulas.
