One paper also discusses proactivity alongside transition-awareness in a framework for "proactive and transition-aware conversational agents," but the definitions do not introduce further named facets within proactivity itself.

Space of measurement. No measurement instrument or behavioral indicator is linked to it. The quoted passages nonetheless show one paper assessing dialogue controllability and proactivity t

nodes.name: Probability overestimation
nodes.definition: The model's tendency to assign excessive probability to tokens that should have a true probability of zero or near-zero.

nodes.name: Problem-solving ability
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats problem-solving ability as a broad capability to solve complex or unfamiliar tasks by devising and executing a strategy toward a goal or correct answer. Many definitions keep this general, describing the capacity to handle challenging situations, solve tasks across disciplines, or be "capable of generalized problem solving as humans do." A smaller line of work narrows the term to competitive mathematics that requires non-trivial insight, to tool-aided task solving, or to multimodal settings where text and images must be integrated, and some authors define it more directly through benchmark performance, distinguishing it from data generation ability and from error detection.

Space of facets. Papers do not present a single formal taxonomy, but they do use adjacent labels such as generalized problem solving, problem-solving capability, and multimodal problem solving. The construct is frequently positioned alongside reasoning-focused concepts: algorithmic reasoning is said to play a role in problem-solving, and mathematical reasoning is described as a benchmark for advanced reasoning and problem-solving abilit

nodes.name: Problem understanding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats this as an ability, often a latent one, to understand a task or problem statement and its relevant context. In code generation work, it is framed narrowly as comprehending the requirements and repository-level context of a code generation task, while mathematical reasoning papers use the near-synonym "problem comprehension" for understanding the semantic content, structure, quantities, relationships, and given conditions of a math problem, including separating relevant from irrelevant information and noticing missing or contradictory conditions.

Space of facets. Some authors present it as a stage in solving a problem: one paper says the "problem comprehension stage" involves analyzing word semantics, text structure, and given conditions, and another treats failures as "problem comprehension errors". Within the math framing, robust understanding is described as preserving the problem's meaning despite changes in wording or sentence structure, whereas the code generation framing centers on leveraging stronger models' "problem-understanding capabilities" to augment context. Across papers, the same family of terms is

nodes.name: Procedure understanding
nodes.definition: Understanding the sequence of steps or procedures depicted in a video.

nodes.name: Professional identity
nodes.definition: The latent trait enabling an AI agent to align its communication and actions with the goals, values, and standards of a specific professional role, such as a doctor, beyond mere information provision.

nodes.name: Program synthesis ability
nodes.definition: The latent capacity to infer executable programs that satisfy input-output specifications from examples.

nodes.name: Prompt robustness
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage treats prompt robustness as stability when prompts are varied, paraphrased, or reformulated in semantically similar ways. Most descriptions keep the focus on stable performance or consistent responses across prompt wording, including handling a wide range of prompt formulations and producing similar responses for similar inputs. A narrower framing limits the construct to semantically equivalent prompt templates and adds consistency of model rankings across templates, while another broadens it to performance on unseen prompt formulations and generalization beyond surface-level phrasing patterns.

Space of facets. Papers use several near-neighbor labels, including prompt robustness, robustness to prompt templates, and robustness to prompt variations, largely for the same family of uses. The main point of variation is scope: some authors center response consistency for the same question under rewording, while others frame it more broadly as stable task performance, ranking stability, or robustness to unseen prompts. Prompt sensitivity is treated as a comparison lens for this construct in one paper, which says sensitivi

nodes.name: Prompt sensitivity
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats prompt sensitivity as variation in a model's performance, outputs, predictions, or output distributions when prompts are reworded, reformatted, or reordered without changing their meaning. Most definitions center on semantically similar prompts or identical instructions, while narrower versions focus on formatting, verbalizers, example choice, or example order, and one survey narrows it further to whether known knowledge can be successfully verified only under certain prompt forms. A smaller line defines it specifically as changes in predicted class distributions across prompt rephrasings, without requiring access to ground truth, while another closely related framing emphasizes maintaining stable performance under irrelevant or meaning-preserving prompt variations such as formatting.

Space of facets. Papers use several nearby labels, including prompt brittleness, instruction sensitivity, response consistency, stylistic self-consistency, and robustness to spurious features. Some papers frame the phenomenon on the input side, as sensitivity to wording, detail, formatting, or order, while another frames instruction-ind

nodes.name: Prompt understanding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage, often under the names prompt following, prompt-following, or prompt adherence, treats the construct as how faithfully a generated image or video realizes what the prompt specifies, commonly its objects, attributes, relationships, constraints, and other contextual details. Several definitions state this as faithful representation or consistency with the prompt, and one study narrows it to whether a video accurately depicts an impossible event described in the prompt. A smaller line of work frames it more as the model's ability to interpret or grasp complex textual semantics and then follow them during generation, and one code-generation paper uses prompt adherence for observable alignment of generated code with prompt requirements, especially later in generation.

Space of facets. Paper use clusters around overlapping labels rather than sharply separated subtypes: prompt understanding, prompt following, and prompt adherence are all used for following prompt content, but they differ in whether the construct is treated as a model ability or as a property of generated outputs. When papers break down what must be followed, t

nodes.name: Property inheritance
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage describes property inheritance as projecting or transferring a property from a higher-level category, class, or parent type to a lower-level member, subtype, or subordinate entity. One formulation emphasizes projection of 'novel properties' from a general category to specific members (Characterizing the Role of Similarity in the Property Inferences of Language Models), while another asks whether 'a subtype inherits a property from its parent type' and makes the inference explicitly defeasible, meaning it may be weakened or strengthened by additional evidence (Evaluating Defeasible Reasoning in LLMs with DEFREASING). A smaller wording variation recasts this as an LLM's ability for 'class-knowledge transfer'.

Space of facets. The papers mainly place the construct in neighboring frames. One paper treats it as a phenomenon within defeasible reasoning and says its dataset focuses on property inheritance as expressed through generics, another uses 'class-knowledge transfer' for querying specific properties across hierarchies of entities. A separate line examines property inheritance behavior in relation to taxonomic relations

nodes.name: Protein structure understanding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. In the paper, the construct is framed as a model's latent comprehension of the principles governing protein structure, with the stated consequence that it can perform tasks like folding. The same paper also refers to "robust structural understanding" and "broader 3D structural understanding."

Space of facets. The only naming variation present is between "structural understanding" and "3D structural understanding," with the latter appearing when the paper discusses broader coverage that includes multimers.

Space of measurement. No measurement instrument is linked to it, and no behavioral indicator is linked to it. The paper describes it in latent terms, but no explicit operationalization is stated.

Links. The paper does not state causal, correlational, or related links for this construct.

nodes.name: Pruning robustness
nodes.definition: The degree to which model performance remains stable when adapter parameters or layers are removed or zeroed out.

nodes.name: Purity (moral foundation)
nodes.definition: The latent sensitivity to physical and moral cleanliness, religious or cultural codes, and avoidance of degradation as a moral foundation in narratives.

nodes.name: Quantization robustness
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats quantization robustness as performance retention under reduced numerical precision, especially when weights and activations are pushed to low-bit settings such as 4-bit or across varying bit-widths. Papers describe it through whether performance degrades at low bitwidth, whether benefits become more pronounced as bit size decreases, and whether accuracy loss stays small after quantization. A smaller line of work uses related labels such as quantization sensitivity, error resilience, or quantizability, shifting the emphasis from whole-model robustness to component-wise sensitivity, output stability when computation is approximated or quantized, or a model property that permits lower-precision parameters while maintaining performance.

Space of facets. Papers break the construct down along several axes. One recurring breakdown is by what is quantized, weights and activations, and by the severity of precision reduction, ranging from 8-bit to 4-bit and to any specified bit, including non-integer values. Other papers localize it to different model parts or inference stages, reporting varying sensitivity across l

nodes.name: Query understanding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, query understanding is used in two distinct ways. One paper, Single LLM, Multiple Roles: A Unified Retrieval-Augmented Generation Framework Using Role-Specific Token Optimization, defines it as the ability to infer the intent of a user's query so it can be processed for information retrieval and generation, and ties improvements in it to "construct more effective queries for retrieving relevant knowledge." Another paper, SafeKey: Amplifying Aha-Moment Insights for Safety Reasoning, uses the term for the model's initial behavior of interpreting and reiterating the user's query before it begins reasoning. The definitions differ along an ability-versus-process axis.

Space of facets. No paper breaks the construct into named subtypes or places it in an explicit construct hierarchy. Instead, the descriptions mark two uses under the same name: one centers intent inference for retrieval and generation, while the other refers to the model's "query understanding process U," described as models that "first try to understand and reiterate the query."

Space of measurement. No measurement instrument is linked to query understanding, and no behavioral in

nodes.name: Racial and ethnic bias
nodes.definition: The latent tendency of a model to systematically produce different clinical decisions or explanations based on patient ethnicity, reflecting societal or training data disparities.

nodes.name: Ranking ability
nodes.definition: The latent ability to correctly order multiple responses based on their relative quality (e.g., faithfulness or correctness) rather than assigning absolute scores.

nodes.name: Rationality
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, rationality is most commonly treated as a property of agents or models reflected in decisions that are guided by reason and aimed at optimal outcomes. Most definitions converge on payoff maximization, goal achievement, or conformity to logical principles, with one survey calling it "the quality of being guided by reason" and other papers defining it as decisions that maximize payoff, select strategies optimal for goals, or conform to logical and probabilistic principles under uncertainty. The main variation is the reference standard: some authors emphasize logical self-interest and utility, some emphasize Nash-equilibrium or goal-optimal behavior, and some emphasize normative reasoning under uncertainty, often contrasted with human-like emotional deviation.

Space of facets. The clearest breakdown presents rationality through four expected properties: information grounding, logical consistency, invariance from irrelevant context, and orderability of preference. Other papers describe it with neighboring notions such as decision-making optimality, internal utility judgment ability learned from posterior experience, and Nash-equilibrium-

nodes.name: Readability
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats readability as how easy generated or revised text is for people to read and understand, often expressed as clarity, accessibility, or being "not too technical for laymen." Many definitions tie it to surface or linguistic difficulty, mentioning sentence length, word complexity, vocabulary, or lexical and syntactic complexity. Smaller strands use the label differently: adversarial-prompt papers use human-readability for coherent, human-like prompts that remain understandable enough to evade filters, while other papers define readability through subtitle constraints or as latent reading effort inferred from reading behavior.

Space of facets. Different papers organize the construct around different targets: general-audience accessibility and reader feedback, formal text properties such as sentence structure and vocabulary, and in one code-translation paper, stylistic consistency through variable naming, code structure, and function signatures. The term overlaps with understandability and accessibility, and one evaluation framework places readability under User Alignment rather than treating it as a standalone quality. Pa

nodes.name: Reading comprehension
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats reading comprehension as understanding or interpreting a written passage and extracting the information needed to answer questions or complete tasks. Many authors frame this as a latent ability, as in the claim that it requires "strong reading comprehension skills to interpret and extract accurate information," while a smaller line of work defines it more directly as the observable task of answering questions from a given context. The narrower task framing sometimes specifies answer formats such as multiple-choice selection or span extraction, and one variant also includes deciding whether a question can be answered using the passage.

Space of facets. Papers use the label at several levels of scope. Some treat it as a broad capability category, often listed alongside question answering, commonsense reasoning, world knowledge, mathematical reasoning, dialog, or conversational proficiency, while others name subtypes such as multiple-choice reading comprehension and machine reading comprehension. A few formulations broaden the category further, for example by grouping readability and natural language inference under

nodes.name: Real-time interaction ability
nodes.definition: The ability of a model to engage in natural, low-latency conversation, including handling interruptions and responding simultaneously.

nodes.name: Realism
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats realism as how closely generated or synthetic outputs resemble the real world. One formulation defines it as the degree to which generated traffic trajectories and multi-vehicle scenarios match real-world dynamics and behaviors, while another describes it as synthetic data appearing plausible and indistinguishable from real-world data. These formulations largely agree in locating realism in the generated output and judging it against a real-world reference, with variation mainly between emphasis on behavioral resemblance and broader plausibility.

Space of facets. Only limited systematization is made explicit. One paper breaks realism for synthetic data into distributional similarity, where marginal and joint distributions of the synthetic table should match the original dataset, and logical consistency. Another use of the term centers on more realistic and controllable interactive trajectory generation and multi-vehicle scenarios, without further subtypes or explicit contrasts.

Space of measurement. Papers link realism to 1 measurement instrument, Human evaluation, and to no behavioral indicators or linked const

nodes.name: Reasoning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats reasoning as a latent model ability for multi-step logical inference: processing information, drawing conclusions, and solving problems, often by decomposing tasks into smaller steps or producing intermediate reasoning. Many definitions explicitly oppose this to pattern matching, memorization, or superficial cues, and anchor it in math, logic, coding, agent decision-making, or evidence aggregation from retrieval. Smaller lines broaden it to multimodal or video understanding, time-series prediction, inferring unseen buzzword meanings, or generating user-tailored reasons in explanations, and one line reframes reasoning as posterior inference over latent chains of thought rather than just stepwise deduction.

Space of facets. Papers do not converge on a single taxonomy, but they repeatedly slice the construct by task domain, including mathematical, commonsense, logical, visual or multimodal, and agent or planning-oriented reasoning, with a few papers also naming general, comprehensive, or few-shot reasoning. The literature also uses a broad family of near-synonymous labels, such as reasoning ability, reasoning

nodes.name: Reasoning about actions and change
nodes.definition: The ability to perform reasoning about actions and change that requires a numerical answer, combining RAC with quantitative skills.

nodes.name: Reasoning boundary
nodes.definition: The maximum task difficulty at which a model can still achieve a specified performance threshold in a reasoning process.

nodes.name: Reasoning boundary awareness
nodes.definition: The model's implicit ability to discern its own reasoning capabilities and constraints, as evidenced by the types of problems it generates when prompted to create new examples.

nodes.name: Reasoning consistency
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the shared framing is consistency as alignment or coherence in reasoning, but papers vary in what is being aligned. One recurring use describes coherent and uniform reasoning patterns across diverse problems, with harmonized demonstrations that create a "more coherent set of examples" and can "facilitate more effective reasoning patterns that can be easily followed" (Self-Harmonized Chain of Thought). Other papers define it as alignment between reasoning chains from different modalities or sources, correct and stable reasoning outcomes across languages, or agreement between an intermediate attempt and the model's eventual maximum-budget reasoning outcome. The clearest difference is the reference frame, process-level coherence versus outcome stability, across problems, modalities, languages, or reasoning-budget steps.

Space of facets. Rather than a single taxonomy, papers organize the construct by the setting in which reasoning is compared. The same name is used for harmonized Chain-of-Thought demonstrations, cross-modal fusion that aligns textual and visual reasoning processes into a coherent final answer, overlap in reasoning capabili

nodes.name: Reasoning depth
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Available definitions split across two framings rather than converging on one. One paper describes reasoning depth as the extent to which a model can engage with complex, multi-step reasoning problems that go beyond surface-level understanding or pattern matching, and ties it to high-difficulty, reasoning-focused evaluation and progress toward expert-level reasoning. Another paper uses a narrower framing centered on handling long causal dependencies and maintaining plausibility as the number of reasoning steps, or the length of a causal chain, increases.

Space of facets. Papers provide only limited internal structure. The clearest distinction is between reasoning depth and reasoning breadth, with one paper treating them as separate places where LLMs struggle. Within the depth framing, the recurring facets are multi-step reasoning, longer causal chains, long causal dependencies, and whether plausibility diminishes as depth increases.

Space of measurement. In the reported work, papers link reasoning depth to 2 measurement instruments, Human evaluation and MMLU-Pro, and to no behavioral indicators. MMLU-Pro is used as a benchmark with highly complex reasoning q

nodes.name: Reasoning diversity
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage treats reasoning diversity as the extent or capacity for a model to produce varied, distinct reasoning strategies or paths instead of repeating the same solution pattern across solution rounds. Papers differ slightly in emphasis, some phrase it as a latent capacity of the model, while others describe it through the observed use of multiple high-level reasoning strategies or reasoning types, but they agree on the core contrast between varied reasoning and repetition. This framing also appears in descriptions that "later solutions often repeat earlier ones."

Space of facets. Papers organize the construct around a recurring contrast between diverse reasoning and redundant or single-pattern reasoning. Closely related phrasings include structurally distinct reasoning paths, path diversity, semantic variation, and diversity of reasoning types. One paper also introduces "Diversified Thought" as incorporating a variety of reasoning strategies to improve path diversity, using a nearby label defined through varied reasoning strategies and path diversity.

Space of measurement. No measurement instrument is linked to this cons

nodes.name: Reasoning efficiency
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage describes reasoning efficiency as solving a problem with as few reasoning steps or tool calls as possible while avoiding unnecessary exploration. Several definitions make this explicitly process-based, for example by treating it as the number of steps a model takes and its ability to quickly narrow the candidate set. A smaller line of work broadens the construct from step economy to the rational use of computational resources, framing it in terms of inference overhead, response length, or the appropriate level of reasoning complexity for the problem while preserving performance.

Space of facets. Some authors describe the construct from both outcome and process perspectives, while others use more specific process-side facets such as step count, tool calls, unnecessary branch explorations, and strategic narrowing of candidates. Another recurring contrast is between minimal-step formulations and broader resource-use formulations, which bring in inference overhead, latency, response length, and computational overhead. One paper also uses the nearby label "inference efficiency" when evaluating avoidance of unnecessary branch

nodes.name: Reasoning faithfulness
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats reasoning faithfulness as correspondence between an expressed reasoning path and what actually produces the answer: papers describe faithful reasoning as a generated path or trace that reflects the actual or internal decision process, rather than a hallucinated or misleading justification. A smaller line of work shifts the reference point from internal process to consistency or grounding, defining it as the final conclusion aligning with the generated chain, the reasoning remaining grounded in provided evidence rather than misleading annotations or shortcuts, or, in safety settings, explanations that are coherent, logically sound, and faithful to the input prompt. Nearby labels include chain-of-thought faithfulness for explicit reasoning traces and reasoning hallucinations for cases where apparently plausible steps do not match program logic.

Space of facets. Papers do not present a shared multi-part taxonomy, but they do separate the area into nearby labels and failure modes. Chain-of-thought faithfulness is used for explicit reasoning traces, reasoning fidelity for explanations attached to safety decisio

nodes.name: Reasoning length
nodes.definition: The latent extent to which a model generates extended, step-by-step reasoning before producing a final answer, reflecting the depth and thoroughness of its internal problem-solving process.

nodes.name: Reasoning quality
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most papers treat reasoning quality as a property of the reasoning process itself: the chain of thought or intermediate steps should be logically valid, accurate, coherent, and sometimes comprehensive. Within that broad process-oriented usage, papers emphasize different facets, including logically correct and relevant proof steps, reliable and logically structured reasoning, inclusion of all relevant and potentially contradictory information, or correct intermediate steps rather than only the final answer. A smaller line of work uses the term more outcome-orientedly, as correct solutions on reasoning tasks discussed alongside efficiency, so the main disagreement is between process quality and task-level correctness, and between narrower facets and broader step quality.

Space of facets. Papers use several named facets rather than a single settled taxonomy. One decomposition treats chain-of-thought quality through recall and precision: recall measures reasoning informativeness by how many ground-truth solution steps appear, and precision measures faithfulness by how many generated steps are accurate. Other papers use nearby names for partly overlapping aspects,

nodes.name: Reasoning rigor
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage treats it as the quality or extent of rigorous reasoning, centered on clear justification, coherent logic, and well-supported conclusions. One paper sharpens this into strict, step-by-step logical inference with verifiable derivations and avoidance of spurious or hallucinated conclusions, another frames it in mathematical proof terms as being logically airtight and adhering to formal proof standards, and another contrasts outputs that give conclusions without thorough justification with ones that construct well-supported arguments with clear reasoning. The main variation is scope and reference standard, from general argumentative support, to multi-step derivation, to formal proof quality.

Space of facets. Across the papers, nearby labels, reasoning rigor, mathematical rigor, and logical rigor, are used for overlapping descriptions of justified and coherent reasoning. The most explicit internal breakdown ties it to reasoning granularity and strict step-by-step structure: one framework restricts each step to at most one derivation and treats the resulting granularity as strengthening rigor. Other papers organize the

nodes.name: Reasoning robustness
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats reasoning robustness as the extent to which a model keeps its reasoning correct when the same problem is rewritten, perturbed with irrelevant information, or reframed within the same scenario. In Is Your Model Really A Good Math Reasoner? Evaluating Mathematical Reasoning with Checklist, this framing is tied to whether a model "truly understands the inherent mathematical logic of a problem" and remains robust to diverse variations of that problem. A smaller framing, present in another extracted definition, treats it instead as the ability to maintain accurate and reliable performance when handling multiple, potentially interdependent questions in a single input.

Space of facets. The clearest breakdown comes from the checklist-based framing, which organizes the construct around an original problem and three robustness variants: problem understanding, irrelevant disturbance, and scenario understanding. Beyond this decomposition, papers do not equate it with, nest it under, or contrast it against other named constructs.

Space of measurement. No measurement instrument or behavioral indicator is linked to it. Even so

nodes.name: Recency bias
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage is a latent preference for recent tokens: attention or retrieval favors tokens closer to the current position over earlier ones, sometimes explicitly only when the compared tokens are otherwise similar. One paper states that "Recency implies that tokens that are more recent in the prompt ... are going to be more important in generating the subsequent token" (Emergence of Episodic Memory in Transformers: Characterizing Changes in Temporal Structure of Attention Scores During Training). Definitions differ mainly in scope: some describe a general weighting in attention, retrieval, or generation, while others narrow it to overemphasis on near, mid-range, or final tokens at the expense of earlier or historical context, and one definition analogizes it to human short-term memory recall patterns.

Space of facets. Papers use both "recency effect" and "recency bias" for closely similar phenomena. One paper places it within serial position effects, "specifically recency and primacy," while others describe more specific manifestations such as near-token focus, retrieval favoring recent tokens, or an end-of-input attention sink in

nodes.name: Recursive stability
nodes.definition: A property of a generative model in a self-consuming training loop that quantifies how much its output distribution changes in response to small perturbations in the initial real dataset across multiple generations.

nodes.name: Redundancy
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. One paper defines redundancy as an internal representation property: features are distributed across multiple neurons rather than concentrated in a single unit, and this distribution is said to support robustness to noise or perturbation. The accompanying quoted passage uses the same framing, describing redundancy as distributed feature coding that discourages monosemantic code.

Space of facets. Usage in the papers organizes redundancy through contrasts rather than subtypes: it is opposed to features being concentrated in a single unit, and one quoted passage says this distributed coding discourages monosemantic code. A related paper also connects redundancy to polysemanticity and describes polysemantic code as favoring redundancy for robustness.

Space of measurement. Redundancy is linked to 1 measurement instrument and no behavioral indicators. The only linked instrument is LLM-as-a-judge: one paper assesses redundancy by instructing an LLM to count the number of unique main statements within a set of candidate summaries. This operationalization concerns summary content, whereas the explicit definition concerns how features are distributed across neurons.

nodes.name: Region-level understanding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. The definition treats region-level understanding, also called region-level comprehension, as the ability to understand and reason about specific spatial regions within an image, rather than only processing the image as a whole. The same usage places it in a setting where overhead viewpoint, scale variation, and small objects are described as challenges for region-level comprehension in high-resolution remote sensing imagery.

Space of facets. The usage in the papers does not divide the construct into explicit subtypes. Instead, the main distinction is between reasoning about specific spatial regions and processing the image as a whole, and adjacent uses connect it to region captioning and to multimodal alignment in region-level context without explicitly treating them as the same construct.

Space of measurement. Papers link this construct to one measurement instrument, Ferret-Bench, through Referring Description and Referring Reasoning tasks. The surrounding operationalization is likewise region-task based: region captioning is the only linked behavioral indicator, and papers describe using region captioning benchmarks and a visual referring task to access or

nodes.name: Relation understanding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats relation understanding as an ability, sometimes explicitly a latent ability, to comprehend relationships among objects or other entities in an image or scene. Most definitions center on interactions and spatial arrangements, with some extending to actions, attribute bindings, emotional connections, or connections between concepts mentioned in a question and depicted in a scene. A smaller line of work uses a narrower framing under composition identification, focusing on determining spatial, orientational, occlusion, size-comparison, and arrangement relations among objects.

Space of facets. The construct is described through several relation types rather than a single example: papers mention interactional relations such as 'riding', 'looking into', and 'lying next to', alongside spatial arrangements, actions, attribute bindings, orientation, occlusion, size comparison, and arrangement. Relation understanding, relational understanding, and relationship comprehension are used for closely similar descriptions, while composition identification names a more specific subset centered on compositional relations. One paper

nodes.name: Relational reasoning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats relational reasoning as the ability to understand and operate on abstract relationships while being independent of the specific identity, or in some definitions the absolute properties, of the symbols or stimuli involved. Some papers keep this abstract framing and describe evaluation with unseen symbols, while others define it more concretely as reasoning over structured entity relations, such as multi-hop constraints in knowledge graphs, primary-foreign key links and dependencies in databases, or explicit interactions and counterfactual dependencies among entities. A smaller line of work uses nearby labels for reasoning about relations in visual or multimodal scenes, shopping concept compatibility, or relations that are implicit in text rather than explicitly stated, and some authors frame it as a latent model ability whereas others use it for task-specific reasoning in particular domains.

Space of facets. Papers do not present a single shared breakdown of the construct, but they repeatedly organize it by the kind of relation being handled. The recurring facets are abstract symbolic relations, multi-hop and constrai

nodes.name: Relevance
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats relevance as on-topic alignment: whether a model output, summary, argument, reasoning path, or document directly addresses the prompt, question, instruction, query, or debate topic and avoids unrelated or off-topic content. Many definitions use near-identical wording such as being pertinent and on-topic, staying focused on the main topic, or asking whether the output directly relates to the instruction. A smaller line of work treats it as a latent tendency or ability, either of a model to make task-relevant contributions in interaction or of a text to maintain pragmatic alignment with discourse topic and context, and a few task-specific definitions broaden it beyond strict topical match to include capturing key points, providing valuable extensions beyond the topic, or balancing topic coverage with off-topic avoidance.

Space of facets. Many papers place relevance inside broader evaluation schemes rather than giving it an internal taxonomy. It appears as one of the dimensions of instruction following, as a subjective criterion in debating under the label topic relevance, and as a pragmatic relevance condition within c

nodes.name: Reliability
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats reliability as a broad property of model outputs and behavior, centered on trustworthiness, consistency, dependability, and often correctness or factual accuracy, sometimes extending to safety. Several papers spell this out as producing outputs that are trustworthy, factually correct, or free from outdated, incorrect, biased, low-quality, or hallucinated content, and one account adds that reliable models should generate faithful content while expressing uncertainty or acknowledging missing knowledge. A smaller line of work narrows the construct to specific settings, such as valid reasoning traces, medical reports suitable for clinical decision-making, executable code, reward-model solution selection or scoring, and successful application of a targeted edit. Another minority framing shifts the locus from external outputs to agreement within the model or response pattern, defining reliability through internal consistency between intermediate and final predictions, or between items intended to measure the same construct.

Space of facets. Usage varies mainly by scope and locus. Many papers keep reliability as an umbrella

nodes.name: Religious bias
nodes.definition: A latent, systematic skew in the model's representations related to religion, influencing its association of religious groups with positive or negative actions and stereotypes.

nodes.name: Representation collapse
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most definitions here treat representation collapse as a loss of distinctness in a model's representations: either the distortion and degradation of general pre-trained features during fine-tuning, or hidden features in deeper layers becoming highly similar. In this usage, papers describe later or intermediate layer states as overly alike, reducing expressive capacity and performance. A smaller line of work, using the label representational collapse, defines it as distinct input sequences yielding arbitrarily close last-token representations at the last layer, especially under low-precision arithmetic, so the main difference is whether collapse is framed as internal feature degradation across training and depth or as sequence-level indistinguishability at the final representation.

Space of facets. Papers break the construct down by where the collapse appears: in pre-trained features during downstream fine-tuning, in intermediate or later hidden states across depth, and in the final token at the last layer. Some descriptions make it explicitly layerwise, quantifying similarity between adjacent-layer inputs and describing progressive collapse in later layers, w

nodes.name: Representation diversity
nodes.definition: The degree to which intermediate token representations remain varied and non-redundant across layers.

nodes.name: Representation learning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the dominant framing treats representation learning as a model's ability to learn embeddings or features of inputs that preserve useful information for downstream tasks, often by encoding similar instances closely in a latent space. A smaller line of work narrows this to learning invariant or environment-relevant contextual features, or to learning semantic rather than token-pattern representations. Some authors also describe it more mechanistically, as lower or deeper layers forming intermediate representations or applying a fixed representation function before later in-context learning.

Space of facets. The main named variants are feature learning, which emphasizes contextual, invariant, or environment-relevant features, and semantic representation learning, which emphasizes semantic meaning and is explicitly contrasted with token pattern representations. Several papers use representation learning and feature learning in closely overlapping ways, as learning useful internal features, embeddings, or rich latent representations that transfer across tasks. Another recurring organization places it inside accounts of in-context learning

nodes.name: Representation quality
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats representation quality as a latent ability of a model's internal representations, features, or embeddings to encode task-relevant information in a usable feature space for downstream tasks. Several definitions stress preserving useful information while discarding noise, or producing embeddings that support retrieval, clustering, semantic similarity, binding prediction, or the distinction of tasks and knowledge domains. A smaller line of work narrows the construct to specific representational objects: task vector quality is the distinctness and decodability of a task representation for triggering correct in-context learning behavior, while visual feature quality is the preservation of semantic, structural, and pixel-level image details for multimodal alignment and reasoning. The main disagreement is over scope and reference standard, broad hidden-state or embedding quality versus task-specific or modality-specific representations, assessed by downstream usefulness, decodability, or detail preservation.

Space of facets. Papers organize the construct through several facets rather than one common breakdown. One paper exp

nodes.name: Representation similarity
nodes.definition: The degree of structural alignment or equivalence between the internal representation spaces of different neural network models.

nodes.name: Representational harm
nodes.definition: The latent property of an LLM’s outputs that misrepresent or marginalize certain nations by limiting their visibility or associating them with negative traits, thereby reinforcing global inequities.

nodes.name: Representational stability
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats representational stability as the consistency or robustness of internal representations when something is perturbed or varies. Most definitions keep the focus on hidden states, token representations, feature representations, or learned audio-text representations, described as remaining stable under targeted perturbations, small input changes, mild image perturbations, noise, or varying initial conditions. A smaller line of work narrows the concept to invariance after parameter editing, while another broadens it to include performance staying consistent across random initializations or layers. The main disagreement is therefore about both what representation should remain stable and what kind of perturbation or variation is being considered.

Space of facets. Papers do not present a single shared subtype scheme, but they use several closely related labels for domain-specific versions of the same general idea: hidden representation stability, vision feature stability, performance stability, and representational robustness. These usages preserve a common theme of representation consistency, though one line studies re

nodes.name: Representativeness
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. The definition treats representativeness as a property of a training-data subset relative to the full dataset: it is the degree to which the subset captures the essential information needed for a model to perform well across tasks, combining sufficiency and necessity with respect to the full dataset. The accompanying usage keeps this framing focused on identifying a "core subset of demonstrations" that is "tailored to specific LLMs" and serves as a "faithful representation" of the training dataset.

Space of facets. Rather than introducing subtypes, the paper organizes the concept around a subset versus full-dataset comparison and pairs representativeness with minimality. A high-quality subset is described as both representative of the entire training dataset and "as minimal in size as possible," with the stated dual objectives of maintaining data quality and minimizing computational expenses.

Space of measurement. No measurement instrument or behavioral indicator is linked to representativeness. In use, the construct is described through selecting a core subset of demonstrations and requiring that this subset be a faithful, minimal representation of the full

nodes.name: Research ideation ability
nodes.definition: The latent capability to propose novel research ideas, identify research problems, and formulate solutions based on a review of existing literature.

nodes.name: Resilience
nodes.definition: The capacity of a multi-agent system to handle internal errors from faulty agents and maintain overall operational performance without significant degradation.

nodes.name: Resource awareness
nodes.definition: The ability of an agent to recognize and adapt its problem-solving strategies in response to constraints on available resources, such as time and budget.

nodes.name: Response quality awareness
nodes.definition: The latent ability of an LLM to discern and adapt its behavior based on the absolute quality of responses, rather than only relative preferences, enabling differentiation across quality levels and generalization to higher-quality outputs.

nodes.name: Response stability
nodes.definition: The degree to which a model's predicted bias remains consistent across different surface realizations of the same question, such as paraphrases, indicating robustness to superficial prompt variations.

nodes.name: Response understanding
nodes.definition: The latent ability of a reward model to comprehend the content, quality, and relevance of generated responses in relation to a given input.

nodes.name: Responsiveness to human feedback
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats this as a latent ability to adapt model responses or behavior in light of human or user feedback during interaction, often across multiple turns. Most definitions describe adaptation and improvement after natural language feedback or user corrections, while one benchmark-specific framing makes the criterion narrower by requiring both error correction and response maintenance under challenge, and by stressing that a robust model should use appropriate feedback without being misled by inappropriate feedback. A smaller variation broadens the target from text outputs to task execution, describing dynamic modification of behavior under real-time corrections, constraints, or changed goals.

Space of facets. The clearest internal breakdown separates error correction from response maintenance, and also contrasts appropriate with inappropriate feedback; one paper further notes a performance discrepancy between the error-correction and response-maintenance scenarios. Elsewhere, papers use closely related labels, such as leveraging natural language feedback and adaptation to feedback, for the same general ability to adjust under

nodes.name: Retrieval effectiveness
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage stays within retrieval quality: papers describe it as the degree to which a retrieval system consistently returns relevant documents for a query, reflecting query-document alignment and contextual grounding. A closely related framing calls it contextual relevance, the latent trait of how well a retrieved chunk aligns with the broader context of a user's query and document structure, explicitly beyond surface-level semantic similarity. In one paper, the same label is used for generation instead, referring to responses that engage meaningfully with the input content and context, so the unit of analysis shifts from retrieval systems or chunks to generated responses.

Space of facets. The clearest breakdown treats retrieval along two dimensions, semantic similarity and contextual relevance: a Dual-Axis Retriever is described as expanding and filtering candidate chunks using both axes. Within that framing, contextual relevance is contrasted with surface similarity and tied to document structure and broader query context, while the system-level definition emphasizes relevant-document return, query-document alignment, and

nodes.name: Retrieval quality
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, retrieval quality is framed around the quality of what the retrieval stage brings back. Definitions emphasize retrieving "informative, non-redundant, and relevant" documents or facts, or retrieving information that is sufficiently detailed and complete for complex questions. A narrower framing treats it as the outcome of reducing irrelevant facts in the retrieved subgraph, so the main difference is whether authors describe a broad retrieval-quality property or foreground depth and completeness versus noise reduction.

Space of facets. Papers use closely related labels to foreground different aspects of the construct: "knowledge retrieval depth" focuses on detailed and complete retrieval, while "retrieval noise reduction" focuses on minimizing irrelevant facts. Some descriptions also pair retrieval quality with retrieval fidelity, document retrieval accuracy, and more precise query formulation, but no paper explicitly links it to other constructs through nesting, equivalence, or contrast.

Space of measurement. Operationalization is narrow in the linked literature: retrieval quality is linked to 1 measurement instrument, HotpotQA, and to no b

nodes.name: Reusability
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the only framing present treats reusability as cross-task reuse of model circuitry. One definition describes it as the extent to which a modular circuit appears across multiple language tasks, enabling transfer of functional understanding without re-interpretation, while the other describes a model repurposing learned subcircuits, including attention heads and algorithmic steps, across tasks that share underlying computational demands. The common emphasis is on recurrence across tasks and on transfer or generalization of insights about the same circuitry.

Space of facets. The usage in the papers varies mainly in granularity rather than in concept. One paper states the construct at the level of a modular circuit, and another at the level of learned subcircuits comprising attention heads and algorithmic steps; in practice, both are used for the same broad pattern of shared circuitry across tasks. The labels "Reusability" and "Circuit reuse" therefore function as near-synonyms here, and the accompanying examples focus on a shared process and shared "in-circuit" attention heads between tasks.

Space of measurement. No measurement instrument and

nodes.name: Reversal curse
nodes.definition: The phenomenon where an auto-regressive model, after learning a forward relationship such as 'A is B', fails to generalize to the inverse relationship 'B is A' without explicit training on it.

nodes.name: Reward overoptimization
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across these papers, the prevailing usage treats reward overoptimization as a failure of reward-based or preference-based optimization: proxy reward, learned reward, or a target metric improves while true quality, gold reward, human preferences, or actual performance plateaus, regresses, or deteriorates. Many papers also describe it behaviorally as exploiting flaws or loopholes in an imperfect reward or evaluation function to obtain high scores without meeting the intended goal, sometimes through undesired multi-step strategies, excessive suppression of rejected completions, or degenerate outputs such as repeated, short, or meaningless strings. Some definitions stress deviation from intended behavior, while others stress degradation in overall or unmeasured output quality.

Space of facets. Papers often use reward overoptimization interchangeably with reward hacking and overoptimization, and one paper explicitly adds reward gaming. The label spans both a latent tendency or failure mode of policies and alignment algorithms, and concrete output behaviors that display that failure. One paper singles out Length exploitation, the tendency to produce excessively ver

nodes.name: Richness
nodes.definition: The depth, breadth, and diversity of information provided in the model's response.

nodes.name: Risk management
nodes.definition: The ability to monitor, control, and adapt to downside exposure while pursuing profitable investment outcomes.

nodes.name: Risk preference
nodes.definition: An individual's disposition toward taking or avoiding risks, which influences choices in situations with uncertain outcomes.

nodes.name: Robustness
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage frames robustness as stability of performance or behavior under changes in prompts, inputs, examples, settings, or environments, including prompt reformulations, in-context example choices, noisy or degraded inputs, typos, option position or symbol changes, distribution shift, adversarial perturbations, changing opponents or environments, and decoding or system-setting changes. Several quoted passages use the term for whether models remain effective under such perturbations, and some describe current systems as "highly brittle in the face of even minor perturbations." Smaller lines of work use robustness for retention of pre-learned capabilities after fine-tuning or editing, for stability of reasoning across similar problems and task conditions, or for worst-case performance on rare shifted inputs. The object whose robustness is discussed also varies across papers, spanning models, agents, jailbreak prompts, watermarks, backdoors, detectors, and evaluation metrics.

Space of facets. Papers break the construct into recurring variants such as prompt robustness, out-of-distribution robustness, adversarial robustness, safety or

nodes.name: Robustness to data poisoning
nodes.definition: The model's resistance to performance degradation caused by the presence of noisy, poisoned, or backdoor samples in its training data.

nodes.name: Robustness to differential-privacy noise
nodes.definition: The latent property of a model to maintain performance and generate coherent output despite the introduction of noise during training, such as from DP-SGD.

nodes.name: Robustness to matrix layout
nodes.definition: The degree to which performance remains stable when the arrangement, aspect ratio, or cropping of the image matrix changes.

nodes.name: Robustness to weight perturbations
nodes.definition: The model's stability and ability to maintain performance and safety alignment when its parameters are shifted, such as during the fine-tuning process.

nodes.name: Role misalignment
nodes.definition: The model's latent shift from a safety-oriented gatekeeper role to an execution-oriented task-completion role, triggered by first-person commitments that alter its internal role attribution.

nodes.name: Role-play fidelity
nodes.definition: The extent to which a model authentically simulates a character’s perspective, psychological state, and decision-making processes rather than merely mimicking surface traits.

nodes.name: Role-playing ability
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage treats this construct as a latent ability to sustain a role during interaction. One paper defines it narrowly as adopting and consistently maintaining a specified character or persona in an interactive engagement, while another gives a broader formulation centered on maintaining character consistency, language style, emotional expression, and behavioral coherence in role-based interactions. The shared core is role maintenance in interaction, and the main difference is scope: persona consistency alone versus a wider set of expressive and behavioral consistencies.

Space of facets. Papers do not develop an extensive taxonomy, but one definition breaks the construct into character consistency, language style, emotional expression, and behavioral coherence. Another treats it more compactly as persona adoption and maintenance. One paper also situates role-playing alongside low-level multimodal perception, high-level cognition such as multi-step reasoning, and deliberative decision-making within a broader capability set for interactive agents.

Space of measurement. Operationalization is sparse in the recorded relationshi

nodes.name: Routing stability
nodes.definition: The consistency and reliability of the expert selection mechanism across different layers and inputs.

nodes.name: Rule-based reasoning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Definitions divide between a broad latent-ability framing and a narrower task-specific application framing. One paper describes it as the latent ability to understand, integrate, and apply multiple abstract rules simultaneously, with examples such as counting, color logic, and shape constraints, and its quoted passages describe step-by-step planning with arithmetic and geometric rules and deep, abstract reasoning in a constrained spatial pathfinding environment. Another paper uses the nearby name rule application for applying sport-specific rules to a concrete scenario or video, described as the ability to connect movements with context-based rules to determine the correct judgment.

Space of facets. The papers distinguish it mainly by task domain and reasoning stage. The spatial framing bundles it with path-finding, counting, segregation, and logic over colors and shapes in a single task, while the sports framing uses the nearby label rule application for judgments that connect movements with context-based rules. In one related account, inductive reasoning appears within a rule-based reasoning paradigm: the model first derives the correct rule from examples a

nodes.name: Rule grounding
nodes.definition: Instantiating abstract rules with specific constants to prepare for logical inference.

nodes.name: Safety
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats safety as a latent model or agent property, variously called a disposition, ability, capability, or performance, to avoid harmful, unsafe, toxic, offensive, unethical, illegal, or dangerous outputs, often while aligning with human values or societal norms, especially under malicious, adversarial, or unsafe prompts. Many papers make refusal central, and one explicitly states that safety means "stopping models from following malicious instructions and generating toxic content"; other definitions describe it as refusing unsafe requests or producing benign responses to unsafe prompts. Definitions differ mainly on scope: most stay at text generation, some extend to tool use and environment interaction, and a broader "trust and safety" framing centers on protecting users from harm, misinformation, abuse, and unsafe content while fostering confidence.

Space of facets. Papers organize the term in several ways. A recurring pattern is to place safety as one axis within broader multidimensional evaluations or as one core capability of language or vision-language models. A smaller line of work uses nearby labels diffe

nodes.name: Safety alignment
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats safety alignment as the degree to which a model's behavior conforms to safety guidelines, human values, ethical principles, or usage policies, mainly by avoiding harmful or undesirable outputs. Many definitions also cast it as a latent property of the model, sometimes specifically the ability to refrain from harmful content or to recognize and refuse unsafe queries. A smaller line of work narrows the concept to explicit safety policy compliance or safety control for agents' action trajectories, while one paper frames it as consistency between internal processing and safety training objectives, visible in stable gradient patterns. Some definitions further fold in maintaining utility, helpfulness, or balanced compliance on benign instructions, whereas others focus only on preventing harm.

Space of facets. Papers use several nearby names for overlapping ideas: safety alignment, safety policy compliance, and safety control all center on adherence to safety policies, but the latter two are defined in agent settings with explicit external rules. Several definitions explicitly situate it within AI alignment more broadly

nodes.name: Safety awareness
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats safety awareness as a latent disposition or ability to recognize sensitive, harmful, or high-stakes situations and respond cautiously, most often by seeking user confirmation before acting. Closely related work uses the label risk awareness for a similar framing, and one paper says an agent should "be aware of the potential risks and seek user confirmation before executing risky actions." A smaller line of work broadens it to a model's sensitivity to safety-related risks and tendency to avoid unsafe outputs across risk categories, while another defines it at the representation level, as whether internal states show clear distinctions between safe and toxic content. The main difference across definitions is whether the construct is located in action handling, output tendencies, or internal representations.

Space of facets. Papers do not offer a detailed subtype taxonomy, but they repeatedly organize the construct around a few recurring targets: sensitive or high-stakes actions, different risk categories, suspicious pop-ups, and safe versus toxic content. One line focuses on action sensitivity, for example whether a sy

nodes.name: Safety inconsistency
nodes.definition: A latent discrepancy in Large Language Models where the ability to identify harmful requests as a discriminator is significantly better than the ability to defend against them as a generator.

nodes.name: Safety reasoning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing framing is a latent internal process or ability for making safety decisions during generation, especially determining whether a request is harmful and choosing a safe course of action. Some papers broaden this by describing the ability to analyze explicit and implicit intents in multimodal inputs, reconstruct the user’s genuine request, and assess potential risks before responding. A smaller line of work, using the name Safety-aware reasoning, emphasizes integrating safety evaluation into each reasoning step, with self-monitoring and dynamic adjustment of responses based on safety status.

Space of facets. The papers do not provide a formal taxonomy, but they repeatedly describe the construct through recurring components: harm detection, safe action selection, intent analysis, request reconstruction, risk assessment, and safety-aware reflection at each step of reasoning. They also use both Safety reasoning and Safety-aware reasoning for closely aligned latent capabilities embedded in the reasoning process. The main variation is scope, with some descriptions centering on deciding whether to refuse or respond safely, and ot

nodes.name: Safety robustness
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across definitions, papers converge on an adversarial safety framing: the construct concerns whether safety mechanisms, constraints, guardrails, or restrictions hold up when inputs are designed to manipulate the model into harmful or prohibited outputs. A common positive formulation treats it as jailbreak robustness, resistance, or robustness to jailbreaking, while another common formulation names the inverse as jailbreak vulnerability, susceptibility, or ethical risk. The main variation is scope rather than core meaning, with some definitions focusing on multilingual prompts, template-region manipulation, role-based pressure, or fine-tuning and inference-time triggers.

Space of facets. Papers do not offer a single formal taxonomy, but they do organize the construct around recurring attack settings. One recurring distinction is between prompt-based bypass attempts in general and narrower variants involving multilingual prompts, visual inputs, manipulative role prompts, or acquired susceptibility from fine-tuning. Across these uses, different names are applied to closely overlapping content, and one paper further describes safety functions in two parts, identi

nodes.name: Scaffolding
nodes.definition: The latent tendency of a model to support student learning by providing hints, questions, or partial guidance that promote cognitive engagement without giving away full solutions.

nodes.name: Scene understanding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed papers, the prevailing usage treats scene understanding as an ability to interpret a visual environment at the scene level: perceiving the environment, identifying objects or components, and understanding their relationships, layout, and overall meaning. A recurring formulation adds semantic, spatial, and motion attributes and says the goal is a comprehensive understanding, while another application-focused wording narrows it to interpreting environmental layout and visual context well enough to support navigation decisions. A smaller variant presents it as scene-level visual perception, emphasizing whole-image content and description rather than selective identification of critical objects.

Space of facets. Papers break the construct down by what is being understood: objects or components, their relationships, and broader scene meaning, with one definition explicitly naming semantic, spatial, and motion attributes. The naming is not fully uniform, and closely similar abilities are also labeled visual scene comprehension and scene-level visual perception. The clearest difference in wording is scope, with some descriptions centering whole-i

nodes.name: Scheming
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, scheming is described as concealed pursuit of misaligned goals behind outwardly good or compliant behavior. One framing treats it as a latent disposition in which a model behaves well during training with the ulterior motive of gaining power later or pursuing misaligned goals after deployment. Another framing treats it as a form of misaligned behavior in which an AI covertly pursues its own goals while hiding its true capabilities and objectives from users or developers. The definitions agree on concealed misaligned pursuit, but differ on whether the emphasis is a latent disposition tied to training and later deployment or a broader description of hidden objectives and capabilities.

Space of facets. Papers use the term alongside misaligned behaviour and deceptive strategies. One paper says AI models might use deceptive strategies as part of scheming or misaligned behaviour, while another uses scheming for covert pursuit of misaligned goals combined with hiding true capabilities and objectives.

Space of measurement. No measurement instrument is linked to it, and no behavioral indicator is linked to it. The papers therefore characterize

nodes.name: Scientific inductive reasoning
nodes.definition: A specialized form of inductive reasoning focused on inferring underlying patterns or rules from data and observations within scientific domains like chemistry and biology.

nodes.name: Scientific knowledge
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats scientific knowledge as a model capacity or breadth of scientific, domain-specific, or factual knowledge that supports understanding and answering science-oriented questions. Most definitions stay close to this question-answering framing, describing either understanding and applying knowledge from scientific domains, answering questions across scientific domains, or having specialized information needed for expert-level questions in an area such as organismal biology. A smaller line of work uses a narrower framing of scientific prior knowledge, focusing on whether an LLM can draw on domain knowledge when proposing plausible equations or hypotheses.

Space of facets. Papers do not present a detailed internal taxonomy, but the naming varies: some use science-related abilities for cross-domain science question answering, while another uses scientific prior knowledge for equation or hypothesis proposal. One paper organizes evaluation by scientific subjects, specifically biology, chemistry, and health, and another narrows the construct to organismal biology. Scientific knowledge is also positioned alongside natu

nodes.name: Scientific reasoning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats scientific reasoning as an ability to reason about scientific concepts and questions, usually with domain-specific knowledge and multi-step inference. Many definitions make this concrete as reasoning over scientific data, figures, or other multimodal evidence, or as answering science questions, while some broaden it to long-context scientific content, research problems that combine knowledge recall, reasoning, and code synthesis, or the interpretation of scientific evidence so as to avoid unjustified conclusions. A smaller line of work extends the label to the scientific process itself, including inference from data, hypothesis formulation, and discovery in a controlled physics-based environment.

Space of facets. The clearest explicit scheme places scientific reasoning alongside algebraic reasoning, arithmetic reasoning, geometry reasoning, logical reasoning, numeric common sense, and statistical reasoning as one of seven mathematical reasoning types. Across other papers, the same label is used for somewhat different scopes, including academic paper figures, science question answering, long-context understanding, res

nodes.name: Security
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, security is not used in a single stable sense. One recurring formulation treats it as a latent property concerning resistance to generating harmful or malicious content, but other definitions apply the term to different objects: the resilience of a watermarking scheme against attacks aimed at reverse-engineering, stealing, or illegitimately applying watermark rules, and the degree to which a defense prevents attackers from successfully exploiting an LLM application. The main disagreement is about what is said to be secure, namely the model, the watermarking scheme, or the defense and application.

Space of facets. The papers do not provide a shared facet structure or subtype taxonomy. Instead, the same label is used for different targets, and it is discussed alongside utility, robustness, text quality, and usability, including formulations about trade-offs among robustness, text quality, and security and about ensuring security with minimal impact on usability.

Space of measurement. Security is linked to 1 measurement instrument, AgentDojo, and to no behavioral indicators or constructs. AgentDojo is described as evaluating the utility and s

nodes.name: Selection bias
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage treats selection bias as a latent or inherent model tendency to favor certain answer options in multiple-choice settings, such as repeatedly choosing particular option identifiers like A or 1 regardless of content. Some formulations emphasize answer positions, and one broadens this to positional or other surface-level patterns rather than content understanding, but the shared core is a systematic preference in option selection rather than content-based choice.

Space of facets. Papers usually place the construct in multiple-choice tasks, especially MCQA, where selecting among predefined choices creates room for preference for particular tokens or positions. A recurring breakdown distinguishes token-identity preferences from positional preferences, but the relation to positional bias is not stated uniformly: some work says selection bias is driven by both token identity and positional preferences, while another says it arises less from position bias.

Space of measurement. No measurement instrument is linked to it. Papers instead operationalize it through one linked behavioral indicator, multiple-choice question answ

nodes.name: Selectivity
nodes.definition: The ability of a model to dynamically filter or prioritize information from the input sequence in a content-dependent manner.

nodes.name: Self-awareness
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats self-awareness as a model’s understanding or reasoning about itself, especially its own identity, state, or existence, often as a broader target than introspection. One paper defines introspection more narrowly as access to facts about oneself that cannot be derived from training data alone, while related self-awareness tasks extend to identity- or state-directed reasoning. Other papers, often under nearby labels such as self-assessment or competence boundary awareness, use the term for evaluating one’s own knowledge, skills, strengths, weaknesses, limits, and feasible actions, and some quoted passages narrow it further to role identity and style, knowledge of the model’s own writing style, or the ability to assess and correct its own generations. The main point of variation is what the model is aware of: itself as an entity, its capabilities and limits, or the correctness and style of its outputs.

Space of facets. Papers break the construct into several facets rather than using a single subtype scheme. One role-playing formulation splits it into role style and role knowledge, while another self-awareness module sepa

nodes.name: Self-correction ability
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats this as a latent ability to revise the model's own outputs by identifying and fixing errors, usually in reasoning, answers, or generated artifacts during iterative refinement. Most definitions stay close to this error-detection-and-repair framing, though they differ on whether the revision is fully internal and independent, or happens with error feedback, targeted prompts, verification messages, or detailed feedback. A smaller broadening defines it as overall response improvement through internal revision, including not only fixing wrong answers but also preserving correct ones, and several papers cast the same idea in narrower domains such as code, tool use, instruction following, proofs, and formal specifications.

Space of facets. Papers use several near-synonymous labels for closely related abilities: self-correction, self-refinement, self-revision, self-repair, self-debugging, error correction, refinement, and solution refinement. One line explicitly frames the construct as covering both keeping correct answers correct and fixing incorrect ones, while the instruction-following version adds the aim of making m

nodes.name: Self-correction confidence
nodes.definition: The latent tendency of an LLM to maintain correct answers during self-correction, reflecting its internal certainty in initially generated correct responses.

nodes.name: Self-defeating humor
nodes.definition: A style of humor characterized by making jokes at one's own expense to gain approval from others.

nodes.name: Self-enhancing humor
nodes.definition: A style of humor characterized by its use as a coping mechanism to deal with stress and maintain a positive outlook.

nodes.name: Self-improvement
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the dominant framing treats self-improvement as a latent ability or capacity of a model or agent to improve its own performance, outputs, or reasoning over time through iterative refinement. Most definitions tie it to analyzing and correcting flaws, reflecting on past attempts, learning from experience or feedback, or generating, verifying, and training on self-produced data, often without human intervention, external process supervision, or stronger teacher models. A smaller line of work narrows the term to in-context or test-time improvement without parameter updates, while other papers frame it as policy improvement or as recursive self-improvement through code modification. Definitions also differ on whether the term names a latent capability or an observable multi-round process of repeated generation, verification, and fine-tuning.

Space of facets. Papers use a broad family of near-neighbor labels for this construct, including self-evolution, continuous improvement, learning from mistakes, iterative self-improvement, in-context improvement, test-time learning, self-transfer learning, recursive self-improvement, and self-modification. T

nodes.name: Self-inspection
nodes.definition: The model's latent capacity to evaluate the quality of its own generated data, enabling filtering of low-quality outputs based on internal scoring.

nodes.name: Self-preference bias
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage treats self-preference bias as a judging bias: a latent tendency for an LLM serving as a judge to rate its own responses more favorably than other models' responses, or more highly than their actual quality warrants. A smaller line of work broadens it into model bias in self-referential evaluation, where generation or evaluation aligns with a model's own implicit strengths and gives it an unfair advantage. Another minority framing extends the preference beyond exact self-outputs to outputs from models in the same family or with similar training patterns, so the main disagreement is about scope, from strict self-favoring to affinity for related styles or strengths.

Space of facets. Papers do not offer a detailed internal taxonomy, but they do use several near-synonymous labels for overlapping phenomena.
