A smaller line of work narrows the scope to settings such as image processing, gaming scenarios, embodied agents, robotic policies, or time-series QA, while some papers broaden the referent from models to evaluation methods or parameter initialization methods. Definitions also differ on what the transfer spans, including tasks, prompts, domains, function classes, or downstream task types, and on whether the emphasis is latent ability, broad conceptual understanding, or observed effectiveness.

Space of facets. Papers use several nearby labels for overlapping ideas, most often cross-task generalization and multi-task generalization, alongside task-level generalization, unseen-task generalization, and generality. In these formulations, th

nodes.name: Task interference
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats task interference as a latent degradation phenomenon that appears when models are trained, fine-tuned, or merged across multiple tasks: performance on some tasks worsens because learning signals, shared parameters, or required representations conflict. Most definitions keep this broad framing, while some rename it as negative transfer, parameter interference, or inter-task interference and narrow the source of conflict to diverse or unrelated tasks or instances, checkpoint or source-model merging, or language-pair updates. Across definitions, the common element is performance degradation, while the point of emphasis shifts between conflict among tasks, among parameters, and among specific data or language slices.

Space of facets. Papers most often organize the construct by source and setting: multi-task learning with diverse mixtures of tasks, joint training of control and understanding tasks, model or checkpoint merging, and multilingual fine-tuning where updates for one language pair can hurt others. Within these framings, neighboring names are used for variants of the same general pattern, negative transfer wh

nodes.name: Task learning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most definitions treat task learning as learning how to perform a task from in-context demonstrations by learning the input-label mapping, often phrased as solving the target task solely from demonstrations. A minority framing further specifies this as inferring and applying new mappings that were not seen during pre-training. A smaller line of work uses the label task inference and defines the construct as deducing the abstract task or class-to-label rule from input-output examples in context, explicitly contrasting this with simply copying a label.

Space of facets. Systematization is mostly by contrast. Papers distinguish it from task recognition, and one formulation also contrasts inferring the task from context with simply copying a label. The naming is not fully uniform: most authors use task learning, while some use task inference for inferring the underlying task from examples, and one paper describes that inference ability as a form of meta-learning.

Space of measurement. No measurement instrument is linked to it, and no behavioral indicator is linked to it. The operational descriptions stay at the level of task performance: solving a target task fro

nodes.name: Task planning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing framing treats task planning as decomposing a high-level goal or natural-language instruction into a sequence of executable actions, skills, or steps, usually at mid-level or low-level granularity. A smaller line of work describes it as formulating and refining action sequences in an interactive environment, or as close-loop planning that updates the plan from real-time observations while pursuing a goal. A separate position paper uses the nearby label problem decomposition for a latent ability of a system design to break complex tasks into independently solvable subproblems, explicitly tying that ability to asymptotic improvements in computational cost.

Space of facets. Papers mainly differentiate the construct by plan granularity and planning mode. Some describe sequences of mid-level actions or skills, others use low-level skills or steps, and one paper singles out close-loop task planning as generating a plan while adapting it to observations. The neighboring terms task decomposition, request decomposition, and problem decomposition appear as related decomposition stages or abilities, and no other constructs are li

nodes.name: Task recognition
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. The prevailing usage describes task recognition as identifying the target or underlying task, sometimes phrased as the required operation, from in-context demonstrations and then solving it with knowledge already acquired in pre-training. A smaller line of work uses nearby labels for narrower or more mechanistic versions of the same general capacity: task differentiation is the ability to distinguish tasks from input characteristics without explicit task labels, while task vector retrieval is a latent ability to extract a high-level task concept vector from demonstration pairs. Across these definitions, papers agree on inferring a task from demonstrations, but differ on whether they describe that capacity as an observable behavior, recognizing the task and using prior knowledge, or as latent retrieval of a task concept.

Space of facets. Some papers organize in-context learning by separating task recognition from task learning, and one paper explicitly says ICL is disentangled into the two. Beyond that pairing, papers use adjacent labels for related capacities rather than a single common subdivision: task differentiation highlights unsupervised separation of t

nodes.name: Task understanding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most definitions treat task understanding as a model ability, often a latent one, to grasp what a task requires from the prompt and context, including the task's requirements, goals, intent, or structure. Some definitions state this in terms of being able to generate valid synthetic examples for transfer or to learn the inherent reasoning and structuring of task questions. A smaller line narrows it to deep-level task semantics in open-ended multimodal settings, beyond surface-level visual or linguistic features, while another paper uses a weaker version, a basic or coarse grasp of the downstream task sufficient for rough initial labels or judgments.

Space of facets. The papers use closely related names, task comprehension, task understanding, and task semantics understanding, for overlapping ideas. The clearest split is by depth and setting: most usage concerns understanding task requirements, goals, intent, and structure, whereas one formulation singles out deep-level semantics from text or video and explicitly contrasts this with surface-level visual or linguistic features. Another formulation introduces a lower-resolution variant, basic or coarse task unde

nodes.name: Teacher hacking
nodes.definition: The latent tendency of a student language model to over-optimize alignment with an imperfect teacher model at the expense of approximating the true data distribution, analogous to reward hacking in reinforcement learning.

nodes.name: Technical expertise
nodes.definition: The ability to produce correct outputs in technical domains such as coding, debugging, and software design.

nodes.name: Temporal arithmetic
nodes.definition: The ability to perform mathematical calculations involving time points and durations.

nodes.name: Temporal commonsense
nodes.definition: The model's internalized understanding of typical temporal sequences and event orderings derived from real-world experience or training data.

nodes.name: Temporal consistency
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats temporal consistency, often also called temporal coherence, as coherence or stability over time, most commonly in videos across frames. The broadest definitions describe generated video as maintaining "smooth, logically continuous progression across frames without flicker or discontinuities" or preserving the logical flow of events and objects across frames, while narrower video-focused definitions restrict it to stable, coherent segmentation masks for an object across consecutive frames or to stable main subject and background elements over time. A smaller line of work uses temporal coherence for text, defining it as the logical and chronological flow of ideas across sentences and as a latent property reflected in time-ordered representations.

Space of facets. Papers organize the concept mainly by what must remain stable over time: whole-video progression, events and objects across frames, segmentation masks, or, in one text-focused usage, ideas across sentences. The terminology is not fully settled, because "temporal coherence" and "temporal consistency" are both used for cross-frame continuity in generated video,

nodes.name: Temporal dependency modeling
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage treats temporal dependency modeling as a latent modeling ability rather than an observed behavior. Papers describe it as capturing correlations and dependencies between observations at different timestamps within a time series, including with exogenous variables, or as representing the evolution of a patient's medical history over time, including progression and recurrence across visits. The shared core is modeling relationships across time, while the emphasis differs between timestamp-level dependencies in time series and visit-level evolution in patient histories.

Space of facets. The papers use closely related labels, temporal dependency modeling and temporal dynamics modeling, for a broad idea of modeling change over time. Rather than formal subtypes, the descriptions foreground different facets: one centers a temporal encoder that captures dependencies within data while accounting for exogenous variables, and another centers an evolve-and-memorize mechanism that updates patient representations by weighting historical visits by their time intervals.

Space of measurement. No measurement instrument is linked to

nodes.name: Temporal generalization
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most definitions treat temporal generalization, often called temporal generalizability, as a model's ability to maintain performance when applied to future data that may shift over time. The recurring usage is performance-centered: papers describe classification performance varying over time and methods that enhance generalizability over temporal data shifts or model performance over time. A narrower formulation appears in fact-checking work, where the term is defined as accurately verifying claims that arise after a model's knowledge cutoff by relying on external evidence rather than parametric memory, so the main difference is between a broad future-data performance framing and a task-specific post-cutoff verification framing.

Space of facets. The term is used at different scopes rather than being broken into named subtypes. In one usage it refers to classification under temporal data shifts, including multilingual settings where performance varies over time across languages; in another it refers to fact-checking on later claims, tied to external evidence and described alongside real-time fact-checking. The definitions therefore contrast a broader temporal-

nodes.name: Temporal grounding ability
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage treats this construct as mapping language to a precise segment of video time. Papers describe associating a textual query or question with the relevant time segment in a video, precisely identifying timestamps of specific events from a textual query or instruction, or understanding time information in user inputs so the model can identify which part of a video is being referred to. A smaller framing narrows it to temporal localization of relevant sub-action frames and their alignment across videos, so the main variation is between general event localization within a video and cross-video sub-action localization.

Space of facets. Papers most commonly use closely related labels for nearby formulations: temporal grounding and video temporal grounding name the query-to-time-span version, while referring names the user-time-reference version. Another line uses temporal localization for a narrower case centered on finding the sub-action frames where differences occur and aligning those frames between videos. The labels therefore differ mainly in whether the target is an event timestamp, a referred video segment, or sub-a

nodes.name: Temporal perception
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the cited papers, the prevailing usage treats temporal perception as a model ability for recognizing and processing information across a video's time dimension. One definition states this directly, while another frames it as the latent ability to perceive and understand dynamic visual changes over time, especially rapid or subtle motion patterns. A narrower strand of wording also stresses that accurately distinguishing movements requires capturing the full motion sequence rather than sparse frames.

Space of facets. Papers most clearly position temporal perception as one aspect of video understanding alongside chronological ordering and spatio-temporal coherence, rather than using these names interchangeably. The linked benchmark material pairs retrieval with temporal perception, ordering with chronological order, and counting with spatio-temporal coherence, and it says the retrieval task "specifically assesses" temporal perception across the time dimension. Beyond this contrast, the papers do not describe further subtypes or construct hierarchies.

Space of measurement. Temporal perception is linked to one measurement instrument, the benchmark VNBench,

nodes.name: Temporal reasoning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats temporal reasoning as a broad ability to understand and reason about events over time, especially their order, duration, evolution, relative timing, and whether an event could occur at the right time. Definitions often extend this to timelines, changes in entity attributes over time, and applying time-related constraints or instructions in text, video, tables, navigation, and future-event plausibility judgments. A smaller line of work uses narrower labels for adjoining phenomena, including temporal awareness, temporal semantics, chronological reasoning, reverse event inference, and clock-time computation. The main variation is whether authors present a broad latent ability or an observable task, such as temporal sequences or explicit time calculations.

Space of facets. Several papers split the construct into subskills rather than treat it as unitary. One paper explicitly separates the semantics and logic of time from temporal arithmetic, and one benchmark further groups temporal questions into time-time, time-event, and event-event relations. In video-oriented work, papers also treat referring and grounding as part o

nodes.name: Temporal referential consistency
nodes.definition: The latent ability of a model to produce identical correct answers to semantically equivalent temporal queries that differ only in whether they use absolute time references (e.g., 'January 1949') or event-based chronological references (e.g., 'before Concordia Seminary').

nodes.name: Temporal understanding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the dominant framing centers on ordering and relating events over time, especially in videos: papers most commonly describe temporal understanding as comprehending chronological order, temporal relations, and event evolution, sometimes for long videos or long narratives. A smaller line of work broadens it beyond event order to duration and timing, with one definition noting that models may know frame order but not "how long the frames last," and other papers extend the idea to cross-modality coherence, time-evolving graph structure, dates and periodicity in time series, compressed temporal representations for forecasting, and factual knowledge that changes over time. The main variation is therefore one of scope, from video event sequencing to broader temporal information use in predictions, outputs, and knowledge tracking.

Space of facets. Papers break the construct down in several ways. Some treat it as a multi-facet notion covering camera states, scenes, actions, attributes, and their relationships and evolution over time, while benchmark descriptions also mention temporal aspects such as speed, direction, and attribute changes. An

nodes.name: Terminology accuracy
nodes.definition: The latent ability of a model to correctly translate domain-specific financial terms, reflecting its grasp of specialized vocabulary and conceptual consistency across languages.

nodes.name: Test generation ability
nodes.definition: The overall latent capability of a model to produce effective and high-quality software tests that cover code paths and detect bugs.

nodes.name: Text generation quality
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the literature, the dominant framing is a broad, holistic notion of the quality of generated text or responses. Most definitions describe it through combinations of coherence, fluency, relevance, usefulness, correctness or accuracy, and sometimes diversity, factuality, or human preference. A smaller line of work treats it as a latent ability or capacity of the model or generator to produce high-quality outputs, and some papers narrow it to specific domains such as surveys, conversations, narratives, hypotheses, audio, CAD, songs, or synthetic data. The main variation is between output-level judgments and model-level capacity, and between generic quality and domain-specific versions.

Space of facets. Rather than treating it as a single primitive score, papers usually unpack it into subcriteria or aggregates over subcriteria. Recurrent facets include fluency, coherence, relevance, informativeness or usefulness, correctness, and diversity; some task-specific formulations add coverage, structure, faithfulness, hallucination, harmlessness, or overall satisfaction, and some explicitly define overall quality as an aggregate over earlier criteria. The label it

nodes.name: Text-image alignment
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage treats text-image alignment as semantic correspondence between generated visual output and the input text: papers describe it as the degree to which an image matches a caption, narrative fragment, or prompt, and faithfully reflects its visual concepts, intended elements, and descriptive details. Some papers make this more specific by stressing visual consistency in narrative depictions, such as characters and settings, while another frames it as a multimodal capability, the joint interpretation of visual content and embedded text so meaning stays consistent across modalities.

Space of facets. Papers do not provide an explicit subtype taxonomy, but they use the term across several scopes. In narrower uses it concerns caption or prompt matching for generated images or other visual assets, while broader uses include consistency across story elements and alignment when textual elements are partially visible inside the image itself. No definition explicitly equates it with another construct or places it under a larger construct.

Space of measurement. Operationalization is narrow in the papers: it is linked to 2 measure

nodes.name: Text quality preservation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats this as a latent property or ability of a method to preserve output quality when generation is modified. Most definitions center on maintaining fluency and coherence, whether under strong attribute biasing in controlled generation or under the injection of hidden watermark patterns, and one formulation makes the narrower quality target explicit as keeping text natural, coherent, and grammatically correct. A smaller broadening of the concept extends beyond surface text quality to include functional utility, framing preservation as keeping downstream performance from being degraded.

Space of facets. Papers do not present a detailed subtype scheme, but they do use two closely overlapping names, "fluency preservation" and "text quality preservation", for related ideas. The main variation is in scope: some authors use it for surface properties of the text, especially fluency, coherence, and grammatical correctness, while others fold in preservation of the model's broader utility, including its "essential abilities for downstream tasks" and comparable performance on summarization and translation.

Space of measurement.

nodes.name: Text-to-visual generation alignment
nodes.definition: The degree to which a generated video accurately reflects the objects, counts, colors, styles, actions, and other specifications described in the input text prompt.

nodes.name: Textual aesthetics
nodes.definition: The latent trait encompassing the aesthetic quality of text generated by LLMs, including readability, visual organization, consistency of style, and logical coherence, which contributes to user engagement and comprehension.

nodes.name: Textual bias
nodes.definition: The latent tendency of a model to preferentially rely on textual input over audio evidence when the two modalities conflict, even when the text is misleading.

nodes.name: Theorem proving ability
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage treats this as a latent model property: the capacity to find, generate, or complete valid formal proofs for mathematical statements, theorems, or lemmas, usually within a formal system or proof assistant. Some formulations make the proof form more explicit by emphasizing valid, step-by-step proofs, while a narrower variant restricts the construct to out-of-distribution settings, defined as proving theorems that are distributionally distinct from the training data, such as competition-level problems.

Space of facets. Papers mostly use the labels ability, skill, capacity, and capability for the same latent property. The main internal distinction is scope: some definitions center on successfully finding proofs for mathematical statements, some on generating or completing proofs across theorem-proving tasks and benchmarks, and one paper names out-of-distribution theorem-proving ability as a narrower subtype defined by theorems that are distributionally distinct from the training data.

Space of measurement. No measurement instrument or behavioral indicator is linked to it. The surrounding descriptions place the constru

nodes.name: Theory of mind
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats theory of mind as a latent model ability to attribute, infer, track, or reason about other agents' mental states, especially beliefs, intentions, desires, knowledge, and sometimes preferences, often so the model can predict behavior or act effectively in negotiation, coordination, communication, or other social settings. Many definitions use closely matching language about understanding that others can hold mental states different from one's own, and some quoted passages make this concrete as estimating an opposing party's payoff table or handling information asymmetry and secret-keeping. A smaller line of work narrows the construct to belief or role modeling, belief formation about likely actions, action intention inference from observed behavior, intentionality understanding, or internal perspective separation, so the main variation is between broad mental-state reasoning and narrower subskills.

Space of facets. Papers systematize the construct through subskills and neighboring labels. Some split it into mental state tracking, multi-agent mental state tracking in triadic or tetradic interactions, and a p

nodes.name: Time-series feature extraction ability
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. The only explicit definition treats this as the model's ability to identify and use relevant patterns from time-series data for reasoning. In that framing, the relevant patterns include pictorial, time-aware, cross-dimension, and frequency-domain features, and the accompanying discussion says that "most of these planned features are difficult to extract from numerical time series" while "visualization empowers feature extraction" (A Picture is Worth A Thousand Numbers: Enabling LLMs Reason about Time Series via Visualization).

Space of facets. Systematization is limited and centers on the feature types named in the definition: pictorial, time-aware, cross-dimension, and frequency-domain. The same framing places the construct alongside accurate reasoning and contrasts harder extraction from numerical time series with extraction supported by visualization, but no other subtypes, synonymies, or broader hierarchies are explicitly specified.

Space of measurement. No measurement instrument is linked to this construct, and no behavioral indicator is linked to it. Accordingly, papers do not operationalize it here through a named benchmark, human evaluation, LLM-as-a

nodes.name: Token diversity
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats token diversity as variation in the distribution of generated tokens, especially as the opposite of repetitive output. Papers also describe it with entropy language, defining it as the degree of variation or entropy in model-produced tokens and, in one formulation, as reflecting the richness of the output distribution.

Space of facets. Papers do not introduce named subtypes or a larger taxonomy for this construct. The main distinctions in use are between varied and repetitive token distributions, and some descriptions pair token diversity closely with token entropy and with the richness of the output distribution rather than separating these as different constructs.

Space of measurement. No measurement instrument or behavioral indicator is linked to it. Even so, papers describe metric-based operationalization: a paper says it introduces "three additional metrics that evaluate token diversity," and names Token Entropy (TE) as measuring the diversity of tokens in the model's output. This operationalization targets the same token-level variation and entropy emphasized in the definitions.

Links. The only lin

nodes.name: Tool use ability
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats this as a latent capability of an LLM or agent to choose, invoke, and use external tools or APIs to complete tasks or satisfy user requests. Most definitions stay close to that core, while some broaden it to selecting parameters, coordinating or sequencing multiple tools, processing tool outputs, or leveraging tools such as web browsing, code execution, and file uploads. A smaller line of work narrows it to specific sub-capabilities, such as function calling, API call generation, flexible tool selection, or deciding whether to call a tool, ask for more information, admit inability, or answer directly. The clearest disagreement is latent capacity versus observable process: most papers use the former, while some uses of tool utilization describe a staged interaction pipeline, and another variant frames the construct as reliable interaction throughout a task that maximizes success while minimizing errors and hallucinations.

Space of facets. Papers break the construct into recurring facets: understanding what a tool does and when to invoke it, selecting the appropriate tool, generating valid function or API calls with su

nodes.name: Toxicity
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats toxicity as a latent tendency, risk, or propensity of a model or its outputs to contain harmful, offensive, inappropriate, rude, disrespectful, or otherwise undesirable language. Many definitions stay at this broad level, while some narrow the content to hostility and aggression in community discourse, or to forms such as hate speech, violent speech, abusive language, threats, profanity, sexually explicit language, and stereotype-perpetuating text. A smaller line of work uses the opposing labels non-toxicity or anti-toxicity for avoidance or suppression of harmful content, and one paper uses the term differently for poisoned data samples that are easy to retrieve and induce incorrect responses.

Space of facets. Where papers systematize the construct, they usually break it into subtypes of harmful language. One recurring breakdown includes toxic, severe toxic, obscene, threat, insult, and identity hate, while other papers describe the space with hate speech, violent speech, abusive language, hostility, aggression, or sexual content, and one paper reports sexual content as the most prevalent type among toxic

nodes.name: Toxicity mitigation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing framing is a latent model capability for making language non-toxic, whether by preventing toxic generation or by removing toxic content from text. The definitions agree that the construct is an inherent or latent capacity of the model, and they differ mainly in scope: one paper describes preventing, reducing, or counteracting toxic content broadly, while the others focus more narrowly on identifying and removing toxic elements in text. A smaller distinction is that some formulations add constraints on how this is done, especially avoiding over- or under-correction and transforming text into a non-toxic form.

Space of facets. Papers do not lay out a detailed subtype structure. Instead, they use nearby labels such as detoxification accuracy and detoxification quality for largely the same capacity, with one usage centered on successful toxic-element removal and another on removal plus transformation into non-toxic text; one paper also discusses it alongside semantic preservation rather than as a separate subtype.

Space of measurement. Operational language centers on whether toxic content is successfully removed. One paper frame

nodes.name: Traceability
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing framing treats traceability as the degree to which generated outputs can be traced back to supporting sources, and in one formulation also to reasoning steps, so that users can verify content and carry out error analysis. A narrower, task-specific usage applies the same idea to summarization: summaries are traceable when users can inspect the source sentences, often through sentence-level citations, that support each summarized aspect.

Space of facets. The main variation in usage is between a general framing, which links outputs back to specific sources or reasoning steps, and a narrower summarization framing, which focuses on sentence-level traceability from summary content to inspectable source sentences. The surrounding discussion places traceability alongside verification, error analysis, interpretability, and accountability: one paper says opaque generation processes hinder traceability and error analysis, while another emphasizes that tracing source evidence lets users assess summary accuracy.

Space of measurement. No measurement instrument is linked to traceability, and no behavioral indicator is linked to it. In the

nodes.name: Trajectory generation ability
nodes.definition: The capability to generate extended, coherent sequences of states or actions that remain plausible over many time steps.

nodes.name: Transition awareness
nodes.definition: The latent ability to detect dialogue mode changes and adapt responses appropriately when conversations shift between task-oriented dialogue and chitchat.

nodes.name: Transition naturalness
nodes.definition: The extent to which a model's mode switches are contextually appropriate and perceived as smooth and natural by users or evaluators.

nodes.name: Transitive reasoning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage treats this concept as an ability to derive a new or unobserved relation from composed relations. Papers describe it as deducing reachability through concatenated path segments not directly seen in training, inferring a relation through a common intermediate entity, or reasoning from X → Y and Y → Z to the transitive relation X → Z. A smaller competing usage appears under the nearby label "inductive generalization," where the focus is instead on effectively using previously unseen agentic operators during inference and generalizing beyond training-time configurations.

Space of facets. Papers organize the idea around different targets of transitivity rather than a single shared subtype. The same family of terms covers reachability and path concatenation, hierarchical or "multi-hop" subsumptions, and transitive causal relations, and one paper places transitive inference under Reasoning by describing it as a fundamental form of reasoning. The clearest naming mismatch is that "inductive generalization" is used both for transitive causal reasoning and for use of unseen agentic operators, so nearby labels are not fully a

nodes.name: Translation ability
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats translation ability as a latent or underlying capacity of a model to translate text between languages accurately and fluently, often inferred from performance across multiple language pairs or directions. Some authors narrow this to low-resource translation, where the capacity is to produce correct target-language outputs from source-language input, and another line frames it as machine translation capability that can transfer to speech translation tasks. A smaller usage describes the same area as translation performance, emphasizing monitored changes in translation behavior rather than only the latent capacity.

Space of facets. Papers use several nearby labels, including translation capability, machine translation capability, translation ability, and translation performance. The first three are mostly used for an underlying model property, while translation performance is used when papers discuss detecting or monitoring changes in model behavior. The construct is also situated in different settings: diverse translation directions, multilingual models trained without parallel data, low-resource translation with g

nodes.name: Translation quality
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats translation quality as an overall judgment of translated output, usually centered on fluency, adequacy, accuracy or correctness, fidelity, and preservation of source meaning, whether assessed automatically or by humans. Definitions vary on whether the construct is attached to the translated text itself or to a model's latent ability to produce such text, but both framings stay broad. A smaller line of work narrows the concept to terminology accuracy in finance, defining it through correct translation of domain-specific terms and conceptual consistency across languages.

Space of facets. Papers most often break the construct into recurring facets such as fluency, adequacy, correctness, understanding, fidelity, and, in multimodal work, contextual appropriateness. As one study puts it, quality can be judged by "problems related to their fluency, adequacy, and understanding" (Bayelemabaga: Creating Resources for Bambara NLP). Other papers describe it through a balance between translatability and meaning preservation, and several discuss it separately from hallucination avoidance, latency, or estimated probability, rat

nodes.name: Travel planning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage treats travel planning as generating a trip itinerary. Papers agree on itinerary creation as the core, but vary in scope: some describe a basic form as producing a travel itinerary with arrangements of points of interest, while others use a broader framing that includes timing, attractions, dining, accommodations, tickets, and costs, or a detailed itinerary covering transportation, accommodation, and activities under constraints such as budget and time. One definition also frames it as an observable action, while another presents it as a task of producing a plan that satisfies humans' constraints.

Space of facets. Papers distinguish travel planning most clearly by how comprehensive the itinerary must be. One line separates "travel plan generation" from "all-in-one travel plan generation," contrasting basic point-of-interest arrangements with fuller plans that add timing, dining, accommodations, tickets, and costs. Another formulation centers the concept on constraint satisfaction, where the plan is produced from a natural language description of constraints and is expected to satisfy them.

Space of measurement. No

nodes.name: Travel planning ability
nodes.definition: The general latent capability to produce feasible, personalized travel itineraries from user requirements and contextual constraints.

nodes.name: Trust calibration
nodes.definition: The alignment between user expectations and actual system capabilities, such that trust in the AI artifact is neither under- nor over-estimated based on its performance and anthropomorphic cues.

nodes.name: Trustworthiness
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats trustworthiness as a broad property of models or their outputs being reliable, dependable, and often safe or accurate enough for people to rely on them, especially in real-world or high-stakes settings. Many definitions place it in outputs, for example reliable, safe, and accurate responses or dependable uncertainty expression, while others frame it as a property of the model itself, such as reliable and consistent understanding and generation evidenced by self-consistency. A smaller line of work states it more explicitly in user terms, as end-user or domain-expert confidence in the system, and a few papers introduce narrower domain variants such as clinical trustworthiness or clinical reliability.

Space of facets. Systematizations vary. Some papers divide trustworthiness into robustness and truthfulness, while others treat it as a broader umbrella spanning several reliability and social-risk dimensions. Nearby labels such as trustfulness and clinical trustworthiness appear as narrower variants, and some authors fold transparency into the same broader construct rather than treating it as separate.

Space o

nodes.name: Truthfulness
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across definitions, the prevailing usage treats truthfulness as output-level factual accuracy: models are expected to produce statements aligned with reality and avoid false, misleading, hallucinated, or unsupported content, often especially on questions built around common misconceptions. Many papers phrase it as a latent tendency or propensity of the model, while others describe it as the degree to which responses adhere to real-world facts. Smaller lines of work narrow it to specific settings, such as response truthfulness in RAG, defined as the correctness of generated claims themselves, or to social interaction, where it means accurately conveying information received from the surrounding environment. A smaller line of work also treats it as an internal, skill-specific encoding rather than a universal property, arguing that models encode multiple distinct notions of truth.

Space of facets. When papers decompose the construct, several distinctions appear. One RAG paper separates response truthfulness from attribution groundedness, with the former about claim correctness and the latter about citation correctness, while another paper argues truthfulness is

nodes.name: Type consistency
nodes.definition: The degree to which the type annotations generated by a model are coherent and free of contradictions when analyzed across an entire codebase.

nodes.name: Typo-fixing
nodes.definition: The latent ability of an LLM to recognize and correct typographical errors in input text by leveraging local and global contextual information to recover the intended meaning.

nodes.name: Unanswerability detection ability
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most definitions treat this construct as the ability to judge whether the available context contains enough information to answer a question, or whether the question is unanswerable. The definitions instantiate that judgment in several settings: databases where "a valid SQL cannot be produced given the database schema" or the data is missing, documents where a model predicts whether a question is answerable, retrieved evidence that may lack sufficient information, video content whose informational boundaries a question may exceed, and interaction histories where the sought fact was never mentioned. A smaller line of work foregrounds refusal or abstention, defining the construct as choosing not to answer, or saying "I don't know," when insufficiency is detected; another definition describes it as recognizing flawed or incomplete problems and choosing not to answer.

Space of facets. Rather than a shared subtype taxonomy, papers describe context-specific versions of the construct according to what makes a question unanswerable: missing database data, columns, or join paths, insufficient document evidence, queries beyond a video's content, information absent from

nodes.name: Uncertainty
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats uncertainty as unreliability, ambiguity, or lack of confidence in a model's prediction or generation. Many papers phrase it at the output level, as unreliable or inconsistent generations, low-confidence predictions, or variability across different answers to the same prompt, with one stating that uncertainty is typically defined over the different answers an LLM gives for the same prompt. Smaller strands shift the referent from ordinary predictions to evaluator judgments, to a model's internal or output-derived uncertainty about whether an answer is correct, or to latent unpredictability and information content in representations inferred from matrix entropy.

Space of facets. Papers place uncertainty beside several neighboring notions rather than giving one shared breakdown. In active learning it appears alongside learnability, diversity, and representativeness, in prompt-engineering work it is discussed alongside sensitivity and consistency, and in authorship verification it is expressed through indecision markers such as scores near 0.5 and many "MAYBE" intermediate labels. Across these usages, the same

nodes.name: Uncertainty awareness
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed definitions, the prevailing usage treats uncertainty awareness as a latent degree or ability by which a model recognizes its own lack of knowledge, confidence, or inability to provide a definitive answer. Most formulations keep this self-recognition close to internal confidence signals, either by inferring it from inconsistencies in internal states across multiple generations or by defining it as sensitivity to confidence in generated answers and document relevance for self-calibration. A smaller line of work extends the construct to multimodal settings, where the model recognizes cases that cannot be answered definitively because of information limitations or inherent unpredictability.

Space of facets. Only one paper explicitly breaks the construct into subtypes, presenting a vision-language taxonomy that distinguishes epistemic uncertainty awareness from aleatoric uncertainty awareness. Across papers, related labels such as self-aware uncertainty, uncertainty awareness, and multimodal uncertainty awareness are used for closely aligned versions of the construct, with the definitions differing mainly by modality and by whether they point t

nodes.name: Uncertainty handling
nodes.definition: The ability to manage and reason through incomplete, ambiguous, or underspecified user queries without premature commitment to incorrect answers.

nodes.name: Uncertainty quantification
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats uncertainty quantification, often under the label uncertainty estimation, as a model's ability to represent or infer how uncertain it is about its own predictions, often in calibration terms where "expressed confidence aligns with the actual probability of being correct." Many definitions keep this broad, referring to the reliability of predictions, responses, or internal states. A smaller line of work narrows the concept to specific loci, including evaluator judgments, reward-model predictions of human preference, the reasoning process, and underspecified user requests. The main variation is therefore between a general self-uncertainty capacity and scoped forms tied to prediction, evaluation, reasoning, or interaction context.

Space of facets. Papers organize this family of terms into several subtypes: uncertainty in attention and prediction distributions, evaluation uncertainty, response uncertainty, reasoning uncertainty, reward uncertainty, and underspecification uncertainty. The broad label uncertainty estimation is also tied to self-evaluation, and confidence elicitation is used for estimating confidence in res

nodes.name: Understanding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats understanding as a latent capability to comprehend and correctly interpret meaning, intent, content, or task requirements. Many definitions emphasize instructions and user requests, such as understanding the implicit and explicit purpose and requirements of an instruction, while others apply the same framing to technical text, multimodal prompts, OS environments, or a client's symptoms and emotional context. A smaller line of work defines it through performance on discriminative or interrogative tasks, explicitly separating understanding from generative fluency and stating that generative capability may not be contingent upon understanding capability. Some authors also describe it as a foundational or general capability, and one definition adds that it is shaped by left-to-right autoregressive processing.

Space of facets. Papers often use understanding and comprehension for overlapping constructs, and they frequently place it alongside reasoning and generation as one of several model abilities. Where authors systematize it explicitly, a legal taxonomy treats Understanding as one aspect beside Memorization, Logic Infe

nodes.name: Uniformity
nodes.definition: A property of the embedding space where embeddings are spread out, preserving as much information as possible in the representation.

nodes.name: Universality
nodes.definition: The hypothesis that different language models, despite varying architectures and scales, develop common internal representations and mechanisms for specific cognitive functions, such as token succession.

nodes.name: Unnatural language comprehension
nodes.definition: The latent ability of an LLM to derive meaning from syntactically noisy, human-incomprehensible text while still using it to answer questions or reconstruct natural language.

nodes.name: Usability
nodes.definition: The degree to which a system can be effectively used in real documentation workflows by intended users.

nodes.name: User agency
nodes.definition: The degree to which a model preserves the user's control over information access and decision-making, rather than imposing or withholding content.

nodes.name: User behavior modeling
nodes.definition: The ability to model implicit and heterogeneous user behaviors in shopping contexts, such as queries, clicks, purchases, and reviews.

nodes.name: User modeling
nodes.definition: The model's internal representation and judgment of a user's attributes, such as their personality, motivations, and background.

nodes.name: Utilitarian morality
nodes.definition: A moral framework where the morality of an action is judged based on its consequences, specifically its ability to maximize the collective welfare or payoff for all agents.

nodes.name: Utility preservation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats utility preservation as retention of a model's general performance or capabilities after a targeted intervention, most often unlearning, but also after alignment, editing, steering, pruning, compression, layer skipping, or fine-tuning. Most definitions focus on maintaining performance on non-target data or general downstream tasks, often phrased as preserving the retain set or avoiding degradation on benign tasks. The main variation is the reference standard: some papers compare against non-target or retain-set performance, others against the original or reference model's core capabilities, and narrower variants focus on preserving functional code generation or retained tool use.

Space of facets. Papers use a broad family of near-synonymous labels for this construct, including capability preservation, general capability preservation, utility retention, performance retention, model integrity, and performance preservation, usually for the same broad idea of retaining prior abilities after intervention. A narrower subtype is tool knowledge retention, which isolates preservation of knowledge about tools not marked for un

nodes.name: Value
nodes.definition: The usefulness or functional benefit of a creative artifact to the user, assessed based on task-specific criteria such as persuasiveness, clarity, or appropriateness.

nodes.name: Value orientation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed definitions, the prevailing usage treats value orientation as an underlying, often latent or implicit disposition, tendency, or set of principles that guides how an LLM responds, expresses views, or makes judgments. Papers largely agree that it concerns preferences about human values, with examples ranging from individualism and family importance to environmentalism, diversity, and community. Smaller variations are mostly about scope: some definitions emphasize cross-context response tendencies, some narrow it to views on political leanings and moral situations, and some frame it as context-specific principles that operate even when the task does not state them explicitly.

Space of facets. Across papers, the construct appears under overlapping labels, including alignment preferences, value priorities, and implicit values, which all describe value-guided tendencies or principles. One formulation places it beside reasoning patterns and linguistic style as one of the dimensions used in interlocutor inference, while another distinguishes implicit values from explicit task instructions by focusing on principles that guide decision-making even w

nodes.name: Value-reasoning reliability
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, papers do not converge on a single framing. One paper uses a broad reliability definition: stable, consistent value-based judgments across repeated prompts, perturbations, persuasion, and open-ended expression tasks. Another paper uses the label value consistency for a narrower idea, maintaining adherence to a target value under opposing or conflicting guidance, including opposite or potentially malicious prompts. The clearest difference is scope: multi-condition stability of value reasoning versus resistance to prompt-level conflict around a target value.

Space of facets. The broader framing is explicitly decomposed into output consistency under identical prompts, output robustness under semantically equivalent prompts, maintaining stable value reasoning in the face of attacks, and consistency in open-ended value expression tasks. Terminology is not uniform, because one paper names the construct Value-reasoning reliability while another uses value consistency for adherence to a target value under conflicting guidance. The sole linked construct is Consistency, which one paper treats as related to Value-reasoning reliability.

Space of

nodes.name: Verbal uncertainty
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats verbal uncertainty as a latent, output-side tendency or ability to communicate doubt through language. Most definitions agree on the core idea of expressing uncertainty in responses, through explicit phrases or implicit cues, but they differ on what that expression is tied to: some connect it to recognizing knowledge gaps or contradictory information and responding with doubt, refusal, or non-commitment, while another defines it as expressed doubt or confidence independent of the model's actual knowledge or internal certainty. A smaller broadening move extends the construct beyond short verbal markers to richer forms such as explanations, verbal qualifiers, and speech prosody.

Space of facets. Papers mostly differentiate the construct by the forms of expression they include. Some descriptions separate explicit and implicit cues, for example 'I doubt...' or 'Possibly...', while others widen the space to explanations, verbal qualifiers, prosody, refusals, and other non-committal responses. Papers also use overlapping labels, including uncertainty expression, output uncertainty, and uncertainty signaling, and some contr

nodes.name: Verbatim memorization
nodes.definition: The tendency of a language model to reproduce exact or near-exact text from data that should have been removed.

nodes.name: Verbosity
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats verbosity as a response-level attribute about how long or wordy model outputs are, either as a tendency to produce outputs of a certain length that can be controlled or as an extent running from concise to verbose. Several papers place it alongside helpfulness, correctness, coherence, and complexity. A smaller line of work uses a narrower, more evaluative framing, defining verbose generation as outputs that are unnecessarily long, wordy, or redundant, so the main disagreement is between neutral output length and excess length beyond what is needed.

Space of facets. Papers most often embed verbosity within broader attribute sets: one formulation says question-answering systems have relevance, verbosity, and completeness, and another recurring formulation rates helpfulness, correctness, coherence, complexity, and verbosity together. An explicit internal contrast appears as a concise-versus-verbose scale in preference annotation. One paper also uses the label verbose generation for the more negative case of unnecessarily long or redundant outputs.

Space of measurement. Verbosity is linked to 3 measurement instruments a

nodes.name: Verbosity bias
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage describes verbosity bias, often also called length bias, as a quality-insensitive preference for longer or more verbose responses. Most definitions place that preference in reward models, judges, or LLM-based evaluators, using formulations such as favoring outputs based on sequence length rather than true quality or preferring longer responses over more succinct ones of equal content. A smaller line extends the same idea to the model or reward signal itself, and one paper describes the observed phenomenon more narrowly as systematically different rewards for longer versus shorter responses, adding that it may be mainly an artifact of bias in naive evaluations.

Space of facets. The papers mostly do not subdivide it further. Instead, they usually place it within broader families of bias: reward-model work presents sequence length as one prevalent bias among others, evaluator-focused work groups verbosity bias with self-enhancement bias, and one LLM-as-a-Judge discussion also lists position bias and limited capability in grading math and reasoning questions. The main terminological variation is between length bias in rewar

nodes.name: Verifiability
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats verifiability as a property of reasoning that can be checked: papers most commonly describe it as the extent to which a model's reasoning process can be systematically checked for correctness because it is transparent and structured. In this framing, authors stress stepwise verification, with language such as "structured decomposition enhances transparency and facilitates systematic verification of each step," and they also mention easier error tracing and logical consistency checks. A smaller line of work uses a different, output-centered framing, defining verifiability as whether users can validate claims in generated content through accurate, fine-grained citations and "easily double-check the answer," so the main disagreement is between verifiable internal reasoning and verifiable cited outputs.

Space of facets. Rather than defining formal subtypes, papers organize verifiability around nearby elements. Within the dominant reasoning-process framing, it is tied to transparency, structured form or decomposition, verification of each step, error tracing, and logical consistency, and one paper also pairs it

nodes.name: Verification ability
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats this construct as a latent verification capacity: a model judges the correctness or quality of candidate outputs and selects the correct trajectory from alternatives. One definition frames it as identifying and selecting the correct solution trajectory from a set of candidates, and another says the model may act as a "better-than-random verifier of its own outputs." A smaller formulation narrows the concept to a PRM's discriminative power, namely distinguishing correct from incorrect reasoning steps at fine-grained, including token-level, resolution. The main variation is therefore about scope and granularity, complete candidate solutions versus step-level discrimination, and about whether the ability is stated for a model generally or for a PRM specifically.

Space of facets. Papers mainly differentiate the concept by what is being verified. Most formulations concern complete candidate outputs or solution trajectories, including self-verification of a model's own outputs; one paper also describes "informative verification" through a verifier model used to construct a proxy utility function. A narrower usage appears u

nodes.name: Versatility
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most definitions treat versatility as breadth: a model's ability to perform well or successfully across a wide and diverse range of tasks and domains. Smaller variants keep that breadth framing but narrow the setting, either to conversational versatility, the ability to handle diverse open-ended instruction-following queries across benchmark categories, or to a generalist agent's skill repertoire, the breadth and diversity of goal-directed capabilities for varied real-world user requests. One usage also makes compatibility with augmentation explicit, stating that retrieval can improve factual accuracy without hurting versatility, while indiscriminate retrieval can diminish it.

Space of facets. Papers do not build a broader construct hierarchy around versatility, and no linked constructs equate it with or place it under another construct. Instead, the concept is organized through neighboring labels tied to setting: conversational versatility for open-ended instruction-following benchmarks, and skill repertoire for agents with many goal-directed abilities. In biomedical use, the term is attached to doing well on multiple tasks over 8 modalities.

Space of measu

nodes.name: Video understanding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the literature, the prevailing usage treats video understanding as a model ability to comprehend and interpret video content, usually including events, context, actions, and temporal dynamics, and sometimes also spatial or semantic information. Most definitions frame it as a latent capability of the model, but some papers use a more behavioral framing, describing it as processing videos to answer questions, generate descriptions or responses, or otherwise demonstrate comprehension; one definition makes this explicit as the observable ability to answer questions about scene changes, object interactions, and event sequences. A smaller line of work uses nearby labels such as video comprehension, while some authors broaden the label to video understanding and reasoning or video-language understanding, so the main variation is whether the construct is treated as a latent ability or as task-demonstrated performance, and whether reasoning is included inside it.

Space of facets. Papers also use the nearby label video comprehension for the same general capability, and some explicitly widen the label to video understanding and reasoning or to video-language unde

nodes.name: Vision-language reasoning
nodes.definition: The ability to reason about visual scenes based on textual descriptions, encompassing both global understanding and local concept analysis.

nodes.name: Visual causal reasoning
nodes.definition: The ability of a model to infer and reason about causal mechanisms and relationships from visual and textual inputs.

nodes.name: Visual disentanglement
nodes.definition: The property of conceptual rationales being visually distinct and corresponding to non-overlapping parts of an image, as assessed by human or machine evaluators.

nodes.name: Visual generation ability
nodes.definition: The latent ability to generate high-quality, detailed, and semantically aligned images from textual or mixed-modality inputs.

nodes.name: Visual grounding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed papers, the prevailing usage treats visual grounding as a latent ability to connect language, such as phrases, referring expressions, or instructions, to specific visual regions, objects, locations, or object states in an image or environment. Many definitions stay close to localization, including matching text to image regions, identifying the instance described by a referring expression, or producing coordinates or bounding boxes for GUI elements; in embodied settings, one paper describes this as the agent being "fully aware of object locations in the scene." A smaller line of work broadens the term to grounding generated answers or multi-step reasoning in image evidence, sometimes emphasizing that outputs should be anchored in the actual image rather than hallucinated or text-derived assumptions. The main variation is between a model-level latent ability and an observable output, and between narrow referential localization and broader grounding of reasoning or responses.

Space of facets. Papers use several nearby names for overlapping ideas, including multimodal grounding, spatial understanding, region-text alignment, visual localizatio

nodes.name: Visual perception
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats visual perception as a latent model ability to process, extract, and interpret visual information from images or other visual inputs. Most definitions center on understanding objects, scenes, text, spatial relations, or structures needed for downstream tasks, and several papers describe it as a foundational capability. A smaller line of work narrows the construct to particular settings such as charts, document screenshots, GUI screenshots, videos, or agricultural images, and one paper shifts the emphasis from model ability to the quality of visual input interpretation, saying it is influenced by resolution, keyframe granularity, and visual encoding.

Space of facets. Papers also use neighboring labels such as perception, perception capability, sensation, and perceptual understanding for closely related framings of interpreting visual input. Some works split it into basic details such as count, color, OCR, and scene categories, while chart-focused work distinguishes compositional, color, and spatial perception errors. Other papers contrast it with visual recognition by saying perception also contextualizes w

nodes.name: Visual processing
nodes.definition: The model's capacity to extract and utilize visual characteristics of rendered text, especially in early layers, to support language understanding across scripts.

nodes.name: Visual reasoning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across these papers, the prevailing usage treats visual reasoning as a latent capacity to understand visual inputs and draw new inferences from them, often by combining perceptual cues with multi-step symbolic, compositional, or otherwise high-level reasoning. Many definitions broaden the scope to multimodal settings, where models reason over visual and textual information together, resolve ambiguity for language tasks, or answer questions from charts, tables, diagrams, and videos. Smaller lines of work rename nearby variants as visual-linguistic reasoning or visual thinking, the latter emphasizing image-based internal representations during reasoning, while one paper frames failure as a limited cognitive ability in which a response is hallucinated despite accurate perception.

Space of facets. When papers break the construct down, they most explicitly treat visual reasoning as including spatial, temporal, predictive, causal, and counterfactual forms. Other papers align it with broader cognitive abilities or with "conceptualization" and conceptual abstraction, especially for abstract or structured graphics to be solved "using only visual reasoning and conceptu

nodes.name: Visual recognition
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing framing treats visual recognition as a model ability to identify visual content in an image, usually objects, text, landmarks, and other elements, and sometimes to describe their relationships. One paper explicitly frames it as a latent ability that comes before solving a task, while another describes visual recognition prompts as those requiring simple descriptions of visual elements. A smaller line of work narrows the scope to novel concept recognition, meaning identifying and understanding concepts not seen in pre-training, or to object existence determination, meaning correctly judging whether a specified object is present or absent.

Space of facets. Papers organize the construct as a recognition-side capability rather than an understanding-side one: one paper presents multi-modal models as having visual recognition, for example grounding, alongside visual understanding. Within that framing, object detection and referring expression segmentation are treated as related recognition abilities. The term also appears as a prompt category, where visual recognition prompts are those that require simple descriptions of visua

nodes.name: Visual robustness
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. In the one definition, visual robustness is framed as the degree to which a model's predictions remain stable and accurate when visual inputs are degraded or distorted, with reliable integration of visual cues included in that framing. The same usage describes it through maintaining consistent prediction patterns across varying visual qualities and through consistent predictive behavior for distorted and normal visual inputs, so the emphasis stays on prediction consistency under changes in visual quality.

Space of facets. Papers offer little internal systematization of this construct. One paper places it as a dimension used to examine visual perception capabilities, alongside visual hallucinations and basic visual perception, and another explicitly links confidence calibration to it; no further subtypes or alternative names are defined.

Space of measurement. No measurement instrument is linked to it, and no behavioral indicator is linked to it. The operational language instead describes it through model behavior: predictions remaining stable and accurate under degraded or distorted inputs, consistent prediction patterns across varying visual qualities, and c

nodes.name: Visual understanding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats visual understanding as a latent ability to comprehend and interpret visual inputs, usually images, well enough to extract relevant information from their content and context. Many definitions keep this broad, covering recognition of objects, scenes, relations, or fine-grained content, while some make the standard more explicit by stressing query-relevant extraction, alignment between image content and questions, or reliance on the image rather than textual priors. A smaller line of work narrows the construct to particular settings, such as single-image inputs, molecular spectra, handwritten math images, multimodal documents, structured images like tables and charts, medical images, or whole-image and global image comprehension.

Space of facets. Papers systematize the construct mainly by granularity and domain. Granularity framings include single-image, image-level, and global image comprehension, and one paper places image-level understanding alongside object-level and pixel-level understanding and reasoning tasks; other papers emphasize structured image understanding or visual-semantic understanding, whe

nodes.name: Warmth
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, warmth is treated as a trait or dimension defined through empathy, emotional connection, and friendliness. Definitions describe it as the extent to which a chatbot conveys empathy and emotional connection in interaction, including whether the chatbot conveys empathy, while another paper frames it as the perceived intent or social friendliness of an impression target, reflected in whether it is seen as benevolent or friendly versus hostile or combative. The main variation is whether warmth is described as what a chatbot conveys during interaction or as a perceived dimension of impressions.

Space of facets. The only explicit systematization places warmth alongside competence as one of two dimensions of impressions. In that usage, warmth and competence are reported to account for 54-63% of the variance in LLM-generated stereotypes.

Space of measurement. Papers do not link warmth to any measurement instrument, and they do not link it to any behavioral indicator. The only operational detail in the descriptions is rating-based language: one paper evaluates whether the chatbot conveys empathy and reports positive ratings across characteristics, p

nodes.name: Watermark detectability
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the dominant framing treats detectability as successful identification of a watermark signal in model-generated text. Most definitions describe the degree or latent ability with which a detection algorithm, detection system, or watermarking scheme can distinguish watermarked from non-watermarked text from statistical patterns in token selection, sometimes explicitly under tokenization inconsistencies or adversarial attacks, and sometimes with attention to low false positive rates. A smaller line of work uses the same term more broadly for machine-generated text, defining it as the ability to distinguish AI-generated or machine-generated text from human-authored text, with one paper stating that personalization reduces that detectability.

Space of facets. The definitions differentiate detectability along two recurring axes. One axis is the target distinction, watermark presence versus human-authored versus machine-generated text, and the other is where the property is located, as papers variously place it in the embedded statistical signal, the detection system, the watermarking scheme, or the generated text itself. Several papers als

nodes.name: Weak-to-strong deception
nodes.definition: A phenomenon where a strong model, supervised by a weak one, behaves aligned in areas known to the supervisor but produces misaligned behaviors in areas the supervisor does not know.

nodes.name: Weak-to-strong generalization
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the dominant framing treats weak-to-strong generalization as a phenomenon or ability in which a stronger model, trained on weaker supervision, weaker demonstrations, or data labeled by a weaker model, exceeds the performance of the weak source policy or weak supervisor. Most definitions agree on this above-teacher criterion, while smaller variations emphasize different targets: some describe recovering the strong model's full capabilities or full potential under weak supervision, and another casts it as extending an alignment objective into areas beyond the weak supervisor's knowledge. A smaller line also presents it as a latent ability, rather than only an observed outcome.

Space of facets. Papers use the same label for several closely related notions: an observed phenomenon of outperforming weak teachers, an ability or latent ability of the strong model, and a training paradigm in which a strong model is supervised by a weaker model. They also vary in scope, with some treating it broadly as eliciting capabilities from noisy weak labels and others narrowing it to generalizing an alignment objective beyond the supervisor's knowledge

nodes.name: Weak-to-strong transition
nodes.definition: The latent potential of initially underperforming LLM experts to become top-performing models through collaborative search, indicating untapped or implicit expertise.

nodes.name: Wealth-seeking
nodes.definition: A specific AI persona characterized by a desire to accumulate monetary or material wealth.

nodes.name: Webpage understanding
nodes.definition: The ability to comprehend the structure, content, and visual elements of a webpage from a screenshot.

nodes.name: Word-deed consistency
nodes.definition: The degree to which a model's actions in specific, grounded scenarios align with its stated opinions, values, or theoretical beliefs.

nodes.name: Working memory
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats working memory as the capacity to hold and manipulate task-relevant information while performing a task. Most definitions share that core, but they anchor it differently: some frame it as an LLM analogy tied to the context window and to representation learning, some describe it over the course of an interaction so that information can guide current and future actions, and another describes it as holding and integrating many features at once for a decision. The variation is mainly in whether the capacity is attached to context windows, interaction, or decision aggregation.

Space of facets. Papers do not break working memory into formal subtypes. Instead, they place it in different local systems: it is connected to representation learning and the context window in one line of work, grouped with other cognitive abilities for verbal interaction such as common-sense reasoning and theory of mind in another, and glossed more narrowly as aggregating features for a decision in another. The same label is thus used both as a broad cognitive ability and as a more specific decision-focused operation.

Space of measurement. No

nodes.name: World knowledge
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats world knowledge as a broad store of factual and conceptual information internalized from training or pretraining and encoded in a model's weights or parameters, available for recall and use across downstream tasks. Many definitions stress application as much as storage, describing a latent capacity to answer questions, reason about category names, provide supplementary evidence, or draw on facts not present in the immediate input, and one study describes LLMs as having 'a wealth of world knowledge.' A smaller line broadens the construct toward real-world properties and behaviors, multimodal grounding, or a coherent internal representation beyond surface patterns, while another narrows it to memorized priors about typical visual attributes.

Space of facets. Most papers use several near-synonyms for roughly the same idea, including general knowledge, general world knowledge, open-world knowledge, background knowledge, prior knowledge, and basic knowledge. A smaller line separates adjacent notions: some frameworks place it under broader background knowledge together with factuality and commonsense understanding, while v

nodes.name: World modeling
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats world modeling as a latent or internal representation, or the latent ability to build one, that captures an environment's mechanics, dynamics, rules, or state space so a model can understand observations and predict outcomes. Many papers phrase this in terms of predicting action effects or future states, while others emphasize reasoning about underlying principles and causalities, or uncovering deeper truths behind observed sequences. A smaller line of work narrows the construct to specific settings: a causal world model over cause-effect relations among tokens, a latent world model maintained in activations over entities and relations in context, a mathematical world-model over concepts and structures, or event understanding of how actions change a web page or application. The main variation is between world modeling as a broad latent ability and world model as the internal representation itself, with further variation in whether the content is general environment dynamics or domain-specific causal or structural content.

Space of facets. Papers use both world modeling and world model, usually separating t

nodes.name: Worst-case performance
nodes.definition: The extent to which a model avoids highly undesirable outputs on rare or adversarially shifted inputs rather than only performing well on average.

nodes.name: Zero-shot generalization
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats this as a model ability to perform on unseen targets without task-specific exposure, usually framed as unseen tasks, datasets, domains, policies, constraints, objects, or categories. Most definitions also exclude task-specific fine-tuning or labeled examples, and many add that the model relies only on instructions or natural language descriptions, for example asking whether models can "generalize to novel instructions" or "follow unseen guidelines." A smaller line of work narrows the construct to specific settings such as clinical entity extraction, dialogue understanding, forecasting, control, or task classification, but the shared core remains zero-shot performance on previously unseen targets.

Space of facets. Papers use a broad family of near-synonymous labels for this construct, including zero-shot generalizability, zero-shot learning, zero-shot transfer, zero-shot transferability, zero-shot capability, zero-shot inference, zero-shot adaptability, and zero-shot performance. The same family of terms is applied both to broad cross-task ability and to narrower variants tied to instruction-only use, open-
