nodes.name: 20 Newsgroups
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats 20 Newsgroups, also written 20NG or 20NewsGroups, as a dataset of newsgroup posts for document understanding and text classification. Definitions describe it as containing approximately 20,000 documents partitioned across 20 different newsgroups, and as a benchmark used to evaluate model performance and robustness in federated learning settings. A smaller usage repurposes it to define an in-domain task from its computer science categories and an out-of-domain set from the remaining categories.

What it is claimed to measure. In the recorded relationships, papers use it to measure one construct, Natural language understanding, and one behavioral indicator, Text classification. One paper includes 20NG among "4 NLU benchmarks," while another uses 20 Newsgroups as the proxy dataset for a topic classification task under the Text classification label. The linked measurement claims therefore span these two framings rather than a broader set of constructs or indicators.

Space of uses. Papers typically use it alongside other evaluation datasets rather than on its own. In federated fine-tuning work it appears with BANKING77 f

nodes.name: 2WikiMultiHopQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing description is a Wikipedia-based multi-hop question answering dataset or benchmark. Most definitions emphasize multi-document reasoning, with answers requiring models to combine information from multiple documents, evidence pieces, paragraphs, or sources; some add that it includes up to 5-hop questions synthesized from Wikipedia passages through manually designed templates. A smaller line of work narrows this to reasoning over two linked facts or entity-centric questions that combine information from two or more distinct Wikipedia articles, and one paper presents it as a more challenging benchmark with many comparison and composition questions. Some papers also refer to a LongBench form of the benchmark under the name 2WikiMQA.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, it is linked to 5 constructs and 4 behavioral indicators. The prevailing use is to measure multi-hop question answering and multi-hop reasoning. Papers also use it to measure question answering and chain-of-thought reasoning, while the remaining links spread across several other QA and reasoning framings.

Space of uses. It is most commonly used alongside HotpotQA and Mu

nodes.name: 3MDBench
nodes.definition: Medical Multimodal Multi-agent Dialogue Benchmark, a framework simulating telemedicine consultations to evaluate LVLMs on diagnostic accuracy and communication quality using patient and assessor agents.

nodes.name: 42D
nodes.definition: Multi-domain challenge benchmark for word sense disambiguation that spans 42 domains aligned with BabelNet, designed to test generalization across diverse topics.

nodes.name: A-OKVQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, A-OKVQA is most commonly described as a visual question answering dataset or benchmark of image-question pairs whose answers require knowledge beyond direct visual evidence, usually framed as external real-world, commonsense, or world knowledge about objects or actions in the image. Some definitions add that it supports open-ended and multiple-choice settings, and one paper describes MSCOCO images with one correct answer and three distractors written by English speakers on Mechanical Turk. A smaller line of work presents it more broadly as a general-purpose VQA benchmark for larger visual concepts.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link A-OKVQA to 6 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators. The most recurrent measurement claim is that it measures commonsense knowledge, and papers also report it as measuring cultural bias, fairness, generalization, multilingual ability, and robustness; among behavioral indicators, it is used to measure visual question answering and object hallucination. Overall, the measurement claims are spread across several targets rather than concentrated on one alone, although knowledge and world-knowledge reasoning is the prevaili

nodes.name: Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus
nodes.definition: The Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC) is a benchmark designed to test abstract reasoning capabilities by requiring the solution of novel visual puzzles.

nodes.name: AbsVis
nodes.definition: Dataset of 675 images with 14,175 concept–explanation pairs from humans and VLMs, used to benchmark abstract concept attribution and explanation in visual contexts.

nodes.name: AccessEval
nodes.definition: A benchmark dataset and evaluation framework for assessing disability bias in LLMs, consisting of paired neutral and disability-aware queries across six domains and nine disability types.

nodes.name: ACE05
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, ACE05 is most commonly described as a news-domain information extraction benchmark. Definitions present it either broadly, as covering named entity recognition, relation extraction, and event extraction over news text, or more narrowly as a sentence-level event extraction dataset with news articles annotated for 33 event types, with one quoted passage adding that the documents come from 6 news sources. Some authors shorten the name to ACE for a news event detection dataset with 33 event types, while one paper uses the surface form ACE differently, for a 21-question multiple-choice computational-thinking assessment aimed at the Bloom levels Analyzing, Evaluating, and Creating.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to measure 1 behavioral indicator, Event detection, and it is linked to no constructs. The recorded claim is concentrated rather than spread across many outcomes: one paper benchmarks an event detection system on ACE alongside other domain datasets.

Space of uses. Papers use ACE05 alongside other benchmarks rather than in isolation. It appears with CASIE and PHEE in evaluations from the TextEE framework, and with ACE04 in a broader s

nodes.name: ACRE
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most commonly, papers describe ACRE as the Abstract Causal REasoning dataset, a diagnostic benchmark for causal induction. Definitions recurrently present it as identifying which Blicket objects trigger a machine or detector, and one paper says it evaluates how well vision systems perform causal induction. A smaller line of work frames it as a rule-induction benchmark in which the model infers a hidden mapping from input-output examples and generates new examples consistent with the shared rule.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link ACRE to 3 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator. They use it to measure inductive reasoning, causal reasoning, and visual reasoning, and they also report it as measuring causal inference, described in one paper as testing an LLM's ability to identify causal relationships. Across these claims, its measurement role is spread across several reasoning targets rather than converging on one alone.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it. In use, papers place it alongside CATER, Something-Else, and STAR for diverse visual reasoning tasks, and alongside List Functions as an inductive reasoning benchmark. They also position it

nodes.name: ActivityNet
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers here, ActivityNet is most commonly treated as a large-scale video dataset or benchmark for activity or human activity understanding. Some descriptions emphasize diverse web videos, while others use it as a source of time-aligned captions and denser event pairs for temporal reasoning question creation. It also appears as the basis for an activity generation task in InterleavedBench and as a benchmark for evaluating video-based multimodal models.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use ActivityNet to measure two behavioral indicators, Action recognition and Natural language planning, and it is not linked to any construct. The reported measurement claims are limited to those two indicators: one paper evaluates action recognition on ActivityNet, and another uses activity generation from ActivityNet for natural language planning.

Space of uses. Papers position it both as a standalone benchmark and as a source dataset inside other evaluations. It is used alongside Something-Something V2, UCF-101, YouCook2, DAVIS, and QVHighlights, and appears in action recognition evaluation, conditional video generation, video understanding, and QA data creation from ca

nodes.name: ActivityNet Captions
nodes.definition: An English dense video captioning dataset referenced as a prior benchmark for video-language evaluation.

nodes.name: ActivityNet-QA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, ActivityNet-QA is most commonly described as an open-ended video question-answering benchmark or dataset built on ActivityNet videos. Definitions repeatedly frame it as covering complex web videos, longer activity videos, and complex human activities or events, with some papers emphasizing zero-shot video understanding evaluation and others describing it in terms of human activity understanding. One paper further states that it contains human-annotated QA pairs on 5,800 videos derived from ActivityNet and is designed for long-term spatiotemporal reasoning.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to 2 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator. The prevailing usage is to measure video question answering: many papers evaluate zero-shot or open-ended VideoQA on ActivityNet-QA and refer to it directly as a video QA benchmark. A broader framing treats it as measuring video understanding, while a smaller line of work reports it as assessing spatiotemporal reasoning.

Space of uses. Papers usually position ActivityNet-QA as one item in broader evaluation suites, describing it as part of classical, widely used, or general video QA and video understan

nodes.name: Adaptive attack
nodes.definition: A custom jailbreak evaluation procedure designed to prevent backtracking by optimizing prompts while discouraging generation of the [RESET] token.

nodes.name: AddSub
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the dominant framing treats AddSub as an arithmetic word-problem dataset or benchmark centered on addition and subtraction. Definitions repeatedly describe it as containing addition and subtraction word problems for arithmetic, basic operational reasoning, or basic mathematical reasoning, and one evaluation section describes it as containing simple math word problems on addition and subtraction. One paper additionally frames it as a near-shift out-of-distribution benchmark, while another uses it as a seed dataset and as a well-defined evaluation set within PMC.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use AddSub mainly to measure Mathematical reasoning. It is linked to 1 construct and 1 behavioral indicator: the construct is Mathematical reasoning, which papers evaluate through arithmetic datasets and mathematical reasoning testbeds, and the behavioral indicator is Mathematical problem solving, which one paper measures with AddSub as part of a more general benchmark suite. The reported measurement claims therefore converge on Mathematical reasoning rather than spreading across many targets.

Space of uses. Most papers use AddSub as one dataset wi

nodes.name: AddSub+
nodes.definition: A dataset for arithmetic reasoning that involves addition and subtraction problems, used here with variants of different digit lengths.

nodes.name: ADE20K
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, ADE20K is most commonly described as a large-scale scene parsing or semantic segmentation benchmark, sometimes specified as ADE20K (A-150). Definitions describe it as containing densely annotated images across a wide range of scenes, with a diverse set of objects and stuff classes. A smaller line of work treats it differently, either as a source dataset for constructing evaluation data with instance-level semantic annotations or as an alternative dataset for patch-level probing.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link ADE20K to 3 behavioral indicators and to no constructs. The prevailing usage is that it measures semantic segmentation, with several papers describing evaluation, fine-tuning, or reported results on ADE20K for that purpose. A smaller line of work uses it to measure open-vocabulary semantic segmentation, and one paper reports it as measuring image segmentation.

Space of uses. Most papers position ADE20K as a benchmark or transfer target for semantic segmentation, often reporting results on it, fine-tuning on it, or using it as a downstream check after image restoration. It appears alongside PASCAL Context, PASCAL VOC 20, COCO

nodes.name: AdvBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most papers treat AdvBench as an adversarial or jailbreak benchmark built from harmful instructions, prompts, queries, questions, or behaviors that are used to test whether models will produce harmful responses. The prevailing framing is a text benchmark of harmful requests, though some definitions describe separate "Harmful Behaviors" and "Harmful Strings" components, and multimodal work reuses or refines it for vision-language or audio attack settings. Definitions also differ on exact scope, with some papers describing the full dataset and others focusing on curated or refined subsets.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use AdvBench to measure 6 constructs and 6 behavioral indicators. The dominant measurement claims center on safety and safety alignment, and on the behavioral side on jailbreaking, harmful content generation, and harmful request refusal; the remaining links cover 4 other constructs and 3 other indicators. Authors operationalize these uses through attack or jailbreak rates, refusal-based metrics, unsafety detection, and harmfulness scoring.

Space of uses. Papers do not link it to other measurement instruments, but they often deploy it alongside Har

nodes.name: AdversarialQA
nodes.definition: Question answering dataset with adversarially constructed questions designed to challenge model robustness and reasoning.

nodes.name: AG News
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats AG News as a benchmark or corpus for news topic classification, usually described as news articles assigned to four classes or categories. Many definitions specify the categories as World, Sports, Business, and Sci/Tech, while some describe the material more generally as short news articles from diverse domains or as a collection drawn from more than 2000 sources. A smaller line of work refers to AG News Title and Description, AGT and AGD, as title and description subsets used for semantic classification and retrieval.

What it is claimed to measure. Measurement claims are dominated by text classification: papers use AG News to measure 3 behavioral indicators in total, with text classification the prevailing one, downstream task performance another recurring use, and one other behavioral indicator appearing less often. It is also used to measure 5 constructs, with zero-shot generalization the most recurrent named construct, while papers also use it for adversarial robustness, calibration, and 2 other constructs. Some papers make the task explicit as categorizing a news article into one of the 4 categories, World, Spo

nodes.name: Agent-as-a-Judge
nodes.definition: Framework that uses agentic systems to evaluate other agentic systems by analyzing step-by-step task-solving processes, incorporating modules for reading, locating, retrieving, and judging based on hierarchical requirements.

nodes.name: AgentBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing treatment is of AgentBench as a benchmark or evaluation suite for LLMs as agents, and some definitions use it as a comparison point for multi-round and task-diverse agent evaluation. Papers describe its contents in different ways: as diverse or 8 distinct environments, as environments for intrinsic reasoning and adaptation to environment feedback across OS, DB, HH, KG, WB, and WS, and as agent application tasks such as OS interaction, web browsing, and web shopping. Reported scoring also varies by environment, with success rate for OS, DB, HH, and WB, F1 for KG, and reward score for WS.

What it is claimed to measure. Its reported measurement role is distributed across several targets rather than a single construct: papers link it to 7 constructs and 3 behavioral indicators. Commonly named targets include Agency, Decision-making, Knowledge acquisition, Logical reasoning, and Instruction following, and papers also frame it more broadly as evaluating agent performance and core abilities.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it. Papers nevertheless use it alongside other agent benchmarks, including ToolBench and AgentBoard, a

nodes.name: AgentBoard
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing framing is of AgentBoard as a standardized or comprehensive benchmark for evaluating LLM agents. Definitions describe it as a unified, open-source evaluation framework for multi-turn agents, with diverse tasks in partially-observable environments and analytical metrics beyond success rates; other papers describe it more broadly as a collection of diverse tasks, or as a benchmark spanning various environments to assess agent performance in tasks such as reasoning and planning.

What it is claimed to measure. Measurement claims converge on a single construct: papers use AgentBoard to measure Agency. The linked evidence describes it as a collection of diverse tasks for evaluating language models' agentic capabilities, and another paper places it under real-world applications; no behavioral indicators are linked to it.

Space of uses. Papers position AgentBoard as a benchmark and evaluation framework for agent evaluation, including analytical evaluation of LLM agents. In use, it appears alongside AgentBench in standardized agent evaluation setups, and some descriptions also group it with ToolBench in broader benchmark suites for assessing agent

nodes.name: AgentDojo
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the cited work, AgentDojo is consistently described as a benchmark or evaluation framework for agent vulnerabilities in dynamic, tool-using settings, especially susceptibility to prompt injection attacks. Definitions emphasize a dynamic environment with untrusted data, and one paper further describes it as a benchmark of stateful, multi-turn tool-use tasks that simulates realistic environments such as email clients, online banking systems, and Slack channels. That description also specifies 97 tasks across four domains: Workspace, Slack, Travel, and Banking.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use AgentDojo to measure three constructs, adversarial robustness, security, and utility preservation, and one behavioral indicator, prompt injection. The recorded claims describe it as measuring the adversarial robustness of AI agents, evaluating the utility and security of AI agents in dynamic tool-calling environments with untrusted data, and testing prompt injection attacks, so the reported measurement claims cover several targets rather than a single construct.

Space of uses. In use, papers treat AgentDojo as an evaluation benchmark for methods in indirect or promp

nodes.name: AgentHarm
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing framing is a safety benchmark, though its content is described in two ways. One description presents it as 110 malicious tasks for general agents, designed to evaluate general agent safety and vulnerability to harmful instructions. Another describes it as providing detailed safety measurements for tool-using LLMs through 176 examples, including harmful and benign samples and multi-step trajectories with harmful tool outputs to test refusal behavior.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to measure two constructs, Harmlessness and Safety, and no behavioral indicators are linked to it. One line of work reports that Harmlessness is measured by AgentHarm, describing it as a benchmark proposed for measuring harmfulness in LLM agents, while another reports that Safety is measured by AgentHarm, saying it measures the potential harm from agents executing malicious tasks. The reported uses therefore span two construct labels rather than centering on a single one.

Space of uses. Papers position it as an evaluation benchmark rather than alongside other named instruments, and no other measurement instrument is linked to it. In ShieldAgent: Shi

nodes.name: AggreFact
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across these papers, AggreFact is most commonly described as a benchmark dataset for evaluating factual consistency in summarization. Definitions portray it as providing fine-grained annotations and summary-level labels across multiple domains, while a narrower description presents it as a summary evaluation benchmark built around the CNN and XSum datasets. One paper also refers to the AGGREFACT-FTSOTA split, indicating use of a named split or subset.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use AggreFact to evaluate factual consistency in summarization, and some also frame it more broadly as a benchmark for summary evaluation. The recorded links do not connect it to any construct or behavioral indicator, so the explicit measurement claims here do not extend beyond those benchmark descriptions.

Space of uses. The quoted passages position AggreFact as one benchmark used alongside other summarization evaluation datasets, especially TRUE and SUMMAC, in model testing. Papers also use it with specific summarization datasets, describing it as consisting of or evaluating CNN or CNN/DM and XSum, and one paper specifies evaluation on the AGGREFACT-FTSOTA split.

nodes.name: AGIEval
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats AGIEval as a human-centric benchmark for evaluating foundation models or language models on standardized exams. Most definitions describe it as drawing on exam questions such as the Gaokao, SAT, GRE, law school admission tests, college admission tests, and civil service examinations, and some papers specify fields like English, Math, Law, and Logic. A smaller line of work describes it more broadly as an aggregated benchmark for overall model capabilities or artificial general intelligence across a wide range of tasks and skills, and one paper calls it a bilingual benchmark for exam performance.

What it is claimed to measure. The recorded measurement claims are concentrated rather than spread across many targets: papers link AGIEval to 1 construct, Generalization, and to no behavioral indicators. One paper reports that Generalization is measured by AGIEval, using all English tasks in zero-shot settings, while many descriptions more broadly say the benchmark evaluates general abilities, overall model performance, reasoning capabilities, knowledge, or general world knowledge.

Space of uses. Papers use AGIEval alongsid

nodes.name: AGIEval-Math
nodes.definition: Out-of-distribution test set used to evaluate mathematical reasoning generalization beyond the training domain.

nodes.name: AI2-THOR
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, AI2-THOR is most commonly described as a simulation environment or interactive 3D simulator for embodied AI in realistic or photorealistic home-like indoor scenes. Definitions emphasize household tasks with natural language instructions and egocentric visual observations, where agents navigate and interact with household items; a smaller line of work presents it as the base environment for multi-agent setups and for benchmarks built on top of it, including MAP-THOR.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use AI2-THOR to measure one construct, Planning, and one behavioral indicator, Causal inference. These claims are concentrated on that small set of targets: one paper reports "planning results" and "N-step causal inference accuracies" across environments and step lengths using AI2-THOR.

Space of uses. Papers position AI2-THOR as an evaluation environment for embodied agents. In the quoted passages, it is used for evaluations across multiple scenarios, including alongside LEGENT, and as the underlying simulator for open-ended, long-horizon home-like tasks in a multi-agent setup.

nodes.name: AI2D
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across definitions, AI2D is most commonly described as a benchmark or dataset for diagram understanding and question answering. Papers variously specify science, textbook, or grade school science diagrams, and some describe multiple-choice questions, diagram parsing, or exhaustive annotations of constituents and relationships over more than 5,000 diagrams and 15,000 question-answer pairs. A few papers refer to variants or subsets such as AI2D-Test and AI2D-RST, the latter described as "a multimodal corpus of 1000 primary school science diagrams".

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use AI2D to measure 3 behavioral indicators and 3 constructs. The recurring behavioral claims are diagram understanding, chart and diagram understanding, and multiple-choice visual question answering, while the construct-level claims link it to multimodal perception, multimodal reasoning, and visual reasoning. Across these links, the prevailing framing stays close to diagram comprehension: papers say it gauges "diagram comprehension," "science diagram comprehension," or challenges of "diagram interpretation and reasoning."

Space of uses. Across evaluation setups, papers usually place AI2D

nodes.name: AIAH
nodes.definition: A benchmark used to evaluate the safety-alignment of Large Audio Language Models (LALMs) against harmful questions across audio-text, text-only, and audio-only modalities.

nodes.name: AIME
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across definitions, papers most commonly treat AIME as the American Invitational Mathematics Examination, used as a benchmark or dataset for advanced mathematical reasoning or problem solving. It is also described as a challenging high school mathematics competition. Some papers specify particular slices rather than the exam in general: one uses the AIMO validation set with 90 questions from AIME 22, 23, and 24, another evaluates on AIME 2025, Parts I and II, and one reference describes AIME as 15 competition math problems.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link AIME to two constructs and two behavioral indicators. The prevailing use is to measure mathematical reasoning, with several papers describing it as a math reasoning benchmark; it is also reported as measuring reasoning more generally. Among behavioral indicators, papers link it to mathematical problem solving and, in one paper, to chain of thought.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it. In reported evaluations, papers usually place AIME in broader benchmark suites alongside Omni-MATH, MATH, GPQA, math500, and gsm8k, and they commonly position it as a challenging or widely used benchmark

nodes.name: AIME 2024
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing description is a benchmark or dataset of problems from the 2024 American Invitational Mathematics Examination, used to test advanced mathematical reasoning or problem solving. Definitions commonly call it challenging, competition-level, or Olympiad-level, and some specify that it contains 30 questions whose answers are integers from 0 to 999; one paper also describes the problems as spanning algebra, counting, geometry, number theory, and probability. Descriptions differ at the margins: some papers frame it as a high-school competition, one as a middle school competition, and some explicitly present it as an out-of-distribution benchmark.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use AIME 2024 to measure three constructs and one behavioral indicator. The dominant use is for mathematical reasoning, with many papers evaluating models' mathematical reasoning ability on it; several others use it for broader reasoning, and papers also report it as measuring mathematical problem solving. A smaller line of work uses it to verify generalization, explicitly treating it as coming from a different distribution than training data.

Space of uses. Most pap

nodes.name: AIME 2025
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly describe AIME 2025, sometimes written AIME25, as a benchmark or benchmark dataset derived from the 2025 American Invitational Mathematics Examination. The definitions converge on its use for testing advanced mathematical problem-solving skills or evaluating mathematical reasoning performance, and one study also classifies AIME25 among "smaller benchmarks."

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, the dominant use is to measure Mathematical reasoning: it is linked to two constructs overall, most often Mathematical reasoning and, in a smaller line of work, Self-improvement. This appears in language such as evaluations of "performance (%) on mathematical benchmarks" and of models' "mathematical reasoning capabilities"; one paper instead uses this recent mathematics benchmark to examine test-time learning capabilities in solving high-level mathematical problems, which is recorded as measuring Self-improvement. Papers do not link it to any behavioral indicator.

Space of uses. Reported evaluations often place AIME 2025 alongside other mathematics benchmarks. Papers commonly pair it with AIME24, and some also include AMC23, MATH500, Minervamath, and

nodes.name: AIR-Bench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, AIR-Bench is most commonly treated as an aggregated or holistic evaluation suite for large audio or audio-language models, covering audio understanding or general auditory processing across speech, audio, and music. Some authors describe it more specifically as an open-ended question-answering benchmark, and another paper refers to AirBench-Chat as a conversational ability evaluation based on text-based interactions. A smaller framing uses the same name for a benchmark dedicated to retrieval performance, with test data automatically generated by large language models without human intervention.

What it is claimed to measure. The prevailing usage is to evaluate audio-centered capabilities: papers describe AIR-Bench as assessing audio understanding, general auditory processing, spoken language comprehension, and conversational ability in the AirBench-Chat subset. A smaller line of work presents it as measuring retrieval performance instead. No constructs or behavioral indicators are linked to it by the papers.

Space of uses. Papers commonly discuss AIR-Bench alongside AudioBench, often as another aggregated evaluation set for large audio mode

nodes.name: AIR-Bench 2024
nodes.definition: A language-model safety benchmark containing 5,694 risky instruction prompts grounded in the AIR 2024 taxonomy of regulation- and policy-derived risk categories.

nodes.name: AIR-Bench (information retrieval)
nodes.definition: An information retrieval benchmark that covers a range of out-of-domain topics, including long document and question-answering sections, to test model generalization.

nodes.name: AitW
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most papers treat AitW as a large-scale dataset or benchmark for Android device control, used to evaluate mobile or GUI agents. Definitions also describe it as containing diverse natural language instructions and operation trajectories, with subsets such as General and Web Shopping, and some authors add that it provides an evaluation environment for real-world tasks. A smaller line of work presents it more specifically as a mobile navigation benchmark, and one paper describes it as an open-source mobile control dataset that lacks UI trees.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the surveyed work, claims about what AitW measures are concentrated on a small set of outcomes: papers link it to 2 behavioral indicators and 1 construct. The prevailing usage is to use it to measure GUI automation, papers also use it to measure task completion, and a smaller line of work reports that it measures Adaptability.

Space of uses. Papers commonly position AitW as an evaluation benchmark for Android, mobile, or GUI control agents. Some also use it as a training or fine-tuning source and then evaluate on test subsets derived from AitW, while others use it as a comparison point or evalua

nodes.name: ALERT
nodes.definition: An evaluation dataset designed to test the safety of responses generated by large language models.

nodes.name: ALFRED
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the dominant framing is a benchmark or dataset for embodied household tasks in simulation, used for planning and instruction following with human-annotated, formally verifiable tasks that involve object manipulation and state changes such as heating, cooling, and cleaning. Definitions and quoted passages variously place it in a simulated Unity environment or describe it as built on the AI2-THOR simulator, and some papers also present it as providing vision-and-language navigation and rearrangement tasks for everyday household settings. A smaller usage writes it as ALFRed and emphasizes long-horizon embodied tasks and task decomposition, while another paper curates an ALFRED test set for 3D evaluation.

What it is claimed to measure. Its reported measurement role is limited and split across 2 constructs, with no linked behavioral indicators. One paper uses it to measure 3D perception through a curated ALFRED test set for "3D evaluation" (LLaVA-Interleave: Tackling Multi-image, Video, and 3D in Large Multimodal Models), while another uses it to measure robustness by reporting experiments in "VirtualHome, ALFRED, and CARLA" (Exploratory Retrieval-Augmented P

nodes.name: ALFWorld
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, ALFWorld is most commonly described as a text-based or text-only household environment for embodied agents, variously called a game suite, benchmark, simulator, or dataset. The prevailing description is that agents follow natural language instructions and act through high-level or low-level text actions to complete housework tasks such as navigation, object manipulation, picking, cleaning, heating, or moving objects; several papers also say it is based on, or aligned with, ALFRED and implemented in TextWorld. A smaller line of work emphasizes logs or next-action prediction rather than online interaction, describing navigation logs from a text-based world simulator. Papers also describe it as having six task types and 134 unseen environments or evaluation tasks.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to measure 8 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators, so its claimed targets are spread across several framings rather than concentrated on a single one. The prevailing use is for decision-making, followed by generalization and sequential decision-making; among behavioral indicators, task completion and embodied planning are the linked uses. In the p

nodes.name: AlignBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing description is a Chinese benchmark of 683 samples for evaluating LLM alignment. It is commonly presented as multidimensional, with a rule-calibrated LLM-as-judge procedure and Chain-of-Thought reasoning for evaluation, and some descriptions add that different question types have manually set evaluation dimensions. One paper also treats it as a benchmark from which Clarity, Completeness, and Factuality are drawn.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to evaluate alignment, variously phrased as LLM alignment, alignment capabilities of LLMs in Chinese, or model alignment across multiple dimensions. One paper further reports using Clarity, Completeness, and Factuality from AlignBench for quality assessment. No constructs and no behavioral indicators are linked to it in the reported relationships.

Space of uses. Most papers position it as an evaluation benchmark rather than alongside other named instruments. A smaller use treats it as a source of metrics, where a model predicts instruction and instruction-response scores based on Clarity, Completeness, and Factuality from AlignBench. No other measurement instruments are linked to it.

nodes.name: Alpaca instruction dataset
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing description is an instruction-following dataset, often described as 52,000 instruction-following demonstrations or instruction-response pairs. Some definitions make its format more explicit as instruction, input, output triples, and papers also refer to the Alpaca training dataset, a cleaned version of Alpaca, code prompts from Alpaca, and an Alpaca subset without unsafe instructions. A smaller line of work uses it less as a standalone tuning set and more as a source of human-written prompts, out-of-domain queries, seed data, or target and anti-target prompts.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to 5 constructs and 4 behavioral indicators, and the dominant measurement claim is instruction following. It is also reported as measuring helpfulness and question answering, while smaller lines of work use it for general ability and text generation. Overall, papers spread its use across several targets rather than tying it to a single construct.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it. In practice, papers position it in several roles: as a fine-tuning or supervised instruction-tuning set, as calibration and recovery-tun

nodes.name: AlpacaEval
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, AlpacaEval is most commonly described as an automatic, LLM-based benchmark or evaluation framework for instruction-following and open-ended text generation. The prevailing setup compares a model's outputs pairwise against a reference, usually text-davinci-003, with GPT-4 judging and a win rate reported; many descriptions also refer to an accompanying leaderboard or dataset of 805 prompts or instructions from diverse domains, while one paper instead treats it as an out-of-distribution evaluation test set drawn from open-source instruction-following and dialogue data. Papers distinguish v1.0, where the default setup computes win rate against text-davinci-003, and some also mention length-controlled AlpacaEval 2 or AlpacaEval 2.0; smaller uses draw on the helpful_base subset of 129 prompts or on 17701 human annotations.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link AlpacaEval to 13 constructs and 5 behavioral indicators, so claims about what it measures are broad. The dominant use is to measure instruction following, phrased either as instruction following ability or instruction following, and it is also frequently used to measure text generation quality, flue

nodes.name: AlpacaEval 2.0
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage is as an automatic, LLM-as-a-judge benchmark for instruction-following and open-ended chat evaluation: a model answers 805 instructions or questions, often described as drawn from five datasets or representative real user interactions, and its responses are compared pairwise with a reference or baseline response. Most definitions say the judge is GPT-4, GPT-4 Turbo, or GPT-4o, with outputs reported as win rate and often length-controlled win rate, sometimes against GPT-4 Turbo or Text-davinci-003. Many papers also refer to variants such as AlpacaEval 2.0 Length Controlled or Length-Controlled AlpacaEval, while a smaller set frames it more specifically as question answering, conversation quality, or a text-only human preference alignment benchmark.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to measure 9 constructs and 6 behavioral indicators. The prevailing claims are that it measures instruction following and instruction following ability, and many papers also use it to measure human preference alignment, helpfulness, and alignment. Beyond these common framings, papers spread it across several other targets rather than tying it to

nodes.name: AlpacaFarm
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most commonly, papers treat AlpacaFarm as an evaluation framework, benchmark, or dataset for open-ended instruction-following or conversation models. Across definitions, it is described as using human preference data and pairwise or model-based comparisons over model outputs, with content such as instructions, output pairs, demonstrations, and human preference annotations; some papers highlight a test set of 805 instructions, training and validation splits, and use of all 9.69k instructions, while a smaller line of work refers to the AlpacaFarm codebase or software framework for judging responses with a model evaluator.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link AlpacaFarm to 2 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator. The named constructs are Helpfulness, where a paper uses its 805-instruction test set for assessing helpfulness, and Instruction following ability, where another paper uses the AlpacaFarm codebase to judge model responses; it is also reported as measuring Pairwise comparison, with one paper describing open-ended instruction-following benchmarks such as Alpacafarm as primarily relying on pairwise comparison.

Space of uses. In use, papers sample from multipl

nodes.name: Amazon Books
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers treat Amazon Books as an Amazon dataset centered on products in the Books category, with user-item interactions and product metadata. In the one definition, it is described as being used to evaluate recommendation performance, and no versions or subsets are described.

What it is claimed to measure. The only explicit measurement claim in the material is that papers use Amazon Books for evaluating recommendation performance. No construct is linked to it, and no behavioral indicator is linked to it, so the recorded claims do not converge on any named construct beyond that general evaluation use.

Space of uses. The paper positions Amazon Books as an evaluation dataset rather than describing it alongside other instruments. No other measurement instrument is linked to it in the recorded relationships.

nodes.name: Amazon Mechanical Turk
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats Amazon Mechanical Turk as a crowdsourcing platform for collecting human annotations and human evaluations. Most definitions describe it as a platform, while one frames it as a crowdsourced evaluation procedure; the reported uses include collecting valid versus invalid labels to train critic models, rating generated plans, comparing outputs on fluency and descriptiveness, evaluating model outputs across a test set, building an annotation platform for splitting and labeling interaction sequences, verifying benchmark samples and human performance, and collecting open-ended answers and ratings for visual riddle tasks.

What it is claimed to measure. Across these papers, Amazon Mechanical Turk is not explicitly linked to named constructs or behavioral indicators. Instead, it is used to gather task-specific human judgments and annotations, including fluency and descriptiveness comparisons, ratings of generated plans, subjective ratings on generated diagrams, human verification and human performance on image-caption matching tasks, and human answers and ratings for visual riddles.

Space of uses. Papers position Amazon Mechanical

nodes.name: Amazon Polarity
nodes.definition:
What it is. The prevailing description treats Amazon Polarity, sometimes written as Amazon or AmazonPolarity, as a sentiment classification benchmark for product reviews and, more broadly, an NLP text classification dataset. Some papers instead describe "Amazon" differently: as a product co-purchasing network, where nodes are products and edges connect items frequently bought together, used for node classification in a text-attributed heterophilic graph, or as a temporal point process benchmark where the goal is to predict the timestamp and category of the next reviewed product among 16 categories.

What it is claimed to measure. In recorded relationships, papers link it to 1 behavioral indicator, Text classification, and to no constructs. The relationship is stated directionally as text classification being measured by Amazon Polarity, with the supporting use describing it as part of sentiment analysis, so the measurement claims converge on a single behavioral indicator rather than being spread across many targets.

Space of uses. Papers place it alongside other evaluation datasets rather than describe a separate protocol. It appears with SST-2 and Yelp in sentiment analysis evalu

nodes.name: Amazon Reviews
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, Amazon Reviews is treated as a product review dataset, most commonly described as Amazon reviews across multiple categories. One use presents it as a sentiment analysis dataset for evaluating model performance on commercial user feedback, while another describes the public Amazon Reviews dataset as adapted with simulated user consultation texts, user profiles, and interaction behaviors for evaluation. In a separate experimental description, the Amazon product reviews are also said to be labeled into a three-layer taxonomy DAG.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link Amazon Reviews to one behavioral indicator and no constructs. The reported measurement claim is concentrated on hierarchical text classification: papers use it to measure that indicator, with one description specifying Amazon product reviews labeled into a three-layer taxonomy DAG rather than spreading the instrument across several reported constructs or behaviors.

Space of uses. No other measurement instrument is linked to Amazon Reviews. In the papers, it is used as a task dataset for sentiment analysis, as a public dataset adapted for evaluation with simulated user consultat

nodes.name: Amazon Reviews 2023
nodes.definition: A dataset of user reviews on Amazon products, used here for the task of personalized review generation, covering categories like Books, Movies & TV, and CDs & Vinyl, and preprocessed with splits from the DPL framework.

nodes.name: Amazon Video Games
nodes.definition: An Amazon dataset containing user-item interactions and metadata for products in the 'Video Games' category, used for evaluating recommendation performance.

nodes.name: AMBER
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, AMBER is most commonly described as a hallucination benchmark that extends POPE beyond existence checks to cover attribute and relation hallucinations as well. Several papers also present it as spanning both discriminative and generative tasks, and one description says it evaluates multimodal hallucinations through 15,220 yes-or-no questions. Smaller descriptions treat it as a dataset for image description tasks, or note implementation details, such as the use of CHAIR as the evaluation metric; one paper further describes it as designed to be evaluated without LLM assistance, with metrics including response-level hallucination and human cognition hallucination.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use AMBER to measure 2 behavioral indicators and 2 constructs. The prevailing use is to measure hallucination, especially hallucination and object hallucination, with papers also using it to measure hallucination resistance and visual recognition. These links are concentrated on hallucination-related targets, while visual recognition appears as a smaller additional use.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it. Papers usually position AMBER as

nodes.name: AmbigNQ
nodes.definition: A dataset of naturally occurring ambiguous questions from Google search logs, which served as the origin for the queries used in AmbigQA and subsequently CondAmbigQA.

nodes.name: Ambrosia
nodes.definition: A benchmark containing human-crafted databases and questions specifically designed to incorporate ambiguities for evaluating semantic parsing.

nodes.name: AMC 2023
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing description is of a benchmark or dataset drawn from the 2023 American Mathematics Competitions, used for standardized or competition-style math questions. Most definitions frame the content as challenging high school-level problems and describe it as a benchmark, dataset, or exam for mathematical reasoning or problem solving. A smaller line of description differs, calling AMC2023 a middle school math competition covering arithmetic, algebra, and geometry and noting that it contains 40 questions. Papers refer to it under several surface forms, including AMC, AMC2023, AMC23, and AMC 2023.

What it is claimed to measure. The measurement claims converge rather than spreading across many targets. Papers link AMC 2023 to one construct, Mathematical reasoning, and one behavioral indicator, Mathematical problem solving, with Mathematical reasoning the prevailing usage and Mathematical problem solving appearing in a smaller line of work. In these uses, papers place it within benchmark sets for assessing models' reasoning or problem-solving abilities on math tasks.

Space of uses. Papers usually deploy AMC 2023 as one item in broader math benchmark s

nodes.name: AndroidControl
nodes.definition:
What it is. Definitions mostly treat AndroidControl as a benchmark for evaluating mobile agent tasks on Android platforms. One description is more specific, calling it an offline GUI benchmark and an in-distribution offline dataset, while another highlights two variants: AndroidControl-Low, where both low-level and high-level instructions are provided, and AndroidControl-High, where only high-level instructions are given. One paper also describes it as a UI control dataset with 14,548 unique tasks over 833 Android apps.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use AndroidControl to measure three constructs, Agency, Generalization, and Out-of-distribution generalization, and no behavioral indicators are linked to it. These measurement claims are spread across those constructs rather than centered on one: one paper presents it as a mobile-agent benchmark, another frames evaluation on it as a test of out-of-distribution performance because only 20 of the 833 apps had been encountered during data synthesis, and another says its task and app coverage allows analysis of performance in and out of the training domain.

Space of uses. When papers place AndroidControl within broader evaluation

nodes.name: AndroidWorld
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the dominant framing is of an online or dynamic Android benchmark for mobile or autonomous agents, usually running in Android emulators or a virtual Android environment. Definitions mostly converge on a suite of 116 tasks across 20 real-world apps, with reward signals or automated evaluation based on final device states, and with task-specific initialization, success-checking, and tear-down logic; one paper also describes a Pixel 6 phone simulator. A smaller line of work treats it more broadly as an Android virtual agent benchmark used for both trajectory collection and evaluation.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to three constructs and no behavioral indicators. The most common claim is that it measures adaptability: papers say it enables finer-grained analyses of agent adaptability and use results on AndroidWorld to report adaptability across real-time dynamic OS tasks. Smaller uses report it as measuring robustness, through performance across different random seeds and task parameters, and chain-of-thought reasoning, in work that describes AndroidWorld as an online environment requiring multi-step reasoning. Overall, the measur

nodes.name: ANLI
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats ANLI as Adversarial Natural Language Inference, a benchmark or dataset for natural language inference, often described as large scale and collected through an iterative, adversarial human-and-model-in-the-loop process. Several definitions stress that it was created to be challenging, with one describing the primary aim as making state-of-the-art models fail, and another framing it as a textual entailment task for natural language understanding and reasoning. Some authors also describe open-domain questions enhanced through an iterative adversarial procedure and report using its challenging subsets for evaluation. A table caption in one paper uses ANLI as a label alongside adversarial attacks, but most definitions describe a benchmark dataset.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use ANLI mainly to measure Natural language inference: it is linked to one behavioral indicator, Natural language inference, and the relationship is recorded as measured_by. A smaller line of work uses it to measure Commonsense reasoning, where it is linked to one construct with a measured_by relationship. The recorded claims are therefore

nodes.name: ANLI R2
nodes.definition: The second round of the Adversarial Natural Language Inference (ANLI) dataset, a challenging benchmark for sentence pair classification.

nodes.name: AnnoMI
nodes.definition: Expert-annotated counseling dataset with 133 dialogues and 9 therapist strategies, used for evaluating emotional support dialogue strategy prediction.

nodes.name: Anthropic Red Team
nodes.definition: An adversarial dataset of potentially harmful queries designed to test the safety of language models.

nodes.name: API-Bank
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, API-Bank is most commonly treated as a benchmark or dialogue-style dataset for evaluating tool calls by LLMs in conversational or tool-augmented settings. Definitions vary in scope: some emphasize single- and multi-turn scenarios, one describes calling predefined local Python tools from user requirements, and others frame it as evaluating planning, retrieval, and API calling. Several papers distinguish two retrieval-call variants, either Call versus Retrieve + Call or L-1, invoking a known API, versus L-2, retrieving and calling from multiple candidates; reported contents also differ, from 314 tool-use dialogues and 753 API calls to 2,138 distinct APIs, 1,888 dialogues, and 4,149 API calls, with another description emphasizing general-purpose tools across 1,000 domains.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link API-Bank to one behavioral indicator and two constructs. The prevailing usage is to measure Tool use and Tool use ability: papers describe it as evaluating tool use, tool-utilization capabilities, or tool-calling capability, including planning, retrieval, and API-calling proficiency. A smaller line of work uses it to measure Generalization, speci

nodes.name: APIBench
nodes.definition: A benchmark focused on APIs that load machine learning models, used to train and evaluate LLMs' ability to interface with ML services.

nodes.name: APPS
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats APPS as an algorithmic programming or code generation benchmark or dataset. Definitions usually describe natural language programming problems paired with test cases and solutions, often Python solutions, and several papers specify 10,000 problems split evenly between training and test sets across introductory, interview, and competition levels. Some authors instead foreground competitive programming, program synthesis, or code synthesis with public or hidden unit tests, and several evaluations use subsets such as 500 interview-level problems, 500 sampled test questions, or the competition split of 1,000 problems.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers most commonly use APPS to measure code generation, with smaller lines of work using it to measure code debugging and clarifying question generation. Papers link it to 3 behavioral indicators and 1 construct: code generation, code debugging, clarifying question generation, and functional correctness. The claims mostly converge on code generation, while the construct-level use is concentrated on functional correctness through execution against test cases.

Space of uses. No mea

nodes.name: AQuA-RAT
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the dominant framing treats AQuA-RAT, often written AQuA or AQUA-RAT, as a dataset or benchmark of algebraic word problems in multiple-choice format. Many definitions add rationales and multi-step reasoning, and one study describes it as containing approximately 100,000 algebraic word problems, each with a rationale leading to one of five answer options, while others characterize it more broadly as algebraic and quantitative reasoning or as reasoning over quantitative and qualitative relationships. Papers also differ slightly in presentation, with one calling it a 4-option multiple-choice benchmark and another a five-option one, and with difficulty described both as relatively simple and as harder math word problems.

What it is claimed to measure. The prevailing usage is as a measure of Mathematical reasoning: papers say it is used to assess varying levels of mathematical reasoning abilities, mathematical reasoning capacity, and arithmetic reasoning. Papers link it to 3 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator overall, with claims concentrated on Mathematical reasoning; a smaller line of work uses it to measure Mathematical problem solving, and single paper

nodes.name: ArabicMMLU
nodes.definition: An Arabic-specific variant of MMLU that evaluates knowledge across subjects with regional relevance to Arab countries, used in a zero-shot setting with option logit probability.

nodes.name: AraEval
nodes.definition: A comprehensive Arabic multi-task evaluation suite assessing knowledge, reasoning, truthfulness, and instruction-following in LLMs, comprising seven datasets with 24,378 samples.

nodes.name: ARC
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most papers treat ARC as the AI2 Reasoning Challenge, a multiple-choice question answering benchmark of grade-school science questions used to test knowledge and reasoning, often described as difficult for simple retrieval or word co-occurrence methods. Definitions commonly note the ARC-Easy and ARC-Challenge splits, and some papers specify about 7.8k questions or say the questions are drawn from standardized tests. A smaller line of work uses the same name for the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus or Challenge, a visual or grid-based benchmark in which models infer transformation rules from input-output examples and apply them to a test grid, sometimes framed as abstract or fluid-intelligence evaluation.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use ARC to measure 8 constructs and 9 behavioral indicators. The prevailing claims center on commonsense reasoning, broader reasoning, question answering, multiple-choice question answering, and machine reading comprehension. Beyond those recurring uses, papers spread ARC across additional reasoning-, ability-, and zero-shot-oriented targets, so it is used for multiple targets rather than only one.

Space of uses. Across papers, AR

nodes.name: ARC-AGI
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, ARC-AGI is most commonly described as the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus, a grid-based benchmark where models infer a transformation rule from input-output examples and then produce the correct output for a new test grid. One definition says the original dataset contains 900 reasoning tasks. A smaller line of description refers to it more specifically as an ARC reasoning benchmark, a visual inductive reasoning benchmark, or a program synthesis benchmark designed to challenge core reasoning capabilities.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link ARC-AGI to 7 constructs and no behavioral indicators. The prevailing use is to measure Reasoning and Generalization: papers describe it as designed to assess core knowledge and the ability to generalize in AI, and as a benchmark that challenges core reasoning capabilities. Other papers use it to measure Abstract reasoning, Core knowledge, and Inductive reasoning; overall, these claims are spread across several constructs rather than centered on one, with 2 additional construct links beyond these, one of them a related rather than measured_by connection.

Space of uses. No other measurement instrument is linked

nodes.name: ARC-Challenge
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing description is the challenge subset of the AI2 Reasoning Challenge, a harder benchmark of difficult multiple-choice science questions, often grade-school level or drawn from scientific exams and standardized natural science tests, and often said to be hard for simple retrieval or word co-occurrence methods. Many definitions frame it as a harder split of ARC or ARC-Easy for question answering and reasoning, and papers variously describe it as 4-option MCQs, a closed-set reasoning dataset, a commonsense or scientific reasoning benchmark, and in one case an open-book QA dataset. Several papers note that the challenge test set has 1,172 examples or questions.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use ARC-Challenge to measure a broad mix of targets, with 15 linked constructs and 12 linked behavioral indicators. The most common construct-level uses are commonsense reasoning, reasoning, and natural language understanding, while the recurring indicator-level uses are multiple-choice question answering and scientific question answering. The claims spread across many targets rather than converging on one framing.

Space of uses. The prevailing use i

nodes.name: ARC-Easy
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, ARC-Easy is most commonly described as the easy split or easy set of the AI2 Reasoning Challenge, a multiple-choice science question-answering benchmark, often framed as grade-school or elementary-level science questions and frequently used in zero-shot evaluation. Several definitions say the easier questions can be answered with simple retrieval or text-matching, while others describe them as testing basic factual knowledge or reasoning. As one appendix notes, the easy subset "consists of 5,197 of the relatively easier reasoning questions" within an ARC collection of 7,787 items (LLM Circuit Analyses Are Consistent Across Training and Scale).

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link ARC-Easy to 10 constructs and 10 behavioral indicators, so its reported measurement role is broad rather than confined to one target. The prevailing usage is as a measure of commonsense reasoning, with recurring links to reasoning and natural language understanding; smaller lines of work also use it to measure general ability, world knowledge, benchmark overfitting, emergent abilities, factual knowledge, functional linguistic competence, and out-of-distribution generalizat

nodes.name: Arena-Hard
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, Arena-Hard is most commonly described as a hard benchmark of 500 prompts or queries, often drawn from challenging user queries or live Chatbot Arena data. The prevailing description emphasizes technical problem-solving and open-ended instruction-following, sometimes with pairwise comparisons against a baseline such as GPT-4-0314 using GPT-4 or GPT-4-Turbo as judge, while some authors instead describe it as a real-world chatbot evaluation set, a benchmark concentrated on coding and debugging, or a v0.1 dataset that also includes responses from 63 systems and about 32K instruction-response pairs. A smaller line of work discusses automated variants, Arena-Hard-Auto and Arena-Hard-Auto-v0.1, which use LLM judges, and one definition says they automate LMSYS Chatbot Arena evaluation with 89% agreement with human rankings.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link Arena-Hard to 8 constructs and 6 behavioral indicators. The prevailing usage is to measure instruction following, often phrased as instruction following ability, and papers also use it for human preference alignment, conversational ability, general ability, and helpfulness. Taken together, the report

nodes.name: ARES
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, ARES is described in two ways. In Probabilistic Soundness Guarantees in LLM Reasoning Chains, it is introduced as Autoregressive Reasoning Entailment Stability, a probabilistic framework that evaluates each reasoning step by its expected entailment probability, conditioned only on previously verified premises or previously occurring sound claims. RAGChecker: A Fine-grained Framework for Diagnosing Retrieval-Augmented Generation instead describes ARES as an automated evaluation framework for RAG systems that uses LLM-based classifiers to predict fine-grained scores, and says it followed the RAG Triad concept and improved score prediction approaches on different datasets.

What it is claimed to measure. The reported measurement claims are concentrated on one construct: papers link ARES to 1 construct, Error propagation, and to no behavioral indicators. That link is recorded as a measured_by relation, so papers use ARES to measure Error propagation, with one study reporting that it "excels at identifying propagated errors, especially in long chains."

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it. The descriptions position it either as a frame

nodes.name: ArgCMV
nodes.definition: A key point extraction benchmark dataset comprising ~12K arguments from real multi-turn debates on Reddit’s r/ChangeMyView, spanning ~3K topics, designed to evaluate long-context argument understanding and summarization.

nodes.name: ArgKP21
nodes.definition: ArgKP21 is a prior key point extraction benchmark consisting of crowd-sourced arguments on controversial topics with human-created gold key points and argument-to-key-point mappings.

nodes.name: Arithmetic
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, Arithmetic is described as an evaluation task built from arithmetic questions or expressions, though the exact format varies. One description uses natural language addition and subtraction questions with at most 5-digit numbers, another uses mathematical expressions with six unique two-digit numbers and addition, multiplication, and subtraction, and another describes 1,000 generated problems in the form a + b · c + d − e · f.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use Arithmetic to measure one construct, Mathematical reasoning, and no behavioral indicators are linked to it. The measurement claim therefore converges on a single construct rather than being spread across several: the paper that makes this link describes Arithmetic as evaluating a model's fundamental mathematical reasoning abilities.

Space of uses. Papers use Arithmetic in different evaluation setups. In Benchmarking and Improving Generator-Validator Consistency of Language Models, it is used to instantiate generator-validator consistency by randomizing correctness, prompting a generator to produce a correct or incorrect response and having a validator check it; elsewhere, papers place i

nodes.name: ARITHMETIC context-sensitivity dataset
nodes.definition: A synthetically generated dataset of simple arithmetic expressions where contexts provide reassignments of subexpressions to create counterfactual answers.

nodes.name: ArmoRM
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage is as a reward model and automated judge for LLM responses. Most descriptions present it as a multi-dimension or multi-objective model, while some papers refer to specific 8B Llama3 variants, including ArmoRM-8B, ArmoRM-Llama3-8B, and ArmoRM-Llama3-8B-v0.1 or v0.13. Definitions and quoted passages place these variants in several roles: evaluating alignment from various perspectives, scoring model outputs, filtering synthetic preference data, creating preference pairs, and assigning ground-truth quality labels or acting as a proxy judge.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link ArmoRM to two constructs and two behavioral indicators overall. The most common reported measurement claim is that it measures text generation quality, while smaller lines of work use it to measure helpfulness and instruction following, sometimes by selecting its instruction-following dimension as the main evaluation metric. It is also related to preference ranking, with papers employing it to score and rank responses, so its reported use covers a small set of different evaluation targets rather than a single one.

Space of uses. Most commonly, papers positio

nodes.name: Arxiv
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, Arxiv is most commonly treated broadly as a dataset of scientific or academic texts from the arXiv repository, but the format varies by task. Some definitions present it as a directed citation network of Computer Science papers, while others use the same name for a long-document summarization corpus of scientific articles, a subset of paper abstracts used through validation splits, a citation recommendation benchmark derived from arXiv preprints, or a short-form academic-text dataset. The prevailing usage is therefore task-specific rather than tied to a single format.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use Arxiv to measure 2 constructs, Length generalization and Zero-shot generalization, and 1 behavioral indicator, Node classification. For node classification, one paper frames the task as predicting which arXiv CS sub-category a paper belongs to. Other papers report Arxiv as part of real-world or out-of-domain evaluations for length generalization and zero-shot generalization, so the measurement claims span several targets rather than converging on one.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is explicitly linked to Arxiv through instrument relation

nodes.name: ArxivCorpus
nodes.definition: Dataset of Arxiv paper abstracts used for pretraining and evaluating text regeneration, with test sets containing texts published after January 2024 to ensure strict unseen evaluation.

nodes.name: ArXivQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats ArXivQA as a question answering resource built from arXiv or academic-paper figures, most commonly as a VQA dataset consisting of questions about figures from ArXiv academic papers. A smaller line of work instead frames it as a page-level retrieval task, where the question is used as the query and the associated page as the gold document, or as a multiple-choice dataset for document visual question answering in closed- and open-domain settings. One survey describes ArxivQA differently again, as a QA test set generated from recent arXiv abstracts.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to 3 behavioral indicators and no constructs. Its measurement claims are spread across information retrieval, question answering, and visual question answering: papers use it as a QA benchmark where answers are produced in natural language, as a VQA dataset targeting figure types, and as question-document pairs for retrieval evaluation.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is directly linked to it. Papers often use it alongside ChartQA, InfographicsVQA, PlotQA, MP-DocVQA, and SlideVQA in document or figure evaluations, and one QA setu

nodes.name: ASAP
nodes.definition:
What it is. The description treats ASAP as the Hewlett Foundation Short Answer Scoring dataset, containing short essay responses across science and biology topics for evaluating automated scoring systems. The description does not mention versions or subsets.

What it is claimed to measure. The paper describes ASAP as a dataset used for evaluating automated scoring systems, but papers do not link it to any named constructs or behavioral indicators.

Space of uses. No other measurement instruments are linked to ASAP. The paper presents it as a dataset of short essay responses on science and biology topics for evaluating automated scoring systems.

nodes.name: Asch conformity experiment
nodes.definition: A series of classic social psychology experiments studying how individual judgment is influenced by a majority group opinion, which inspired the design of the Trust and Doubt protocols.

nodes.name: ASDiv
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, ASDiv is most commonly described as a benchmark, dataset, or corpus of diverse arithmetic or math word problems used in reasoning evaluation. Definitions emphasize diversity in problem types, operations, and difficulty levels, and one paper further describes it as an English math word problem corpus with 2,305 instances typically found in elementary schools. A smaller line of work frames it as an out-of-distribution or out-of-domain benchmark or as a held-out test set, and papers vary in its expanded name, including A Set of Diverse Math Word Problems, Another Solved Dataset of Diverse Word Problems, and Another Simple Math Word Problem Set.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link ASDiv to 3 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator. The prevailing usage is to measure Mathematical reasoning, with many papers listing it among math reasoning benchmarks or using it to assess mathematical reasoning aptitude. Smaller uses report it as measuring the behavioral indicator Mathematical problem solving and the constructs Reasoning and Generalization, and the claims overall converge mainly on Mathematical reasoning rather than being evenly spread across many tar

nodes.name: ASQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most papers describe ASQA as a benchmark or dataset for long-form question answering over ambiguous, often factoid, queries, where systems are evaluated on answers that cover multiple valid or plausible interpretations. Some definitions emphasize attributable factoid and long-form QA tasks, while a smaller one frames it around long-form, multi-hop answers with supporting evidence and citation quality; papers also describe it as collected from, or extending, AmbigQA.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers tie ASQA to several targets rather than only one. It is used to measure 3 constructs, Factuality, Trustworthiness, and Unanswerability detection ability, and 2 behavioral indicators, Ambiguous question answering and Long-form question answering; the reported operationalizations include official ASQA metrics where Disambiguous-Rouge combines ROUGE-L and Disambig-F1 for factual correctness, as well as TRUST-SCORE and Grounded Refusals F1 on ASQA.

Space of uses. Papers commonly include ASQA in multi-dataset evaluations, often alongside ELI5 and QAMPARI, and sometimes with SituatedQA, to evaluate LLM outputs on long-form or ambiguous QA. Some papers evaluate on its test se

nodes.name: AssoCiAm
nodes.definition: A multimodal benchmark designed to evaluate the associative ability of MLLMs by presenting multiple-choice visual association tasks where ambiguity has been systematically mitigated.

nodes.name: ATIS
nodes.definition: The Air Travel Information System (ATIS) dataset, used for intent classification to source seed samples and evaluate downstream classifier performance.

nodes.name: AudioBench
nodes.definition: Open-ended QA benchmark assessing LALMs’ performance on a range of auditory processing tasks, including speech and environmental sound understanding.

nodes.name: AudioCaps
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats AudioCaps as an audio captioning benchmark or dataset of AudioSet clips paired with human-written captions or natural-language descriptions. Some definitions add that the captions are in English, and one specifies one or two captions per clip. A smaller line of work also describes it as being used for audio retrieval, semantic retrieval, or question answering, and a few papers refer to AudioCapsZS, AudioCaps-QA, or an AC evaluation set.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use AudioCaps to measure 3 behavioral indicators and no constructs. The dominant use is for Audio captioning: papers evaluate generated captions on AudioCaps, sometimes on its test set, and report conventional captioning metrics such as CIDEr. More occasionally, papers report it as measuring Cross-modal retrieval through semantic retrieval on AudioCaps, and Text-to-audio generation through evaluation on the AC evaluation set, so the measurement claims extend beyond captioning but remain centered on it.

Space of uses. In practice, papers most often use AudioCaps alongside Clotho or Clotho v2, and some also report it together with MusicCaps or Clo

nodes.name: AUTO-J
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, AUTO-J is most commonly treated as an automated judge, described as a 13B-parameter generative judge model or more generally an LLM-based evaluator. Definitions emphasize its use for rating response helpfulness on a numeric scale, while another description says it is used to assess the distance between a reference answer and a model output. Some authors distinguish AutoJ Eval, an in-domain pairwise-comparison test set from AUTO-J with 58 prompts and 1,392 response pairs labeled by human annotators as win, tie, or lose.

What it is claimed to measure. The reported measurement claims are narrow rather than spread across many targets: papers link AUTO-J to one construct, Helpfulness, and one behavioral indicator, Text summarization. For Helpfulness, papers use it to provide ratings on a 1 to 10 scale for model responses; for Text summarization, a paper reports using the Auto-J model to measure the win rate of model-generated summaries against human summaries.

Space of uses. Papers position AUTO-J mainly as an automated evaluator or judge. It is used alongside other evaluators in some reports, including joint rating with GPT-4, and one paper mentions it

nodes.name: Auto-J test set
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage treats Auto-J as a curated or automated judge benchmark. Papers describe it as a benchmark for meta-evaluation of LLM judges, and one definition also presents it as a benchmark for evaluating reward models, particularly by examining correlation with human expert judgments. A smaller line of description specifies "Auto-J (Eval-P test set with ties)," a pairwise evaluation benchmark that includes tie outcomes.

What it is claimed to measure. The descriptions say papers use Auto-J to evaluate LLM judges and reward models, with the most common framing centered on meta-evaluation of judges and a secondary framing centered on correlation with human expert judgments. Papers in this literature do not link it to any named constructs or behavioral indicators, so the record does not attach it to any explicitly named construct.

Space of uses. Where usage is described, one paper places AutoJ alongside RewardBench and MT-Bench as one of three reward model benchmarks. Another paper uses the tie-enabled version for pairwise evaluation, describing it as a way to test judge models on indeterminate comparisons.

Concerns raised. One paper note

nodes.name: AutoDAN
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats AutoDAN as an automated jailbreak attack procedure, most commonly a genetic algorithm, sometimes a hierarchical genetic algorithm, that searches for adversarial prompts intended to bypass LLM safety alignment. Definitions vary on how the attack is characterized: some call it white-box, gradient-based, query-based, instruction-based, or optimization-based, and some emphasize that it produces high-perplexity, human-readable, or stealthier prompts through controllable text generation or an added loss term. A smaller line of work instead treats AutoDAN as a public dataset for jailbreak detection, or as an attack represented within the EasyJailbreak dataset for transferability evaluation.

What it is claimed to measure. The reported measurement claims concentrate on a small set of targets.
