Papers use AutoDAN to measure one construct, adversarial robustness, and one behavioral indicator, jailbreak resistance, rather than a broad range of targets. In these uses, it appears as a jailbreak attack for evaluating robustness, with one paper explicitly reporting adversarial robustness as attack success rate and another evaluating robustness

nodes.name: Automated interpretability
names: Automated simulation evaluation with language models
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most definitions describe it as an LLM-based evaluation procedure for SAE latents: the judge is given activating examples, works from a proposed or generated textual feature description, and is used to predict when the latent will activate or to score the explanation's predictive success. Some papers specify GPT-4o or GPT-4o-mini, one paper frames the protocol as automated interpretability classification with validation on new activating and non-activating examples, and another describes a related automated simulation evaluation that measures the correlation between actual activations and activations predicted from the explanation. One paper also applies the same prompting pattern to explain meta-latent groupings.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, claims converge on one construct: it measures Interpretability and explainability. The linked evidence describes this as evaluating the human-understandability of learned latents with an LLM as judge, or as using GPT-4o for automated interpretability classification. It is linked to one construct and no behavioral indicators, so the reported measurement claims do not spread across multiple constructs.

Space of use

nodes.name: AUXDATASET
nodes.definition: A 10-terabyte web-text corpus used as a proxy for proprietary training data when searching for exact substring matches in model outputs.

nodes.name: AV-Human
nodes.definition: The human-annotated subset of AVUT containing 698 videos and 1,734 question-answer pairs created by trained annotators.

nodes.name: bAbI
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing usage is to treat bAbI as a reasoning benchmark. One description presents it as a benchmark of 20 synthetic tasks designed to evaluate basic aspects of reasoning, while another uses it more narrowly for deductive reasoning questions requiring inference from a short passage; a smaller line of description cites it as a set of prerequisite toy question-answering tasks and an example of a language-based reasoning benchmark.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the papers, bAbI is used to measure three constructs and one behavioral indicator. The most common claim is that it measures Logical reasoning, and smaller lines of work also report it as measuring Spatial reasoning and Temporal reasoning; one paper further links it to the behavioral indicator Coreference resolution, describing the benchmark as assessing "spatial and temporal reasoning, deduction, and coreference resolution" ("BABILong: Testing the Limits of LLMs with Long Context Reasoning-in-a-Haystack").

Space of uses. In use, papers link bAbI to one other measurement instrument, BABILong, and characterize that instrument as extending bAbI. Outside that relation, authors employ

nodes.name: BABILong
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, BABILong is most commonly described as a long-context benchmark for evaluating reasoning over extended narratives or extremely long documents, and some papers describe it as a long-context extension of bAbI. Definitions emphasize that models must find, retrieve, and reason over multiple supporting facts or pieces of evidence distributed through a long sequence, sometimes described as randomly placed in the context. The descriptions are not identical: one paper presents it as a benchmark of 5 tasks, while another says it includes 20 reasoning tasks.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link BABILong to 8 constructs and 3 behavioral indicators. The prevailing measurement claim is long-context reasoning, and papers also use it to measure commonsense reasoning, inductive reasoning, logical reasoning, long-context understanding, and 3 other constructs, so the reported construct links spread across several reasoning-related targets. For behavioral indicators, papers link it to counting, information retrieval, and single-hop question answering, and related evidence also mentions fact chaining, deduction, and handling lists or sets among its tasks.

Space of us

nodes.name: BabiStories
nodes.definition: A dataset of simple stories, which is a reproduction of TinyStories, used for training and evaluating language models in a controlled setting.

nodes.name: BabyAI
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, BabyAI is most commonly described as a procedurally generated, partially observable 2D gridworld for evaluating agent capabilities on tasks given as textual or visual goals, especially navigation and object manipulation. Some authors describe it more specifically as an interactive 20x20 grid with a limited sight range for text-based agent evaluation, while others frame it as a grid-world benchmark with discrete navigation and interaction actions where an agent completes an instruction, including evaluation on instructions rephrased with synonyms.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link BabyAI to 3 behavioral indicators and no constructs. The prevailing measurement use is Navigation, with papers describing grid-world tasks in which agents navigate and interact with objects, and one paper referring to five types of navigation tasks. Smaller lines of work use it to measure Embodied planning and Instruction following, including natural language goal instructions such as Go to the tile (3,2) and Look behind the green locked door.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it. Across the papers, BabyAI is used as an embodied or grid-world ev

nodes.name: BACE
nodes.definition: A dataset from the MoleculeNet benchmark for the binary classification task of predicting binding results for the inhibition of human β-secretase 1.

nodes.name: Bamboogle
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, Bamboogle is most commonly treated as a question answering benchmark for complex questions, often described as a multi-hop dataset involving web search and reasoning over multiple documents. It is also used as an unseen or out-of-domain evaluation task for RAG-tuned models, and one paper describes it as containing questions that Google answers incorrectly. The descriptions vary on coverage: some authors place it with datasets "derived from Wikipedia documents", while another says it "requires knowledge beyond Wikipedia's coverage".

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link Bamboogle to 2 behavioral indicators and 2 constructs. The prevailing usage is to measure multi-hop question answering, with a broader question answering framing also recurring. A smaller line of work reports that it measures compositional reasoning and generalization, including out-of-domain generalization.

Space of uses. Papers usually use Bamboogle directly alongside other question answering benchmarks, especially HotPotQA, MuSiQue, 2WikiMultiHopQA, WebQuestions, and PopQA. They variously position it as one of several established or widely used multi-hop QA datasets, as an unseen

nodes.name: BANKING77
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats BANKING77, also written as BANKING, Banking-77, or Banking77, as a banking-domain intent classification benchmark built from customer banking or online banking queries and organized into 77 intent classes or categories. Definitions commonly frame it as a fine-grained intent detection or classification resource for domain-specific language understanding, and some papers place it among benchmarks used for in-context learning. A smaller line of work uses the name Bank77 and describes it instead as an intent discovery dataset for finding unknown intents in user utterances.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link BANKING77 to 1 construct and 2 behavioral indicators. The prevailing reported use is to measure Intent classification, with additional papers using it to measure Text classification; one paper also reports it as measuring Reasoning, describing evaluations of reasoning accuracy with prompt engineering and demonstration selection across BANKING77 and other benchmarks. Taken together, papers more often report it as measuring classification behaviors than as measuring a construct.

Space of uses. Across papers, BANKING77 of

nodes.name: BBBP
nodes.definition: A dataset from the MoleculeNet benchmark for the binary classification task of predicting whether a molecule can penetrate the blood-brain barrier.

nodes.name: BBH Object Counting
nodes.definition: A benchmark task used here as one of the general evaluation tasks for zero-shot and in-context performance.

nodes.name: BBQ
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the dominant framing is of BBQ as a question-answering benchmark or dataset for evaluating social bias, societal bias, or stereotype reliance. Most definitions describe ambiguous and disambiguated, or ambiguous and unambiguous, contexts with closed-ended answer choices, often multiple choice; one paper specifies three labels, Stereotyped, Unknown, and Unstereotyped. Papers also differ on scope and size, describing nine social dimensions or protected groups in several places, but also 11 bias categories in one account, and giving totals of 31,372 question-answer pairs or 58,492 unique questions in others.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers connect BBQ to three constructs and one behavioral indicator. The prevailing use is to measure social bias: several papers describe it as evaluating biases against protected classes or groups, sometimes across nine social dimensions. Smaller lines of work use it to measure stereotyping and, in one case, social reasoning, while papers also report it as measuring question answering when bias is operationalized through QA tasks.

Space of uses. Papers usually position BBQ as a direct evaluation benchmark for bias, for e

nodes.name: BBQ Lite
nodes.definition: The Bias Benchmark for Question Answering (BBQ) Lite, a subset of the full benchmark designed to measure social biases in language models across various demographic axes.

nodes.name: BC5CDR
nodes.definition: A document-level biomedical relation extraction dataset focused on binary relations between chemical and disease entities.

nodes.name: Beaver
nodes.definition: An enterprise database benchmark with 99 tables used to evaluate ambiguous and unanswerable semantic parsing tests in a real-world setting.

nodes.name: BeaverTails
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, BeaverTails is most commonly described as a safety and alignment evaluation dataset or benchmark for model responses, especially response safety classification. Papers describe it in several ways: as a human-preference dataset with helpfulness and harmlessness annotations for query-answer interactions, as advice queries with candidate answers across 14 harm categories, as human annotations over a 14-category safety taxonomy, and as either a 700-prompt evaluation set or a larger collection of 330k annotated sentences; one paper also refers to safe and unsafe samples from its alignment data.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use BeaverTails to measure 4 constructs and 3 behavioral indicators, so the reported targets are spread across multiple safety-related concepts. The prevailing claims are that it measures harmlessness and helpfulness, while other papers use it to measure safety, harmful content generation, harmful content detection, and response harmfulness classification; one paper also reports BeaverTails as related to safety alignment by using its safe samples for an alignment task.

Space of uses. Papers commonly use BeaverTails alon

nodes.name: BeaverTails-Evaluation
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing description is of an evaluation benchmark for LLM harmlessness on harmful instructions, with definitions emphasizing both content safety and refusal behavior. One paper also refers to its 700 test prompts that can potentially elicit harmful responses. A smaller line of work uses the name Beaver-eval for a public dataset of malicious instructions and describes it as one source used to construct SG-Bench.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to two constructs and no behavioral indicators. The dominant use is to measure Harmlessness: papers say it is used to evaluate a model's harmlessness, and one paper uses its harmful-response prompts for that purpose. A smaller usage treats it as measuring Safety more broadly, with one paper listing it among benchmarks that address safety.

Space of uses. Most papers use it directly as an evaluation benchmark. One paper includes it in a broader safety benchmark suite alongside XSTest, while another treats Beaver-eval as source material for constructing SG-Bench. No measurement instruments are linked to it.

nodes.name: BEHAVIOR-1K
nodes.definition: A benchmark of 1,000 everyday activities in realistic simulation, cited to show that daily tasks often involve multiple objects.

nodes.name: BEIR
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most commonly, papers describe BEIR as a diverse collection or suite of retrieval datasets for evaluating out-of-domain or zero-shot performance. Definitions vary in expansion and scope, calling it the "Benchmark for Evaluation of Information Retrieval", "Benchmarking-IR", or, in one paper, "Broad Evaluation of Information Retrieval", and they frame it as supporting retrieval, ranking, and re-ranking across domains. The reported coverage also varies by paper: one refers to 18 datasets from various domains, another to 14 public retrieval datasets excluding MS MARCO, another to 15 retrieval tasks, and one definition names Covid, SciFact, DBpedia, and NFCorpus.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the linked claims, papers use BEIR to measure two constructs, Generalization and Retrieval effectiveness, and two behavioral indicators, Information retrieval and Ranking. The dominant measurement claim is information retrieval, usually framed as zero-shot or out-of-domain retrieval performance, while a smaller line of work uses it to assess generalization. More specific uses, reported by individual papers, treat it as measuring retrieval effectiveness or evaluating ranking and

nodes.name: Belebele
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most papers describe Belebele as a multilingual reading comprehension benchmark, usually framed as multiple-choice questions about short passages. Several definitions specify 122 language variants or language-dialect combinations, sometimes with parallel passages and questions, while one paper describes it as translated into over 200 languages and another uses official Moroccan and Egyptian dialect sets. Some papers describe its passages as sourced from FLORES-200, and one refers to it as another benchmark extended from the FLORES family of multilingual evaluation resources.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link Belebele to two behavioral indicators and two constructs. The prevailing usage is to measure machine reading comprehension, and a smaller line of work uses it for multiple-choice question answering; at the construct level, papers also report it as measuring natural language understanding and cross-lingual alignment. Overall, the measurement claims center on reading comprehension, with the broader construct claims spread across those two constructs.

Space of uses. Papers usually use Belebele as part of a broader benchmark suite rather than on its own. It a

nodes.name: BFCL
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most papers describe BFCL, often expanded as the Berkeley Function-Calling Leaderboard or Benchmark for Function Calling, as a comprehensive benchmark or leaderboard for evaluating LLM function calling or tool use. Definitions variously say it covers single-turn, multi-turn, hallucination, and executable settings, or Non-live, Live, Multi-turn, and Hallucination samples, with evaluation through AST, executable function evaluation, and relevance detection. A smaller line of description presents it as assessing an agent's ability to reason and execute function calls across programming languages and application domains, including simple, multiple, and parallel calls. Some papers also mention real-world APIs and use-cases such as agent tasks and enterprise workflows, and refer to BFCL v2 and BFCL v3.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, the claims cluster around tool use and closely related function-calling ability. BFCL is linked to 2 behavioral indicators and 1 construct, and papers most often use it to measure Tool use, with additional uses for Hallucination and for the construct Tool use ability. The supporting language stays near whether models can invoke fun

nodes.name: BFCL-v2
nodes.definition: A tool-calling benchmark with Python-style tool call data across four categories (Simple, Multiple, Parallel, Parallel Multiple) to evaluate a model's ability to correctly call tools.

nodes.name: BIG-bench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across these papers, the prevailing usage treats BIG-bench as a large, collaborative evaluation suite, usually described as Beyond the Imitation Game, with 204 or over 200 diverse tasks for probing the capabilities and limitations of language models. Definitions vary in emphasis: some highlight reasoning and comprehension tasks, others say it covers both traditional NLP tasks and novel problems, and several papers use narrower slices such as BIG-BENCH LITE, the BBII subset, the verb tense subset, or single tasks such as Date Understanding and Sudoku.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link BIG-bench to 6 constructs and 4 behavioral indicators, so its reported measurement role spans multiple targets. The construct links are measured_by claims, with papers using it to measure Calibration, Emergent abilities, Logical reasoning, and Social bias, plus 2 other constructs. Behavioral uses are also reported, including Multi-digit multiplication, plus 3 other indicators, and one of those behavioral links is only related rather than measured by the benchmark.

Space of uses. Most commonly, papers position BIG-bench as a broad benchmark or as a source of subtasks for targeted

nodes.name: BIG-Bench Hard
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats BIG-Bench Hard, usually abbreviated BBH, as a challenging subset of BIG-Bench or the Beyond the Imitation Game benchmark, centered on tasks that were difficult for contemporary language models and used for reasoning-focused evaluation. Most descriptions emphasize complex, multi-step, logical, or general reasoning, while some also frame it as covering language understanding, world knowledge, compositionality, and generalization; one paper describes 23 multiple-choice tasks and 4 free-form generation tasks, while others report 21, 23, or 27 tasks, sometimes across 23 task types. Some papers use only selected BBH subtasks, including DATE and Navigate, and one paper refers to BBH-COT as a chain-of-thought variant.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link BBH to 20 constructs and 7 behavioral indicators, so its measurement claims are spread across many targets rather than converging on a single one. The dominant claim is that it measures reasoning, followed by general ability, natural language understanding, chain-of-thought reasoning, and complex reasoning. The remaining links extend to 15 other constructs and the 7 behavioral i

nodes.name: BIG-Bench Logical Deduction
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats BIG-Bench Logical Deduction as a BigBench task or benchmark for deduction. Definitions describe it as testing deductive reasoning from a set of premises, evaluating logical reasoning capabilities, and, in one description, as a symbolic reasoning benchmark for deduction over structured premises. Papers also refer to it simply as Logical Deduction or as Deduction from the BigBench collaborative benchmark.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to measure logical reasoning and symbolic reasoning, and the linked construct set contains two constructs; no behavioral indicator is linked to it. One framing places it among logical reasoning tasks, while another uses it within a symbolic reasoning evaluation, so the measurement claims span both of those constructs rather than a single reported target.

Space of uses. Papers include it within broader reasoning suites. One logical reasoning evaluation pairs it with AR-LSAT, ZebraLogic, FOLIO, and other reasoning tasks, while another symbolic reasoning setup pairs it with Date Understanding and other BigBench datasets. Papers also relate it to one other measurement instrument, BI

nodes.name: bigcode-evaluation-harness
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, bigcode-evaluation-harness is most commonly treated as an evaluation framework or harness for running code-generation benchmarks and assessing models on coding tasks. Definitions largely converge on that role, while a smaller variation describes it as a software library, one paper highlights its use for HumanEval because it supports safe code execution, and others mention use with benchmarks such as HumanEval and MBPP and for assessing non-Python versions of APEval.

What it is claimed to measure. The measurement claims are narrow rather than spread across many targets: papers use it to measure Code generation, and it is linked to one behavioral indicator and no constructs. In relationship evidence, authors describe using the Bigcode Evaluation Harness as the evaluation tool for coding tasks, with one example reporting Pass@1 and Pass@10.

Space of uses. Papers commonly use it alongside Eleuther Harness or lm-evaluation-harness, with those paired with natural language tasks while bigcode-evaluation-harness is used for coding tasks; one paper also says evaluations are run under the same settings with lm-evaluation-harness and bigcode-evaluation-harness

nodes.name: BigCodeBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, BigCodeBench is most commonly described as a code generation benchmark centered on completion or function completion tasks that require correct use of library APIs and multiple function calls. Definitions also portray it as a Python benchmark with execution-based evaluation over 1,140 fine-grained, rich-context, multi-tool-use tasks drawn from 139 libraries and 7 domains, while another paper describes 148 function completion problems requiring multiple Python libraries. Some papers further describe it as covering diverse problems from cryptography to data visualization, and a smaller usage mentions the BigCodeBench Leaderboard plus the BigCodeBench-Hard and BigCodeBench-full subsets.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link BigCodeBench to 3 behavioral indicators and 1 construct. The prevailing use is to measure code generation, with papers describing it as a benchmark for code generation, a harness for running and evaluating LM-written code, and a dataset attached to the code generation task. A recurring secondary framing says it measures tool use and instruction following, especially in tasks that require using tools and following complex instruc

nodes.name: BigCodeBench-Complete
nodes.definition: The structured-docstring version of BigCodeBench used to evaluate code generation from verbose programming prompts.

nodes.name: BigCodeBench-Instruct
nodes.definition: A variant of BigCodeBench that evaluates instruction-to-code generation, where models generate code from short, natural-language-oriented instructions.

nodes.name: BigMath
nodes.definition: Dataset of multi-step math problems used to evaluate tutoring models, containing problems of medium-to-high difficulty with annotated solve rates.

nodes.name: BioASQ
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most descriptions treat BioASQ as a biomedical question answering dataset or challenge, often tied to scientific literature or PubMed abstracts, while some definitions frame it more broadly as a resource for biomedical semantic indexing and question answering. Papers describe its contents in several ways, including human expert-written question-answer pairs with ground truth documents based on PubMed abstracts, and they vary in the question types they foreground: several mention factoid, list, and yes/no questions, while another mentions factoid, list, and summary questions. A narrower use focuses on Tasks 2B, 3B, and 4B and disregards long answers to assess the precision of short responses.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, the prevailing measured use is question answering. BioASQ is linked to 2 behavioral indicators, Question answering and Text generation, and to no constructs; the more common claim is that it measures question answering, including PubMed-based biomedical QA for specialized domains and biology and medicine tasks. A smaller line of work also uses it to measure text generation in the biology and medicine domain.

Space of uses. Papers commo

nodes.name: Biography
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, Biography is most commonly described as a fact-seeking long-form generation dataset centered on biographical information, used to evaluate factual consistency in narrative generation. Some authors instead describe it as a test set for biography generation used for out-of-domain evaluation of factuality. The descriptions differ on format details: one gives 181 prompts, while another says it uses a subset as the test set with 183 questions about biography generation.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link Biography to 2 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator. The linked behavioral indicator is biography generation, and papers also use Biography to measure factuality, including by reporting FactScore on the out-of-domain Biography dataset. A smaller line of work uses a synthetic Biography dataset to measure knowledge forgetting.

Space of uses. It is linked to 1 other measurement instrument, FActScore, which papers use alongside Biography for fact-verification. In that pairing, Biography is positioned as the out-of-domain test set and FActScore as the corresponding evaluation strategy; elsewhere papers simply refer to evaluating a biography-generation ta

nodes.name: BIRD
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across definitions, BIRD is most commonly described as a large-scale, cross-domain, database-grounded benchmark for Text-to-SQL, sometimes written as BIRD-Bench. Papers repeatedly describe it as built from real-world databases and as more challenging than Spider or previous datasets, citing complex databases or schemas, difficult questions, external knowledge, dirty values, varied cell formats, challenging value mappings, and value-based reasoning. The descriptions vary in detail: some give train, development, and test split sizes, some focus on the dev set and a 20240627 BIRD-dev version, and others describe it as containing over 12,751 question-SQL pairs across 95 databases spanning 37 domains.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link BIRD to 2 behavioral indicators and 2 constructs. The prevailing usage is to measure Text-to-SQL: several papers evaluate Text-to-SQL tasks or generation on BIRD, including settings where models generate SQL or SQLite programs from natural language instructions over real-world databases. A smaller line of work uses it to measure schema linking, and individual papers report it as measuring cross-domain generalization and table reasonin

nodes.name: BiRdQA
nodes.definition: A benchmark dataset for question answering that, according to the paper's analysis, contains a non-trivial amount of answer ambiguity.

nodes.name: BizsRE
nodes.definition: BizsRE is a multilingual dataset created using machine translation models like Google Translate.

nodes.name: BLEnD
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, BLEnD is most commonly described as a culture-specific benchmark dataset for everyday knowledge questions across diverse cultures and languages, with data sourced from authentic, real-world scenarios in native-speaking regions. Some authors describe it through particular parts or settings, such as its short-answer questions in native languages, while another presents it as a traditional annotation setup in which annotators answered fixed questions from 500 pre-defined templates for Indonesian and Nigerian cultural knowledge. One description also expands the name as the Benchmark of Linguistic and ENcyclopedic Diversity and frames it around culturally diverse inputs.

What it is claimed to measure. Most descriptions frame BLEnD as testing everyday knowledge across cultures and languages. One paper describes it as designed to measure model performance on culturally diverse inputs, and another uses it to assess generalization of cultural awareness in LLMs. Papers do not explicitly link BLEnD to any constructs or behavioral indicators.

Space of uses. BLEnD appears as a standalone evaluation benchmark in the papers. Reported uses include adopting and exte

nodes.name: BLiMP
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, BLiMP is most commonly treated as an English benchmark or corpus of linguistic minimal pairs for grammaticality or acceptability judgments. It is usually described as minimally different pairs of acceptable and unacceptable, or grammatical and ungrammatical, sentences, with evaluation based on identifying the grammatical item or assigning it lower perplexity; several definitions present it as a multi-task benchmark spanning syntax, morphology, and semantics. Most descriptions specify 67 subtasks, datasets, or paradigms with 1,000 pairs each, often grouped into 12 categories or phenomena and sometimes summarized as 67,000 pairs, and some add that the examples are template-generated or built from manually crafted sentence templates, though one paper describes 13 linguistic phenomena. A smaller usage selects an 11-dataset subset that can be used for text generation.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link BLiMP to 5 constructs and no behavioral indicators. The prevailing claim is that it measures syntactic competence, with papers using it for syntactic generalization, grammatical learning, and grammatical competence; some papers also report it as measuri

nodes.name: BLINK
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats BLINK as a multi-image benchmark for reasoning over multi-view and spatial relationships. Some papers describe it more broadly as a benchmark, or collection, of 14 visual perception tasks across indoor, outdoor, and natural scenes, noting that some tasks involve multiple images, such as visual similarity and multi-view reasoning, and that the suite also includes relative depth, spatial reasoning, and correspondence tasks. A smaller set of definitions frames it as testing whether multimodal large language models can perceive as well as see, and one paper specifically refers to its Jigsaw and Multi-view reasoning splits.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link BLINK to 4 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator. Among the measured_by links, the prevailing claim is that it measures multi-image reasoning, with additional work using it to measure visual perception and, through a reported BLINK spatial reasoning task, spatial reasoning; a smaller line of work also cites it as measuring hallucination. Overall, the reported measurement claims spread across several targets rather than converging on a single construct.

Space

nodes.name: Blocksworld
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, Blocksworld is most commonly treated as a classical planning benchmark or domain in which blocks are rearranged from an initial or source configuration to a specified goal configuration, often on a table and sometimes with the explicit rule that only one unstacked block may be moved at a time. Definitions vary at the margins: some papers formulate it in PDDL, some describe it as a symbolic or commonsense domain, some call it a planning dataset, and some place it within PlanBench or describe it as a real-world task planning benchmark that corresponds to path-finding in a state transition graph. A smaller line of work also defines task-specific splits inside it, including plan-length train, validation, and test partitions and in-distribution versus out-of-distribution block-count ranges.

What it is claimed to measure. Its reported measurement use is concentrated on Planning. Papers use Blocksworld to measure 2 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator, with Planning the prevailing target, described in relationship evidence as a real-world task planning benchmark, a symbolic planning problem, or simply the planning task on which a framework is evaluated. Smalle

nodes.name: BMIKE-53
nodes.definition: BMIKE-53 is a multilingual dataset created using LLMs for translation.

nodes.name: BOLD
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats BOLD as a benchmark or evaluation dataset for open-ended language generation, with English text prompts used for bias benchmarking. Definitions most often describe prompts spanning five domains, and one definition specifies Wikipedia-derived prompts covering race, gender, profession, religion, and politics. Papers variously frame it as evaluating fairness, social bias, and toxicity, and some describe it as assessing sentiment or the affective properties of model outputs for diverse demographic prompts.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link BOLD to 2 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator. The dominant measurement claim is that it measures social bias, with several papers describing it as a bias evaluation dataset or as designed to evaluate social biases in generative language models. A smaller line of work uses it to measure gender bias, and one paper reports that it measures biased content generation, so the reported links are concentrated on social bias with narrower uses for the other targets.

Space of uses. In use, papers place BOLD alongside other generation and fairness benchmarks, most commonly RealToxic

nodes.name: Bongard Problems
nodes.definition: A family of abstract reasoning tasks consisting of two sets of six images each, where the model must identify the conceptual rule distinguishing the sets and express it in natural language.

nodes.name: BookMIA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most papers treat BookMIA as a benchmark or dataset of book excerpts, passages, or paragraphs, used as a membership inference benchmark and as a dataset for evaluating memorization. Descriptions differ in detail: some specify excerpts from copyrighted books, some specify books published after model knowledge cutoffs or model release as "unseen" examples, and one description pairs those with passages from popular books as memorized examples. One paper also characterizes it as a prior temporal detection dataset, and another use selects only the "unseen" subset.

What it is claimed to measure. The recorded measurement claims are narrow rather than spread across many targets: papers link BookMIA to one construct, Memorization, and one behavioral indicator, Pre-training data detection. One paper uses it to measure memorization by treating 2023 book excerpts as unseen text and passages from popular books as memorized examples, while another uses it to evaluate pre-training data detection methods.

Space of uses. When papers situate BookMIA relative to other evaluations, they present it as one benchmark among others, using it alongside WikiMIA, BookTection, ArXivTection, and P

nodes.name: Books3
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the dominant framing treats Books3 as a large collection of books used as a dataset or benchmark for language model evaluation, especially on long-context or extremely long documents. Definitions describe it as an extensive collection of books, a large-scale dataset of text from a wide variety of books, or a large dataset for long-context sequences, and one paper uses the spelling Book3.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link Books3 to one construct and no behavioral indicators, and the measurement claims converge on length generalization. In that usage, Books3 is reported as measuring length generalization through language modeling evaluations such as perplexity, with one quoted passage stating that perplexity on Books3 'shows better extrapolation' and another using Books3 among real-world datasets when reporting length generalization gains.

Space of uses. Most papers position Books3 as an evaluation dataset or benchmark rather than as a standalone target. It is used alongside PG-19 or Gutenberg in evaluations over book datasets and alongside Arxiv in model-performance experiments, and papers link it to one other measurement instrument, The Pil

nodes.name: BookSum
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, BookSum is most commonly described as a benchmark dataset for book or long-form narrative summarization on long inputs. The descriptions differ on granularity and content: some papers frame it as evaluating summaries of entire books, others call it a collection of datasets for long-form narrative summarization over novels, plays, and stories, and another describes each example as a book chapter paired with a summary of that chapter’s content.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use BookSum to measure Text summarization, and it is linked to one behavioral indicator in total. No constructs are linked to it, so the reported measurement claims are concentrated on summarization rather than spread across multiple constructs.

Space of uses. Papers use BookSum as a standalone evaluation dataset rather than alongside other linked measurement instruments. In the descriptions, it is used to assess long-context and long-response generation capabilities, to evaluate models on a book summarization dataset, and to evaluate takedown methods in the books domain.

nodes.name: BookTection
nodes.definition: A membership inference benchmark for book excerpts used as a prior temporal detection dataset.

nodes.name: BoolQ
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, BoolQ is most commonly described as a dataset or benchmark of yes/no question answering grounded in a passage, with each example consisting of a question, a passage, and a binary answer. The prevailing descriptions frame it as reading comprehension or binary QA, and many also present it as testing commonsense reasoning or factual reasoning. Some authors further emphasize that the questions are naturalistic, naturally occurring, or unprompted, and one paper specifies 15,942 examples split into 9,427 train, 3,270 validation, and 3,245 test; smaller departures describe it as a closed-book QA dataset or use it as a text classification task.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use BoolQ to measure 9 constructs and 8 behavioral indicators. At the construct level, the prevailing framing is commonsense reasoning, with recurring use for natural language understanding, reasoning, short-context ability, and benchmark overfitting, plus 4 other constructs. At the behavioral level, it is most often reported as measuring machine reading comprehension, question answering, zero-shot question answering, multiple-choice question answering, and downstream task performance

nodes.name: BorderLines
nodes.definition: Benchmark containing multilingual questions about disputed territories, designed to test model consistency and handling of conflicting claims.

nodes.name: BRIGHT
nodes.definition:
What it is. In the papers, BRIGHT is treated as a text retrieval benchmark centered on reasoning in retrieval. It is described as focusing on complex queries that require deep reasoning to identify useful passages beyond simple semantic relevance, and one abstract presents it as the first text retrieval benchmark requiring intensive reasoning to retrieve relevant documents.

What it is claimed to measure. Its measurement claims are narrow rather than spread across many targets. Papers link BRIGHT to 1 construct, Information retrieval ability, and to no behavioral indicators; the recorded relationship is that Information retrieval ability is measured by BRIGHT. In those uses, BRIGHT is presented as benchmarking retrieval on challenging, reasoning-intensive queries.

Space of uses. Papers position BRIGHT as a challenging benchmark for evaluating retrieval systems. In LimRank: Less is More for Reasoning-Intensive Information Reranking, it is used alongside FOLLOWIR, with BRIGHT covering reasoning-intensive retrieval and FOLLOWIR covering instruction-following retrieval. No other measurement instrument is linked to it in the recorded relationships.

nodes.name: C3
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, C3 is most commonly treated as a Chinese reading comprehension benchmark or dataset, described both as Chinese Cloze-style Reading Comprehension and as a Chinese machine reading comprehension benchmark for evaluating reading comprehension in Chinese. A smaller variation in wording presents it as a modern Chinese reading comprehension dataset used to test the generalizability of a procedure, while other descriptions add that it covers Chinese passages and questions and is a free-form multiple-choice dataset.

What it is claimed to measure. Its measurement claims are concentrated rather than spread across many targets: papers link it to one behavioral indicator and one construct. One paper uses it to measure Machine reading comprehension, describing C3 as a free-form multiple-choice Chinese machine reading comprehension dataset, and another reports it as measuring Chinese language understanding through Chinese comprehension.

Space of uses. Papers use C3 as an evaluation benchmark or test set. One study explicitly marks it as a test benchmark, and another uses it to evaluate a procedure on a modern Chinese reading comprehension dataset to demonstrate th

nodes.name: C4
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across these papers, the prevailing description of C4 is the Colossal Clean Crawled/Common Crawl corpus, a large cleaned web-text dataset derived from Common Crawl. Some authors refer specifically to the English subset, the validation split or c4 en-validation, including C4 validation loss, while a smaller line uses C4 Corpus for neuron-activation analysis inputs. Beyond evaluation, papers also use it for pre-training or continual language modeling, as calibration data for quantization or pruning, and as a prompt source for text generation.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link C4 to 2 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator. The prevailing use is to measure language modeling ability, typically through perplexity or validation loss on C4 or its validation split; a smaller line of work uses it to measure generative ability, and papers also use it to measure the behavioral indicator text generation. Taken together, the linked claims center on language modeling and generation.

Space of uses. Most papers position C4 as one of several evaluation corpora, commonly alongside WikiText2 and often PTB when reporting perplexity. Several papers also use it as calibration data,

nodes.name: C-Eval
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most commonly, papers treat C-Eval as a comprehensive Chinese benchmark or evaluation suite for foundation models. Definitions repeatedly describe it as multi-level and multi-discipline, usually spanning 52 subjects or disciplines, with one paper adding four difficulty levels and another specifying 13,948 multiple-choice questions; some definitions say it covers STEM, humanities, and social sciences or broader academic and professional domains, and targets factual knowledge, foundational knowledge, reasoning, and problem solving. A smaller set of papers describes particular slices of the suite, such as the logic subject or eight selected subjects, and some frame its use as assessing multi-task language understanding in a cross-linguistic setting or Chinese instructions.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link C-Eval to 3 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators. The prevailing usage is to measure General ability, with several papers placing CEval among general-domain or authoritative benchmarks and reporting changes on C-Eval as changes in general abilities; smaller strands use it to measure Cross-lingual generalization and Multilingual understanding, and to evaluate

nodes.name: CAA
nodes.definition: Contrastive Attribute Analysis, a method and dataset for extracting steering vectors using binary-choice contrastive prompts and evaluating model behavior via output probabilities and GPT-4o mini scoring.

nodes.name: Caltech101
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most definitions describe Caltech101 as an image or object classification dataset or benchmark with 101 object categories, used for visual recognition evaluation. Papers also place it in broader evaluation setups, for example among nine benchmark datasets for image classification and in an 11-dataset image-classification suite, and one paper reports 4,331 test images from 101 classes.

What it is claimed to measure. Across reported links, papers use it to measure one behavioral indicator and two constructs. The recurring claim is that it measures image classification, while a smaller line of work reports that it is used to measure personalization and generalization, so the recorded uses extend beyond a single construct.

Space of uses. Papers commonly include it as one dataset within larger image-classification suites rather than presenting it on its own. It appears alongside datasets such as ImageNet, StanfordCars, Flowers102, CUB, and OxfordPets, with several other classification datasets also used, and papers position it in zero-shot and linear-probe evaluations as well as in multi-dataset studies of personalization and generalization.

nodes.name: Candle
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, CANDLE is most commonly treated as a cultural benchmark or dataset, though one definition instead describes Candle as an international research program studying human values that is used with the World Values Survey to select sensitive topics. Papers describe the benchmark form as a multiple-choice question benchmark, larger in sample size at 1.1M, with a focus on cultural norms and commonsense knowledge. Another paper frames it as a prior dataset for culture-specific items that extracts cultural commonsense knowledge from web-scale corpora.

What it is claimed to measure. The recorded measurement claims are concentrated rather than spread across many targets: papers link it to 1 construct, Cultural knowledge, and to no behavioral indicators. In that usage, it is reported as measuring general cultural knowledge, and no other construct is linked to it here.

Space of uses. Papers most often position it as part of a suite of cultural evaluations. One study says it is used with CULTURALBENCH as a multiple-choice benchmark, and another places it alongside CULTURALBENCH and ETICOR for general cultural knowledge evaluation; elsewhere it is used as

nodes.name: CapsBench
nodes.definition: A benchmark used to evaluate fine-grained captioning and visual perception.

nodes.name: CASIE
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, CASIE is most commonly described as a cybersecurity event extraction or event detection dataset. Definitions converge on its focus on cybersecurity incidents and on a five-event-type schema, often named as Databreach, Phishing, Ransom, Discover, and Patch; some descriptions also note trigger and argument annotations, while others frame it as identifying security-related incidents from technical reports and news or as evaluating event detection in cyber threat reports.

What it is claimed to measure. Across these papers, CASIE is presented as a benchmark dataset rather than as an instrument explicitly said to measure a named construct or behavioral indicator. No papers link it to any constructs or behavioral indicators, so the descriptions emphasize task evaluation instead of an explicit measurement claim.

Space of uses. Papers use CASIE in experiments on event extraction and event detection, and one study places it within a broader benchmark suite by reporting results on "16 IE benchmarks" (Label Drop for Multi-Aspect Relation Modeling in Universal Information Extraction). No other measurement instrument is linked to it, so the papers present it with

nodes.name: CausalVLBench
nodes.definition: A comprehensive benchmark for evaluating visual causal reasoning in Large Vision-Language Models, encompassing tasks of causal structure inference, intervention target prediction, and counterfactual prediction.

nodes.name: CB
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, CB is most commonly described as CommitmentBank, a SuperGLUE natural language inference or textual entailment task, dataset, or benchmark built around short premise-hypothesis pairs or short texts. The prevailing descriptions frame it as evaluating entailment, with some definitions adding whether a sentence or statement commits the author to a belief or entailment, one definition specifying entailment, contradiction, or neutrality, and another highlighting pragmatic inference. A smaller usage treats it more broadly as a general NLU task for textual entailment or related classification evaluation.

What it is claimed to measure. In the reported literature, CB is only claimed to measure one behavioral indicator, Natural language inference, and it is not tied to any construct. That use converges on NLI rather than spreading across several targets, sometimes stated as textual entailment and, in one definition, textual entailment with an emphasis on pragmatic inference.

Space of uses. Papers usually use CB as one task within larger evaluation bundles rather than in isolation. The only instrument relationship reported for CB is a related link to SuperGLUE,

nodes.name: CC3M
nodes.definition: The Conceptual Captions 3M dataset, containing millions of image-URL/alt-text pairs, used for pretraining and, in this paper, for a large-scale compositional evaluation.

nodes.name: CCBench
nodes.definition: A benchmark used to assess the general multimodal capabilities of models.

nodes.name: CelebA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, CelebA is most commonly described as a large-scale face or facial-attributes dataset, often said to contain over 200K celebrity images with 40 binary attribute annotations. Some authors narrow the setup to predicting 'Blond Hair' with 'Male' as the sensitive attribute, while others treat it as facial attribute recognition data or as source images for emotion-comparison examples. One paper also preprocesses CelebA by cropping, resizing, and flattening pixel values into space-separated numerical sentences for language-model inputs.

What it is claimed to measure. Recorded measurement claims are narrow. Papers link CelebA to one behavioral indicator, Image reconstruction, and link it to no constructs or other measurement instruments. In that usage, a paper evaluates reconstruction quality on CelebA and reports results on CelebA alongside LSUN-horse and LSUN-bedroom.

Space of uses. Papers position CelebA mainly as an evaluation dataset, with uses that include fairness evaluation, robustness testing under spurious correlations and distribution shifts, facial attribute recognition, early-exit diffusion image generation, and disentanglement, reconstruction, and

nodes.name: CFBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, CFBench is most commonly described as a complex instruction-following benchmark built around instructions with multiple constraints. Definitions emphasize coverage of a comprehensive range of constraint types, including format, content, and style. A less common description presents it as a comprehensive Chinese benchmark for evaluating constraint comprehension and following capabilities through a multi-dimensional evaluation framework, and shared definitions also state that it is evaluated with GPT-4 as a judge.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link CFBench to 2 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator. The prevailing claim is that it measures Complex instruction following ability, with papers using it for evaluations where instructions consist of multiple constraints and for comprehensive assessment of model capabilities. Papers also use it to measure Instruction following ability and the behavioral indicator Instruction following, so the linked uses are concentrated on instruction following, especially formulations centered on multiple constraints.

Space of uses. Papers commonly use CFBench alongside FollowBench, and some evaluations also place it w

nodes.name: CHAIR
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the cited definitions, CHAIR is most commonly described as a benchmark, metric, or evaluation protocol for hallucination in image captioning, especially object hallucination. The prevailing description is that it compares generated captions with ground-truth objects or annotations and computes the proportion or ratio of mentioned objects that are not present in the image; most papers describe instance and sentence variants, written as CHAIRi and CHAIRs, for hallucinated object instances and sentences containing hallucinated objects. Some papers describe the same evaluation as open-ended captioning on sampled MS-COCO images, and a smaller line describes broader sentence- or image-level checks such as object, attribute, count, or positional correctness.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link CHAIR to five behavioral indicators and one construct. The most frequent use is to measure Hallucination, Image captioning, and Object hallucination, with papers saying that CHAIR assesses hallucination by comparing objects mentioned in generated captions with ground-truth or reference objects; additional links treat it as measuring Text generation in open-ended generation

nodes.name: Charades-STA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats Charades-STA as a benchmark dataset for temporal grounding: localizing a video segment, or identifying the start and end timestamps of video content, from a natural language sentence. A smaller framing describes it as a temporal activity localization dataset, and one definition says it is used as a source for event-caption alignment and temporal video grounding. One paper summarizes it as "temporal activity localization via language query" (E.T. Bench: Towards Open-Ended Event-Level Video-Language Understanding).

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use Charades-STA to measure temporal grounding, the only linked behavioral indicator; no constructs are linked to it. The relationship evidence describes this as evaluating the ability to locate specific activities described in text, including moment retrieval with recall at IoU thresholds and tasks that identify start and end timestamps from a query sentence. In these links, claims converge on this single behavioral indicator rather than spreading across multiple constructs.

Space of uses. Papers position Charades-STA mainly as an evaluation benchmark or test set for tempora

nodes.name: ChartGaze
nodes.definition: A high-precision eye-tracking dataset for chart question answering that pairs chart images and questions with human gaze annotations.

nodes.name: ChartMimic
nodes.definition: Benchmark for evaluating chart-to-code generation, assessing both code executability and chart fidelity through high-level (image similarity) and low-level (code similarity) metrics.

nodes.name: ChartQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, ChartQA is most commonly described as a benchmark or dataset for question answering about charts, often framed as requiring both visual perception and logical reasoning. Several descriptions make that more specific by mentioning item comparison, counting, numerical computation, or even complex, multi-step logical and visual reasoning; a smaller set of papers frames it more broadly as figure QA or a document task dataset, and one paper refers to it as VQAChart. Papers also vary in how they describe its contents, including real-world charts from sources such as Statista and Pew Research, human-created and LLM-augmented questions in one account, and a mixture of handwritten and machine-generated questions in another; one reuse paper states that it contains 18K real-world charts and 23.1K human-authored QA pairs.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link ChartQA to 5 behavioral indicators and 4 constructs, so its reported measurement role is spread across chart-specific evaluation and broader multimodal assessment rather than concentrated on a single target. Among behavioral indicators, papers most often use it to measure chart and diagram understanding

nodes.name: ChartX
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing framing is a chart-to-code benchmark for assessing text and data reproducibility in generated code, with attention to accurate rendering of chart content. A smaller usage treats ChartX as a figure description dataset, specifically as one of the sampled sources for F2TBenchmark. One paper further describes it as providing fixed instructions to GPT-4 to write code that procedurally generates predefined chart types and settings in bulk.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link ChartX to 2 behavioral indicators and no constructs. The recorded uses are Code generation, where one paper says it evaluates MLLMs' code generation ability, especially for text and data reproducibility, and Figure-to-text generation, where another paper lists it under figure description. The measurement claims therefore spread across 2 behavioral indicators rather than converging on a construct.

Space of uses. In chart-to-code work, papers use ChartX alongside ChartMimic and Plot2Code as one of the benchmarks on which methods are evaluated. In figure-to-text work, one paper uses it differently, as one of the sampled sources for F2TBenchmark.

Concerns raised. A

nodes.name: CharXiv
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly describe CharXiv as a benchmark or comprehensive evaluation suite for chart understanding, built from real-world charts drawn from arXiv papers or preprints. Definitions emphasize natural, challenging, and diverse charts, and one description specifies 2,323 charts with hand-curated descriptive and reasoning questions. A smaller framing presents it as a benchmark dataset for evaluating complex visual reasoning through the interpretation of charts and graphs across scientific and technical domains.

What it is claimed to measure. The linked measurement claims center on 2 behavioral indicators, Chart and diagram understanding and Complex reasoning question answering, and no construct is linked to CharXiv. One paper says it provides "a more realistic and faithful measure of progress" in MLLM chart understanding. The same paper also presents it as measuring complex reasoning question answering through reasoning questions that require synthesizing information across complex visual elements.

Space of uses. No other measurement instrument is linked to CharXiv. Papers present it as an evaluation benchmark: one study reports results on its validation set to

nodes.name: Chatbot Arena
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, Chatbot Arena is most commonly described as a crowdsourced evaluation platform or leaderboard for open-ended conversational tasks, where two anonymous model outputs are compared side by side, users cast pairwise preference votes, and Elo or related rankings are produced from these battles. Some authors instead refer to the underlying evaluation set, datasets, or prompts built from real-world user-assistant interactions and human preference labels, and one paper calls LM Arena, formerly LMSYS Chatbot Arena, a community-driven collection of such head-to-head matchups. A smaller line of work describes it as an evaluation framework or benchmark that uses LLMs to judge responses, and one paper uses the similar name ChatArena for a multi-agent language game framework.

What it is claimed to measure. Most measurement claims center on Human preference alignment and Conversational ability, with papers using Chatbot Arena to evaluate human preferences in open-ended, real-time, or multi-turn dialogue. It is linked to 5 constructs, most often Human preference alignment, Conversational ability, Multilingual understanding, Positional bias, and Reasoning, and to 5 behav

nodes.name: Chatbot Arena Conversations
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, it is most commonly described as the LMSys Chatbot Arena Conversations dataset, a collection of real-world user preferences gathered from user votes on pairwise comparisons of LLM outputs. Another paper describes it as a dataset of human-annotated pairwise model comparisons.

What it is claimed to measure. The papers do not link this dataset to any named constructs or behavioral indicators. In their own descriptions, they use it to capture real-world user preferences and to compute human agreement with LLM judge decisions.

Space of uses. One paper positions it as a usage dataset for broader real-world preferences, stating that "the usage datasets capture broader real-world preferences" (HumT DumT: Measuring and controlling human-like language in LLMs). Another uses it to compute human agreement and evaluates agreement on held-out test instructions not used for model selection; the papers do not link it to other measurement instruments.

nodes.name: ChatEval
nodes.definition: ChatEval is an evaluation framework that uses multi-agent collaboration to assess model outputs, aiming for preference judgments that are better aligned with humans.

nodes.name: ChatRAG-Bench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats ChatRAG-Bench as a benchmark for retrieval-augmented generation and conversational question answering. Definitions differ on the task framing: some describe short-context evaluation within a 4K token window, including "nine short context (within 4K) tasks," while others describe multi-turn question answering with retrieved text chunks; another paper-level description presents it as a benchmark for evaluating RAG and conversational question answering capabilities of LLMs.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to one behavioral indicator, conversational question answering, and to no constructs. The recorded measurement claim uses ChatRAG-Bench to measure conversational question answering, with one paper describing it as "the RAG benchmark for conversational QA tasks within a 4K context window," so the reported measurement use is focused on that single behavioral target rather than spread across multiple constructs or indicators.

Space of uses. Papers use it as an evaluation benchmark for conversational QA and short-context RAG settings. One paper states, "We use ChatRAG Bench (Liu et al., 2024) as our benchmark for

nodes.name: ChEBI-20
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, ChEBI-20 is most commonly described as a dataset used in molecule-text tasks: one definition says it is widely used for text-based molecule generation, where a model generates a molecular sequence from a textual description, and another says it contains molecules and their corresponding text descriptions for molecule-text alignment and caption generation. A smaller line of work describes it differently, as the molecular graph VQA ChEBI-20 used for fine-tuning and copyright-tracking evaluation. One paper also reports using a restricted subset by selecting molecules containing fewer than 100 atoms.

What it is claimed to measure. The recorded measurement use is concentrated rather than spread across many targets: papers use ChEBI-20 to measure one behavioral indicator, Molecule captioning, and it is not linked to any constructs. The evidence is performance-focused, with papers reporting the performance of molecule captioning on ChEBI-20 and using it to test molecule description generation.

Space of uses. Papers use ChEBI-20 both as a direct evaluation dataset and in conjunction with other resources. In captioning evaluations, it is used alongs

nodes.name: CheckEval
nodes.definition: Checklist-based LLM-as-a-Judge framework that evaluates text generation by decomposing criteria into binary yes/no questions and computing scores based on the proportion of affirmative responses.

nodes.name: ChemProt
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most commonly described as a labeled biomedical dataset for identifying chemical-protein interactions in scientific literature, papers frame ChemProt as a relation extraction, relation/classification, or text classification dataset. One description specifies five relation classes, while a smaller line of work treats it as a named entity detection source with annotations for chemical compounds and gene or protein-related objects, and derives ChemProt-Chem and ChemProt-Gene for detecting chemicals and genes.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link ChemProt to one behavioral indicator and no constructs. The recorded measurement claim is concentrated on relation extraction: one paper reports that Relation extraction is measured by ChemProt, describing it as a chemical-protein dataset featuring five relation classes.

Space of uses. In the reported uses, ChemProt appears with other biomedical datasets in evaluation and as a downstream domain adaptation task. Papers place it alongside RCT, PubMedQA, MQP, and USMLE, and another paper repurposes it for named entity detection through derived subsets for chemicals and genes.

nodes.name: CHENGYU-BENCH
nodes.definition: A comprehensive benchmark for Chinese idiom understanding, assessing models across three tasks: evaluative connotation (sentiment classification), appropriateness (misuse detection), and open cloze (idiom generation in context), with 2,937 human-verified examples covering 1,765 idioms.

nodes.name: Chess
nodes.definition: An evaluation task using a textual representation of the game of chess, where the agent's goal is to make moves that result in victory.

nodes.name: ChID
nodes.definition: A large-scale cloze test dataset for Chinese idiom comprehension, containing 581k passages with multiple-choice idiom selection tasks from news, novels, and essays.

nodes.name: CHIME
nodes.definition: CHIME (Hsu et al., 2024), a taxonomy-generation baseline that extracts claims and frequent entities and prompts an LLM to build a hierarchical structure.

nodes.name: Chinese SimpleQA
nodes.definition: A benchmark introduced by Alibaba Group comprising concise, fact-oriented questions to assess the factual capabilities of LLMs in a Chinese context, focusing on general knowledge.

nodes.name: CIFAR-10
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the dominant framing is a standard or benchmark image classification dataset, most often described as 60,000 32x32 color images in 10 classes. Some definitions compress this to a 10-class object recognition or small-image classification benchmark, while a few papers describe it more situationally, for example as a testbed for clustering comparisons, automated accuracy prediction under synthetic and natural shifts, dirty-sample detection under poisoned or noisy samples, or zero-shot adversarial robustness.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to 1 behavioral indicator and 3 constructs. The prevailing use is to measure Image classification, with studies using it for finetuning, zero-shot classification, linear probing, and downstream performance evaluation. One paper each also uses it to measure Generalization, Label noise robustness, and Multimodal alignment, so the measurement claims are centered on image classification rather than distributed evenly across several constructs.

Space of uses. Most papers position it as one benchmark within broader image-evaluation suites, often alongside CIFAR-100 and ImageNet, and also with STL-10, CUB, and Pla

nodes.name: CIFAR-100
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, it is most commonly described as an image classification benchmark or dataset with 100 classes, often framed as 100 fine-grained object classes or categories. Some definitions add that it consists of 32x32 color images, and several papers explicitly contrast it with CIFAR-10 as a more challenging or more complex setting; papers also use both spellings, CIFAR-100 and CIFAR100.

What it is claimed to measure. The prevailing use is to measure Image classification, which is the only linked behavioral indicator and the one attached to most papers, covering finetuning, zero-shot classification, linear probing, transfer learning, and downstream performance. Papers also link it to 2 constructs, Generalization and Multimodal alignment: one paper evaluates the generalization of discrete prompts on CIFAR-100, and another reports alignment scores on CIFAR-100 to measure multimodal alignment. Overall, the measurement claims concentrate on image classification rather than spreading evenly across constructs.

Space of uses. Papers do not link it to other measurement instruments directly, but they commonly use it inside multi-benchmark evaluation suites, most often along

nodes.name: CipherChat
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, the prevailing usage treats CipherChat as a jailbreak method or framework that encodes prompts in cipher, most often a Caesar cipher, to bypass safety alignment and probe a model's intrinsic or inherent characteristics. Most descriptions emphasize the cipher-based prompting itself, with some specifying a three-letter Caesar shift, while one paper gives a fuller procedural account: user instructions are enciphered, a system prompt and few-shot enciphered demonstrations are added, the model is checked for responding in cipher, and the output is then deciphered.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link CipherChat to one construct and no behavioral indicators. The linked construct is Safety alignment, and the claims converge on that single target: papers use CipherChat to measure or examine safety alignment, including a report that it is used to "systematically examine the generalizability of safety alignment to non-natural languages, ciphers" (GPT-4 Is Too Smart To Be Safe: Stealthy Chat with LLMs via Cipher).

Space of uses. Papers use it by encoding user instructions or questions in cipher, commonly a Caesar cipher with shift three, and the

nodes.name: CiteSeer
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, CiteSeer is most commonly described as a real-world citation network dataset of scientific papers or publications. The prevailing usage treats its nodes as papers and uses the dataset for node classification evaluation. A smaller line of work describes a modified CiteSeer for link prediction, with nodes from the original node classification test set removed.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use CiteSeer to measure two behavioral indicators, with claims concentrated on node classification and a smaller usage for link prediction. Across the papers, the dominant framing is that CiteSeer measures node classification, while a single paper reports it as evaluating link prediction. No constructs are linked to it.

Space of uses. Papers commonly place CiteSeer in multi-dataset evaluations, most visibly alongside Cora and, in broader benchmark suites, PubMed, ogbn-arXiv, ogbn-products, and Wiki-CS. In node classification studies it appears as one dataset among several benchmark datasets, while in the link prediction use it is paired with a modified Cora and treated as an evaluation dataset after removing the original node classification test nodes.

nodes.name: CLAIR
nodes.definition: Automated evaluation metric that measures overall caption quality by assessing alignment with reference captions using GPT-4o.

nodes.name: ClassEval
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, the dominant framing is of a benchmark for object-oriented, class-level code generation. Definitions describe it as assessing object-oriented programming skills and class-level code generation abilities, and some descriptions add that it is a manually crafted collection of 100 class-level Python code generation tasks. Papers also describe it as containing 100 standalone programming tasks from seven domains, and one evaluation setup further specifies 100 classes, 410 methods, an average of 33 tests per class, and 8 tests per method.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to measure one behavioral indicator, code generation, and do not link it to any constructs. The prevailing claim is specifically class-level code generation: papers state that they evaluate code LLMs on class-level code generation using ClassEval and list it with other benchmarks for code generation, so the reported measurement role converges on that single indicator rather than spreading across multiple targets.

Space of uses. In use, papers usually place it within broader benchmark suites, listing it alongside LiveCodeBench, BigCodeBench, HumanEval, MBPP, and DevEval

nodes.name: CLEVR
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing description is a visual reasoning benchmark or diagnostic dataset for compositional language and elementary visual reasoning. Some authors frame it differently in use: as an image classification task, as a scene reasoning domain for inductive program synthesis, or as an image-based dataset for multimodal data understanding and retrieving. One definition specifically uses the val split, described as containing 15,000 images with cylinders, cubes, and spheres that vary in number, size, and color.

What it is claimed to measure. Claims about what it measures are narrow. Papers link it to 1 construct and no behavioral indicators, and the only recorded measurement claim is that it measures Complex reasoning: one paper refers to "complex reasoning in CLEVR" when using it alongside Winoground. Across papers, measurement claims center on a single construct rather than multiple targets.

Space of uses. Papers use it in several roles rather than a single fixed protocol. It appears alongside SVHN and EuroSAT in image classification experiments, alongside REGEX and LOGO as one of three inductive program synthesis domains, and as a multimodal data under

nodes.name: Climate-FEVER
nodes.definition: Climate-FEVER is a benchmark for fact checking focused on claims about climate change.

nodes.name: CLIMATEVIZ
nodes.definition: A benchmark dataset for scientific fact-checking over climate-related charts, containing 49,862 claims paired with 2,896 expert-curated visualizations, each labeled as support, refute, or not enough information, and including structured knowledge graph explanations.

nodes.name: CLINC150
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the dominant description of CLINC150 is an English intent classification or intent detection benchmark organized around 150 intents or classes. Papers agree on the 150-class framing but describe the domain structure differently: one definition says 10 domains, another says multiple domains such as banking and travel, and one paper describes 150 classes across five domains. A smaller line also treats it as an intent clustering benchmark, and one dataset-construction paper uses sample sentences from CLINC while extracting 40 intents from five domains for culturally adapted utterance generation.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link CLINC150 to one behavioral indicator, Intent classification, and one construct, Reasoning. The prevailing usage is to measure Intent classification or intent detection: one relationship says it is designed for intent classification, and another paper reports using CLINC for intent detection. A smaller usage reports it as measuring Reasoning, describing evaluations of reasoning accuracy across benchmark datasets that include CLINC150.

Space of uses. Papers often position CLINC150 as one benchmark among several. It appears a

nodes.name: ClinTox
nodes.definition: A dataset from the MoleculeNet benchmark for the binary classification task of predicting the clinical toxicity of a molecule.

nodes.name: Clotho
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats Clotho as an audio captioning dataset or benchmark, though one definition also frames it as a benchmark for audio-retrieval tasks. Definitions consistently describe paired audio and text data: audio clips with natural-language captions, with some papers adding that it contains long, diverse soundscapes, is human annotated, and is composed of FreeSound samples. A more detailed description gives 6,000 clips of 15 to 30 seconds with five captions per clip, and another paper likewise describes each sample as having five different captions. A smaller usage refers to Clotho Caps, and one retrieval study explicitly uses the original, non-spatial version.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link Clotho to one construct and two behavioral indicators. The prevailing claim is that it measures Audio captioning, with several papers evaluating models on Clotho for audio captioning tasks; a smaller line of work uses it to measure Cross-modal retrieval through semantic retrieval scores such as R@1, R@5, and R@10. One paper also reports that Clotho measures Generalization, stating that a model trained solely on AudioSet’s audio excerpts and

nodes.name: ClothoAQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly describe ClothoAQA as an audio question-answering benchmark or dataset derived from Clotho for evaluating audio-language understanding. One definition gives more detail, describing 1,991 audio samples from the Clotho dataset, each paired with six crowdsourced questions and corresponding answers, and says it is used to evaluate natural language understanding of general audio content.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the papers here, its use converges on one target: Audio question answering is measured by ClothoAQA. Papers link it to one behavioral indicator, Audio question answering, and to no constructs; the definitions also describe it as evaluating audio-language understanding or natural language understanding of general audio content.

Space of uses. No other measurement instrument is linked to it. Papers instead use it as the audio question-answering evaluation, with one paper listing it among "foundational benchmarks" and another using it as the audio question-answering task in a broader audio evaluation setup.

nodes.name: CLTE
nodes.definition: Chinese Language Teaching Evaluation benchmark, a comprehensive framework assessing LLMs across three dimensions: basic knowledge, international teacher certification, and teaching practice via student model improvement.

nodes.name: CLUTRR
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers variously describe CLUTRR as a benchmark or dataset for reasoning over family relations in text. Definitions frame it as relation inference from partial graph descriptions in natural language, family relation path reasoning, and a diagnostic benchmark for inductive reasoning from text; other descriptions call it a deductive reasoning dataset requiring multi-hop reasoning over family relationships or a relational reasoning benchmark based on human-written stories about family relations. One paper also uses the CLUTRR dataset as the basis for the NoRa-Commonsense task.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link CLUTRR to 4 constructs and no behavioral indicators.
