The recorded measured_by links span Inductive reasoning, Logical reasoning, Multi-hop reasoning, and Relational reasoning, so papers use it to measure several reasoning constructs rather than a single one. In the relationship evidence, authors describe it as a "deductive reasoning dataset requiring multi-hop reasoning over family relationships" and as a relational reasoning benchmark.

Space of uses. Papers do not link CLUTRR to any other measurement instrument. Instead, they position it as a direct bench

nodes.name: CMATH
nodes.definition: Chinese math reasoning benchmark assessing mathematical problem-solving ability in Chinese, evaluated under 0-shot or 5-shot settings.

nodes.name: CMB-Clin
nodes.definition: Open-domain medical Q&A dataset used to assess LLM performance on real-world clinical consultation scenarios.

nodes.name: CMB-Exam
nodes.definition: Medical examination dataset used for evaluating LLMs on standardized medical knowledge and clinical reasoning tasks.

nodes.name: CMedCalc-Bench
nodes.definition: CMedCalc-Bench is a Chinese clinical calculation benchmark containing 69 calculators and 1,143 real-world patient cases for evaluating medical LLMs.

nodes.name: CMMLU
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most papers treat CMMLU as a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating knowledge and reasoning in Chinese, often under the name Chinese Massive Multitask Language Understanding. Several descriptions add that it covers 67 subjects from basic to advanced or professional levels, and one definition says it uses multiple-choice questions across diverse academic disciplines. A smaller set of papers frames it more specifically as Chinese language understanding or proficiency, while a few describe it differently, including as multilingual or multimodal, and one quoted passage mentions a 5-shot setting.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, its measurement claims are spread across 4 constructs and no behavioral indicators, rather than concentrating on a single target. The most frequently linked constructs are Chinese language understanding, general ability, reasoning, and generalization. Papers use it to assess "Chinese language understanding," to check that general capabilities are not compromised, and in one out-of-domain evaluation to test generalization.

Space of uses. CMMLU is usually used as one component of a broader evaluation suite, commonly alongside MMLU and al

nodes.name: CNN/DailyMail
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, CNN/DailyMail is most commonly described as a large-scale news summarization dataset or benchmark, built from CNN and Daily Mail articles paired with human-written summaries. The prevailing description is for text or abstractive summarization, with summaries often described as multi-sentence and sometimes as highlights; a few papers further frame it as a single-document generative summarization corpus. Definitions differ in minor details, with one paper describing it as containing just over 300k unique news articles and another using article-highlight pairs from it for citation attribution.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to 4 behavioral indicators and 2 constructs. The dominant measurement claim is Text summarization, and papers also use it to measure Abstractive summarization, News summarization, and Text generation. Construct links are narrower: one paper uses it to measure Out-of-distribution generalization by treating CNN/DailyMail as an OOD test set for summarization, and another reports it as measuring Text generation quality, with quality measured by ROUGE-2 for CNNDM.

Space of uses. No other measurement instrument is linked to it.

nodes.name: CoBia
nodes.definition: A suite of lightweight adversarial attacks using constructed conversations to expose hidden societal biases in LLMs, with two main variants: history-based constructed conversation (HCC) and single-block constructed conversation (SCC).

nodes.name: COCO Caption
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the dominant framing is a COCO-based image captioning benchmark or dataset used to evaluate models that generate textual descriptions for images. Definitions vary at the margins: some describe a large-scale captioning benchmark, some describe the captioning portion of a broader object detection and segmentation dataset with multiple short human-written descriptions per image, and some use it as a source of prompts for text-to-image evaluation. Specific descriptions mention the validation set, the validation split, and the karpathy-test split, and one paper describes over 330,000 images with more than 1.5 million captions and five human-generated captions for each image.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to 2 behavioral indicators and 2 constructs. The prevailing usage is to measure image captioning, with several papers explicitly evaluating caption tasks on this benchmark and reporting caption metrics such as BLEU, METEOR, CIDEr, SPICE, ROUGE-L, or BertScore. Smaller lines of work also use it to measure image generation, fine-grained perception, and visual understanding.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it. Papers usuall

nodes.name: CodeAttack
nodes.definition: CodeAttack is a jailbreak attack method used to embed harmful requests in seemingly harmless task templates.

nodes.name: CodeContests
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats CodeContests as a benchmark dataset for competitive programming and code generation, commonly described as featuring challenging code competition problems. Some definitions further specify that each problem includes multiple human-written correct and incorrect solutions, while others describe it as requiring a code solution from a problem specified in natural language together with public test case descriptions. Papers also note variant uses, including splitting test problems into basic and advanced levels by difficulty tag and evaluating on selected subsets.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers most often use CodeContests to measure code generation, the most frequently linked behavioral indicator, and it is also linked to coding. On the construct side, papers report it as measuring algorithmic reasoning and functional correctness, so the claims span 2 behavioral indicators and 2 constructs. The linked targets remain tightly code-focused, with one paper placing it among complex algorithmic reasoning tasks and another describing evaluation against private test cases to check execution correctness.

Space of uses. No

nodes.name: Codeforces
nodes.definition: A competitive programming website that serves as a longitudinal benchmark for code generation, featuring problems released over time with public and private test cases for evaluation.

nodes.name: CodeMixBench
nodes.definition: A comprehensive benchmark introduced in this paper for evaluating the performance of LLMs on multilingual code-mixing, encompassing eight tasks and 18 languages.

nodes.name: CodeNet
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across these papers, the dominant framing treats CodeNet as a source corpus for code research rather than as a standalone evaluation protocol. Definitions describe it as a competitive programming dataset, and one paper adds that it "collects data from online judge websites" (DCE-LLM: Dead Code Elimination with Large Language Models). Papers use different slices of that corpus: C++ submissions and problem trajectories for constructing PIE, material for extending a code-to-code semantic search evaluation set to more languages, and source code for a dead-code dataset.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers do not link CodeNet to any constructs or behavioral indicators through explicit measurement claims. Instead, they report it as underlying data for resources such as PIE, a code-to-code search evaluation set, and a dead-code dataset, so these papers do not state that CodeNet measures a particular construct.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it. The recurring use is as upstream data for derived resources: one paper states, "Our dataset is constructed based on performance-improving edits (PIE) made by human programmers in a range of competitive programm

nodes.name: CodeParrot
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the definitions, CodeParrot is treated as a code-focused evaluation resource. One paper describes it as a "code-oriented long-context benchmark" used in length extrapolation evaluation, while another describes it as a code modeling dataset for assessing language modeling performance on programming language sequences.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to one construct, Length generalization, and to no behavioral indicators. The measurement claim is concentrated on that single construct: one paper places CodeParrot within "length extrapolation on six long benchmarks," so it is reported as measuring Length generalization.

Space of uses. The papers position it in two ways: as part of a long-benchmark suite for length extrapolation, and as a dataset on which perplexity is evaluated. In the latter use, one paper evaluates perplexity on it alongside PG19 and Proof-Pile, and beyond that co-usage papers do not report links to other measurement instruments.

nodes.name: CodeQL
nodes.definition: A semantic code analysis engine used as an instrument to automatically detect security vulnerabilities in the code generated by a model.

nodes.name: CodeSearchNet
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, the dominant framing is as a benchmark for function-level text-to-code retrieval, using natural language queries and code snippets. Some papers describe it more broadly as a dataset for evaluating code generation and understanding, with code snippets and natural language descriptions across multiple programming languages. One definition presents the CodeSearchNet Corpus as covering six programming languages and containing over 2 million (comment, code) pairs extracted from GitHub.

What it is claimed to measure. Measurement claims stay with behavioral indicators rather than constructs: papers link it to three behavioral indicators, Code generation, Code retrieval, and Ranking, and to no constructs. Papers use it to measure Code retrieval and Ranking in text-to-code retrieval evaluation, while one paper reports using the CodeSearchNet dataset for Code generation evaluation.

Space of uses. Where evaluation setups are described, it appears alongside AdvTest as a text-to-code retrieval benchmark. Some work also uses code search and summarization datasets from CodeBERT that are described as extensions of CodeSearchNet, while another paper selects

nodes.name: CodeXGLUE
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, CodeXGLUE is most commonly treated as a benchmark for code tasks, but its scope is described in more than one way. Some authors present it narrowly as a code-to-text benchmark for evaluating natural-language explanations of code snippets, where the task is to generate a natural language explanation from a code snippet. Others describe it more broadly as a benchmark suite for code intelligence, including code defect detection in C, or as a public benchmark for programming language models with single-file code completion datasets such as PY150 and Github Java Corpus.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link CodeXGLUE to 2 behavioral indicators and no constructs. The prevailing recorded use is to measure vulnerability identification, through the CodeXGLUE code defect detection task in C, which papers describe as a binary defect detection setting with a label for whether code is insecure and may attack software systems. A smaller usage links it to code summarization, with papers reporting that they use the CodeXGLUE benchmark for that task.

Space of uses. No other measurement instrument is linked to it. Papers use it directly as a benchmark,

nodes.name: CoGS
nodes.definition: Construction Grammar Schematicity corpus, a dataset of 10 construction types used to evaluate model performance on partially substantive and schematic constructions.

nodes.name: Coin Flip
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats Coin Flip as a simple symbolic or rule-based reasoning benchmark in which a model tracks a coin's state through a sequence of flips and non-flips and gives a binary answer, usually Yes or No or the final face, heads or tails. Definitions often make the setup explicit, including questions with named agents performing or not performing flips; one paper uses versions with 2, 3, and 4 rounds of potential flips, and another describes scalable versions. A smaller line of work instead describes it as testing simple probabilistic scenarios or as a knowledge-free reasoning task without factual knowledge.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use Coin Flip overwhelmingly to measure Symbolic reasoning: it is linked to one construct, Symbolic reasoning, and the recurring description is a symbolic reasoning benchmark or dataset. The measurement claims converge on that single construct rather than spreading across many. It is also linked to one behavioral indicator, State tracking, but only as a related indicator rather than as something the benchmark directly measures.

Space of uses. Papers commonly pair Coin Flip with Last Letter when ev

nodes.name: CoIR
nodes.definition: CoIR, a benchmark covering code-to-text, code-to-code, hybrid code retrieval, and text-to-code retrieval tasks.

nodes.name: CoLA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, CoLA is most commonly described as the Corpus of Linguistic Acceptability, usually framed as a GLUE task or benchmark for grammatical or linguistic acceptability. The prevailing usage treats it as a binary, often single-sentence classification task in which English sentences are judged as grammatically acceptable or unacceptable, or simply grammatically correct. Some papers use the surface names GLUE-COLA or GLUE-CoLA, and one definition instead describes GLUE-CoLA as a dataset of text from books and journal articles used in TDDBench.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use CoLA to measure 3 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators. The dominant behavioral claim is that it measures grammatical acceptability judgment, with papers describing the task as deciding whether a sentence is acceptable or unacceptable; a smaller line of work also treats it as text classification. At the construct level, it is most often used to measure natural language understanding, and some papers also report it as measuring general ability and generalization, so its measurement claims are spread across several constructs rather than centered on one alone.

Space of uses. Most p

nodes.name: Cola (compositional image retrieval)
nodes.definition:
What it is. The prevailing usage treats Cola or COLA as a text-to-image retrieval benchmark for compositional ability or compositional reasoning: captions describe relations between entities, or specific configurations of attributes and objects, and the task is to retrieve the correct image from candidate images or from a database with distractor images. Definitions commonly emphasize composing objects with their relations or retrieving images with the correct attribute-object configuration. One quoted passage using the same name, COLA, refers instead to the Corpus of Linguistic Acceptability for linguistic acceptability, so papers do not use the label uniformly.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the papers that link it to other entities, Cola is used to measure compositional reasoning, and that is the only linked construct. No behavioral indicators are linked to it, so the reported measurement claims converge on compositional reasoning rather than spreading across multiple targets.

Space of uses. Papers use it as part of compositional evaluation. One paper describes an evaluation procedure that calculates perplexity between a caption and all candidate images and then selects

nodes.name: COLD
nodes.definition: Chinese Offensive Language Dataset, a benchmark dataset that categorizes sentences into fine-grained types such as personal attacks and anti-bias expressions concerning race, gender, and region.

nodes.name: Collab-Overcooked
nodes.definition: A benchmark built on the Overcooked-AI game, designed to evaluate LLM-based multi-agent systems on 30 collaborative tasks that require resource isolation and asymmetric task knowledge.

nodes.name: CollegeMath
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most descriptions frame CollegeMath as a college-level mathematical reasoning benchmark, often presented as a more challenging or out-of-domain evaluation set beyond high school material. Papers variously describe it as college-level math problems, advanced topics beyond the high school curriculum, or an out-of-domain benchmark for generalization; one description in DART-Math specifies 2,818 test problems drawn from 9 textbooks across 7 domains such as linear algebra and differential equations. A smaller line of description differs: Logits-Based Finetuning calls it "a mathematical reasoning dataset created using MathScale, containing two million math question-answer pairs."

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use CollegeMath mainly to measure mathematical reasoning. Across recorded relationships it measures 2 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator: mathematical reasoning is the prevailing target, while a smaller number of papers use it to measure generalization and mathematical problem solving. The reported measurement claims therefore center on reasoning, with only limited extension to other targets.

Space of uses. Papers typically use CollegeMath inside multi-bench

nodes.name: CommonGen
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across definitions, CommonGen is most commonly described as a commonsense-guided or constrained text generation benchmark or dataset. Papers consistently define the task as generating a coherent or natural sentence from a given set of concepts or keywords, often three to five per example, with the sentence required to contain all of them; some frame this as describing an everyday scenario or as a struct-to-text task, and one definition notes that inflections of the keywords are allowed. A smaller usage modifies the data split by restricting the training set to samples having "man" while leaving validation and test unchanged.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use CommonGen to measure 3 constructs and 3 behavioral indicators, so its reported measurement role is spread across several targets rather than centered on one. The linked constructs are Constraint satisfaction, Evaluation ability, and Generative ability, and the linked behavioral indicators are Commonsense generation, Constrained decoding, and Text generation. In these uses, papers describe CommonGen as a way to compare text generation and evaluation abilities, to evaluate commonsense generation and constrain

nodes.name: Commonsense170K
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing description is a large-scale commonsense reasoning dataset for supervised fine-tuning, usually presented as a mixture or combination of eight datasets or subtasks. Definitions variously call it a training dataset, a benchmark, or a language evaluation suite, and several specify components such as BoolQ, PIQA, SIQA, HellaSwag, Wino or WinoGrande, ARC-Easy or ARC-Challenge, and OpenBookQA or OBQA. One paper also describes it as "a comprehensive collection of commonsense reasoning questions" with 170020 training samples and 400 validation samples.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to 1 construct, Commonsense reasoning, and to no behavioral indicators, so the reported measurement claims concentrate on a single construct. The dominant wording is that Commonsense reasoning is measured by Commonsense170K, while some papers frame the connection more loosely by describing fine-tuning or evaluation on a combined dataset of eight commonsense reasoning tasks.

Space of uses. Most papers use it as the resource on which models are fine-tuned for commonsense reasoning, often before evaluation on downstream tasks or benchmarks, and some explic

nodes.name: Commonsense reasoning benchmark
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing description is a composite commonsense evaluation suite built from eight tasks or datasets. Definitions usually list BoolQ, PIQA, SIQA, HellaSwag, WinoGrande, and other ARC/OBQA components, and describe either aggregated training with individual test evaluation or a suite for commonsense question answering and inference. A smaller difference is whether ARC is split into ARC-e and ARC-c or referred to more broadly as ARC, and one definition frames the suite as covering factual, physical, social, and scientific inference.

What it is claimed to measure. Its measurement claims are focused: papers link it to one construct, Commonsense reasoning, and one behavioral indicator, Catastrophic forgetting. The prevailing usage is to measure commonsense reasoning, with papers reporting evaluation on the benchmark or on its constituent tasks for that purpose. A smaller usage treats performance on the commonsense reasoning QA task after instruction-following training as measuring catastrophic forgetting, described as assessing knowledge forgetting.

Space of uses. Papers commonly use it as a composite benchmark rather than as a standalone single dataset,

nodes.name: CommonsenseQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats CommonsenseQA as a multiple-choice commonsense question-answering benchmark or dataset for everyday or real-world knowledge. Definitions usually say it evaluates commonsense reasoning, and several specify five answer options, or four distractors, with questions that require identifying relevant knowledge and ruling out plausible distractors; some add that the questions are designed to resist superficial cues. A smaller line of work frames it as testing general understanding or general knowledge, one description says it covers social, physical, and psychological domains, some report more than 10,000 or 12,102 questions, and one paper describes CSQA as comprising seven multiple-choice tasks. A few papers also describe it as built on or using ConceptNet, and one uses it as the basis for the ACCORDCSQA benchmark suite.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use CommonsenseQA to measure 14 constructs and 4 behavioral indicators overall, but the dominant link is to Commonsense reasoning. The most frequently listed construct links after that are General ability, General reasoning, Reasoning, and Editing locality. On the behavioral sid

nodes.name: CommonsenseQA 2.0
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across these papers, the prevailing description is a dataset for commonsense reasoning. Definitions differ in emphasis: one describes CSQA2 as containing "a large number of questions about entity knowledge and commonsense reasoning," while another presents CommonsenseQA 2.0 as a dataset for evaluating commonsense reasoning through multiple-choice questions.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to 2 constructs and no behavioral indicators. The most common claim is that it measures Commonsense reasoning, with papers using it within commonsense QA evaluations, while a smaller line of work also treats it as measuring Factual reasoning.

Space of uses. Papers use it as one dataset in broader evaluation suites. In a factual reasoning setup, it appears alongside CREAK and StrategyQA, and in a commonsense QA suite it appears with CommonsenseQA, OpenBookQA, ARC-Easy, and several other datasets described as widely utilized.

nodes.name: CommonsenseQA-CoT
nodes.definition: A version of the CommonsenseQA dataset augmented with 8.1k Chain-of-Thought examples generated by GPT-4o-mini to facilitate CoT-based training.

nodes.name: ComplexBench
nodes.definition: Evaluation suite for complex instruction-following abilities, focusing on multi-step and multi-constraint reasoning, assessed via GPT-4 judgment.

nodes.name: ComplexOR
nodes.definition: A benchmark for optimization problem solving that requires models to use an optimization solver, focusing on linear programming without explicit input numbers.

nodes.name: ComplexTempQA
nodes.definition: A large-scale dataset of over 100 million temporal question-answer pairs used to evaluate temporal reasoning, with questions categorized into attribute, comparison, and counting types, and enriched with metadata such as time span and popularity.

nodes.name: CompreCap
nodes.definition: Evaluation framework using a Directed Scene Graph to assess the correctness of object mentions, attributes, and their relationships in image captions.

nodes.name: ComVE
nodes.definition:
What it is. The paper describes ComVE as a natural language reasoning dataset where the task is to identify which of two sentences violates common sense. In that same description, it is presented as being used to evaluate commonsense reasoning and explanation generation, and it is also grouped with ECQA and e-SNLI as a widely used natural language reasoning dataset with NLEs (Self-Critique and Refinement for Faithful Natural Language Explanations).

What it is claimed to measure. The definition says that papers use ComVE to evaluate commonsense reasoning and explanation generation. Beyond that definition-level claim, papers do not explicitly report that it measures any construct or behavioral indicator.

Space of uses. In the one quoted passage, ComVE is used alongside ECQA and e-SNLI: the paper says its experiments were conducted on these three natural language reasoning datasets with NLEs. This positions ComVE as one of the datasets on which the study's experiments are run.

nodes.name: ConceptARC
nodes.definition: An ARC-style benchmark where each task is designed to exemplify a single, isolated high-level concept, allowing for more targeted evaluation of specific reasoning abilities.

nodes.name: ConceptVectors
nodes.definition: A benchmark designed to evaluate unlearning, used as a source of concepts for the erasure experiments.

nodes.name: CondAmbigQA
nodes.definition: A benchmark and dataset of 2,000 ambiguous questions with condition-answer-citation triples, designed to evaluate models' ability to resolve ambiguity through explicit condition identification and conditional answer generation.

nodes.name: ConflictingQA
nodes.definition: Benchmark dataset containing controversial yes/no web search queries and labeled support/refute web pages, used to evaluate model performance on debatable query summarization.

nodes.name: ConflictQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the dominant framing treats ConflictQA as a contradiction-checking benchmark built around questions paired with both aligned and conflicting evidence. Most descriptions emphasize samples containing a PopQA question, correct aligned evidence, and ChatGPT-generated contradictory evidence; one benchmark-oriented description adds that each question also comes with matched and contradictory evidence plus the answer. Some authors instead foreground its counterfactual contexts, noting that these questions often lack descriptors, and some studies report using only a subset.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link ConflictQA to 1 construct and no behavioral indicators. The measurement claims converge on a single construct, Context utilization: one paper uses ConflictQA as a measurement instrument for context utilization, in a comparison that places it alongside CounterFact rather than spreading its use across multiple constructs.

Space of uses. Papers use it as an evaluation dataset for contradiction checking and for testing performance under conflicting or unhelpful contexts, and some explicitly work with a subset rather than the full benchmark. It is linked

nodes.name: ConflictQA+
nodes.definition: An extension of the ConflictQA dataset, constructed to evaluate LLM performance by adding distracting, ambiguous, and duplicated contexts to the original set of counterfactual contexts.

nodes.name: CoNLL-2003
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, CoNLL-2003 is most commonly described as a named entity recognition benchmark or dataset. When papers specify its content, they describe news text and four entity types, persons, locations, organizations, and miscellaneous, and one paper further says these are tagged using the IOB scheme, resulting in nine distinct IOB labels. One definition also presents it as an English flat NER dataset for benchmarking sequence labeling models, while another broadens its use to token-level representation learning through tasks such as NER, chunking, and POS tagging.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, its measurement claims concentrate on 1 behavioral indicator and no constructs: papers use CoNLL-2003 to measure named entity recognition. This framing is consistent across the relationship evidence, which repeatedly presents it as the dataset used for NER experiments. A broader evaluative role for token-level representation learning appears in one definition, but no additional behavioral indicators or constructs are linked to it.

Space of uses. Papers use it mainly as an experimental dataset for named entity recognition, and one paper explicitly st

nodes.name: Consensual Assessment Technique
nodes.definition: A psychometric method for evaluating creative products through holistic judgments by domain experts, adapted here for LLMs to assess poetry across criteria like creativity and quality.

nodes.name: ContextHub
nodes.definition: A benchmark for propositional logic, used to evaluate the generalization of the model's complex logical reasoning capabilities to an unseen domain.

nodes.name: ConvAI2
nodes.definition: A multi-turn open-domain dialogue dataset with persona profiles and conversational history.

nodes.name: COPA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats COPA, the Choice of Plausible Alternatives, as a benchmark or dataset for causal, often commonsense causal, reasoning. It is most often described as asking a model to choose the more plausible cause or effect for a given premise or situation, and one paper says it provides "a premise event and a corresponding causal query question along with two choices"; papers variously frame this as a multiple-choice task, a sentence completion task, or a SuperGLUE task. A smaller line of work describes it more broadly as an NLU benchmark, one paper adds counterfactual reasoning, one paper notes a COPA-0-shot setting, and another says the dataset includes 1000 causal questions.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link COPA to 2 constructs and 5 behavioral indicators. The dominant measurement claims are causal reasoning and commonsense reasoning, with papers explicitly saying it evaluates causal reasoning abilities or placing it under commonsense reasoning. More narrowly, papers also use it to measure causal discovery, downstream task performance, multiple-choice question answering, sentence completion, and zero-shot task performance, so t

nodes.name: COPAL-ID
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, COPAL-ID is treated as an Indonesian evaluation resource. One definition describes it broadly as a benchmark used to assess downstream model performance after safety fine-tuning, while another paper describes it more specifically as an Indonesian causal reasoning dataset written from scratch by native speakers in both standard and Jakartan Indonesian. Papers therefore describe it both as a benchmark and as a task-specific dataset.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link COPAL-ID to 2 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator. The construct links are divided between causal reasoning and cultural understanding: one paper reports that COPAL-ID measures causal reasoning, and the same line of work uses it to assess models' ability to reason within the Indonesian cultural sphere, treating it as a measure of cultural understanding. Another paper uses COPAL-ID as one of the benchmarks that measure downstream task performance after safety fine-tuning.

Space of uses. In use, papers position COPAL-ID as part of broader model evaluation. One study includes it in a suite of Indonesian benchmarks alongside IndoMMLU, IndoCareer, IndoCulture, MAPS, and IndoCl

nodes.name: Copy-paste attack
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the dominant framing is a watermark-robustness test built around mixing texts. Most definitions describe inserting a watermarked or machine-generated span into a larger human-written or hand-written document, while one definition instead describes inserting copied original text before generated text. Reported setups vary, including embedding watermarked fragments in a surrounding un-watermarked document, inserting 600 tokens from the origin text before generated text, or inserting a 200-token watermarked span into a 1000-token human-written passage.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to measure Robustness, the only linked construct, and no behavioral indicators are linked to it. One paper explicitly assesses the robustness of different watermarking methods under various attacks, including the copy-paste attack, so the claims converge on robustness rather than spreading across multiple targets.

Space of uses. Papers use it as a scenario-based attack within broader watermark evaluations, and some describe the same setup as text mixing or a Copy-Paste scenario where watermarked text appears inside a larger hand-written passage. One pap

nodes.name: CoQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most papers treat CoQA as a conversational question answering dataset or benchmark for dialogue-based evaluation. The prevailing description is passage-based conversational comprehension: papers say it requires understanding a text passage and answering a series of interconnected questions in conversation, and one description adds that it requires coreference and pragmatic reasoning. Descriptions differ on access conditions, with several papers calling it open-book, one calling it a closed-book reading comprehension dataset, and some referring to specific subsets such as the development split or coqa-dev-v1.0.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link CoQA to 4 behavioral indicators and 1 construct. The dominant measurement claim is conversational question answering, and papers also use it to measure machine reading comprehension, question answering, and extractive question answering. These measurement claims spread across several task labels rather than one label only, while a smaller line of work reports it as measuring the construct Reasoning, including evaluation framed as commonsense and math reasoning on CoQA with exact match accuracy.

Space of uses. Papers usu

nodes.name: Cora
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, the prevailing framing is of Cora as a citation network benchmark: nodes are described as scientific publications, documents, or academic papers, and edges as citation links. Most definitions place it in text-attributed graph or node classification settings, though some papers also use it for node-level and edge-level tasks, and one paper evaluates perplexity, structural understanding, and zero-shot node and link classification on forms labeled Cora-Node and Cora-Link. A smaller line of work also mentions an expanded version of Cora.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link Cora to three behavioral indicators and no constructs. The dominant use is to measure node classification, with papers reporting node classification accuracy on Cora and describing it as widely adopted for that task; smaller lines of work report it as measuring link prediction and graph partitioning, including multi-scale graph partitioning datasets based on Cora. Overall, the measurement claims are concentrated on node classification rather than spread evenly across tasks.

Space of uses. Papers do not explicitly relate Cora to another measurement instrument, but they

nodes.name: CosmosQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, CosmosQA is most commonly described as a large-scale commonsense-based reading comprehension benchmark or dataset, usually framed as multiple-choice question answering. Definitions consistently say its passages and questions require commonsense reasoning, while some descriptions are more specific, presenting it as common-sense questions about human behaviors, intentions, and social interactions with four answer options each, and another places it among real-world NLP classification datasets.

What it is claimed to measure. The prevailing usage is as a measure of commonsense reasoning: papers link it to 1 construct, Commonsense reasoning, and 1 behavioral indicator, Question answering. Most measurement claims treat it as evaluating commonsense reasoning, including work that explicitly labels it a common sense reasoning dataset, while a smaller line of work reports it as measuring question answering by listing it among question answering datasets. Overall, the claims center on a single construct and a single behavioral indicator rather than spreading across many targets.

Space of uses. No paper links it to another measurement instrument. Papers usually pos

nodes.name: CoSQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, CoSQA is most commonly described as a natural-language-to-code semantic search or code search benchmark, using natural language queries to retrieve relevant code and to evaluate alignment between code and intent expressed in natural language. A smaller line of work treats CosQA as a code-oriented question answering dataset of natural language-code pairs, used to test model performance on a code question-answering task and, in one definition, a model's ability to understand and reason about code semantics.

What it is claimed to measure. The prevailing usage presents CoSQA as evaluating natural-language-to-code semantic search, code search, and alignment between code and natural language intent. One paper also describes it as testing code question answering and understanding and reasoning about code semantics. No paper explicitly links it to a named construct or behavioral indicator.

Space of uses. Papers commonly position CoSQA as one benchmark within a small group of code search evaluations, most often alongside AdvTest and a third benchmark named as CSN in one paper and CodeSearchNet in another. In that role it is described as one of the "

nodes.name: CoSQL
nodes.definition: CoSQL is a conversational text-to-SQL dataset referenced as prior work with limited ambiguous and unanswerable questions.

nodes.name: CounterFact
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most commonly, papers treat CounterFact as a factual question-answering or prompt dataset for evaluating factual knowledge and knowledge editing. Definitions often describe samples as (subject, relation, answer) tuples with paraphrased prompts, while a recurring alternative framing emphasizes counterfactual statements, or false facts, used as new knowledge for editing; some descriptions also mention neighboring datapoints, rephrased or unrelated queries, and prompt pairs. Papers sometimes use task-specific subsets or reformulations, including the first 1000 examples, filtered fact pairs the model already recalls, a subset restricted to one relation with a fixed target label, question reformulations, and old versus new knowledge partitions.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link CounterFact to 8 constructs and 3 behavioral indicators, so its reported measurement role is spread across several targets rather than concentrated on one. The prevailing usage is to measure knowledge editing, and recurring work also uses it to evaluate editing locality, factual recall, factual knowledge, and fact checking. Across these claims, papers describe it as testing whether models re

nodes.name: CoVoGER
nodes.definition: A multilingual multitask benchmark for speech-to-text generative error correction, covering ASR and ST across 15 languages and 28 language pairs, using N-best lists from Whisper and SeamlessM4T models.

nodes.name: CoVoST 2
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across these papers, CoVoST 2 is most commonly described as a multilingual speech-to-text translation corpus or benchmark derived from Common Voice, used for training and evaluation. Definitions differ on the source-target setup: some describe English speech translated into multiple typologically diverse languages, with one use case noting 15,500 English examples into seven languages, while others focus on general-domain French-English and German-English subsets or on 14 non-English source languages paired bidirectionally with English for 28 directions. A smaller framing presents it as the speech translation source corpus used inside CoVoGER to generate N-best lists.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link CoVoST 2 to one construct and two behavioral indicators. The prevailing usage is to measure speech translation, with papers stating that speech translation is tested on CoVoST 2 and reporting settings such as En-De or English-to-multiple-language translation; a smaller line of work also uses it to measure speech recognition in joint ASR and ST evaluation. Separately, one paper reports CoVoST 2 as measuring cross-lingual alignment, saying its results confirm superi

nodes.name: CR
nodes.definition: Customer Reviews sentiment classification benchmark used to evaluate polarity labeling.

nodes.name: Creak
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, the prevailing usage treats Creak as a fact-checking dataset or benchmark. Definitions describe it as evaluating verification of claims against a knowledge graph using Wikidata, while a smaller framing presents CREAK as a benchmark for fact-checking and commonsense reasoning that assesses whether statements are supported by commonsense knowledge.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link Creak to 2 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator. The most common claim is that it measures fact checking, with papers describing it as a fact-checking or fact verification dataset; some also use it to measure commonsense reasoning, and a single paper reports it as measuring factual reasoning.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it. In use, papers pair it with FEVER in fact verification settings, and with StrategyQA and CSQA2 in evaluations described as containing many questions about entity knowledge and commonsense reasoning; one paper also places it under a "Factual Reasoning Task."

nodes.name: CREPE
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, CREPE is not described in one uniform way. The prevailing benchmark-style usage treats it as an evaluation dataset for reasoning: some papers describe a causal reasoning dataset for identifying cause-effect relationships in natural language, while others describe CREPE or Crepe as a compositional reasoning benchmark that tests systematicity and productivity, including an image-text retrieval dataset with hard negatives for compositional understanding. A separate paper uses the same name for a different instrument, CREPE as "Rapid Chest X-ray Report Evaluation by Predicting Multi-category Error Counts," described as a domain-specific BERT-based, multi-head regression metric that predicts error counts in six clinical categories.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link CREPE to 3 constructs and no behavioral indicators. The recorded measurement claims are spread across Causal reasoning, Compositional reasoning, and Compositionality, rather than converging on a single construct: one paper uses it for causal reasoning, one reports it as evaluating compositional reasoning, and one uses it for compositionality with a focus on systematicity and productivi

nodes.name: CRITICTOOL
nodes.definition: A self-critique evaluation benchmark for LLMs in tool-calling scenarios, assessing performance across internal and external error types using evolved data strategies.

nodes.name: CrossCodeEval
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats CrossCodeEval as a repository-level, cross-file benchmark. One definition describes it broadly as evaluating code generation and understanding, while another presents it more narrowly as a diverse, multilingual benchmark, and also as a repository-level code completion dataset, for cross-file code completion.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to 1 behavioral indicator, Code completion, and to no constructs. The recorded use converges on that single indicator: one paper uses CrossCodeEval to measure code completion in repository-level, cross-file settings, specifically for code Fill-in-the-Middle scenarios.

Space of uses. In use, papers report performance on CrossCodeEval as an evaluation dataset for repository-level code completion. One paper uses it alongside CrossCodeLongEval and RepoEval to evaluate repository-level code Fill-in-the-Middle in cross-file scenarios, and a survey mentions it together with RepoBench when discussing repository-level tasks.

nodes.name: CrossNER
nodes.definition: A benchmark dataset for evaluating zero-shot NER that includes five domains: Movies, AI, Literature, Politics, and Science.

nodes.name: CrowS-Pairs
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, CrowS-Pairs is most commonly described as a crowdsourced dataset or benchmark of sentence pairs that contrast stereotypical with anti-stereotypical, or less stereotypical, formulations, often as minimal pairs differing in a demographic-group or social-group reference. Papers describe the task in slightly different ways: models may be asked which sentence is more likely, which is more natural or reasonable, or be checked for whether they assign higher probability to the biased variant. Most descriptions place it in English or U.S. English and focused on stereotypes tied to historically disadvantaged groups, while some papers discuss multilingual adaptations or translations, including French, Dutch, German, Spanish, and Catalan, as well as multilingual and Spanish-subset versions.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link CrowS-Pairs to 3 constructs and no behavioral indicators. The prevailing measurement claim is social bias: papers say it evaluates social bias, includes sentences with social biases, or checks a model's propensity to generate biased outputs. A smaller but recurring line of work uses it to measure stereotyping, and one paper pl

nodes.name: CRUXEval
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the cited papers, CRUXEval is most commonly described as a benchmark for code reasoning, code understanding, and execution. Many definitions make this concrete as execution-result, code-output, or input-output prediction, and some papers explicitly split it into CruxEval-I for input prediction and CruxEval-O for output prediction; one paper further describes it as 800 Python functions created with a "generate-and-filter" approach with CodeLlama. A smaller framing refers to it more broadly as a benchmark for reasoning abilities in code generation and understanding.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use CRUXEval to measure 3 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators. The prevailing usage is to measure code reasoning, followed by abductive code reasoning and broader reasoning; among behavioral indicators, code output prediction is the more common use, followed by code input prediction. The linked claims largely converge on reasoning about code execution, including tasks that ask a model to predict the input given the output of a function and vice versa.

Space of uses. Papers typically position CRUXEval as an evaluation benchmark within broader suites, often along

nodes.name: CSCD-NS
nodes.definition:
What it is. The definitions treat CSCD-NS as a Chinese Spelling Correction benchmark dataset, described as high-quality and as containing character errors that primarily stem from pinyin input methods, with many homophonic and word-level errors. In Enhancing Character-Level Understanding in LLMs through Token Internal Structure Learning, it is grouped with LEMON as one of two newer CSC benchmarks, in contrast to earlier datasets such as SIGHAN.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it in a focused way rather than across many targets: it is linked to 1 behavioral indicator, Chinese spelling correction, and to no constructs. One paper explicitly uses CSCD-NS as one of two CSC benchmarks for evaluating Chinese spelling correction.

Space of uses. Usage is shown mainly as a paired benchmark: papers use it alongside LEMON, and one study says the pair was selected to address limitations identified in previous datasets like SIGHAN. No other measurement instruments are linked to it.

nodes.name: CSRT
nodes.definition: Code-Switching Red-Teaming, a framework that synthesizes multilingual code-switching adversarial prompts to evaluate both safety and multilingual understanding of LLMs.

nodes.name: CTC
nodes.definition: An automated evaluation procedure used to compare generated chain-of-thought rationales against manually created golden references.

nodes.name: CUAD
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers describe CUAD as a specialized contract understanding dataset, specifically a corpus of commercial legal contracts used for evaluating automated contract review and provision extraction. One paper further describes it as consisting of 510 labelled documents across 25 contract types, and no versions or subsets are described.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use CUAD to measure contract understanding. It is linked to 1 construct, Contract understanding, and to no behavioral indicators, so the measurement claims reported here center on a single construct rather than being spread across multiple targets.

Space of uses. In the descriptions, CUAD is positioned as an evaluation dataset for automated contract review, provision extraction, and contract understanding. No measurement instrument is linked to it, so the evidence does not show it being used alongside other named benchmarks.

nodes.name: CUB-200-2011
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats CUB-200-2011, also written as CUB-200, CUB, CaltechUCSD Bird-200, Birds-200-2011, and Caltech-UCSD Birds, as a fine-grained bird image benchmark or dataset for 200 bird species. Most definitions frame it as an image classification or fine-grained visual classification benchmark, often within FGVC, while some papers also describe it as a fine-grained image dataset used for image captioning and generation, or as a source of bird attributes for evaluating attribute relativity in the animal domain. A smaller line of work describes it in terms of detailed visual understanding, localization, and concept-based evaluation.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link this instrument to 5 behavioral indicators and 1 construct. The dominant measurement claim is image classification, while smaller lines of work use it to measure cross-modal retrieval, image captioning, image reconstruction, and object recognition. Papers also report it as measuring interpretability and explainability, with one study stating that CUB offers image-level concept annotations that enable quantitative evaluation.

Space of uses. Papers usually use it as one data

nodes.name: CultSportQA
nodes.definition: A multilingual, multicultural benchmark containing 33,000 multiple-choice questions across text and image modalities, assessing models on history-based, rule-based, and scenario-based understanding of traditional sports from 60 countries and 11 languages.

nodes.name: CURIE GEO
nodes.definition: Geospatial Dataset Extraction task in the CURIE benchmark where the model must identify all datasets used in a research paper, including their sources, variables, and time/spatial ranges.

nodes.name: CV-Bench 2D
nodes.definition: A vision-centric benchmark specifically for evaluating 2D visual understanding capabilities of models.

nodes.name: CVQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, CVQA is most commonly described as a culturally diverse, multilingual visual question answering benchmark and dataset for culturally specific or culturally diverse images and questions. Definitions describe it as a large-scale resource spanning 31 languages and 30 countries, written in both English and local languages, while one definition instead calls it a cross-lingual VQA dataset. Its questions are described as multiple choice, with one correct answer and three distractors, and the benchmark is also said to be convertible into free-text open-ended QA.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use CVQA to measure three constructs and three behavioral indicators, with claims spread across several targets rather than centered on one alone. The prevailing construct-level uses are for cultural bias, cultural understanding, and multilingual understanding: papers say it can assess the cultural capability and bias of multimodal models, and use it to assess a model's ability to reason about and understand culturally diverse visual content. At the behavioral level, it is reported as measuring visual question answering, and descriptions of its format also link it t

nodes.name: CWQ
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, CWQ is most commonly treated as ComplexWebQuestions, a benchmark dataset for multi-hop knowledge base or knowledge graph question answering. The prevailing description places it on Freebase and frames it as testing complex, compositional, or knowledge-intensive reasoning over a knowledge graph, with some definitions noting conjunction, composition, comparison, or superlative reasoning and natural language questions paired with SPARQL queries. A smaller line of work describes it instead as multi-hop, web-based questions for reasoning over web content.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use CWQ to measure three constructs and two behavioral indicators. The most common use is to measure Knowledge graph question answering, and papers also report it as measuring Multi-hop reasoning; less common links use it to measure Reasoning, World knowledge, and Question answering. Overall, the reported measurement claims cluster around KGQA and multi-hop reasoning, while the other uses appear as smaller framings.

Space of uses. In use, papers usually include CWQ in a small suite of KGQA benchmarks, most often alongside WebQSP and often GrailQA; some also pair it

nodes.name: D4RL
nodes.definition:
What it is. The paper treats D4RL as Datasets for Deep Data-Driven Reinforcement Learning, described as a benchmark suite for offline reinforcement learning. In that usage, it appears specifically in risk-sensitive variants, with experiments run on four risk-sensitive D4RL tasks using public human preferences, as described in A Distributional Approach to Uncertainty-Aware Preference Alignment Using Offline Demonstrations.

What it is claimed to measure. The papers do not report D4RL as measuring any construct or behavioral indicator, and no measured_by relationship is recorded for it.

Space of uses. Usage is illustrated in one paper as an experimental benchmark: the authors report that they "conduct experiments using public human preferences from Yuan et al. (2024) on four risk-sensitive D4RL tasks." No other measurement instrument is linked to it.

nodes.name: DailyDialog
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing description is of a dataset of human-written dialogues or human conversation transcripts about everyday life, used to evaluate dialogue generation or conversational performance. Definitions variously say it covers "various topics of daily life," consists of "transcripts of conversations between humans," or comprises sequences of everyday conversations. A minority description adds that it contains 13,118 dialogues annotated with 7 emotions for emotion recognition and dialogue generation.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use DailyDialog to measure one behavioral indicator, Dialogue generation, and do not link it to any constructs. The claims converge on dialogue generation rather than several outcomes: papers describe "dialogue generation with the DailyDialog dataset" and report using it to "assess performance in conversation scenarios."

Space of uses. Papers position it both as a case-study setting and as one dataset within multi-dataset evaluations. One line of work describes "a single setting as a case study: dialogue generation with the DailyDialog dataset," while other work evaluates systems across diverse datasets or d

nodes.name: DAN
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most commonly, papers treat DAN, often expanded as Do Anything Now, as a benchmark or prompt-based test for whether models resist malicious or jailbreak-enhanced instructions. Definitions describe it as a benchmark collection of jailbreak-enhanced instructions for evaluating resilience against diverse jailbreak attacks, or more generally as a benchmark for model safety against malicious instructions and jailbreak attacks. Some authors use a narrower prompt-level framing, calling DAN 13.0 a well-known jailbreaking prompt and baseline that overrides AI safety restrictions, and one paper refers to a dataset of forbidden prompts from the Do Anything Now jailbreak family. Separately, one paper uses the same name for "Expose Backdoors on the Way," a feature-based textual backdoor defense method evaluated against Query-Attack and Observation-Attack on WebShop.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the linked relationships, papers use it to measure two constructs, Safety and Safety robustness, and no behavioral indicators are linked to it. The reported measurement claims stay within this safety framing: one paper says it uses AdvBench and DoAnythingNow to assess the safety of

nodes.name: DART
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the cited papers, DART is most commonly described as a dataset or benchmark for structured-data-to-text generation: definitions call it a large, open-domain resource with 82,191 examples from various domains, and describe the task as turning structured records, graphs, or RDF triples into natural language. Most descriptions use struct-to-text, data-to-text, or graph-to-text language, though one paper describes it as employed for evaluating text-to-data generation.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to measure 2 behavioral indicators and no constructs. The linked indicators are Data-to-text generation and Text generation, both via measured_by relations; one paper further specifies RDF-to-text generation in that usage, while another places it inside a Natural Language Generation task and says it is employed for evaluating text-to-data generation.

Space of uses. Papers most often position it as an evaluation benchmark. As one study states, "We conducted all of our experiments on the following three benchmarks: WebNLG17, WebNLG20, DART", while other papers use it in broader NLG evaluation and in LoRA merging evaluation for converting structured data to na

nodes.name: Databricks Dolly-15k
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing framing is an instruction-following dataset, often described as open-source and based on human-generated records, and used to fine-tune large language models for instruction following or dialogue generation. Some authors instead present it as an evaluation task or benchmark dataset, including use in decoding experiments, Diff-eRank computation, and federated LLM fine-tuning across multiple NLP tasks. Papers also describe its contents with some specificity: one account says it contains 15,000 human-written instruction-response pairs, another says it includes categories such as brainstorming, classification, closed QA, generation, information extraction, open QA, and summarization, and one paper uses a 500-sample test split.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to 1 construct and 2 behavioral indicators overall. The direct measurement claims span both a construct and a behavioral indicator: papers use it to measure Helpfulness, in work that selects Dolly samples to assess whether LLMs retain usefulness after fine-tuning, and Dialogue generation, where Dolly is treated as the dialogue generation task. One additional paper reports tha

nodes.name: Date Understanding
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most definitions describe Date Understanding as a task, benchmark, or benchmark dataset for reasoning about dates and temporal information. The prevailing framing places it in BigBench, with papers also describing it as a symbolic reasoning task, a logical reasoning task, or a commonsense reasoning task; one paper specifically places it in BIG-Bench-Hard. Across descriptions, the content is natural-language date reasoning, including calendar dates, temporal relationships, contextual clues, calendar logic, and, in one paper's wording, "inferring dates from natural language descriptions" and "performing arithmetic operations on dates".

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use Date Understanding to measure three constructs and one behavioral indicator. The construct links are to commonsense reasoning, logical reasoning, and symbolic reasoning, and one paper uses it to measure date inference as a behavioral indicator. Taken together, these measurement claims are spread across several reasoning framings rather than centered on a single construct.

Space of uses. In use, papers usually include it as one evaluation task within broader benchmark sets, pairing it with Object C

nodes.name: DBPedia
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most papers describe DBPedia as a benchmark dataset for topic or ontology classification based on Wikipedia articles. The prevailing description is a 14-way, 14-class task for categorizing text into non-overlapping ontological classes, and some papers frame it more generally as multi-class text classification or text categorization. A smaller line of work describes DBpedia as a hierarchical text classification benchmark, with Wikipedia articles organized in a three-layer taxonomy tree with 9/70/219 classes.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use DBPedia to measure two behavioral indicators, and the dominant link is to text classification. In those papers it is reported as evaluating classification tasks, topic classification, or multi-class classification of Wikipedia articles. A smaller line of work uses it to measure hierarchical text classification. No constructs are linked to it.

Space of uses. Papers often present DBPedia as a public evaluation dataset within multi-dataset experiments rather than as a standalone protocol. It appears alongside other classification benchmarks such as AGNews, SST2, Yelp Polarity, and TREC, and one paper also uses it among other p

nodes.name: DBpedia Class
nodes.definition: A dataset used to examine watermark decryption accuracy by analyzing word frequencies within specific semantic classes.

nodes.name: DCLM
nodes.definition:
What it is. The definition treats DCLM as the pre-training data of the DCLM-7B model, and one paper explicitly uses it as a calibration source. Another paper uses a subset of DCLM and describes DCLM as a high-quality corpus carefully curated with complex pipelines.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the linked uses, papers use DCLM to measure Language modeling ability, and this is the only construct tied to it. It is reported as testing language modeling capability on a subset of DCLM, "to examine how well LMs capture broad and diverse knowledge," and no behavioral indicators are linked to it.

Space of uses. In the papers, DCLM is positioned both as calibration data and as an evaluation subset for language modeling tests. No other measurement instrument is linked to it.

nodes.name: DDXPlus
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across these papers, DDXPlus is most commonly described as a medical diagnosis dataset or benchmark used to evaluate models on complex and diverse conditions. Definitions differ in how they describe its contents: one treats it as a large-scale Electronic Health Record dataset, another as clinical vignettes with synthetic patient information for differential diagnosis, and another says agents must choose among 49 diagnoses from patient profiles detailing symptoms (StreamBench: Towards Benchmarking Continuous Improvement of Language Agents).

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use DDXPlus to measure 2 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator. The prevailing claim is that it measures Medical diagnosis, with papers saying it tests models on diagnosing complex and diverse medical conditions and requires a diagnosis from symptom profiles. Smaller uses report it as measuring Medical reasoning, through clinical vignettes that evaluate diagnostic reasoning abilities similar to a clinical setting, and Domain knowledge, through assessing continuous improvement in applying expert knowledge.

Space of uses. Across the papers, DDXPlus is used as an evaluation dataset for models or ag

nodes.name: DecodingTrust
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats DecodingTrust as a benchmark dataset for evaluating LLM trustworthiness, and often safety, with several papers describing it as covering multiple perspectives. Some papers narrow that broad framing to particular components, especially a stereotypes partition, described in one study as 48 statements for race groups black and white, and a privacy dataset centered on the Enron email extraction task. A smaller framing presents it as a public leaderboard that integrates large amounts of new test data to evaluate and rank safety and trustworthiness, and another describes it through red-teaming prompts or instructions.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link DecodingTrust to 2 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator. Most definitions frame it as measuring Trustworthiness, while other papers use it to measure Stereotyping and Privacy leakage, with the privacy use tied to the Enron email extraction task and data leakage. The measurement claims therefore span both a broad construct and more specific targets, rather than converging on only one use.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it through formal relat

nodes.name: DeepCAD
nodes.definition: A dataset of CAD parametric sequences used as the source for training and test data in the sequential learning stage.

nodes.name: DeepInception
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage treats DeepInception as a manually crafted jailbreak prompt template that uses imaginary scenes and characters to attack target LLMs. One paper describes it as a meticulously crafted manual prompt template that incorporates imaginary scenes with various characters. Other papers use a broader framing, treating it as a jailbreak method or as one of the evaluated state-of-the-art jailbreak attacks.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link DeepInception to one construct, Harmlessness, and to no behavioral indicators. The recorded relationship is that Harmlessness is measured by DeepInception, with supporting evidence coming from an evaluation table that compares harmfulness scores for jailbreak attacks and shows attack success rates in brackets. The measurement claims are therefore concentrated on Harmlessness rather than distributed across multiple constructs.

Space of uses. In the usage in the papers examples, papers place DeepInception inside multi-attack evaluations rather than presenting it by itself. One study evaluates it alongside GCG and PAIR, and another lists it with AutoDAN, ReNeLLM, and CodeAttack among jailbreak

nodes.name: Defects4J
nodes.definition: Real-world Java bug-fix benchmark containing 806 bugs from 15 open-source projects, used to evaluate automated program repair systems on repo-level debugging tasks.

nodes.name: DeliData
nodes.definition: A dataset of multi-party, problem-solving dialogues where participants propose and score solutions, used to evaluate controlled dialogue generation and hallucination.

nodes.name: Detoxify
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, Detoxify is most commonly described as a model-based toxicity scoring or classification tool for text. Papers variously refer to it as a machine learning model, library, classifier, or evaluation procedure, but the prevailing usage is to assign a toxicity score to generated text, responses, or continuations, with higher scores indicating more toxic generation; some authors also describe it as automatically generating disutility measures for LLM outputs. One paper uses the classifier with six attributes, toxicity, severe toxicity, obscene, threat, insult, and identity attack, and another reports retraining Detoxify on a biased subset of the Jigsaw Unintended Bias in Toxicity Classification dataset.

What it is claimed to measure. The reported links are concentrated rather than spread across many targets: papers use Detoxify to measure one construct, Toxicity, and one behavioral indicator, Harmful content generation. The prevailing use is for Toxicity, with papers describing it as assessing the toxicity of responses, generated text, continuations, or tweets; some operationalizations use the raw score, while others derive metrics such as Toxicity

nodes.name: DialogSum
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most papers treat DialogSum as a dialogue summarization dataset or benchmark. Definitions and quoted passages describe it as a large-scale resource of dialogues paired with manually labeled summaries, and one description adds topics and a total of 13,460 dialogues. A smaller line of work uses it beyond dialogue summarization evaluation, rebuilding it for instruction tuning, using it as dialogue context for grammar analysis, or using it for summary-to-dialogue generation.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, DialogSum is linked to 3 behavioral indicators and no constructs. The prevailing use is to measure Dialogue summarization, and papers also use it to measure Text summarization and, in a smaller framing, Abstractive summarization. All 3 linked behavioral indicators are summarization-related.

Space of uses. No other measurement instrument is linked to it. Papers most often position it as an evaluation benchmark, including zero-shot generative evaluation, decoding-stage experiments, assessment of efficient inference methods, and evaluation after coreset selection or alignment; some papers instead rebuild it for fine-tuning an event summary module, use it as c

nodes.name: Dictator Game
nodes.definition: A one-shot bargaining game used to measure altruism and fairness, where one player unilaterally decides how to split a sum of money with a passive recipient.

nodes.name: DiDeMo
nodes.definition: Describe, Detect and Moment dataset focused on moment-level video grounding and retrieval, where models must align natural language queries with specific video segments.

nodes.name: DiscoveryBench
nodes.definition: A benchmark for data-driven analysis that uses expert-curated analytics to assess agent performance against human experts.

nodes.name: DIWALI
nodes.definition: A large-scale dataset of Culture Specific Items (CSIs) for India, containing approximately 8,000 concepts from 17 cultural facets across 36 sub-regions, used for evaluating cultural text adaptation.

nodes.name: DMDTEval
nodes.definition: A systematic evaluation framework for assessing LLMs' disambiguation capabilities in multi-domain translation, including a multi-domain ambiguous word dataset, disambiguation prompt strategies, and disambiguation accuracy metric.

nodes.name: DnD
nodes.definition: Role-playing dataset involving 10 fantasy characters and 129 in-game situations with 3 possible actions each, used to evaluate alignment with character-specific behavioral preferences.

nodes.name: DocBench
nodes.definition: Document understanding benchmark containing 229 long documents and 1,102 questions across five domains—Academia, Finance, Government, Laws, and News—with evaluation by evidence source and document type.

nodes.name: DOCCI
nodes.definition: A dataset containing 15,000 image-caption pairs with highly detailed, hallucination-free captions, used for evaluating caption quality.

nodes.name: DocVQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most papers treat DocVQA as a document visual question answering benchmark or dataset for document images, where models answer questions from document text and layout. Some descriptions add scanned or photographed documents, and characterize the task as extractive, span or segment based, or as testing extraction and reasoning over document images. Papers describe its scope differently: some say it is limited to single-page documents, while another defines it as covering single-page and multi-page document QA and retrieval; one paper also uses the name VQADoc, and another refers to a DocVQAVAL split.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, the prevailing claim is that DocVQA measures document understanding. It is linked to 4 constructs and 4 behavioral indicators overall: beyond document understanding, papers use it to measure fine-grained visual understanding, long-context understanding, and multimodal perception, and among behavioral indicators it most often measures optical character recognition, with additional uses for document question answering, information retrieval, and machine reading comprehension. The reported measurement claims therefore spread across

nodes.name: Dolos
nodes.definition: A state-of-the-art plagiarism detection tool used to assess the degree of copying or approximate memorization in generated code.

nodes.name: DOSA
nodes.definition: A community-driven dataset of cultural artifacts for a sub-regional culture in India, built through a gamified data collection process.

nodes.name: DOTA
nodes.definition: A large-scale dataset for object detection in aerial images.

nodes.name: DoTA (traffic accident analysis)
nodes.definition: An academic benchmark dataset for traffic accident analysis, providing annotations for captions, temporal localization, and bounding boxes.

nodes.name: DreamBooth
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers commonly treat DreamBooth as a subject-focused text-to-image resource, but they describe its format in several ways: as a dataset and method for fine-tuning on subject-specific data, as a subject-driven image generation benchmark or test set, and as a text-to-image personalization evaluation setup. The described contents center on subject examples and reference images, including a DreamBooth dataset that "includes 30 different subjects" and settings with "30 new concepts" from DreamBooth used as reference images; some descriptions also frame the setup around subject-driven generation with special identifier tokens.

What it is claimed to measure. The papers do not explicitly link DreamBooth to any named constructs or behavioral indicators. Instead, they describe it in task terms, reporting its use for subject generation evaluation in diffusion models, for evaluating reference-based image compositing on test images and generated variants, and for text-to-image personalization or subject-driven generation.

Space of uses. In use, papers position DreamBooth mainly as an evaluation setup, benchmark, or test set, rather than alongside any linked measurement instrument

nodes.name: DRISHTIKON
nodes.definition: A multimodal, multilingual benchmark for evaluating cultural understanding in vision-language models, consisting of 64,288 aligned text-image multiple-choice questions across 15 Indian languages and all 36 states and union territories, covering cultural themes like festivals, attire, cuisine, and heritage.

nodes.name: DroidTask
nodes.definition: An existing benchmark for GUI agents consisting of 162 tasks across 12 English-language Android applications.

nodes.name: DROP
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, DROP is most commonly described as the Discrete Reasoning Over Paragraphs reading comprehension benchmark or dataset, built around paragraph-level content and questions that require discrete reasoning such as addition, counting, arithmetic, and sorting. Some authors frame it more specifically as grounded question answering, open-book QA, or a generation task for phrase or numeric answers. One paper uses a decontextualized subset, and another says its queries mainly address History, Politics, Sports, Demographics, and Societal Issues.

What it is claimed to measure. In the surveyed work, papers use DROP to measure 6 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators, so the reported measurement claims are spread across several framings rather than concentrated on one. Across constructs, the prevailing links are to discrete reasoning and reasoning, with contextual understanding also present; on the behavioral side, it is linked to machine reading comprehension and question answering. Papers also report 3 other construct links, and some describe this use as testing reading comprehension abilities or question answering where models must ground answers in in-context docum

nodes.name: DS-1000
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly describe DS-1000 as a benchmark of 1000 data science coding problems, workflows, or challenges, usually spanning seven widely used Python libraries such as NumPy and Pandas. The prevailing framing is data science code generation, though some definitions narrow this to code completion of partial quoted passages, and one description adds two evaluation modes, completion and insertion. Several papers also describe the problems as real-world StackOverflow questions with unit tests or test cases, while one paper characterizes them as non-standalone functions with contextual dependencies.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the surveyed work, papers use DS-1000 to measure code generation, and it is linked to one behavioral indicator and no constructs. The claims concentrate on that single indicator: authors describe tasks as generating Python code for data science questions written in natural language, using standard data science libraries, and passing executable test cases. Some papers frame the same use more specifically as data science code completion.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to DS-1000. In use, papers often place it alon

nodes.name: DTD
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, DTD is most commonly described as the Describable Textures Dataset, a dataset or benchmark for texture classification and texture recognition. Some definitions add that it contains texture images in the wild annotated with describable attributes and is used for fine-grained visual classification based on descriptive attributes, while another frames it as a benchmark for recognizing and differentiating textures within images. A smaller line of work refers to it simply as Texture and uses it as an out-of-distribution texture dataset.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, DTD is linked to 1 behavioral indicator and no constructs. The recurring claim is that papers use DTD to measure Image classification: they report image recognition or classification evaluations on DTD in settings such as fine-tuning, transfer learning, and zero-shot or linear-probe image classification. The measurement claims therefore center on one behavioral indicator rather than multiple constructs.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to DTD directly. In practice, papers usually place it inside multi-dataset evaluation suites alongside benchmarks such as CIF

nodes.name: DUDE
nodes.definition:
