What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing framing is as a benchmark for multi-page document understanding, with coverage limited to documents up to 20 pages. One paper gives a more task-specific account, describing DUDE as a multi-page visual question answering dataset containing financial reports, and highlighting the "diverse domains and complex document structures" associated with it.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers do not formally link DUDE to any construct or behavioral indicator. Instead, they describe it at the task level: most commonly as a benchmark for multi-page document understanding, and in one paper as a dataset used to evaluate retrieval and question answering performance.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is formally linked to DUDE, but papers do use it alongside other benchmarks. One paper reports using DUDE together with MPVQA, CUAD, and MOAMOB, while another discusses DUDE alongside MP-DocVQA as an example of a current multi-page document benchmark.

Concerns raised. The main limitation raised is document-length coverage. As noted in LongDocURL: a Comprehensive Multimodal Long Document Benchmark Integrating Understanding, Reasoning, and Locatin

nodes.name: DynaMath
nodes.definition: Benchmark evaluating dynamic mathematical reasoning with visual inputs, used to assess model performance on evolving problem structures.

nodes.name: DynamicNER
nodes.definition: A multilingual, multi-granular Named Entity Recognition dataset with dynamic categorization, designed to evaluate LLM-based NER methods across varying entity type lists and granularity levels.

nodes.name: DynamicQA
nodes.definition: A benchmark for evaluating LLMs' ability to handle knowledge conflicts arising from evolving real-world information, including static, temporal, and disputable cases.

nodes.name: E2E NLG Challenge
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing description is a benchmark or dataset for natural language generation from structured input in the restaurant domain. Authors variously refer to it as E2E NLG Challenge, E2E NLG, or simply E2E, and most describe the task as generating natural language from structured meaning representations; some instead phrase it as data-to-text or table-to-text generation, and one description specifies that it verbalizes key-value attribute pairs in English.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to two behavioral indicators and no constructs. The more prevalent recorded use is to measure Text generation, with papers describing it as an NLG or text generation benchmark, and it is also used to measure Data-to-text generation, including table-to-text generation and verbalizing structured attributes, so the recorded claims cluster around those two behavioral indicators rather than a broader construct set.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it. In practice, papers often use it alongside WebNLG, and one text generation setup also groups it with CommonGen and an Adidas product description dataset; a recurring usage is as a benchmark

nodes.name: E-GSM
nodes.definition: Extended Grade-School Math, a benchmark of math word problems with lengthy narratives, created by iteratively extending problems from the GSM8K test set.

nodes.name: e-SNLI
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across these papers, e-SNLI is most commonly described as an extension of the SNLI corpus or dataset that adds human or human-annotated explanations to premise-hypothesis pairs. The prevailing description emphasizes entailment-style natural language inference, including labels such as contradiction, neutral, and entailment, while another recurring framing treats it as a multi-premise setting because the premise and explanation are described as jointly entailing the hypothesis. A smaller usage highlights it as a held-out test for generalization.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link e-SNLI to 2 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator. The most common claim is that it measures natural language inference, with papers describing its task as determining the logical relationship between a premise and a hypothesis; papers also report it as measuring logical reasoning ability and interpretability and explainability, including through human explanations that support explicit reasoning and interpretability benchmarks. Taken together, the reported uses are spread across this small set rather than tied to only one target.

Space of uses. No other measurement instrument is linke

nodes.name: ECL
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across definitions, the prevailing usage treats ECL, often called Electricity, as a benchmark electricity-consumption time series dataset. Most descriptions say it contains hourly data for 321 clients or customers, sometimes specifying 2012 to 2014 and a 1-hour recording frequency, and papers place it in real-world or benchmark suites for long-term forecasting. A smaller line of work describes ECL as a subset of the Electricity dataset with hourly kilowatt-hour consumption from 19 clients, and one paper describes Electricity as a dataset for evaluating self-healing adaptation strategies across different data distributions.

What it is claimed to measure. Most papers report ECL as a benchmark for evaluating long-term time series forecasting, forecasting models, or forecasting accuracy. One paper instead describes Electricity as being used to evaluate the performance of self-healing adaptation strategies across different data distributions. No construct is linked to it, and no behavioral indicator is linked to it.

Space of uses. Papers usually use ECL as one member of a broader benchmark suite rather than as a standalone instrument. It appears alongside ETTh1, Weather, T

nodes.name: ECQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, ECQA is most commonly treated as a commonsense question-answering dataset or benchmark that requires models to answer questions and provide explanations. Definitions differ in how they expand the name, including Explainable CommonsenseQA, Explanations from Commonsense Knowledge Acquisition, and Explanation-based Commonsense Question Answering. One paper additionally describes it as a knowledge QA dataset with chain-of-thought reasoning, while another uses it as source data for constructing fine-tuning datasets.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link ECQA to one construct and one behavioral indicator. The prevailing use is to measure commonsense reasoning, with papers describing it as used for explainable commonsense reasoning and including it in commonsense evaluations; a smaller use treats it as measuring question answering by adopting its test split for evaluation. These claims concentrate on commonsense reasoning and question answering rather than spanning many targets.

Space of uses. Most papers position ECQA as an evaluation set, either as a benchmark or through its test split. No measurement instrument is linked to it, but papers use it alongs

nodes.name: EDUADAPT
nodes.definition: A benchmark dataset of nearly 48,000 grade-labeled question-answer pairs across nine science subjects for Grades 1–12, designed to evaluate grade-level adaptability in LLMs through both multiple-choice and open-ended questions.

nodes.name: Ego4D
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, Ego4D is most commonly described as a large-scale egocentric video dataset. Definitions emphasize everyday activities, and one paper adds that it has dense annotations for various aspects of the videos. Papers often discuss it as source material for derived benchmarks: HourVideo is curated from Ego4D, with 500 videos covering 77 daily life scenarios, and another line of work recasts Ego4D into an offline procedural mistake detection format for Ego4D-PMD using individually annotated video frames.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the papers, Ego4D is linked to 1 construct and no behavioral indicators. The measurement claims center on Egocentric video understanding: one paper reports that Ego4D offers human-annotated videos and labels for certain egocentric video understanding tasks, particularly episodic memory.

Space of uses. No other measurement instrument is linked to it. Instead, papers mainly position Ego4D as a source dataset from which other evaluations are built or reformatted, including curation for HourVideo and recasting into an offline mistake detection setting for Ego4D-PMD.

nodes.name: EgoSchema
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, EgoSchema is most commonly treated as a benchmark, often called a benchmark dataset, for long-form or long video question answering on egocentric videos. Some descriptions frame it more broadly as a benchmark for very long-form or long-context video-language understanding, but the recurring details are multiple-choice questions over egocentric videos, often described as over 5K videos or 5000 questions and as three-minute videos or videos with an average length of 3 minutes. Some papers further specify evaluation slices such as a 500-question subset, the full test split, or a 5031-video test set.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link EgoSchema to 4 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator. The prevailing measurement claims are that it measures video understanding and long video understanding, and papers also use it to measure egocentric video understanding, temporal reasoning, and the behavioral indicator video question answering. Overall, papers use it across several targets rather than tying it to only one.

Space of uses. Papers do not describe EgoSchema through direct instrument-to-instrument relationship claims. Instead, they usually deploy it as

nodes.name: EHRNoteQA
nodes.definition: A clinical benchmark comprising 962 QA pairs linked to distinct patients' discharge summaries from MIMIC-IV EHR, evaluated in both open-ended and multi-choice formats.

nodes.name: EIFBENCH
nodes.definition: Extremely Complex Instruction Following Benchmark, a multi-instruction, multi-constraint evaluation framework assessing LLMs across diverse task types and constraint categories in plain text, dyadic dialogue, and multi-party dialogue scenarios.

nodes.name: ELI5
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, ELI5 is most commonly described as an open-ended, long-form question-answering dataset. Definitions usually emphasize user-generated questions about science, history, and everyday life, often sourced from the Reddit "Explain Like I’m Five" forum, with answers expected to be simple and easy to understand, paragraph-length, or otherwise comprehensive and multi-aspect. Some papers foreground factual question answering and helpfulness, while others describe complex QA or LFQA settings, including a WebGPT-collected version with questions, model-generated answers, and supporting context.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link ELI5 to two behavioral indicators and two constructs. The prevailing usage is to measure long-form question answering, and more broadly question answering. A narrower use treats evaluations on ELI5 as measuring trustworthiness and unanswerability detection ability, with table-based evaluations referring to TRUST-SCORE and Grounded Refusals F1.

Space of uses. Papers usually position ELI5 as an evaluation benchmark or prompt source for long-form QA and retrieval-augmented generation. It is often used alongside ASQA, and also with NQ-Op

nodes.name: EMBODYGUARD
nodes.definition: A PDDL-grounded benchmark containing 942 LLM-generated scenarios for evaluating physical safety in embodied decision-making, split into EMBODYGUARDmal (malicious commands) and EMBODYGUARDsit (situational hazards).

nodes.name: Emotion (dair-ai)
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats Emotion (Saravia et al., 2018) as a text classification dataset or benchmark for fine-grained emotion classification. One definition specifies six classes, joy, sadness, anger, fear, love, and surprise, and one study describes these as six "nuanced" classes in a more complex evaluation. Another definition also presents it as a six-category emotion benchmark but lists anger, disgust, fear, joy, sadness, and surprise, so papers do not describe the label set identically.

What it is claimed to measure. Most papers use it to measure Text classification, describing Emotion among "Text Classification datasets" and text classification benchmark suites. A smaller line of work uses it to measure Sentiment analysis, with one paper describing it as text data labeled with various emotions and suitable for sentiment analysis tasks. Papers link it to 2 behavioral indicators, Text classification and Sentiment analysis, and to no constructs.

Space of uses. Papers often place it inside multi-dataset evaluation suites. In those setups it appears alongside other text classification datasets such as CoLA, AG News, Stanford Sentiment Tr

nodes.name: EmpatheticDialogues
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the cited definitions, the prevailing treatment is as a dialogue dataset centered on emotional situations. Papers describe it as conversations grounded in specific emotional situations and, more specifically in one definition, as 24,850 multi-turn speaker-listener conversations annotated with one of 32 emotions for fine-grained emotion classification. Another naming variant in the papers, E-Dialogue, is described as a benchmark for evaluating empathetic capabilities in open-domain conversation models, so the descriptions emphasize either fine-grained emotion labels or empathetic evaluation.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it most often as a task or evaluation dataset for fine-grained emotion classification and emotion detection in dialogue, while another definition says it evaluates empathetic capabilities in open-domain conversation models. No construct or behavioral indicator is linked to it, so the papers here describe its measurement role through tasks rather than explicit construct mappings.

Space of uses. Papers position it as a benchmark or task dataset. No measurement instrument is linked to it, but one paper reports using E-Dialogue alongside

nodes.name: Enron email dataset
nodes.definition: A standard dataset of emails from which personally identifiable information is sampled to construct prompts for privacy evaluation.

nodes.name: EntityQuestions
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers describe EntityQuestions as a question answering dataset. The prevailing description is a closed-book QA specific dataset containing knowledge across 24 topics extracted from Wikipedia and used to construct training and testing sets, while another paper frames it more broadly as a fact-seeking QA dataset centered on entity-related factual knowledge.

What it is claimed to measure. In the recorded relationships, papers link it to one behavioral indicator, Closed-book question answering, which is measured by EntityQuestions, and no constructs are linked to it. Separately, one definition describes it as being used to evaluate non-factuality prediction in fact-seeking question answering.

Space of uses. Papers use EntityQuestions in different evaluation roles. One paper uses it to construct training and testing datasets for experiments, while another poses questions from it alongside PopQA and Natural Questions as one of three widely-used QA datasets; papers do not link it to any other measurement instrument.

nodes.name: Enwik8
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most commonly, papers treat Enwik8 as a Wikipedia language modeling benchmark built from 100 million bytes of unprocessed English-language text. Definitions usually frame it as byte-level and as a dataset for compression and sequence prediction, with one paper noting long-term dependencies that can span tens of thousands of bytes and another describing it as a standard English Wikipedia dataset for training and evaluating compression models. A smaller line describes EnWik-8 as a character-level language modeling benchmark for evaluating pretraining performance, so the prevailing framing is byte-level but not uniform. One paper also contrasts it with enwik9, described there as an extension, while enwik8 contains the first 100 million bytes.

What it is claimed to measure. The papers do not explicitly report Enwik8 as measuring any named construct or behavioral indicator. Instead, they use it as an evaluation setting and report outputs such as test bits-per-byte and, in the character-level framing, test bytes-per-character.

Space of uses. Across the papers, Enwik8 is used for both training and evaluation: one paper states that it trains vanilla Transformer models on enwi

nodes.name: EQ-Bench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers describe EQ-Bench in two different ways. One treats it as a benchmark for creative writing, specifically a creative writing leaderboard scored by other LLMs. Another describes it as an emotional intelligence benchmark that incorporates human survey ratings and allows multiple correct answers through cosine similarity to weighted choice distributions.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, EQ-Bench is linked to three constructs and no behavioral indicators. Those measurement claims are spread across emotion understanding, emotional intelligence, and social and emotional intelligence: papers report using it to evaluate emotional understanding ability, treat it as a benchmark from a similar emotional-intelligence domain, and place it within socio-emotional evaluation.

Space of uses. Papers use EQ-Bench as an evaluation benchmark. No measurement instrument is linked to it, though one paper groups it with LM-Pragmatics, SocialIQA, and SimpleToM under a socio-emotional category, and another uses it as a comparison point alongside other benchmarks from a similar domain.

nodes.name: EquiBench
nodes.definition: A benchmark consisting of 2400 program pairs in Python, C, CUDA, and x86-64, designed to evaluate an LLM's ability to reason about program semantics via equivalence checking.

nodes.name: ESC-50
nodes.definition: Environmental sound classification benchmark with 50 classes, used to evaluate zero-shot audio classification performance.

nodes.name: ESC-Judge
nodes.definition: An automated, LLM-driven evaluation framework that compares emotional-support LLMs using synthetic help-seeker roles and a judge model guided by Hill’s Exploration–Insight–Action rubric across nine fine-grained dimensions.

nodes.name: ESConv
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly describe ESConv as a benchmark dataset for emotional support conversations. The definition presents it as collected in a help-seeker and supporter mode, with approximately 1K conversations and 31K utterances, and with utterances annotated with one of eight support strategies.

What it is claimed to measure. In the linked work, ESConv is used to measure 1 behavioral indicator, Text generation, and it is not linked to any constructs. The reported measurement claim is narrow rather than spread across multiple outcomes: one paper says it conducts experiments on ESConv when applying IntentionFrame to enhance downstream response generation.

Space of uses. Across the cited work, ESConv is positioned as an experimental benchmark for emotional support conversation systems. No other measurement instrument is linked to it. Papers use it for experiments on response generation and framework evaluation, including studies that report experiments on ESConv when assessing emotional support performance and support strategy selection.

nodes.name: ESOL
nodes.definition: A dataset from the MoleculeNet benchmark for the regression task of predicting the log water solubility of a molecule.

nodes.name: ETHICS
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across definitions, ETHICS is most commonly described as a benchmark dataset for machine ethics or ethical reasoning built from morally charged, scenario-based examples. Papers variously describe first-person descriptions of morally relevant actions with binary labels, tasks where models categorize scenarios as "wrong" or "not wrong," and subsets such as Commonsense, Justice, and Deontology; one description highlights the Commonsense subset as featuring scenario-based moral recognition tasks. A smaller framing treats it more narrowly as a zero-shot benchmark or as a dataset assessing whether described actions are wrong.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link ETHICS to 2 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators, and the prevailing use is as a measure of Moral reasoning. A smaller line of work treats it as measuring Ethical decision-making, while behavioral-indicator links report its use for Binary classification and Zero-shot task performance. Overall, the claims concentrate on moral reasoning, and one relationship explicitly states that ETHICS mainly measures an LLM's moral reasoning ability.

Space of uses. No other measurement instrument is linked to it by an expli

nodes.name: ETHOS
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the usage in the papers, ETHOS is described as a dataset for detecting hate speech. The only definition further presents it as a binary classification benchmark on which papers report F1 score under optimized prompts.

What it is claimed to measure. The papers here use ETHOS for hate-speech detection evaluation via F1 in binary classification. No papers link it to any constructs or behavioral indicators.

Space of uses. In the only described usage, ETHOS is reported alongside ArSarcasm, Liar, and BBH-navigate, with F1 used as the evaluation metric in the same setup.

nodes.name: ETTh1
nodes.definition: A real-world benchmark dataset for long-term time series forecasting, consisting of seven factors related to electricity transformers.

nodes.name: ETTm1
nodes.definition: A time series benchmark dataset used in long-term forecasting evaluations, part of the Electricity Transformer Temperature datasets with hourly and minute-level sampling.

nodes.name: EuroGEST
nodes.definition: A multilingual dataset for measuring gender stereotypes in 30 European languages, consisting of gendered minimal sentence pairs (EuroGESTG) and gender-neutral sentences (EuroGESTN) that can be placed in gendered templates.

nodes.name: EuroSAT
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, EuroSAT is most commonly described as a satellite imagery or satellite image classification benchmark or dataset used for image classification. Some definitions narrow this to land use and land cover classification, with one description calling it a dataset and deep learning benchmark for that task, and another specifying Sentinel-2 satellite images covering 10 land use and land cover classes. A smaller line of description frames it through particular evaluation settings, such as remote sensing image understanding or the evaluation of descriptions for rare or abstract visual concepts.

What it is claimed to measure. In the recorded links, papers use EuroSAT to measure the behavioral indicator Image classification. It is linked to one behavioral indicator, Image classification, and to no constructs. Several papers describe evaluations on EuroSAT as part of image recognition or classification benchmarks, including formulations such as satellite image classification and standard benchmark datasets for multiple classification domains.

Space of uses. Papers usually position EuroSAT as one dataset within broader benchmark suites for image recognitio

nodes.name: EvalPlus
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing description is an augmented evaluation framework or suite for HumanEval and MBPP that adds more test cases for more rigorous assessment of Python code generation and functional correctness. Definitions regularly refer to its plus versions, HumanEval+ and MBPP+, and one paper notes that scores are reported both on HE and MBPP base test cases and on HE+ and MBPP+ plus test cases. A smaller line of work describes it more narrowly as the test set used to augment HumanEval, while some definitions focus specifically on MBPP+ as the extended MBPP portion covering human-written basic Python tasks.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers most commonly use EvalPlus to measure code generation, and that is the dominant role across the surveyed work. More broadly, papers link it to 3 behavioral indicators, Code generation, Code debugging, and Coding, and to 2 constructs, Inductive reasoning and Self-correction ability. The overall pattern is therefore concentrated on code generation, with smaller uses that report it as evaluating coding, code debugging, self-correction ability, or, through MBPP+, inductive reasoning.

Space of uses. In use, papers relate

nodes.name: Event-Bench
nodes.definition: A benchmark for evaluating long video understanding, with a specific focus on the challenging task of episodic reasoning.

nodes.name: EvoEval
nodes.definition: Benchmark with 828 programming problems evolved from HumanEval using GPT-4, including semantic-altering and semantic-preserving variants to test robustness and efficiency.

nodes.name: Evol-Instruct
nodes.definition: Evol-Instruct, an instruction-following benchmark used to compare model responses under pairwise judgment.

nodes.name: EVOUNA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the cited papers, EVOUNA is most commonly described as a question answering benchmark augmented with LLM-generated responses and human annotations of whether each response is semantically equivalent to the golden answer. A smaller framing presents it as a dataset containing human evaluations of reader models on question answering tasks, rather than only as a benchmark.

What it is claimed to measure. The papers describe EVOUNA around human judgments of semantic equivalence in question answering, and one description frames it more broadly as containing human evaluations of reader models on QA tasks. Papers do not link it to any named constructs or behavioral indicators, so the surveyed usage does not converge on a recorded construct that it measures.

Space of uses. Papers use EVOUNA directly as a QA benchmark, and one paper also uses it as source data for constructing EMBERQA. No other measurement instrument is linked to it, so the usage in the papers mainly positions it as a standalone benchmark or as material reused in another benchmark-building setup.

nodes.name: Execution-based evaluation
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing description is of an evaluation method or protocol that verifies success through execution, rather than relying on static demonstrations or string matching. Most definitions instantiate this either as running generated code against test cases and checking whether outputs match expected results, or as using custom scripts to check the final state of a computer environment. A narrower variant, called execution-based focused evaluation, has annotators obtain database results programmatically and write scripts that focus on the essential components of the answer while ignoring non-essential columns, and one paper describes sandbox execution in a secure, isolated Docker-based environment for validating code and test cases.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link this instrument to 1 behavioral indicator and no constructs. The measurement claim converges on code generation: papers report that the execution-based method runs generated code against test cases to measure success rate, with generated outputs expected to equal the target outputs.

Space of uses. Papers link it to 1 other measurement instrument, OSWorld, and describe that bench

nodes.name: Expert evaluation
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage is a domain-specific human assessment protocol: experts or other qualified evaluators manually review model outputs, annotations, or benchmark items against references, task requirements, or explicit rubrics. Definitions vary in name, including human expert evaluation, expert annotation, expert review, reader study, validation, and human-as-a-judge, but most describe independent scoring or comparison by clinicians, physicians, radiologists, legal experts, translators, researchers, or other subject-matter specialists; some papers instead use native speakers, students, or trained participants. Common formats include pairwise comparisons, rubric-based ratings, binary judgments, blind or randomized review, and consensus adjudication after disagreements, and some papers use the protocol not only to assess model outputs but also to validate labels, benchmark items, or human performance baselines.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use expert evaluation to measure five constructs, Accuracy, Faithfulness, Fluency, Legal accuracy, and Relevance, and one behavioral indicator, Hallucination. The linked claims are spread across several dimens

nodes.name: FActScore
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most commonly described as a reference-based evaluation procedure for long-form generation, especially biographies, papers say it decomposes generated text into atomic facts or claims and verifies each one against a knowledge source, reference passages, or retrieved Wikipedia evidence. Across definitions, authors alternately call it a tool, benchmark, framework, suite, fact evaluator, or automated retrieval augmentation pipeline, and describe outputs as a precision or percentage of supported atomic facts, or counts of true and false facts. A smaller naming family in the papers includes FACTSCORES, defined as the proportion of cited sub-facts that are supported, and FactScore-Bio, described as a long-form QA dataset of biography questions from Wikipedia.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to 2 constructs and 3 behavioral indicators. The prevailing usage is to measure Factuality: papers describe it as reference-based truthfulness scoring, as evaluating factuality of biographies or generated summaries, and as assessing factuality degradation by comparing generations with original text. A smaller line of work uses it to measure Faithfulness, including faithful b

nodes.name: FairEval
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly treat FairEval as a benchmark dataset for open-ended question answering: definitions describe 80 open-ended questions drawn from a wide array of categories, including common-sense, counterfactual, and coding, with corresponding human annotations. Some papers describe it differently, casting it as a meta-evaluation benchmark for assessing the performance and biases of LLM evaluators, while another paper uses it as a fairness-oriented evaluation procedure adopted to eliminate positional bias.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the surveyed work, the recorded measurement claim concentrates on one behavioral indicator: papers use FairEval to measure Open-ended question answering. No construct is linked to it, so the reported use converges on that single behavioral indicator rather than spreading across multiple constructs or behaviors.

Space of uses. Papers use FairEval both as a benchmark in model evaluation and as a reference point in evaluator meta-evaluation. One paper evaluates a system on FairEval alongside Topical-Chat, where FairEval represents the open-ended question answer category, another compares evaluator accuracies on FairEval agains

nodes.name: FaithEval
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers describe FaithEval as an evaluation benchmark. One framing presents it as designed to measure and reduce model hallucination across different challenging scenarios, while another presents it as a novel and comprehensive benchmark for evaluating the faithfulness of LLMs in contextual scenarios. One paper further describes it as comprising 4.9K high-quality problems built through a four-stage context construction and validation framework.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use FaithEval to measure 1 construct and 1 behavioral indicator. The construct link is Context faithfulness, with papers describing the benchmark as tailored to evaluate the faithfulness of LLMs in contextual scenarios. It is also linked to Hallucination, in work that cites an ablation study on FaithEval as showing reduced hallucinations.

Space of uses. In use, papers relate FaithEval to 2 other instruments, Human evaluation and LLM-as-a-judge. One description says its problems are validated through LLM-based auto-evaluation and human validation, and another says a separate LLM judge is used to verify whether a new answer is valid given the context. It also appears as an ablation benchmark i

nodes.name: Fann or Flop
nodes.definition: A benchmark comprising 6,984 poem-explanation pairs across 12 historical eras and 14 genres of Arabic poetry, designed to evaluate semantic, metaphorical, prosodic, and cultural understanding through QA-style tasks.

nodes.name: FANToM
nodes.definition: A theory-of-mind dataset containing questions based on multi-party dialogues, some of which rest on false premises, to test a model's ability to handle such scenarios.

nodes.name: Fashion-MNIST
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, Fashion-MNIST is described as a dataset of Zalando article images with 60,000 training examples and 10,000 test examples. The definitions agree on that format, while differing slightly in emphasis: one paper presents it as used for image classification, and another describes it as a drop-in replacement for MNIST.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers do not report Fashion-MNIST as measuring any linked constructs or behavioral indicators. The recorded links include no constructs and no behavioral indicators, so the descriptions frame it as a dataset without explicit measured concepts attached to it.

Space of uses. The descriptions place Fashion-MNIST in training setups rather than in explicit measurement claims. One study states that "The MNIST (Deng, 2012) and FashionMNIST (Xiao et al., 2017) datasets are used for pretraining and fine-tuning, respectively" (Beyond Zero Initialization: Investigating the Impact of Non-Zero Initialization on LoRA Fine-Tuning Dynamics), while another simply cites "Fashion MNIST (Xiao et al., 2017)" as the dataset used.

nodes.name: FB15k-237
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the definitions, papers most commonly treat FB15k-237 as a benchmark dataset, or standard benchmark, for knowledge graph completion, derived from Freebase or from the original FB15k. The prevailing description is that it is a subset built by removing inverse relations to reduce or prevent test set leakage, and one definition adds that it focuses on common knowledge. A smaller line of work instead describes it as a large-scale knowledge graph with complex relational semantics.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use FB15k-237 to measure four behavioral indicators and do not link it to any constructs. It is most often used for link prediction, and is also reported as measuring fact checking, graph partitioning, and knowledge graph completion. Overall, the reported uses spread across multiple behavioral indicators rather than converging on a single linked construct.

Space of uses. Papers commonly use it alongside WN18RR, and some also pair it with YAGO3-10, PrimeKG, FB15k-237N, or the FEVER fact verification challenge. In these studies it is positioned as one of the benchmark datasets used for experimental evaluation, for example as one of "two large datasets" f

nodes.name: FB-Bench
nodes.definition: A fine-grained, multi-task benchmark in Chinese for evaluating LLMs’ responsiveness to human feedback across error correction and response maintenance scenarios, using a weighted checklist evaluated by GPT-4o.

nodes.name: Feedback Bench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the definitions, papers treat Feedback Bench as a benchmark for evaluating judge models or LLM-as-a-judge. The fuller description presents it as the official test set of Feedback Collection, with 1K responses to evaluate and instructions and scoring rubrics that do not overlap with the training set, while a briefer description frames it as a benchmark for single-instance rating tasks.

What it is claimed to measure. In the reported relationships, papers use it to measure one construct, Evaluation ability, and no behavioral indicators are linked to it. The claims therefore converge on a single construct rather than spreading across many: one paper reports measuring evaluation ability by checking correlation with GPT-4 across customized score rubrics on Feedback Bench.

Space of uses. Papers use it as an evaluation benchmark for judging tasks, including single-rating evaluation. One study places it alongside MT Bench, Vicuna Bench, and Flask Eval when measuring correlation with GPT-4 across multiple benchmarks, which positions it as one component of a broader evaluation setup.

nodes.name: Ferret-Bench
nodes.definition: A benchmark of multimodal dialogue-style VQA tasks for referring and grounding, constructed with GPT-4.

nodes.name: FeTaQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across these papers, FeTaQA is most commonly described as a table question answering benchmark or dataset with open-ended, free-form, long-form natural-language answers. Definitions repeatedly say that answering requires fetching multiple entities from a table, aggregating or reasoning over them, sometimes across multiple table sections, and producing a coherent response; one paper also describes it as an English dataset of Wikipedia tables paired with questions, answers, and supporting table cells. A smaller use treats FetaQA as table-language data adapted into training formats for table-language interleaved learning and for training column embeddings, rather than only as an evaluation benchmark.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link FeTaQA to 3 behavioral indicators and 1 construct. The prevailing use is to measure Table question answering, with several papers explicitly naming it as a TableQA benchmark or dataset. Smaller lines of work also report it as measuring Data-to-text generation and Long-form question answering, and one paper uses it to measure Table reasoning, so the recorded links are concentrated on table question answering with a few additional fram

nodes.name: FEVER
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, FEVER is most commonly described as a fact verification benchmark or dataset of human-written claims about Wikipedia, paired with evidence from Wikipedia and labeled as Supported, Refuted, or NotEnoughInfo, though one definition gives the third label as neutral. Several papers present it under the full name Fact Extraction and VERification, while smaller usages describe it as a fact-checking task, a natural language inference benchmark, a KILT subset task, or a closed-book fact verification dataset. One paper further describes it as a large-scale resource with 185,000 annotated claims.

What it is claimed to measure. The prevailing usage is to treat FEVER as measuring fact checking: across papers it is linked to one behavioral indicator, Fact checking, and to no constructs. This matches the dominant framing of FEVER as a fact-checking or fact verification task, usually cast as three-class claim classification with evidence. Some papers also describe it as testing world knowledge and factuality, and one paper uses it for factual consistency.

Space of uses. Papers commonly use FEVER as an evaluation task: one study says it uses FEVER 'for all our experimen

nodes.name: FEVEROUS
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, FEVEROUS is most commonly described as a fact-verification or complex claim-verification dataset or benchmark built around mixed evidence. Definitions usually say it combines structured or semi-structured tables with unstructured text or sentences, often from Wikipedia, and several descriptions add complex or multi-hop reasoning, sometimes with evidence annotated at the sentence or table-cell level. A smaller line of work adapts it for open-domain table reasoning by restricting attention to table-only claims and framing the task as identifying relevant evidence tables.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link FEVEROUS to 1 construct and 2 behavioral indicators. The prevailing use is to measure fact checking: papers describe it as a fact verification, claim verification, or fact-checking benchmark for deciding whether evidence supports or refutes claims. Smaller usages treat it as measuring table reasoning, through an open-domain adaptation, and entity disambiguation, through a reported FEVEROUS partition.

Space of uses. Papers do not link FEVEROUS to another measurement instrument. It is nevertheless used alongside other benchmarks, most commonly HOVE

nodes.name: FewEvent
nodes.definition: A dataset for type discovery focused on identifying event types from text.

nodes.name: FewRel
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, FewRel is most commonly described as a benchmark dataset for few-shot relation extraction, used to evaluate model performance in low-resource relation classification scenarios. A recurring variant of this description places it in continual learning settings with limited data. A smaller framing describes it more broadly as a dataset for type discovery that focuses on identifying relation types from text.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use FewRel to evaluate model performance in few-shot relation extraction, especially in low-resource relation classification scenarios and continual learning settings with limited data. Some authors also present it as supporting relation type discovery from text. No construct or behavioral indicator is explicitly linked to it.

Space of uses. Most commonly, papers use FewRel alongside TACRED and position it as a benchmark for experiments and baseline comparisons, including paired FCRE benchmark evaluations. A smaller use groups it with FewEvent and FewNerd as information extraction datasets focused on event, entity, and relation type discovery.

nodes.name: FFHQ
nodes.definition: A high-resolution face image dataset used for unconditional and conditional image generation evaluation.

nodes.name: FGSM
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly describe FGSM as the Fast Gradient Sign Method, an adversarial attack method. The definitions converge on the same mechanism: it generates adversarial examples by adding a small perturbation in the direction of the sign of the loss gradient with respect to the input, and one definition explicitly presents it as a white-box attack.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers do not use FGSM to measure any construct or behavioral indicator, and no measurement links connect it to linked outcomes.

Space of uses. Where papers describe its use, they apply FGSM as an adversarial attack procedure. One paper reports using it together with SI-NI-FGSM and varying the attack strength, stating, "We apply two adversarial attacks FGSM and SI-NI-FGSM with various attack strengths."

nodes.name: FGVC
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, FGVC is treated as a Fine-Grained Visual Classification benchmark for specialized image classification, covering bird, flower, dog, and car recognition. Definitions describe it as five specialized tasks; one source names CUB-Birds, NA-Birds, Oxford Flowers, Stanford Dogs, and Stanford Cars, while a related description says FGVC includes CUB-200-2011, Oxford Flowers, Stanford Dogs, and Stanford Cars.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link FGVC to 1 construct and 1 behavioral indicator, both centered on image-focused evaluation. The prevailing usage is to use FGVC to measure Image classification, and one paper also reports Visual recognition as measured by FGVC.

Space of uses. Papers use FGVC alongside other evaluation settings: one evaluation quote groups it with VTAB-1K, few-shot learning, and domain adaptation as visual classification adaptation tasks, and another reports evaluation on VTAB-1k and the FGVC benchmark. Papers also relate FGVC to 4 instruments, CUB-200-2011, Oxford Flowers-102, Stanford Cars, and Stanford Dogs, describing them as included datasets within the benchmark.

nodes.name: FGVC-Aircraft
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, FGVC-Aircraft is most commonly described as a fine-grained aircraft image classification dataset or benchmark. Definitions converge on aircraft model recognition, with papers variously describing it as focusing on aircraft categories and as containing images of 100 or over 100 different aircraft model variants. A smaller framing specifies the evaluation setting rather than the content, describing it as used for few-shot learning performance, while another definition says it is used to assess visual classification and explanation quality.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to two behavioral indicators and no constructs. The reported measurement claims center on fine-grained visual recognition and image classification: one paper uses FGVC-Aircraft to measure image classification, describing it as part of "12 image recognition datasets" for "aircraft model classification," and another uses it to measure fine-grained visual recognition as one of several "popular FGVR datasets."

Space of uses. Papers typically include it within broader benchmark suites, for example alongside CUB-200, Stanford Dogs, OxfordPets, StanfordCars, and Flowers1

nodes.name: FigStep
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, FigStep is most commonly treated as a multimodal safety benchmark, sometimes described as a harmful-question dataset, for testing vision-language or multimodal models on unsafe prompts. Definitions vary in what they foreground: attacks involving figures and text, harmful-response behavior from image-based prompts, typography that transfers unsafe text into images, and adversarial step-by-step harmful task instructions, with one definition also noting unsafe and benign variants. One paper adapts it by excluding legal, medical, and financial advice categories and converting the questions to speech.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use FigStep to measure three constructs: Safety alignment, Safety, and Safety robustness. The recorded links are all measured_by relations from those constructs to FigStep, and it is not linked to any behavioral indicator. In the papers' own terms, it is used to evaluate safe alignment, multimodal safety, or jailbreak robustness.

Space of uses. FigStep is usually deployed alongside other safety benchmarks, most often MM-SafetyBench and SIUO, and also JailBreaKV, VL-Guard, and MOSSBench. Papers generally position it as o

nodes.name: FilBench
nodes.definition: FILBENCH, a Filipino-centric benchmark suite that evaluates LLMs across cultural knowledge, classical NLP, reading comprehension, and generation tasks in Filipino, Tagalog, and Cebuano.

nodes.name: FIMO
nodes.definition: A formal dataset for automated theorem proving containing challenging Olympiad-level math problems.

nodes.name: FinanceBench
nodes.definition: An English-language financial benchmark consisting of 1 dataset for 1 task.

nodes.name: Financial PhraseBank
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats Financial PhraseBank, also written as FPB or FP, as a benchmark dataset for sentiment analysis or text classification in financial text. Definitions consistently describe sentences from financial news, and one definition broadens this to financial statements and news, annotated for sentiment. Most descriptions specify positive, negative, and neutral categories, while one paper describes its task setup on the dataset as positive or negative.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use Financial PhraseBank to measure 2 behavioral indicators and link it to no constructs. The dominant claim is that it measures sentiment analysis, with papers describing it as extracting positive, negative, or neutral sentiment from financial texts. A smaller but recurring line of work uses it as a text classification benchmark, describing it among several text classification datasets.

Space of uses. Papers often use it within multi-dataset evaluations, for example alongside FiQA-SA and TSA in financial sentiment analysis, or alongside Tweet Irony and MRPC in broader text classification comparisons. Some papers also frame it as a focused t

nodes.name: FineDiving
nodes.definition: A dataset of Olympic diving performances, used as a source for the 'Diving' category videos in the VidDiffBench benchmark.

nodes.name: FinEval
nodes.definition: Benchmark for evaluating financial domain understanding and reasoning in language models.

nodes.name: FineWeb
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, FineWeb is described as a web-text or pretraining corpus. Definitions variously call it a web-text corpus for analyzing bilinear transformer feature interactions, a high-quality LLM pretraining dataset used to synthesize prompts, and a large corpus of deduplicated English web documents from which one study samples 10k examples to evaluate negative log-likelihood. One paper also refers to "two FineWeb models" with 12 and 16 layers, labeled "fw-small" and "fw-medium."

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link FineWeb to one construct and no behavioral indicators. The only recorded measurement claim is that papers use it to measure Generalization: one study evaluates a model trained on C4 on FineWeb as one of several other datasets. In the recorded relationships, measurement claims therefore center on Generalization rather than spreading across multiple constructs.

Space of uses. Papers use FineWeb in several ways: as a prompt source for base LLMs, as a source of deduplicated English web documents for negative log-likelihood evaluation, and as data for analyzing bilinear transformer feature interactions at different model sizes. In one evaluation setu

nodes.name: FineWeb-Edu
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, FineWeb-Edu is most commonly described as a curated educational web-text dataset used in language model training and evaluation. Definitions present it as high-quality educational text from CommonCrawl, while one paper instead treats Fineweb-Edu as an English LLM-annotated dataset with approximately 450,000 document assessments of educational value. Another description presents it as educational text filtered from FineWeb, comprising 1.3T tokens with documents up to 339K tokens long, and mentions a curated subset of 1,000 texts of 128K tokens each for perplexity assessment.

What it is claimed to measure. The papers do not link FineWeb-Edu to any construct or behavioral indicator through measured_by relations, so no prevailing claim appears about what it measures. In the descriptions, it is used as training, evaluation, sampling, or perplexity material rather than being tied to a recorded construct-level or behavioral measurement claim.

Space of uses. Papers position it mainly as source material rather than as an instrument used alongside other named instruments, and no other measurement instrument is linked to it. The recurring uses are training on

nodes.name: FinQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, FinQA is most commonly described as a financial question-answering benchmark or dataset. The most specific definition presents it as a held-out dataset where answering requires generating a Python-executable math expression from a question and financial tables, while other papers describe it more broadly as a benchmark focused on knowledge-based question answering or as a financial QA dataset that primarily assesses text generation.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, it is linked to 1 construct and no behavioral indicators, and the linked construct is Financial reasoning. The only recorded measurement claim is that papers use FinQA to measure Financial reasoning, with one paper describing FinQA and ConvFinQA as datasets developed to benchmark models for numerical reasoning tasks in the financial domain, so the reported use converges on that single construct rather than spreading across several.

Space of uses. Papers usually position FinQA as an evaluation resource. One paper uses it as a held-out dataset to evaluate generalization on questions and tables, another uses it with Fin-Fact to construct reranking tasks, and other discussion pla

nodes.name: FINTRUST
nodes.definition: A comprehensive benchmark with 15,680 question-answer pairs across textual, tabular, and time-series data, designed to evaluate LLM trustworthiness in finance through seven dimensions: truthfulness, safety, fairness, robustness, privacy, transparency, and knowledge discovery.

nodes.name: FiQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly treat FiQA as a retrieval benchmark within BEIR. Definitions variously describe it as a single-hop retrieval benchmark whose corpus consists of human-written responses to the search queries, as a dataset from the BEIR benchmark for financial question answering, and as a financial QA benchmark used for downstream evaluation; one paper also describes using it as a retrieval dataset for generating and evaluating adversarial passages in corpus-poisoning experiments.

What it is claimed to measure. Measurement claims are concentrated on one target: papers link FiQA to no constructs and to one behavioral indicator, financial question answering. In Co-Eval: Augmenting LLM-based Evaluation with Machine Metrics and Training a Utility-based Retriever Through Shared Context Attribution for Retrieval-Augmented Language Models, papers use it to measure financial question answering, including the label "FiQA (Maia et al., 2018), Financial QA."

Space of uses. Papers usually position FiQA within BEIR, and BEIR is the only linked measurement instrument through a related link. In use, papers include it among BEIR retrieval benchmarks, pair it with NFCorpus, SciFact,

nodes.name: FiQA-SA
nodes.definition: A dataset for sentiment analysis in the financial domain.

nodes.name: FLAN
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across these papers, FLAN is described as a benchmark or collection of datasets covering diverse NLP tasks, including free-form generation tasks such as translation and summarization, with datasets expressed through natural language instructions. The prevailing usage is as a broad multi-task evaluation set, and papers also describe it as a mix of multiple NLP tasks used as a reference dataset.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use FLAN to measure two constructs, Generalization and Robustness. These measurement claims cover both constructs rather than a single repeated target, and FLAN is also related to one behavioral indicator, Text generation, through descriptions of its free-form generation tasks.

Space of uses. Papers mainly position FLAN as a broad evaluation benchmark. It is used as a large multi-task evaluation set, as a reference dataset when demonstrating generalization and robustness, and alongside Wikitext and Gigaword for evaluation across various tasks. No other measurement instrument is linked to it.

nodes.name: FLAN Collection
nodes.definition: The FLAN Collection is a dataset composed of various tasks formatted as instructions, used to evaluate instruction-following, chain-of-thought, and few-shot learning capabilities.

nodes.name: FLASK
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing framing is FLASK as a fine-grained benchmark or evaluation protocol for particular LLM skill sets. Definitions vary in emphasis: some describe a benchmark for fine-grained evaluation, others a model-based protocol for assessing generated text such as rationales across dimensions like logical thinking, and one defines it more concretely as 200 test prompts paired with 2000 responses from Alpaca-7B, Vicuna-13B, Bard, and GPT-3.5-Turbo-0613 to assess LLM-as-a-judge performance across diverse outputs. A smaller line of work treats it as a benchmark for judge models on single-instance rating tasks, and one usage focuses on its logical thinking category, covering logical correctness, logical robustness, and logical efficiency.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use FLASK to measure 4 constructs and no behavioral indicators, and the reported targets are spread across those constructs rather than centered on one recurring claim. The linked constructs are Insightfulness, Text generation quality, Logical consistency, and Logical reasoning. One paper describes FLASK as offering "12 skill-specific scores," while another uses its logical thinking ca

nodes.name: FLenQA
nodes.definition: Flexible Length Question Answering, a benchmark that assesses a model's reasoning capabilities over contexts of varying lengths by asking True/False questions.

nodes.name: FLEURS
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats FLEURS as a multilingual speech benchmark or dataset, often for automatic speech recognition, and one definition expands its name as the Few-shot Learning Evaluation of Universal Representations of Speech. Some papers narrow this to the English test split or test subset, where WER is computed, while a smaller line of work describes it as a multilingual or massively multilingual speech translation benchmark, including translation between English and German, Spanish, and French in both directions. One paper describes it as speech for 102 languages, and another says it covers 21 African languages.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link FLEURS to 2 behavioral indicators and no constructs, so the claims about what it measures concentrate on behavioral indicators rather than constructs. The most common claim is that it measures Speech recognition, including ASR evaluations and WER on the English test split, and a smaller line of work also uses it to measure Speech translation through ST tasks on several language pairs.

Space of uses. Papers commonly position FLEURS as a standard multilingual benchmark for ASR and AST

nodes.name: FLEURS-ASL
nodes.definition: A benchmark for American Sign Language to English video translation, extended from the multilingual FLORES/FLEURS benchmarks and featuring vocabulary from Wikipedia articles.

nodes.name: Flickr30k
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, Flickr30k is most commonly described as a benchmark dataset for image captioning: papers depict it as 30,000 images from Flickr paired with descriptive captions, often five per image, and sometimes emphasize human-annotated captions. A smaller but recurring framing treats it as an image-text retrieval benchmark, where models match images to captions or the reverse, and some papers also use it for text-to-image generation. One paper further specifies evaluation on the Flickr30k Karpathy split test set.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the papers, Flickr30k is linked to 3 behavioral indicators and 2 constructs. The prevailing measurement claim is image captioning, with papers using it to evaluate image-level caption ability, zero-shot caption generation, and general image captioning; a smaller line of work uses it to measure cross-modal retrieval, including image-to-text and text-to-image retrieval, and a few papers use it for image generation. At the construct level, papers report it as measuring visual perception through captioning scenarios and as evaluating multimodal understanding.

Space of uses. Papers commonly position Flickr30k as

nodes.name: Flickr30k Entities
nodes.definition: Benchmark dataset for phrase grounding, where models are evaluated on their ability to localize text phrases in images; uses recall at K (R@1, R@5, R@10) with IoU > 0.5.

nodes.name: FLORES
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, FLORES is most commonly described as a benchmark dataset for machine translation, often framed as multilingual or massively multilingual and used across many languages. Definitions describe it as evaluating text-to-text translation across over 200 languages, with one paper paraphrasing it as a set of short documents translated into 200 languages, while other papers emphasize low-resource evaluation, translation across languages and scripts, or high-quality translation between language pairs. A smaller line of work describes Flores as a dataset for bitext mining where the same sentences are shared across several language pairs, and some papers refer specifically to FLORES devtest for npi and gug.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link FLORES to one behavioral indicator, Machine translation, and one construct, Translation quality, so the named measurement claims focus on these outcomes rather than a wider set. The prevailing usage is to measure machine translation: papers say they use or adopt FLORES to assess machine translation performance, including English to non-English and non-English to English settings and experiments on 100 languages. A smalle

nodes.name: Flores-101
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across definitions, Flores-101 is most commonly described as a multilingual benchmark dataset with aligned translations or translation pairs across 101 languages. Papers variously describe the content as professionally translated sentences, aligned translations, or human-written translation pairs, and one usage specifically refers to the devtest. A smaller description treats it more broadly as a benchmark for machine translation and cross-lingual generation, with BLEU and COMET used to assess translation quality.

What it is claimed to measure. In the linked literature, papers use Flores-101 to measure Machine translation. It is linked to 1 behavioral indicator, Machine translation, and to no constructs, so the reported use converges on a single behavioral indicator rather than spreading across multiple constructs. The relationship evidence describes it as an evaluation set for translation, as a benchmark for translation tasks from FLORES-101, and as covering bidirectional Eng→X and X→Eng machine translation.

Space of uses. Papers most often position Flores-101 as an evaluation benchmark, using it to test models on translation tasks and multilingual capabilities. It ap

nodes.name: FLORES-200
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most definitions treat FLORES-200 as a multilingual machine translation benchmark spanning 200 languages, often emphasizing low-resource coverage. Papers variously use its development, test, and devtest splits; some explicitly describe it as parallel text, and one definition says it contains short paragraphs sampled from Wikimedia and translated by skilled human translators into 204 languages, whereas most others describe 200 languages. A smaller line of work also uses its development and test sets as high-quality parallel training data, and one paper notes that Belebele passages are sourced from FLORES-200.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the linked claims, papers use FLORES-200 to measure 1 behavioral indicator, Machine translation, and 1 construct, Generalization. The prevailing usage is machine translation evaluation, including low-resource, multilingual, English-to-X, X-to-English, and many-to-many settings; papers report chrF1, spBLEU, COMET, or BLEU on the benchmark. Only one construct link appears: one paper uses Flores200 for zero-shot evaluation as a measure of generalization in En-Zh and En-De translation.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is l

nodes.name: FLORES+
nodes.definition:
What it is. In the definitions, FLORES+ is treated as a multilingual parallel-sentence dataset. The only described use frames it as an out-of-domain dataset for visualizing cross-lingual alignment with t-SNE, and one paper says it "randomly sample[s] 100 parallel sentences" for that examination (Debiasing Multilingual LLMs in Cross-lingual Latent Space).

What it is claimed to measure. Papers in the evidence do not link FLORES+ to any construct or behavioral indicator through explicit measurement claims. The only stated evaluation target is cross-lingual alignment in a visualization setting, where authors examine sentence representations with t-SNE rather than report it as measuring a broader construct.

Space of uses. The documented usage is narrow: papers use FLORES+ as an out-of-domain set for visualization. In the reported procedure, authors sample 100 parallel sentences and inspect their cross-lingual alignment with t-SNE; no linked instruments are reported alongside it.

nodes.name: FLUID QA
nodes.definition: A multilingual benchmark that evaluates figurative language usage in multi-turn dialogue across English, Korean, and Chinese, using a cloze-style multiple-choice format to assess pragmatic appropriateness.

nodes.name: FM2
nodes.definition: Fact verification benchmark assessing whether models can verify claims using retrieved evidence.

nodes.name: fMoW
nodes.definition: The Functional Map of the World (FMOW) dataset, a satellite imagery benchmark for object classification that includes multiple classes and spurious groups, used to test model performance in complex settings.

nodes.name: FoCus
nodes.definition: A dialogue dataset focused on conversational information-seeking scenarios, used for developing and evaluating personalized dialogue systems.

nodes.name: FOLIO
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most commonly, papers treat FOLIO as a benchmark dataset for natural language reasoning with first-order logic, where models infer or assess conclusions from given premises. Several definitions emphasize that it is human or expert annotated and includes first-order logic annotations, while a smaller translation-oriented use describes it as English statements paired with logical forms for NL-FOL generation. Papers describe it at different granularities, from around 1,000 human-annotated deductive reasoning questions overall to a validation split of 203 expert-written natural language reasoning instances with corresponding first-order logic annotations, and some mention evaluation on the validation set or an original and perturbed version.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, the prevailing usage is that FOLIO measures Logical reasoning. It is linked to 3 constructs and no behavioral indicators, and the other reported measurement claims are less common: some papers use it to measure Chain-of-thought reasoning or Reasoning more broadly. Overall, the measurement claims converge mainly on logical reasoning rather than being spread evenly across many constructs.

Sp

nodes.name: FollowBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the dominant description is of a fine-grained constraint-following benchmark with five levels of difficulty, built from diverse, open-ended instructions and evaluated by strong LLMs such as GPT-4. Some authors frame it more specifically as a benchmark for complex, multi-constraint instruction-following tasks, while others describe it as covering more general instructions that require LLM-based judgment rather than simple code execution.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to 3 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator. The prevailing use is to measure instruction following ability and complex instruction following ability, with instruction following also measured by it; one paper additionally uses it to measure generalization on more general instructions not verifiable by simple code executions. Overall, the recorded claims cluster around instruction following and its complex variant, with generalization appearing as a less common target.

Space of uses. Papers typically deploy it alongside other instruction-following benchmarks rather than on its own. It often appears with IFEval and CFBench, and also with ComplexBench, Multi-IF, and Sy

nodes.name: FollowIR
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, FollowIR is most commonly described as a benchmark for instruction-following document retrieval, or more broadly for instruction following in information retrieval, used to assess how well models adapt to user instructions in search queries. A narrower description adds that it is built from three TREC collections and uses a pairwise evaluation framework to measure how models respond to altered instructions. One paper also presents FOLLOWIR as more than a benchmark alone, pairing it with training data that includes diverse and realistic instructions.

What it is claimed to measure. The reported measurement claims converge on a single behavioral indicator: papers use FollowIR to measure Instruction following, describing it as a benchmark that explicitly measures the instruction-following ability or capabilities of retrieval models. It is linked to one behavioral indicator, Instruction following, and to no constructs.

Space of uses. Papers use FollowIR as an evaluation benchmark for retrieval models, including reporting performance on instruction-following retrieval tasks and evaluating models' instruction-following capabilities on the benchmark. One paper

nodes.name: Food-101
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most papers describe Food-101 as a food image classification dataset or benchmark organized around 101 food categories. Several definitions also frame it as a fine-grained image classification or recognition resource, and some add that it contains 101,000 images and is challenging. Some papers describe it more specifically as being used for zero-shot class descriptions, zero-shot transfer, or few-shot learning performance, while others use it more generally for image classification and prediction-correctness evaluation.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link Food-101 to 1 behavioral indicator and no constructs. The reported relationship is consistent: papers use Food-101 to measure Image classification, and no other behavioral indicators are linked to it. The measurement claims therefore converge on a single behavioral target rather than spreading across multiple constructs.

Space of uses. Papers usually place Food-101 within larger benchmark suites rather than using it alone, often alongside CIFAR-100, CUB, Caltech101, OxfordPets, and SUN397. The reported settings include fine-tuning, transfer learning, zero-shot and linear-probe evaluation, and fine-grained imag

nodes.name: FrameNet 1.7
nodes.definition: An expanded FrameNet benchmark with more annotated examples, more defined frame definitions, and increased lexical diversity, used for frame identification evaluation.

nodes.name: FreebaseQA
nodes.definition: A question answering dataset where questions are centered around entities and relations in the Freebase knowledge graph.

nodes.name: FreeSolv
nodes.definition: A dataset from the MoleculeNet benchmark for the regression task of predicting the hydration free energy of a molecule.

nodes.name: FreshQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the dominant framing is a question-answering dataset or benchmark. Definitions converge on questions with varying time sensitivity and complexity, with papers describing it as assessing factuality and reasoning; some add paired correct and incorrect contexts, while others emphasize up-to-date information and questions whose answers change over time, framing it as a benchmark for freshness and factuality of LLM responses.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use FreshQA to measure 4 constructs, and it is not linked to any behavioral indicators. The measurement claims are spread across compositional reasoning, factuality, generalization, and knowledge conflict resolution rather than centered on a single construct: papers variously list it among factuality benchmarks, use it in benchmarking situated faithful reasoning on question-answering tasks, and report it as evaluating compositional reasoning or generalization.

Space of uses. Papers do not link FreshQA to another measurement instrument, but they do use it alongside NaturalQA, TriviaQA, PopQA, CuQA, and MultiHop-RAG. In those uses it is positioned as one of several question-answering tasks, and in

nodes.name: FreshWiki
nodes.definition: A dataset of high-quality, recent Wikipedia articles used to evaluate a model's ability to perform deep research and generate comprehensive articles on a given topic.

nodes.name: FrontierMath
nodes.definition:
What it is. The definition treats FrontierMath as a benchmark for evaluating the complex problem-solving and reasoning abilities of large language models. The accompanying description also places it within reasoning benchmarks, alongside ARC-AGI, when discussing model performance.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link FrontierMath to one construct, Reasoning, and no behavioral indicators. The recorded relationship is that Reasoning is measured by FrontierMath, and the definition likewise frames the benchmark as evaluating reasoning abilities and complex problem-solving.

Space of uses. In the usage in the papers, papers position FrontierMath as a reasoning benchmark used to report model results, and the description mentions it alongside ARC-AGI in that role. No other measurement instrument is linked to it through the recorded relationships.

nodes.name: FSD50K
nodes.definition: A benchmark for audio event classification.

nodes.name: Functional MATH
nodes.definition: Functional MATH is a transfer evaluation dataset used to test whether reasoning improvements generalize beyond the original training benchmark.

nodes.name: FUNSD
nodes.definition: The Form Understanding in Noisy Scanned Documents dataset, used to evaluate key information extraction and form parsing capabilities.

nodes.name: G-Eval
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats G-Eval as an LLM-based automated evaluation framework for generated text. Most definitions describe GPT-4 assigning criterion-level, often 1-5 Likert-scale, scores from a prompt, sometimes step by step with chain-of-thought prompting; applications mentioned include summaries, patent claims, dialogue responses, and condition, answer, and citation-related outputs. A smaller line of work describes it as an auto-CoT framework that generates evaluation steps, as a GPT-4 rubric for helpfulness, honesty, and harmlessness, or as a logit-weighted scoring method that reweights score tokens by the model's own predicted probabilities. Papers also mention adaptations and variants, including GCC-Eval for chess and G-Eval-4, where GPT-4 is sampled 20 times and the average score is used.

What it is claimed to measure. The measurement claims cover multiple output-quality constructs rather than a single recurring one. Papers link it to eight constructs and one behavioral indicator, most frequently as a measure of Coherence, Fluency, Relevance, Empathy, and Faithfulness, with three other constructs also linked. The behavioral-indicator link

nodes.name: GAIA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, GAIA is most commonly treated as a benchmark for general AI assistants and tool use, with multimodal and information-seeking tasks as the dominant framing. Definitions describe it either as a multi-modal benchmark with 446 tasks and 109 files for document understanding, web surfing, logic reasoning, and answer summarization, or as 466 human-designed and annotated questions covering reasoning, multimodal comprehension, coding, and tool usage. A smaller line of work describes it more narrowly as diverse tool-use and information-seeking tasks such as web browsing and file reading, and one comparison paper characterizes it as focused solely on question answering tasks.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link GAIA to 5 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators. The most recurrent use is to measure tool use, with other recurring claims that it measures reasoning and web navigation; papers also report it as measuring generalization, multimodal understanding, robustness, and tool use ability. The reported measurement scope is spread across several abilities, often framed through real-world questions or scenarios that require reasoning, web browsing, multi-modali

nodes.name: Game of 24
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, Game of 24 is most commonly described as a mathematical reasoning benchmark in which a model or agent must combine four given numbers with basic arithmetic operations to produce an expression or equation that evaluates to 24. Definitions usually add that each of the four numbers is used exactly once, and one paper identifies it as a task from 4nums.com. A smaller line of work also frames it as a reasoning and search benchmark, a planning benchmark, or a mathematical puzzle, and papers refer to it as Game of 24, Game 24, or Game24.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to five constructs and two behavioral indicators. The prevailing usage is as a measure of mathematical reasoning, and other papers use it to measure reasoning, planning, decision-making, and logical reasoning. Among behavioral indicators, papers use it to measure mathematical problem solving, while one paper relates it to self-verification by stating that verification is easier than solving on problems such as Game of 24. Overall, the measurement claims are spread across several reasoning-oriented targets rather than centered on only one.

Space of uses. Papers do not link it to ano

nodes.name: GaoKao
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly treat GaoKao as an exam-oriented dataset tied to the Chinese National College Entrance Examination. Definitions describe it either as derived from exam questions or as simulating the exam, but they converge on academic subject coverage and reasoning demand: it is used for Chinese physical, chemical, and mathematical reasoning, and is described as requiring complex or high-level reasoning and knowledge integration.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, the prevailing usage is that GaoKao measures Mathematical reasoning. It is linked to 1 construct, Mathematical reasoning, and no behavioral indicators, so the reported measurement claims converge on a single construct rather than spreading across many. Relationship evidence also describes GAOKAO, alongside ZHONGKAO, as enabling measurement of "a wider range of abilities," while using it to assess model accuracy under chain-of-thought reasoning settings.

Space of uses. The usage in the papers examples place GaoKao alongside other datasets rather than in isolation. Papers use it together with ZHONGKAO and CN Middle School 24 in broader evaluation setups, and one reported protocol assesses model

nodes.name: GaoKao 2023 En
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing description treats this as an English-language or English-translated benchmark or dataset of mathematics problems from the 2023 Chinese National College Entrance Examination, often phrased as the Gaokao math test in English. Papers also frame it as an out-of-domain or out-of-distribution evaluation set. A smaller description is looser, calling it an out-of-distribution mathematics benchmark drawn from major 2023 exam sources for testing generalization.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to measure two constructs and no behavioral indicators. The dominant claim is that it measures Mathematical reasoning, as papers report results on it among advanced math benchmarks, while a broader reasoning framing also appears in diverse reasoning task suites. Overall, the linked claims are concentrated on Mathematical reasoning and Reasoning rather than spread across many constructs.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it. Across the papers, it is used alongside other evaluation benchmarks such as Minerva Math, OCWCourses, GSM8K, MATH or MATH500, and CollegeMath, and it is positioned as part of broader benchmark su

nodes.name: GAVIE
nodes.definition: An evaluation procedure for assessing generative hallucinations by prompting models to produce open-ended captions.

nodes.name: GCG
nodes.definition:
What it is.
