Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats GCG as a white-box, gradient-based jailbreak attack procedure, usually one that greedily optimizes prompt tokens or an adversarial suffix to induce unsafe, specific, or otherwise target outputs. Most definitions describe suffixes appended to harmful queries, while a smaller line describes attack strings prepended to harmful prompts or universal suffixes used to bypass safety filters; one paper instead refers to filtered GCG-generated jailbreak prompts as a dataset, and another mentions nanoGCG as a lightweight variant.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link GCG to 3 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators. The most common measurement claims use it to measure adversarial robustness and jailbreak resistance, often through attack success or failure under GCG; smaller uses report it as measuring harmlessness, robustness, and harmful content detection. Taken together, these claims spread across several safety-related outcomes rather than one construct only.

Space of uses. Papers often position GCG as a popular or state-of-the-art white-box attack within multi-attack evaluation suites, rather than as a standalone chec

nodes.name: GEMBA-MQM
nodes.definition: A prompting-based automatic evaluation metric that uses an LLM to detect translation quality errors based on the Multidimensional Quality Metrics (MQM) framework.

nodes.name: GenEval
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing framing treats GenEval as a benchmark for whether a model can generate an image that is an accurate depiction of a prompt. Most descriptions emphasize prompt accuracy directly, calling it "a benchmark that examines a model's ability to generate an accurate depiction of the prompt," while one paper instead describes it as a metric of generated image quality and text alignment, based on human preferences and semantic accuracy.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use GenEval most often to measure Visual generation ability, with evaluation quoted passages tying it to visual or text-to-image generation capabilities. A smaller line of work uses it to measure Prompt understanding, with one study saying gains on GenEval reflect enhanced prompt-following capabilities, and it is also reported as measuring the behavioral indicator Image generation. Across papers, it is linked to two constructs and one behavioral indicator, with the claims concentrated on visual generation and a smaller extension to prompt understanding.

Space of uses. Papers use GenEval when reporting benchmark scores and model comparisons for image or visual generation. Although

nodes.name: Geometry3K
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, Geometry3K is most commonly described as a geometry benchmark or dataset centered on plane geometry problems. Definitions differ slightly: one paper calls it an early multimodal reasoning benchmark, while another describes a geometry dataset with human-annotated logical forms that is used to generate factual QA pairs and to evaluate geometry problem solving.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to measure 2 constructs and no behavioral indicators. The linked constructs are geometric reasoning and mathematical reasoning, so the measurement claims focus on reasoning tasks: one paper evaluates effectiveness with “the problems from the Geometry3K dataset,” and another includes Geometry3K in geometry sub-task evaluation.

Space of uses. Papers most often position it as an evaluation source. One study uses its problems directly for evaluation, while another also treats it as source material, stating that “the factual QA pairs in the alignment data are generated using Geometry3K”; the same paper places it alongside GeoQA+, UniGeo, and GEOS in geometry-focused evaluation, and notes that the testmini split of MathVista is collected from GeoQA

nodes.name: GeoQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, GeoQA is most commonly described as a geometry question-answering or geometry problem benchmark for evaluating multimodal geometric problem solving. Definitions vary slightly in what they foreground: one emphasizes questions and images, while another emphasizes diagrams, textual descriptions, and the need for complex reasoning.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the papers, GeoQA is linked to one construct, Geometric reasoning, and to no behavioral indicators. In G-LLaVA: Solving Geometric Problem with Multi-Modal Large Language Model and Theorem-Validated Reverse Chain-of-Thought Problem Generation for Geometric Reasoning, it is used to measure Geometric reasoning, so the measurement claims converge on a single construct rather than spreading across many.

Space of uses. In the cited evaluations, papers use the test set of GeoQA alongside the geometry problem solving task, testmini split, of MathVista. One paper also compares model performance on GeoQA with traditional methods in the geometry problem solving domain, which positions it as an evaluation benchmark for model comparison.

nodes.name: GeoQA+
nodes.definition: An enhanced version of the GeoQA dataset for geometric problem solving.

nodes.name: GEOS
nodes.definition: A dataset for geometry problem solving, included as a subtask within the MathVista benchmark.

nodes.name: Global-MMLU
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly describe Global-MMLU as a multilingual extension of MMLU covering 42 languages, with improved translation quality, expanded language coverage, and subsets labeled as culturally sensitive and culturally agnostic. The fuller description presents it as a comprehensive test set containing MMLU's 14K samples in 42 languages, totaling 589,764 samples.

What it is claimed to measure. The cited papers do not explicitly claim that Global-MMLU measures any construct or behavioral indicator, and no construct or behavioral-indicator links are reported for it.

Space of uses. Across the papers, Global-MMLU is positioned as a multilingual benchmark or comprehensive test set for broader language coverage. One paper cites it as part of broader initiatives extending coverage to 42 languages, and no measurement instrument is linked to it.

nodes.name: GlobalOpinionQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, GlobalOpinionQA is most commonly described as a dataset or benchmark built from the World Values Survey and the Pew Global Attitudes Survey, intended to capture diverse perspectives on global issues and align model responses with human opinions across regions. Definitions largely converge on cross-national survey questions and answers, and one paper further describes it as comprising around 2.5K questions. Some papers frame it more specifically as a multiple-choice evaluation of model opinions against aggregated population opinions from different countries, while others treat it as a template that preserves the original questions and response options for consistent formatting. A smaller line of work uses subsets of countries such as C′1 and C3, and one paper converts the original within-country answer distribution into a single answer by selecting the highest-probability choice.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the papers, it is used to measure three constructs, Personalization, Pluralistic alignment, and Social bias, and no behavioral indicators are linked to it. In work on Personalization, papers use it as one of the multiple-choice QA dataset

nodes.name: GLUE
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, GLUE is most commonly described as a multi-task benchmark or suite of diverse natural language understanding tasks, often sentence-level, used to evaluate model performance. Definitions usually mention sentiment analysis, textual entailment or natural language inference, paraphrasing, linguistic acceptability, and semantic textual similarity; some papers describe it as a collection of nine tasks, while others refer to eight tasks or subtasks, and many studies use smaller subsets such as four binary datasets, five tasks, or six tasks. A smaller line of descriptions also includes question answering or coreference resolution in what the benchmark covers.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link GLUE to 8 constructs and 8 behavioral indicators. The prevailing usage is to measure natural language understanding, and papers also use it to measure text classification, natural language inference, sentiment analysis, and general ability. These claims converge most clearly on natural language understanding, though the recorded links also spread across other constructs and task-level indicators.

Space of uses. Most papers use GLUE as a primary downst

nodes.name: GLUE-X
nodes.definition: An extension of the GLUE benchmark specifically designed to evaluate the out-of-domain robustness and generalization of language models.

nodes.name: GMAI-MMBench
nodes.definition: Medical multimodal benchmark assessing visual question answering across 38 modalities and four clinical tasks including attribute, blood vessel, bone, and cell recognition.

nodes.name: GoEmotions
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, GoEmotions is most commonly described as a multi-label emotion recognition benchmark or dataset with 27 fine-grained emotions. Several definitions say it contains human-annotated Reddit comments, with one paper describing 58,000 comments from popular English subreddits and labels drawn from 27 emotions plus neutral, while a smaller line of work describes it more generally as texts with fine-grained emotions and one definition instead refers to human annotations of tweets. Several papers also use pooled variants, usually seven labels formed by hierarchical clustering, and one paper notes an average of 3.6 annotators per sample.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link GoEmotions to one behavioral indicator and no constructs, and the linked indicator is emotion analysis. The claims are concentrated rather than spread across multiple outcomes: several papers use it to measure emotion analysis, describing it as a multilabel emotion recognition benchmark with 27 emotions.

Space of uses. The prevailing use is as an evaluation benchmark for emotion classification or emotion recognition, including fine-grained, multi-label, and open-set setups. Some papers ad

nodes.name: GossipCop
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the cited papers, GossipCop is most commonly treated as a factuality-labeled dataset for entertainment and celebrity gossip content. The prevailing description is a collection of English-language celebrity gossip news articles, labeled for factuality or as true or false, and one definition also describes it as containing related social media posts alongside news articles.

What it is claimed to measure. In the recorded relationships, papers use GossipCop to measure one behavioral indicator, Misinformation detection, and no constructs are linked to it. The measurement claims converge on that single target: papers describe it as a benchmark for fake news or misinformation detection in entertainment-related domains.

Space of uses. Papers position GossipCop as a benchmark dataset for fake news detection tasks. One study presents it as the second of two benchmark datasets used to evaluate a framework, and another applies open-ended rewriting to fake news and rephrases real news from GossipCop alongside PolitiFact.

nodes.name: GovReport
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most papers describe GovReport as a long-document summarization dataset or benchmark built from U.S. government and congressional reports. The prevailing framing emphasizes long inputs, often stating an average document length of 7,866 tokens; one quoted passage adds that it comprises 19,402 reports, and another places it in the SCROLL benchmark for summarizing long government reports. A smaller naming variant treats it as SUM-GOVREPORT, described as a summarization task over long government reports with complex structure and content.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use GovReport mainly to measure text summarization: it is linked to 1 behavioral indicator and 1 construct, and the recurring behavioral indicator is Text summarization. Several papers explicitly describe evaluation on GovReport as "the summarization task" or as testing "long text summarization capacity." A narrower line of use reports it as measuring Length generalization, with one paper including it in "length extrapolation on six long benchmarks."

Space of uses. No other measurement instrument is linked to it through recorded relationships. In use, papers commonly position GovReport as a long-cont

nodes.name: GPQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, GPQA is most commonly described as a graduate-level, "Google-proof" question-answering benchmark or multiple-choice QA dataset built from expert-written scientific questions. The prevailing description places its content in biology, physics, and chemistry, often as 448 questions written by domain experts or PhD-level experts to test deep reasoning and domain expertise; a smaller set of descriptions broadens this to "various scientific subjects" or "various disciplines."

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link GPQA to 9 constructs and 4 behavioral indicators. The dominant claim is that it measures Reasoning, with additional recurring uses for General ability, Generalization, Chain-of-thought reasoning, and Natural language understanding; taken together, papers use it for a range of targets rather than only one. Behavioral-indicator links are present as well, but are fewer and spread across 4 indicators.

Space of uses. Papers do not explicitly relate GPQA to another named measurement instrument. In practice, they usually place it inside larger benchmark suites, often alongside MMLU, BBH, GSM8K, ARC-C, and MT-Bench, depending on whether the evaluation i

nodes.name: GPQA-Diamond
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, GPQA-Diamond is most commonly described as a challenging expert-level science or STEM question answering benchmark for deep reasoning. Most definitions describe graduate-level or expert-level multiple-choice questions across biology, physics, and chemistry, and one definition specifies 198 questions. A smaller line of work frames GPQADiamond as a challenging subset of GPQA used to assess zero-shot generalization on an unseen task, and some definitions note pass@1 accuracy.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to 2 constructs and no behavioral indicators. The prevailing usage is to measure Reasoning: papers describe evaluating models on reasoning benchmarks that include GPQA-Diamond, selecting it among mathematical and reasoning datasets, and measuring reasoning ability with accuracy on GPQA Diamond. A smaller line of work uses it to measure Generalization, specifically how well a transferring-then-finetuning approach generalizes to the unseen task GPQADiamond.

Space of uses. Papers do not explicitly relate it to other measurement instruments, but they often use it alongside AIME 2024 and MATH-500, and sometimes LiveCodeBench or GSM8K, in mu

nodes.name: GPT-4 Head-to-head Comparison
nodes.definition: An evaluation protocol where an evaluator, such as GPT-4, is prompted to directly compare the outputs of two different models for the same input and decide which is better.

nodes.name: GQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most commonly, papers treat GQA as a visual question answering benchmark or dataset for real-world visual reasoning and compositional question answering over images. Many descriptions emphasize complex, compositional, or multi-hop questions, and some add structured content: scene graph structures from Visual Genome that generate balanced question-answer pairs with one ground-truth answer, or scene graphs plus a SQL-like reasoning path for each VQA pair. A smaller line of work foregrounds particular splits or variants, including balanced-testdev, test-dev, test-balanced, and GQA balanced, while some papers simply describe it as a public VQA benchmark with open-ended questions.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use GQA to measure 12 constructs and 3 behavioral indicators, so the reported uses are spread across many targets rather than concentrated on one. The most recurrent framings are visual understanding, compositional reasoning, visual perception, generalization, and visual question answering; the remaining links cover 8 other constructs and 2 other behavioral indicators. In the recorded language of the papers, GQA is also reported as measuring reasoning-oriented

nodes.name: GrailQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing treatment of GrailQA is as a Freebase-based KBQA or KGQA benchmark and dataset for complex question answering, especially compositional and zero-shot reasoning. Definitions also frame it as a benchmark for evaluating KBQA generalizability and, in one formulation, semantic parsing systems; one description specifies 64,331 questions with target S-expressions and complex questions requiring up to 4-hop reasoning. A recurring description is that it tests three generalization settings: I.I.D., compositional, and zero-shot.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link GrailQA to 4 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator. The reported uses are spread across several targets: papers use it to measure Knowledge graph question answering, and they also report it as evaluating Generalization, Multi-hop reasoning, Robustness, and Zero-shot generalization. This generalization framing is explicit in descriptions that use GrailQA to compare performance across I.I.D., compositional, and zero-shot levels, with one paper stating that validation and test questions are split into 50% unseen KB elements, 25% unseen compositions, and 25% I.I.D.

Space of uses. In

nodes.name: Granite Guardian
nodes.definition: IBM’s Granite Guardian, an open-source LLM designed to detect risks in prompts and responses, including societal bias, harmful content, and unethical behavior, used as a binary classifier for bias detection.

nodes.name: GREEN
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly describe GREEN as an evaluation procedure, Grounded-factual-correctness Evaluation for radioloGy reports, for radiology report evaluation. The definition says it uses a finetuned LLM to assess the factual correctness of generated radiology reports, and one paper further characterizes it as a metric based on a "single-answer reference-guided LLM-as-a-Judge mechanism."

What it is claimed to measure. Across the surveyed work, GREEN is linked to one construct and one behavioral indicator. Papers use it to measure Clinical accuracy, and they also report Radiology report generation as measured by GREEN; the accompanying language emphasizes factual correctness in generated radiology reports and describes it as a metric for radiology report evaluation.

Space of uses. The papers here position GREEN as a primary evaluation metric. One paper calls it a "state-of-the-art metric for radiology report evaluation," and another says results are "primarily" reported with GREEN and F1-SRR-BERT Score to assess clinical accuracy and structural consistency; no other measurement instrument is linked to it.

nodes.name: gRefCOCO
nodes.definition: A benchmark dataset for generalized referring expression segmentation, which includes expressions that refer to multiple objects or no objects at all.

nodes.name: GSM8K
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, GSM8K is most commonly described as a benchmark or dataset of grade-school math word problems for multi-step arithmetic, numerical, or mathematical reasoning, often also described as high-quality and linguistically diverse. Many papers describe it as an about 8.5K-scale collection with 7,473 training and 1,319 test examples, though some give rougher counts such as about 8K or 8.8K, and a few papers label the problems middle-school or high-school level rather than grade-school. Some authors emphasize specific formats or variants: text-only or open-ended text completion rather than multiple choice, the official 1.3K test set, detailed solutions or reasoning traces, and a multilingual version covering English plus 9 other high-resource languages.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link GSM8K to 22 constructs and 11 behavioral indicators. The prevailing claim is that it measures Mathematical reasoning, with broader uses for Reasoning and General ability also recurring; on the behavioral side, it is most often used to measure Mathematical problem solving and Chain of thought. Papers also describe it as evaluating quantitative reasoning, arithmetic reasonin

nodes.name: GSM8K-Aug
nodes.definition:
What it is. Definitions describe GSM8K-Aug as an augmented version of GSM8K with a 385k training set, where intermediate reasoning steps are represented as mathematical equations. A quoted passage further states that it "uses only math equations as the reasoning steps."

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to one construct and no behavioral indicators. The only recorded measurement claim is that it measures Mathematical reasoning, with one study referring to GSM8K-Aug as a "complicated mathematical reasoning benchmark."

Space of uses. In the quoted passages, GSM8K-Aug appears alongside GSM8K-Aug-NL as one of the datasets used in experiments. Papers also position it as a main fine-tuning dataset, stating that they mainly fine-tune models on GSM8K-Aug for mathematical reasoning.

nodes.name: GSM-Hard
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, GSM-Hard, also written GSM-HARD or GSMHard, is most commonly described as a harder GSM8K benchmark or test set of grade-school math problems. Most definitions present it as a more challenging subset or version of GSM8K, while some are more specific and say it is created by replacing the original question numbers with larger-magnitude values to increase calculation difficulty. A smaller line of work describes it as an extended or out-of-distribution version with more complex arithmetic problems, and one definition says it contains problems that state-of-the-art models struggle with and is designed to test the limits of mathematical reasoning.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link GSM-Hard to three constructs and one behavioral indicator. The prevailing claim is that papers use it to measure Mathematical reasoning, with several papers also reporting it as measuring the broader construct of Reasoning; a smaller line uses it to measure Robustness, often in out-of-distribution or perturbation settings, and one paper reports it as measuring Mathematical problem solving. Overall, the linked uses lean most toward mathematical reasoning.

Space of

nodes.name: GSM-IC
nodes.definition: A benchmark of math word problems with irrelevant context, used to evaluate the generalizability of the proposed methods.

nodes.name: GSM-NoOp
nodes.definition: A dataset derived from GSM-Symbolic templates where seemingly relevant but ultimately inconsequential statements are added to problems to test a model's ability to discern relevant information.

nodes.name: GSM-Plus
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, GSM-Plus is most commonly described as an adversarial version or extension of GSM8K for grade-school math evaluation. Definitions converge on a benchmark or test suite of grade-school or grade-level math problems, with the dominant emphasis on being more challenging and on testing robustness or "resilience to adversarial perturbations," though one paper describes it more simply as a held-out set for mathematical reasoning.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link GSM-Plus to three constructs and one behavioral indicator. The prevailing measurement claims are mathematical reasoning and mathematical problem solving, and smaller lines of work report it as measuring robustness and verification ability; one paper explicitly says it "tests model robustness." Overall, papers use it for several related math-performance targets rather than only one construct.

Space of uses. Papers typically use GSM-Plus alongside other math evaluations, especially GSM8k, MATH, SVAMP, ASDiv, and TheoremQA. In those uses it is positioned variously as a grade-school math benchmark, a robustness benchmark, and a held-out test set, with one paper noting that for robustness benc

nodes.name: GSM-Symbolic
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, it is described as a benchmark for symbolic math word problems. One description presents it as a dataset where names and numerical values are replaced with symbolic variables, so models must generate correct symbolic expression solutions; another presents it as an enhanced benchmark built from symbolic templates of GSM8K questions, able to generate diverse variants for more controllable and reliable evaluation.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to measure 1 construct, Mathematical reasoning, and 1 behavioral indicator, Mathematical problem solving. The reported targets are concentrated rather than spread across many outcomes: one paper says it provides more reliable metrics for measuring models' reasoning capabilities, and another uses it to assess mathematical reasoning skills through correct symbolic expression generation.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it in the recorded relationships. In use, one paper places it among "challenging symbolic reasoning benchmarks" alongside FOLIO and uses it as an evaluation benchmark for CRANE, while another positions it as an improved benchmark that generates diverse question variant

nodes.name: GTA
nodes.definition: A benchmark for evaluating multi-modal agents on tasks that require a combination of perception, operation, logic, and creativity using visual data.

nodes.name: GTZAN
nodes.definition: A music genre classification benchmark.

nodes.name: GuessingGame
nodes.definition: An open-domain, open-ended evaluation protocol where a 'Guesser' LLM identifies a hidden object by asking free-form questions to an 'Oracle' LLM.

nodes.name: GUI-Odyssey
nodes.definition: A benchmark for evaluating mobile agent capabilities, assessing step-wise task completion on Android platforms.

nodes.name: GUI-WORLD
nodes.definition: A comprehensive video dataset and benchmark designed to evaluate MLLMs on GUI understanding across six scenarios, with a focus on dynamic and sequential tasks.

nodes.name: HADES
nodes.definition:
What it is. In the definitions, HADES is described as a multimodal jailbreak benchmark for probing multimodal safety under adversarial conditions. Papers characterize it as using crafted images with accompanying typography, with malicious intent embedded and amplified in those visual materials. It is also described as providing 750 samples across five harmful scenarios.

What it is claimed to measure. In the recorded links, papers use HADES to measure jailbreak resistance. It is linked to one behavioral indicator, Jailbreak resistance, and to no constructs, so the reported use centers on that single indicator rather than being spread across multiple constructs. A single paper also frames it as one of the datasets or attack methods used to evaluate the defense capabilities of multimodal large language models against jailbreak attacks.

Space of uses. Papers position HADES as part of a broader evaluation suite rather than as a stand-alone check. In the reported use, it appears alongside SafeBench, MM-SafetyBench, MML, and HIMRD when authors adopt several jailbreak attack methods or datasets to comprehensively evaluate defense capabilities against jailbreak attacks.

nodes.name: HAGRID
nodes.definition: A long-form question answering dataset for attributed generation, containing information-seeking questions with answers that are generated by LLMs and subsequently evaluated by humans.

nodes.name: HallusionBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, HallusionBench is most commonly described as a benchmark or diagnostic suite for assessing hallucination in multimodal or vision-language models. A recurring formulation is that it targets both language or knowledge hallucination and visual illusion, and some papers add that it distinguishes different VLM reasoning error modes or evaluates across question type and difficulty. A smaller line of descriptions treats HallBench or HallB as the same resource and frames it more broadly as a multimodal understanding benchmark with an emphasis on hallucination-related performance, or as an image-context reasoning benchmark built from paired images and questions.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use HallusionBench to measure 1 construct and 4 behavioral indicators. The prevailing use is to measure hallucination, with papers saying it evaluates visual illusions and knowledge hallucinations, or how well multimodal models handle language hallucinations and visual illusions. Smaller strands report it as measuring hallucination detection, visual hallucination, and visual question answering, and one paper uses it to measure the construct hallucination re

nodes.name: HaluEval
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, HaluEval is most commonly described as a large-scale benchmark for evaluating hallucination, especially factual hallucination in model-generated responses. Most descriptions place it in large language model evaluation, often in question answering, while some instead emphasize language-only dialogue, and one paper reuses dialogue and summarization subsets called HaluDial and HaluSum. Papers describe its instances in several ways: one calls it synthetically generated hallucination data, another says each example pairs a user query with factual and hallucinated LLM responses annotated by human evaluators, and another describes a QA track of 10000 questions with reference knowledge, a right answer, and a hallucinated answer. Some uses also frame it as a discriminative yes or no judgment task for deciding whether an answer contains a hallucination.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use HaluEval to measure 3 behavioral indicators and 2 constructs. The prevailing use is for Hallucination and Hallucination detection: papers describe it as evaluating hallucination tendencies, detecting and flagging hallucinations, or judging whether an answer contains a h

nodes.name: HANNA
nodes.definition: Dataset for evaluating short stories generated from prompts, with human ratings on narrative qualities such as surprise and coherence.

nodes.name: HANS
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, HANS is most commonly described as a natural language inference dataset aimed at model sensitivity to lexical overlap and related artifacts. Some descriptions sharpen this by calling it the adversarial dataset Heuristic Analysis for NLI Systems, "generated to contain examples that cannot be solved through heuristics like lexical overlap," and note that it contains 30K examples; others describe it as a stress test set that manipulates lexical overlap, subsequence, and negation. One extracted definition also situates it in a binary classification setting, where it is used to assess length bias.

What it is claimed to measure. Measurement claims are concentrated rather than spread across many targets. HANS is linked to one construct, Out-of-distribution generalization, and one behavioral indicator, Natural language inference. One paper reports using it for NLI, and the same paper also presents it as an OOD benchmark, saying that these NLI datasets are "suitable benchmarks for evaluating the OOD robustness of ICL."

Space of uses. Papers typically use HANS as part of broader evaluation suites rather than in isolation. One paper places it with NAN,

nodes.name: HardEN
nodes.definition: Challenging word sense disambiguation benchmark consisting of instances that were not correctly disambiguated by any system in prior evaluations, used to assess performance on difficult or out-of-distribution examples.

nodes.name: HarM
nodes.definition: Harmful Meme dataset focused on COVID-19-related memes, used to evaluate zero-shot detection of harmful content in a public health context.

nodes.name: HarmBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, HarmBench is most commonly described as a benchmark or dataset of harmful instructions, behaviors, prompts, or questions used to evaluate jailbreak success and safety behavior under adversarial attacks. Definitions also call it a standardized framework or evaluation framework, and some papers emphasize built-in judging machinery, referring to an official classifier of response harmfulness or a default judge. A smaller line of work treats it as an out-of-distribution test set distinct from AdvBench, or uses subsets such as JBB-Behaviors slices to test generalization and avoid leakage.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link HarmBench to 5 behavioral indicators and 5 constructs. The prevailing usage is to measure jailbreaking, often through attack success rate or harmful-response judgments; papers also use it to measure harmful request refusal, adversarial robustness, safety, and attack transferability. Overall, the behavioral claims center on jailbreak-related evaluation, while construct-level claims are spread across several safety-related targets rather than a single construct.

Space of uses. No explicit instrument-to-instrument relatio

nodes.name: HarmBench-adv
nodes.definition: An adversarial evaluation set used to test prompt and response classification under jailbreak attacks.

nodes.name: HarmBench classifier
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats this as a HarmBench safety judge, an LLM-based classifier used to decide whether a model output is harmful or whether a response to a harmful instruction is unsafe. Definitions vary between an official HarmBench classifier of model response harmfulness, an evaluator used for HarmBench results, and a judge that checks whether a target response matches malicious intent and counts as a successful jailbreak. Some authors specify that it is fine-tuned from Llama-2-13B or refer to the HarmBench-Llama2-13B-Chat variant, while one paper places it as a baseline safety evaluator in a meta-evaluation.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to 1 construct and 2 behavioral indicators. They use it to measure harmful content generation, assessing output safety or harmfulness and computing attack or adversarial success rates. They also use it to measure harmlessness, reporting the percentage of harmless responses or classifying whether prompting generated a harmful response, and it is reported as measuring jailbreaking through attack success rate using HarmBench's judge. These measurement claims are distributed across harmful content g

nodes.name: Harmful instructions
nodes.definition: A safety benchmark used to evaluate VLM behavior under harmful multimodal jailbreak prompts.

nodes.name: Harry Potter dataset
nodes.definition: A copyrighted-text unlearning evaluation dataset built from Harry Potter book passages used to test whether the model stops reproducing the source text.

nodes.name: HateCheck
nodes.definition: A benchmark dataset for evaluating hate speech detection models, used in this paper as a source of unsafe, hate-speech-related prompts for the LITMUS benchmark.

nodes.name: Hateful Memes
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats Hateful Memes, also written HATEFUL MEMES, HatefulMemes, or FHM, as a multimodal meme benchmark or dataset built around meme images and their text captions. Papers describe it as classifying whether an image-text combination is hateful, whether a meme "describes hateful intentions," or whether it contains harmful content; some also note that it requires reasoning beyond simple unimodal signals and describe it as a challenge released by Meta or Facebook.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link this instrument to no constructs and to two behavioral indicators, hate speech detection and harmful content detection. The reported measurement claims use both framings: some papers describe it as evaluating multimodal hate speech detection, while others use it to test whether a model can distinguish toxic from non-toxic images or detect harmful meme content.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it. Papers instead use it as an evaluation dataset for multimodal systems, sometimes alongside other public meme datasets, including HarM and MAMI, and sometimes as a specific-mapping task where the model is asked

nodes.name: HateXplain
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing description is a natural-language or toxic text classification benchmark or dataset. It is most commonly framed as classifying sentences as normal versus hateful or offensive, with one quoted passage specifying that the target label is 0 for normal sentences and 1 for those considered hateful or offensive. Some authors describe it more specifically as a dataset with demographic correlation shifts and unwanted correlation between toxicity labels and mentions of demographics, while others present it as a subjective single-label dataset or as a source task for transfer learning in harmful content detection.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it primarily to evaluate classification of normal versus hateful, offensive, or toxic text. Some also report using it to evaluate fairness with respect to gender-related sensitive information, and another paper uses it to evaluate zero-shot robustness in the presence of demographic correlation shifts. No construct or behavioral indicator is explicitly linked to it.

Space of uses. Papers position it as an evaluation dataset in several roles. It appears as one of several text classification data

nodes.name: HC3
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats HC3 as a ChatGPT text detection corpus, described as up-to-date, bilingual in English and Chinese, and organized at multiple text lengths, with full or long-text data and sentence-level or short-text variants for multiscale evaluation. Papers explicitly mention the short-text subsets HC3-English-Sent and HC3-Chinese-Sent. A smaller line of work instead frames it as the Human ChatGPT Comparison Corpus, a set of responses or question-and-answer pairs from humans and GPT-3.5 or ChatGPT to the same questions, used to compare their characteristics or for human-AI text discrimination.

What it is claimed to measure. Among recorded links, papers use HC3 to measure AI-generated text detection. It is linked to 1 behavioral indicator, AI-generated text detection, and to no constructs, so the recorded measurement claims are concentrated on that single indicator. One paper describes using a learned kernel from HC3 to test unseen HC3 texts "to mimic the MGT-detection."

Space of uses. No other measurement instrument is linked to it. Papers position HC3 as an evaluation benchmark or corpus: methods are evaluated on its long or full and short

nodes.name: HealthCareMagic
nodes.definition: Medical consultation dataset containing single-turn patient queries paired with licensed professional responses, used for in-distribution evaluation of medical QA systems.

nodes.name: HellaSwag
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, HellaSwag is most commonly described as a benchmark or dataset for commonsense natural language inference, commonsense inference, or commonsense reasoning, usually framed as sentence or context completion. The prevailing task description is to choose the most plausible ending or continuation for a given text, event, or scenario in a multiple-choice format, and many papers present it as a zero-shot benchmark. Smaller lines of work describe it as grounded or physically situated commonsense, next-event prediction, or natural continuation generation, and some note adversarially filtered examples that are described as difficult for language models but easy for humans.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use HellaSwag to measure 15 constructs and 14 behavioral indicators. The dominant claims center on commonsense reasoning and reasoning, with natural language understanding, general ability, and generalization also recurring; across the linked behavioral indicators, the most common uses are sentence completion, zero-shot task performance, multiple-choice question answering, zero-shot question answering, and downstream task performance. Overall, papers use it

nodes.name: HelloBench
nodes.definition: A comprehensive, in-the-wild, and open-ended benchmark designed to evaluate the performance of large language models in generating long text.

nodes.name: HELM
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, HELM is most commonly described as Holistic Evaluation of Language Models, a large-scale or aggregate benchmark or framework from Stanford for evaluating language models across a wide range of scenarios and metrics. Definitions repeatedly present it as offering broad evaluation across capabilities, limitations, and risks, and papers place it among comprehensive evaluation suites and foundation-model evaluations. A smaller line of work uses the same name differently, describing HELM as a non-adaptive baseline attack that randomly adds typos, lowercases text, or uses contractions.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link HELM to no constructs, one behavioral indicator, and two other instruments. The only behavioral indicator it is recorded as measuring is multiple-choice question answering: one paper states that HELM uses questions from MMLU, with multiple choice questions and labeled correct answers. In the recorded relationships, the measurement use therefore centers on that single behavioral indicator rather than on any linked construct.

Space of uses. Papers commonly use HELM as a broad comparative evaluation or ranking source. One paper

nodes.name: HELMET
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage is as a long-context benchmark for extended text processing tasks. Definitions describe it as application-centric and comprehensive, with a common description noting that it includes portions from RULER and ∞Bench; papers also describe it as covering seven categories of tasks, though one evaluation setup names five task types, synthetic recall, retrieval-augmented generation, many-shot in-context learning, passage re-ranking, and long-document QA, totaling 17 sub-tasks.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link HELMET to 4 constructs and 4 behavioral indicators. The most recurrent measurement claims use it for in-context prediction and synthetic recall, and papers also report it as measuring document question answering and ranking; at the construct level, papers use it to measure length generalization, long-context understanding, long-range dependency modeling, and memory.

Space of uses. Papers most often use HELMET alongside RULER: one study presents it as a main benchmark and notes that it includes portions from RULER, while another evaluates models on HELMET and RULER together. A smaller line of work relates HELMET to HotpotQA,

nodes.name: HelpSteer
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most commonly, papers describe HelpSteer as a multi-attribute dataset for aligning or evaluating LLM outputs against human-preferred characteristics, with human-annotated ratings for helpfulness, correctness, coherence, complexity, and verbosity. Some authors frame it more specifically as a model alignment and steering dataset, while a smaller line of work describes it as a QA dataset for evaluating instruction following across five dimensions, including informativeness and factuality, or as a multi-attribute helpfulness dataset. One paper also treats it as an unpaired dataset with around 35K samples, where each prompt has a single response scored on attributes.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use HelpSteer to measure 6 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators, so its reported measurement role is spread across several targets rather than centered on one. The most frequently linked constructs are helpfulness, coherence, complexity, factuality, and faithfulness. Additional papers also report it as measuring other recorded targets beyond those five.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it. Papers position HelpSteer in several ways: as a dataset used

nodes.name: HelpSteer2
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most commonly, papers describe HelpSteer2 as a preference or multi-aspect alignment dataset used in alignment and reward-modeling workflows. Definitions vary between a validation split used for evaluating alignment across preference dimensions, datasets of prompts and completions with helpfulness or broader multi-attribute annotations, and the original release's larger permissively licensed dataset of prompts with paired responses annotated for helpfulness, correctness, coherence, complexity, and verbosity. A smaller line of work instead treats it as instruction-following data for supervised fine-tuning, or as a subset used to synthesize judge training data, and one paper notes that most prompts are sourced from ShareGPT and that the dataset includes multi-turn prompts.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, measurement claims are spread across several targets rather than converging on one. It is linked to three constructs and one behavioral indicator overall, and papers use it to measure model collapse, personalized alignment, and verbosity; papers also describe it as evaluating alignment across different preference dimensions. The behavioral-indicator link is

nodes.name: HESEIA
nodes.definition: A Spanish-language dataset of 45,416 sentences created by high-school teachers and students in Latin America to evaluate social biases in LLMs, organized by school subject and annotated for intersectional demographic biases.

nodes.name: HEx-PHI
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, HEx-PHI is most commonly described as a harmful query or safety benchmark: a dataset of 330 harmful instructions or queries spanning 11 harmful categories or use cases. Definitions converge on its use for testing whether models comply with harmful requests, produce unsafe outputs, or generate harmful or privacy-invasive responses, though one description narrows this to privacy-harming and personally harmful instructions. A smaller line of work refers to it as the Policy-Oriented Safety Evaluation Benchmarks or the POSE benchmark, describing its categories as derived from Meta's and OpenAI's usage policies or prohibited use cases.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to three constructs and one behavioral indicator. Most often, it is used to measure Harmlessness, followed by Safety and Safety alignment, and the only linked behavioral indicator is Harmful content generation. The recorded relationships keep these claims within safety evaluation, with papers describing the benchmark as assessing harmfulness or evaluating whether a model complies with harmful requests, so its use is spread across three constructs rather than centered on

nodes.name: HEXACO-60
nodes.definition: A 60-item personality inventory used to measure six major dimensions of personality: Honesty-Humility, Emotionality, Extraversion, Agreeableness, Conscientiousness, and Openness to Experience.

nodes.name: HH-Golden
nodes.definition: A preference dataset, modified from HH-RLHF, used to evaluate a model's alignment with a broad spectrum of human preferences.

nodes.name: HH-RLHF
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most commonly described as Anthropic's Helpful and Harmless preference dataset for human-assistant dialogue, it contains prompts or conversation histories with two candidate responses and a human-preferred choice, often framed as chosen-rejected pairs annotated for helpfulness and harmlessness. Papers variously describe it as multi-turn dialogues, human-AI conversation pairs, or single-step human-assistant interactions, and reported sizes include 161K training and 8.55K test pairs, approximately 170K dialogues or chosen-rejected pairs, and more than 160,000 preference comparisons. Several papers treat it as having separate helpfulness and harmlessness subsets or focus only on the helpfulness portion, and one paper defines a 150-instance HH-RLHF* subset for out-of-domain evaluation. Some papers instead describe Anthropic HHH with helpful, harmless, and honest comparisons, sometimes using it as a source of harmful prompts and responses.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, measurement claims converge most strongly on helpfulness and harmlessness, often with separate helpful and harmless splits. It is linked to 9 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator: beyond help

nodes.name: HH-RLHF harmless subset
nodes.definition: A binary human-preference dataset of harmlessness-oriented response comparisons used to test reward-model explanations.

nodes.name: HH-RLHF helpful subset
nodes.definition: A binary human-preference dataset of helpfulness-oriented response comparisons used to test reward-model explanations.

nodes.name: HiTab
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly describe HiTab as a benchmark or table reasoning dataset built around hierarchical or otherwise complex tables from government reports and Wikipedia pages. Definitions emphasize multi-level headers, implicit relationships, and complex structural relationships, and they describe the dataset as used for table transformation and question answering; one paper specifies 3,597 tables from HTML government reports and Wikipedia pages and 10,672 QA pairs. One paper also presents it as designed for table-based question answering and table-to-text generation.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use HiTab to measure 1 construct and 2 behavioral indicators. The construct link is table reasoning, while the behavioral indicator links are data-to-text generation and table question answering. Taken together, papers report it as evaluating several related table tasks rather than only one.

Space of uses. Papers use HiTab as an evaluation benchmark in experiments on table reasoning, question answering, and generation, and one paper places it among three widely used table reasoning datasets. No other measurement instrument is linked to it, though papers evaluate it

nodes.name: HotpotQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage is a multi-hop question answering benchmark or dataset whose questions require combining evidence across multiple supporting documents, passages, or paragraphs, usually from Wikipedia. Some authors instead describe it as multi-hop reading comprehension, multi-document QA, search-based or open-domain QA, and papers mention setups such as fullwiki, distractor, closed-book, inclusion in KILT or LongBench, and a version where retrieval difficulty is manipulated by paragraph ordering. Descriptions of the answer format also vary, with some papers calling it an open-ended task with long answers and others a closed-ended task with short entity or yes or no answers.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use HotpotQA to measure a broad set of targets: it is linked to 9 constructs and 10 behavioral indicators. The leading construct links are to multi-hop reasoning and reasoning; among behavioral indicators, the most common links are to multi-hop question answering and question answering, with some work framing it as complex reasoning question answering. Overall, papers use it for several different reasoning and QA targets rather than a single c

nodes.name: HotpotWikiQA-mixup
nodes.definition: Multi-hop QA dataset derived from Wikipedia, combining elements of HotpotQA with long-context requirements.

nodes.name: HoVer
nodes.definition: Multi-hop fact verification benchmark requiring evidence aggregation across multiple documents, based on Wikipedia, with claims structured in 2-hop, 3-hop, and 4-hop reasoning paths.

nodes.name: How2Sign
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage is as a large-scale American Sign Language dataset drawn from instructional videos and used as a benchmark for translation. Some descriptions make the domain more specific as "how to" instructional videos and as ASL-to-English translation, and another adds that it contains 35,191 samples with a vocabulary of 16K English words.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to 2 behavioral indicators and no constructs. The dominant measured-by use is sign language translation, with papers reporting How2Sign as one of the datasets or benchmarks for that task; a smaller use is sign language identification, where results are reported with top-1 accuracy, while sentence-level translation in the same benchmark setup is scored with BLEURT-20.

Space of uses. Papers commonly mention How2Sign alongside other sign language datasets: the recurring companions are CSL-Daily, with some mentions of OpenASL, PHOENIX14T, and FLEURS-ASL. In these descriptions it is positioned as one of the benchmarks on which models report results in sign language translation experiments or broader benchmark suites, and no measurement instrument is formally li

nodes.name: HSSD
nodes.definition: A dataset of synthesized, single-floor indoor scenes used to create environments for the Habitat-MAS benchmark.

nodes.name: Human annotation study
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across these papers, the prevailing use of "human annotation study" is as a flexible human evaluation protocol, but the concrete protocol varies by task. One framing uses 84 participants who each annotate 18 news stories, 9 real and 9 fake, and classify them as real or fake "without relying on the Internet." Another has humans annotate a subset of 390 examples from DEFREASING*N-alt, following the naturalistic prompt instructions, to compare model behavior with human tendencies. A further version uses three graduate students per episode to annotate an AI agent's truthfulness with fine-grained and coarse-grained categories, with omniscient access to background information, hidden details, and full conversation history.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use this protocol to measure 2 constructs, Coverage and Truthfulness, and it is not linked to any behavioral indicators. The claims are spread across these two constructs rather than converging on a single one: papers report using the results of a human annotation study as ground truth for sentence-level coverage, and they also report having annotators label an agent's truthfulness using fine-grained and coarse-grained

nodes.name: Human baseline
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage is not a single standardized benchmark but a family of human performance reference protocols. Most commonly, humans attempt the same benchmark tasks as models or agents so papers can establish a baseline for performance, success rate, efficiency, time, or accuracy. Some papers define it more narrowly as independent annotators manually synchronizing multilingual tables, a linguist creating vowel prediction baselines, native speakers or untrained annotators labeling benchmark subsets, an offline clue-by-clue survey with guesses and "buzz" decisions, or humans acting as LLM agents to estimate an upper bound. Several versions are run on subsets rather than full benchmarks, including 100 table-updating pairs, 75 abstracts, 1000 questions, and 35-40 held-out questions.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers do not formally link this instrument to any constructs or behavioral indicators. Instead, they use it to measure human task performance for comparison with model outputs, variously reporting success rate and efficiency, performance, time and accuracy, argument classification performance, answerability on document questions, or expert for

nodes.name: Human evaluation
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the term covers several manual assessment protocols rather than one fixed format. The prevailing usage is a human or expert judgment procedure for rating model outputs, often through pairwise preference comparisons, Likert or numeric scoring, or rubric-based review, though some papers narrow it to spot-checking or verification of automated labels, and others use humans to perform the task itself as a baseline. Papers also refer to nearby variants such as human annotation, verification, review, manual evaluation, and user study, and the studies range from small sampled checks to large annotation exercises with over 10,000 judgments.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use human evaluation to measure 49 constructs and 20 behavioral indicators, so its reported scope is broad rather than centered on one agreed target. The most frequent reported targets are helpfulness, conciseness, factuality, fluency, and harmlessness. Behavioral-indicator claims are similarly dispersed across many tasks rather than concentrated on a single behavior.

Space of uses. Among the 12 linked instruments, LLM-as-a-judge is the prevailing companion: papers report that human evalu

nodes.name: Human preference evaluation
nodes.definition:
What it is. The prevailing usage is a pairwise human judgment protocol: evaluators see outputs from two models side by side and choose the better one, often with a tie or no-difference option. Papers describe closely related variants as human preference studies, A/B testing, side-by-side comparisons, human pairwise or comparative evaluation, preference voting, and AB preference tests, with task criteria tailored to the application, such as faithfulness, general response quality, translation quality, plausibility and consistency, argument quality, plan usefulness, or omission, fabrication, distortion, and temporal mismatch in captions. A smaller line of work uses the same label for non-pairwise ratings, including a 5-point Mean Opinion Score setup for naturalness and meaningfulness.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link this protocol to 3 constructs and no behavioral indicators. The linked constructs, listed most often first, are Human preference alignment, Faithfulness, and Text generation quality, and the relationship is always that those constructs are measured by human preference evaluation. The measurement claims are therefore spread across several constructs rather than

nodes.name: Human subject study
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, this label covers several direct-participant methods rather than a single fixed protocol. The prevailing usage is survey-based: papers describe a community survey to gather perspectives on harmful model behaviours and ideal responses, a mixed-methods user survey with open-ended questions and Likert ratings to identify adoption patterns, use cases, and challenges, and a questionnaire on frustrations and the perceived helpfulness of clarifications, entity graphs, and relationship graphs. A smaller line of work uses open-ended interviews to elicit detailed feedback on participants’ experience and workflow fit.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers do not report this instrument as measuring any linked constructs or behavioral indicators, and no construct or behavioral indicator is linked to it. In practice, the studies use it to elicit participants’ perspectives, frustrations, adoption patterns, perceived helpfulness, and experience in the papers’ own terms.

Space of uses. Most papers position human subject studies as an elicitation or validation step alongside broader system or model work, for example to broaden a list of harms, identify user ch

nodes.name: HumanEval
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing description is a Python code generation or code completion benchmark built around functional correctness. Most definitions describe hand-written or hand-crafted programming problems, often 164 in total, with function signatures or docstrings, unit tests, and sometimes reference or canonical Python solutions, evaluated by unit test pass rate, usually pass@1. A smaller line of work refers specifically to HumanEval-Python or HumanEval-python for Python function completion, uses the HumanEvalSynthesize variant, adapts it to a single-line code infilling task, or treats it as the basis for HUMANEVALPACK.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link HumanEval to 12 constructs and 4 behavioral indicators. The prevailing claims are that papers use it to measure code generation and coding ability, with further recurrent uses for reasoning, functional correctness, and code completion. Additional construct and behavioral links are also recorded, so papers do not tie it to only one target concept.

Space of uses. Papers explicitly relate it to 2 other instruments, EvalPlus and MultiPL-E, and many evaluations also pair it with MBPP; some additionally ment

nodes.name: HumanEval-Decompile
nodes.definition: A decompilation benchmark derived from the C-language adaptation of HumanEval, containing 164 C functions compiled with O0–O3 optimization flags and disassembled into X86-64 assembly.

nodes.name: HumanEval+
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across these papers, HumanEval+ is most commonly described as an extended or improved version of HumanEval for code generation, with stronger or more comprehensive unit tests for more rigorous evaluation of functional correctness. Definitions vary in the details they foreground: some describe handwritten Python programming questions with comprehensive, ground-truth unit tests, while others describe function-level problems with docstrings, code headers, and input-output examples, or 164 hand-crafted programming problems with function signatures, docstrings, and unit tests. One description adds that the extension scales the number of test cases by 80x.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link HumanEval+ to three constructs and two behavioral indicators. The prevailing use is to measure code generation, often framed as evaluating whether models generate functionally correct code; smaller lines of work use it to measure coding, algorithmic reasoning, coding ability, and functional correctness. Overall, these claims are spread across several closely related targets rather than centered on a single construct.

Space of uses. Papers usually position HumanEval+ as a standard

nodes.name: HumanEval-X
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats HumanEval-X as a multilingual benchmark for code generation, often described as a multilingual extension of HumanEval. Definitions describe it as translating HumanEval’s Python problems into multiple languages, and one paper further characterizes it as a comprehensive benchmark covering Python, C++, Java, JavaScript, and Go. A smaller naming variant, HumanEval-Multi, refers to the multilingual version of HumanEval and describes it as evaluating the functional correctness of model-generated code, used as a test dataset for utility.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link this instrument to 2 behavioral indicators and to no constructs. The dominant claim is that it measures Code generation: papers report pass@1 on HumanEval-X for multilingual code generation and say it aims to evaluate multilingual code generation abilities. A smaller line of work uses it to measure Code translation, with one paper reporting Java-to-C++ translation performance on the HumanEval-X benchmark.

Space of uses. Papers commonly place it inside broader code evaluation suites, including use as one of several code benchmarks. Some papers use the mu

nodes.name: HumanEvalFix
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the definitions, the prevailing description is a benchmark for fixing bugs in provided functions with accompanying test cases. Papers also frame it as function-level bug fixing, and one usage narrows it to the Python subset and lets models or agents self-debug over multiple turns with feedback from test execution.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use HumanEvalFix to measure one behavioral indicator, Code debugging, and one construct, Code editing ability. The linked claims center on bug fixing and debugging: several papers describe it as measuring Code debugging through tasks where an incorrect function with unit tests is given and the system is asked to fix it, while one paper also reports using it to evaluate Code editing ability.

Space of uses. In the papers, it is used as an evaluation benchmark for code-editing tasks. One paper uses it alongside CanItEdit, NoFunEval, Aider, and Aider Polyglot, while another applies it in a multi-turn setup where the system solves bugs by self-debug using test-execution feedback.

nodes.name: HumanEvalPack
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly describe HumanEvalPack as a code benchmark used to supply prompts for code-domain evaluation. In RM-Bench: Benchmarking Reward Models of Language Models with Subtlety and Style, authors state that prompts for the code domain are sourced from HumanEvalPack. Some authors discuss the HumanEvalSynthesize variant instead, describing it as adapted for instruction-following models, where the task is framed as a natural language instruction to generate a complete program.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to measure 1 behavioral indicator, Code generation, and link it to no constructs. The reported measurement claims converge on code generation, including a setup where, given a natural language docstring or comment describing the desired code, the model is tasked to synthesize the correct code.

Space of uses. Papers relate it to 1 other instrument, RM-Bench, where it is used as a source of prompts for the code domain or code split. Generative Representational Instruction Tuning uses the HumanEvalSynthesize variant and describes that choice as more adequate for instruction-following models.

nodes.name: Humanity’s Last Exam
nodes.definition: Humanity’s Last Exam (HLE) is a challenging benchmark consisting of difficult exam questions across various academic and professional domains.

nodes.name: HumanML3D
nodes.definition: HumanML3D benchmark of human motions and textual descriptions used for evaluating text-to-motion and motion-to-text performance.

nodes.name: Humor Style Questionnaire
nodes.definition: Standardized 32-item psychological assessment measuring four humor styles—affiliative, self-enhancing, aggressive, and self-defeating—using a 5-point Likert scale, used here to probe LLMs' representation of humor-related constructs.

nodes.name: HybridQA
nodes.definition: HybridQA is a question answering benchmark combining table evidence with textual passages for hybrid reasoning.

nodes.name: Hypersim
nodes.definition: A photorealistic synthetic dataset used as a transfer task to evaluate the model's fine-tuned performance on semantic segmentation.

nodes.name: HyPoradise
nodes.definition: A generative error correction benchmark for LLM-enhanced ASR containing over 316K hypotheses-transcription pairs from mainstream ASR corpora, used to evaluate H2T mapping.

nodes.name: ICL CIPHERS
nodes.definition: A cryptographic evaluation framework that applies bijective and non-bijective token-level substitution ciphers to in-context learning inputs to assess task learning by comparing performance gaps between reversible and irreversible mappings.

nodes.name: iCliniq
nodes.definition: Real-world medical consultation records from the iCliniq platform, used as an out-of-distribution test set to evaluate generalization in medical QA.

nodes.name: IconQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly treat IconQA as a visual question answering dataset for diagram understanding. One definition also describes it as "a new benchmark for abstract diagram understanding and visual language reasoning," and another places it as one task within the CMIT benchmark.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link IconQA to 1 behavioral indicator and no constructs. The reported measurement claim is consistent: IconQA measures visual question answering, with the task described as diagram understanding VQA, rather than being used for a wider spread of constructs or behaviors.

Space of uses. Within the reported uses, papers position IconQA as a visual question answering task for model comparison, including comparisons that pair it with ScienceQA and multi-task settings that include both ScienceQA and IconQA. No other measurement instrument is linked to it, and one definition frames it as a task used inside the CMIT benchmark.

nodes.name: IEMOCAP
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers describe IEMOCAP as the Interactive Emotional Dyadic Motion Capture database, used as a benchmark for emotion recognition from speech, and one paper further presents it as a multimodal dataset for emotion classification from spoken dialogue. In that usage, it is also used to evaluate text-based emotion detection in long conversational sequences. The cited evaluations also refer to IEMOCAP Session 5, and one paper specifies 1,241 utterances.

What it is claimed to measure. Among linked entities, papers connect it to one behavioral indicator, Emotion analysis, and to no constructs. The recorded relationship is that Emotion analysis is measured by IEMOCAP, with supporting quoted passages describing emotion recognition as being assessed on IEMOCAP and reporting accuracy for "ER | IEMOCAP Session 5". Its reported measurement role therefore centers on a single named behavioral indicator.

Space of uses. Papers use it as an evaluation benchmark, sometimes alongside other datasets. One study assesses emotion recognition on IEMOCAP and MELD, while another reports "consistent improvements on MultiWOZ 2.2 and IEMOCAP" and reports IEMOCAP accuracy gains over DEEPSEEK and MOD

nodes.name: IFEval
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, IFEval is most commonly described as a targeted benchmark for instruction following, often framed as evaluating whether a model follows explicit instructions or satisfies verifiable prompt constraints. Several definitions make those constraints concrete as format, style, content, or formatting requirements, and one paper places it in the TÜLU-2 evaluation suite under zero-shot settings. A smaller line of work uses adapted forms, including a synthesized spoken version derived from the original text-based IFEval and single-turn tasks adapted from IFEval data.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use IFEval predominantly to measure instruction following: it is linked to one behavioral indicator, Instruction following, and to five constructs, with Instruction following ability as the prevailing construct-level framing. Smaller lines of work also use it to measure Helpfulness, Self-correction ability, Utility preservation, and World knowledge. The recorded measurement claims converge most clearly on instruction following, while the remaining construct links are distributed across several other framings.

Space of uses. In use, papers usually tre

nodes.name: iGSM
nodes.definition: A synthetic dataset of program-generated, elementary-school level math reasoning problems with step-by-step solutions, designed to be controllable and verifiable.

nodes.name: IIRC
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing description is of a reading comprehension benchmark dataset, Iterative Information Retrieval and Comprehension, used for evaluation. Papers also describe it as focused on information integration and reading comprehension, where models answer questions by linking information across document sections, and one paper reports experiments on decontextualized versions of a subset of IIRC.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to measure one behavioral indicator, question answering. In the recorded relationship, it is presented as one of four QA datasets, including multi-hop Wikipedia reasoning datasets, and no papers here link it to any construct, so the reported measurement use is concentrated on question answering rather than spread across multiple targets.

Space of uses. No other measurement instrument is linked to it. Papers position it as an evaluation dataset within QA experiments, including use as one of four QA datasets in a comparison setup; one study also reports results on decontextualized versions of a subset, and another reports a consistent advantage across metrics on IIRC.

nodes.name: IIW-400
nodes.definition: A dataset consisting of 400 image-caption pairs with highly detailed, hallucination-free captions, used for evaluating caption quality.

nodes.name: ImageNet-100
nodes.definition: A subset of the ImageNet dataset used for evaluating image classification performance.

nodes.name: ImageNet-1k
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most papers describe ImageNet-1k as a large-scale image classification or object-recognition benchmark, usually defined over 1,000 categories or classes. Some definitions add scale details, describing over 1.2 million images, or over a million training images plus 50,000 validation images, and papers variously refer to ImageNet1k, ImageNet-1K, ImageNet-2012, or the ILSVRC2012 validation split. A smaller line of work also treats it as a benchmark for class-conditional image generation, while other papers use its images, categories, or class labels to build few-shot classification, fine-grained object VQA, structured-rationale, or attack evaluations.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, ImageNet-1k is linked to 3 constructs and 4 behavioral indicators. The prevailing usage is to measure image classification, with smaller lines of work using it to measure image generation, object recognition, and zero-shot classification. At the construct level, papers also use it to measure multimodal alignment, and more occasionally adaptability and generalization, for example through alignment scores or top-1 zero-shot accuracy on ImageNet, and through 16-shot domain adaptatio

nodes.name: ImageNet-A
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers describe ImageNet-A as an out-of-distribution benchmark for ImageNet that contains natural adversarial examples and is challenging for standard models. Across the definitions, that is the only characterization.

What it is claimed to measure. No papers link ImageNet-A to any construct or behavioral indicator, so the literature here does not specify what it is claimed to measure.

Space of uses. The evidence only shows the benchmark being named in Section 5.1 of "LiNeS: Post-training Layer Scaling Prevents Forgetting and Enhances Model Merging". No papers link it to any other measurement instrument, so its use alongside other benchmarks is not specified.

nodes.name: ImageNet-C
nodes.definition: A standard procedure and dataset used to generate corrupted versions of images with perturbations like snow, brightness changes, and motion blur to test model robustness.

nodes.name: ImageNet-R
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing description treats ImageNet-R as an image classification or out-of-distribution benchmark built from artistic renditions of ImageNet object classes. Definitions repeatedly mention forms such as paintings, cartoons, sculptures, embroidery, and graffiti, and one paper describes these renditions as domains; the benchmark is framed as testing generalization to novel styles, different artistic forms, or transformed visual appearances.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers most commonly present ImageNet-R as evaluating robustness to out-of-distribution images or out-of-distribution robustness, with adjacent descriptions of generalization to novel styles, different artistic forms, and transformed visual appearances. No constructs and no behavioral indicators are linked to it in the recorded relationships, so the claims stay at the level of benchmark purpose rather than explicit construct or behavior mappings.

Space of uses. Papers use it mainly as an evaluation benchmark for out-of-distribution images and artistic renditions of ImageNet classes. Learning from Teaching Regularization: Generalizable Correlations Should be Easy to Imitate uses

nodes.name: ImageNet-Segmentation
nodes.definition: A dataset providing pixel-level segmentation masks for a subset of the ImageNet dataset, used for evaluating semantic segmentation and object localization.

nodes.name: ImageNet-Sketch
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the definitions, papers treat ImageNet-Sketch mostly as an out-of-distribution ImageNet benchmark made up of sketch-like images. The prevailing description is a dataset of sketch-like, sometimes explicitly black-and-white, images derived from ImageNet classes, used to test robustness and generalization; one definition phrases it as an out-of-distribution benchmark for ImageNet, while others describe it as a dataset for evaluating image classification under out-of-distribution conditions.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to one behavioral indicator, Image classification, and to no constructs. The only measured_by claim treats ImageNet-Sketch as measuring Image classification, so the reported measurement use is confined to that single behavioral indicator rather than spread across multiple linked targets.

Space of uses. In the cited uses, papers place it alongside ImageNet, ImageNet-R, and ImageNet-Rendition when evaluating models. One quoted passage describes evaluating ViT-B/16 and ViT-L/16 on ImageNet-R and ImageNet-Sketch to investigate out-of-distribution robustness, and another places it among the image datasets used to evaluate TIMM; papers do

nodes.name: ImageNetV2
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across definitions, papers treat ImageNetV2 as an ImageNet-derived benchmark or test set rather than a new task. The prevailing descriptions say it is used to test robustness under natural distribution shift and to measure generalization to new, similarly distributed data, and one definition also specifies that it was collected with a replicated protocol. Papers use both spellings, ImageNetV2 and ImageNet-V2.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link ImageNetV2 to one behavioral indicator and no constructs. The only recorded measurement claim is that image classification is measured by ImageNetV2, so the reported use converges on a single behavioral indicator rather than spreading across multiple constructs. In the definitions, this evaluation is framed as testing robustness under natural distribution shift or measuring generalization to new, similarly distributed data.

Space of uses. Across the cited uses, papers position ImageNetV2 as one dataset within broader evaluation suites. One paper includes it among a larger collection of image recognition datasets, and another uses it alongside ImageNet-R, ImageNet-A, and ImageNetSketch for evaluation. No measurement instr

nodes.name: IMDb
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, the prevailing usage is as a movie-review sentiment benchmark: definitions most often describe IMDb as a large, binary sentiment classification dataset of movie reviews with positive and negative labels. Some papers make the format more specific, describing a corpus of 50,000 or 50K highly polar reviews, while one definition says it contains movie reviews and ratings and is also used in recommendation system research. A smaller line of work uses it as a controlled-generation testbed for generating positive movie reviews, and one paper treats it as an out-of-distribution target-domain sentiment benchmark.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to three behavioral indicators and three constructs.
