The linked behavioral-indicator uses are sentiment analysis, controlled sentiment generation, and text classification; the quoted passages describe IMDb as supporting binary polarity classification, semantic analysis of user sentiment, and positive-sentiment movie review generation. Beyond those uses, papers also report it as measuring general ability, generalization, and out-of-distribution generalization, so the measurement claims extend acro

nodes.name: IMHI
nodes.definition: In-distribution dataset for MentaLLaMA consisting of approximately 105,000 instruction-response pairs for mental health analysis, including depression detection and wellness classification.

nodes.name: IMPLIRET
nodes.definition: A benchmark for evaluating retrieval and reasoning capabilities when relevance depends on implicit facts in documents, covering arithmetic, temporal, and world knowledge reasoning across uni- and multi-speaker discourse styles.

nodes.name: In-context attack
nodes.definition: A baseline evaluation setting that uses few-shot demonstrations of immoral or harmful behavior to induce the target model to endorse similar unethical behaviors.

nodes.name: INCLUDE
nodes.definition: INCLUDE, a native multilingual benchmark cited as culturally aware but lacking discipline balance and difficulty control.

nodes.name: IndoCulture
nodes.definition: An Indonesian benchmark used to assess downstream model performance after safety fine-tuning.

nodes.name: IndustryOR
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the cited papers, IndustryOR is most commonly described as an open-source dataset of commercial Operations Research problems. One paper says it served as the basis for "a novel benchmark dataset based on the open-source commercial IndustryOR" (Decision Information Meets Large Language Models: The Future of Explainable Operations Research), while another describes it as consisting of 100 real-world optimization problems spanning linear, integer, and mixed-integer programming at various difficulty levels.

What it is claimed to measure. No papers report IndustryOR as measuring any construct or behavioral indicator.

Space of uses. The papers position IndustryOR either as source material for building a new benchmark for explainable OR or as a benchmark used directly for real-world optimization problems at varying difficulty levels. No papers link it to other measurement instruments.

nodes.name: InfiAgent-DABench
nodes.definition: A benchmark for data analysis containing 257 challenges with CSV inputs and multi-level (easy, medium, hard) analysis questions.

nodes.name: InfiniBench
nodes.definition: A large-scale benchmark for long-form video understanding in multi-modal models, assessing eight skills across 87.7K question-answer pairs from 1,000+ hours of movies and TV shows, using both multiple-choice and open-ended formats.

nodes.name: InfiniteBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing usage is a long-context benchmark or benchmark suite for evaluating LLMs on ultra-long inputs, usually described as exceeding 100K tokens. Most descriptions treat it as a diverse collection of synthetic and real-world tasks, sometimes stated as 10 tasks, while narrower descriptions focus on particular subsets such as En.QA, En.MC, En.Sum, Inf.QA, Inf.MC, or specific retrieval tasks. Papers differ in emphasis: some describe long-book or long-novel QA and multiple-choice tasks, while others include multilingual QA, code debugging, dialogue, math, and retrieval, and reported average lengths vary across descriptions, including 100K, 145.1K, 190k, 214k, and 184K tokens for particular setups.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use InfiniteBench to measure 4 constructs and 9 behavioral indicators. The prevailing claim is that it measures Long-context understanding, while smaller lines of work also report it as measuring Length generalization, Long-context reasoning, and Dialogue understanding. At the behavioral level, the named links are spread across several targets rather than one, most often Text summarization, Code debugging, Document

nodes.name: InfoBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing description is an instruction-following benchmark for instruction adherence that decomposes complex instructions into simpler sub-instructions for granular evaluation. One paper adds that it contains 500 diverse instructions and 2,250 decomposed questions across multiple constraint categories, and describes a metric called Decomposed Requirements Following Ratio (DRFR) for assessing instruction-adherence capabilities. Some papers instead describe task-specific views of it: a direct scoring dataset with a 1 to 5 Likert scale and English Easy and Hard subsets, an Expert split used for fine-grained classification, and a benchmark for more general instructions that need LLM-based judgment.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use InfoBench to measure one behavioral indicator, Instruction following, and two constructs, Cross-domain generalization and Instruction following ability. The most common claim is that it measures instruction following: papers describe it as assessing instruction-adherence capabilities and as an instruction benchmark that evaluates whether models comprehend and execute detailed directives, including clear, s

nodes.name: InfoSeek
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the definitions, InfoSeek is treated as a visual question answering dataset centered on knowledge-seeking questions. The recurring description is that it requires identifying an entity in an image and then querying for a related fact, and one paper also places it among "three popular KB-VR benchmarks" alongside A-OKVQA and OK-VQA.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link InfoSeek to two constructs, Generalization and Commonsense knowledge, and no behavioral indicators. In SearchLVLMs: A Plug-and-Play Framework for Augmenting Large Vision-Language Models by Searching Up-to-Date Internet Knowledge, it is used to evaluate "the generalization capability of our framework across datasets that do not necessitate up-to-date knowledge," and the same paper also reports that "InfoSeek and A-OKVQA Rely on Commonsense Knowledge (RCK)," so the uses are split across these two constructs rather than concentrated on one.

Space of uses. The papers use InfoSeek alongside A-OKVQA, OK-VQA, and GQA. One paper positions it as one of three popular KB-VR benchmarks in model evaluation, while another selects it with GQA and A-OKVQA specifically to assess generalization across datasets

nodes.name: InfoVQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly describe InfoVQA, sometimes written as InfographicVQA or InfographicsVQA, as a visual question answering benchmark or dataset for infographics or infographic images. Some descriptions instead frame it as information visual question answering on document images, emphasizing information localization, extraction, or extracting specific information, and one definition places it among prior single-page document understanding datasets. One paper also characterizes the infographics setting as high-resolution and requiring interpretation of charts and graphical data.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link this instrument to 2 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator. The prevailing claim is that papers use it to measure document understanding, while smaller lines of work also report it as measuring fine-grained visual understanding and optical character recognition. Beyond document understanding, its reported measurement use therefore extends to OCR-related and fine-grained visual evaluation.

Space of uses. Papers usually deploy it within broader benchmark suites, commonly alongside DocVQA, ChartQA, TextVQA, and OCRBench, and sometimes with STVQA. In the

nodes.name: InjecAgent
nodes.definition: A red-teaming framework that uses a large language model (GPT-4) to automatically generate adversarial injection prompts for attacking LLM agents.

nodes.name: InstruSum
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, InstruSum is most commonly described as a benchmark dataset for evaluating instruction-controllable summary generation. Definitions describe it as containing articles or a source article, summary requirements expressed as a specific or complex instruction, and model outputs; one description also says it contains human annotations, and another states that it contains 400 samples. A smaller line of work instead frames it as a summarization-focused pairwise comparison benchmark for evaluating instruction-following and content quality in summaries.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link InstruSum to one behavioral indicator, Pointwise scoring, and to no constructs. The reported use is that it measures pointwise scoring of instruction-controllable summarization, so the measurement claims are concentrated on that single behavioral indicator rather than spread across multiple constructs or behaviors.

Space of uses. Papers use InstruSum as an evaluation benchmark for instruction-controllable summarization. In one evaluation setup it appears alongside LLMBar, with the two benchmarks described as respectively representing pairwise evaluation of ins

nodes.name: IOI task
nodes.definition: The Indirect Object Identification task, used to evaluate model understanding of internal circuits by testing if a model can identify the indirect object in sentences with a known structure.

nodes.name: IPIP-NEO-300
nodes.definition: A 300-item personality questionnaire from the International Personality Item Pool used to measure the Big Five personality traits, used in this paper as a generalization target for models aligned on IPIP-NEO-120 data.

nodes.name: Isaac Gym
nodes.definition: A GPU-accelerated physics simulation environment for reinforcement learning, used to evaluate performance on nine challenging robotic locomotion and manipulation tasks.

nodes.name: IU-Xray
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, IU-Xray is most commonly described as a dataset of chest X-ray images paired with associated medical or radiology reports, mainly used for evaluating medical report generation. Definitions largely converge on that image report format, while a smaller line of work broadens the description to a chest X-ray dataset used for both report generation and medical visual question answering.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use IU-Xray to measure 2 behavioral indicators, and the linked claims are concentrated on behavioral indicators rather than constructs. The prevailing usage is Medical report generation: papers describe evaluating models on the report generation task with IU-Xray and refer to it as a report generation dataset. A smaller line of work also uses it to measure Medical visual question answering, including definitions that place IU-Xray among medical VQA datasets; no constructs are linked to it.

Space of uses. In practice, papers most often use IU-Xray alongside MIMIC-CXR for report generation evaluation; as one study puts it, "For medical report generation, we use MIMIC-CXR and IU-Xray" (Focus on What Matters: Enhancing Medical Visi

nodes.name: IWSLT 2017
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most commonly described as a benchmark dataset from the International Workshop on Spoken Language Translation 2017 for evaluating machine translation systems, papers treat IWSLT 2017 as a translation benchmark rather than defining it in broader terms. Some definitions are more specific, describing parallel documents sourced from TED talks, and one paper focuses on the tst2017 test sets covering 12 language pairs. A smaller line of usage calls it an international speech translation benchmark and notes its use in zero-shot prompting experiments, while another paper refers to extracting its training and test sets and using it to evaluate translation performance for low-resource language pairs.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the surveyed papers, the measurement claim converges on one behavioral indicator: Machine translation. IWSLT 2017 is linked to one behavioral indicator and no constructs, and papers use it to measure machine translation in settings described as text translation, context-aware machine translation from English to French, and additional translation evaluation in a generation scenario. The reported use is therefore concentrated on this single indica

nodes.name: JailbreakBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the dominant framing treats JailbreakBench as an open or standardized benchmark for evaluating jailbreak attacks and model safety or robustness. Most descriptions present it as a dataset of harmful queries, unsafe behavior prompts, or instructions, often using 100 prompts or instances, though some papers define it more narrowly as an evaluation protocol that uses an LLM judge to detect detailed disallowed responses, and one describes a leaderboard that collects attacks designed to bypass safety filters. A smaller line of work refers to template and direct variants, and some authors use the names JBB, JBB-Behavior, or JBB-Behaviors for harmful-query or harmful-behavior versions used in evaluation.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link JailbreakBench to three constructs, Harmlessness, Adversarial robustness, and Safety, and to one behavioral indicator, Jailbreaking. The prevailing use is to measure jailbreak performance, success, or resistance, often through Attack Success Rate, while other papers use it to assess harmlessness on mixed harmful-query sets, adversarial robustness to prompt injection, or safety on harmful prompts. Taken together, the

nodes.name: JailbreakV
nodes.definition: A multimodal safety dataset used to evaluate jailbreak resistance and safety performance, identified in the paper as suffering from visual safety information leakage.

nodes.name: JAMA Clinical Challenge
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats JAMA Clinical Challenge as a benchmark or dataset drawn from the JAMA Network Clinical Challenge archive, made up of challenging or complex real-world clinical cases for diagnosis or treatment decision-making. Definitions agree on a multiple-choice format built from case narratives: papers describe a long or detailed patient case followed by a clinical question, four answer choices, and a discussion or expert explanation; one description also includes the correct answer index and a medical speciality classification. One paper further specifies a size of 1,524 cases.

What it is claimed to measure. The measurement claims are concentrated on a small number of targets: papers link it to 1 construct and 1 behavioral indicator. Most commonly, papers use it to measure Clinical decision-making, with the cases described as testing decision-making skills in realistic clinical scenarios; it is also reported as measuring Multiple-choice question answering, since the benchmark is described as structured as a multiple-choice question-answering task with expert-written explanations.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it.

nodes.name: JEEBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, JEEBench is most commonly treated as a challenging mathematics benchmark or dataset for benchmarking LLM performance on hard, exam-style problems. Some descriptions are more specific, portraying it as a collection of math problems from Indian Institute of Technology entrance exams that assesses advanced mathematical reasoning, while another paper says it covers some college-level topics, including simple ODEs and multivariable calculus. Papers also place it among more challenging mathematics problem sets.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use JEEBench to evaluate mathematical reasoning on exam-style problems, advanced mathematical reasoning, and LLM performance on challenging mathematics problems. These claims cluster around mathematical reasoning and benchmark performance, but papers do not explicitly link it to any construct or behavioral indicator.

Space of uses. Papers do not explicitly link it to other measurement instruments, but they mention it alongside other hard math benchmarks, especially OmniMATH and a subset of MATHBENCH. The quoted passages position it as an additional challenging benchmark for comparative studies, includi

nodes.name: Jigsaw
nodes.definition: A toxicity classification dataset where each sample is a sentence and sensitive attribute value is identified by humans.

nodes.name: JIGSAWS
nodes.definition: A dataset of surgical activities, used as a source for the 'Surgery' category videos in the VidDiffBench benchmark, featuring procedures like knot tying.

nodes.name: JudgeBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, JudgeBench is usually presented as a benchmark for evaluating LLM-based judges on challenging or difficult response pairs, and one definition also describes it as testing the robustness and accuracy of LLM-as-a-Judge systems across challenging evaluation cases. The prevailing description says it spans knowledge, reasoning, mathematics, and coding, and one definition adds that it uses responses from strong models like GPT-4o. Smaller descriptions frame it more generally as challenging questions for various reasoning tasks, or as an additional case study for judge behavior and agreement under uncertainty.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link JudgeBench to three constructs and no behavioral indicators. The most common claim is that it measures factuality: papers say its focus is on evaluating the factual and logical correctness of complex responses to challenging questions, and they note that it includes response pairs involving factual correctness. A smaller line of work treats it as measuring reasoning, through difficult response pairs that require advanced reasoning abilities, and evaluation ability, through challenging response pairs spanning

nodes.name: JudgeLM
nodes.definition:
What it is. The definition treats JudgeLM as a judge model for automated evaluation of LLM responses, used to score or select outputs. One paper also refers to multiple named variants, including JudgeLM-7B, JudgeLM-13B, and JudgeLM-33B.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers describe JudgeLM as evaluating responses by scoring or selecting outputs, but they do not link it to any named construct or behavioral indicator. No named construct is reported as being measured by it, and no behavioral indicator is reported either.

Space of uses. In xFinder: Large Language Models as Automated Evaluators for Reliable Evaluation, JudgeLM is discussed as one option within a group of judge models, mentioned alongside PandaLM and GPT-4. The same paper refers to several model sizes, so its use is presented through multiple variants rather than a single named configuration.

nodes.name: Just-Eval
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most descriptions treat Just-Eval as an evaluation framework or benchmark for scoring model outputs, though one paper also presents it as a dataset of diverse instructions. Across these descriptions, the recurring content is the same five dimensions, helpfulness, clarity, factuality or factual accuracy, depth, and engagement, and one paper says the official prompt is used with GPT-4 scoring each dimension from 1 to 5. Papers also use subsets of the instructions, with examples of 1,000 and 800 diverse instructions.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the reported links, Just-Eval is connected to one construct, Helpfulness, and no behavioral indicators are linked to it. Papers use it to measure Helpfulness by evaluating outputs in terms of helpfulness, clarity, factuality, depth, and engagement, and one description explicitly says it is used to measure the helpfulness of edited LLMs. The reported measurement claims therefore center on Helpfulness rather than on multiple constructs.

Space of uses. Most usages present Just-Eval as a direct output evaluation: papers score responses on the named dimensions and report Just-Eval scores, often for edited or defended LLM outp

nodes.name: K-QA
nodes.definition: A real-world medical question-answering benchmark, with a subset of responses verified by physicians.

nodes.name: Keirsey Temperament Sorter
nodes.definition: A self-assessment personality questionnaire, based on the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator, used to classify individuals into one of four temperament groups: Rationals, Idealists, Guardians, and Artisans.

nodes.name: Kitchen
nodes.definition: A simulated benchmark (Gupta et al., 2019; Fu et al., 2020) designed to test an agent's ability to handle sparse terminal rewards and perform long-horizon manipulation in a kitchen setting.

nodes.name: KnowEdit
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the descriptions, papers treat KnowEdit as an integrated benchmark for evaluating knowledge editing methods. The benchmark is described as containing six datasets for different evaluation types, and one paper notes that experiments are conducted on the KnowEdit benchmark (Precise Localization of Memories: A Fine-grained Neuron-level Knowledge Editing Technique for LLMs).

What it is claimed to measure. Papers describe KnowEdit as evaluating knowledge editing methods across criteria such as success, portability, locality, and fluency. Beyond those benchmark criteria, no construct links or behavioral-indicator links are recorded, so the usage in the papers does not connect it to a broader spread of named constructs.

Space of uses. The paper uses KnowEdit as an experimental benchmark for assessing knowledge editing methods. No other measurement instruments are linked alongside it in the recorded relationships.

nodes.name: Konwinski Prize
nodes.definition: A benchmark designed to fairly evaluate state-of-the-art LLMs by using only new GitHub issues, thereby mitigating data contamination.

nodes.name: L-Eval
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats L-Eval as a benchmark, often described as a standardized long-context evaluation suite for language models. Most definitions frame it around long-context capability or performance, with closed-ended tasks, especially multiple-choice and true or false question answering, while some papers describe a broader suite with both closed-ended and open-ended tasks for understanding, reasoning, summarization, and open-format question answering over long inputs. A smaller line of work specifies its contents as 508 long documents from various domains, divided into 20 subtasks or "20 smaller long sequence datasets," and one paper notes that its tasks appear at varying input lengths.

What it is claimed to measure. Relationship claims are concentrated rather than spread broadly: papers link L-Eval to one construct and one behavioral indicator. The dominant claim is that it measures long-context understanding, with several papers describing it as a commonly used long-context benchmark or as part of a "comprehensive evaluation of long-context understanding." A smaller usage links it to long-context generation, where one paper report

nodes.name: LAION-1k
nodes.definition: A set of approximately 1,000 LAION-derived text-image pairs related to human names and personal life, used to assess training data memorization.

nodes.name: LAMBADA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats LAMBADA as a language modeling or word-prediction benchmark or dataset in which models predict the final word of a passage or sentence from full passage, paragraph, or broad discourse context. Definitions repeatedly frame it as testing long-range dependencies, long-context recall, contextual comprehension, or text understanding, and one paper describes it as a collection of narrative passages designed for discourse-based prediction. A smaller line of work instead labels it a reading comprehension benchmark, and papers also refer to variants such as LAMBADA (OpenAI) and LAMBADA-standard (LS).

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use LAMBADA to measure 8 constructs and 5 behavioral indicators, so its reported target is spread across several framings rather than concentrated on one. The most recurrent links are that papers use it to measure Commonsense reasoning, Language modeling ability, Natural language understanding, Downstream task performance, and Zero-shot task performance, with the remaining links covering 5 other constructs and 3 other behavioral indicators.

Space of uses. Most commonly, papers include LAMBADA as one i

nodes.name: Lambada-OpenAI
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly describe Lambada-OpenAI as a benchmark for evaluating language understanding, specifically the ability to model long-range dependencies in text through a text completion task. The operational detail that appears in the descriptions is a 0-shot setting.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the papers here, Lambada-OpenAI is used to measure Natural language understanding. It is linked to 1 construct and no behavioral indicators, so the reported use converges on a single construct rather than spreading across multiple targets.

Space of uses. The usage in the papers descriptions place Lambada-OpenAI within a language-understanding evaluation lineup alongside Hellaswag-0-shot, Winograd-3-shots, and WinoGrande-5-shots. Papers that specify the setup report it in 0-shot form, and no separate linked measurement instruments are recorded for it.

nodes.name: LaMP
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, LaMP is treated as a benchmark or dataset for short-form personalization evaluation. The prevailing descriptions frame it around short-form personalized text generation, including tasks such as news headline generation, scholarly title generation, and tweet paraphrasing, while another description presents it as a public LLM personalization benchmark with named subsets, LaMP-1 through LaMP-5, covering citation identification, movie tagging, Amazon product rating, news headline generation, and scholarly title generation, and says these tasks test surface-level personalization on short-context queries. A broader framing in another paper describes LaMP as consisting of various text classification and generation tasks.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use LaMP to measure 4 behavioral indicators and no constructs. The linked behavioral indicators are headline generation, scholarly title generation, text classification, and text generation, so the recorded uses are spread across several task types rather than converging on any linked construct. In the more task-specific descriptions, papers explicitly tie it to the headline and scholarly title generation s

nodes.name: LaMP-QA
nodes.definition: A benchmark for evaluating personalized long-form question answering, covering questions from Arts & Entertainment, Lifestyle & Personal Development, and Society & Culture, using user profiles and aspect-based evaluation derived from question narratives.

nodes.name: Lap14
nodes.definition: A dataset for aspect-based sentiment analysis from the SemEval 2014 shared task, requiring classification of sentiment towards a particular entity or aspect.

nodes.name: LASER
nodes.definition: An LLM-based ASR evaluation rubric that uses detailed prompts with error type examples to assign no, minor, or major penalties based on semantic impact, producing a sentence-level score.

nodes.name: Last letter concatenation
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing description is a benchmark, dataset, or test set in which a model concatenates the last letters of words in a name or other word sequence. Most definitions frame it as a symbolic reasoning task, while some describe it more narrowly as a simple text-processing or string-manipulation task; one definition also says it is used to evaluate algorithmic reasoning and length generalization in verification settings. Examples in the quoted passages ask for the last letters of names such as "Amy Brown" or "Craig Alice," and some papers specify four-word or four-name inputs.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to 2 constructs and no behavioral indicators. It is most commonly reported as measuring Symbolic reasoning, with papers saying they use Last Letter Concatenation to examine or benchmark symbolic reasoning performance. A smaller line of work uses it to measure Reasoning more broadly, describing it as one of the standard reasoning datasets, so the recorded claims center on Symbolic reasoning with an additional broader reasoning use.

Space of uses. Papers usually use it as one benchmark among several, appearing alongside GSM8K, CSQA, and

nodes.name: LastFM
nodes.definition: A benchmark dataset for recommendation research derived from a popular music service, containing user-artist interaction histories.

nodes.name: LawBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. In the usage in the papers, LawBench is treated as a benchmark focused on Chinese laws, with 20 diverse legal tasks. The definition and source text specifically mention charge prediction and prison term prediction, and the paper places LawBench alongside LegalBench when evaluating LLMs' generalization capability across legal domains.

What it is claimed to measure. The paper links LawBench to 2 behavioral indicators, charge prediction and prison term prediction, both through measured_by relationships. Its quoted use narrows LawBench to these two tasks, and no constructs are linked to it.

Space of uses. The paper uses LawBench as part of a broader legal-domain evaluation and positions it alongside LegalBench. Within LawBench, it concentrates on the two challenging tasks of charge prediction and prison term prediction. No measurement instrument is linked to it.

nodes.name: LeanDojo
nodes.definition: LeanDojo is a Lean theorem-proving benchmark and data-extraction ecosystem used as a comparison point for premise-based theorem proving.

nodes.name: LeetCode
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, LeetCode is most commonly described as a collection of programming problems from the LeetCode platform or website. Some authors use it as a source for building code tasks, including fill-in-the-blank evaluations drawn from approximately 2,000 problems with Python, Java, and C++ solutions. A smaller line of work describes Leetcode as a benchmark of recent scraped problems, and another paper refers to it more generally as a coding benchmark.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to measure one construct and one behavioral indicator. The reported links do not converge on a single target: it is used to measure code understanding in fill-in-the-blank code comprehension tasks, and it is also reported as measuring code generation, where one paper groups HumanEval and LeetCode 'for coding'.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it. In practice, papers position it as part of a broader coding evaluation suite or as a problem source: one paper reports experiments on HumanEval, MBPP, APPS, CodeContests, and Leetcode, while another pairs HumanEval and LeetCode as coding evaluations.

Concerns raised. One paper foregrounds prior trai

nodes.name: LeetCode Contest
nodes.definition: A benchmark consisting of programming contest problems categorized by difficulty (Easy, Medium, Hard) to assess performance on complex problem-solving.

nodes.name: LegalBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly describe LegalBench as a benchmark or benchmark suite for evaluating legal reasoning in language models, and one paper says it consists of 162 tasks covering various aspects of legal reasoning. A smaller line of work calls it a dataset for evaluating reasoning and hallucination in legal contexts and for assessing domain-specific factual accuracy. Papers also refer to specific parts of the benchmark, including the International Citizenship Questions sub-task and the Definition Extraction task, and one paper presents LegalBench-Instruct as derived from LegalBench through prompt refinement.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, claims converge on a single construct: LegalBench is used to measure legal reasoning. It is linked to 1 construct and no behavioral indicators, and several papers describe it as evaluating various aspects of legal reasoning, measuring legal reasoning in large language models, or providing problem templates for profiling legal reasoning. One definition also extends its use to reasoning and hallucination in legal contexts, but the linked measurement claim centers on legal reasoning.

Space of uses. No measurement instrume

nodes.name: LEMON
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers here, LEMON is described as a large-scale, multi-domain Chinese Spelling Correction dataset built from real-world spelling errors. Definitions emphasize seven sub-domains, with examples including game, encyclopedia, contract, medical care, and car, plus two others, and one paper says it typically tests domain correction capabilities in a zero-shot setting. Another paper characterizes it as having test sets from seven domains without in-domain training sets.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to measure two constructs and one behavioral indicator. The construct links are both generalization-oriented, Cross-domain generalization and Generalization: one paper describes LEMON as an ideal benchmark for evaluating a model’s cross-domain generalization capability, and another says it serves as a cross-domain dataset for evaluating generalization capabilities. A separate paper also uses it as a benchmark for Chinese spelling correction.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it. In use, papers position it as an evaluation benchmark centered on cross-domain testing: one definition says it typically assesses domain correction capabilit

nodes.name: LexEval
nodes.definition: Legal domain evaluation suite containing Legal Translation and Legal EssayQA tasks, assessing bilingual translation and open-ended legal reasoning.

nodes.name: LFQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, the dominant framing treats LFQA as a long-form question-answering dataset drawn from Reddit. Definitions say it was created by scraping Reddit questions and pairing them with human-written answers, and one paper further specifies that it is curated from posts and responses on Reddit's "Explain Like I'm Five" forum. A smaller framing presents LFQA as a pairwise comparison benchmark for evaluating long-form question answering.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers do not link LFQA to any constructs or behavioral indicators. Instead, they describe it at the task level, as being used for evaluating watermark robustness in question answering settings and for pairwise comparisons in long-form question answering.

Space of uses. Papers position it mainly as an evaluation set or prompt source. One paper says LFQA was adopted as prompts for a human paraphrasing study, while other definitions describe it as part of evaluation for watermark robustness and as an evaluation set for pairwise comparisons. No other measurement instruments are linked alongside it.

nodes.name: LIAR
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the definitions, papers treat LIAR as a dataset for evaluating claim verification. One paper also places it among "7 standard datasets" used for evaluation and describes its role here as assessing F1 score in true/false classification under prompt optimization.

What it is claimed to measure. The recorded relationships do not link LIAR to any construct or behavioral indicator as a measurement instrument. In the descriptions, its stated evaluative role is claim verification and F1 assessment for true/false classification.

Space of uses. Papers use LIAR as one dataset within a broader evaluation setup alongside other standard datasets, including WSC, Ethos, and ArSarcasm. In the reported use, it appears in prompt optimization experiments, with one result summarized as "improving F1 score by 10.1 on LIAR dataset" (Efficient and Accurate Prompt Optimization: the Benefit of Memory in Exemplar-Guided Reflection).

nodes.name: LIAR2
nodes.definition: Benchmark dataset of approximately 23,000 short statements manually labeled by professional fact-checkers for truthfulness, used for fake news detection evaluation.

nodes.name: LibriSpeech
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most papers describe LibriSpeech as a large corpus, dataset, or benchmark of read English speech derived from audiobooks, often aligned and segmented, and commonly framed as clean read speech for ASR. Definitions usually mention 960 hours of English reading audio, though one paper says it contains roughly 1000 hours and another extracts chunks from it to form a 1GB audio dataset for compression experiments. Papers use several subsets and settings, including train-clean-100, dev-clean, dev-other, test-clean, test-other, and 100-hour and 960-hour setups, while a smaller line simply describes Librispeech as a speech recognition dataset for closed-ended audio evaluation.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, LibriSpeech is linked to 1 construct and 2 behavioral indicators. The prevailing use is to measure Speech recognition: relationship evidence calls it an automatic speech recognition benchmark, a benchmark dataset of clean read speech for standard ASR tasks, and a test set that demonstrates ASR performance in a clean scenario. A smaller line uses it to measure Speech reconstruction, and one paper uses it to measure Utility preservation as part of a general utili

nodes.name: LIMA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the definitions, papers consistently treat LIMA as a dataset, though they describe its role differently. One description presents it as a natural language dataset used to study memorization in a non-code domain and to test whether findings generalize beyond code. Another frames it as a dataset for instruction fine-tuning, consisting of curated prompts and responses designed to teach models to follow specific instructional formats.

What it is claimed to measure. Its measurement role is narrow. Papers link it to 1 construct, Memorization, and to no behavioral indicators; the recorded claim is that Memorization is measured by LIMA. One study uses it to examine memorization on natural language datasets across task domains (Measuring memorization in RLHF for code completion).

Space of uses. The uses split between studying memorization and additional training. One paper studies memorization on LIMA alongside Anthropic HH as a natural language dataset, while another reports additional training using LIMA in an instruction fine-tuning setup (Peri-LN: Revisiting Normalization Layer in the Transformer Architecture). No measurement instrument is linked to it.

nodes.name: LINGOLY
nodes.definition: Benchmark consisting of linguistic puzzles from the United Kingdom Linguistics Olympiad (UKLO), covering six topics: phonology, morphology, syntax, semantics, number systems, and compounding, used to evaluate LLM performance on puzzle solving.

nodes.name: LiRA
nodes.definition: Likelihood Ratio Attack, a membership inference attack that formulates the problem as hypothesis testing, comparing the likelihood of a model's output score under the hypotheses that the sample was or was not in the training data.

nodes.name: List Functions
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing description is a dataset or benchmark for list transformation, where a model infers a rule that maps an input list to an output list from examples. Definitions and quoted passages variously describe the target rule as primitive, compositional, or a general transformation function, and they frame the benchmark as evaluating human and machine concept learning ability and inductive reasoning ability. A smaller line of work presents "List Function" as a Programming by Example task about computable list to list functions using GPL rules. Some descriptions further specify integer-list inputs and outputs, including the possibility of an empty list.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the linked work, papers use List Functions to measure inductive reasoning. It is linked to one construct, Inductive reasoning, and to no behavioral indicators or other measurement instruments. The claims converge on that single construct, with papers describing the benchmark as evaluating "inductive reasoning ability in inferring list transform functions" and as one of the "inductive reasoning datasets" used in experiments.

Space of uses. Papers most often pos

nodes.name: LITRANSPROQA
nodes.definition: An LLM-based question-answering framework for literary translation evaluation that uses professionally curated questions to assess translation quality across multiple dimensions including literary devices, cultural understanding, and authorial voice.

nodes.name: LiveBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing description is of a benchmark from Abacus AI that evaluates models on a large test set of questions with ground truth answers. Most descriptions stress a dynamic setup, with questions compiled from recent sources such as math competitions and the dataset updated periodically, while another description foregrounds coverage across data analysis, language, reasoning, math, instruction following, and coding and says it is built from periodically released exams and competitions to reduce contamination.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use LiveBench to measure 4 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators. The linked constructs are Reasoning, Coding ability, Mathematical reasoning, and Natural language understanding, and the linked indicators are Data analysis and Instruction following; these measurement claims are spread across several capabilities named in papers' descriptions of the tasks.

Space of uses. Across papers, LiveBench is used alongside 6 other instruments. Papers report it as correlating with Arena-Hard, BIG-Bench Hard is related to it through harder, contamination-limited versions of earlier tasks, it is also reported to correlat

nodes.name: LiveCodeBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, LiveCodeBench is most commonly described as a contamination-free benchmark for code generation built from recent competitive programming problems, often from LeetCode, AtCoder, and Codeforces, with date-based segregation to avoid contamination. Some definitions broaden it to a holistic evaluation of models for code, highlight real-world execution-based evaluation, or describe a dynamic collection process that continuously adds new human-authored problems. Papers also mention variants or subsets, including LiveCodeBench-v1.0, an "easy" subset, and the code execution task LCB-Exec; descriptions of scale differ, ranging from over 711 problems to 400 recent Python algorithm challenges or over 300 contest questions.

What it is claimed to measure. The prevailing usage is to measure code generation: papers repeatedly use LiveCodeBench to assess coding capability or function generation, and it is linked to 4 constructs and 3 behavioral indicators. Smaller lines of work use it to measure code debugging through a self-repair scenario, code output prediction through LCB-Exec, test generation ability through test output prediction, abductive code reasoning, coding a

nodes.name: LiveSum
nodes.definition: A synthetic football game comments dataset designed for text-to-table tasks, featuring multi-instance and dynamic data where team statistics are aggregated from individual player scores mentioned in the text.

nodes.name: LIWC
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, LIWC is treated as a text analysis and psycholinguistic feature extraction tool. The prevailing description is that it categorizes words into linguistic and psychological dimensions, including emotion, cognition, and formality, and one paper specifies the LIWC-22 version as calculating the percentage of words in a text that fall into different linguistic and psychological categories.

What it is claimed to measure. No construct or behavioral indicator is explicitly linked to LIWC in these papers. Instead, papers describe it more generally as providing psycholinguistic characteristics and category-based linguistic outputs, including outputs used to build trait-specific linguistic features.

Space of uses. Papers use LIWC as an analysis tool over text and responses. One usage reports segment comparison with LIWC features alongside WritePrint features, while another analyzes responses with LIWC-22 and constructs trait-specific linguistic features from its outputs.

nodes.name: Llama Guard
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, Llama Guard is most commonly described as an LLM-based guard model or safety classifier that judges whether prompts or responses are harmful, unsafe, safe, or harmless. Definitions also refer to LLaMA Guard 7B or LlamaGuard-7B, described as a 7-billion parameter open-source guard model and a dedicated classifier for both prompt classification and response classification. A recurring description is as an evaluation tool that classifies responses so papers can compute Attack Success Rate, though some papers instead frame it as a pretrained text content moderation guardrail, an NSFW filter for user prompts, or a deployed safety mechanism on communication edges in multi-agent systems.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to two constructs and two behavioral indicators. The construct claims are Harmlessness and Toxicity: papers use Llama-Guard to determine the safety of responses for harmlessness evaluation, and one paper uses it as the toxicity classifier for some models. The behavioral-indicator claims are Harmful content generation, measured through ASR, and Jailbreaking, assessed by judging whether a response is safe for the given instruction.

S

nodes.name: Llama Guard 2
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across these papers, the prevailing treatment is as an automated safety classifier and LLM-as-a-judge for judging whether model outputs are safe, unsafe, harmful, or toxic. Definitions commonly describe it as a model fine-tuned from Llama-3-8B, with named variants such as Llama-Guard-2-8B and LLaMA Guard 2 8B, and one definition also describes it as an 8-billion-parameter open-source guard model. Most uses focus on classifying responses or conversations, though some papers additionally use it to identify unsafe documents, derive soft safety scores for rejection sampling, or use its feature layer as a semantic embedding source.

What it is claimed to measure. The reported measurement claims are concentrated rather than spread across many targets: papers link it to 1 construct and 2 behavioral indicators. The prevailing usage is to measure Safety, for example by classifying responses or conversations as safe or unsafe and by reporting unsafe response rates; a smaller line of work reports it as measuring Harmful content generation, including attack success rate based on output safety, and Jailbreaking, by classifying responses as jailbreak or non-jailbreak.

Space of uses.

nodes.name: Llama Guard 3
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the dominant framing is Llama Guard 3 as an automated content safety classifier or judge for prompts and model responses. Most descriptions refer to an 8B variant and describe it as a content safety classification LLM that labels text as safe or unsafe, scores harmfulness or toxicity, or identifies harmful categories such as violence, self-harm, illegal activities, and inappropriate sexual content; one paper also specifies it as a Llama-3.1-8B-based model fine-tuned for content safety classification. A smaller line of work treats it as a moderation defense or external guardrail for detecting jailbreak attempts and unsafe content.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to one behavioral indicator and three constructs. The recurring use is to measure harmful content generation by evaluating the harmfulness of model responses, while other papers report that harmlessness, safety, and safety alignment are measured by it, often through content safety classification or harmfulness scoring. The linked claims therefore center on several named outcomes rather than a single target.

Space of uses. No other measurement instrument is linked to it. Papers m

nodes.name: LLaVA-Bench-in-the-Wild
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing description is of an evaluation benchmark for open-ended multimodal dialogue, image understanding, and visual question answering in unconstrained, real-world settings. Many papers describe it as 24 images with 60 challenging questions spanning conversation, detailed description, and complex reasoning, sometimes framed as multimodal instruction following or visual conversation and often scored with GPT-4, GPT-4V, GPT-4o, or another stronger model as evaluator. A smaller line of work presents it as a case-study set for open-ended responses, distinguishes COCO and Wild variants, or uses it for long-generation settings with single-image contexts and a few hundred tokens.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to measure 6 constructs and 9 behavioral indicators, so the reported measurement claims are spread across several targets rather than centered on one. At the construct level, the most common claims are that it measures visual understanding and helpfulness; at the behavioral-indicator level, the recurring uses are for complex reasoning question answering, visual question answering, and detailed image description. Other pap

nodes.name: LLaVA-Med
nodes.definition: A large-scale instruction-tuning dataset for biomedical vision-language processing, used for training.

nodes.name: LLF-Bench Meta-World
nodes.definition: A simulated benchmark environment featuring a Sawyer robot manipulator for testing an agent's ability to learn from language feedback on tasks like reach, pick-place, and push.

nodes.name: LLM-as-a-judge
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage is an evaluation protocol in which one language model, usually a separate or stronger model, judges another model's outputs. Most definitions describe pairwise comparisons, numeric scoring, binary correctness or harmfulness judgments, or rubric-based classification over open-ended responses, sometimes with references, full dialogue history, source documents, or images as context. A smaller line of work extends the same pattern to VLM or MLLM judges, autonomous evaluators, prompt judges, meta-judges, and ensemble or mixture-of-judges setups, and some papers distinguish prompting styles such as a Vanilla judge or an Arena-Hard judge.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to measure 53 constructs and 33 behavioral indicators, so the claims spread across many targets rather than converging on one construct. The most common construct-level uses are helpfulness, harmlessness, factuality, and text generation quality, and the most frequent behavioral use is text generation, with the remaining links spanning 49 other constructs and 32 other behavioral indicators.

Space of uses. Most papers position it as a scalable proxy for human ann

nodes.name: llm-foundry
nodes.definition: Evaluation suite for benchmarking pretrained language models in an in-context few-shot learning setup across multiple task categories.

nodes.name: LLM Guard
nodes.definition: LLM-Guard, a safety evaluation procedure used to measure safety rates on safety benchmarks.

nodes.name: LLMBar
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across definitions, it is most commonly described as a meta-evaluation benchmark, or dataset, for assessing whether LLM evaluators can distinguish instruction-following outputs. Papers consistently place it in pairwise comparison settings, and one definition says it contains one Natural subset and four Adversarial subsets, Neighbor, GPTInst, GPTOut, and Manual. Other descriptions emphasize that it provides high-quality human annotations with high inter-annotator agreement, and one usage-oriented paper treats it as the source of a judging prompt for pairwise response comparison.

What it is claimed to measure. Measurement claims center on a small set of targets: papers link it to 2 constructs, Evaluation ability and Instruction following ability, and 2 behavioral indicators, Instruction following and Pairwise comparison. The prevailing use is to measure evaluators' judgment or discernment in instruction-following tasks, including their ability to distinguish outputs and, in one formulation, to follow instructions using response pairs with clear ground truth preference labels based on adherence to instructions rather than subjective preferences. A smaller framing describe

nodes.name: LLMEval
nodes.definition: An LLM-based evaluation pipeline used to judge whether model responses are correct, abstentions, or hallucinations.

nodes.name: LM1B
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers treat LM1B as a dataset. One description names it the One-Billion Word Language Model Benchmark and uses it for language modeling evaluation, while another uses it to run experiments and check whether results seen on C4 also appear on a different data source.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link LM1B to one construct and no behavioral indicators. The only reported measurement claim is that it measures Zero-shot generalization: a paper describes out-of-domain unseen datasets as validating models' ability in zero-shot generalization, and LM1B is linked to that evaluation.

Space of uses. Papers do not link it to another measurement instrument. In use, LM1B appears alongside C4, where authors report 'observed similar results,' and alongside the OpenWebText test set in an evaluation that uses out-of-domain unseen datasets to validate zero-shot generalization; elsewhere it is presented as a language modeling benchmark.

nodes.name: lm-evaluation-harness
names: Eleuther AI Language Model Evaluation Harness
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing description is of an open-source, standardized or unified evaluation framework, library, or suite for running language model benchmarks across many downstream tasks. Definitions repeatedly present it as a way to evaluate language-model, reasoning, question answering, and multiple-choice tasks in reproducible settings, most often in zero-shot form, though some papers also use few-shot, 5-shot, or mixed 0-shot to 5-shot setups. Some papers describe narrower slices within the suite, such as text-only task suites or short-context benchmarks including Wikitext, LAMBADA, PIQA, and HellaSwag, while a smaller line of work describes leaderboard-oriented variants or adapted protocols.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link the harness to 10 constructs and 12 behavioral indicators. The prevailing usage is to measure commonsense reasoning, reasoning, and general ability, and to operationalize zero-shot task performance and downstream task performance. Overall, papers report it as evaluating a broad spread of capabilities rather than a single construct, with zero-shot and downstream benchmark performance appearing most often.

Space of uses. In use

nodes.name: LMR-BENCH
nodes.definition: A benchmark designed to evaluate an LLM agent's ability to reproduce code from language modeling research papers by implementing masked functions in a provided code repository.

nodes.name: LMSYS-Chat-1M
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing description is a large dataset of real-world chat interactions. Definitions variously call it a dataset of real-world user prompts and conversations, real-world LLM conversations, or user-model conversations; one paper specifies an open-access collection of 1 million user conversations from the Chatbot Arena platform, while another describes real-world conversations with 25 state-of-the-art LLMs. Papers typically treat it as a source from which prompts or conversation samples are drawn for chat model fine-tuning and evaluation.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers do not explicitly present LMSYS-Chat-1M as measuring any named construct or behavioral indicator. Instead, papers use it as an evaluation source in several ways: to assess non-adversarial reproduction in practical chat settings, to supply out-of-distribution prompts for classifier generalization tests, to represent realistic use cases, and to analyze real-world usage patterns. These uses spread across several evaluation aims rather than converging on one named measured construct.

Space of uses. Most commonly, papers use LMSYS-Chat-1M as a prompt or conversation pool for downstr

nodes.name: LoCoMo
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, LoCoMo is most commonly treated as a long-term conversation benchmark for assessing long-term conversational memory over very long dialogue histories. Definitions describe it as including 50 long-term chat histories with questions, and one paper also calls it the longest conversation dataset to date, while another quoted description instead refers to 30 multi-session dialogues between two speakers. Papers also vary in how they describe its question categories: some list single-hop, multi-hop, temporal, commonsense, world knowledge, and adversarial reasoning, while another lists single-hop, multi-hop, temporal, and open-domain.

What it is claimed to measure. In the recorded relationships, papers use LoCoMo to measure one behavioral indicator, Question answering, and it is not linked to any constructs. The measurement claims converge on that single target: papers report QA performance on LoCoMo and describe it as a dataset for evaluating question answering.

Space of uses. Papers commonly position LoCoMo as one of the long-term conversation benchmarks and mention it alongside Long-MT-Bench+, including in performance comparison tables. No measurement in

nodes.name: LOFT
nodes.definition: A benchmark for evaluating long-context models on real-world retrieval tasks, including argumentative retrieval, fact-checking, web search, and multi-hop reasoning question answering.

nodes.name: LogicBench
nodes.definition: A benchmark comprising various logic questions in both binary classification and multiple-choice formats to assess logical reasoning.

nodes.name: LogicNLI
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly treat LogicNLI as a logical reasoning benchmark, and some describe it more specifically as an NLI-style or natural language inference dataset. Across definitions, the recurring framing is that it assesses hypothesis verification from facts and rules and isolates first-order logic reasoning from commonsense inference; as one study notes, "LogicNLI effectively separates the targeted FOL reasoning from common-sense inference" (Few-Shot Natural Language to First-Order Logic Translation via Code Generation).

What it is claimed to measure. Its reported measurement targets are concentrated: papers link it to 1 construct and 1 behavioral indicator. The prevailing usage is to measure Logical reasoning, with several papers evaluating models on LogicNLI as a logical reasoning dataset, while a smaller usage treats it as measuring Natural language inference, including a paper that selects LogicNLI "for natural language inference."

Space of uses. Most uses here position LogicNLI as one member of a broader evaluation suite rather than a standalone protocol. Papers use it alongside RobustLR, PrOntoQA-OOD, ProofWriter, ParaRules, and ProntoQA in logical reasoning

nodes.name: LogiQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, LogiQA is most commonly described as a machine reading comprehension or question answering benchmark for logical reasoning. Definitions usually present it as multiple-choice questions grounded in a passage or logical text, where models choose the correct option; one paper describes it as expert-written and aimed at human-level logical reasoning across deductive, inductive, and abductive inference, while others frame it as reading comprehension from logic puzzles or as NLI from premises to a conclusion. A smaller line of work places it under commonsense reasoning instead.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link LogiQA to five constructs and one behavioral indicator. The prevailing use is to measure logical reasoning, with broader reasoning as another recurring framing; smaller lines of work use it to measure commonsense reasoning, generalization beyond the pretraining distribution, and question answering, and papers also link it to additional constructs. Overall, the measurement claims concentrate on logical reasoning but spread across several targets.

Space of uses. In use, papers often place LogiQA in broader benchmark suites for reasoning, reading

nodes.name: LogiQA 2.0
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across definitions, the prevailing usage treats LogiQA 2.0, often written as LogiQA2 or LogiQA 2, as a benchmark or dataset for logical reasoning and logical question answering. Papers describe it as requiring logical reasoning over text, and some specify a multiple-choice format, including "logical reasoning multi-choice QA" and multiple-choice questions derived from professional exams that require deductive reasoning. A smaller strand presents it as an improved version of LogiQA for machine reading comprehension, and one quoted passage describes LogiQA2 as a revision and re-annotation of LogiQA.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to 5 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator. The most common claim is that it measures Logical reasoning; other papers use it to measure Commonsense reasoning, Executive function, Generalization, and Reasoning, and one paper uses it for the behavioral indicator Multiple-choice question answering. Overall, its reported measurement role is spread across several reasoning-related constructs rather than confined to a single framing.

Space of uses. Across papers, it is usually one component of broader evaluation suites rather than a st

nodes.name: Logistics
nodes.definition:
What it is. The prevailing description treats Logistics as a PDDL planning benchmark or domain centered on transporting packages between locations with trucks and airplanes. The definitions are closely aligned: one calls it a classical PDDL planning benchmark, while another describes it as a benchmark planning domain specified in PDDL.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use Logistics to measure one construct, Planning, and it is not linked to any behavioral indicators. The reported use converges on that single construct: papers frame it under planning benchmarks and use it when evaluating simple or valid plan generation in the logistics domain.

Space of uses. In practice, papers position Logistics as one task within a broader set of PDDL problems rather than as a standalone instrument. One study includes it among four PDDL tasks, BlocksWorld, Minigrid, Logistics, and Tetris, and another calls it a widely used benchmark when testing whether many-shot in-context learning can improve simple plan generation; no measurement instrument is linked to it.

nodes.name: Long Range Arena
nodes.definition: Long Range Arena (LRA), a pioneering benchmark for long context modeling with tasks ranging from 1k to 16k tokens.

nodes.name: LongBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, LongBench is most commonly described as a multi-task benchmark or benchmark suite for evaluating long-context understanding in LLMs, usually across question answering, summarization, and code completion. Some papers instead call it a collection of long-context benchmark datasets and describe it as bilingual or multilingual, with real-world and synthetic tasks. Reported length characterizations differ: one definition gives evaluation lengths of 5k to 15k tokens, while other papers describe average context around 18K, a 32K maximum length, or use on sequences longer than 32K.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link LongBench to 6 constructs and 13 behavioral indicators. The prevailing claim is that it measures long-context understanding. Among behavioral indicators, it is most often used to measure text summarization, code completion, few-shot task performance, and question answering, while other papers also use it for additional constructs and task indicators.

Space of uses. In use, papers commonly position LongBench as a main downstream evaluation for long-context models and methods, often alongside other long-context benchmarks, and sever

nodes.name: LongBench-E
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly describe LongBench-E as a benchmark covering 13 real-world long-context applications, including coding, question answering, and few-shot learning. Some authors instead describe it as the English-language subset of the LongBench benchmark, used for evaluating long-context understanding. One recurring characterization also calls it a multitask benchmark for long-context understanding, with task lengths averaging between 5k and 32k tokens.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing claim is that LongBench-E measures Long-context understanding: it is linked to one construct, and papers describe it as evaluating large language models' ability to understand long contexts or to find key information within a long multi-document context. It is also linked to two behavioral indicators, Coding and Few-shot task performance, through papers that use its coding and few-shot learning applications. Overall, papers use it mainly for one construct, with two additional task-level indicators attached to it.

Space of uses. Papers use LongBench-E as an evaluation benchmark for comparing models and methods, including experiments with propose

nodes.name: LongBench v2
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing description is a multiple-choice benchmark for long contexts, with contexts ranging from 8K to 2M words. One fuller account specifies 503 multiple-choice questions spanning six tasks, single-document QA, multi-document QA, long in-context learning, long dialogue history understanding, code repository understanding, and long structured data understanding, and presents it as designed to evaluate deep long-context comprehension and reasoning, while a shorter description emphasizes its use for assessing long-context performance and efficiency.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the papers, it is linked to one construct and two behavioral indicators. The only linked construct is long-context reasoning, and the linked behavioral indicators are document question answering and text summarization; one paper describes it as a benchmark for challenging long-context question-answering, another uses it for long-context reasoning, and another groups it with datasets that primarily assess retrieval and summarization rather than complex reasoning.

Space of uses. No other measurement instrument is linked to it. In use, papers position it as a long-

nodes.name: LongEmbed PasskeyRetrieval
nodes.definition: A synthetic benchmark from the LongEmbed study used to evaluate long-context retrieval by requiring the model to retrieve a random 'passkey' from a long, distracting document.

nodes.name: LongEval
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across definitions, LongEval is most commonly described as a benchmark for long-context performance, or for tasks that require understanding long-span context. The prevailing description is a retrieval-focused benchmark composed of topic retrieval and line retrieval tasks with varying prompt lengths, while another paper characterizes it more broadly as an early benchmark with various long context retrieval tasks.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link LongEval to one construct and one behavioral indicator. The prevailing measurement claim is Long-context understanding, with papers describing LongEval as designed to measure long-context performance; a smaller line of work uses it to measure Synthetic recall and describes it as a benchmark for long-context retrieval abilities where answer tokens can be separated from non-answer tokens.

Space of uses. No other measurement instrument is linked to it. Papers use it as a benchmark for additional experiments and more comprehensive analyses of model scalability in long-context settings, and another paper positions StreamEval as a dataset inspired by LongEval.

nodes.name: LongEval (summarization faithfulness)
nodes.definition: Evaluation benchmark for long document summarization factuality, used to assess performance on scientific texts with summary-level correlation metrics.

nodes.name: LongFact
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, LongFact is treated as a resource for evaluating factuality in long-form generation, though its format is described differently. One description presents it as a dataset with 250 prompts, while another describes a GPT-4-generated prompt set for benchmarking long-form factuality in open domains, with 2,280 fact-seeking prompts or questions across 38 manually selected topics; as one paper puts it, it contains "2,280 fact-seeking prompts that solicit long-form responses across 38 manually-selected topics" (Long-form factuality in large language models).

What it is claimed to measure. Papers describe it as evaluating factuality in long-form generation, and the recorded measurement links connect it to two behavioral indicators, Hallucination and Long-form text generation, with no linked constructs. The measurement claims therefore spread across these two indicators: one paper reports "hallucination on LongFact," while another uses it as the measure for Long-form text generation.

Space of uses. No other measurement instrument is linked to it in the papers. Papers position it as a benchmark or evaluation set: one paper includes it among "four fact-seeking long

nodes.name: LongGenBench
nodes.definition: Benchmark designed for extreme-length generation with multi-shot in-context examples, testing long-context reasoning and comprehension.

nodes.name: LongLaMP
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly treat LongLaMP as a benchmark dataset for long-form personalized text generation. The prevailing description is that it covers tasks such as abstract generation, topic writing, and review generation; another description presents it as an extended version of LaMP with longer-form, open-ended, and more subjective personalized generation tasks, including abstract and topic writing.

What it is claimed to measure. In these papers, LongLaMP is not linked to named constructs or behavioral indicators. Instead, papers describe it at the task level as evaluating long-form personalized text generation, with one description further characterizing its tasks as involving more subjective or user-specific expression.

Space of uses. Papers commonly use LongLaMP alongside LaMP, positioning the pair as resources for long-form and short-form personalized text generation, respectively. One study also places it within a set of open-ended personalized text generation tasks drawn from LaMP and LongLaMP.

nodes.name: LongMemEval
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the cited work, LongMemEval is described both as a long-term multi-session conversation dataset for evaluating response generation and memory utilization, and as a benchmark for chat assistants' long-context memory. One description presents it as evaluating five core long-term memory abilities, information extraction, multi-session reasoning, temporal reasoning, knowledge updates, and abstention, while another calls it a challenging benchmark covering six memory tasks. The prevailing usage is therefore as a memory-focused evaluation resource, though papers differ on whether they frame it primarily as a dataset or as a benchmark and on how many task categories it contains.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use LongMemEval to measure 6 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators. The most common links are to multi-session reasoning and temporal reasoning, which multiple papers say the benchmark evaluates; other papers also use it to measure length generalization and the behavioral indicators abstention and information extraction, with 3 other constructs also reported. Overall, the measurement claims are spread across several memory and reasoning targets rather than

nodes.name: LongReport
nodes.definition: A benchmark dataset created for this paper, containing 12 complex prompts designed to elicit comprehensive, long-form reports on time-sensitive topics.

nodes.name: LongVideoBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, LongVideoBench is most commonly described as a benchmark or dataset for long video understanding, often framed as long video question answering. Some papers narrow this further to referred reasoning on long frame inputs or to long-context interleaved video-language understanding: one description says it features "video-language interleaved inputs up to an hour long," with 3,763 web-collected videos and subtitles, plus 6,678 human-annotated multiple-choice questions in 17 fine-grained categories.

What it is claimed to measure. Across linked relationships, papers use it to measure 3 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator. The prevailing usage is to measure long video understanding, with additional use for video understanding and long-context multimodal understanding; one behavioral link treats it as measuring video question answering. Several task descriptions further characterize that measurement as targeting referred reasoning, long-form evaluation, or long-term multimodal understanding.

Space of uses. Papers usually deploy it as one benchmark within a broader evaluation suite rather than in isolation. It appears alongside MLVU, VideoMME, EgoSchema, MVBe

nodes.name: LooGLE
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats LooGLE as a benchmark or workload for long-context evaluation. Definitions describe it as evaluating long document question answering with prompts containing extensive text from which answers must be derived, and more broadly as evaluating long-context understanding through extremely long documents, diverse domains, short- and long-dependency tasks, and long-range dependencies over the full sequence. Papers differ slightly in emphasis, with some foregrounding long document QA and others framing it as a broader long-context benchmark; the descriptions also note documents with over 24,000 tokens and data primarily around 32,000 tokens.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use LooGLE to measure long-context understanding, and this is the only linked construct. It is linked to 1 construct, long-context understanding, while no behavioral indicators are linked. The claims converge on this single construct rather than spreading across multiple constructs.

Space of uses. Papers position LooGLE both as a standalone workload and as part of broader evaluation suites. Some descriptions treat it as one workload among others, f

nodes.name: LoraxBench
nodes.definition: A multitask, multilingual benchmark suite covering 20 Indonesian languages and 3 register variations across 6 tasks: reading comprehension, open-domain QA, natural language inference, causal reasoning, cultural QA, and machine translation.

nodes.name: LSMDC
nodes.definition: Large-Scale Movie Description Challenge dataset featuring movie clips with textual descriptions, designed for evaluating multimodal understanding and retrieval in narrative contexts.

nodes.name: LV-Eval
nodes.definition: Bilingual benchmark assessing long-context understanding through single-hop and multi-hop question answering across 11 datasets, designed to evaluate model performance at varying context lengths.

nodes.name: LVIS
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, LVIS is most commonly described as a large-vocabulary instance segmentation dataset or benchmark used for evaluation. Definitions repeatedly emphasize a long-tail version with annotations for over 1000 object categories, while one paper describes a commonly used zero-shot LVIS with 1,203 categories. Papers also refer to its validation dataset or validation sets, and some describe it as being used to evaluate object-level classification when a model is prompted with a visual region.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use LVIS to measure 2 behavioral indicators, Instance segmentation and Open-vocabulary object detection, and no constructs are linked to it. These linked claims stay at the behavioral level, though some definitions also describe LVIS as assessing object-level classification performance, including referring classification scored with Semantic Similarity and Semantic Intersection over Union.

Space of uses. No other measurement instrument is linked to LVIS. Papers mainly position it as an evaluation benchmark: they report results on object detection, instance segmentation, and open-vocabulary recognition or segmentation, and in one usage the

nodes.name: M3Exam
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers here, M3Exam is most commonly described as a multitask, multilingual benchmark used to evaluate multimodal models. A narrower description in Is Translation All You Need? A Study on Solving Multilingual Tasks with Large Language Models treats it as a multilingual, multi-subject, multiple-choice exam benchmark built from real-world national exam questions, with questions drawn from different languages rather than translated from English.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link M3Exam to 1 construct and no behavioral indicators, so the reported measurement claims converge on a single construct rather than spreading across many targets. Its linked construct is Cultural knowledge: one paper uses M3Exam to measure it, stating that the questions require strong multilingual proficiency and cultural knowledge to perform well.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it in the recorded relationships. In use, papers present M3Exam as an evaluation benchmark or dataset: R2-MultiOmnia: Leading Multilingual Multimodal Reasoning via Self-Training uses it together with XMMMLU and MAXM to study multimodal reasoning performance, while another paper sel

nodes.name: M4
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers describe M4 in two distinct ways. Some definitions present it as a short-term time series forecasting benchmark containing marketing data at different sampling frequencies, and one quoted passage describes it as a testbed with a collection of marketing data in different sampling frequencies. Several quoted passages instead use M4 for a machine-generated text detection dataset or benchmark: documents generated by multiple LLMs in five domains, a multilingual resource with languages such as Chinese, Russian, Urdu, Indonesian, Arabic, and Bulgarian, and in some cases the Urdu subset or a large-scale multi-domain benchmark for cross-domain scenarios.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use M4 to measure two behavioral indicators, AI-generated text detection and time series forecasting, and no constructs are linked to it. The recorded measurement links are split across these two behavioral indicators: one paper reports AI-generated text detection as measured by the Urdu subset of M4, and another reports time series forecasting as measured in work on transfer learning between the M3 and M4 competitions.

Space of uses. Across the papers, M4 is positioned either as a

nodes.name: M-LongDoc
nodes.definition: A benchmark of 851 samples designed to evaluate multimodal long-document understanding through open-ended question answering over real-world documents spanning hundreds of pages, with questions requiring in-depth reasoning across text, figures, and tables.
