nodes.name: M-RewardBench
nodes.definition: A multilingual benchmark for evaluating reward models across 23 languages, assessing chat, safety, reasoning, and translation capabilities through human-validated preference triples.

nodes.name: MAGE
nodes.definition:
What it is. The definition treats MAGE as a supervised fine-tuned model for AI text detection. It is described as classifying text as human or machine-generated through binary classification on linguistic features.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers do not link MAGE to any constructs or behavioral indicators, so the evidence does not specify broader concepts it is used to measure.

Space of uses. The usage in the papers evidence places MAGE among other AI text detectors rather than as a standalone protocol. In Beyond Checkmate: Exploring the Creative Choke Points for AI Generated Texts, it is evaluated as part of a suite of prominent detectors alongside GPT-Zero, Radar, Binoculars, and GPT-Who.

nodes.name: MagicBrush
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most papers describe MagicBrush as a benchmark or manually annotated dataset for instruction-guided image editing, in one case specified as real image editing and in another as evaluation for image editing within an interleaved generation context. Some descriptions emphasize that its editing queries can demand a series of complex edits to an image, and one paper reports using the full test set. A smaller line of work repurposes it to form paired images with subtle differences for existence comparison.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the papers, claims about what MagicBrush measures converge on a single behavioral indicator: papers use it to measure Image editing, often by describing evaluation of image editing capabilities on MagicBrush. It is linked to one behavioral indicator, Image editing, and no constructs are linked to it.

Space of uses. Papers mainly position it as an evaluation set for image editing. One paper uses it alongside EVR and MA5K when evaluating image editing capabilities, another reports an additional evaluation on the full test set, and another adapts it for comparative reasoning by constructing paired images with subtle differences.

nodes.name: MAGPIE
nodes.definition:
What it is. In the surveyed work, MAGPIE is described as a corpus of potentially idiomatic expressions labeled as figurative or literal. The definition also presents it as a resource used to test whether global affinity distinguishes figurative from literal usage.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link MAGPIE to one behavioral indicator, Idiom identification, and to no constructs. The recorded use is as a measure of idiom identification, with one study stating that it adapts the dataset for the identification task.

Space of uses. The reported use treats MAGPIE as a task dataset, with one study noting that it adapts the dataset for the task and applies some filtering. No other measurement instrument is linked to it.

nodes.name: MaliciousInstruct
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most commonly, papers treat MaliciousInstruct as a harmful benchmark or dataset of malicious instructions for testing LLM safety defenses on out-of-domain or out-of-distribution inputs. Definitions converge on that role, while varying in wording between a dataset, a benchmark, and an out-of-domain test set. Another definition states that it contains 100 broader harmful instructions and is used to assess transferability.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the papers, MaliciousInstruct is linked to one construct, Safety, and to no behavioral indicators. The reported measurement claim converges on that single construct: papers use it to measure Safety, including as an out-of-domain test set for evaluating safety defenses and in evaluations that check whether responses lacked keywords indicating instruction rejection.

Space of uses. Papers use MaliciousInstruct alongside AdvBench, and also with HEx-PHI and AdvExtent. It is typically positioned as one of several harmful benchmarks for evaluating defense strategies, or as an OOD check for transferability. A paper also uses jailbreak attacks on MaliciousInstruct and then applies string matching to identify whether respons

nodes.name: MAMI
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the definitions, MAMI is most commonly treated as a publicly available dataset or benchmark of memes for evaluation, especially around misogyny and abusive or harmful content. The prevailing description says it contains memes that are predominantly derogatory towards women, while another recurring framing presents it as a shared-task resource for multimedia automatic misogyny identification with binary and multi-label misogyny classification. Some papers describe it more broadly as a dataset of multimodal abusive memes used to benchmark detection of abusive language and imagery in social media content.

What it is claimed to measure. Across reported links, papers use MAMI to measure one behavioral indicator, Harmful content detection, and it is not linked to any construct. The recorded measured_by relation says Harmful content detection is measured by MAMI, with the dataset used for evaluation in that role. The measurement claims therefore converge on a single reported target rather than being spread across multiple constructs or indicators.

Space of uses. In use, a paper places MAMI alongside HarM and FHM as part of a set of publicly available meme datasets for

nodes.name: MAMO
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing usage is as a benchmark for mathematical or optimization modeling. Some descriptions add that it benchmarks modeling with code solvers and focuses on linear programming problems, while others present it through EasyLP and ComplexLP, either as two optimization datasets or as subsets of varying difficulty.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use MAMO to evaluate mathematical modeling, mathematical optimization modeling, or LLM performance on those tasks. No constructs or behavioral indicators are linked to it in the surveyed papers.

Space of uses. In the surveyed papers, MAMO appears as one benchmark within broader evaluation suites. It is used alongside NL4OPT, IndustryOR, OptiBench, and OptMATH-Bench in one evaluation setup, and another study includes Mamo, specifically EasyLP and ComplexLP, among real-world optimization and operation task datasets; one quoted passage also places it among established modeling benchmarks.

nodes.name: Mantis-Eval
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across definitions, papers most commonly describe Mantis-Eval as an evaluation dataset or benchmark for multi-image reasoning. The prevailing framing is an evaluation set of high-quality, human-annotated multi-image reasoning samples: one description specifies 207 examples and mentions tasks such as size perception and weight comparison, while another highlights co-reference, reasoning, and comparison. A smaller line of work refers to it simply as Mantis and treats it as a multi-image benchmark used to assess performance on multi-image inputs.

What it is claimed to measure. In relationship claims, papers use it to measure 2 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator. The most common measured target is multi-image reasoning, and papers also report it as measuring multimodal reasoning and multi-image visual question answering. Overall, these links cluster around reasoning over multiple images rather than spreading across many different targets.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it. Papers instead position it as one benchmark within broader multi-image evaluation suites, most often alongside MMMU and BLINK, and sometimes with QBench, NLVR2, or MVBench. In

nodes.name: Manual error analysis
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage is a human evaluation protocol in which annotators manually inspect model outputs or rationales against predefined error categories. Definitions range from native English speakers assessing rationale mistakes such as context, word-sense, and pun pair errors, to manual error annotation that counts errors in generated instructions across categories such as incorrect assembly operations or order. Other descriptions emphasize fine-grained taxonomies of linguistic and non-linguistic errors, or manual analysis of incorrect generations.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to measure one construct, linguistic quality, and two behavioral indicators, calculation error and reasoning error. One paper uses manual annotation to investigate inconsistencies and linguistic quality, while another reports that in-depth human analysis identified common error types including calculation error and reasoning error. The reported measurement claims therefore center on this small set: linguistic quality, calculation error, and reasoning error.

Space of uses. Papers position it "beyond standard metrics" or as "in-depth" manual analysis of incorrect g

nodes.name: MASSIVE
nodes.definition: Multilingual dataset for intent and slot detection covering 15 low-resource languages, used to evaluate zero-shot performance on unseen label schemas.

nodes.name: Massive(I)
nodes.definition: A dataset for intent discovery, aiming to identify unknown intents within user utterances.

nodes.name: MATH
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats MATH as a benchmark dataset of challenging competition-level or high school mathematics problems for evaluating advanced mathematical reasoning. Definitions commonly describe problems drawn from competitions such as AMC 10, AMC 12, and AIME, often spanning seven subjects and domains such as algebra, geometry, and number theory; some papers add that it contains 12,500 problems in informal language with step-by-step solutions and boxed answers, and one paper notes a 5,000-problem evaluation split. A smaller line of work further describes internal difficulty levels from 1 to 5 and uses variants such as an algebra subset of 881 problems, MATH-Algebra-Easy, a multiple-choice version, and the MATH-500 test subset.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link MATH to 13 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator. The dominant framing is that it measures mathematical reasoning; a recurring secondary use is mathematical problem solving, and broader work also treats it as measuring reasoning, complex reasoning, and general ability. The remaining links are more dispersed across 9 other constructs, so reported uses spread across many targets eve

nodes.name: MATH-500
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most commonly, papers treat MATH-500, also written MATH500, as a 500-question subset or test set from the MATH benchmark, often described as selected from the original 5,000-question MATH test set. Some authors simply describe it as a mathematical reasoning benchmark containing 500 challenging math problems, while others specify that it is a representative, highly challenging 10% subset. Where papers give more detail on content, they describe high school competition math across seven subjects, with AoPS-based difficulty levels from 1 to 5.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to three constructs and one behavioral indicator. The prevailing usage is to measure Mathematical reasoning, with closely related uses for broader Reasoning; papers also use it to measure Mathematical problem solving, and a smaller line of work reports it as measuring Verification ability. Overall, the reported measurement claims are concentrated on math-focused reasoning constructs rather than spread across many different targets.

Space of uses. Most papers use it within broader evaluation suites rather than alone, most often alongside GSM8K, and often with AIME or GPQA; some also pair

nodes.name: Math Hard
nodes.definition: A difficult mathematics benchmark used to assess complex mathematical reasoning.

nodes.name: MathBench
nodes.definition: Chinese mathematics benchmark requiring models to solve school-level math problems in Chinese, used to evaluate complex task learning.

nodes.name: MathDial
nodes.definition: MathDial, a dataset of tutoring conversations collected by human teachers interacting with simulated students, used for tutoring evaluation and preference data.

nodes.name: Mathematics Dataset
nodes.definition:
What it is. Definitions usually treat Mathematics Dataset, also referred to as Mathematics or DeepMind-Mathematics, as a dataset or benchmark of mathematical problems for evaluating mathematical reasoning. The content is described as covering diverse mathematics topics, including algebra, arithmetic, calculus, and probability, with one description also listing comparison, measurement, and numbers; another says the problems are based on a national school mathematics curriculum up to age 16. A smaller variation in description is whether papers emphasize a curriculum-based generation process, a benchmark format, or a test set of 1000 problems.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to measure Mathematical reasoning. The measurement claims converge on one construct rather than spread across many: it is linked to one construct, Mathematical reasoning, and to no behavioral indicators.

Space of uses. Papers use it both as an out-of-domain evaluation dataset, alongside SVAMP and SimulEq, and as part of HUMANBENCH, which contains 7 datasets from the Mathematics Dataset. Another paper describes DeepMind-Mathematics directly as a test set.

nodes.name: MathGAP
nodes.definition: MathGAP (Mathematical Generalization on Arithmetic Proofs), a synthetic evaluation framework that generates arithmetic word problems and chain-of-thought solutions with controllable proof-tree complexity for out-of-distribution testing.

nodes.name: Mathlib
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most commonly described as Lean's largest community-maintained repository, Mathlib is also treated as the Lean mathematical library that serves as the formal environment for compiling and checking theorem statements and proofs. Papers use it both as a source of evaluation theorems for testing generalization, including newly added theorems in one study, and as the library against which correctness tests are run in a matching Lean and Mathlib setup.

What it is claimed to measure. In the recorded relationships, Mathlib is not claimed to measure any construct, and it is linked to one behavioral indicator, theorem proving. That connection is reported as a related link rather than a direct measurement claim, with one paper stating that most neural theorem provers based on Lean are primarily trained on Mathlib.

Space of uses. No other measurement instrument is linked to it. Across the definitions and quoted passages, papers use Mathlib as shared infrastructure: a repository models may have trained on, a source of evaluation theorems for generalization tests, and the formal environment used to compile, check, and run correctness tests for theorem statements and proofs.

nodes.name: MathOdyssey
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing usage is as a benchmark for math reasoning, especially Olympiad-level mathematical reasoning. One definition describes it more specifically as a set of math problems of varying difficulty, including olympiad-level competition questions, and a quoted passage calls it "a popular benchmark for LLM math reasoning"; another paper refers to it more generally as an olympiad benchmark, and one study focuses on its olympiad-level competition problems.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use MathOdyssey to measure one behavioral indicator, Mathematical problem solving, and two constructs, Generalization and Mathematical reasoning. In the linked claims, it is used as a held-out benchmark for Mathematical problem solving and Generalization, and it is also reported as evaluating Mathematical reasoning, so the measurement claims are spread across these targets rather than centered on a single construct.

Space of uses. Papers do not link it to another measurement instrument, though they use it alongside Hendrycks MATH and Functional Math. In those uses, it is positioned as an additional or challenging held-out benchmark, and elsewhere as one of mu

nodes.name: MathQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across definitions, the prevailing usage is as a math question answering or mathematical reasoning benchmark built from math word problems. Most descriptions present it as multiple-choice and centered on multi-step quantitative reasoning, and one source notes that it offers five answer options per problem and includes geometry, physics, probability, and algebra. A smaller line of work describes the problems as using operation-based formalisms for interpretability, and one paper using the name MQA frames it instead as GRE and GMAT exam questions requiring more diverse and complex reasoning skills.

What it is claimed to measure. Claims concentrate on Mathematical reasoning: papers use MathQA to measure that construct more often than any other, and describe it as assessing mathematical tasks, varying levels of mathematical reasoning ability, and diverse arithmetic and algebraic reasoning challenges. Overall it is linked to four constructs, Mathematical reasoning, Reasoning, Commonsense reasoning, and Problem-solving ability, and to two behavioral indicators, Mathematical problem solving and Classification. The prevailing measurement claim is therefore Mathematical reasoni

nodes.name: MathTutorBench
nodes.definition: A benchmark for measuring open-ended pedagogical capabilities of LLMs in mathematics tutoring, involving task prompts, human evaluation, and scaffolding-focused metrics.

nodes.name: MathVerse
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, MathVerse is most commonly treated as a multimodal or visual math benchmark for evaluating mathematical reasoning with visual inputs, especially diagram understanding. Definitions variously emphasize geometry-related mathematical reasoning, broader multimodal mathematical problem solving, and whether models can interpret or "truly see" diagrams in visual math problems, and one description specifies 2,612 visual math problems. Papers also describe different formats within the benchmark, including multiple-choice questions and a Vision-Only mode where questions are presented in images, alongside text-dominant and vision-integrated presentations.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use MathVerse to measure two constructs and one behavioral indicator. The prevailing measured construct is Mathematical reasoning, while smaller uses treat it as measuring Generalization and as supporting Chain of thought evaluation, with one paper reporting scores on "CoT evaluation and accuracy" on MathVerse. Overall, papers link it to a fairly concentrated set of targets rather than a broad spread of constructs.

Space of uses. Papers often place MathVerse inside broader mul

nodes.name: MathVerse-mv
nodes.definition: A multi-image mathematical reasoning benchmark used for out-domain evaluation.

nodes.name: MathVision
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, MathVision is most commonly described as a visual mathematical reasoning dataset or benchmark for multimodal problem solving. Definitions present it as covering algebra, geometry, combinatorics, and logic, with evaluation by accuracy on complex multimodal problems, while another description says it involves interpreting diagrams and solving quantitative problems. One source also refers to the testmini subset of the MATH-Vision dataset.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link MathVision to 2 constructs and no behavioral indicators. The prevailing usage is to measure Mathematical reasoning: papers place it among math-related benchmarks and describe such benchmarks as designed to evaluate the mathematical abilities of MLLMs. A smaller line of work uses it to measure Calibration under visual mathematical reasoning.

Space of uses. It is frequently used alongside MathVista, and in some benchmark suites also with MathVerse, DynaMath, MMStar, and CharXiv. Papers position it as one benchmark within broader visual reasoning or math-related evaluations, and one paper pairs it with MathVista specifically to evaluate calibration under visual mathematic

nodes.name: MathVista
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, MathVista is most commonly described as a benchmark for mathematical reasoning in visual or multimodal contexts. Definitions emphasize puzzles or math problems that involve images and joint mathematical and visual understanding, often broken down by reasoning type and image context. Some authors describe or use it through the geometry problem solving task, especially the testmini split, while a smaller line of work presents it as a broader benchmark that also includes general visual question answering tasks and questions outside traditional mathematics.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to measure 7 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators. The prevailing usage is mathematical reasoning, often phrased as math reasoning with visual information or visual mathematical reasoning. Other recurring claims are broader reasoning, geometric reasoning, multimodal reasoning, and visual question answering, with 3 other constructs and 1 other behavioral indicator also linked to it. Overall, the claims center on mathematical reasoning but spread across several other reported targets.

Space of uses. Papers usually position it as one benchmark within a larger e

nodes.name: MAWPS
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the dominant framing is MAWPS as a benchmark or dataset of math word problems, often described as arithmetic problems in natural language for evaluating arithmetic or mathematical reasoning; one paper further describes it as consisting of 2,373 elementary-level math word problems. A smaller set of definitions describes it as an out-of-distribution or out-of-domain benchmark repository, one definition says it categorizes and standardizes arithmetic word problems from other datasets, and one paper reports average results over SingleEQ, SingleOP, AddSub, and MultiArith under the collective term MAWPS.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use MAWPS to measure 2 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator. The prevailing claim is that it measures Mathematical reasoning, with papers describing it as a math reasoning or arithmetic reasoning benchmark; less commonly, it is reported as measuring In-context learning and Mathematical problem solving, so the claims are concentrated on Mathematical reasoning rather than spread across many targets.

Space of uses. No other measurement instrument is linked to it, but papers commonly evaluate MAWPS alongside GSM8K and SVAMP,

nodes.name: Maze
nodes.definition: A text-based navigation task in which an agent must choose moves in a maze, including partially observed and fully observed variants.

nodes.name: MBPP
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, MBPP is most commonly treated as a Python programming benchmark or dataset for code generation from natural language descriptions or a textual context. The prevailing framing is entry-level or simple problems with automated tests or unit tests, though some definitions also mention reference code or associated solutions, and a smaller line of work casts it as text-to-code, text-to-Python, program synthesis, or code completion. Papers also refer to variants or subsets such as MBPP(+), MBPP-pro, sanitized versions, and manually verified test splits, and they describe the benchmark with different task totals.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link MBPP to 9 constructs and 3 behavioral indicators. The dominant use is to measure code generation and coding ability: papers use it to test Python writing, coding proficiency, or Python coding skills from natural language, and some explicitly evaluate pass-based functional correctness on it. Claims beyond that are more spread out, with papers also using it to measure generalization and reasoning, alongside other linked constructs and indicators.

Space of uses. No other measurement instrument is linked to it

nodes.name: MBXP
nodes.definition: The MBXP benchmark is a multilingual dataset for evaluating code generation models across multiple programming languages.

nodes.name: mC4
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the definitions, mC4 is most commonly described as the multilingual Colossal Clean Crawled Corpus, or multilingual C4, a large multilingual web-crawl dataset derived from Common Crawl. Papers variously present it as multilingual pre-training data, as a benchmark spanning high-, medium-, and low-resource languages, and as a multilingual partition of CommonCrawl web scrapes; some descriptions focus on particular portions or slices, such as Arabic and English portions, selected linguistically diverse languages, or tokens used to record feature activation ranges.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the papers, mC4 is not explicitly linked to any named construct or behavioral indicator, so it is not presented as measuring a single construct. The reported measurement uses are instead task specific: evaluating multilingual pre-training behavior, computing model perplexity across 50 languages, reporting validation loss on selected languages, and approximating entity occurrence in pre-training data.

Space of uses. The papers do not explicitly relate mC4 to other named measurement instruments. They use it as multilingual experimental data: for pre-training distillation

nodes.name: MCBench
nodes.definition: Metric Calculating Benchmark, a code-verifiable evaluation suite that tests LLMs on their ability to follow complex step-by-step rubrics for computing string-matching NLP metrics, with objective assessment via parallel reference code.

nodes.name: MD-Judge
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, MD-Judge is treated as an automated, LLM-based evaluation procedure for safety judgments. The descriptions converge on its role as an evaluator or classifier, but differ in scope: one paper describes it as assessing whether generated responses appropriately handle fairness and privacy concerns in terms of safety and appropriateness, while another describes it more generally as evaluating the safety of instruction-response pairs.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link MD-Judge to one construct and to no behavioral indicators. The only recorded measurement claim is that it measures Privacy awareness: one paper reports using it to assess generated responses regarding Qf and Qp, so the measurement claims here are concentrated on that single construct rather than spread across multiple linked outcomes.

Space of uses. No other measurement instrument is linked to it here. Papers instead position MD-Judge as the evaluator itself, either by directly employing it to assess model outputs, as in The Tug of War Within: Mitigating the Fairness-Privacy Conflicts in Large Language Models, or by describing it as an evaluation procedure built around an LLM-based

nodes.name: Mean Opinion Score
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the cited definitions, Mean Opinion Score is most commonly treated as a subjective human rating protocol on a 1 to 5, 5-point, or Likert-like scale. The prevailing usage is in speech and audio, where listeners rate synthesized speech or generated responses for naturalness or overall quality, while a smaller usage applies the same format to text, where raters judge quality and diversity.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use MOS to rate a range of output qualities rather than tying it to one named target. The recurring claims are that it gauges naturalness and quality in synthesized speech or generated audio, and quality and diversity in text, with some definitions further describing perceived fluency and coherence; however, papers do not explicitly link it to any construct or behavioral indicator.

Space of uses. Papers typically position MOS as a subjective human evaluation step. In the audio-focused work, it is described as a commonly used crowd-sourced listening test, including collection through Amazon Mechanical Turk, and one paper reports using MOS alongside a separate prosody mean opinion score, P-MOS, when evaluating prosody and naturalness; in the t

nodes.name: MEBench
nodes.definition: A benchmark comprising 4,780 question-answer pairs designed to evaluate LLMs and RAG systems on cross-document, multi-entity question answering across comparative, statistical, and relational reasoning tasks.

nodes.name: Medbullets
nodes.definition: A question answering dataset based on online medical questions.

nodes.name: MEDFACT
nodes.definition: A large-scale Chinese dataset for evidence-based medical fact-checking of LLM-generated claims, containing 1,321 questions and 7,409 claim-evidence pairs with veracity labels across five categories: Supported, Partially Supported, Refuted, Uncertain, and Not Applicable.

nodes.name: MedHallu
nodes.definition: A benchmark of 10,000 medical question-answer pairs with systematically generated hallucinated answers, stratified by difficulty (easy, medium, hard) and hallucination type, used to evaluate medical hallucination detection in LLMs.

nodes.name: Media Frames Corpus
nodes.definition: A dataset of news articles annotated for policy frames such as 'Economic' or 'Morality', used to evaluate alignment with human-constructed framing schemes.

nodes.name: MediaSum
nodes.definition: A summarization dataset used as part of the faithfulness evaluation setup for intrinsic and extrinsic refinement experiments.

nodes.name: Medley-solos-DB
nodes.definition: A benchmark for instrument-related audio classification.

nodes.name: MedMCQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the dominant framing is a large-scale, multi-subject medical multiple-choice question answering benchmark or dataset. Most definitions describe it as built from Indian medical entrance examinations, often naming AIIMS and NEET or NEET PG, and one paper explicitly describes it as a 4-way multiple-choice dataset. Smaller variations describe it as a closed-book medical QA benchmark, one component of the medical MIRAGE benchmark, or a QA dataset that provides plain-text explanations.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link MedMCQA to 2 constructs and 3 behavioral indicators. The prevailing claims use it to measure question answering, medical question answering, multiple-choice question answering, and medical knowledge, with papers describing it as assessing clinical domain knowledge or preliminary knowledge grasp through QA tasks. One paper additionally uses it to measure calibration, reporting ECE and accuracy on MedMCQA.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it. Papers usually place it inside broader evaluation suites, most often alongside MedQA, and also with PubMedQA, MMLU or MMLU-Med, ARC-Challenge, and HotpotQA, or within

nodes.name: MedQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, MedQA is most commonly described as a medical multiple-choice question answering benchmark built from USMLE or other professional medical board exam questions. Definitions usually present it as evaluating medical knowledge and reasoning, with some papers specifying clinical vignettes, patient-profile style contextualized questions, or questions curated by medical examination experts from various question banks; one paper also notes that MedQA included questions from Medbullets. Papers also mention variants: MedQA-USMLE is described either as an NBME-sourced subset or simply as MedQA, and MedQA-US as a challenging USMLE-based version.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link MedQA to 4 constructs and 5 behavioral indicators. The prevailing use is to measure Medical question answering, Multiple-choice question answering, Question answering, Medical knowledge, and Medical reasoning; other papers report four additional linked targets. Overall, the reported measurement claims stay centered on medical QA and knowledge or reasoning evaluation, rather than on one single target.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it. In use, pap

nodes.name: MedQuAD
nodes.definition: A question-answering benchmark with long free-form answers used to evaluate uncertainty methods.

nodes.name: MeetingBank
nodes.definition: A dataset for summarization tasks, specifically from meeting transcripts, used for both intrinsic and extrinsic evaluation of model refinement.

nodes.name: MELD
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, MELD is most commonly described as a multimodal dataset of TV show dialogues annotated for emotion and sentiment, used for evaluating emotion recognition in conversational speech. Some descriptions are more specific, calling it a multimodal multi-party Speech Emotion Recognition dataset from the TV series Friends with over 1,400 dialogues and 13,000 utterances, annotated with seven emotion labels and sentiment, while another paper reports assessing emotion recognition on 2,608 utterances.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use MELD to measure two behavioral indicators, Emotion analysis and Speech emotion recognition, and two constructs, Emotion understanding and Utility preservation. The prevailing usage is emotion-focused: papers describe it as an emotion recognition or emotion classification benchmark, and one paper interprets MELD results as showing "strong emotion perception and contextual understanding"; the links therefore center on emotion-related outcomes, though a smaller line of work also uses it in general utility evaluation.

Space of uses. In the papers here, MELD is positioned as an evaluation benchmark and is used alongside other be

nodes.name: Membership inference attack
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most papers describe it as a privacy evaluation procedure for testing whether a specific datapoint, input fragment, or sample was used in a model’s training or alignment process, typically by distinguishing member from non-member examples. A few papers specify black-box variants that rely only on model outputs or loss values, and others name heuristics such as perplexity, lowercase probability, zlib compression, and Min-K% probability. A smaller line of work extends the same framing to document-level membership, to suspect-dataset inference, or to unlearning settings where membership is inferred by comparing model behavior before and after unlearning.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to 3 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators, so its measurement claims are spread across several privacy- and unlearning-related targets rather than centered on one alone. The prevailing use is to measure privacy preservation, with a smaller but recurring use for privacy leakage, while only a few papers use it to assess forget quality or knowledge memorization. Separately, papers relate it to pre-training data detection, with some describing that task as a special case of memb

nodes.name: MemeReaCon
nodes.definition: A benchmark for evaluating contextual meme understanding in vision-language models, consisting of 1,565 annotated Reddit posts with meme images, post text, and top comments, assessed across four tasks probing interplay, stance, connections, and intent.

nodes.name: Mercury
nodes.definition: Code generation evaluation used as a validation set for tuning hyperparameters in code-related tasks.

nodes.name: MERLIN
nodes.definition: A benchmark focused on entity recognition in multilingual multimodal settings, evaluating the model's ability to identify culturally relevant entities from image-text pairs.

nodes.name: Meta-World
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across definitions, the prevailing usage treats Meta-World as a MuJoCo-based robotic manipulation benchmark, often also framed as a multi-task and meta-reinforcement-learning benchmark. Papers describe an agent controlling a Sawyer robot to manipulate objects such as doors, drawers, and windows, or more generally manipulating an object to achieve a given goal, and they use the benchmark to evaluate generalization across robot manipulation tasks. Some papers refer to specific subsets or settings, including ML10, ML45, MT10, MT50, the ML-45 version with 45 tasks, and a setup with 10 different robot manipulation goals.

What it is claimed to measure. Where papers make explicit measurement claims, they use Meta-World to measure one behavioral indicator, Robotic manipulation, and they do not connect it to any constructs. The reported use is concentrated rather than spread across many targets: relationship evidence describes Meta-World as a robotic manipulation benchmark suite and as a tabletop manipulation benchmark, so the measurement claim converges on robotic manipulation.

Space of uses. Papers position Meta-World mainly as an evaluation or verification benchmark for rob

nodes.name: MetaICL
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, MetaICL is most commonly described as a benchmark dataset or evaluation framework for in-context learning. Definitions repeatedly describe it as covering 142 NLP tasks, with papers variously emphasizing meta-training and meta-testing partitions, seven partitions, or task types such as text classification, question answering, natural language inference, and paraphrase detection. A smaller line of description focuses on a high-to-low resources setting with 61 training tasks and 26 unseen test tasks, where evaluation uses multiple-choice accuracy.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the reported relationships, papers link MetaICL to one construct, In-context learning, and to no behavioral indicators. The claims converge on that single construct rather than spreading across many: papers describe MetaICL as "designed for in-context learning scenarios," use it for "short finetuning and evaluation," and report results as a "MetaICL in-context learning evaluation."

Space of uses. Papers use MetaICL as an evaluation benchmark to validate methods, and some follow its short-finetuning-and-evaluation setup. One paper reports average accuracy across 2

nodes.name: MetaQA
nodes.definition: Multi-hop KBQA dataset requiring reasoning over multiple relations in a knowledge base, available in 1-hop, 2-hop, and 3-hop variants.

nodes.name: MetaTool
nodes.definition: A dataset used to evaluate an LLM's ability to select the correct tool for a given task, assessing a key component of agent-oriented capabilities.

nodes.name: MFCAQ
nodes.definition: The Moral Foundations Character Action Questionnaire, a 16-item instrument designed to assess the moral dimensions of a fictional character's behavior based on Moral Foundations Theory, using a 5-point Likert scale.

nodes.name: MFQ
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, MFQ is described as the original Moral Foundations Questionnaire, a psychometric or psychological survey designed for humans. One definition says it measures how individuals evaluate abstract moral scenarios in relation to their own values, while another describes it as a survey that has been used to analyze which morals are most expressed in language model outputs.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use MFQ mainly in terms of moral evaluation and moral expression: one definition frames it as measuring evaluations of abstract moral scenarios relative to personal values, and another says it has been used to analyze which morals are most expressed in model outputs. The papers do not explicitly link it to any construct or behavioral indicator.

Space of uses. The usage described in the papers treats MFQ as a human psychological survey that is brought into LLM analysis. The papers do not report it being used alongside any other named measurement instrument.

nodes.name: MFRC
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, MFRC is described as the Moral Foundations Reddit Corpus, a dataset of 16,123 English Reddit posts from 12 subreddits, categorized into US politics, French politics, and everyday moral life. Another description presents it as a multi-label moral foundation corpus covering six moral foundations, with three annotators assigned to each sample, so the prevailing usage combines a Reddit post collection with a multi-label annotation setup.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use MFRC to measure one behavioral indicator, Moral foundation classification, and no constructs are linked to it. The measurement claim converges on that single use: papers describe MFRC as a corpus of six moral foundations and, in one definition, as an evaluation resource for subjective multi-label classification and distribution alignment.

Space of uses. Papers do not link MFRC to any other measurement instrument. The descriptions present it as a Reddit-based, multi-label corpus, and one description notes that each sample received three annotators.

nodes.name: MFTC
nodes.definition: The Moral Foundations Twitter Corpus, a dataset of 32,218 tweets annotated for moral dimensions across sociopolitical and cultural contexts including Black Lives Matter and the 2016 US presidential election.

nodes.name: MGSM
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, MGSM is most commonly described as a multilingual grade-school math benchmark or dataset of word problems, used to evaluate mathematical or arithmetic reasoning across languages. Several papers further describe it as extending or translating GSM8K into multiple languages, but the reported coverage differs: some definitions mention 10 languages, others 11 languages, and another refers to nine non-English languages; one relationship statement specifies 250 manually translated GSM8K test problems, and another paper describes 250 QA pairs. A smaller line of work treats it as the source for AfriMGSM, while other papers mention related resources such as MGSM-SYMBOLIC and MGSM8KInstruct, and one definition says evaluation is done with exact match.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use MGSM to measure five constructs and one behavioral indicator. The prevailing usage is to measure Mathematical reasoning, and papers also report using it for Multilingual reasoning, Reasoning, Generalization, and the behavioral indicator Mathematical problem solving, plus one other construct. Overall, the linked claims concentrate on reasoning-oriented constructs rat

nodes.name: MHellaSwag
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers describe MHellaSwag, also referred to as MHELLASWAG or Okapi-HellaSwag, as a multilingual commonsense reasoning benchmark. The prevailing description presents it as sentences or paragraphs where models must choose the most likely continuation or ending, and one paper says it "aims at collecting the multilingual understanding abilities" (P-MMEval: A Parallel Multilingual Multitask Benchmark for Consistent Evaluation of LLMs). Another definition uses slightly different wording, framing Okapi-HellaSwag as evaluating event prediction and situational understanding.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the papers, claims converge on one linked construct: multilingual ability. Papers report it as measuring multilingual ability in evaluations of models' capability across languages, and no behavioral indicators are linked to it.

Space of uses. Papers position it as one benchmark within broader multilingual evaluation efforts rather than alongside any named companion instrument. One paper groups it with multilingual benchmarks that rely on English translation for cross-language evaluation, and no other measurement instrument is linked to it.

nodes.name: MileBench
nodes.definition: A benchmark for evaluating multimodal large language models on tasks involving multiple images, categorized into temporal, semantic, needle-in-a-haystack, and image retrieval tasks.

nodes.name: MIMIC-CXR
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats MIMIC-CXR as a chest X-ray or chest radiograph dataset paired with free-text radiology reports, mainly for report generation and grounded report evaluation. Several definitions add that the studies are de-identified and publicly available, and some describe each study as accompanied by labels as well as a report. A smaller line of work refers to processed or subset versions, and one paper points to a VQA variant, MIMIC-CXR-VQA, for chest-radiograph question answering.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link MIMIC-CXR to 3 behavioral indicators, and to no constructs. The prevailing usage is to measure medical report generation, with additional use for radiology report generation, while a smaller line of work uses it to measure medical visual question answering. These links are all to behavioral indicators, especially report generation tasks, not to any construct.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it directly, but papers commonly use MIMIC-CXR alongside IU-Xray, and sometimes alongside CT-RATE, CheXpert Plus, Harvard-FairVLMed, or PMC-OA. Quoted passages describe it as used for both training an

nodes.name: MIMIC-III
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, MIMIC-III is most commonly described as a publicly available, de-identified in-patient or critical care EHR dataset from the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care project. Definitions consistently tie it to patients who stayed in critical care units, while some papers describe particular contents such as discharge summaries or radiology reports used for clinical NLP evaluation. A smaller strand also treats it as the source dataset for EHRCon and as a database of ICU patient records from Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link MIMIC-III to 2 behavioral indicators and 1 construct. The prevailing usage is to measure mortality prediction, with hospital readmission prediction also reported, and a smaller line of work using it to measure privacy preservation. Overall, the recorded measurement claims are concentrated more on predictive behavioral indicators than on a broad range of constructs.

Space of uses. Papers do not link it to other measurement instruments. In use, one paper places it alongside MIMIC-IV and EHRShot as a public EHR dataset, while other papers use it as the data source for downstrea

nodes.name: MIMIC-IV
nodes.definition:
What it is. In the definitions, MIMIC-IV is described as a large-scale multimodal clinical dataset. Papers pair that description with patient outcome prediction tasks, specifically length of stay and 48-hour in-hospital mortality, and one paper also says its records are converted into test samples for a full-path clinical diagnosis task.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the papers, MIMIC-IV is linked to 3 behavioral indicators and no constructs. Papers use it to measure hospital readmission prediction, medical diagnosis, and mortality prediction. Definitions also describe it as evaluating patient outcome prediction, including length of stay and in-hospital mortality.

Space of uses. Papers use it as an evaluation dataset, and no other measurement instrument is linked to it. Across the uses, models are transferred to MIMIC-IV for length of stay and 48-hour in-hospital mortality tasks, its records are leveraged to create test samples for full-path clinical diagnosis, and results are reported on mortality and readmission prediction.

nodes.name: MIMIR
nodes.definition: A challenging benchmark for pretraining data detection that contains "seen" and "unseen" text samples from the Pile dataset, specifically constructed to have high n-gram overlap between classes.

nodes.name: MIND
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the descriptions, MIND is most commonly framed as a hallucination detection method that automatically labels data during detection to train a classifier. A smaller framing describes it as an unsupervised method: it truncates Wikipedia articles, prompts an LLM to continue the next sentence, and generates truth labels by matching named entities between the continuation and the original source text.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers describe MIND as serving hallucination detection, but no constructs and no behavioral indicators are linked to it.

Space of uses. The usage described in the papers centers on self-generated labeling rather than reliance on pre-annotated datasets. One account explicitly contrasts it with SAPLMA on that basis, and another describes a workflow built from truncated Wikipedia articles, next-sentence continuation, and named-entity matching to produce truth labels. No measurement instrument is linked to it.

nodes.name: Mind2Web
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage is as a real-world web navigation benchmark or dataset built from human demonstrations on real websites. Most definitions describe open-domain, action-annotated tasks, often noting about 2K instructions across 137 websites, and emphasize generalization across tasks, websites, and domains through cross-task, cross-website, and cross-domain settings. Papers differ in emphasis: some call it an offline task planning evaluation, some a demonstration dataset for action prediction, and one paper recasts its tasks as dynamic how-to questions with multiple possible outcomes per step. Evaluation is commonly described with step success rate and element accuracy, while some papers also mention action F1, task-level success rate, or step accuracy.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to measure 3 behavioral indicators and 2 constructs. The prevailing measurement claim is web navigation: several papers describe Mind2Web as evaluating agents' capabilities on web navigation tasks or their capability of performing complex instructions on real-world websites. A smaller line of work uses it for action prediction, especially generaliz

nodes.name: Minecraft
nodes.definition: A 3D open-world video game environment used as a platform for evaluating generally capable agents on tasks involving resource gathering, crafting, and exploration.

nodes.name: MineDojo
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage is as a Minecraft-based simulation suite for embodied-agent research, often also described as a benchmark or research framework. Papers consistently describe it as containing thousands of open-ended, natural language-specified or language-prompted tasks, with task content commonly framed around navigation, harvesting, combat, and crafting. A smaller difference in wording is whether authors call it a benchmark or a framework, and some work uses selected long-horizon tasks from it rather than the full suite.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to one construct and one behavioral indicator. The construct claim is Generalization: one paper reports that validating a single model on diverse challenging tasks in MineDojo indicates promising generalization. The behavioral indicator claim is Navigation, and the benchmark is also described as supporting behaviors such as navigation, harvest, combat, and craft, though only Navigation is explicitly linked as a measured behavior.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it. In practice, papers use it to validate embodied-agent methods: one study evaluates in both

nodes.name: Minerva Math
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across definitions, papers attach the Minerva Math label and closely neighboring names, including Minerva, MinervaMATH, OCW, OCWCourses, and OCW-Math, to two recurring benchmark descriptions. One common framing presents a mathematical reasoning benchmark for scientific and mathematical questions, including undergraduate- or Olympiad-level problems that require advanced quantitative reasoning. Another common framing describes an OpenCourseWare-based benchmark with 272 undergraduate STEM problems with automatically verifiable solutions, spanning areas such as chemistry, information theory, differential equations, and special relativity, and often characterized as requiring multi-step reasoning or serving as an out-of-domain benchmark.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to 2 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator. The prevailing use is to measure Mathematical reasoning, with many papers listing it among mathematical-reasoning benchmarks or mathematical reasoning datasets; a smaller line of work uses it to measure the broader construct Reasoning, and another reports it as evaluating Mathematical problem solving. Overall, the reported measurement claims are concen

nodes.name: miniF2F
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, miniF2F is most commonly described as a benchmark or dataset for formal theorem proving, often for neural theorem proving, used to evaluate whether models can generate proofs verifiable by a theorem prover. Definitions usually portray it as formal mathematical problems or statements drawn from competition mathematics, often high-school or Olympiad-level; several descriptions give 488 items split into 244 validation and 244 test problems, and some say it spans multiple formal systems or four formal languages. Papers also mention a miniF2F-test variant for Lean-based evaluation, while a smaller line of work describes it as standalone competition problems that do not require external context, and one description extends it to Olympiad and undergraduate-style coursework.

What it is claimed to measure. Across surveyed uses, papers use miniF2F to measure 4 constructs and 3 behavioral indicators. The most frequently linked behavioral indicators are Formal theorem proving, Theorem proving, and Autoformalization, and the most frequently linked constructs are Mathematical reasoning, Generalization, Autoformalization ability, and Formal reasoning. The measurement c

nodes.name: Minimal-pair ABX task
nodes.definition: A training-free, zero-shot evaluation framework where a model must determine if a test item X is representationally closer to item A or item B, used to measure the structure of embedding spaces.

nodes.name: MiniWoB++
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats MiniWoB++ as a standard benchmark suite or interactive benchmark for computer control and web navigation in a simulated, simplified web environment. Definitions usually emphasize diverse instruction-following tasks, from low-level actions to complex multi-step decision making, where agents interact with web elements or pages through keyboard and mouse actions; some descriptions also note built-in reward functions or outcome-based checks. A smaller line of work under the name MiniWob describes it instead as a multimodal or open-ended web navigation benchmark in real web environments.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use MiniWoB++ most often to measure web navigation, and some also use it to measure task completion. A smaller strand reports it as measuring adaptability. These claims do not spread across many targets: the benchmark is linked to 2 behavioral indicators, web navigation and task completion, and to 1 construct, adaptability.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to MiniWoB++. In use, papers commonly position it as a standard or representative benchmark for evaluating computer-control or autonom

nodes.name: MinosEval
nodes.definition: Framework for evaluating medical question answering, including Top-1 Hit Rate (GPT-4o ranking) and Average NLI Score using a ClinicalBERT model on MedNLI.

nodes.name: MINT
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly describe MINT as a multi-turn interactive agent evaluation framework or benchmark that adapts existing datasets into interactive, feedback-rich environments. The prevailing description centers on evaluating task-solving through multi-turn interaction, especially by using tools and leveraging natural language feedback; definitions also mention agent capabilities such as tool use and self-debugging, and a curated subset of reasoning, code generation, and decision-making tasks with GPT-4-simulated feedback. Some uses refer to a part of the MINT dataset focused on tool-utilization for reasoning, another use only considers coding and math problems, and related work also refers to it as Mint-Bench.

What it is claimed to measure. Claims about what MINT measures are concentrated rather than spread across many targets. It is linked to 1 construct, Responsiveness to human feedback, and 1 behavioral indicator, Multi-turn interaction: papers use it to measure responsiveness to human feedback through "leveraging natural language feedback," and to measure multi-turn interaction. More generally, papers describe it as evaluating performance or task-solving ability

nodes.name: MIntRec2.0
nodes.definition: Large-scale multimodal intent recognition dataset with 30 fine-grained intent labels across text, video, and audio modalities, used to evaluate performance in complex semantic understanding scenarios.

nodes.name: MIRACL
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the cited definitions, papers describe MIRACL as the Multilingual Information Retrieval Across a Continuum of Languages dataset for multilingual retrieval evaluation across 18 languages. The prevailing description emphasizes native questions and relevance judgements of retrieved passages, while another formulation states more generally that it is used to evaluate retrieval systems across 18 diverse languages.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link MIRACL to one construct and one behavioral indicator. These claims are concentrated rather than spread across many targets: papers use it to measure multilingual ability, with one study saying it helps assess multilingual retrieval capability, and one paper reports it as measuring information retrieval by describing it as a multilingual and cross-lingual IR resource.

Space of uses. In use, papers present MIRACL as a retrieval evaluation dataset and, in one case, as the basis for a broader benchmark. One study pairs it with BEIR for main evaluations of dense retrievers and multilingual retrieval capability, while another builds a benchmark on top of MIRACL using native-language questions and generating responses wi

nodes.name: MixEval
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, MixEval is most commonly described as a hybrid benchmark for language models that combines 18 ground-truth-based tasks. Some definitions broaden this to a benchmark across a diverse mix of tasks and domains, and one paper frames it as an efficient, gold-standard evaluation paradigm built by strategically mixing off-the-shelf benchmarks after matching real-world user queries mined from the web to similar queries from existing ground-truth benchmarks; another reports a 0.96 correlation to human preferences.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use MixEval to measure four constructs and one behavioral indicator. The linked constructs are alignment, conversational ability, general ability, and reasoning, and the linked behavioral indicator is classification, so the recorded measurement claims are spread across several targets rather than centered on one; the papers describe it as evaluating alignment effectiveness, general capabilities, and generalist chat capabilities.

Space of uses. In practice, papers often use MixEval alongside other evaluations rather than alone. It appears with Open LLM Leaderboard v2 for benchmark evaluation, with MT-Bench and A

nodes.name: MixEval-Hard
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across definitions, MixEval-Hard is most commonly treated as the hard subset of MixEval. Papers describe it as a challenging or more challenging subset for difficult tasks or queries, and one definition says it was derived to better differentiate strong language models; a smaller formulation presents it more generally as a benchmark for challenging general-domain tasks.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link MixEval-Hard to 1 construct and no behavioral indicators. The only linked construct is Reasoning: one paper uses MixEval-Hard among datasets spanning instruction-following, reasoning, mathematics, and coding, so in the recorded relationships it is reported as measuring reasoning rather than a wider spread of constructs.

Space of uses. The uses place it within broader evaluation suites. Papers use it alongside several other benchmarks, for example MT-Bench, AlpacaEval 2.0, Arena Hard Auto, and MixEval, and another paper treats it as one of several general-domain tasks. One paper also reports that this harder subset shows a higher correlation of 0.96 with Chatbot Arena Elo.

nodes.name: MKQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, MKQA is most commonly described as a multilingual or cross-lingual question answering benchmark. Definitions differ in emphasis: one describes it as a multilingual open-domain benchmark derived from Natural Questions, another as an open-ended question-answering benchmark used to assess multilingual retrieval-augmented answering, and another as a cross-lingual QA dataset used as a knowledge retrieval benchmark in interpretability analysis. One study further specifies that it consists of 10k knowledge question-answer pairs aligned across 26 languages.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link MKQA to 3 behavioral indicators and no constructs. The prevailing usage is to measure multilingual question answering, including multilingual open-ended QA and multilingual ODQA evaluation. Smaller lines of work use it to measure knowledge retrieval, where it is selected as a representative dataset for interpretability analysis, and information retrieval, where a paper uses it to evaluate cross-lingual retrieval performance.

Space of uses. In use, papers usually place MKQA alongside other QA benchmarks rather than presenting it alone. One setup uses it with MLQA

nodes.name: MLaKE
nodes.definition: MLaKE is a multilingual dataset created using LLMs for translation.

nodes.name: MLDR
nodes.definition: Long-context information retrieval benchmark consisting of over 200,000 long documents, used to evaluate single- and multi-vector retrieval performance in out-of-domain and in-domain settings.

nodes.name: MLogiQA
nodes.definition: Multilingual logical reasoning benchmark derived from LOGIQA, assessing the ability to make logical inferences from complex texts.

nodes.name: MLQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly describe MLQA as a multilingual question answering dataset or benchmark with extractive question-answer instances in SQuAD format across seven languages. One recurring description says it contains over 5K instances in English, Arabic, German, Spanish, Hindi, Vietnamese, and Simplified Chinese, and another emphasizes its aligned structure, with each question-answer pair present in multiple languages. Smaller descriptions frame it more functionally, as a benchmark for cross-lingual reading comprehension, answer extraction, or comprehension skills across seven languages, and one study uses it as the source for the MLNeedle test.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, MLQA is linked to one construct and two behavioral indicators. The prevailing usage is to measure multilingual question answering: several papers describe it as facilitating cross-lingual evaluation of QA systems or as representing multilingual open-ended question-answering tasks, and one definition says it evaluates extractive question answering capabilities in multiple languages. Smaller usage treats it as measuring question answering more generally, or natural language understan

nodes.name: MLVU
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats MLVU as a long-video or long-form video understanding benchmark for multimodal models. Definitions often add that it is multi-task or oriented to question answering, with videos described as ranging from 3 minutes to 2 hours; some papers specify a test set of over 500 QA pairs and multiple-choice accuracy, and one paper instead highlights an average video duration of 15.5 minutes. Other descriptions emphasize long-context comprehension, extended temporal reasoning, or complex scene dynamics, but the common framing remains a benchmark for understanding long videos.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link MLVU to 3 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators. The dominant claim is that papers use it to measure long video understanding; other papers report it as measuring video understanding and, in a smaller line of work, temporal reasoning across diverse domains. Among behavioral indicators, it is used for video question answering, and one paper points to MLVU subtasks for counting.

Space of uses. Papers often use MLVU alongside other video benchmarks, especially VideoMME, LongVideoBench, and EgoSchema, and also with MVBench and

nodes.name: MM-ID
nodes.definition: A benchmark designed to evaluate a model's ability to remember and recognize instance identities across four tasks: matching, location, question-answering, and captioning.

nodes.name: MM-NIAH
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly describe MM-NIAH as a benchmark for long multimodal or mixed-modality contexts built around a needle-in-a-haystack setup. One line of work presents it as a mixed video-text retrieval benchmark, where 25% of the input is text segments inserted across frames and the model must locate relevant content, with tests reaching up to 4.5k frames, about 1.1M tokens. Another description is broader, framing it as a benchmark for long multimodal documents with interleaved text and images and tasks in retrieval, counting, and reasoning.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link MM-NIAH to one behavioral indicator and two constructs. The prevailing uses are to measure Synthetic recall and Long-context multimodal understanding, with papers describing it as detecting image and text needles within hybrid long contexts and as evaluating the capability to comprehend long multimodal documents. A narrower link treats it as measuring Multimodal reasoning, in line with the benchmark's reasoning task alongside retrieval and counting.

Space of uses. In use, papers position MM-NIAH as an evaluation for mixed-modality or long-context multimodal scenarios, including settings

nodes.name: MM-SafetyBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, MM-SafetyBench is most commonly described as a multimodal safety benchmark for testing whether vision-language models produce unsafe responses to harmful inputs. A smaller set of descriptions makes the content more specific: one defines it as 5,040 text-image pairs across 13 scenarios for assessing safety and robustness against multimodal jailbreak attacks, while another treats it as a dataset of typographical images, stable diffusion-generated images, Typo + SD images, and text-based attack samples. Papers also mention alternate forms or subsets, including an official tiny version with 168 samples, a sampled set of 100 harmful and safe images, and the abbreviation MMSafe.

What it is claimed to measure. Its recorded uses are concentrated on safety-related outcomes. Papers link it to 2 constructs, Safety and Safety robustness, and to 2 behavioral indicators, Harmful content generation and Jailbreak resistance; in the relationship evidence, it is used to assess multimodal safety, judge resiliency under harm-inducing instructions, evaluate jailbreak robustness and defense capabilities against jailbreak attacks, and test whether image-query-related inputs el

nodes.name: MM-Vet
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, MM-Vet is most commonly described as a comprehensive multimodal benchmark for integrated capabilities, visual reasoning, and understanding across diverse scenarios. Several definitions make it more specific: it is presented as an open-ended or free-form question answering benchmark, sometimes as an in-the-wild or zero-shot evaluation, and some papers note that scoring is done by GPT-4 through comparative judging of predicted and ground-truth answers. A recurring characterization says it contains 217 challenging open-ended tasks that require multiple capabilities at once, and another says it defines six core vision-language abilities and 16 combinations, including recognition, OCR, knowledge, spatial awareness, language generation, and math; a smaller line of work describes it as evaluating visual conversations.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use MM-Vet to measure 9 constructs and 4 behavioral indicators, so its reported target is spread across several abilities rather than centered on a single one. The prevailing construct links are visual understanding, multimodal understanding, reasoning, spatial understanding, and fine-grained visual unders

nodes.name: MMAU
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, MMAU is most commonly described as a benchmark for expert-level audio reasoning and audio understanding, with sound and music subsets. Definitions also frame it as a Massive Multi-Task Audio Understanding and Reasoning Benchmark for large audio-language models, and one description says it includes information extraction and reasoning questions. The reported results for "MMAU Sound" and "MMAU Music" further show that papers treat those subsets as distinct reported parts of the benchmark.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use MMAU to measure 5 constructs and 3 behavioral indicators, so its reported measurement role is spread across several targets rather than centered on a single one. The most frequently named construct links are audio understanding, audio perception, audio reasoning, domain knowledge, and reasoning, while the linked behavioral indicators are information extraction, knowledge retrieval, and tool use. In the relationship evidence, papers describe it as evaluating understanding and reasoning in complex audio QA tasks, advanced perception and reasoning with domain-specific knowledge, expert-level multimodal reasoning and knowledge-ret

nodes.name: MMBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing framing is a comprehensive multimodal benchmark for large vision-language or multimodal models, used across diverse tasks that require perception and reasoning, and sometimes knowledge-based or commonsense questions. Many descriptions present it as a multiple-choice or VQA-style evaluation: one paper describes approximately 3000 multiple-choice questions covering 20 capability dimensions, while others describe thousands of VQA-format questions spanning both perception and reasoning, and several authors explicitly cast it as testing whether a model is an "all-around player." Some authors distinguish English and Chinese variants, including MMBench-Chinese, Dev-EN, and version 1.1, while a smaller line of work refers more broadly to an MMBench-series with additional variants. A minority description emphasizes its answer-robustness setup, stating that MMBench and its CN version use all-round shuffling on multiple-choice answers.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use MMBench to measure 13 constructs and 5 behavioral indicators, so its measurement claims are spread across many targets. The most frequent construct framings are multimodal unde

nodes.name: MMBench-CN
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most commonly, papers treat MMBench-CN, also written as MMBench-Chinese, MMBCN, or MMB-CN, as the Chinese version of the MMBench benchmark for evaluating multimodal models. Some descriptions narrow this to answer robustness under shuffled multiple-choice answers, while others frame it more broadly as evaluating multimodal tasks, multimodal understanding and generation in a Chinese-language context, or vision-language capabilities in a non-English setting. A smaller usage presents it as a standard evaluation for single-image QA performance, and one paper refers specifically to the MMBCN dev split.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link MMBench-CN to 2 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator. The construct claims are split across Multimodal understanding and Robustness: one paper says MMBench and its CN version evaluate a model's answer robustness with all-round shuffling on multiple-choice answers, while another uses MMBCN for comprehensive evaluation of multimodal understanding. The behavioral-indicator claim is narrower, with one paper placing MMB-CN among conventional visual question answering and single-image QA tasks.

Space of uses. Papers typically use MMBench-

nodes.name: MMBench-Video
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most descriptions treat MMBench-Video as a video-focused version of MMBench for evaluating multimodal understanding. A more detailed framing presents it as a quantitative benchmark built from long-form, multi-shot web videos and human-annotated, free-form questions, intended to evaluate LVLMs' video understanding capabilities across a hierarchical taxonomy. Papers also describe the videos as long-form and diverse, covering a broad spectrum of topics.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use MMBench-Video to measure 6 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators, so its reported measurement role is spread across several targets rather than concentrated on one. The most frequently named construct links are Commonsense reasoning, Long video understanding, Spatial understanding, Temporal reasoning, and Temporal understanding; papers also connect it to 1 other construct and 2 behavioral indicators. In the relationship evidence, it is described as probing models through human-annotated ability taxonomies and free-form questions.

Space of uses. Across the papers, MMBench-Video is positioned as a benchmark for evaluating LVLMs on longer, multi-shot video tasks, and as a VideoQA be

nodes.name: MMC
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly describe MMC as a benchmark for evaluating chart understanding, with charts drawn from diverse sources. Another definition frames it as a recent benchmark for multimodal chart understanding and notes that some questions require external domain-specific knowledge.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link MMC to one behavioral indicator and to no constructs. The recorded measurement claim centers on Chart and diagram understanding, with one paper explicitly labeling MMC as chart understanding.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is formally linked to MMC. In practice, papers use or discuss it alongside other multimodal and chart benchmarks: one paper includes it in a broader benchmark suite and contrasts it with MMMU and MathVista by noting that those include mathematical figures, whereas MMC contains charts from diverse sources, and another discusses it alongside ChartBench and ChartX3 as a recent chart-understanding benchmark.

Concerns raised. Concerns appear in one paper, which says that some MMC questions require external domain-specific knowledge. The same paper also groups MMC with benchmarks that have issues with the source or diversi

nodes.name: MMCU-Medical
nodes.definition: Multi-task medical dataset used to evaluate LLM performance on medical question answering and diagnostic reasoning.

nodes.name: MME
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, MME is most commonly described as a comprehensive multimodal or vision-language benchmark for large multimodal language models, covering perception and cognition across 14 sub-tasks or visual question answering tasks. Definitions often specify content such as OCR, color, counting, scene understanding, recognition, commonsense reasoning, and attribute or relation judgments; one paper further describes the 14 tasks as ten perception-related subtasks and four cognition-focused ones, and another calls the benchmark human-annotated. Papers also refer to named components and subsets, including MME-Perception and MME-Cognition, an aggregate score over those two parts, a perception component built from yes/no questions, and a hallucination subset over existence, count, position, and color. A smaller line of work instead frames it as true/false questions or as a benchmark for following single-image instructions.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use MME to measure 13 constructs and 5 behavioral indicators. The dominant claims frame it as measuring multimodal understanding, visual perception, visual understanding, cognition, and general ability, which matches

nodes.name: MME-P
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers describe MME-P as a multimodal benchmark for visual understanding, with one definition specifying OCR and fine-grained visual reasoning as prominent task types. A second description treats MME Perception as a sub-benchmark of the MME suite for evaluating visual perception capabilities, and one paper explicitly inspects OCR-related tasks within MME-P.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the reported relationships, papers use it to measure Visual understanding, and this is the only construct linked to it. No behavioral indicators are linked to it, so the reported measurement claims concentrate on a single construct rather than spreading across multiple outcomes.

Space of uses. No other measurement instruments are linked to it. In use, one paper includes MME Perception among several mainstream benchmarks in a broader evaluation suite, while another reports an overall MME-P score under visual understanding benchmarking and then examines OCR-related tasks within the benchmark.

nodes.name: MME-RealWorld
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, MME-RealWorld is most commonly described as a multimodal benchmark for real-world scenarios and real-world multimodal tasks, used to assess vision-language performance. The prevailing descriptions present it as manually curated or manually annotated, with one line of description specifying five primary categories and 43 sub-class tasks, including monitoring, autonomous driving, OCR, property, and text/address tasks, and another noting an average resolution of 2000×1500. A smaller line of work also refers to an MME-RealWorld-Lite Reasoning subset and a remaining Reasoning subset.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use MME-RealWorld to measure 2 constructs and 4 behavioral indicators. The construct links are to Reasoning and Generalization, while the behavioral indicators linked to it are Agent intention prediction, Diagram understanding, Multiple-choice question answering, and Object counting, so the recorded uses span both broad constructs and task-level behaviors. The supporting descriptions also frame the benchmark as covering 43 perception and reasoning subtasks, and the multiple-choice question answering setup is described as using four manual

nodes.name: MMHal-Bench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, MMHal-Bench is most commonly described as a benchmark for multimodal or vision-language hallucination. Most definitions portray it as 96 image-question pairs, or questions, spanning eight question types, including object attributes, adversarial objects, comparisons, counting, and spatial relations; one paper additionally describes 12 object topics, and some authors frame it as a question-answering or generative benchmark. Many papers also describe GPT-4-based evaluation, variously for hallucination severity, response quality, hallucination rate, or agreement with human responses, object labels, or ground-truth answers, and a few papers add response informativeness or information richness.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, it is linked to six behavioral indicators and one construct. The prevailing usage is to measure hallucination: papers say it quantifies hallucinations, evaluates the degree of hallucination, or assesses response-level hallucination rates. Smaller lines of work also use it to measure attribute recognition, hallucination detection, object hallucination, and, in one paper, faithfulness by identifying hallucinations in outputs,

nodes.name: MMLongBench-Doc
nodes.definition:
