What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage is as a benchmark dataset for multi-modal long-context document understanding or document question answering on long, information-rich PDFs. Papers refer to it both as MMLongBench-Doc and MMLongBench, with descriptions emphasizing extensive documents, diverse multi-modal elements, complex layouts, and questions whose answers may require integrating text, images, and charts across many pages; one definition also notes expert-annotated questions and several document categories.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to three constructs and one behavioral indicator, so its reported measurement role is spread across several targets rather than centered on one. It is reported as measuring localization ability, multimodal document understanding, and retrieval effectiveness, and papers also use it to measure hallucination; one description says its question types evaluate long-context document understanding from complementary aspects, including localization ability and hallucination severity, while another uses it to compare retrieval accuracy.

Space of uses. Most papers position it as one benchmark within a broader evaluation suite

nodes.name: MMLU
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing description is a broad multiple-choice benchmark, usually expanded as Massive Multitask Language Understanding, though some definitions say Measuring or Massively Multitask Language Understanding, and covering 57 subjects across areas such as STEM, humanities, social sciences, law, health, and related domains. Authors variously call it a benchmark, dataset, test set, quiz bank, or evaluation framework, and they report slightly different scales, including 14 042, 14 079, 14 421, or about 16,000 questions; one paper instead describes 22 high-school subjects. A smaller line of work uses subject subsets or variants, including legal, medical, scientific, math, history, policy, and multilingual subsets or variants, as well as updated forms such as MMLU-Pro.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link MMLU to 37 constructs and 20 behavioral indicators, so the claims are spread across many targets rather than centered on one. The most common construct-level claims are that papers use it to measure general ability, natural language understanding, reasoning, world knowledge, and generalization, while the remaining claims cover 32 other constructs and

nodes.name: MMLU-Math
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, the dominant description treats MMLU-Math as the mathematics subset of the Massive Multitask Language Understanding benchmark, used in a multiple-choice format to evaluate knowledge and problem-solving skills. Definitions vary in how they specify its coverage: some describe it broadly as covering topics from elementary to advanced math or various math subjects, while another specifies Algebra, Probability, Number Theory, and Calculus and says its evaluation setup follows MAmmoTH.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link MMLU-Math to one behavioral indicator, Mathematical problem solving, and one construct, Mathematical reasoning. The prevailing usage is as a measure of Mathematical problem solving, with papers reporting evaluation on MMLU-Math when assessing models on math benchmarks across different domains; a smaller line of work reports it as measuring Mathematical reasoning by including it among representative math datasets. The reported measurement claims are concentrated on these two targets rather than spread across many constructs or indicators.

Space of uses. No paper links it to another measurement instrument. Across the papers,

nodes.name: MMLU-Med
nodes.definition: A medical examination question-answering dataset used to evaluate retrieval performance in the medical domain, part of the broader MMLU benchmark.

nodes.name: MMLU-Medical
nodes.definition: A subset of the MMLU benchmark containing exam questions from nine subjects relevant to medicine, used to assess broad medical knowledge.

nodes.name: MMLU-Pro
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most commonly, papers describe MMLU-Pro as an enhanced, more robust and more challenging version of MMLU, a multi-task, multiple-choice benchmark for proficient-level language understanding. Definitions emphasize more complex reasoning questions, more distractor answer choices, and, in one description, a different evaluation protocol; papers also describe it as covering a wide range of academic and professional subjects, or 14 domains/categories, and one paper specifies a multiple-choice format with 10 options. A smaller line of work describes it more functionally, as a benchmark used to assess general knowledge, validate that adding a vision modality does not reduce text-task performance, or serve in out-of-distribution evaluation.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use MMLU-Pro to measure 13 constructs and 3 behavioral indicators, rather than tying it to a single reported target. The prevailing links are to natural language understanding, reasoning, and world knowledge, and papers also use it for multiple-choice question answering and classification. Other reported uses extend to additional reasoning, knowledge, generalization, and question-answering targets.

Spa

nodes.name: MMLU-Pro Math
nodes.definition: A subset of the MMLU benchmark focused on professional-level mathematics problems.

nodes.name: MMLU-ProX
nodes.definition:
What it is. Available definitions describe MMLU-ProX as a multilingual benchmark of parallel multiple-choice questions for advanced LLM evaluation. It is presented as covering 29 languages, with 11,829 questions in its full version, and as maintaining the high difficulty level and reasoning focus of MMLU-Pro while assessing advanced reasoning in diverse linguistic and cultural contexts.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use MMLU-ProX to measure two constructs, multilingual ability and multilingual reasoning, and no behavioral indicators are linked to it. The claims cluster around cross-lingual capability and reasoning: one paper says it "enables comprehensive evaluation of LLMs’ cross-lingual reasoning abilities" (MMLU-ProX: A Multilingual Benchmark for Advanced Large Language Model Evaluation), while another places it among benchmarks used "to evaluate the LLMs’ capability across languages."

Space of uses. In the recorded relationships, no other measurement instrument is linked to MMLU-ProX. Papers position it as a benchmark for evaluating LLMs across languages: one introduces it as "a comprehensive benchmark covering 29 languages," while another cites it alongside other mul

nodes.name: MMLU-Redux
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most papers describe MMLU-Redux as a zero-shot or revised variant of MMLU used as an evaluation benchmark for general knowledge, language understanding, and reasoning. Several descriptions present it as multiple-choice or closed-form question answering across a wide range of subjects, with one definition placing those subjects from elementary to professional level. Papers differ on its scope: some describe a manually re-annotated subset of 3,000 questions across 30 subjects, while others describe 5,700 manually re-annotated questions across all 57 subjects, with corrections to ground truth answers and question clarity.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use MMLU-Redux to measure 3 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator. The prevailing link is to Reasoning: papers call it a logical reasoning or reasoning benchmark and use it to verify reasoning abilities or performance after editing. Smaller lines of work use it to measure Mathematical reasoning and Robustness, and one paper reports that it can also measure Error detection. The reported uses therefore span several targets rather than centering on only one, though Reasoning is the most common framing.

Space of uses. P

nodes.name: MMLU-STEM
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing description is a STEM-focused subset of the MMLU benchmark, covering science, technology, engineering, and mathematics subjects. Most definitions present it as evaluating broad STEM knowledge and reasoning, while some narrow this to mathematical and scientific reasoning or to knowledge and problem-solving skills. Format details are only occasionally made explicit: papers describe it as a multiple-choice dataset or as multiple-choice questions for human exams across math and other STEM disciplines; Llemma: An Open Language Model for Mathematics specifies a subset of 18 out of 57 MMLU subjects, and another paper reports a STEM subset with 3.13K problems.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to 3 constructs and no behavioral indicators. The prevailing usage is to measure Mathematical reasoning and Reasoning, while a smaller line of work reports it as measuring Domain knowledge. Correspondingly, relationship evidence places it in evaluation suites for reasoning abilities across domains and for mathematical reasoning, and one paper treats performance on it as evidence about specialized knowledge.

Space of uses. Although no measurement

nodes.name: MMMLU
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, MMMLU is most commonly described as a multilingual version of MMLU, often specifically a human-translated or professionally translated variant used across multiple languages and subjects. Definitions vary in emphasis, framing it as testing general language understanding, reasoning performance, knowledge comprehension, or world knowledge. One description also notes that answers are extracted from generated outputs rather than token probabilities, and another use draws on its test sets to create "easy" and "hard" evaluation sets.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use MMMLU to measure four constructs and two behavioral indicators. The named targets include cross-lingual alignment, knowledge understanding, multilingual ability, multilingual reasoning, and language mixing, with one additional behavioral indicator also linked to it. Overall, papers distribute its measurement claims across several named targets rather than centering on only one.

Space of uses. Several papers place MMMLU inside broader multilingual evaluation suites. It appears with Belebele and m-ARC in cross-lingual alignment evaluations, with Belebele again for multiple-choice question a

nodes.name: MMMU
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, MMMU is most commonly described as a large multi-discipline multimodal understanding and reasoning benchmark for college- or university-level problems that require expert knowledge and complex reasoning. Definitions vary on scope and size: some describe six core disciplines, others 30 college-level subjects or domains, several specify 11.5K questions, one describes about 12.5K questions, and one notes 30 types of images. Papers also describe different formats and subsets, including VQA or image+text-to-text settings, multiple-choice and free-form questions, both single- and multi-image questions, and dev or validation subsets used for evaluation.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link MMMU to 14 constructs and 6 behavioral indicators, so its reported use is spread across many abilities rather than centered on only one, though the prevailing framing is multimodal understanding. It is most often used to measure multimodal understanding, reasoning, visual understanding, visual reasoning, and multi-image reasoning, with 9 other constructs also linked. At the behavioral level, papers most often use it for visual question answering, with additional use for

nodes.name: MMMU-Med
nodes.definition: The medical subset of the Massive Multi-discipline Multimodal Understanding (MMMU) benchmark, used for evaluating advanced comprehension.

nodes.name: MMMU-Pro
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across definitions, papers treat MMMU-Pro as a challenging multimodal benchmark for advanced, professional-level vision language model capability. The prevailing description emphasizes complex knowledge and reasoning tasks across disciplines, with a vision component that requires deep understanding of images. Some authors further frame it as an advanced version of MMMU, with more challenging questions and stricter evaluation settings, including a 10-option multiple-choice format, and one reported setting is MMMU-Pro-std with 10 options.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to 4 constructs and no behavioral indicators. It is used to measure calibration, general ability, multimodal reasoning, and multimodal understanding: one paper adopts it to measure calibration on complex, multidisciplinary image understanding and reasoning problems, another says it is designed to assess true multimodal understanding and reasoning across a wide range of academic disciplines, and another uses it among comprehensive benchmarks and VQA datasets to evaluate the general capabilities of VLMs. Across these claims, papers position it against several broad capabilities rather than a s

nodes.name: MMStar
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, MMStar is most commonly described as a benchmark for evaluating large vision-language models, often framed as a single-image or image question-answering benchmark for visual-language understanding. A recurring description presents it as an elite, vision-indispensable multimodal benchmark with 1,500 human-selected or curated samples, six core capabilities, and 18 detailed axes, with papers also noting minimal data leakage and that visual content is necessary for correct answers. Some authors instead emphasize different task scopes, describing it as assessing general understanding and reasoning across visual and textual tasks, while a smaller line of work describes it as an extensive static-content image VQA benchmark, a multimodal mathematical reasoning benchmark, or a benchmark built around high-quality multiple-choice questions.

What it is claimed to measure. Across relationships, papers use MMStar to measure 10 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator, so the reported targets are spread across many concepts rather than centered on one. The most frequent links treat it as measuring Logical reasoning and Reasoning; papers also use it for Fine-grained percep

nodes.name: MMT-Bench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers describe MMT-Bench as a multimodal benchmark drawn from existing datasets. The most detailed definition says it covers 162 concrete sub-tasks, is primarily focused on perception, and uses a multiple-choice question format; a quoted passage also says it supports in-depth analysis through its "taskonomy" and diverse input forms. Another paper frames it more broadly as a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating large vision-language models on multitask performance.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the papers, MMT-Bench is not explicitly linked to any constructs or behavioral indicators. Instead, papers describe it as evaluating large vision-language models on multitask performance, and one quoted passage places it among visual question answering benchmarks rather than tying it to a named construct.

Space of uses. Papers use MMT-Bench as part of broader benchmark reporting, describing it as one of the widely adopted VLM benchmarks and including it in comparative tables of results on leading methods. No papers report links between MMT-Bench and other measurement instruments.

nodes.name: MMToM-QA
nodes.definition: A real-world multimodal dataset combining video and text to assess machine learning models’ ability to infer mental states, used here to validate the generalizability of probing methods.

nodes.name: MMVP
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, MMVP is most commonly described as a fine-grained visual benchmark built from visually similar, CLIP-blind image pairs. Definitions say it evaluates visual details or fine-grained visual recognition, with one paper stating that it "collects CLIP-blind pairs" and contains "150 image pairs, each accompanied by a binary-option question," another describing paired classification over 9 visual patterns, and another referring to MMVP(-VLM) for testing object existence, orientation, and counting. A smaller line of work instead places it under single-image VQA, treats it as a multi-image benchmark for image-caption alignment, or describes it as exposing the visual shortcomings of CLIP-based multimodal models.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use MMVP to measure 8 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators, which places it across several nearby targets rather than only one. The most recurrent links frame it as measuring visual understanding, compositional reasoning, and fine-grained perception, while behavioral-indicator uses include fine-grained visual recognition and visual question answering, with 5 other construct-level targets also linked. Overall, papers d

nodes.name: MNIST
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the dominant framing is of MNIST as a benchmark or classification dataset for handwritten digits. Most descriptions treat it as a handwritten digit recognition or image classification benchmark, while some position it more narrowly as a dataset for controlled finetuning experiments, shallow-network training and evaluation, or robust hyperparameter optimization. A smaller usage treats it as a test of digit recognition and number comprehension from images, with one study noting that models "struggle on simple digit recognition and counting tasks, e.g. MNIST."

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link MNIST to 3 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator. The reported measurement claims are spread across image classification, optical character recognition ability, model collapse, and visual perception, rather than concentrated on one target. In these accounts, papers use it to measure image classification, to assess "the models’ ability to identify digits and count objects within images" for optical character recognition ability, to measure model collapse in experiments with shallow networks fully trained on MNIST, and to test visual perception.

Space of uses.

nodes.name: MNLI
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, MNLI is most commonly described as a natural language inference benchmark, dataset, or corpus for sentence-pair entailment classification. Definitions repeatedly describe large-scale, crowdsourced premise-hypothesis pairs labeled as entailment, contradiction, or neutral, often across multiple genres; some papers frame it more narrowly as a multi-class classification problem or as an alternative to SNLI with more genres and more challenging examples, and some use the name MultiNLI. A smaller line of work emphasizes particular versions or reporting splits, including match and mismatch, hard-match and hard-mismatch, and m/mm results.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link MNLI to three constructs and two behavioral indicators. The prevailing claim is that it measures natural language inference, with papers using it to benchmark understanding of entailment, contradiction, and neutrality; more occasional framings use it to measure natural language understanding, in-context learning performance, reasoning or inference ability, and text classification. Overall, the measurement claims center on NLI and otherwise spread across a few neighboring labels.

Space

nodes.name: ModelNet40
nodes.definition: A benchmark dataset consisting of 3D CAD models from 40 categories, used for tasks like 3D point classification.

nodes.name: Mol-Instructions
nodes.definition: Mol-Instructions is a benchmark dataset for molecular generation tasks including retrosynthesis, reagent prediction, and forward reaction prediction.

nodes.name: MoleculeNet
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers consistently treat MoleculeNet as a benchmark suite, or benchmark dataset, for molecular machine learning and molecular property prediction. The prevailing description emphasizes a collection of tasks and public datasets, sometimes used for classification evaluation on multiple molecular datasets; some papers additionally describe its tasks as spanning properties from quantum mechanics, physical chemistry, biophysics, and physiology. Papers often work with subsets rather than only the full resource, commonly naming BBBP, BACE, ClinTox, ESOL, and FreeSolv.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, the reported measurement target converges on a single behavioral indicator: MoleculeNet is used to measure Molecular property prediction. It is linked to 1 behavioral indicator and no constructs, so papers do not link it to other constructs or behavioral indicators. Relationship evidence frames this use as evaluation, validation, or fine-tuning on MoleculeNet for molecular property prediction tasks.

Space of uses. In use, papers most often position MoleculeNet as an evaluation benchmark: models are evaluated on it, validated on datasets drawn from it, or fine-tuned

nodes.name: MOLERR2FIX
nodes.definition: A structured benchmark assessing LLMs on chemical error detection, localization, explanation, and revision using 1,193 expert-annotated molecular description errors.

nodes.name: MORABLES
nodes.definition: A human-verified benchmark built from fables and short stories from historical literature, designed to assess abstract moral reasoning in LLMs through a multiple-choice question answering task.

nodes.name: MORBENCH
nodes.definition: Multilingual Over-Refusal Benchmark, a large-scale, automatically constructed evaluation set designed to assess overrefusal behaviors in LLMs across 7 languages and 12 safety categories by targeting prompts near the safety decision boundary.

nodes.name: MovieChat
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly treat MovieChat, often named MovieChat-1K, as a long video or long-form video understanding benchmark built from movie clips. Definitions vary slightly between calling it a dataset and a benchmark: one describes 1,000 movie clips with an average duration of 9.4 minutes and 14K annotations, while several others describe roughly 10-minute movie clips. A smaller description emphasizes question-answer pairs about movies, and another adds two evaluation modes, a global mode for overall long-term understanding and a breakpoint mode for detailed analysis of specific moments.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use MovieChat to evaluate long-form or long video understanding rather than to measure a named construct. It is described as evaluating long-form video understanding, overall long-term understanding in a global mode, and detailed analysis of specific moments in breakpoint mode. No papers explicitly link it to any construct or behavioral indicator.

Space of uses. In use, papers position MovieChat as one of the long video benchmarks for model evaluation, sometimes alongside EgoSchema and MovieNet-QA. One paper reports evaluations on more challengin

nodes.name: MovieLens
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly describe MovieLens as a widely used benchmark dataset for recommendation systems, centered on user movie ratings and movie metadata. Some descriptions are more task-specific, presenting it as movie-rating data for evaluating recommendation systems, query modification in LLM-based recommenders, simulation platforms, or personalized cover generation; one paper also describes it as including movie metadata, user demographics, and covers, and reports "86K movies, 0.3M users, and 3.3M ratings".

What it is claimed to measure. The reported measurement claims converge on one construct: MovieLens is linked to one construct, Generalization, and to no behavioral indicators. One paper, Customizing Language Models with Instance-wise LoRA for Sequential Recommendation, uses it to measure Generalization, stating that MovieLens was included "to validate the generalization ability" of the model in real-world recommendation scenarios.

Space of uses. Papers typically place MovieLens within multi-dataset evaluations. It is used alongside LastFM and Steam in sequential recommendation experiments, alongside Google Local and AmazonBook in simulation-platform evaluation,

nodes.name: MovieLens-25M multi-tabular
nodes.definition: A multi-tabular dataset adapted from the MovieLens-25M dataset, used to evaluate graph construction methods on a relation attribute prediction task.

nodes.name: MP-DocVQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. The definition treats MP-DocVQA as a benchmark for multi-page document question answering. The same description limits it to documents under 20 pages, and a paper further states that benchmarks such as MP-DocVQA do not assess documents exceeding 20 pages. In retrieval-oriented uses, papers also describe it as covering industrial documents.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use MP-DocVQA to measure two behavioral indicators, Visual question answering and Information retrieval, and no constructs are linked to it. These claims are spread across those two task framings rather than centered on a linked construct, and both uses rely on question-document pairs drawn from MP-DocVQA.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it, but papers use MP-DocVQA alongside other VQA datasets. One paper groups it with DUDE as a current multi-page document question answering benchmark, while another combines its question-document pairs with ArXivQA, ChartQA, InfographicsVQA, and SlideVQA, plus another figure-focused dataset, to target different document types.

Concerns raised. The stated concern is page-length coverage. Papers note that MP-DocVQA is limited to documents u

nodes.name: MPQA
nodes.definition: The Multi-Perspective Question Answering dataset, used for opinion and sentiment analysis tasks.

nodes.name: MQAR
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, MQAR is most commonly treated as a benchmark for associative recall, and one paper further describes it as a synthetic diagnostic task. Definitions describe sequences or contexts with multiple query tokens, where the model must retrieve and output the value associated with each queried item from the surrounding context; some descriptions add multiple pairs and distractors, and one paper notes that this can require multiple associative recalls in a single forward pass at varying sequence positions.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link MQAR to one construct, Associative recall ability, and one behavioral indicator, Key-value retrieval. The prevailing usage is concentrated rather than spread across many targets: papers say a model's recall capability is assessed using the MQAR task, and that the task's goal is to correctly predict the associated value at the query positions while non-query positions are ignored.

Space of uses. The papers do not link MQAR to other measurement instruments. Instead, they position it directly as an evaluation benchmark for associative recall capabilities and retrieval from context; one paper presents analytical solut

nodes.name: MQM
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most descriptions treat MQM as a framework or guided error annotation scheme for translation evaluation that defines categories, dimensions, and severities for translation errors. Papers describe it as covering dimensions such as accuracy, fluency, and style, and one description specifies six major categories: terminology, accuracy, fluency, style, locale-convention, and non-translation. A smaller use treats the MQM evaluation framework as a source from which manual metrics, in that case fluency and idiom translation, are derived.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the surveyed work, MQM is linked to one construct, Translation quality, and one behavioral indicator, Machine translation. Papers use it to measure translation quality, and one paper also treats machine translation as measured by MQM, describing that setting as having substantial amounts of fine-grained MQM data already available. No other construct or behavioral indicator is linked to it.

Space of uses. No other measurement instrument is linked to MQM by the surveyed papers. Papers position it as guided human error annotation, where evaluators read a source and candidate translation, identify error span

nodes.name: MQP
nodes.definition: The Medical Question Pairs dataset, a benchmark for detecting duplicate questions in a medical domain.

nodes.name: MQuAKE
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, MQuAKE is most commonly described as a benchmark or dataset for knowledge editing on multi-hop knowledge questions, especially question-answering tasks that require reasoning over edited facts. Definitions also frame it as testing whether edited knowledge propagates to related facts and as evaluating knowledge editing generalization through multi-hop questions. Another paper describes each case as a multi-hop question built from a chain of single-hop subquestions, while some authors describe variants by hop count, from 2 to 4, by the position of the knowledge used in the questions, and in one definition by temporal knowledge.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to one behavioral indicator and three constructs, so its reported measurement role is spread across several targets rather than centered on one. It is used to measure Multi-hop question answering, with papers reporting Multi-hop Accuracy and Hop-wise Answering Accuracy for performance on the benchmark, and it is also reported as measuring Multi-hop reasoning, Context faithfulness, and Portability. In the portability framing, papers describe it as evaluating whether modified knowledge

nodes.name: MQuAKE-CF
nodes.definition: A dataset used for evaluating multi-hop reasoning capabilities in the context of model editing.

nodes.name: MR-Ben
nodes.definition: A benchmark for error detection covering domains such as natural sciences, coding, and logic.

nodes.name: MR-GSM8K
nodes.definition: A benchmark for reasoning step error detection based on a subset of the GSM8K dataset, with manual annotations for the reason behind the first error.

nodes.name: MRDA
nodes.definition: ICSI Meeting Recorder Dialog Act corpus, a multiparty dialogue dataset with 50 fine-grained DA classes, used to evaluate dialogue act classification and related pre-tasks.

nodes.name: MRPC
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, MRPC is most commonly described as the Microsoft Research Paraphrase Corpus, usually treated as a benchmark or dataset for paraphrase identification or detection between two sentences. Many papers place it within GLUE, while some frame it more specifically as a sentence-pair text classification task, a binary paraphrase detection task, or a test of whether two sentences are semantically equivalent. A few papers simply list it as one item in broader evaluation suites.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link MRPC to 2 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator. The prevailing usage is to use it to measure paraphrase detection, often described as paraphrase identification or paraphrase tasks; a smaller line of work reports it as measuring natural language understanding or general ability. Overall, the measurement claims are concentrated on paraphrase detection rather than spread across many constructs.

Space of uses. In use, MRPC is usually positioned as one task inside a larger benchmark suite rather than a standalone instrument. The only linked instrument is GLUE, and papers often describe MRPC as a GLUE task or dataset used alongside SST-2, RTE

nodes.name: MS-COCO
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing description is a large-scale vision dataset and benchmark for object detection, segmentation, and captioning, often narrowed to an image-caption dataset with complex scenes and multiple objects, or to the validation set used for zero-shot captioning and text-to-image evaluation. Papers also refer to specific versions and subsets, including MSCOCO-2014, the COCO-2017 validation set, COCO-Val, the Karpathy test split, and an MS-COCO-30K evaluation benchmark. A few descriptions add dataset details, such as images annotated with 80 categories, or a Karpathy-style setup with about 120,000 training images, 5,000 validation and 5,000 test images, and five captions per image.

What it is claimed to measure. Rather than converging on a single target, papers link it to 9 behavioral indicators and 4 constructs. The prevailing use is to measure image captioning, with recurring use for cross-modal retrieval and image generation; at the construct level, papers also report it as measuring multimodal alignment and visual generation ability. The remaining links cover 6 other behavioral indicators and 2 other constructs.

Space of uses. Most paper

nodes.name: MS MARCO
nodes.definition:
What it is. The prevailing usage treats MS MARCO as a large-scale retrieval, question answering, or machine reading comprehension benchmark built from queries or questions and passages, sometimes with ground-truth answers. Several papers narrow it to particular components, such as only the question-and-answer pairs or the passage set, and one description says the public dev split has 101.09k examples, each with a simple question and 10 relevant passages. Variants and subsets also appear, including MARCO QA, msmarco-passages, MS MARCO Dev, and the TREC Deep Learning subsets DL19 and DL20, and one use frames the task as answering real-user Bing queries from 10 retrieved passages.

What it is claimed to measure. Claims about what it measures are spread across several targets rather than centered on one: papers link MS MARCO to three behavioral indicators and two constructs. The linked behavioral indicators are Open-domain question answering, Information retrieval, and Ranking, and the linked constructs are Retrieval effectiveness and Robustness. In the recorded relationships, papers use it to measure open-domain question answering in simple open QA and MARCO QA settings, to measure In

nodes.name: MSR-VTT
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most papers describe MSR-VTT as a large video description or video captioning benchmark used for video-language evaluation. Definitions variously frame it as an English video captioning dataset, a text-to-video retrieval benchmark with 10,000 video clips and associated natural language descriptions, and a benchmark for short video understanding; one source also notes 10K open-domain videos, while another refers to a test set of 2,990 videos that are 10 to 30 seconds long. A smaller line of work treats it as the large unannotated dataset in active-learning experiments.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the surveyed work, the dominant use is to measure behavioral indicators rather than constructs: papers link it to 3 behavioral indicators and no constructs. Most commonly, papers use it to measure video captioning, while smaller lines of work use it to measure video generation and cross-modal retrieval. These reported uses stay at the level of behavioral indicators.

Space of uses. Papers often use MSR-VTT alongside other video-language benchmarks, most often MSVD, and also VATEX, LSMDC, DiDeMo, and UCF-101. It is positioned both as a benchmark for evaluating zero-sho

nodes.name: MSRVTT-QA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing description is a video question answering benchmark based on or derived from the MSR-VTT dataset, also expanded in some definitions as Microsoft Research Video to Text. Definitions differ mainly in label and emphasis: some call it a benchmark, others a dataset or benchmark dataset, and several specify that it is open-ended, testing comprehension of video content through associated questions or answers about video clips. One description also notes that MSRVTT-QA, together with MSVD-QA, is derived from video retrieval datasets.

What it is claimed to measure. Measurement claims are concentrated rather than spread across many targets. Papers link it to 1 behavioral indicator, Video question answering, and this is the dominant usage: relationship evidence describes MSRVTT-QA as a benchmark for open-ended or zero-shot video question answering. Papers also link it to 1 construct, Video understanding, typically when placing it inside broader video understanding benchmark suites.

Space of uses. No paper directly links it to another measurement instrument, but papers usually use it alongside other video QA benchmarks, most often MSVD-QA and Activit

nodes.name: MSVD
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, MSVD is most commonly framed as a video understanding benchmark, including for assessing short video comprehension and for evaluating multimodal video question answering or captioning performance. A smaller framing describes it as a benchmark dataset for video captioning: one paper specifies that it contains 1,970 open-domain videos collected from a commercial video search engine, with about 41 human-annotated captions for each video.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link MSVD to 1 construct and 2 behavioral indicators. The construct-level claim is that video understanding is measured by MSVD, while the behavioral indicators are video question answering, where it is listed as an open-ended VideoQA dataset, and cross-modal retrieval, where it appears as one of the retrieval benchmarks. These claims spread across a small set of evaluation targets rather than only one task framing.

Space of uses. In use, papers often place MSVD alongside other benchmarks in evaluation suites. It appears with MSR-VTT in video captioning experiments, with MUSIC-AVQA in open-ended VideoQA evaluation, and with MSR-VTT, LSMDC, and DiDeMo in cross-modal retrieval benchm

nodes.name: MSVD-QA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, MSVD-QA is most commonly treated as a video question-answering benchmark, often described as open-ended and frequently used for zero-shot evaluation. Definitions repeatedly tie it to the Microsoft Video Description dataset or the Microsoft Research Video Description Corpus, and the name also appears as MSVDQA and, in one formulation, MVSD-QA. Some descriptions add that it assesses understanding of video content through natural-language answers to video-based questions, sometimes over short video clips, and one paper notes that MSVD-QA is derived from video retrieval datasets.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link MSVD-QA to 1 construct and 2 behavioral indicators. The prevailing usage is to measure Video question answering, with many papers explicitly calling it a video QA, open-ended VideoQA, or zero-shot video question answering benchmark. A smaller line of work reports it as measuring Video understanding by placing it among video understanding benchmarks, and a minority framing uses it for Visual question answering. These claims concentrate most strongly on Video question answering rather than spreading evenly across targets.

Space of uses.

nodes.name: MT-Bench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing description is of a multi-turn, open-ended conversation benchmark for instruction-following and chat evaluation, usually graded by GPT-4 or another strong LLM judge. Most papers describe 80 human-crafted or predefined multi-turn questions or dialogues, often organized into 8 domains or categories such as writing, roleplay, reasoning, math, coding, extraction, STEM, and humanities, and several papers say these are two-turn items totaling 160 prompts; some papers instead emphasize one-turn plus multi-turn reasoning and instruction-following examples or call it an open-source multi-turn conversation benchmark. A smaller line of work treats MT-Bench as a human-annotated benchmark or preference dataset, noting expert-level pairwise annotations or human preferences over model responses.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use MT-Bench to measure 23 constructs and 13 behavioral indicators, so claims about what it measures are spread across many targets rather than converging on one. The prevailing claims are that it measures instruction following ability and conversational ability, and papers also use it for generalization; at the be

nodes.name: MT-Bench-101
nodes.definition: Multi-level benchmark using multi-turn questions to assess model understanding and consistency in complex dialogues.

nodes.name: MTEB
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, MTEB is most commonly described as a comprehensive, standard, or general-purpose suite for evaluating text embedding models. A recurring specification presents it as 56 English tasks across 7 types: classification, clustering, pair classification, reranking, retrieval, semantic textual similarity, and summarization. Some papers describe narrower or different slices, including ten STS tasks for sentence embeddings, or a holistic assessment of sentence representations across 8 task types. Some authors also refer to an MTEB leaderboard and collection of benchmarks when citing top or leading embedding models.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use MTEB to measure 6 behavioral indicators and 3 constructs. The prevailing measurement claims concern information retrieval, semantic textual similarity, text clustering, text embedding, and pair classification, with 1 other behavioral indicator and 3 constructs also reported. Across those links, the reported uses are spread across multiple embedding-related behaviors rather than centered on a single target.

Space of uses. In use, papers often treat MTEB as the main embedding benchmark, either evaluating on the f

nodes.name: MTOP
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers here, MTOP is most commonly treated as a benchmark dataset for multilingual task-oriented semantic parsing, with definitions centering on intent and slot filling. It is also described as containing compositional representations for complex nested queries across multiple languages and domains, and one description says it covers 6 languages and 11 domains.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use MTOP to measure one behavioral indicator, Semantic parsing, and no constructs are linked to it. The linked claims converge on semantic parsing: papers describe MTOP as a semantic parsing benchmark and as a benchmark for multilingual task-oriented semantic parsing, with attention to intent and slot filling.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to MTOP, but papers do use it alongside other semantic parsing benchmarks. One paper presents it with SM-CalFlow and GeoQuery as part of "three popular diverse semantic parsing benchmarks," and another evaluates across four semantic parsing tasks that span "intent and slot filling (MTop)."

nodes.name: MTOP(I)
nodes.definition: A dataset for intent discovery, aiming to identify unknown intents within user utterances.

nodes.name: MUCAR
nodes.definition: A benchmark for evaluating multilingual cross-modal ambiguity resolution, consisting of 1278 samples in Chinese, English, and Malay, including dual-ambiguity cases where both text and image are ambiguous but jointly resolve to a single interpretation.

nodes.name: MuirBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly describe MuirBench as a multi-image, multimodal benchmark for evaluating understanding or reasoning across multiple images. The definitions converge on its focus on integrating information from diverse visual inputs and assessing image relationships, and one paper introduces it as a "comprehensive benchmark" for multi-image understanding; the documented task areas include counting, diagram understanding, image-text matching, scene understanding, and visual retrieval.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the linked uses, papers use MuirBench to measure 2 constructs and 4 behavioral indicators, rather than tying it to a single target. The construct-level claims center on multi-image reasoning and scene understanding, and the behavioral indicators are counting, cross-modal retrieval, diagram understanding, and information retrieval; the task descriptions say these cover counting specific objects across multiple images, understanding diagrams, matching text and visual content, understanding scenes from multiple surveillance images, and retrieving images that contain the same building.

Space of uses. No other measurement instrument is linked to MuirBe

nodes.name: Multi30k
nodes.definition: Multilingual dataset for machine translation, containing image captions in English and German.

nodes.name: Multi-IF
nodes.definition: Benchmark designed to evaluate instruction-following with multiple independent constraints.

nodes.name: Multi-Needle-in-a-Haystack
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across definitions, the prevailing usage treats this as a long-context retrieval variant of Needle-in-a-Haystack: a model must locate multiple needles, hidden targets, or pieces of information within a single long context, sometimes with multiple distractor facts mixed in. A smaller line of usage casts it as a multi-turn evaluation in which different specific pieces of information are retrieved from the same long context across successive conversational turns, with questions issued one-by-one.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link this instrument to one construct, Long-context understanding, which is reported as being measured by it. No behavioral indicators are linked to it, and no other constructs are named, so the measurement claim converges on that single construct rather than spreading across several targets.

Space of uses. No other measurement instrument is linked to it. Where papers describe its role, they present it as a more complex or harder needle retrieval evaluation by mixing multiple needles and by running multi-NIAH alongside single-NIAH in longer contexts; another paper uses it following NeedleBench and frames it as a multi-turn conversation setti

nodes.name: MultiArith
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, MultiArith is most commonly described as a benchmark dataset of arithmetic word problems, often grade-school or general math word problems that require multiple operations or multi-step reasoning. Some definitions frame it more broadly as a quantitative or mathematical reasoning dataset, and one paper describes it as a subset of MAWPS containing multi-step mathematical word problems. A few papers add corpus details, reporting either a data size of 600 or a split of train: 420 and test: 180.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link MultiArith to 2 constructs, Mathematical reasoning and Robustness, and to 1 behavioral indicator, Mathematical problem solving. The prevailing usage is to measure Mathematical reasoning, with papers using it to verify mathematical reasoning capacity or assess arithmetic reasoning tasks. A smaller line of work uses it to measure Robustness through out-of-domain evaluation, and it is also used to measure Mathematical problem solving on general benchmark suites.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it. In practice, papers usually evaluate MultiArith alongside GSM8K and, in smaller benchmark suites, SVAMP, AddSu

nodes.name: MultiHiertt
nodes.definition: A question answering dataset in the finance domain designed to support compositional reasoning by encoding hierarchical table structures for multi-step questions.

nodes.name: MultiHop-RAG
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the definitions, papers describe MultiHop-RAG as a benchmark or dataset for multi-hop reasoning and question answering, with one definition placing it in retrieval-augmented generation settings and emphasizing integration across multiple documents. One description says it assesses whether LLMs can extract and synthesize relevant information from multiple documents, while another specifies four question types, Inference, Comparison, Temporal, and Null; a relationship description also says it includes 2,556 multi-hop questions.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to measure two constructs, Generalization and Multi-hop reasoning, and one behavioral indicator, Multi-hop question answering. The reported uses are spread across these targets rather than centered on a single construct: multi-hop question answering is the most common framing, multi-hop reasoning is another recurring target, and one paper uses it to assess generalization by treating it as a recent and challenging OOD dataset; one definition also says it is used to evaluate reasoning adaptability across question types.

Space of uses. Across papers, MultiHop-RAG is usually used as one component of

nodes.name: MultiJail
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing description is a multilingual benchmark for adversarial or harmful prompts across languages. One definition describes it as a red-teaming dataset covering nine languages, used to sample and translate adversarial prompts for non-English safety evaluation, while another describes it as a multilingual harmful-prompt benchmark; one paper further mentions 315 queries when using it as seed data.

What it is claimed to measure. Its reported measurement role is narrow rather than spread across many targets. Papers link it to one behavioral indicator, harmful content detection, and to no constructs, using it specifically to evaluate the accuracy of detecting harmful prompts in multilingual benchmarks.

Space of uses. Papers position it both as a benchmark in multilingual safety evaluation and as seed data for another dataset. It is related to one other instrument, CSRT, which one paper constructs by leveraging MultiJail's 315 queries as seed data, and another paper evaluates on it alongside other text attack benchmarks such as RTP-LX and AyaRedTeaming.

nodes.name: Multimodal Mind2Web
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most descriptions treat Multimodal Mind2Web as a multimodal extension of Mind2Web used for offline evaluation of web or GUI agents. Papers describe it as evaluating web agent task completion from cached screenshots and high-level task instructions, with a test split of 1,013 tasks spanning over 100 websites; another recurring framing is that it evaluates increasingly difficult cross-task, cross-website, and cross-domain generalization. A smaller line of work describes it as an in-distribution offline dataset for GUI-agent tasks involving web browsers.

What it is claimed to measure. Where papers make explicit measurement claims, they use it to measure 1 construct and 1 behavioral indicator. One paper uses it to measure Generalization, stating that it evaluates generalization across cross-task, cross-website, and cross-domain settings. Another paper uses it to measure Action grounding, using its test data to further assess GUI grounding models after alignment.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it. Papers position it as an offline evaluation benchmark for realistic web tasks, and one paper also describes it as a challenging benchmark on which evaluati

nodes.name: MultiNERD
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most commonly, papers describe MultiNERD as a named entity recognition dataset, with one definition presenting it as a NER pre-training dataset based on Wikipedia and Wikinews, containing 164K instances in the English split and 17 label names, and used as a baseline for IE pre-training. A smaller line of work treats it as the named entity recognition dataset used to examine chain-of-thought prompting under few-shot open-set conditions, including seen and unseen classes.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the papers here, MultiNERD is not explicitly linked as measuring any construct or behavioral indicator. Instead, papers use it for task evaluation in named entity recognition and, in one case, for reporting seen-class and unseen-class F1 under few-shot open-set classification.

Space of uses. Papers position MultiNERD in two main ways: as a baseline dataset for IE pre-training, and as an evaluation dataset for reasoning-based prompting. In "Few-Shot Open-Set Classification via Reasoning-Aware Decomposition," it is the dataset on which chain-of-thought prompting is examined, and the paper reports that a method achieves the highest F1-score in 50/54 settings for seen

nodes.name: MultiNews
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across definitions, MultiNews is most commonly described as a dataset or benchmark for multi-document summarization. One description specifies that it consists of news articles and human-written summaries from newser.com, and one source further describes 56k article-summary pairs with summaries written by professional editors (GraphRouter: A Graph-based Router for LLM Selections). A smaller line of description places it within LongBench as a multi-document summarization dataset, while another simply frames it as a dataset for summarization tasks that require synthesizing multiple documents.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use MultiNews to measure 1 behavioral indicator, Text summarization, and link it to no constructs. The recorded uses converge on summarization rather than spreading across multiple outcomes: papers describe it as a summarization task, use it in summarization evaluations, and report it as evaluating multi-document summarization. One paper adds that the task "requires synthesizing information from the entire context" (APE: Faster and Longer Context-Augmented Generation via Adaptive Parallel Encoding).

Space of uses. In the cited evaluations, Mult

nodes.name: MultiPL-E
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats MultiPL-E as a multilingual code generation benchmark formed by translating HumanEval, and often MBPP, into multiple programming languages. Several definitions describe parallel datasets in 18 programming languages, sometimes as translations of two unit-test driven Python benchmarks to 18 other languages; as one paper puts it, it is "translated from the Python benchmark ... into parallel datasets in 18 programming languages" (Knowledge Fusion of Large Language Models). Some authors also call it a multi-language parallel benchmark for text-to-code generation, and papers report evaluations on subsets such as 8 languages, 5 languages, or cpp/go. A smaller line of work describes it more narrowly as translated HumanEval problems, while one paper instead describes a Bash-focused benchmark with 540 scripting tasks checked by unit tests.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link MultiPL-E to 2 behavioral indicators and no constructs. The dominant claim is that papers use it to measure code generation, with evaluations reported on MultiPL-E using metrics such as pass@1, pass@k, Avg. Pass@(1+10), and pass@100. A smaller line uses i

nodes.name: MultiRC
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, MultiRC is most commonly described as a multi-sentence reading comprehension dataset or benchmark for question answering. Definitions present it as a multiple choice dataset, sometimes evaluated with exact-match accuracy, and several quoted passages say its questions require reasoning over, or synthesizing information from, multiple sentences in a passage; some also note that a passage question may have multiple correct answers. A smaller line of work phrases it as the task itself, namely answering a question by combining information from multiple sentences, and one definition places it within SuperGLUE.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link MultiRC to one construct and one behavioral indicator. The more common measurement claim is that it measures machine reading comprehension, with papers describing it as a question-answering dataset testing reading comprehension and using it among validation sets that cover reading comprehension. A separate use treats it as measuring general ability by including it in a broader cross-domain evaluation set, so the reported measurement claims span both a behavioral indicator and a construct rather than c

nodes.name: MultiWOZ
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers commonly treat MultiWOZ as a task-oriented, multi-domain Wizard-of-Oz dialogue dataset or benchmark. Definitions describe conversations where one human acts as a booking system for domains such as hotels and restaurants and the other acts as the user, while other papers frame it more broadly as a large-scale dataset for bookings and information requests. Papers also describe it differently by evaluation task: some use it as a dialogue state tracking benchmark, and another uses a later version built on an earlier release with corrections and enhancements to the test set.

What it is claimed to measure. No constructs or behavioral indicators are formally linked to MultiWOZ. Even so, papers use it to evaluate several targets rather than one recorded construct: dialogue state tracking, user satisfaction estimation, and first-order uncertainty quantification, including prediction of how certain the user is that they are more satisfied than would occur by chance, with average crowd-worker user-satisfaction annotations treated as ground truth.

Space of uses. No other measurement instrument is formally linked to MultiWOZ. In practice, papers position it both as a widely

nodes.name: MUSE
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, MUSE is most commonly described as a comprehensive machine unlearning evaluation benchmark for language models, framed as Machine Unlearning Six-Way Evaluation and said to evaluate unlearned models across six desiderata or facets. Definitions place it in news and book materials, with verbatim-text and question-answer knowledge sets, though some papers narrow the description to copyrighted-information removal and emphasize two scenarios, Books from the Harry Potter series and News from BBC News. A smaller description focuses only on the BBC News portion, where passages are split into Forget and Retain sets to evaluate knowledge removal and utility preservation through question answering.

What it is claimed to measure. In the recorded relationships, MUSE is linked to 3 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator, so papers use it across several measurement targets rather than centering it on a single construct. The explicit links are to Knowledge memorization, Utility preservation, and Verbatim memorization, plus the behavioral indicator Privacy leakage, and one definition also frames MUSE as evaluating six desirable properties of unlearning more broa

nodes.name: MUSE-Books
nodes.definition:
What it is. The only available paper treats MUSE-Books, under the name BOOKS, as a dataset within the MUSE benchmark. In Catastrophic Failure of LLM Unlearning via Quantization, it is described as featuring the Harry Potter series, with the original novels as the forget set and related FanWiki materials as the retain set.

What it is claimed to measure. The paper does not explicitly report that MUSE-Books measures any construct or behavioral indicator, and papers do not link it to any constructs or indicators.

Space of uses. Papers position it as a component of the MUSE benchmark rather than as a standalone protocol. The described use pairs the original Harry Potter novels as the forget set with related FanWiki materials as the retain set, with the retain set used to preserve domain knowledge post-unlearning, and no other measurement instrument is linked to it.

nodes.name: MUSIC-AVQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers describe MUSIC-AVQA as a multimodal question answering benchmark over audio and video. One definition calls it an open-ended VideoQA dataset used for multimodal question answering, while another paper uses the name MUSIC-QA and frames it as a benchmark for music-related audio-visual understanding and reasoning.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, it is linked to two behavioral indicators and no constructs. Papers use it to measure Audio-visual question answering and Video question answering, with one paper presenting fine-tuning results on Audio-Video Question Answering using MUSIC-AVQA and another listing it among open-ended VideoQA datasets.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it through the recorded relationships. In practice, papers evaluate with it alongside other benchmarks, for example with MSVD as an open-ended VideoQA dataset, and in a broader audio-visual QA suite that also includes AVSD, AVSSD, MSVD-QA, and MSRVTT-QA, along with other benchmarks.

nodes.name: MusicCaps
nodes.definition: Benchmark for music captioning with rich textual descriptions, used to evaluate open-domain music understanding and description.

nodes.name: MuSiQue
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats MuSiQue as a challenging multi-hop question answering dataset or benchmark built from composable pairs of single-hop questions, so models must connect multiple pieces of information across multiple paragraphs, passages, or documents. Many descriptions add that it supports up to four-hop reasoning or at least two reasoning steps, and several say it was designed to reduce reasoning shortcuts or require connected or disentangled reasoning. A smaller line of work refers to named variants or slices, including the answerable version, MuSiQue-Ans, 2-hop questions, and 3-hop or 4-hop portions; one definition also mentions adversarially written paragraphs, and another describes diverse domains with minimal lexical overlap.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use MuSiQue to measure 3 constructs and 4 behavioral indicators. The dominant claims center on multi-hop reasoning and multi-hop question answering, and papers repeatedly use the benchmark to assess multi-step reasoning over complex information dependencies. More selectively, papers also report it as measuring question answering, generalization, and chain of thought, w

nodes.name: MuSR
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, MuSR is most commonly described as a benchmark from the Open LLM Leaderboard for reasoning-oriented evaluation, especially reasoning over social or multi-step scenarios. Some definitions specify Open LLM Leaderboard v2, while others refer to the Open LLM Leaderboard more generally. One paper calls it "the semi-symbolic MUSR" and notes that "All tasks are multiple-choice" (Analysing Chain of Thought Dynamics: Active Guidance or Unfaithful Post-hoc Rationalisation?), and papers describing its domains mention murder mysteries, object placement, and team assignment.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link MuSR to 6 constructs, with commonsense reasoning the most frequent linked construct, followed by chain-of-thought reasoning, logical reasoning, physical world understanding, and social reasoning; no behavioral indicators are linked to it. The measurement claims are spread across several reasoning-oriented constructs rather than one: one description ties its domains to commonsense reasoning about physical and social situations, another says it is designed to assess multistep reasoning, and a separate paper places it with formal logic "to a lesser degree."

nodes.name: MuST-C
nodes.definition: A multilingual speech translation corpus created from English TED Talks, widely used for evaluating speech translation systems.

nodes.name: MuTual
nodes.definition: A dataset for multi-turn dialogue reasoning, adapted from Chinese high school English listening comprehension exams.

nodes.name: MVBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing description is a video or video-language understanding benchmark centered on temporal sensitivity. Definitions often say it covers nine core temporal tasks with 20 subtasks, and that each task cannot be solved from a single frame; some authors instead describe it as a reorganized benchmark containing 20 video understanding tasks, or as a multi-choice QA benchmark with 4,000 QA pairs derived from 11 public video benchmarks. A smaller line of work highlights specific subsets, especially action-related subtasks such as Action Antonym, Action Count, Action Sequence, Action Prediction, Action Localization, Fine-grained Action, and Unexpected Action.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link MVBench to 3 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator. The dominant use is to measure video understanding, with several papers treating it as one of the general benchmarks for that construct; a recurring second use is to measure temporal reasoning, with papers describing it as concentrating on temporal reasoning skills or video temporal reasoning. A smaller usage treats it as measuring multi-image reasoning, and a single paper uses it to measure the behavioral

nodes.name: MVSA-M
nodes.definition: A multimodal sentiment analysis benchmark for post-level sentiment classification on image-text posts.

nodes.name: MVSA-S
nodes.definition: A multimodal sentiment analysis benchmark for post-level sentiment classification on image-text posts.

nodes.name: Mystery Blocksworld
nodes.definition: An obfuscated version of the Blocksworld planning domain from the PlanBench suite, designed to be more challenging by obscuring the commonsense nature of the task.

nodes.name: MzsRE
nodes.definition: MzsRE is a multilingual dataset created by translating full sentences with Google Translate.

nodes.name: NarrativeQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing description of NarrativeQA is a long-context question-answering or reading-comprehension benchmark over narrative texts, usually entire books and movie scripts or transcripts. Papers describe question-answer pairs tied to full stories or long text segments, with the task framed as generating free-form answers from the text; one account says the questions are concatenated to text segments, while another says each example includes a full story and corresponding QA pairs. Some authors place it within SCROLL or SCROLLS, and one paper instead describes annotators reading novel summaries to write questions.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link NarrativeQA to 2 behavioral indicators and 2 constructs. The most common use is to measure Question answering and Document question answering: it is described as an established QA dataset, a single-doc QA benchmark, and a long-document question-answering dataset about stories, books, or movie scripts. A smaller line of work uses it to measure Long-context understanding, including claims that it assesses comprehension of long-form narrative structures beyond simple content matching, and one

nodes.name: Natural Instructions
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the cited work, Natural Instructions is described as a dataset for evaluating a model's ability to follow natural language instructions across a wide range of tasks. One quoted passage also places it in generation-task testing, where papers report testing method effects on Natural Instructions.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use Natural Instructions to measure Instruction following. It is linked to one behavioral indicator, Instruction following, and to no constructs, so the measurement claims converge on that single target rather than being spread across multiple outcomes.

Space of uses. In the usage in the papers evidence, papers position Natural Instructions as a training and evaluation dataset alongside XSum and the WMT-14 en-de translation dataset. Another paper uses it to test generation-task effects of different methods.

nodes.name: Natural Questions
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, Natural Questions is most commonly treated as a question answering benchmark built from real user Google Search queries, usually paired with Wikipedia answers or passages. The dominant framing is open-domain, knowledge-intensive, and often single-hop, though some authors instead describe it as closed-book, fact-recall, world-knowledge, or retrieval evaluation. Papers also refer to an open-domain variant, NQ-Open or NaturalQuestions-Open, and to versions with short and long answers, golden and distractor passages, or retrieved documents with the gold document placed at different positions; some studies evaluate it in 0-, 3-, 5-, or 32-shot form, or use subsets such as 10,000 queries and the 3,610-pair NQ-Open validation set.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link Natural Questions to 9 constructs and 9 behavioral indicators. The prevailing use is to measure question answering, especially open-domain question answering, and some work also uses it for text generation. Construct claims are less concentrated on a single target: world knowledge is the most recurrent framing, editing locality is another recurring use, and papers also attach the benchmar

nodes.name: NBA
nodes.definition: Natural Backdoor Attacks (NBA), a baseline backdoor attack method that injects fixed, non-learnable 'natural triggers' like rain or a whistle at the beginning of an audio waveform.

nodes.name: Nectar
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers here, Nectar is treated as a dataset rather than a protocol. The more detailed description presents it as a dataset of human-labeled responses in seven distinct rankings, used to evaluate question answering performance, with one paper stating, "We began our experiments using the Nectar dataset, which includes human-labeled responses categorized into seven distinct rankings" (RED: Unleashing Token-Level Rewards from Holistic Feedback via Reward Redistribution). A smaller description refers to Berkeley Nectar simply as a dataset used in direct and indirect transfer evaluations of decoding-time alignment, without further detail on contents or format.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers here do not explicitly link Nectar to any construct or behavioral indicator through recorded measurement relationships. Instead, the definitions describe it more narrowly as being used to evaluate question answering performance in one paper, while another paper uses Berkeley Nectar in transfer evaluations of decoding-time alignment; these usages do not converge into an explicit measured construct in the recorded links.

Space of uses. The prevailing usage in these papers

nodes.name: Needle-in-a-Haystack
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, Needle-in-a-Haystack, often abbreviated NIAH, is most commonly described as a synthetic long-context retrieval benchmark or evaluation procedure, and several authors call it a popular or widely used pressure or stress test. The prevailing setup inserts a fact, statement, answer, sentence, or key-value pair, the "needle", at varying depths or positions inside a long irrelevant or distracting document or text, the "haystack", then queries the model to retrieve it. Some definitions emphasize controlled insertion depth, and one reported setup uses a four-needle variant with multiple inserted items.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to measure five constructs and three behavioral indicators. The most frequently linked constructs start with long-context understanding and contextual understanding, while the most frequent behavioral links are synthetic recall, context retrieval, and information retrieval; the remaining links cover three other constructs. These claims are spread across several constructs, though the recurring use is to assess retrieval from long contexts, including correct answer rate on the task and whether models can locate inserted

nodes.name: NeedleBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly describe NeedleBench as a long-context benchmark built around recall-intensive retrieval tasks. One definition frames it as evaluating whether models can comprehend and retrieve information from long input sequences, while another describes it as a suite of recall-intensive tasks for long-context retrieval and information finding. One paper adds that it tests retrieval and reasoning in complex contexts through three subtasks: Single-Needle Retrieval, Multi-Needle Retrieval, and Multi-Needle Reasoning, and another groups it with synthetic benchmarks that offer control over sequence length and complexity.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the papers here, the reported measurement use centers on one behavioral indicator: Synthetic recall. Papers claim NeedleBench measures this indicator, describing it as testing retrieval and reasoning in complex contexts and using it to assess recall or retrieval capabilities. Papers do not link it to any construct or to additional behavioral indicators.

Space of uses. In use, papers position NeedleBench as one of the long-context benchmarks focused on models' ability to understand long-context input sequences.

nodes.name: NegHalu
nodes.definition: A constructed dataset for evaluating hallucination detection in negated text, derived from HaluEval, BamBoo, and SelfCheckGPT-WikiBio by applying post-negation transformations and reassigning hallucination labels based on logical consistency.

nodes.name: NESTFUL
nodes.definition: A benchmark dataset designed to evaluate LLMs on nested sequences of API calls in mathematical reasoning and generic coding domains, assessing five dimensions of performance including F1 scores and sequence accuracy.

nodes.name: NewsQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, NewsQA is most commonly described as a question answering or machine comprehension dataset built from news articles, with questions answered from long passages. Definitions emphasize comprehension, extraction of answers from realistic passages, and, in one description, synthesizing information from long passages. A narrower characterization specifies CNN articles paired with questions and answers derived from those articles, and one quoted passage refers specifically to the MRQA version of NewsQA.

What it is claimed to measure. A paper uses NewsQA to measure Question answering. Across the recorded links, it is connected to one behavioral indicator, Question answering, and to no constructs, so the reported measurement use is concentrated rather than spread across multiple constructs.

Space of uses. Papers use it as an evaluation dataset for question answering over news passages or articles. One quoted passage lists the MRQA version of NewsQA alongside HotpotQA among the datasets tested, and another paper uses it for the news articles domain when evaluating takedown methods. No other measurement instrument is linked to it.

nodes.name: NExT-QA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing usage is as a video question answering benchmark, often described as multiple choice, for evaluating causal and temporal reasoning over video events. Several definitions add that it targets everyday activities, natural videos, or explanations of temporal actions, and some descriptions also mention descriptive question types; one paper additionally names a subset, NExT-GQA, with timestamp annotations to locate the answer moment. Papers describe its video scope somewhat differently: some call it a long-form or minute-long video dataset with thousands of multiple-choice questions, while others describe it as measuring temporal dynamics over short clips or focusing on short videos.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to one behavioral indicator, Video question answering, and to seven constructs. The dominant measurement claim is that papers use NExT-QA to measure video question answering, while construct-level uses are spread across long video understanding and video understanding, followed by causal reasoning, compositional reasoning, reasoning, spatiotemporal reasoning, and temporal reasoning. The recorded relationship language

nodes.name: NFCorpus
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, the prevailing usage treats NFCorpus, also written NFCORPUS or NF-Corpus, as an information retrieval dataset or benchmark, often described more specifically as medical information retrieval. Definitions add that it contains queries in simple English and technical documents extracted from PubMed, and one paper states that its test split has 323 queries and the corpus has 3.6k documents. Some papers describe it more generally as a retrieval dataset from BEIR used for query generation and retrieval or for generating and evaluating adversarial passages, while another frames it as a medical dataset for domain-specific factual questions involving single entities.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link NFCorpus to two behavioral indicators, Factual question answering and Information retrieval, and to no constructs. One paper uses it to measure information retrieval in long-document retrieval scenarios, reporting recall and precision on NFCORPUS, while the same paper also says that SQUAD, NFCORPUS, and SCI-DOCS contain factual questions involving single entities. In the linked relationships, the measurement claims stay at the level of behaviora

nodes.name: NL4OPT
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, closely related labels, NL4OPT, NL4Opt, and NLP4OPT, are used for what is most commonly described as a benchmark or benchmark dataset for turning natural language optimization problems into mathematical formulations. The prevailing description emphasizes question text in natural language, named entity recognition to extract entities and numerical values, and subsequent formulation into mathematical models. A narrower description presents it as a curated set of 244 linear programming problems used to evaluate autoformulation systems, while a smaller framing describes it as a dataset from the NL4Opt competition for solving optimization problems described in natural language.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers mainly use NL4OPT to evaluate whether models can construct or extract optimization formulations from natural language descriptions or questions. In that usage, it is reported as assessing named entity and numerical value extraction as part of formulating mathematical models, and a narrower description limits the task to linear programming autoformulation. Papers do not link it to named constructs or behavioral indicators.

Space of uses. In the

nodes.name: NLGraph
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, NLGraph is most commonly described as a benchmark or evaluation framework for graph reasoning tasks presented in natural language. Some definitions frame it broadly as assessing whether language models can handle graph tasks and basic graph properties, including counting node degrees or finding shortest paths, while one usage narrows to the shortest-path subset, where models find the shortest path between two nodes in a weighted undirected graph.

What it is claimed to measure. The recorded measurement claims link NLGraph to two constructs, Reasoning and Generalization, and no behavioral indicators. Papers use it to measure Reasoning in benchmark suites, and another paper reports that simpler tasks in NLGraph evaluate Generalization, so the measurement claims are spread across more than one construct rather than centered on a single one.

Space of uses. Papers position NLGraph as an evaluation benchmark for graph-task performance, sometimes as an extensive framework and sometimes through a specific subset or simpler tasks. One line of use employs only the shortest-path subset, and another refers to the simpler tasks in NLGraph when evaluating generalizati

nodes.name: NLP4LP
nodes.definition: A benchmark for solving linear programming problems where models must use an optimization solver, with problem data presented implicitly in the text.

nodes.name: NLVR2
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing description treats NLVR2 as an extension of the NLVR dataset built from pairs of real-world photographs and natural language statements, used to test visual reasoning. A compatible framing presents it as a benchmark for evaluating reasoning over paired visual inputs and related language statements, and some papers refer to it simply as a dataset for visual reasoning.
