What it is claimed to measure. Papers use NLVR2 to measure three constructs: Multi-image reasoning, Visual reasoning, and Visual understanding, and no behavioral indicators are linked to it. These claims are spread across those constructs rather than concentrated on one: some papers place NLVR2 among multi-image benchmarks, another uses it for visual reasoning, and another reports it as measuring visual understanding.

Space of uses. Across the papers, NLVR2 is commonly positioned as one item in a broader evaluation suite rather than as a standalone protocol. As one study notes, "we select five multi-image benchmarks" including NLVR2, while another uses it within a broader set of image-text tasks; papers do not link it to any other measurement instrument.

nodes.name: NoCaps
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, NoCaps is most commonly treated as an image captioning benchmark or dataset for testing captions on novel objects or classes not seen during training, often in zero-shot settings. Some authors describe it as large-scale or open-domain; one paper labels it a captioning task for natural images, another says it is derived from Open Images, and another uses it as an out-of-domain benchmark for transferability and robustness tests. The recurring content description is images with diverse objects and scenes, especially categories not seen frequently in training.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use NoCaps to measure 2 behavioral indicators and no constructs. The prevailing use is Image captioning: papers describe it as evaluating image-level caption ability, zero-shot image captioning, or image-to-text captioning. A smaller line of work uses it to measure Object hallucination, with one paper evaluating object hallucination in visual caption and checking transferability and robustness on out-of-domain images.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it. In practice, papers commonly report it alongside Flickr30K and COCO, and some also place i

nodes.name: NormAd
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, NORMAD is most commonly described as a benchmark or hierarchical evaluation framework for LLM cultural adaptability, though one paper also refers to it as a dataset. Definitions converge on a multi-country set of free-text or short social situations, reported as 2,600 stories from 75 countries, where a character either adheres to or violates a cultural norm; models judge the acceptability of these situations under different levels of cultural context specificity, from abstract values to explicit social norms and etiquette.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use NORMAD to measure Cultural adaptation, and this is the only linked construct. It is linked to one construct and no behavioral indicators, so the reported measurement claims converge on cultural adaptation, including judging social acceptability across varying levels of cultural norm specificity.

Space of uses. Papers position NORMAD mainly as a direct evaluation setup for studying cultural adaptability in LLMs. One paper introduces it as a multi-level framework for social acceptability judgments, and another reports using the NORMAD dataset "to study cultural adaptability in LLMs"

nodes.name: NOVA-63
nodes.definition: A native multilingual benchmark containing 89,107 multiple-choice questions across 14 languages and 63 academic disciplines, designed to assess multilingual and multidisciplinary capabilities of LLMs with native content, difficulty control, and disciplinary balance.

nodes.name: NovelHopQA
nodes.definition: A benchmark for evaluating multi-hop question answering over long narrative contexts, featuring 4,000 questions with 1-4 reasoning hops across 64k-128k token excerpts from public-domain novels.

nodes.name: NQ-Swap
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, NQ-Swap is most commonly described as a counterfactual version of Natural Questions, where incorrect answers are swapped into the context to test whether a model relies on correct evidence. A closely related description treats it as a knowledge conflict dataset based on Natural Questions, consisting of synthetic conflicting data to test a model's ability to handle discrepancies. Papers also position it as a counterfactual QA benchmark that offers a more challenging and complementary evaluation of whether models can identify and rely on the correct evidence.

What it is claimed to measure. The reported measurement claims are concentrated rather than spread across many targets: papers link NQ-Swap to one construct, Context faithfulness, and one behavioral indicator, Question answering. The prevailing usage is to measure Context faithfulness, with papers describing it as evaluating a model's ability to identify and rely on the correct evidence, or to follow instructions and contexts on knowledge conflict datasets. A smaller line of use reports it as measuring Question answering, where it appears as one of the QA datasets used in task evaluation.

nodes.name: NTREX-128
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, NTREX-128 is described as a document-translation dataset. Definitions place it in FILBENCH for English-to-Filipino translation evaluation, and quoted passages describe it as part of a "diverse set of test examples" that include documents.

What it is claimed to measure. In the recorded relationships, papers use NTREX-128 to measure Machine translation. It is linked to one behavioral indicator, Machine translation, and to no constructs, so the reported use centers on a single behavioral target rather than multiple constructs or indicators.

Space of uses. Papers position NTREX-128 as part of a broader machine translation evaluation setup rather than as a standalone protocol. One paper lists it alongside FLORES-200, AfroLingu-MT, TICO-19, and MAFAND-MT under MT datasets, and no measurement instrument is formally linked to it in the recorded relationships.

nodes.name: Nucleotide Transformer Benchmark
nodes.definition: A collection of 18 downstream tasks for evaluating DNA foundation models, covering histone marker prediction, regulatory annotation, and splice site prediction.

nodes.name: NumGLUE
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, NumGLUE is most commonly described as a suite of mathematical or numerical reasoning tasks, though one definition frames it as a benchmark for numerical and quantitative reasoning. The definitions emphasize tasks that require understanding of numerical concepts and language, handling numbers in natural language contexts, and, in one paper’s phrasing, tasks that fundamentally involve arithmetic formula evaluation.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use NumGLUE to measure Mathematical reasoning. It is linked to 1 construct, Mathematical reasoning, and to no behavioral indicators, so the reported measurement use centers on that single construct; papers place it among in-domain datasets for mathematical reasoning and also group NumGLUE1 and NumGLUE2 under math-related tasks.

Space of uses. Papers typically use NumGLUE alongside other evaluation datasets, including GSM8K, MATH, Mathmeticas, SVAMP, and MathQA. In these accounts it appears as one part of a broader evaluation setup, for example as an in-domain dataset in a comprehensive assessment or as one of several benchmarks used to evaluate numerical reasoning.

nodes.name: OASST1
nodes.definition: OpenAssistant Conversations dataset, a human-generated and human-annotated assistant-style conversation dataset used to train and evaluate reward models.

nodes.name: Object HalBench
nodes.definition: Object HalBench is a benchmark for evaluating model hallucination at both the response level and mention level, focusing on object presence and attributes.

nodes.name: OCR-VQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across definitions, OCR-VQA is most commonly described as a visual question answering benchmark or dataset centered on text in images. Papers characterize it as requiring understanding, reading, or reasoning about text within images, using labels such as "text understanding VQA" and "text-in-image understanding"; the name also appears as OCRVQA and OCR VQA.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use OCR-VQA to measure 2 behavioral indicators and 2 constructs. The linked behavioral indicators are optical character recognition and visual question answering, and the linked constructs are document understanding and generalization. These measurement claims are spread across several targets rather than centered on a single one.

Space of uses. Papers do not relate OCR-VQA to any other measurement instrument. They more often place it inside broader evaluation suites, alongside datasets such as TextVQA, GQA, OKVQA, DocVQA, and VQAv2. Within those suites, it is used as a text-in-image evaluation, and some papers use it specifically to assess learned generalization ability or document understanding.

nodes.name: OCRBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, OCRBench is most commonly described as a benchmark for optical character recognition, often framed as evaluating OCR capabilities or text reading and text understanding in images or other visual inputs. Some authors use the spelling OCR-Bench, and one source abbreviates it as OCRB. A smaller line of description says it assesses a model's ability to recognize and reason about text within images using OCR tasks, but the prevailing usage remains an OCR-focused benchmark for large multimodal models.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use OCRBench to measure one behavioral indicator and three constructs. The dominant measurement claim is optical character recognition, and additional papers report it as measuring fine-grained visual understanding, fine-grained perception, and multimodal perception. Overall, the measurement claims center on OCR, with some broader perception-oriented framing around the same benchmark.

Space of uses. Across papers, OCRBench is usually used as part of broader evaluation suites rather than in isolation. It is frequently grouped with DocVQA, ChartQA, TextVQA, and InfoVQA in OCR-related, OCR-extensive, or OCR/document/chart under

nodes.name: ogbn-arxiv
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing description is a large-scale citation network benchmark for node classification in text-attributed graphs. Papers commonly describe nodes as papers, usually with title and abstract text, and edges as citations; some definitions further specify that it is an Open Graph Benchmark dataset, a directed graph of arXiv papers, or more specifically arXiv computer science papers.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link ogbn-arxiv to 2 behavioral indicators and no constructs. The dominant use is to measure Node classification, with relationship evidence describing node classification accuracy on ogbn-arxiv and listing it among datasets widely adopted for node classification; a smaller line of work uses it to measure Zero-shot classification, described as an initial investigation into leveraging GPT-3.5 on the dataset.

Space of uses. Papers usually position it as one benchmark within broader multi-dataset evaluations, often alongside Cora and PubMed, and sometimes with ogbn-products, CiteSeer, or Wiki-CS. It appears in performance tables and comparative experiments for node classification, and papers also use it for zero-shot classific

nodes.name: ogbn-products
nodes.definition: A large-scale graph dataset from the Open Graph Benchmark representing an Amazon product co-purchasing network, used for node classification.

nodes.name: OK-VQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats OK-VQA as an open-ended visual question answering benchmark or dataset whose questions require knowledge beyond what is directly visible in the image. Most definitions describe this as external or outside knowledge, while some specify commonsense, world knowledge, reasoning, or general knowledge questions; one study describes it as focusing on knowledge-based questions, one calls it open-domain, and some papers refer specifically to the validation split.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use OK-VQA to measure one behavioral indicator, Visual question answering, and six constructs. The most frequently linked constructs are Multimodal understanding, World knowledge, Generalization, and In-context learning, and papers also link it to other constructs, so the reported measurement claims are spread across several uses rather than centered on one; in these accounts it is used to assess multimodal vision-language capabilities, generalization ability, few-shot or in-context learning, and questions requiring outside or world knowledge.

Space of uses. In practice, papers usually place OK-VQA inside broader multimodal or VQA eva

nodes.name: OKTest
nodes.definition: A benchmark dataset for evaluating over-refusal, which includes 300 benign examples that contain sensitive terms but are fundamentally safe.

nodes.name: OLMES
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers describe OLMES as an evaluation suite for language models, covering multiple-choice and cloze-format tasks across knowledge and reasoning domains; one definition also says it uses manually curated in-context examples and calibration methods to improve reliability. Its contents are presented as a suite of benchmark tasks, with papers listing MMLU, ARC-Easy, ARC-Challenge, and CommonsenseQA among them, and another description also including BoolQ in a suite of 10 multiple choice question answering benchmarks.

What it is claimed to measure. The measurement claims converge on one behavioral indicator rather than spreading across constructs. Papers link OLMES to 1 behavioral indicator, Multiple-choice question answering, and to no constructs, and one paper explicitly describes it as a suite of multiple choice question answering benchmarks.

Space of uses. In use, papers adopt OLMES for evaluation and present it as a grouped suite of benchmarks. Across papers it is related to 10 instruments, including ARC-Challenge, HellaSwag, OpenBookQA, PIQA, and WinoGrande.

nodes.name: OlympiadBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Definitions split between two recurring descriptions: one line portrays it as an Olympiad-level benchmark for challenging mathematics problems, spanning high-school, college-level, and competition material, while another describes a bilingual multimodal version with 8,476 problems from Olympic-level mathematics and physics competitions. Across both descriptions, papers say it assesses advanced mathematical reasoning, and the multimodal framing adds high-level visual and logical reasoning. One paper also shortens the name to Olympiad and describes a challenging mathematical problem-solving dataset aimed at advanced reasoning and proof-like capabilities.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to 3 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators. The most common use is to measure Mathematical reasoning, while smaller strands use it to measure Reasoning and Generalization; papers also report it as measuring Mathematical problem solving and Scientific problem solving. Overall, the reported targets spread across several reasoning-related abilities, but they most often center on mathematical reasoning.

Space of uses. Across evaluations, it is commonly used alongside MATH or MA

nodes.name: OMMO
nodes.definition: A large-scale outdoor multimodal dataset and benchmark used as a test source for evaluating camera-operation performance.

nodes.name: Omni-Judge
nodes.definition: An open-source evaluation model developed to assess the consistency between model-generated solutions and reference answers for the Omni-MATH benchmark at a low cost.

nodes.name: Omni-MATH
OmniACT
nodes.definition: An existing dataset for desktop agent tasks, used as a source for constructing the GroundUI benchmark.

nodes.name: OmniEval
nodes.definition: An omnidirectional RAG benchmark in the financial domain that evaluates systems across 16 topics and 5 tasks using both rule-based and LLM-based metrics on auto-generated and human-annotated datasets.

nodes.name: OMOMO
nodes.definition: A dataset of human-object interactions used to assess the model's performance with novel objects not seen during training.

nodes.name: Online A/B testing
nodes.definition: A real-world evaluation method comparing user engagement metrics (PV CTR, UV CTR) between the proposed model and a baseline over a two-week period with live traffic.

nodes.name: OntologyRAG-Q
nodes.definition: A retrieval-augmented generation framework for Qur’anic Tafsir featuring Ayat-Ontology chunking, designed to evaluate verse-level retrieval and question answering using structured ontological context.

nodes.name: OntoNotes
nodes.definition: Coreference resolution dataset evaluating the model's ability to track entities across long texts.

nodes.name: Open LLM Leaderboard
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most papers describe the Open LLM Leaderboard as a public HuggingFace leaderboard or evaluation suite for ranking open or open-access LLMs on standardized downstream or academic benchmarks. The prevailing framing is an aggregate suite over reasoning and knowledge tasks, with recurring task lists that include ARC, HellaSwag, MMLU, TruthfulQA, and GSM8K, though other papers describe different subsets or broader versions. Some papers also treat it as an evaluation methodology, including few-shot or zero-shot/few-shot setups, and refer to versions such as v1, v2, and OpenLLM Leaderboard 2.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to 9 constructs and 3 behavioral indicators, so its reported measurement role is spread across many targets rather than centered on a single one. The most prominent construct links use it to measure general ability, truthfulness, alignment tax, commonsense reasoning, and instruction following ability, with four other construct links beyond these. Papers also describe the suite as giving a glimpse into model knowledge, reasoning, and truthfulness, and a smaller line of work uses it for three behavioral indicators.

Space of uses. In use, paper

nodes.name: Open LLM Leaderboard V1
names: Hugging Face Open LLM Leaderboard v1
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the definitions, the prevailing framing is of a public leaderboard and benchmark suite for open-source large language models. One paper describes v1 as evaluating and ranking models with publicly available weights, while another specifies that it covers MMLU, ARC-Challenge, GSM8K, HellaSwag, Winogrande, and TruthfulQA, using both log-likelihood and text-generation evaluations.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers describe it as assessing question-answering and reasoning tasks, and the task-level descriptions attached to the suite mention grade school math, world knowledge and reasoning, language understanding, and factual correctness. No named constructs or behavioral indicators are linked to it in the recorded relationships.

Space of uses. Papers use it as a public, and in one description popular, leaderboard that evaluates and ranks models with publicly available weights. Among the recorded instrument links, it is related to GSM8K and MMLU, and one paper states that these benchmarks are included in it; the suite definition also places it alongside ARC-Challenge, HellaSwag, Winogrande, and TruthfulQA.

nodes.name: Open LLM Leaderboard v2
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers commonly describe Open LLM Leaderboard v2, also written as Open LLM Leaderboard 2 or Huggingface Leaderboard v2, as a Hugging Face evaluation suite or public leaderboard for benchmarking and ranking LLMs on challenging downstream tasks. The prevailing description specifies six tasks, BBH, GPQA, IFEval, MATH-Hard or MATH Level 5, MMLU-Pro, and MuSR or MUSR, covering reasoning, knowledge or expert knowledge, advanced math, and instruction following, usually with accuracy-based scoring. Some definitions additionally frame it as a more challenging version of the earlier Open LLM Leaderboard, and one description notes that its scores are normalized to a 0 to 100 scale.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link this instrument to 3 constructs and no behavioral indicators. Different papers use it to measure General ability, Knowledge understanding, and World knowledge, so the recorded measurement claims name several broad constructs rather than a single one. The relationship language is consistent in treating the leaderboard as the instrument that measures those constructs.

Space of uses. In use, papers position it as a benchmark evaluation suite for model performanc

nodes.name: Open VLM Leaderboard
nodes.definition: An evaluation protocol and leaderboard for assessing the performance of vision-language models on a variety of tasks.

nodes.name: OpenAI Moderation API
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats OpenAI Moderation API as an OpenAI-provided content-safety tool or evaluation procedure for classifying text under safety policies. Definitions commonly describe it as assigning violation categories or scores for harms such as hate, harassment, self-harm, sexual content, and violence, and some papers add that it returns both a binary safe or harmful tag and a continuous harmfulness score. Papers use it to tag unsafe conversations, assess the safety of text data before and after alignment rewriting, detect and filter toxic or inappropriate content, and evaluate moderation or jailbreak responses; a smaller line of work refers to OpenAI Moderation as a query-classification benchmark or as a defense strategy in jailbreak evaluation.

What it is claimed to measure. In the recorded relationships, papers use it to measure 3 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators. The construct links are Toxicity, Harmlessness, and Safety, and the behavioral-indicator links are Content moderation and Harmful content generation. Across those claims, papers use it to flag unsafe or harmful text, judge whether a response is safe, and determine harmful con

nodes.name: OpenAI Moderation dataset
nodes.definition: A standard safety dataset used to evaluate the performance of guardrail models in detecting unsafe content.

nodes.name: OpenBookQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most descriptions frame OpenBookQA as a multiple-choice question answering benchmark or dataset modeled after open-book exams and centered on elementary science questions. Papers usually say it requires reasoning over a provided small set of science or common-knowledge facts, often together with external or general common knowledge, and some further describe it as commonsense, knowledge-intensive, or multi-hop reasoning. A smaller line treats it more broadly as open-domain or scientific-domain QA, and one paper describes OBQA as a VoiceBench subset. Papers also describe its size differently, with one stating 500 multiple-choice questions and others describing 5,957 science questions with four options.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use OpenBookQA to measure 12 constructs and 8 behavioral indicators. The prevailing framing is Commonsense reasoning, with recurring use for Natural language understanding and Reasoning; at the behavioral level, it is also used for Question answering and Multiple-choice question answering. Other construct and behavioral uses are also reported, so papers do not treat it as tied to only one target.

Space of uses. It is related to two o

nodes.name: OpenCompass
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most papers describe OpenCompass as an open-source evaluation framework or toolkit for standardized assessment of large language models across multiple benchmarks. Some narrow that description to a suite for several widely used zero-shot benchmarks, while another paper presents it as a platform that includes datasets such as MMBench v1.1, MMStar, MMMU val, MathVista, and OCRBench. One paper further describes using its official scripts, PPL mode, and zero-shot or few-shot prompting to score models across reasoning, language, knowledge, examination, and understanding.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, OpenCompass is linked to 1 construct, General ability, and no behavioral indicators. Papers use it to measure General ability by evaluating seven distinctive capabilities across 17 representative NLP datasets and by running regression tests on mainstream tasks for models' general capabilities. Claims about what it measures therefore converge on that single construct in the papers.

Space of uses. Papers usually position OpenCompass as the platform or framework used to evaluate benchmarks. It is related to 8 instruments, including PIQA, ARC-Challenge, ARC-Easy, C

nodes.name: OpenEQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. In the one definition, OpenEQA is treated as a dataset for Embodied Question Answering that offers "rich scenarios" for the task. It is described as providing instances that include a question, a ground truth answer, and associated episode memory from 3D environments.

What it is claimed to measure. The papers do not state that OpenEQA measures any named construct or behavioral indicator. In this literature, it is described as a dataset for the task rather than linked to particular constructs through reported measurement claims.

Space of uses. Usage is described narrowly. In "EQA-RM: A Generative Embodied Reward Model with Test-time Scaling," the authors say their dataset construction process "builds upon" OpenEQA, using its question, answer, and episode-memory format as a basis, and they also cite datasets like OpenEQA as offering rich scenarios for the task. No other instruments are described alongside it.

nodes.name: OpenHermes-2.5
nodes.definition: A dataset used for supervised fine-tuning and for constructing in-domain test sets to evaluate model perplexity.

nodes.name: OpenLID
nodes.definition: A language identification model used as an instrument to evaluate whether machine translation models generate outputs in the correct target language.

nodes.name: OpenOrca
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, OpenOrca is most commonly treated as an instruction and reasoning dataset used in supervised fine-tuning and evaluation. Some definitions broaden this to an ORCA family, including OPENORCA and SLIMORCA, described as fine-tuning datasets for instruction-following and as derived from explanations of chain-of-thought reasoning steps from larger models. A smaller framing presents Orca as an SFT collection that combines prior instruction-tuning data such as FLAN, T0, NIV, and CoT, and one paper describes OpenOrca as augmented FLAN collection data.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use OpenOrca to evaluate general reasoning and comprehension performance and instruction-following capabilities, and one paper also describes it as supporting in-domain test sets for model perplexity. These descriptions do not converge on one named construct, and no construct or behavioral indicator is linked to it.

Space of uses. Papers most often position OpenOrca as a supervised fine-tuning corpus, with some also using it as an evaluation or validation dataset. In reported setups it appears alongside GSM8K and ChatDoctor in fine-tuning experiments, alongside OpenHermes-2

nodes.name: OpenReview
nodes.definition: A benchmark dataset of ICLR 2023 peer reviews used for evaluating text classification in a centralized differentially private setting.

nodes.name: OpenTuringBench
nodes.definition: A large-scale benchmark (>500K texts) for evaluating machine-generated text detection and authorship attribution, featuring diverse OLLMs and challenging tasks including out-of-domain texts, unseen models, and human-machine mixing.

nodes.name: OpenWebText
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, OpenWebText is most commonly described as a large-scale text corpus or dataset, often an open-source replication of the WebText dataset, used for pre-training and validating language models. Some authors make the content more specific, describing it as a large-scale English, web-scraped corpus, and size estimates differ slightly, with definitions giving approximately 8 billion or 9 billion tokens. A smaller line of work defines it by experimental role, as a source of prompts for sentence continuation or as a text generation dataset for open-ended language completion evaluation.

What it is claimed to measure. Its recorded measurement links converge on one behavioral indicator: papers link it to 1 behavioral indicator, Text generation, and to no constructs. This aligns with definitions that describe it as evaluating open-ended language completion performance and with relationship evidence where papers report text generation experiments on OpenWebText or compare unconditional samples on OpenWebText.

Space of uses. Papers most often use OpenWebText as training data, especially for GPT-2 style pretraining, and some also use it for validation, including valid

nodes.name: OpenWebText2
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the definitions, OpenWebText2 is most commonly described as a large-scale web-text corpus or dataset. Papers characterize it as text extracted from URLs shared on Reddit and used to evaluate language model performance via perplexity, while another description treats it more generally as an evaluation corpus for computing Diff-eRank and reduced loss.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers do not explicitly link OpenWebText2 to any construct or behavioral indicator. Rather than presenting it as a measure of a named construct, they describe it operationally as a corpus used for evaluation through perplexity, Diff-eRank, and reduced loss.

Space of uses. The reported usage is mainly evaluative. One paper compares model performance on OpenWebText2, and another considers including it when computing Diff-eRank and also lists it alongside Wikipedia and other pre-training datasets for OPT models.

nodes.name: OpinionQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats OpinionQA as a survey-based benchmark or dataset built from Pew Research's American Trends Panel, using public opinion questions and demographic-group response distributions to compare model outputs with those of U.S. respondents. Definitions often describe it as multiple-choice survey or QA data covering topics such as science, politics, health, and personal relationships, and some specify versions such as a subsampled train/test split or a U.S. opinions subset labeled OQA or OpinionQA W27. A smaller line of work refers to "OpinionsQA" as persona data used in prior work to learn persona embeddings and soft prompts.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use OpinionQA to measure 2 constructs and no behavioral indicators. The linked constructs are Personalization and Pluralistic alignment, both through measured_by relations: personalization work describes it as a dataset proposed to measure the steerability of LLMs for specific users or social groups, while pluralistic-alignment work places it among datasets for quantifying distributional alignment. These claims therefore span more than one construct, although the dominant d

nodes.name: OPUS-100
nodes.definition: A multilingual machine translation dataset used for training and robustness experiments across multiple language directions.

nodes.name: OR-Bench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across definitions, OR-Bench is most commonly described as a large-scale benchmark for over-refusal in LLMs: papers describe it as the first large-scale over-refusal benchmark, with 80,000 prompts across 10 common rejection categories, framed as safe prompts that are likely to be incorrectly rejected. Some papers refer specifically to OR-Bench-80K, while later uses also mention a 1k-prompt subset and a moderated prompt pool following the canonical OR-Bench methodology. A smaller use treats it as a source of complied benign inputs contrasted with complied harmful inputs.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link OR-Bench to 1 behavioral indicator, Overrefusal, and to no constructs. The measure claim converges on that single indicator: papers say they evaluate over-refusal using OR-Bench, introduce it as an over-refusal benchmark, and use 1k prompts from it to represent overrefusal behaviors. Some descriptions also frame this use as evaluating false-positive refusal rates in LLMs.

Space of uses. No other measurement instrument is linked to OR-Bench. Papers position it both as the released benchmark itself and as a comparison or baseline resource: some use OR-Bench-80K

nodes.name: OR-Bench-Hard-1K
nodes.definition: A challenging subset of OR-Bench containing 1,000 safe prompts that are rejected by at least three state-of-the-art models, used to evaluate over-refusal in high-performance LLMs.

nodes.name: OR-QuAC
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the cited definitions, OR-QuAC is treated as a conversational question answering dataset. The prevailing description emphasizes open-retrieval settings with conversational, multi-turn queries and associated passages, while another paper highlights that it includes context-independent rewrites of dialogue questions, allowing those questions to be posed without prior context and used in both dialogue-based and isolated-question evaluation.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers do not explicitly link OR-QuAC to any construct or behavioral indicator, so the sources do not frame it as measuring a named construct. Instead, they describe it as an evaluation dataset for conversational QA, including use in dialogue-based settings and in settings where rewritten questions can be asked independently of earlier turns.

Space of uses. In the papers, OR-QuAC appears as part of broader evaluation suites alongside QuAC, CoQA, and DoQA. One study includes it in the main evaluation on widely used conversational search datasets, and another uses it to assess generalization beyond the training distribution.

nodes.name: OSWorld
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats OSWorld as a real computer environment and benchmark for open-ended computer tasks with multimodal or OS agents. Definitions commonly describe it as an interactive testbed spanning Ubuntu, Windows, and macOS, with 369 tasks involving real web and desktop applications and execution-based evaluation; some authors stress that agents must interact with the operating system step by step and wait for a response before continuing, while another paper uses it more briefly as a desktop virtual agent benchmark for trajectory collection and evaluation.

What it is claimed to measure. Claims about what OSWorld measures are spread across five constructs and one behavioral indicator rather than concentrating on a single target. Papers most often use it to measure Generalization, while smaller lines of work use it for Adaptability, Agency, Commonsense reasoning, and Robustness; it is also linked to one behavioral indicator, with one benchmark description saying results reveal weaknesses in GUI grounding and operational knowledge.

Space of uses. In use, papers position OSWorld as a challenging or comprehensive benchmark for evaluating multi-s

nodes.name: Overcooked-AI
nodes.definition: An open-source, multi-agent collaborative game environment involving chefs preparing and serving meals, which serves as the foundation for the Collab-Overcooked benchmark.

nodes.name: OWL
nodes.definition: A dataset of 31.5K aligned literary excerpts from 20 books in ten languages, including original English texts, official translations, and newly machine-translated texts in six low-resource languages, used to probe multilingual and cross-lingual memorization in LLMs.

nodes.name: Oxford Flowers-102
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the dominant framing is a flower image classification benchmark for fine-grained recognition. Definitions variously call it Flowers-102, Flower-102, Flowers102, Oxford Flowers, OxfordFlowers, or the Oxford 102 Flowers dataset, and some descriptions specify fine-grained classification of 102 different flower species or categories. Most papers describe it broadly as an image or visual classification dataset, while smaller lines of work describe it more specifically as a zero-shot classification benchmark, a few-shot learning dataset, a fine-grained visual recognition dataset, or a benchmark used to evaluate personalized and generalized performance across clients.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to 2 behavioral indicators and no constructs. The prevailing use is to measure Image classification: papers report using Flowers102 among image classification benchmarks, to test downstream performance, or for zero-shot classification. A smaller line of work uses it to measure Fine-grained visual recognition, so the linked claims stay with behavioral indicators rather than constructs.

Space of uses. Papers usually place it inside broader benchmark sui

nodes.name: Oxford-IIIT Pets
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most commonly, papers treat Oxford-IIIT Pets as an image or visual classification benchmark. Definitions describe it as an image classification benchmark used for evaluating prediction correctness, while some papers frame it more specifically as a fine-grained pet-breed dataset, including a version described as pet images grouped into 37 breeds and used for fine-grained classification or few-shot learning. Quoted passages also place it in broader evaluation suites, for example as one of several datasets used for zero-shot and linear-probe image classification or as one of several visual classification datasets used to study personalization, generalization, and privacy.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link this instrument to one behavioral indicator, Image classification, and to no constructs. The prevailing measurement claim is focused: papers use it to measure Image classification, rather than a wider set of linked outcomes. Definitions also say it is used to evaluate prediction correctness, few-shot learning performance, and personalized and generalized performance across clients, but papers do not link it to additional constructs or behavioral indicators.

Spa

nodes.name: P-MMEval
nodes.definition: A parallel multilingual multitask benchmark covering fundamental NLP and capability-specialized tasks across 10 languages, designed for consistent evaluation of LLMs.

nodes.name: P(True)
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing usage is a prompt-based self-assessment method: a model is queried directly, often with a simple template, to judge whether its own generated answer is correct, and the probability of outputting "True" is taken as the score. Definitions variously present it as hallucination detection, error detection, or uncertainty quantification, but they converge on self-critique of a generated response. A smaller framing names a "P(True) baseline" protocol that first generates a completion for an input, concatenates the input and completion, and then asks the model to answer with "true" or "false" only.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to score the model's own assessment of answer correctness, and they also describe that score as a confidence or uncertainty measure. No constructs are linked to it and no behavioral indicators are linked to it, so the papers do not connect it to a named construct; instead they describe it at the level of correctness, confidence, uncertainty, hallucination detection, or error detection.

Space of uses. When papers position it relative to other methods, the prevailing role is as a baseline or representative

nodes.name: PAIR
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats PAIR as Prompt Automatic Iterative Refinement, a black-box jailbreak attack or procedure in which an attacker or red-teaming LLM automatically and iteratively generates or refines prompts until a target model is jailbroken. Several papers phrase this as a multi-turn conversation approach, a query-based attack, or a prompt-level jailbreak that uses prompt optimization, and some describe it more generally as an algorithmic attack method for generating jailbreak prompts. A smaller set of definitions departs from this framing, with one paper describing PAIR as population-based and another using the name for a Likert-style prompt that assesses whether a response "violates ethical, legal, or safety guidelines."

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link PAIR to one construct and two behavioral indicators. It is reported as measuring Jailbreaking and Jailbreak resistance, and one line of work also uses it to measure Harmlessness, including benchmark comparisons that report harmfulness scores and attack success rates under PAIR. Overall, the recorded links are narrow, covering those three targets.

Space of uses. It is comm

nodes.name: PakBBQ
nodes.definition: Pakistani Bias Benchmark for Question Answering, a culturally and regionally adapted bias benchmark for QA tailored to the Pakistani context, with versions in English and Urdu.

nodes.name: PandaLM
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the definitions, PandaLM is most commonly described as a fine-tuned LLM judge, based on Llama-7b, for preference judgment and automated evaluation of other LLMs. Some papers refer to the model specifically as PandaLM-7B and describe it as scoring or selecting outputs, while another definition presents it as a fine-tuned judge benchmark, trained on human preference data, that is used to evaluate model outputs.

What it is claimed to measure. In the recorded links, papers use PandaLM to measure one construct and one behavioral indicator: Helpfulness and Instruction following. The helpfulness link is explicit, with one paper saying it uses PandaLM "to evaluate the helpfulness of various models," while another paper frames PandaLM as addressing "relative conciseness, clarity, adherence to instructions, comprehensiveness, and formality," which is recorded as measuring instruction following.

Space of uses. In the descriptions, PandaLM is used as an automated judge in evaluator comparisons, and no measurement instrument is linked to it. Papers place it alongside other judge models such as JudgeLM and GPT-4, and another paper uses it as a comparison point when assessing

nodes.name: PAP
nodes.definition: Benchmark that uses persuasive language to evade safety filters, testing a model's ability to resist manipulation through rhetorical techniques.

nodes.name: ParaDetox
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across definitions and quoted passages, ParaDetox is described as a dataset of paired toxic and non-toxic paraphrased sentences. Papers characterize it as containing pairwise toxic and non-toxic sentences generated using paraphrasing, and one definition says it is used to identify toxicity-related features in a model's activations.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use ParaDetox to measure one construct and one behavioral indicator. One usage measures Toxicity from its paired toxic and non-toxic sentences, while another reports using it for Conditional text generation and describes it as imposing the strongest conditional constraints among the compared datasets.

Space of uses. Papers do not link ParaDetox to other measurement instruments. In the usage in the papers evidence, one paper uses it alongside RocStories when contrasting datasets with different levels of conditional constraints, positioning ParaDetox as the more strongly constrained option rather than the relatively open-ended one.

nodes.name: ParaRel
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, ParaRel is treated as a factual knowledge dataset for studying relational knowledge in language models. The prevailing description is a collection of paraphrased relational facts, formatted as ⟨subject, relation, object⟩ triples with multiple query variations; another definition also describes it as being used in an independent multi-problem question answering setting.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link ParaRel to 2 behavioral indicators and no constructs. Its reported measurement use is concentrated on question-answering behavior: papers use it to measure Question answering and Open-domain question answering, including one formulation where "Given a question, the model directly predicts its answer" and another where it provides "factual information from open-domain question answering (OQA)".

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to ParaRel. In the papers, it is used as a named evaluation dataset that authors "employ," and one paper places it alongside HotpotQA within a question-answering evaluation.

nodes.name: PartNet-Mobility
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, PartNet-Mobility is most commonly described as a large-scale dataset of 3D articulated objects with part-level segmentation and kinematic information, used for training and evaluating articulation and reconstruction tasks. A smaller framing presents it as articulated 3D objects used within the SAPIEN simulation environment to define seen and unseen manipulation tasks for evaluation. One paper also specifies a subset of five categories: Laptop, Box, Refrigerator, Storage-Furniture, and Table.

What it is claimed to measure. Its reported measurement role is narrow rather than spread across many targets: papers use it to measure one construct, Generalization, and one behavioral indicator, Joint prediction. The Generalization link is described through validation on an extensive test set of unseen objects, while the Joint prediction link is described through quantitative analysis on the entire dataset and reported success-rate gains over prior work.

Space of uses. Papers commonly position PartNet-Mobility as an evaluation resource: one paper says it validates performance on the dataset and fine-tunes a pre-trained model using its data, and another uses it

nodes.name: Pascal Context
nodes.definition: A dataset providing dense semantic labels for the PASCAL VOC images, used for open-vocabulary segmentation.

nodes.name: PASCAL VOC
nodes.definition: The PASCAL Visual Object Classes benchmark, used here for open-vocabulary segmentation.

nodes.name: Passkey retrieval
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats passkey retrieval as a synthetic long-context task or benchmark in which a model must recover a random passkey, usually a five-digit number, hidden at some depth in a long document or in long, meaningless or distracting text. Definitions differ slightly in calling it a task, benchmark, or evaluation protocol, but they converge on the same setup: the model is asked to find, retrieve, and sometimes repeat a short target token embedded within a lengthy context. Some papers further describe it as a needle-in-haystack setting for testing long-range dependency, information retention, or the maximum distance that a token can attend to during inference.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link this instrument to 1 construct and 2 behavioral indicators. The most common use is to measure Synthetic recall, with papers describing it as assessing whether a model can retrieve an n-digit or five-digit passkey from a large context, and one paper reporting "perfect memory recall on the Passkey Retrieval task." A smaller line of work uses it to measure Context retrieval, and another uses it to measure Long-context understanding, describing th

nodes.name: PatentScore
nodes.definition: A multi-dimensional evaluation framework for patent claims that integrates structural, legal, and semantic metrics through LLM-based prompting and weighted aggregation, aligned with WIPO and USPTO standards.

nodes.name: PathVQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most commonly, papers describe PathVQA as a medical or biomedical visual question answering dataset or benchmark centered on pathology images. The definitions mostly converge on that framing, while differing in emphasis: one says the pathology images are drawn from textbooks and online libraries, others say it tests a model's ability to answer questions about histopathology slides, and another says it targets interpretation of complex visual medical information.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link PathVQA to 2 behavioral indicators and no constructs. The prevailing usage is to treat it as measuring medical visual question answering, with papers using it as a Med-VQA benchmark and reporting performance on it for medical VQA tasks; some papers use it more broadly to measure visual question answering, including statements that PathVQA and Q-VQA assess VQA performance. In these papers, its measurement claims stay within VQA-related behavioral indicators rather than extending to other constructs.

Space of uses. Papers usually position PathVQA as one dataset within a broader evaluation suite, most often alongside SLAKE and VQA-RAD, and in some cases with IU-Xray, Omn

nodes.name: PAWS
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing framing is PAWS as a benchmark or dataset for paraphrase detection or paraphrase identification. Definitions describe it as evaluating whether two sentences are semantically equivalent and helping assess whether models distinguish paraphrases from non-paraphrases, and one paper further characterizes it as sentence pairs with high lexical overlap that may still have different meanings. Some authors also expand the name as Paraphrase Adversaries from Word Scrambling.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers most commonly use PAWS to measure paraphrase detection, and it is linked to 1 behavioral indicator, Paraphrase detection. Beyond that dominant use, it is linked to 1 construct, Out-of-distribution generalization: a smaller line of work uses PAWS as an OOD evaluation dataset for paraphrase identification and reports it as suitable for evaluating OOD robustness.

Space of uses. No other measurement instrument is linked to it. Papers position PAWS as one task within broader evaluation suites, including dataset compositions for paraphrase detection, multi-task finetuning across diverse tasks, OOD evaluation for paraphrase identificati

nodes.name: PAWS-X
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, PAWS-X is most commonly treated as a multilingual benchmark or dataset for paraphrase identification, where the model must decide whether two sentences have the same meaning. Some authors frame it more broadly as a multilingual natural language understanding benchmark for evaluating performance across languages, while others describe paired sentences across seven languages, adversarially constructed paraphrase pairs, and a task of distinguishing semantically equivalent sentences from near-duplicates. Definitions also mention both full multilingual use and, in one application, the Spanish portion of the dataset.

What it is claimed to measure. Its reported measurement role is concentrated: papers link it to 1 behavioral indicator, Paraphrase detection, and to no constructs. The prevailing usage is to treat PAWS-X as measuring paraphrase identification or paraphrase detection, including in descriptions of a cross-lingual adversarial dataset for paraphrase identification.

Space of uses. No other measurement instruments are linked to it. Papers commonly place it inside broader multilingual evaluation suites, for example among several benchmarks covering reas

nodes.name: PCam
nodes.definition: A benchmark for medical imaging, specifically for identifying metastatic tissue in histopathologic scans of lymph node sections.

nodes.name: PCFG SET
nodes.definition: A dataset of ten string-edit operations based on a probabilistic context-free grammar, used to evaluate compositional sequence-to-sequence behaviors in language models.

nodes.name: PDDL
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers describe PDDL as a benchmark for evaluating LLM agents on planning tasks expressed in PDDL-style environments. In AgentSquare: Automatic LLM Agent Search in Modular Design Space, it appears within a broader evaluation set described as "covering diverse use cases in web, embodied, tool use and game scenarios."

What it is claimed to measure. Papers do not link PDDL to any constructs or behavioral indicators through explicit measurement relationships. The only stated target is evaluating LLM agents on planning tasks expressed in PDDL-style environments, rather than a named construct or behavioral indicator.

Space of uses. The paper uses PDDL as a benchmark within an evaluation suite for LLM agents. No other measurement instruments are linked to it, so the evidence does not show a recurring pattern of using it alongside particular named benchmarks or as an auxiliary check.

nodes.name: Perception Test
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across these papers, Perception Test is most commonly described as a video perception or video understanding benchmark, often framed as a diagnostic for multimodal video models or MLLMs. Definitions recurrently say it assesses visual understanding over video sequences and fine-grained perception, and several also extend this to reasoning, logical inference, scene understanding, object tracking, and spatial awareness. Some authors narrow it to a video multiple-choice question answering dataset, while others describe an open-set benchmark with action-related questions or a diagnostic that covers skills such as memory, abstraction, physics, and semantics across video, audio, and text modalities.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the surveyed use, claims mostly converge on Video understanding: papers use Perception Test to measure that construct, and papers link it to 2 constructs in total and no behavioral indicators. One paper additionally reports that Perception Test is related to Reasoning, describing it as focused on skills and types of reasoning such as descriptive, explanatory, predictive, and counterfactual reasoning.

Space of uses. Most papers position Percep

nodes.name: Perspective API
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing description is an external API or automated tool for toxicity assessment, used to score text for harmful language. Most definitions describe an overall toxicity score, often on a 0 to 1 scale, plus finer-grained attribute scores such as severe toxicity, threat, profanity, insult, and identity attack. The granularity varies across papers: some refer to six toxicity attributes, some select five aspects for safety evaluation, and one paper uses eight attributes including sexually explicit and flirtation. A smaller line of work describes it as a moderation tool, or as a benchmark or model for toxic detection.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to two constructs and one behavioral indicator. The dominant use is to measure Toxicity, with papers describing it as toxicity evaluation, toxic language and hate speech detection, or a toxicity behavior function for model generations. More narrowly, some papers use Perspective API metrics such as Expected Maximum Toxicity and Toxicity Probability to measure Harmlessness, and several papers report it as measuring Harmful content generation or the harmfulness of responses. Overall, these claims

nodes.name: PG-19
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing description is a long-context or long-form language modeling dataset or benchmark built from Project Gutenberg books. Some authors specify it as an open-vocabulary collection with 11 gigabytes of text from over 28,000 books published before 1919, while others describe evaluation slices such as 100 books, 100 long books, 25 sampled documents, or samples averaging about 69k words, and they use validation, test, held-out, or truncated documents for extended-context next-token or perplexity evaluation.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link PG-19 to five constructs and no behavioral indicators. The most common measured_by claims use it to measure Length generalization and Long-context understanding, usually through perplexity at varying context lengths or length extrapolation on held-out documents, while other papers use it to measure Continual learning, Fluency, and Language modeling ability.

Space of uses. In use, papers most commonly report perplexity, word-level perplexity, or next-token generation on long books and long documents, including streaming or infinite-length settings and context-length sweeps from 4k to 32k tokens. A small

nodes.name: PGD
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the definitions, PGD is treated as an iterative adversarial attack that repeatedly takes small steps in the gradient direction and projects each update back into a constrained perturbation space. One definition further specifies it as a white-box attack, and some usage is stated specifically as PGD-l∞, where the projection keeps perturbations within ε∞ constraints; papers also describe it as a method for crafting or generating adversarial examples.

What it is claimed to measure. The papers do not report PGD as measuring any construct or behavioral indicator, and no linked target construct is identified.

Space of uses. One paper explicitly employs PGD-l∞ alongside CW-l2 as two standard adversarial attack methods, while other papers refer to PGD more generally as an iterative approach for crafting adversarial examples.

nodes.name: PGPS9K
nodes.definition: A benchmark dataset for geometry problem solving that includes high-quality diagrams and detailed annotations.

nodes.name: PHEME
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers describe PHEME as a benchmark dataset for fake news detection made up of tweets related to five major news events. One definition also specifies its split and scale, stating that it contains 1,414 training tweets and 608 testing tweets.

What it is claimed to measure. In the recorded uses, papers use PHEME to measure misinformation detection. It is linked to 1 behavioral indicator and no constructs, so the reported measurement claim is concentrated on that single behavioral indicator rather than spread across multiple outcomes.

Space of uses. Across the cited studies, PHEME is used alongside Twitter and Weibo in one evaluation setup, and alongside Weibo21 and LLM-mis in another. Papers position it as one of several public or widely-used benchmark datasets for experiments, rather than as a standalone evaluation protocol.

nodes.name: PHTest
nodes.definition: Benchmark dataset for assessing over-refusal behaviors in language models using pseudo-harmful prompts.

nodes.name: Pick-a-Pic
nodes.definition:
What it is. In the description, Pick-a-Pic is framed as a large-scale open dataset derived from a web platform that collects real users' creative intention, and papers present it as being used to evaluate generation alignment with user preference.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link Pick-a-Pic to one construct, Text-image alignment, and to no behavioral indicators. In the recorded measured_by relationship, it is used to measure Text-image alignment, with one paper describing it as one of several text-to-image evaluation benchmarks used to score agreement with human judgments of alignment for images generated from complex text prompts, so the reported claims converge on a single construct rather than spreading across many.

Space of uses. The recorded relationships do not link Pick-a-Pic to other measurement instruments, but one paper positions it alongside DrawBench, EditBench, COCO-T2I, and TIFA160 as one of five text-to-image evaluation benchmarks. In that usage, it appears as part of a benchmark set for evaluating alignment against human judgments on generated images.

nodes.name: Pile-10k
nodes.definition: A 10,000-document subset of The Pile, a large and diverse text corpus, used for evaluating language model perplexity.

nodes.name: Pile-CC
nodes.definition: A component of The Pile dataset derived from the CommonCrawl web corpus, used in this study as a key validation set to predict downstream performance.

nodes.name: PIQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, PIQA is most commonly described as the Physical Interaction: Question Answering benchmark or dataset for physical commonsense reasoning about everyday objects and situations. Definitions usually present it as multiple-choice question answering, often asking a model to choose the more physically plausible solution or action, and many papers use it in zero-shot evaluation. Some papers also refer to it as "Reasoning about Physical Commonsense in Natural Language"; a few descriptions instead call it a generative QA dataset or use the name "Physical Interaction Quality Assessment," and one paper says it contains 21k questions across different subsets.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link PIQA to 11 constructs and 11 behavioral indicators. The prevailing claim is that it measures Commonsense reasoning, and it is also repeatedly used to measure Reasoning and Physical world understanding, while the remaining construct links are spread across eight other framings. At the behavioral level, papers most often use it for Zero-shot question answering and Zero-shot task performance, with nine other indicators also linked.

Space of uses. In use, papers usually pl

nodes.name: PKU
nodes.definition: Chinese word segmentation dataset used to evaluate tokenization performance in character-dense language processing.

nodes.name: PKU-SafeRLHF
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most commonly, papers treat PKU-SafeRLHF, also written SafeRLHF or Safe-RLHF, as a human-annotated preference dataset or public benchmark for safety alignment. Definitions usually describe prompt or instruction-response comparisons with paired responses and labels for helpfulness and harmlessness or safety, and some papers further describe safe and unsafe response pairs, conversation comparisons, and safety-focused coverage such as insults, immorality, crime, emotional harm, and privacy. A smaller line emphasizes it as a harmful-query or red-teaming test set for out-of-distribution evaluation, and papers describe its overall scale differently.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, the dominant use is to measure harmlessness and helpfulness: papers link it to five constructs and no behavioral indicators, with harmlessness and helpfulness appearing most often. Smaller lines of work use it to measure generalization or safety, and one paper relates PKU-SafeRLHF to safety alignment rather than treating it as a direct measure. Overall, the measurement claims are concentrated on harmlessness and helpfulness rather than evenly spread across the linked constructs.

Spac

nodes.name: PKU-SafeRLHF-10K
nodes.definition: A dataset containing 10,000 human-labeled preference pairs on the helpfulness and harmlessness of responses, used for fine-tuning and aligning large language models for safety.

nodes.name: Places365
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, Places365 is most commonly described as a large-scale scene-centric image dataset with 365 scene categories, used for scene recognition or classification tasks. A smaller framing presents it as a scene classification benchmark used to evaluate descriptions on scene categories, so papers alternate between calling it a dataset and a benchmark while keeping the same scene-category focus.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the papers, Places365 is used to measure Image classification, and this is its only linked behavioral indicator. It is not linked to any constructs, so the reported measurement use centers on 1 behavioral indicator rather than multiple constructs or indicators.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it. Papers position Places365 as part of broader multi-dataset evaluations, for example alongside CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and CUB, and another paper includes it among 12 image recognition datasets; one study also notes that "BLIP2 FlanT5 performs better on the Places365 dataset," explicitly treating it as a scene classification dataset.

nodes.name: PlanBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the cited definitions, the prevailing framing is as a benchmark for evaluating planning in LLMs. One definition narrows this to planning and Reasoning about Actions and Change, while another describes PlanBench as using Planning Domain Description Language problems converted into natural language to evaluate planning and reasoning abilities.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link PlanBench to one construct and no behavioral indicators, and the linked construct is Planning. The measurement claims therefore converge on planning rather than spreading across multiple targets, with one paper citing PlanBench among specialized benchmarks used in discussions of complex planning or multi-step reasoning challenges.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it. In the papers that mention it, PlanBench is used chiefly as a comparison point for other benchmarks, including side by side contrasts with prior Reasoning about Actions and Change benchmarks, and it is also grouped with closely related work that converts Planning Domain Description Language problems into natural language.

nodes.name: PLLuM-Align
nodes.definition: Polish preference dataset containing human-annotated response ratings, rankings, and multi-turn dialogues for evaluating alignment in Polish LLMs.

nodes.name: Plutus-ben
nodes.definition: The first Greek financial evaluation benchmark, assessing LLMs across six tasks: numeric NER, textual NER, question answering, extractive summarization, abstractive summarization, and topic classification using expert-annotated Greek financial datasets.

nodes.name: PMC-VQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, PMC-VQA is described as a medical or clinical visual question answering dataset. Definitions differ in emphasis: one treats it simply as a clinical VQA dataset mentioned for comparison, another calls it a multi-modal, multiple-choice VQA dataset derived from medical literature where models choose the correct answer from four options, and another describes a large-scale medical VQA dataset that evaluates deriving answers from both text and images in scientific publications.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link PMC-VQA to 2 behavioral indicators and no constructs. The reported measurement use is concentrated on medical visual question answering and visual question answering: papers use it to measure those VQA-related behaviors, including as a medical VQA dataset in evaluation and under the task type Visual Question Answering. The recorded relationships do not extend beyond these VQA-related behavioral indicators.

Space of uses. In use, papers place PMC-VQA among other medical VQA evaluation datasets. One paper evaluates a method on PMC-VQA alongside SLAKE and VQA-RAD, another lists it under the task type Visual Question Answering, and a

nodes.name: PMO
nodes.definition: Practical Molecular Optimization (PMO), a benchmark of molecular generation tasks used to evaluate optimization performance across many target properties and structures.

nodes.name: Pointwise rating
nodes.definition: An evaluation method where an LLM is prompted to assign a numerical score to individual answers based on their correctness, which are then compared to establish a preference.

nodes.name: PoisonedRAG
nodes.definition: A baseline RAG attack method that uses poisoned documents to manipulate retrieval and responses.

nodes.name: PolitiFact
nodes.definition: A dataset of real-world viral claims spread online, verified by journalists, used to assess models' ability to handle real-world misinformation.

nodes.name: PolitiFact (FakeNewsNet)
nodes.definition: A real-world human-written misinformation dataset focused on political fake news, used as a source for generating new misinformation and as a baseline for comparison.

nodes.name: POPE
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most papers describe POPE as a benchmark or dataset for evaluating object hallucination in multimodal or vision-language models through binary questions about whether an object is present in an image, often with short yes/no or true/false answers. The common format is three balanced splits or sampling settings, Popular, Random, and Adversarial, and some definitions say objects not present in the image are sampled under these strategies; several papers also call it a polling-based evaluation, a binary classification query dataset, or a VQA protocol, and one paper describes it as using MSCOCO object annotations. A smaller line describes it more broadly as a hallucination VQA benchmark, one paper labels it multi-choice VQA, and one paper instead expands it as "Positional Object Perception Evaluation" for fine-grained localization and counting.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, the dominant claim is that papers use POPE to measure object hallucination, and more broadly hallucination, in multimodal or vision-language models. Papers also report it as measuring visual question answering, visual hallucination, and visual understanding, but these are secondary frami

nodes.name: PopQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, PopQA is most commonly described as an open-domain question-answering dataset or benchmark, often entity-centric and focused on rare entities, long-tail knowledge, or questions spanning a wide range of entity popularity. Some descriptions make this more concrete by calling it a large-scale resource with 14K questions or 14k entity-centric QA pairs, while a smaller line of work says it is derived from Wikidata triples or frames it as single-hop QA that is difficult to answer from parametric memory alone. Variants and formats also differ by use: one study uses a long-tail subset of 1,399 rare entity queries, and another turns its questions into a closed-book sentence-completion task.

What it is claimed to measure. Measurement claims center on 2 behavioral indicators, especially open-domain question answering and a broader question-answering framing. Papers also use PopQA to measure 4 constructs, most visibly factual knowledge, knowledge conflict resolution, memorization, and out-of-distribution generalization. Taken together, the construct-level uses are spread across several targets rather than concentrated on one.

Space of uses. Papers usually include P

nodes.name: PoSum-Bench
nodes.definition: A bilingual benchmark for evaluating positional bias in conversational summarization, covering English and French datasets across formal meetings, casual dialogues, and customer service interactions, with a reference-free evaluation framework based on semantic similarity.

nodes.name: Prefilling attack
nodes.definition: An adversarial attack method used for evaluation where the model's generation is prefixed with an affirmative phrase (e.g., 'Sure, I’m happy to help with that.') to test its vulnerability to jailbreaking.

nodes.name: Presidio
nodes.definition: Data protection and de-identification API used to identify and classify personally identifiable information (PII) types in text, including name, gender, race, date-time, and location.

nodes.name: PricingLogic
nodes.definition: Benchmark comprising 300 natural-language questions derived from 42 real-world tourism pricing policies, assessing LLMs on customer-type pricing and bundled-tour discount reasoning across three difficulty levels.

nodes.name: PRISM
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most descriptions treat PRISM as a chat or preference dataset built from multi-turn conversations between humans and LLMs. In that usage it is described as globally diverse, focused on values and controversial opinions, and as containing 27,172 conversations used to solicit human feedback for preference alignment across 9 speaker features and 60 demographic groups; papers also differ on annotation format, describing both N-way preference ratings and binary choices. A smaller line of work uses the same name differently, either for Posterior-Refined Inference for Subset Membership, which updates an LR-Attack score with a world-model prior, or for a reference-free quality estimation procedure that uses a multilingual machine translation model with forced decoding to score other models’ outputs.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers do not link PRISM to any constructs or behavioral indicators through measured_by relationships. Where authors describe its target directly, the dataset form is framed around collecting preference ratings and human feedback for preference alignment, evaluating conversational preferences, and focusing on values and controversial opinions, rather

nodes.name: PRM800K
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most commonly, papers describe PRM800K as a dataset for mathematical reasoning with step-by-step, human or manually annotated process-level feedback. The descriptions vary in emphasis: some present mathematical or MATH problems with step-by-step solutions labeled for correctness, some describe each reasoning step as positive, negative, or neutral, and one paper describes 80,000 incorrect stepwise student solutions from MATH, with 2,077 test examples marked at the first error step. A smaller usage note refers to the easy, level 1-3 portion of the dataset.

What it is claimed to measure. Across these papers, PRM800K is described through its annotations on reasoning steps, but it is not linked to any named construct or behavioral indicator through explicit measurement claims. No constructs and no behavioral indicators are linked to it.

Space of uses. The prevailing usage is as a training or benchmark resource for process-supervised or step-level modeling in math reasoning. Papers describe training a step-level PRM on PRM800K, training policy and reward models on its easy portion, and using it as a benchmark dataset for labeled MATH solutions; one study also pairs training

nodes.name: PRMBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, PRMBench is most commonly described as a benchmark dataset for process-level reward models in reasoning chains, built on the PRM800K corpus and focused on step-level correctness in multi-step problem solving. Definitions describe it as covering about 6k math problems across 9 error categories, while one benchmark description gives a more exact inventory of 6,216 problems and 83,456 step-level labels, aimed at reasoning correctness and error detection.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to measure 2 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator. The prevailing links are that PRMBench measures Soundness and Simplicity, and one paper also reports it as measuring Error analysis, describing the benchmark as supporting granular error diagnosis; the reported uses therefore span a small set of process-evaluation targets rather than a single repeated construct.

Space of uses. Papers typically position PRMBench as one evaluation dataset within a broader suite. As one study notes, "We evaluate on four datasets: PRMBench, DeltaBench, ClaimTrees, and CaptainCookRecipes" (Probabilistic Soundness Guarantees in LLM Reasoning Chains), while another paper re

nodes.name: ProcessBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, the prevailing description is a benchmark for mathematical reasoning that provides step-by-step solutions with human annotation of where errors occur. One recurring formulation is that it contains 3,400 test cases or problems, mainly competition- and Olympiad-level math, with annotations by multiple human experts and four subsets, as described in ProcessBench: Identifying Process Errors in Mathematical Reasoning. Other papers describe the same resource more generally as containing human-annotated stepwise labels for mathematical solutions, with emphasis on the earliest or first incorrect step.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers most commonly describe ProcessBench as evaluating a model's ability to identify erroneous steps in mathematical reasoning, especially step-level error identification focused on the earliest or first incorrect step. Definitions also frame it as assessing detection of the first incorrect step in LLM-generated mathematical solutions. Papers do not link it to named constructs or behavioral indicators.

Space of uses. In the descriptions, papers use ProcessBench as an evaluation benchmark for step-level error identifica

nodes.name: Project Euler
nodes.definition: Test set consisting of 45 C implementations of Project Euler mathematical challenge problems, used to evaluate transpilation accuracy on algorithmic code.

nodes.name: Prometheus
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing treatment is as an LLM-based evaluator or open-source LM judge for scoring generated outputs. Most definitions describe it as a model trained to evaluate other language models or for general human preference evaluation in natural language generation, with some papers referring to a later Prometheus variant. The task framing varies across papers: it is used for summaries, literary translation, text-to-SQL assessment, and generated articles, and different definitions name dimensions such as interest, coherence, relevance, coverage, diversity, breadth, depth, and novelty.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to score output quality across several task-specific dimensions, but no constructs and no behavioral indicators are explicitly linked to it. The reported targets do not converge on one recurring linked construct: papers describe it as assessing summarization quality, translation quality, text-to-SQL assessment, general human preference evaluation in natural language generation, and article quality through dimensions like relevance, breadth, depth, and novelty.

Space of uses. In use, papers position it as an automatic judge fo

nodes.name: PrOntoQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most papers treat PrOntoQA, sometimes written ProntoQA, as a synthetic benchmark for logical or multi-step reasoning. Definitions differ in emphasis: some describe data points that assign hierarchical relationships among objects and ask whether a multi-step reasoning chain is correct, while others describe question-answering examples with explicit chains of thought, or a synthetic first-order logic benchmark with problems derived from ontologies and axioms over structured knowledge.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, the prevailing use is to measure logical reasoning. It is linked to two constructs, Logical reasoning and the broader Reasoning, and to two behavioral indicators, Logical problem solving and Question answering; most claims center on logical reasoning, while a smaller line frames it as measuring general reasoning, and isolated papers use it for logical problem solving or as question-answering examples.

Space of uses. Papers usually position it as one benchmark among several for logical or deductive reasoning evaluation, and some explicitly use it for out-of-distribution evaluation. Among linked instruments, it is related to ProofWriter, and one

nodes.name: PrOntoQA-OOD
nodes.definition: An out-of-distribution logical reasoning benchmark used to evaluate multi-step hypothesis verification.

nodes.name: Proof-pile
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, Proof-pile is most commonly described as a long-context language modeling dataset centered on mathematical material, either as a cleaned Arxiv Math dataset or, more specifically, as a 13GB collection of long mathematical documents. The descriptions converge on long-form technical or scientific content with many long sequence samples, though some authors describe it more broadly as scientific and technical texts rather than emphasizing Arxiv Math.

What it is claimed to measure.
