Papers use Proof-pile to evaluate language modeling performance on long sequences, most often through perplexity, including long-sequence or long-context performance in technical, scientific, or mathematical domains. No paper links it to a named construct or behavioral indicator, so the recorded descriptions stay at the level of language modeling performance and perplexity rather than a broader measurement claim.

Space of uses. Papers most often use Proof-pile alongside GovReport for long-context evaluation, and another study places it beside PG19 and CodeParrot in a perplexity comparison. It is typically used in evaluation settings, with papers reporting perplexity o

nodes.name: ProofNet
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing description is of a Lean benchmark for undergraduate or college-level mathematics, usually used for theorem proving or autoformalization. Definitions describe 371 exercises or informal-statement and formalization pairs from standard textbooks, with problems spanning areas such as real analysis, complex analysis, linear algebra, abstract algebra, and topology; some descriptions emphasize isolated or less context-dependent problems, and one paper instead treats it as a source dataset of high-quality mathematical proofs. Papers also refer to variants: ProofNet-test for formal statements of college-level questions, and ProofNet#, a corrected version kept close to the original while updating reference formalizations; descriptions variously specify Lean 3, Lean 4, or Lean-formatted problems.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use ProofNet to measure 3 behavioral indicators and 2 constructs. Among behavioral indicators, the most common uses are autoformalization, formal theorem proving, and theorem proving, with papers describing evaluation by comparing predictions with ground truths, assessing theorem-proving capabilities, or reporting whole-

nodes.name: ProofWriter
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing framing is a deductive or logical reasoning benchmark, sometimes called a dataset, for logical inference over written or natural language rules and facts. Definitions variously describe first-order logic rules, small rule-bases composed of facts and rules, and tasks that determine whether a query can be proved, including multi-step deduction and proof construction under a closed-world assumption. Some papers emphasize generating natural language proofs for conclusions, while others highlight moderately complex logical structures such as conjunctions and disjunctions. A smaller strand refers to the ProofWriter family, which includes Birds-Electricity and ParaRules.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use ProofWriter mainly to measure Logical reasoning, and the relationship claims mostly converge there: it is linked to 2 constructs, with Logical reasoning the dominant one and Chain-of-thought reasoning appearing in a smaller line of work that treats it as a multi-step reasoning dataset. The definitions align with this usage by describing it as assessing deductive reasoning abilities, logical inference, and implication eliminatio

nodes.name: PropBank
nodes.definition: A corpus of verb argument annotations (Kingsbury and Palmer, 2002) applied to the Penn Treebank, providing the verb-specific tense and aspect labels used in this study.

nodes.name: ProteinGym
nodes.definition: A benchmark suite composed of hundreds of deep mutational scan (DMS) studies used to evaluate the zero-shot fitness prediction capabilities of protein language models.

nodes.name: PStance
nodes.definition: Large-scale dataset focusing on individuals' stances toward U.S. political figures (Trump, Biden, Sanders) with binary labels (favor or against), used to evaluate performance in real-world political discourse.

nodes.name: PTB
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, PTB is most commonly described as the Penn Treebank, a language-modeling benchmark, corpus, or dataset used for evaluating models on text prediction. The prevailing description is evaluation via perplexity, though some definitions frame it more specifically as a benchmark for next-token prediction, zero-shot performance, or log-loss under canonicality enforcement. A few papers specify particular forms of the resource, including a test split with 3761 strings, 82k words, and 439k characters, validation-set use, and a version preprocessed by Dyer et al. (2016); one paper instead uses PTB sentences annotated with PropBank as source material for analyzing grammatical features.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link PTB to one construct and one behavioral indicator, so the reported measurement claims are concentrated rather than spread across many targets. The most common claim is that papers use PTB to measure language modeling ability, typically by reporting perplexity on PTB, and a separate line of work uses it to measure text generation, again through perplexity in language generation experiments. The relationship language is consistent across these c

nodes.name: PubHealth
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, PubHealth is most commonly described as a fact verification dataset or claim verification benchmark in the public health domain, often grouped with closed-set tasks. Definitions consistently emphasize public health or medical claims, and several descriptions frame it as evaluating closed-set factual verification or the truthfulness of health-related statements. A smaller line of work instead describes it as a closed-set generative dataset comprising medical claims on various biomedical topics.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link PubHealth to one construct and one behavioral indicator. The prevailing linked use is to measure fact checking: papers describe it as requiring a system to verify a given claim based on retrieved documents. One paper also uses sampled claims from PubHealth to investigate domain-specific factual knowledge in the public health domain, so it is also reported as measuring domain knowledge; overall, the claimed measurement scope is concentrated rather than spread across many targets.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it through explicit relationships. In practice, papers often use PubHealth ins

nodes.name: PublicViews
nodes.definition: A dataset extracted from TwinViews-13k containing political statements across 31 topics and explicitness variants for evaluating political bias and factuality in generated news.

nodes.name: PubMed
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the dominant framing treats PubMed as a citation-network or text-attributed graph benchmark derived from the PubMed database, where documents or scientific publications are the nodes and node classification is the usual evaluation task. Some definitions make this more specific by describing it as a biomedical citation network or as publications related to diabetes. A smaller line of work uses the same name for different resources: one paper refers to "PubMed1" as a collection of biomedical paper abstracts used as a representative domain corpus for finetuning, another defines PubMed as medical scientific articles for summarizing authors' conclusions from experiment descriptions, and another uses Scientific Papers (Pubmed) as an out-of-domain benchmark; one graph paper also uses PubMed for node-level and edge-level tasks.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link PubMed to 3 behavioral indicators and 1 construct. The prevailing use is to measure node classification, with papers describing it as a widely adopted or well-established dataset for that task and reporting node classification accuracy on it. Other papers use it to measure link predict

nodes.name: PubMedQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, PubMedQA is most commonly described as a biomedical question-answering benchmark built from PubMed abstracts or articles, usually asking yes, no, or maybe questions grounded in a corresponding abstract. Some definitions say its QA pairs are formulated from PubMed articles, with questions derived from titles; several also describe corresponding contexts and sometimes long-form or free-form explanations or answers, while a smaller line of work treats it as a biomedical multiple-choice dataset or simply as a held-out evaluation benchmark. Papers mention multiple reused portions of the resource, including validation and test sets and the pqa_labeled split.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link PubMedQA to 2 constructs and 3 behavioral indicators. The prevailing usage is to measure medical question answering, and smaller lines of work use it to measure knowledge-based question answering and natural language inference; on the construct side, papers also use it to measure contextual reasoning and medical knowledge. Overall, papers use it for several different targets rather than only one, although medical question answering is the most recurrent behavioral

nodes.name: PUNMEMECN
nodes.definition: A multimodal benchmark for Chinese pun memes that assesses vision-language models on pun detection, sentiment analysis, and contextual meme response selection using annotated memes and simulated chat conversations.

nodes.name: PutnamBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly describe PutnamBench as a benchmark of undergraduate-level mathematics competition questions used to evaluate theorem proving on challenging problems. Some definitions give a fuller format, describing a multi-language benchmark with 1692 hand-constructed formalizations of 640 theorems from the William Lowell Putnam Mathematical Competition in Lean 4, Isabelle, and Coq, while shorter descriptions refer more simply to formalized problems from the Putnam competition.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, the measurement claims are concentrated rather than spread widely: PutnamBench is linked to 2 behavioral indicators, theorem proving and formal theorem proving, and to 1 construct, problem-solving ability. The prevailing usage is to evaluate theorem proving, including neural, symbolic, and domain-agnostic theorem provers, while a narrower framing says it measures problem-solving ability by requiring problem-solving and proficiency across a broad range of topics taught in undergraduate mathematics courses.

Space of uses. One usage pattern is to report PutnamBench together with miniF2F and ProofNet for whole-proof generation methods. More broad

nodes.name: PWWS
nodes.definition: Probability Weighted Word Saliency, an adversarial text attack procedure that uses WordNet synonym replacements guided by saliency to reduce classifier prediction confidence.

nodes.name: Q-Bench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, Q-Bench is most commonly described as a benchmark for low-level vision tasks or for assessing the low-level visual capabilities of multimodal or general-purpose foundation models. One definition further specifies that it is divided into perception, description, and quality assessment sections. A smaller usage treats it as an existing benchmark for in-domain multi-image evaluation, and one paper refers to a QBench-Testset, abbreviated QBenchT, as a named test set.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link Q-Bench to 1 construct and no behavioral indicators. The only recorded measurement claim is that it measures Multi-image reasoning, with a paper including QBench among the benchmarks incorporated for multi-image tasks. The reported measurement use therefore centers on a single construct rather than spanning multiple constructs or indicators.

Space of uses. In practice, papers often present Q-Bench as one benchmark within broader evaluation suites. It is adopted alongside NLVR2 in multi-image evaluation, appears with Mantis-Eval and BLINK for multi-image tasks, and is also reported together with SEED-Bench Image Part and MM-Vet in result summaries.

nodes.name: QAMPARI
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed definitions, QAMPARI is most commonly described as a benchmark dataset for attributable, factoid question answering, used for evaluation. The definitions converge that questions may have multiple answers, and one paper specifies this more narrowly as a factoid QA dataset in which each answer is "a list of entities drawn from different passages." Papers also describe it as a setting for evaluating precision and recall in attributed generation.

What it is claimed to measure. The recorded measurement claims do not converge on a single target. Papers link QAMPARI to 2 constructs and no behavioral indicators: it is reported as measuring Trustworthiness and Unanswerability detection ability, in both cases through measured_by links. One definition also frames it as evaluating precision and recall in attributed generation, so its documented use spans these evaluation targets rather than centering on only one.

Space of uses. Papers use QAMPARI as an evaluation dataset, often alongside ASQA and ELI5. As one study puts it, "Evaluations on the benchmark datasets ASQA, QAMPARI, and ELI5 show that models trained with TRUST-ALIGN outperform the competitive baseli

nodes.name: QASC
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing description treats QASC as a question-answering benchmark or dataset for science questions that require multi-step or multi-hop reasoning, often by integrating, composing, or reasoning over multiple facts from multiple sentences. Some authors instead place it under commonsense reasoning or multiple-choice comprehension, one definition says it provides questions and associated facts, and another expands the name as "Question Answering via Sentence Composition". A smaller line of work also presents it as an elementary science or scientific reasoning benchmark.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link QASC to 1 construct and 1 behavioral indicator. The prevailing measurement claim is that it measures Question answering, with papers using it for evaluation or fine-tuning under that label; a smaller line of work reports it as measuring Commonsense reasoning by including it among commonsense QA datasets. The reported measurement uses are therefore concentrated on those two targets rather than spread across many constructs or indicators.

Space of uses. Papers commonly present QASC as one dataset in broader evaluation suites. It is often used a

nodes.name: Qasper
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, Qasper is most commonly described as a question-answering benchmark or dataset over full NLP or research papers, used for retrieval, open-book QA, and answering from long scientific documents. Definitions consistently frame its contexts as full papers or scientific articles, and one study describes it as including 5,049 questions across 1,585 NLP papers, with each question probing information embedded in the full text. Several papers note that it contains extractive, abstractive, yes/no, and unanswerable questions, and some definitions add that questions may be unanswerable from the provided abstract or full text. A smaller line of work refers to it as part of SCROLL or SCROLLS, one paper uses a Qasper subset from LongBench, and another filters and augments QASPER to derive 493 questions for a derived evaluation.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link Qasper to 2 constructs and 3 behavioral indicators, and the prevailing use is to measure question answering. Several papers use it for question answering over research or NLP papers, while smaller uses treat it as measuring document question answering and synthetic recall, and as measuring th

nodes.name: QM9
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, QM9 is described as a quantum-chemistry or molecular property prediction benchmark for small molecules, with ground-state 3D structures and use in computed property prediction. One paper states that it "contains over 130,000 molecules with ground-state 3D structures obtained through DFT computations" (3D-MolT5: Leveraging Discrete Structural Information for Molecule-Text Modeling). Another paper treats it as a regression benchmark for quantum chemistry properties, including HUMO, LUMO, and HUMO-LUMO gap.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link QM9 to no constructs and to two behavioral indicators. It is reported as measuring Molecular property prediction and Molecule generation, so the recorded claims are spread across task-level indicators rather than concentrated on any linked construct. The more detailed measurement framing is for computed or molecular property prediction, while a separate paper also reports molecule generation on QM9.

Space of uses. Papers use QM9 mainly as an evaluation dataset. In one study it appears alongside PubChemQC and PubChem as one of three datasets used to evaluate performance on computed property prediction, and a

nodes.name: QMSum
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the definitions, QMSum is most commonly described as a query-based, multi-domain meeting summarization dataset or benchmark, usually placed in SCROLL or SCROLLS. Papers generally describe meeting transcripts paired with summaries conditioned on specific questions about the dialogue, and one paper describes it as a human-annotated benchmark with 1,808 query-summary pairs over 232 meetings. Some authors add that it covers multiple domains or aggregates ICSI, AMI, and Parliament meetings, while a smaller framing under the label SUM-QMSUM treats it more generally as a benchmark for generating summaries of meeting transcripts.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use QMSum to measure 2 constructs and 3 behavioral indicators. The behavioral uses cover text summarization, dialogue summarization, and query-focused summarization, while the construct uses are length generalization and long-context understanding. Taken together, these links span both summarization behaviors and broader long-context constructs.

Space of uses. As another measurement instrument, papers only explicitly relate QMSum to SCROLLS, and several definitions place it within SCROLL or SCROLLS, someti

nodes.name: QNLI
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, QNLI is most commonly described as a question-answering natural language inference benchmark or dataset, often said to be derived from SQuAD. The prevailing formulation is an entailment-style, usually binary, classification task over question-sentence pairs, though some papers describe question-paragraph pairs instead, where the model determines whether the context sentence contains the answer to the question. A smaller set of definitions frames the same setup as question answering cast as textual entailment.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link QNLI to 2 constructs and 3 behavioral indicators, and the dominant claim is that it measures natural language inference. Smaller lines of work also report it as measuring question answering and text classification, while only a few papers treat it as measuring natural language understanding or reasoning. Overall, the reported measurement claims center on natural language inference, with a smaller set of broader or alternative framings.

Space of uses. The only linked instrument is GLUE, to which QNLI is related, and many papers position it as one task within GLUE evaluations. In practice, papers

nodes.name: QQP
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, QQP is most commonly described as the Quora Question Pairs dataset or benchmark, a paraphrase or duplicate-question task in which a pair of questions is labeled for semantic equivalence. Definitions repeatedly frame it as deciding whether two questions are paraphrases, duplicates, or semantically equivalent, and one description specifies more than 400,000 question pairs with a binary paraphrase label. A smaller line of work describes it more broadly as sentence paraphrase judgment, and one paper uses an adversarially perturbed form for robustness testing.

What it is claimed to measure. The prevailing use links QQP to one behavioral indicator, paraphrase detection, and papers do not link it to any construct. Relationship claims describe it as measuring paraphrase detection or paraphrase identification, including formulations such as duplicate-question detection and deciding whether two questions are "equivalent" or "not equivalent". The recorded claims therefore converge on a single behavioral target rather than spreading across multiple constructs.

Space of uses. In use, papers most often position QQP as part of GLUE, which is its only linked instrument

nodes.name: QuAC
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, QuAC is most commonly described as the Question Answering in Context benchmark or dataset for conversational question answering. Definitions converge on a format with interconnected questions in a conversational, multi-turn dialogue, and one paper adds that it evaluates whether a model can understand context and participate in a dialogue about a text. In On Synthesizing Data for Context Attribution in Question Answering, it is further described as featuring coreferences across turns, challenging models to track context across multiple turns.

What it is claimed to measure. Recorded uses link QuAC to one construct, Reasoning, and to no behavioral indicators. The reported measurement claim is narrow rather than spread across many targets: one paper lists QUAC among the benchmarks used "for reasoning abilities," so papers use it to measure Reasoning rather than a wider set of constructs.

Space of uses. Papers use QuAC alongside other benchmarks rather than in isolation. One usage places it with ARC-Easy, ARC-Challenge, SIQA, PIQA, and WinoGrande in an all 0-shot evaluation for reasoning abilities, while another uses it with CoQA, OR-QuAC, and DoQ

nodes.name: QualBench
nodes.definition: A multi-domain Chinese question-answering benchmark for assessing localized, vertical-domain knowledge in LLMs, comprising over 17,000 questions from 24 Chinese professional qualification exams across six domains.

nodes.name: QuALITY
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most papers describe QuALITY as a long-document or long-context question answering benchmark built from stories, articles, or other long passages, usually in a multiple-choice format. Definitions commonly emphasize long inputs, with one description saying passages average about 5,000 tokens and another describing English context passages between 2K and 8K tokens. A smaller line of work recasts the benchmark for different answer formats, including direct answer generation without the four options and a binary-choice extractive reading-comprehension form.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, QuALITY is linked to 1 construct and 3 behavioral indicators. The prevailing measurement claim is question answering, with papers describing it as a QA dataset over stories and articles; smaller lines of work use it to measure multiple-choice question answering and machine reading comprehension. Papers also report it as evaluating long-context understanding, especially when they frame it as a longer-sequence or long-context ability benchmark.

Space of uses. Papers usually use QuALITY as one benchmark inside broader question-answering or long-context evaluation suites, often

nodes.name: QuaRel
nodes.definition: A question answering dataset that tests qualitative reasoning about the relationships between quantities.

nodes.name: QuoteSum
nodes.definition: A long-form question answering benchmark where the task is to generate answers that are semi-extractive, meaning they are composed of direct quotes from multiple provided source documents.

nodes.name: QVHighlights
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most descriptions treat QVHighlights as an evaluation benchmark for highlight detection, or more broadly for detecting moments and highlights in videos from natural language queries. In that usage, models are asked to identify highlight moments and their saliency scores for a given query. A smaller line of work treats it as a video dataset for QA creation, describing YouTube videos with sparsely annotated captions or events and event pairs; one paper says it features over 10,000 videos across various themes.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, the measurement claims converge on Temporal grounding. QVHighlights is linked to one behavioral indicator, Temporal grounding, and no constructs, and papers report using it for the video grounding task and for identifying relevant moments and highlights in response to user queries.

Space of uses. Papers commonly position QVHighlights as an evaluation benchmark rather than as an auxiliary check. It is used for experiments on video grounding and temporal localization, appears alongside Charades-STA in zero-shot temporal localization reporting, and is selected with ActivityNet for QA data creation. One definition also say

nodes.name: R-GSM
nodes.definition: A math reasoning dataset used to evaluate reasoning performance under swapped conditions.

nodes.name: R-Judge
nodes.definition: Benchmark for coding and software engineering tasks involving high-risk bash commands or API calls, assessing safety and alignment in programming environments.

nodes.name: RACE
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, RACE is most commonly described as a large-scale reading comprehension dataset or benchmark drawn from English examinations for middle and high school students, built around passage-based multiple-choice questions. Several papers explicitly separate RACE-High and RACE-Middle, and one paper refers to the high test portion. A smaller line of descriptions frames it more specifically as coming from English exams for Chinese students, or more broadly as factual QA or exam-style passages and questions.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link RACE to 6 constructs and 3 behavioral indicators. The prevailing measurement claims are reading comprehension and machine reading comprehension, and one paper describes it as a multiple-choice task used to evaluate reading comprehension abilities and requiring reasoning over provided passages. More occasional uses treat it as measuring general ability, long-context understanding, and natural language understanding, with several other linked targets appearing more sparsely.

Space of uses. Papers do not link RACE to another measurement instrument directly, but they frequently place it inside broader benchmark suites. It

nodes.name: RAGAS
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, the dominant framing is of RAGAS as an automated, LLM-based evaluator for Retrieval-Augmented Generation. Definitions variously describe it as a pointwise evaluation system, a Retrieval-Augmented Generation Assessment framework, and an automated evaluation framework, with one description adding that it uses prompted frontier models and embedding models to score responses. The outcomes it evaluates are usually described through metrics such as faithfulness and context relevance, with some definitions also naming refusal, answer relevance, and claim-level decomposition.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link RAGAS to 1 construct and no behavioral indicators, so the recorded use is concentrated rather than spread across many outcomes. The only explicit measured_by relation says that RAGAS measures Faithfulness. More broadly, definitions and quoted passages also report it as assessing metrics such as context relevance, answer relevance, and refusal.

Space of uses. Papers mainly position RAGAS as a reference or comparison evaluator within broader RAG assessment setups. One study says it is run as a reference point, another cites it with RAG-

nodes.name: RAGTruth
nodes.definition: A high-quality, manually annotated benchmark dataset specifically designed for evaluating RAG hallucination detection, covering tasks like question answering, data-to-text writing, and news summarization.

nodes.name: RAID
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the cited papers, RAID is treated as a dataset or benchmark for machine-generated text detection, most commonly described as spanning multiple domains and supporting cross-domain evaluation. Definitions mention domains such as Abstracts and Wiki, and one paper states that it uses those two domains as out-of-domain evaluation data. A smaller framing presents RAID as covering multiple domains and models and including adversarial examples, while another uses it to evaluate detector performance on more advanced models with human-written and model-generated text.

What it is claimed to measure. In the descriptions, papers use RAID to evaluate machine-generated or LLM text detection and detector performance. The papers do not explicitly link it to any named construct or behavioral indicator.

Space of uses. Papers use RAID alongside other detection datasets rather than as a standalone protocol. It appears with RealDet, M4, and MAGE as a representative evaluation dataset, and with Yelp as an out-of-domain dataset. Another paper positions RAID as a way to test performance on more advanced models.

nodes.name: RAVDESS
nodes.definition: The Ryerson Audio-Visual Database of Emotional Speech and Song (RAVDESS), used for emotion classification.

nodes.name: RAVEL
nodes.definition: A knowledge retrieval task involving factual recall of biographical information about historical figures.

nodes.name: RAVEN
nodes.definition: A non-verbal intelligence test, adapted as a visual reasoning benchmark (Zhang et al., 2019a), that requires identifying the missing element in a matrix of abstract patterns.

nodes.name: RCT
nodes.definition: A biomedical dataset for sequential sentence classification, used to evaluate domain adaptation.

nodes.name: RE-Bench Scaling Law Experiment
nodes.definition: An RE-Bench environment that tasks the agent with predicting the optimal hyperparameter tradeoff for a large model by extrapolating from smaller-scale experiments.

nodes.name: Real-MM-RAG
nodes.definition: A multimodal retrieval benchmark with four high-difficulty evaluation sets used to assess reranking and robustness, including a rephrased version.

nodes.name: RealTimeQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing framing is a time-sensitive question-answering benchmark or dataset about real-time events, developed after LLM knowledge cut-off dates to avoid data contamination. One paper further describes it as multiple-choice, while another emphasizes that it requires periodic manual updates.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the papers, no constructs or behavioral indicators are explicitly linked to RealTimeQA. One paper does describe it as being used to evaluate zero-shot knowledge recall in continual learning settings, but that use is not tied to a named construct or behavioral indicator.

Space of uses. Papers mainly position it as one testbed among other time-sensitive QA benchmarks. One study discusses it alongside FreshQA and TAQA as benchmarks designed to avoid data contamination, and another uses it as a second testbed of downstream tasks for evaluating zero-shot knowledge recall.

Concerns raised. The recurring concern is maintaining its post-cutoff, time-sensitive character. One paper notes that it requires periodic manual updates and that it "stopped its manual updates in January 2024," making it likely that newer LLMs with later

nodes.name: RealToxicityPrompts
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats RealToxicityPrompts as a dataset or benchmark of text prompts, often described as web-derived, naturally occurring, or sentence-level prompts for text continuation or sentence completion that are likely to elicit toxic generations from language models. Several definitions further describe the prompts as incomplete, seemingly benign or neutral, or divided into toxic and non-toxic prompts for controlled testing. Papers also mention variants and subsets, including a challenge or challenging split of 1,199 prompts, a 10K non-toxic sample, toxic and non-toxic 10K samples, and an adapted version of the 100,000-prompt dataset for sentiment, toxicity, and counterfactual fairness under gendered inputs.

What it is claimed to measure. Claims about what it measures mostly converge on Toxicity. Papers link it to 3 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator: it is most often used to measure Toxicity, while smaller lines of work use it to measure Safety and Harmlessness, and the linked behavioral indicator is Harmful content generation. The evidence quotes commonly describe prompting models with challenge prompts and evaluating the res

nodes.name: RealWorldQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, RealWorldQA is most commonly described as a benchmark or dataset of questions about real-world images. The most specific definition presents it as multiple-choice questions over anonymized outdoor and indoor images, scored by accuracy, and aimed at basic real-world spatial understanding. Other papers frame it more broadly as practical, real-world visual understanding, or as a multimodal question-answering benchmark used to assess general capability in real-world question answering.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use RealWorldQA to measure a range of constructs rather than a single shared target. It is linked to 7 constructs and no behavioral indicators, with the listed uses covering fine-grained perception, multimodal perception, multimodal understanding, reasoning, and spatial understanding, with additional papers placing it under other perception and understanding constructs. Across the relationship evidence, papers state that these constructs are measured by RealWorldQA.

Space of uses. No other measurement instrument is linked to it. In practice, papers often evaluate it alongside MMMU, MMVP, ScienceQA, MME, and SEED-Bench, usually as part of

nodes.name: ReasonSeg
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly describe ReasonSeg as a benchmark dataset for reasoning segmentation, designed to evaluate segmentation based on complex reasoning. Some descriptions narrow it to an image reasoning segmentation benchmark used to assess reasoning capability on images, while another describes it as a referring expression segmentation benchmark used to assess pixel-level grounding. In use, authors also call it a challenging dataset and report CIoU, GIoU, and gIoU results on it.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the linked relationships, papers use ReasonSeg to measure one behavioral indicator, Reasoning segmentation, and no constructs are linked to it. This is the prevailing usage: papers say it evaluates the model's reasoning ability and use it to assess reasoning capability on images. The linked claims therefore converge on a single behavioral indicator rather than spreading across many constructs or indicators.

Space of uses. Papers use it as an evaluation benchmark and report performance with CIoU, GIoU, and gIoU. No measurement instrument is linked to it, and the quoted passages mainly show it being used to compare model performance, including improvements

nodes.name: REBEL
nodes.definition: A benchmark dataset for relation extraction, from which a 1,000-sample subset is used for evaluation.

nodes.name: ReClor
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage is a reading comprehension or multiple-choice question answering benchmark for logical reasoning. Definitions commonly say it is sourced or derived from standardized tests, especially LSAT and GMAT, or from American graduate school entrance exams and their preparatory materials. Some authors describe it more specifically as the Reading Comprehension with Logical Reasoning dataset, and some descriptions frame it as assessing the ability to draw correct inferences from complex textual premises or to perform logical reasoning from provided text.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, the measurement claims converge on 1 construct, Logical reasoning, and no behavioral indicators are linked to it. Papers use it as a logical reasoning dataset or benchmark, including descriptions that they use ReClor for logical reasoning and for overall comparisons on logic tasks. The measurement claims therefore center on a single construct rather than spreading across multiple constructs.

Space of uses. Papers commonly include it alongside other benchmarks, for example ARC and CSQA in natural language reasoning question-answering exper

nodes.name: Red-teaming
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats red-teaming as an adversarial testing or stress-testing procedure aimed at uncovering safety vulnerabilities, harmful capabilities, biases, or unsafe outputs. Definitions differ, though: some authors describe a manual assessment or a process run by human experts or automated systems, while another use treats it as data generation, for example a set "consisting of 100 harmful examples generated via red-teaming" (Durable Quantization Conditioned Misalignment Attack on Large Language Models). One reported variant evaluates safeguards with 28 test-time adversaries that are variations of fine-tuning attacks.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use red-teaming to evaluate safeguards and expose safety vulnerabilities, and to probe a model's propensity to produce inaccurate, biased, offensive, or unsafe responses. No constructs or behavioral indicators are linked to it.

Space of uses. No other measurement instruments are linked to it. Papers position it in several roles: as a step for generating harmful examples for fine-tuning, as an "extensive red teaming" evaluation against test-time adversaries, and as manual or multilingua

nodes.name: Reddit TL;DR
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats Reddit TL;DR as a Reddit-based summarization dataset or benchmark, usually described as posts paired with short, human-written summaries. Some definitions add that a post may come with several short summaries judged by human evaluators for quality and informativeness, while others describe preference-labeled comparison data or multiple generated summaries with human preference data. A smaller line describes it more generally as a summarization benchmark of articles and summaries, but most descriptions specifically center Reddit posts, with papers also referring to train and test splits, a comparison-data variant, and a subset restricted to relationship-oriented subreddits.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to measure 3 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators. The prevailing use is to measure Text summarization, and a smaller line of work uses it to measure Alignment; individual papers also use it to measure Abstractive summarization, Summary quality, and Out-of-distribution generalization. Taken together, these claims mostly converge on summarization, with additional use for Alignment, Summary quality, and

nodes.name: ReDial
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, ReDial is described in two distinct ways rather than with a single settled format. One paper introduces it as Reasoning with Dialect Queries, a human-annotated benchmark with over 1.2K parallel Standardized English and African American Vernacular English query pairs spanning algorithm, logic, math, and integrated reasoning tasks, and describes it as an end-to-end SE-AAVE parallel dataset for reasoning. Another paper uses the same name for a movie recommendation dialogue dataset, described as a collection of movie recommendation conversations annotated with user satisfaction labels and used in task-oriented dialogue experiments.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use ReDial to measure one construct and one behavioral indicator. The construct link is Reasoning, with a paper describing ReDial as a dataset for reasoning tasks, while the behavioral indicator link is Conversational recommendation, with another paper treating ReDial as one of two real-world conversational recommendation benchmarks. The measurement claims therefore point to two different targets rather than converging on only one.

Space of uses. In experiments, papers place ReDial alongside

nodes.name: RedPajama
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing framing is a pretraining or training corpus of web text. Definitions describe it as a multi-domain pretraining corpus used to sample general web data for language modeling perplexity, as an open-source project creating a large, high-quality dataset for training language models, and as a pre-training dataset derived from CommonCrawl; one paper specifically uses the CommonCrawl split. Another paper uses it as a calibration dataset, describing it as a large collection of web text meant to represent typical input distributions.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link RedPajama to one construct and no behavioral indicators. The only reported measurement claim is that it measures Editing locality: in model editing work, locality data is described as the irrelevant data of the editing process. The measurement claims therefore center on a single construct rather than being spread across many targets.

Space of uses. Papers use RedPajama in several operational roles, and no other measurement instrument is linked to it. It appears as evaluation data for language modeling perplexity on general web data, as part of averaged throughput simulations a

nodes.name: RedPajama-V2
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, RedPajama-V2 is most commonly treated as a large-scale web-text or web-corpus resource for training or pretraining language models. Definitions also describe it as a preprocessed dataset from diverse internet sources, in one case specifying 30 trillion tokens, while narrower variants include the "sample" and "sample-100B" subsets and, in another use, the validation split.

What it is claimed to measure. Most descriptions do not present RedPajama-V2 as a benchmark for named constructs. One paper defines its validation set as a benchmark to measure forgetting by tracking changes in pretraining loss, and papers otherwise do not link it to any constructs or behavioral indicators.

Space of uses. The prevailing usage is as pretraining data: papers use it as the corpus on which language models are trained, or as a starting point for a general-domain pretraining dataset. A smaller line of work uses it more instrumentally, as the source of pretraining text domains on which model losses are measured for data selection, and one paper uses both the pretraining set and its validation loss in analyses of forgetting. No other measurement instruments are linked to i

nodes.name: RefCOCO
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing description is a benchmark or dataset for visual grounding and referring expression comprehension: models must locate the object named by a natural-language referring expression in an image, often by predicting a bounding box from image-text input. Several definitions call it a visual grounding dataset or a referring expression comprehension benchmark, and one paper describes it as assessing localization together with fine-grained spatial and semantic relationships. A smaller group of papers instead treats RefCOCO as a referring expression segmentation benchmark, evaluating localization at the pixel level, and papers often mention it together with RefCOCO+ and RefCOCOg.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, RefCOCO is linked to two constructs and three behavioral indicators. The most common measurement claims are visual grounding and referring expression understanding; papers also use it for referring expression segmentation, and only isolated papers use it for object localization or spatial reasoning. Across these uses, the recurring task is locating a referred object or region from language in an image.

Space of uses.

nodes.name: RefCOCO/g/+
nodes.definition: A referring-expression benchmark suite consisting of RefCOCO, RefCOCOg, and RefCOCO+ for evaluating object localization from language descriptions.

nodes.name: RefCOCO+
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the cited definitions, RefCOCO+ is most commonly described as a benchmark or dataset for referring expression tasks, usually paired with RefCOCO and RefCOCOg. The prevailing description treats it as similar to RefCOCO but with constraints that exclude spatial or location words, shifting descriptions toward appearance-based language; a smaller line of work describes it as an extension used for referring expression segmentation and as featuring more complex language. Papers also variously label it as a referring expression comprehension benchmark, a visual grounding benchmark, or a referring expression segmentation dataset.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use RefCOCO+ to measure two behavioral indicators, Referring expression segmentation and Referring expression understanding, and one construct, Visual grounding. The recurring uses are to assess referring expression understanding or comprehension, referring expression segmentation, and visual grounding, so the measurement claims are spread across these tasks rather than concentrated on only one framing. Relationship evidence describes it as evaluating recognition ability on referring expression comprehensio

nodes.name: RefCOCOg
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats RefCOCOg as a benchmark or dataset for referring expression comprehension, visual grounding, and object localization from natural language descriptions. Definitions repeatedly emphasize longer or more descriptive referring expressions, sometimes with spatial relations, and some papers specify grounding a described region to a single bounding box. A smaller line of work describes refCOCOg as a version of the refCOCO series for referring expression segmentation, with natural language queries paired with object masks, while some papers also use it for referring expression generation and region-level captioning.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link RefCOCOg to 1 construct and 4 behavioral indicators. The most common reported use is to measure Referring expression understanding, followed by Referring expression segmentation, Region captioning, and Referring expression generation, and it is also reported as measuring the construct Visual grounding. Overall, papers use it across several task framings rather than centering it on only one reported target.

Space of uses. Papers most commonly use RefCOCOg alongside RefC

nodes.name: Repetition Task
nodes.definition: A few-shot evaluation task where the model must repeat a given sentence, used to test the ability to steer generation when the model's default behavior is to follow a contextual pattern.

nodes.name: RepoBench-P
nodes.definition: A benchmark for evaluating code-related tasks, specifically code retrieval and completion, used as part of the LongBench evaluation.

nodes.name: RepoEval
nodes.definition: Benchmark for repository-level code completion, assessing line-, API-, and function-level code generation using real-world codebases.

nodes.name: RepoQA
nodes.definition: A benchmark for question answering over entire code repositories to assess deep code comprehension.

nodes.name: RESISC45
nodes.definition:
What it is. The prevailing description treats RESISC45 as a publicly available remote-sensing image or land-scene classification benchmark with 45 classes. Definitions describe it as a benchmark for Remote Sensing Image Scene Classification and as a land use dataset involving land scene classification over 45 classes. A smaller variation in wording presents it more generally as a vision benchmark, and one evaluation setup frames the task as selecting a class from a provided list.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, its measurement role is narrowly focused: it is linked to 1 behavioral indicator, Image classification, and to no constructs. Papers use RESISC45 to measure image classification, with evidence phrased as reporting performance on image classification benchmarks that include Resisc-45 and as part of evaluations spanning multiple classification domains. The claims therefore converge on a single behavioral indicator rather than being spread across multiple constructs or behaviors.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it. Papers usually position RESISC45 as one component of broader benchmark suites, for example alongside CIFAR-100, Food101, Flower

nodes.name: RestBench
nodes.definition: A benchmark of real-world API tasks involving authentic calls to TMDB and Spotify with dynamic responses.

nodes.name: ResumeBench
nodes.definition: A multilingual benchmark comprising 2,500 synthetic resumes across 50 templates and 5 languages, designed to evaluate LLMs on structured resume parsing with realism and privacy compliance.

nodes.name: ResumeBench-Mix
nodes.definition: ResumeBench-Mix, a combined real-synthetic dataset created by pairing public real resumes with an equal number of synthetic resumes in five languages for evaluation.

nodes.name: RETAIL
nodes.definition: A real-world tourism all-in-one interactive planning dataset containing 10,182 dialogues that supports evaluation of decision-making for implicit queries, environmental awareness, plan revision, and all-in-one travel planning with rich POI details.

nodes.name: RewardBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, RewardBench is most commonly described as a benchmark for evaluating reward models on preference judgments, often framed as prompt, chosen, rejected triples or binary preference tasks. Definitions repeatedly describe 2,985 tasks drawn from 23 subtasks or datasets, usually organized into Chat, Chat-Hard, Safety, and Reasoning; one paper also describes it as English-only and says the triples are human-validated. Smaller lines of work describe it more specifically as a public benchmark for generative judges on preference-related subtasks, or as an out-of-distribution benchmark for testing generalization.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link RewardBench to 6 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators, so its reported measurement role is spread across several targets rather than confined to one. The prevailing usage is to measure Reasoning and Safety, and some papers also use it for Out-of-distribution generalization; among behavioral indicators, it is used for Pairwise comparison and Preference prediction, with 3 other construct links appearing less often. In these claims, papers describe reasoning through preferences over correct versus incorrect response

nodes.name: ReXVal
nodes.definition: A dataset containing ground-truth and generated radiology reports annotated by radiologists with six categories of errors, classified as clinically significant or insignificant.

nodes.name: RGB
nodes.definition:
What it is. The definitions treat RGB as a retrieval-augmented generation benchmark, and one paper also describes it as an open-source general-domain QA dataset. Across these descriptions, it is used for questions that require grounding in retrieved documents, with emphasis on robustness, generalization, and the ability to effectively use retrieved information while withstanding imperfections in the retrieval process.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link RGB to 1 behavioral indicator and no constructs. The only reported measurement claim is that it measures question answering, with papers describing it as evaluating whether language models can effectively use retrieved information under imperfect retrieval conditions.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it through the recorded relations. In the papers, RGB appears as one dataset within broader retrieval-augmented generation evaluations, placed alongside PopQA, Natural Questions, TriviaQA, and KNOT.

nodes.name: RiddleSense
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the cited papers, RiddleSense is most commonly described as a benchmark dataset of riddle-style questions for evaluating commonsense reasoning. The prevailing wording presents it as complex commonsense reasoning in the framework of riddle-style, multiple-choice questions, while another definition more generally calls it a commonsense reasoning benchmark involving riddles. Some authors also place it among lateral thinking-related benchmarks.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use RiddleSense to measure a single construct, Commonsense reasoning, and no behavioral indicators are linked to it. The claims converge on that construct rather than spreading across several: it is described as evaluating complex commonsense reasoning, including in out-of-domain evaluation settings.

Space of uses. Papers position RiddleSense mainly as an existing benchmark used in broader benchmark comparisons and out-of-domain evaluation. It is analyzed alongside BiRdQA and BrainTeaser in benchmark analysis, included with Story Cloze Test, HellaSwag, and NumerSense in out-of-domain commonsense reasoning evaluation, and cited as a lateral thinking-related benchmark to which another benc

nodes.name: RLBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, RLBench is most commonly treated as a simulated, and in one definition large-scale, benchmark and learning environment for robotic manipulation. Definitions vary in emphasis: some describe tabletop tasks and a Franka robot performing both prehensile and non-prehensile tasks, while others frame it as a benchmark for language-conditioned or language-guided robotic manipulation. Papers also describe it as being used to generate trajectories and to evaluate manipulation-related path prediction or other challenging simulation tasks.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link RLBench to one behavioral indicator, robotic manipulation, and to no constructs. The recorded measurement claim is concentrated rather than spread across multiple targets: RLBench is used to measure robotic manipulation, with the supporting description referring to tabletop manipulation in simulation.

Space of uses. Across the papers, RLBench is positioned as a simulation benchmark or learning environment rather than being linked to other measurement instruments. Authors use it for evaluation, including generating trajectories or episodes and assessing model performance on manipulati

nodes.name: RM-Bench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the definitions, papers most commonly describe RM-Bench as a benchmark for evaluating reward models through preference pairs with subtle differences, with emphasis on sensitivity to subtle content variations and resistance to style biases. One description adds that it is designed to correlate with downstream policy performance across chat, math, code, and safety tasks. A related paper situates it alongside RewardBench and says it covers the Chat, Code, Math, and Safety domains, with code prompts sourced from HumanEvalPack.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link RM-Bench to 2 constructs, Robustness and Factuality, and no behavioral indicators. Most descriptions frame it in robustness terms: one paper says RM-Bench is designed to assess the robustness of reward models through their sensitivity and resistance to subtle content differences and style biases. A smaller use treats it as measuring factuality, with one study using it because RM-Bench includes response pairs involving factual correctness, so the reported measurement claims are concentrated in these two constructs rather than spread across many.

Space of uses. Papers position RM-Bench as an evaluation

nodes.name: RoBERTa harmfulness classifier
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly describe this instrument as an external safety evaluator: a harmfulness detection model that assigns a probability score indicating whether a given response is harmful. In Refusal-Aware Red Teaming: Exposing Inconsistency in Safety Evaluations, it is used among "state-of-the-art harmfulness detection models" that assign harmfulness probabilities to each response.

What it is claimed to measure. The description uses it to score whether a response is harmful by assigning a harmfulness probability. No constructs and no behavioral indicators are linked to it through recorded measurement claims.

Space of uses. The only described usage places it alongside WildGuard as part of an evaluation setup, where both models act as external safety evaluators for response harmfulness. No other measurement instrument is linked to it.

nodes.name: RocketEval
nodes.definition: An automated evaluation framework that uses a lightweight LLM to grade responses against an instance-specific, multi-faceted checklist.

nodes.name: ROCStories
nodes.definition:
What it is. Definitions mostly describe ROCStories as a story-generation dataset built from short stories with exactly 5 sentences, often characterized as coherent narrative or commonsense stories. The prevailing usage is open-ended conditional generation or title-to-story generation, including evaluation of a model's ability to generate a five-sentence story from a title. A smaller framing treats ROC Stories as a story-completion or infilling setup, where a middle sentence is masked and the generated replacement is assessed for coherence.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link ROCStories to 1 behavioral indicator and no constructs. The only recorded measured_by relationship is with Text infilling, so papers use ROCStories to measure text infilling; in that use, one paper describes the corpus as 'a dataset of short stories containing exactly 5 sentences each.' The claims therefore center on a single behavioral indicator rather than multiple constructs.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to ROCStories. Across the papers, it is used in several evaluation setups: for title-to-story generation, for relatively open-ended conditional generation, and for story comple

nodes.name: RoDEval
nodes.definition: A comprehensive evaluation framework for assessing the word sense disambiguation capabilities of LLMs, comprising four novel metrics and associated evaluation tasks.

nodes.name: Rotten Tomatoes
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, the prevailing usage treats Rotten Tomatoes as a sentiment classification dataset or benchmark built from movie reviews, typically for binary polarity labeling. Some authors refer to it as MR or Movie Review, and one description specifies movie reviews from the Rotten Tomatoes website, while others describe it more generally as a text classification dataset or benchmark used in projected-embedding, in-context learning, and prompt-based evaluations.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to measure 2 behavioral indicators, Text classification and Sentiment analysis, and no constructs are linked to it. The linked claims stay within classification behavior: papers describe it as one of the datasets that 'all admit classification tasks' and as a benchmark for binary polarity tasks on movie reviews.

Space of uses. Papers most commonly use it as one dataset within a larger evaluation suite rather than in isolation. In the excerpts, it appears alongside SST-2, IMDB, AG News, Subj, and TREC, and it is used to evaluate projected embeddings, in-context learning and activation-vector methods, few-shot classification, polarity labeling, and non-r

nodes.name: RTE
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the dominant framing treats RTE as a textual entailment or natural language inference benchmark built from premise-hypothesis sentence pairs, where the task is to judge whether one sentence entails or can be inferred from the other. Several definitions make the label space explicit as a binary decision, such as entailment versus not entailment or "True" versus "False," and one definition describes it as a collection or series of textual entailment challenges. Papers place it in both GLUE and SuperGLUE, and one paper describes a negation-focused use with versions framed as entailment, contradiction, or neutral.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link RTE to 3 constructs and 3 behavioral indicators. The prevailing measurement claim is that papers use it to measure Natural language inference, often described as textual entailment; additional papers use it to measure Binary classification and Fact checking. At the construct level, it is used to measure General ability, Natural language understanding, and Language modeling ability, so the reported measurement claims extend beyond a single construct.

Space of uses. Papers usually use RTE as one

nodes.name: Rule-based judge
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, the prevailing usage is a rule-based or heuristic evaluation procedure, often described as keyword matching over model outputs. Most definitions say it searches for predefined refusal-related keywords, rejected words, or strings that indicate refusal to comply with a harmful instruction, and uses that to judge whether a jailbreak attack was successful. A smaller line of work describes keyword matching differently, as checking specific keywords in factual-query answers to measure information overlap.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it primarily to measure Jailbreaking: it is linked to one behavioral indicator, Jailbreaking, and to no constructs. In the recorded relationships, Jailbreaking is measured by the Rule-based judge, and the accompanying descriptions operationalize that judgment through searches for refusal-indicating strings or related rules. The measurement claims therefore converge on jailbreak evaluation rather than spreading across multiple constructs.

Space of uses. Papers position it as an automatic evaluator, sometimes alongside other judges and sometimes as the default or a baseline evaluator. Quoted passages show

nodes.name: RULER
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most papers describe RULER as a synthetic long-context benchmark or dataset for evaluating LLMs, often emphasizing controllable or customizable sequence lengths and task complexity. The prevailing description is a suite of 13 tasks across four categories, with papers variously spelling these out as Needle-in-a-Haystack retrieval, multi-hop tracing or variable tracking, aggregation or common and frequent word extraction, and question answering; some also say it challenges the true context window length or evaluates effective context length. A smaller description treats it more generally as a benchmark suite for long-context capabilities, and one mention refers to five categories.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link RULER to 5 constructs and 9 behavioral indicators. The dominant use is to measure long-context understanding, while smaller lines of work use it for length generalization, long-context reasoning, long-range dependency modeling, and multi-hop reasoning. At the behavioral level, it is most often used for synthetic recall and state tracking, with additional uses for question answering, context retrieval, and document question answering, plus 4 other indic

nodes.name: RuleTaker
nodes.definition: Automatically generated logical reasoning dataset using formal connectives (¬, ∧, →), requiring models to apply logical rules across multiple inference steps.

nodes.name: SAEBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the cited work, SAEBench is most commonly treated as a benchmark or evaluation suite for sparse autoencoders. Definitions differ in the metrics they foreground: one describes feature absorption, splitting, composition, probing, and concept isolation across multiple tasks and models, while another emphasizes downstream SAE-specific metrics such as spurious correlation removal, targeted probe perturbation, sparse probing, automated interpretability, and feature absorption. One paper also characterizes it as a benchmark of SAE metrics "faithful to possible real world use cases."

What it is claimed to measure. It is linked to 1 construct, interpretability and explainability, and to no behavioral indicators. Papers use it to measure that construct through "interpretability benchmark results from SAEBench" and through a "detection score ... implemented in SAE Bench" that is used to validate interpretability, so the reported use centers on a single construct rather than a broader set.

Space of uses. No other measurement instrument is linked to it. Papers use its evaluations to compare SAE variants across a wide variety of tasks, to calculate specific metrics such as a

nodes.name: SAFE
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, SAFE is most commonly presented as Search-Augmented Factuality Evaluator, an LLM-based search procedure, sometimes framed as an investigative agent, that uses iterative Google Search queries to assess whether generated facts are supported by external evidence. In Long-form factuality in large language models, it is described more specifically as splitting a long-form response into individual facts, checking relevance, searching the web, and labeling each fact as supported, not supported, or irrelevant; other definitions use the broader formulation of asking whether search results support a fact.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link SAFE to 3 behavioral indicators and no constructs. The prevailing measurement claim centers on Hallucination: one paper uses SAFE to quantify LLM hallucinations, and related evidence says it enables direct measurement of hallucination. The other linked indicators, Fact checking and Search query generation, are reported as related to SAFE rather than as additional things it measures, so the explicit measurement claims converge on hallucination.

Space of uses. Papers use SAFE as an evaluation procedure for long

nodes.name: SafeBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the definitions, SafeBench is most commonly described as a safety benchmark for VLMs or MLLMs. The prevailing description says it contains 500 malicious questions organized into 10 categories based on AI usage policies. Some authors frame it more specifically as a benchmark for evaluating defense against jailbreak attacks or the ability to perceive multimodal risks, and one paper refers to SafeBench11, described as constructed with FigStep and sampled at 200 items.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use SafeBench to measure two behavioral indicators, Jailbreaking and Jailbreak resistance, and no construct is linked to it. The linked uses converge on jailbreak-related behavior: one paper reports attack success rates on SafeBench as evidence for Jailbreaking, while another uses it among jailbreak attack methods or datasets to evaluate defense capabilities against jailbreak attacks, that is, Jailbreak resistance.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it through recorded relationships. In use, papers most often place it alongside MM-SafeBench or MM-SafetyBench and HADES or HADES-Dataset, and also alongside MML, HIMRD, and AdvBench. The recurring

nodes.name: SALAD-Bench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, SALAD-Bench is most commonly described as a safety benchmark for LLMs. Definitions present it as an established benchmark that provides prompts and safety scores for evaluating LLM safety and its relationship to value systems, and another description calls it a hierarchical benchmark covering different task types and jailbreak attack methods. A smaller line of work treats it as a dataset source of harmful prompts used in training and evaluating refusal mechanisms.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers portray it as measuring more than one target rather than centering on a single construct. In the recorded links, it is used to measure one construct, privacy awareness, where authors extract the "privacy infringement" category, and one behavioral indicator, jailbreaking, where it is used as a safety benchmark to assess the generalizability of a weak-to-strong attack. Definitions also frame it more broadly as evaluating LLM safety, and in one paper its prompts and safety scores are used to study safety in relation to value systems.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it. Papers mainly position it as an evaluation source: one study draws pr

nodes.name: SAMSum
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, SAMSum is most commonly described as a dialogue summarization dataset or benchmark built from chat or messenger-like conversations paired with short or human-written summaries. Definitions variously emphasize daily-life messenger conversations, multi-turn or multi-party dialogues, and human-annotated abstractive summarization, and some papers use few-shot variants such as "SAMSUM Few shot" or describe it as a few-shot summarization benchmark. A minority description diverges, with one quoted passage characterizing it as using news articles and machine-generated summaries.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to 2 behavioral indicators and 1 construct. The prevailing usage is to measure Text summarization, with a smaller line of work using it for Dialogue summarization, and one paper also uses summarization on SAMSum as part of assessing General ability. Overall, the measurement claims are concentrated on summarization rather than spread broadly across constructs.

Space of uses. Across papers, SAMSum is commonly used as one benchmark within broader evaluation suites, though some studies make it the task-specific dataset for text or dia

nodes.name: SAT
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly treat SAT as a standardized test used for college admissions in the United States and used to evaluate model performance. A narrower description in one paper treats it as a set of math problems from the Scholastic Aptitude Test, and notes that this version contains 32 four-choice problems.

What it is claimed to measure. Across these papers, SAT is used to evaluate model performance, and one paper specifies quantitative reasoning as the target of the SAT math problems. Papers do not explicitly link it to named constructs or behavioral indicators.

Space of uses. One paper places SAT alongside other standardized tests such as GRE and AP when comparing model and human test-takers, stating that GPT-4 scores on these tests are comparable to those of human test-takers. Another paper uses the SAT math problems as a small evaluation set and averages results over the last three checkpoints when available.

Concerns raised. The only explicit concern raised is the small size of the SAT math-problem version: one paper notes that it has only 32 four-choice problems, which leads the authors to average results over multiple checkpoints.

nodes.name: SAT-Math
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most papers treat SAT-Math as a standardized SAT mathematics benchmark used to evaluate mathematical reasoning under standardized conditions. The definitions differ slightly in granularity: some describe standardized test math problems from the SAT or a benchmark of SAT mathematics problems, others specify that it is composed of multiple-choice questions from the math section, and one paper describes the task coverage as Intermediate Algebra, Probability, and Calculus.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the papers, the linkage converges on 1 construct, Mathematical reasoning, and no behavioral indicators. Papers use SAT-Math to measure Mathematical reasoning, describing it as one of the datasets used for math-domain evaluation, a representative evaluation dataset, or part of a collection of mathematical reasoning benchmarks that papers say covers diverse domains, question formats, and difficulty levels.

Space of uses. Papers usually report SAT-Math alongside other math benchmarks, most often GSM8K and MATH, and also AQuA or AQuA-RAT, MMLU-Math, and MMLU-STEM. It is often positioned as one component of broader math evaluation, for example as a term in a math-domain

nodes.name: SATBench
nodes.definition: A benchmark consisting of 2100 logical puzzles derived from SAT formulas, presented in natural language, used to evaluate models' ability to perform search-based logical reasoning and produce valid reasoning traces.

nodes.name: SBIC
nodes.definition: The Social Bias Inference Corpus (SBIC) is a labeled dataset of social media posts used for assessing societal biases in language, which served as a source for the CoBia dataset.

nodes.name: sBLIMP
nodes.definition: A ZeroSpeech paired-choice evaluation using grammatically correct versus incorrect sentence speech examples.

nodes.name: SC-Safety
nodes.definition: Chinese-language safety benchmark focusing on compliance with ethical and legal standards in LLM responses.

nodes.name: ScanNet
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats ScanNet as an indoor 3D scene dataset, with definitions alternating between real indoor room scenes, a 3D indoor scene dataset, and richly annotated 3D reconstructions of indoor scenes. The content described for it varies by paper: some authors use scenes from it to construct scenarios, others highlight annotations supporting object classification, visual question answering, and captioning in point cloud modality, and another describes it as a segmentation dataset with 1,201 training scenes, 312 validation scenes, and 20 semantic classes.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link ScanNet to one behavioral indicator, Semantic segmentation, reporting that semantic segmentation is measured by the ScanNet segmentation dataset. The recorded links do not connect it to any constructs. Beyond that linked use, some papers also report evaluating classification, captioning, and QA on its test split, and one paper reports building a partial scene registration benchmark from it.

Space of uses. Papers position ScanNet both as source material for derived resources and as a direct evaluation dataset. It is used alongside PartNet

nodes.name: ScanQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, ScanQA is most commonly described as a benchmark dataset for question answering in 3D scenes, with questions grounded in objects within ScanNet scans. Some definitions present it more specifically as a 3D visual question answering dataset focused on spatial relationships and object properties, while another describes a challenging indoor 3D VQA dataset with over 41,000 question-answer pairs. A smaller line of description treats it as a multi-modal 3D scene dataset for spatial scene understanding, and one quoted passage says it is centered on ScanNet and pioneered human annotations and template-based generation.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use ScanQA to measure 3 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators. The prevailing construct-level use is for 3D understanding, with additional papers reporting it as measuring 3D perception and vision-language reasoning; at the behavioral-indicator level, it is linked to 3D question answering and visual question answering. One paper explicitly says evaluations on ScanQA and SQA3D do not require object referencing and grounding while being used to demonstrate overall 3D scene understanding and reasoning, so the me

nodes.name: SciBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, SciBench is most commonly described as a benchmark suite for scientific reasoning or college-level scientific problem solving. Most definitions emphasize complex, multi-step scientific questions, and one paper says the objective is to answer questions that require integrating knowledge, reasoning over evidence, and applying scientific principles (Fleet of Agents: Coordinated Problem Solving with Large Language Models). Subject coverage is described differently across papers, with some referring to physics, chemistry, and biology, another to physics, chemistry, and mathematics, and another focusing on a math-related subset with calculus, differential equations, and statistics.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the papers, SciBench is linked to three constructs and three behavioral indicators. The prevailing construct link is scientific reasoning, while smaller lines of work report it as measuring chemical reasoning and out-of-distribution generalization; on the behavioral side, papers use it for mathematical problem solving, scientific problem solving, and scientific question answering. These measurement claims therefore span several labels rather

nodes.name: SCIDOCS
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly treat SCIDOCS, also written SciDocs, as a retrieval dataset for scientific literature. The prevailing description is an information retrieval dataset dedicated to scientific scholarly articles or scientific document retrieval, and some authors place it within BEIR as a single-hop retrieval benchmark for re-ranking scientific documents. Another description presents it as a document retrieval dataset based on citation networks in scientific literature, used to assess whether embeddings retrieve semantically related academic papers.

What it is claimed to measure. These papers do not explicitly link SCIDOCS to any named construct or behavioral indicator. Instead, they use it to evaluate retrieval tasks, especially retrieval of scientific scholarly articles, single-hop re-ranking of scientific documents, and retrieval of semantically related academic papers.

Space of uses. Papers usually deploy SCIDOCS alongside other retrieval datasets. It appears within BEIR evaluations for re-ranking, in corpus-poisoning experiments to generate and evaluate adversarial passages, and in embedding evaluation with nDCG@10 alongside MS MARCO and NFCorpus.

Concerns rais

nodes.name: ScienceAgentBench
nodes.definition: A multidisciplinary benchmark for evaluating LLMs operating within agent frameworks on explorative scientific tasks.

nodes.name: ScienceQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, ScienceQA is most commonly described as a multiple-choice science question answering benchmark, usually multimodal, spanning diverse science topics or knowledge domains. The prevailing descriptions say samples pair a question and options with visual and textual context, and some definitions add optional lecture or context text, background knowledge, and explanations; a smaller line of work narrows evaluation to questions with images or refers to image-based forms such as ScienceQA-Image, while some work also uses text-only samples. Papers also describe it as covering science questions with diagrams and as a benchmark for scientific or complex reasoning from visual and textual inputs.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use ScienceQA to measure 10 constructs and 3 behavioral indicators, so its use is spread across several framings rather than centered on one. The most frequent construct claims treat it as measuring multimodal reasoning and scientific reasoning, followed by knowledge reasoning, multimodal perception, and multimodal understanding, with 5 other constructs also linked. At the behavioral-indicator level, the clearest recurring use is visual

nodes.name: ScienceQA-IMG
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats ScienceQA-IMG, also written as SciQA-IMG, SQAI, or SQA-I, as a multimodal science question answering benchmark with image or visual context. Most descriptions say it contains image-based questions and evaluates reasoning over visual and textual context in science-related problems, while one definition presents SQA-I more specifically as the image-based subset of the ScienceQA benchmark.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to measure two constructs and no behavioral indicators: Language bias and Visual understanding.
