One paper reports zero-shot performance on ScienceQA-IMG and says a model outperforms others by "successfully alleviating language bias," while another uses it when reporting "superior image understanding capabilities"; the reported uses are therefore split across those two constructs rather than centered on a single named target.

Space of uses. Papers often position it as one member of broader evaluation suites: quoted passages describe evaluating models across eight vision-language tasks, 11 mainstream benchmarks, or widely-adopted VLM benchmarks that include ScienceQA-IMG. In these descriptions it appe

nodes.name: ScienceWorld
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing description is a text-based or textual simulation benchmark, or interactive environment, for basic or elementary science experiments. Definitions repeatedly say agents receive natural-language goals and must interact with objects by navigating, manipulating objects, and observing outcomes; several papers also frame it as an embodied or embodied-AI setting for long-horizon, large-action-space tasks. A smaller line of work emphasizes the abilities it requires, describing it as involving long-term memory, subtask decomposition, and scientific and commonsense knowledge, and one paper uses the surface form SciWorld for science-oriented interactive tasks.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use ScienceWorld to measure 3 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators. The most recurrent construct framing is generalization, including evaluation on unseen tasks; a smaller set of papers uses it to measure commonsense knowledge and task decomposition ability. It is also reported as measuring embodied planning and scientific experimentation, so papers attach it to several distinct capabilities rather than only one.

Space of uses. Papers commonly use Scienc

nodes.name: SciERC
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, SciERC is treated as a computer science evaluation resource, but the descriptions are not identical. One paper presents it as an evaluation task in SciRIFF-Eval for relation extraction, with a computer science abstract as input and six entity types as output. Another paper describes it as a computer science dataset for text classification over scientific articles, focused on identifying entities, relations, and coreference.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use SciERC to measure two behavioral indicators, Information extraction and Knowledge graph construction, and no construct is linked to it. The more direct framing is that it measures Information extraction, stated as "IE(Rel)" with a CS abstract and six entity types as the task format. Another paper reports it as measuring Knowledge graph construction by using it as one of the domain-specific datasets with golden ground truth KGs.

Space of uses. Papers use SciERC within broader evaluation setups, and no measurement instrument is linked to it. In one usage it appears inside SciRIFF-Eval as the relation extraction task over computer science abstracts. In another, it is grouped with REBEL-Sub,

nodes.name: SciEval
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing description of SciEval is a benchmark for scientific-domain evaluation. Definitions variously present it as a multi-level benchmark for scientific research, a benchmark for understanding and reasoning about scientific content, and a comprehensive, multi-disciplinary benchmark that assesses scientific reasoning, problem solving, and subjective question answering.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use SciEval to evaluate scientific reasoning most often, with closely related descriptions emphasizing scientific research reasoning, problem solving, understanding scientific content, and subjective question-answering capabilities. Papers do not explicitly link it to named constructs or behavioral indicators through measurement relationships, so its measurement role is described in these broader capability terms.

Space of uses. In use, papers refer to "benchmark tests on SciEval" and place it within broader evaluation suites alongside instruments such as MedQA, MedMCQA, FinEval, FinanceIQ, and MMLU-Sci. They position it as a multi-level scientific benchmark, and one description further calls it a comprehensive, multi-disciplinary benchmark fo

nodes.name: SciFact
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing description is a scientific fact-checking dataset or benchmark in which claims are verified using evidence from research papers. Definitions commonly say the evidence comes from sentences in papers and may require citation context, while some papers instead describe verification against scientific abstracts or a corpus of research abstracts. One paper also reports a split of 809 training claims and 300 test claims.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link SciFact to one behavioral indicator, fact checking, and one construct, domain knowledge. The dominant use is to measure fact checking, with several papers explicitly listing it as a fact-checking dataset or among popular fact-checking datasets. A smaller line of work uses it to measure domain knowledge by sampling claims from SciFact in the science domain to investigate domain-specific factual knowledge.

Space of uses. Papers relate SciFact to one other instrument, BEIR. Some authors place it inside the BEIR benchmark, and one paper selected it for a challenging subset based on high ratios of out-of-corpus terms. In evaluation setups, papers also use it alongside other datasets in broa

nodes.name: SciQ
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, SciQ is most commonly described as a benchmark or dataset for scientific question answering built from multiple-choice science exam questions. Several definitions also call it a crowdsourced science-question dataset, and some add supporting paragraphs or annotated support. A smaller line of work describes its use more broadly, as reading comprehension, commonsense question answering, natural language understanding, or phrase-level and free-form question answering; one paper uses a LitCab test split, and another uses it for short responses.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link SciQ to 6 constructs and 3 behavioral indicators. The prevailing usage is to measure Commonsense reasoning, with additional papers using it to measure General ability, Scientific knowledge, Scientific reasoning, Out-of-distribution generalization, and 1 other construct. At the behavioral level, it is used for Multiple-choice question answering most often, and also for Question answering and Open-ended question answering. One line of work explicitly says it measures scientific reasoning by challenging models to apply scientific concepts beyond mere fact recall.

Sp

nodes.name: SciQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, SciQA is most commonly presented as a science question-answering resource. Definitions describe it as a dataset of science exam questions with "rich domain-specific language and complex reasoning," while some authors instead present it as a science question answering benchmark for visual question answering, including scientific diagrams that require scientific reasoning; another usage places it among reading comprehension tasks.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use SciQA to measure one construct and two behavioral indicators. It is reported as measuring Visual understanding, and it also measures Knowledge-based question answering and Machine reading comprehension, so the recorded uses are spread across several targets rather than centered on a single reported construct.

Space of uses. Papers often list SciQA as one item in broader evaluation suites. It appears with ARC-Challenge, ARC-Easy, LogiQA, PIQA, and LAMBADA in downstream-task testing, and other papers include it in collections of vision-understanding or visual question answering benchmarks.

nodes.name: SciVerse-mv
nodes.definition: A multi-image scientific reasoning benchmark used for out-domain evaluation.

nodes.name: ScreenSpot
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing description is a benchmark for single-step or cross-platform GUI grounding. Definitions describe it as assessing whether a predicted location falls within the ground truth element bounding box, and one paper further presents it as a GUI visual grounding benchmark containing 1,200 instructions with target element bounding boxes across mobile, desktop, and web or website environments. A smaller variation in wording frames it more broadly as part of multi-modal task performance evaluation, though the recurring content is GUI grounding across platforms.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use ScreenSpot to measure 3 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator. The dominant claims are that it measures Action grounding and Visual grounding, with papers also using it to measure Grounding and, in a smaller line of work, Adaptability. Across these links, the named targets are mostly grounding-related.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is explicitly linked to it, but several papers use it within broader benchmark suites. It appears alongside VisualWebBench and RefExp for GUI grounding, and alongside MiniWob, AITW, and Mind2Web in broader evaluat

nodes.name: SCROLLS
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most commonly, papers treat SCROLLS as a benchmark suite for long-text or long-context evaluation, often explicitly as a suite of 7 datasets. Its task mix is described as question answering and summarization, with some descriptions adding classification, and one definition frames SCROLL as evaluating language models' ability to reason over and synthesize information from long texts. A smaller framing discusses Scrolls together with ZeroSCROLLS as realistic long-input tasks from real-world scenarios, and one quoted passage reports average lengths ranging from 1.7k to 49.3k tokens.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use SCROLLS to measure 2 constructs and no behavioral indicators, most often Long-context understanding and Long-context reasoning. These claims are concentrated on long-context capabilities rather than spread across many concepts: one line of work places Scrolls within long-context modeling and QA evaluation, while another describes it as evaluating models' ability to synthesize information over long texts.

Space of uses. Across papers, SCROLLS is used as a finetuning and comparison benchmark for long-sequence tasks, including baseline comparisons and lo

nodes.name: Seal-Tools
nodes.definition: A dataset of held-out tasks used to evaluate the generalization ability of models on function call scenarios.

nodes.name: SEED-Bench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, SEED-Bench is most commonly described as a comprehensive multimodal or vision-language benchmark for multimodal comprehension or generative comprehension. Many definitions present it as a multiple-choice benchmark, with one recurring description calling it a human-annotated dataset of 19K multiple-choice questions spanning 12 evaluation dimensions across image and video modalities, while another describes a visual question-answering benchmark with 9 dimensions scored by MCQ accuracy. Some authors narrow it to complex visual scene comprehension, broad cognitive tasks such as instance interaction, text understanding, and spatial relations, or video comprehension tasks such as action prediction, action recognition, and procedure understanding; papers also refer to image, video, all, and SEED-Image subsets, and sometimes to the image part simply as SEED.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link SEED-Bench to 5 constructs and 3 behavioral indicators. The prevailing construct-level use is to measure visual understanding, with additional papers using it to measure multimodal perception, multimodal understanding, reasoning, and visual perception. At the be

nodes.name: SEED-Bench-2
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, SEED-Bench-2 is most commonly described as a multimodal benchmark for evaluating models on multimodal inputs, especially cases with multiple images. Definitions variously say it evaluates the ability to comprehend and reason about multimodal inputs containing multiple images, serves as a benchmark for general performance of Vision-Language Assistants after debiasing methods, and is used as a non-synthetic comparison point for LVLM evaluation rankings. Descriptions also differ on context length: one survey places it in long-context tasks that require identifying relevant information from image sequences, while another paper groups it with multi-image benchmarks that consist of short contexts.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link SEED-Bench-2 to 2 constructs and no behavioral indicators. The only direct measurement claim is for Multi-image reasoning: one paper says it measures this by evaluating the ability to comprehend multimodal inputs containing multiple images. Long-context understanding appears only as a related construct, with one paper discussing SEED-Bench-2 in connection with that capability by arguing that it does not evaluate long-con

nodes.name: SEED-Bench Image
nodes.definition: SEED-Bench Image Part (SEEDI) is a benchmark focusing on generative comprehension for multimodal LLMs, specifically its image-related tasks.

nodes.name: Self-Instruct
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats Self-Instruct as an instruction-following evaluation dataset or test set, sometimes written as Self-Instruct Eval or SelfInst. Definitions describe it as based on self-instructed prompts and used to assess responses to self-instruction-style prompts, while one paper describes a test set of human-generated instructions from various tasks and sources. A smaller line of work also presents it as a framework and dataset that uses the model itself to generate new instructions, inputs, and outputs, and one paper characterizes it as generating approximately 82k instances from 175 human-created handwritten instructions.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link Self-Instruct to 1 behavioral indicator, Instruction following, and no constructs. In the recorded relationship, a paper uses it to measure instruction following by evaluating trained student models on Self-Instruct alongside other instruction-following datasets. One definition also describes it as testing model generalization and response quality across a wide range of tasks, but the recorded measurement link centers on instruction following.

Space of uses. Papers commonly us

nodes.name: SelfCheckGPT
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing description is a suite or method for hallucination detection: it samples multiple stochastic responses from a model and checks their consistency or support for the original answer to assess veracity, often in zero-resource black-box or gray-box settings. Some authors narrow this to a baseline for self-consistency or zero-resource fact-checking, and a smaller line of work instead describes it as a benchmark or dataset for hallucination correction, assessing whether a model can rectify factual inconsistencies. One paper also uses the variant name Self-CKGPT for the consistency-based baseline.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to 3 behavioral indicators and no constructs. The linked indicators are Knowledge editing, Hallucination, and Hallucination detection, so the reported uses are distributed across several behavioral targets rather than tied to a construct. In these links, papers use it to evaluate the ability to correct hallucination in knowledge editing, to assess hallucination or response veracity, and to measure hallucination detection through inconsistency among sampled responses.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument

nodes.name: SemEval-2007
nodes.definition: A dataset from the SemEval-2007 workshop, commonly used as a validation set in WSD research.

nodes.name: SemEval 2010 Task 8
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most papers treat it as a standard or widely used relation extraction benchmark dataset. Definitions describe it as sentence-level and general-domain, and as evaluating semantic relation extraction between pairs of nominals; the prevailing description says it contains 19 relation types, though a smaller usage describes ten relation classes. Some definitions also present it as spanning diverse domains and as a benchmark used to evaluate few-shot learning and generalization.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the surveyed papers, claims converge on a single behavioral indicator: SemEval 2010 Task 8 is used to measure Relation extraction. Papers connect it to 1 behavioral indicator, Relation extraction, and to no constructs. The relationship language is consistent, with papers describing RE as being evaluated on this dataset or including it among standard RE benchmarks.

Space of uses. Papers usually use it alongside TACRED and its variants, including TACREV or TACRED-Revisit, and ReTACRED or Re-TACRED. They generally position it as one benchmark within a multi-dataset RE evaluation, for example as part of a set of widely used or standard benchmarks, while a smaller us

nodes.name: SemEval-2016 Task 5
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the definitions, this instrument is described as a benchmark dataset for aspect-based sentiment analysis built from restaurant reviews in multiple languages and used to evaluate cross-lingual performance in end-to-end ABSA. One paper specifies that it includes real user restaurant reviews in English, Spanish, French, Dutch, Russian, and Turkish.

What it is claimed to measure. In the papers, papers use this dataset to measure aspect-based sentiment analysis. Its reported measurement links converge on a single behavioral indicator, Aspect-based sentiment analysis, and no constructs are linked to it.

Space of uses. The observed usage frames it as an evaluation dataset for a proposed framework rather than alongside other named instruments. Papers describe evaluating on SemEval-2016 to assess cross-lingual performance in end-to-end ABSA, and no other measurement instruments are linked to it.

nodes.name: SemEval 2018 Task 1 E-c
nodes.definition: Multi-label emotion recognition task with 11 emotion categories on English tweets, used to analyze LLM generation dynamics despite lacking individual annotator labels.

nodes.name: SentEval
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most directly, papers describe SentEval as a standard transfer learning evaluation suite for sentence embeddings, with tasks such as sentiment classification (MR, SST-2), subjectivity detection (SUBJ), and question classification (TREC). One paper adds that it provides standard transfer learning tasks including MR, CR, SUBJ, MPQA, SST-2, TREC, and MRPC (Token Prepending: A Training-Free Approach for Eliciting Better Sentence Embeddings from LLMs). A separate paper uses SentEval as an evaluation tool for semantic textual similarity and says it contains seven STS subsets: STS 2012-2016, the STS-Benchmark, and SICK Relatedness.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link SentEval to no constructs and no behavioral indicators. Instead, they report it as evaluating sentence embeddings through standard transfer learning tasks, and one paper relates it to STS tasks where model performance is measured with Spearman's correlation. No paper explicitly names a construct that SentEval measures.

Space of uses. The only linked measurement instrument is STS tasks. One paper relates SentEval to STS tasks by adopting it as the evaluation tool for seven STS subsets and measuring model p

nodes.name: SENTIBENCH
nodes.definition: Benchmark for evaluating sentiment analysis models across multiple tasks including basic, multi-faceted, and fine-grained sentiment analysis, covering domains like IMDb, Yelp, and Twitter.

nodes.name: SENTIMENT
nodes.definition: A dataset for sentiment analysis, typically involving classifying text into positive, negative, or neutral categories.

nodes.name: seqBench
nodes.definition: A tunable benchmark for sequential reasoning in LLMs, featuring synthetic pathfinding tasks with orthogonal control over logical depth, backtracking count, and noise ratio, enabling fine-grained analysis of reasoning failure modes.

nodes.name: Sequential-NIAH
nodes.definition: A benchmark for evaluating sequential information retrieval from long contexts, featuring synthetic-temporal, real-temporal, and real-logical order needles embedded in texts from 8K to 128K tokens.

nodes.name: SGD
nodes.definition: The Schema-Guided Dialogue (SGD) dataset, a challenging benchmark for multi-domain task-oriented dialogue that includes unseen domains in its test set to evaluate generalization.

nodes.name: SGHateCheck
nodes.definition: A curated multilingual dataset containing parallel toxic content across Singlish, Chinese, Malay, and Tamil, used to source hateful statements for red-teaming evaluations.

nodes.name: ShareGPT
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, ShareGPT is most commonly described as a dataset, or a collection from sharegpt.com, of user-shared conversations with ChatGPT. Definitions also frame it as real-world user requests, dialog, instruction-response pairs, and, in some systems work, as real user conversations with LLMs or conversation traces; one description calls sharegpt.com "a platform where ChatGPT users voluntarily share their conversations." Some papers use selected portions or derivatives of it, including 10,000 instruction-response pairs for supervised fine-tuning, another 1,000 instructions for evaluation, subsampled workload types, and synthetic workloads built from its real input and output texts.

What it is claimed to measure. The recorded measurement claims are narrow rather than spread across many targets: papers link ShareGPT to one construct and one behavioral indicator. One paper reports that Robustness is measured by ShareGPT, assessing robustness against fine-tuning by fine-tuning on ShareGPT and Evol-Instruct to try to overwrite embedded watermarks. Separately, one paper relates ShareGPT to Instruction following, describing it as a general instruction tuning set that focu

nodes.name: ShieldGemma-9B
nodes.definition: A large language model used as an automated evaluator to assess the safety and alignment of other models' generated responses.

nodes.name: SHP
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most commonly, papers describe SHP, usually expanded as Stanford Human Preferences, as a human-preference dataset used in alignment or reward-model evaluation, though one definition calls it Shared Human Preferences. The prevailing format is prompts, questions, or posts paired with responses or comments plus a preference label, sometimes described as human annotation and sometimes as preference inferred from likes or from Reddit users rating one comment as more helpful. Descriptions differ on the source material: several papers present Reddit posts, prompts, or comments, while another describes pairs of responses to StackExchange questions; some papers also frame SHP as an out-of-distribution benchmark for reward models.

What it is claimed to measure. In the linked claims, papers use SHP to measure 1 construct and 1 behavioral indicator. The construct link is out-of-distribution generalization, where SHP is included among datasets for testing reward models' out-of-distribution generalization, and the behavioral-indicator link is question answering, where a paper reconstructs SHP from Reddit questions and user answers for a QA task. These measurement claims are concentr

nodes.name: SHQ-NPOV
nodes.definition: A dataset of 300 human-written queries and answers on controversial topics, with each answer rated for its adherence to a Neutral Point of View (NPOV).

nodes.name: SIB-200
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing description is a multilingual text classification benchmark spanning 204 languages and multiple domains, used to evaluate cross-domain generalization and classification accuracy. Some papers describe it more narrowly as a seven-way topic classification dataset, and one paper describes it as representing 200 languages. Papers also note that it supports both high and low-resource languages.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use SIB-200 to measure one behavioral indicator, Text classification, and no constructs are linked to it. The reported use converges on text classification rather than spreading across multiple outcomes, with several papers describing the task more specifically as topic classification, including a seven-label setup.

Space of uses. Papers position SIB-200 both as a widely adopted multilingual benchmark in zero-shot evaluation and as a main grounding dataset for research. One reported use chooses it for topic classification because it has seven labels and supports a variety of high and low-resource languages, while another reports instruction tuning on each domain and evaluation across all other domains within SIB-

nodes.name: SimpleQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly describe SimpleQA as an OpenAI benchmark made up of numerous concise, fact-oriented, fact-seeking questions for assessing LLM factual capabilities in general knowledge. A narrower description presents it specifically as a factuality benchmark in which model responses are categorized as correct, incorrect, or not attempted.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use SimpleQA to measure two constructs, Factuality and Truthfulness, and one behavioral indicator, Factual question answering. The prevailing usage stays within factual evaluation: one paper says it was proposed to measure short-form factuality in LLMs, another takes it for truthfulness, and another describes it as evaluating the ability of language models to answer fact-seeking questions.

Space of uses. The clearest paired use is alongside FreshQA-2025-04-28, where a paper presents the two as factuality benchmarks for fact-seeking questions. Otherwise, no measurement instrument is linked to it, and papers position SimpleQA as a benchmark used for short-form factuality or truthfulness evaluation.

nodes.name: SimpleSafetyTests
nodes.definition: SimpleSafetyTests, a safety evaluation dataset used to probe whether models refuse or avoid unsafe requests.

nodes.name: SimulatorArena
nodes.definition: Benchmark of 909 annotated human–LLM conversations in math tutoring and document creation, used to evaluate user simulators on message realism and alignment with human assistant ratings.

nodes.name: SimulEq
nodes.definition: Dataset focused on solving systems of equations, used to evaluate symbolic and algebraic reasoning capabilities in language models.

nodes.name: SingleEq
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most papers treat SingleEq as a dataset or benchmark of arithmetic or math word problems solvable with a single equation. The prevailing wording is that the problems are solvable with a single equation, while some papers narrow this to single-equation algebraic word problems or say the benchmark contains algebraic word problems that are parsed into equations. Several papers also position it as a distribution-shift, near-shift, or out-of-domain test set, and one definition explicitly says it has simpler reasoning demands.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use SingleEq to measure one construct, Mathematical reasoning, and one behavioral indicator, Mathematical problem solving. The dominant claim is Mathematical reasoning: papers list it among arithmetic or math reasoning datasets and describe it as covering problems "solvable using a single linear equation." One paper also uses it to measure Mathematical problem solving in a broader benchmark set.

Space of uses. Most papers use SingleEq alongside other arithmetic or math benchmarks, most often MultiArith, SVAMP, GSM8K, AddSub, and SingleOp, with some papers also pairing it with AQuA or MATH. A recurring usage is as

nodes.name: SinhalaMMLU
nodes.definition: A multiple-choice question answering benchmark for Sinhala, containing over 7,000 questions aligned with the Sri Lankan national curriculum across six domains and 30 subjects, designed to evaluate multitask language understanding in a low-resource language.

nodes.name: SIQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, SIQA is most commonly described as a benchmark or dataset for multiple-choice question answering about social situations or interactions. Papers variously call it SocialIQA, Social IQA, Social Interaction QA, or Social-I-QA, and they usually describe it as testing social commonsense reasoning, including understanding people's actions, feelings, social implications or consequences, likely outcomes, human motivations, and reactions. Some papers frame it more broadly as a downstream task benchmark or a socio-emotional-skills evaluation item, and a smaller line adapts or re-annotates it, either using it to construct situational questions for another benchmark or using a version with Likert-scale answer plausibility ratings.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use SIQA to measure 8 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator. The prevailing usage is to measure commonsense reasoning, often as one of several commonsense reasoning tasks; smaller lines of work report it as evaluating question answering, general ability, social and emotional intelligence, and social reasoning, with additional papers linking it to other constructs. Overall, the measurement claims cente

nodes.name: SIUO
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing framing is of a multimodal safety benchmark. Definitions most commonly describe it as a safety-awareness benchmark that assesses a model's ability to infer user intent and identify safety risks in multimodal inputs through visual and textual reasoning, while another paper describes it more broadly as assessing safe and effective responses under different risk combinations. One study also notes that higher scores denote better safety performance.

What it is claimed to measure. Its measurement claims are spread across 3 constructs rather than concentrated on one: papers use SIUO to measure Safety, Safety alignment, and Safety awareness, and no behavioral indicators are linked to it. The phrasing varies by paper, with one using it for multimodal safety, another to evaluate safe alignment, and another for assessment of safety-awareness.

Space of uses. Papers typically use SIUO within broader benchmark suites, alongside FigStep, VLGuard, MOSSBench, MSS-Bench, and MM-Safetybench. In these studies it is used as an evaluation dataset with reported SIUO scores, including a "safe&effective score"; another paper states that higher SIUO sc

nodes.name: SLAKE
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats SLAKE as a medical visual question answering benchmark or dataset built from image and question-answer pairs. Several definitions further describe it as semantically labeled and knowledge-enhanced, and some add radiology images, physician annotation, region-level annotations of organs and diseases, or multiple imaging modalities such as CT and MRI across different pathologies and modalities. A smaller set of descriptions specifies versions and question formats: some papers describe English and Chinese versions, one evaluation keeps only the English portion with 641 images and 7,033 question-answer pairs, and others note open and closed questions or Yes/No and single-word answers.

What it is claimed to measure. In these papers, SLAKE is linked to 2 behavioral indicators and no constructs. The prevailing claim is that it measures Medical visual question answering, and a smaller but closely aligned usage treats it as measuring Visual question answering; overall, the reported links stay within VQA rather than spreading across other outcomes.

Space of uses. Papers most often position SLAKE as one benchmark within a bund

nodes.name: SlideVQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, SlideVQA is most commonly described as a public, open-source dataset for visual question answering on presentation slides. The prevailing description adds that each document consists of 20 pages, and one paper further specifies splits of 1,919 slides for training, 400 for test, and 300 for development. A smaller usage describes it more generally as a visual document question-answering dataset that can serve as source material for query refinement.

What it is claimed to measure. Across reported uses, papers use SlideVQA to measure 2 behavioral indicators and no constructs. The linked indicators are Information retrieval and Visual question answering, so its reported measurement use is spread across those two tasks rather than centered on any construct. One paper evaluates retrieval accuracy on SlideVQA, while another includes it among VQA datasets used for presentation slides.

Space of uses. Papers use SlideVQA in several roles. In one evaluation setup, it appears alongside MM-LongBench, DUDE, DocVQA, and VisR-Bench when comparing retrieval accuracy baselines. Other papers use it as a source of question-document pairs for presentation slides, or desc

nodes.name: SlimPajama
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, SlimPajama is most commonly treated as a large-scale text corpus or pre-training dataset. Several definitions present it simply as the corpus from which files are selected or as the data source for language-model pretraining, while some papers describe it more specifically as a cleaned and deduplicated version of RedPajama and a high-quality corpus with diverse sources such as C4, ArXiv, GitHub, and Books. A smaller line of work foregrounds subsets within it, either by selecting categories such as StackExchange, Github Codes, ArXiv, and Book, or by drawing token subsets for experiments.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers do not report SlimPajama as measuring any construct or behavioral indicator. The descriptions instead use it as experimental data for training, post-training, pruning recovery, and related model-development procedures.

Space of uses. Most papers position SlimPajama as a training or continued-training corpus rather than a standalone evaluation protocol. Papers use it for file selection, post-prune recovery, continual pre-training after architectural changes, post-training after pruning, general language-model training, and finetun

nodes.name: SLUE
nodes.definition: A spoken language understanding evaluation benchmark listed in the comparison of spoken language and audio comprehension benchmarks.

nodes.name: SLURP
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, SLURP is most commonly described as a spoken language understanding dataset. Definitions describe a corpus of 16.5k sentences and 72k audio recordings of single-turn interactions with a home assistant, annotated with scenarios, actions, and entities; some uses keep only the reference transcriptions for slot filling, while others treat it as a seed corpus for generating dialogues with diverse intents and interwoven mode switches.

What it is claimed to measure. In these papers, SLURP is linked to 3 behavioral indicators and no constructs. The prevailing usage is to measure Information extraction, and papers also use it to measure Intent classification and Sequence understanding, with evidence phrased as "SF SLURP," "intent classification ... with SLURP," and "Sequence Understanding on SLURP."

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it. Papers position SLURP both as a benchmark for common speech tasks, including slot filling and intent classification, and as source material for broader dialogue construction, including work that constructs flows from MultiWOZ2.2 and SLURP and then builds TACT variants from both.

nodes.name: SMNLI
nodes.definition: A synthetic Natural Language Inference (NLI) dataset created by subsampling the MNLI dataset to induce specific spurious correlations between text genres and labels for evaluation purposes.

nodes.name: SMS Spam
nodes.definition: A dataset for binary classification of SMS messages as either legitimate (ham) or spam.

nodes.name: SNIPS
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most descriptions treat SNIPS as a benchmark dataset for intent classification. One definition places it in a voice assistant setting with seven user intents and says it is used for evaluating task-oriented dialogue systems, while another presents it as a multi-domain dataset, mentioning restaurants, movies, and music, reporting 13,084 training utterances, and describing it as used to evaluate model reasoning on diverse and balanced data.

What it is claimed to measure. Claims about what SNIPS measures converge on a single behavioral indicator, intent classification. Papers use it to measure intent classification, and the linked measurement claims do not extend beyond that: it is linked to one behavioral indicator, Intent classification, and to no constructs.

Space of uses. Papers treat SNIPS as a benchmark used within evaluation setups rather than as a standalone protocol. One study pairs it with ATIS as one of two intent classification benchmark datasets, and another includes SNIPS as the intent classification dataset within a broader text classification comparison; papers do not otherwise link it to measurement instruments.

nodes.name: SNLI
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most papers describe SNLI as the Stanford Natural Language Inference dataset or benchmark, a large-scale corpus of sentence pairs for textual entailment or natural language inference. One paper explicitly states that it labels pairs of strings as entailment, neutral, or contradiction, and another describes it more specifically as using image captions as premises paired with hypotheses elicited from crowdworkers. Some papers work with adapted versions or slices, including entailment-only pairs, SNLI-TEST-SAMPLE original examples, and negation benchmarks for SNLI.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, the prevailing use is to measure natural language inference, which is also the most frequently linked behavioral indicator. Papers link SNLI to two behavioral indicators and two constructs overall: it measures natural language inference most often, one paper also uses it to measure multiple-choice question answering, and papers additionally use it to measure generalization and logical consistency. The reported uses therefore cluster around NLI, while the construct-level links are divided between generalization and logical consistency.

Space of uses. No measurement

nodes.name: Social Chemistry 101
nodes.definition: A dataset encompassing diverse social norms and moral judgments about everyday actions, used to evaluate morality.

nodes.name: SocioBench
nodes.definition: A large-scale, cross-national benchmark derived from the International Social Survey Programme (ISSP) that evaluates LLMs' ability to simulate human responses in sociological surveys across 10 domains and over 30 countries.

nodes.name: SolEval
nodes.definition: Repository-level benchmark for Solidity smart contract generation, consisting of 1,507 real-world function samples from 28 repositories, with human-annotated requirements, contextual dependencies, and test cases to assess functional correctness, gas efficiency, and vulnerability rates.

nodes.name: Something-Something V2
nodes.definition: A large-scale video dataset for action recognition that focuses on fine-grained human-object interactions, often requiring temporal reasoning.

nodes.name: SORRY-Bench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across definitions, the prevailing usage treats SORRY-Bench as a benchmark dataset of unsafe or harmful prompts and instructions for evaluating model refusal, safety alignment, or harmfulness. Papers variously describe it as a dataset of unsafe prompts used to evaluate and train models, a harmfulness benchmark in the HarmfulQA context, a jailbreak evaluation benchmark, and a dataset for assessing whether an LLM rejects questions with harmful intent. Its content is described as 450 harmful instructions, with one definition adding that the prompts span 45 categories and another referring to 450 unseen harmful test sets.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers connect SORRY-Bench to 1 construct and 3 behavioral indicators. It is used to measure Safety, and the named behavioral indicators, in the order most frequently linked, are Harmful content generation, Harmful request refusal, and Jailbreaking. The measurement language varies across papers, including "text-only safety," "LLM safety refusal," and "harmfulness in the HarmfulQA context."

Space of uses. Papers use SORRY-Bench both as an evaluation benchmark and as source material for derived datasets. It appears alongside

nodes.name: SOTOPIA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing description is of an open-ended, interactive benchmark environment for simulating complex social interactions between artificial or LLM agents and assessing social intelligence. Definitions consistently refer to scenarios in which agents have character or role profiles and private goals, and one paper specifies simulated social tasks defined by a scenario, two role profiles, and private goals. A more detailed usage description says it includes 90 scenarios with 5 role pairs, yielding 450 self-chat tasks and 900 non-self-chat tasks, while another paper describes it more broadly as a platform or framework for simulation and evaluation.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link SOTOPIA to 2 constructs and no behavioral indicators. The most common linkage is that it measures Strategic reasoning: papers report evaluating strategic reasoning in SOTOPIA, including social interaction with goals and as one of the social intelligence tasks in a broader strategic-reasoning evaluation. A smaller line of work presents it as measuring Social intelligence directly, matching descriptions of the benchmark as evaluating agents' social intelligence.

Space

nodes.name: SPaRC
nodes.definition:
What it is. The descriptions do not converge. In "SPaRC: A Spatial Pathfinding Reasoning Challenge," the name refers to a benchmark of 1,000 2D grid pathfinding puzzles used to evaluate spatial and rule-based reasoning under multiple constraints. In "Track-SQL: Enhancing Generative Language Models with Dual-Extractive Modules for Schema and Context Tracking in Multi-turn Text-to-SQL," SParC is described instead as a benchmark dataset for multi-turn Text-to-SQL, with 4,298 dialogue sequences and over 12,000 questions paired with SQL queries, used to evaluate cross-domain semantic parsing in interactive settings.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the recorded relationships, papers use it to measure 4 constructs and no behavioral indicators. The linked constructs are constraint satisfaction, multi-step planning, rule-based reasoning, and spatial reasoning, with the evidence stating that the benchmark reveals limitations regarding all four.

Space of uses. Usage details are limited. No measurement instrument is linked to it in the recorded relationships, but a reported evaluation uses SParC alongside CoSQL as a benchmark dataset for validating a method.

nodes.name: Speech Quality Dataset
nodes.definition: A dataset from Slonim et al. (2021) containing over 600 debate speeches annotated by 15 human raters each, used to benchmark LLM judges.

nodes.name: SPEED
nodes.definition: Event detection dataset in the epidemiology and social media domain, containing 7 event types related to disease outbreaks and public health responses.

nodes.name: Spider
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats Spider as a large-scale, complex, cross-domain text-to-SQL benchmark or dataset. Papers commonly describe it as natural-language questions paired with SQL queries over multiple databases or database schemas, sometimes emphasizing executable SQL and syntactic and semantic correctness. A smaller line of work describes it as a benchmark for text-to-SQL semantic parsers or parsing over one or more relational tables, and some papers also refer to train, development, and test splits and a range of difficulty levels.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers overwhelmingly use Spider to measure Text-to-SQL, including generating SQL queries from natural-language questions and schemas. Beyond that dominant use, papers link it to two behavioral indicators, Text-to-SQL and Schema linking, and to two constructs, Cross-domain generalization and General ability. The claims are concentrated on Text-to-SQL, while a single paper each reports Spider as measuring schema linking, evaluating cross-domain generalization, or testing general downstream performance.

Space of uses. Papers usually position Spider as a standard or prominent bench

nodes.name: Spider-DK
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, Spider-DK is most commonly treated as a variant of the Spider benchmark, and one definition describes it as a robust variant. The shared characterization is that it incorporates domain knowledge into the questions and introduces domain knowledge reasoning challenges for correctly generating SQL queries; one paper also places it among datasets derived from Spider.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link Spider-DK to one behavioral indicator, Text-to-SQL, and to no constructs. The only reported measurement claim is that it measures Text-to-SQL: one paper evaluates NL2SQL using SPIDER-DK alongside other datasets, so the reported use is concentrated on that single behavioral indicator rather than spread across multiple constructs.

Space of uses. Across the papers, Spider-DK is used alongside other Spider-based evaluations rather than with separate linked instruments. One paper uses it together with Spider and Spider-Realistic as prevalent NL2SQL datasets, and another evaluates it with the same demonstration pool as Spider-Realistic and Spider-Syn, describing these as derived from Spider.

nodes.name: Spider-Realistic
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, Spider-Realistic is most commonly described as a Spider-derived benchmark or variant that removes explicitly mentioned column names from questions. The descriptions converge on this format, with one paper specifying that the removals are made in the SPIDER development set, and they frame the change as simulating more realistic question settings or better reflecting real-world scenarios.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use Spider-Realistic to measure one behavioral indicator, Text-to-SQL, and they do not link it to any constructs. The reported measurement claim centers on Text-to-SQL rather than multiple named targets: one paper on NL2SQL evaluation lists SPIDER, SPIDER-DK, and Spider-Realistic as datasets adopted for the task.

Space of uses. Papers do not link it to other instruments, and instead place it alongside other Spider-derived evaluations. One description evaluates on Spider-DK, Spider-Realistic, and Spider-Syn using the same demonstration pool, while another paper positions SPIDER, SPIDER-DK, and Spider-Realistic together in evaluation for NL2SQL.

nodes.name: Spider-Syn
nodes.definition: A variant of the Spider benchmark where schema-related words in the questions are replaced with their synonyms to test model robustness to lexical variation.

nodes.name: SPSA
nodes.definition: Simultaneous Perturbation Stochastic Approximation, a black-box adversarial attack that estimates the gradient using a small number of queries.

nodes.name: Spurious correlation removal
nodes.definition: Spurious correlation removal (SCR), a procedure that trains classifiers on biased data and ablates latents encoding the spurious signal to test concept isolation.

nodes.name: SQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, SQA is most commonly described as a science question answering or ScienceQA benchmark, usually multimodal: definitions mention science questions that require complex reasoning, often with diagrams, reasoning over text and diagrams, scientific knowledge, and, in one description, a focus on model reasoning capability. A smaller line of work uses the same acronym for sequential question answering over tabular data in multi-turn or logically related settings, and one paper uses it for a 3D question answering benchmark with over 33K question-answer pairs from 650 indoor scenes.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link SQA to one behavioral indicator and one construct. The prevailing measurement claim is that it measures visual question answering, with papers explicitly evaluating methods on visual or image question-answering benchmarks including SQA; a smaller line of work reports it as measuring multimodal reasoning by listing it among multimodal benchmarks.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it through recorded relationships. In use, papers usually include SQA as one benchmark within broader evaluation suites, often alongside VQAv2, Vi

nodes.name: SQA3D
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across definitions, SQA3D is most commonly described as a situated 3D dataset or benchmark for situated question answering in 3D scenes. Papers variously call it human-annotated, multi-modal, and a dataset for situated understanding in real-world scenes, and one definition adds that it contains over 33,000 question-answer pairs for evaluating vision-language reasoning. Several descriptions emphasize questions posed from an embodied agent's perspective or under imaginative situations, and one paper says it emphasizes the role of "situation" in the scene context.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use SQA3D to measure 3D question answering and situated question answering, and they also report it as measuring 3D understanding and vision-language reasoning. Across linked concepts, claims are spread across 3 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators rather than converging on one target. Separately, one paper says SQA3D is related to spatial reasoning, citing question types that include object identification, spatial relationships, scene-level understanding, and general reasoning.

Space of uses. In use, papers commonly evaluate SQA3D alongside ScanQA, describing the pair as

nodes.name: SQUAB
nodes.definition: An automatic dataset generator for ambiguous and unanswerable questions in semantic parsing, producing annotated tests across six categories: Column Ambiguity, Scope, Attachment, Column Unanswerable, Calculation Unanswerable, and Out-of-Scope.

nodes.name: SQuAD2.0-Eval
nodes.definition: Evaluation dataset derived from SQuAD2.0, designed to assess adherence and robustness in retrieval-augmented language models under complex retrieval scenarios with conflicting and irrelevant contexts.

nodes.name: SQuAD 2.0
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, this benchmark appears under several surface forms, including SQuAD v2, SQuAD v2.0, SQuADv2, and SQuAD2, but the prevailing description is the Stanford Question Answering Dataset v2.0, a reading comprehension or question answering benchmark built from Wikipedia articles or passages. Most definitions emphasize span-based answering with some unanswerable questions, so models are expected either to extract an answer or abstain, including to "reject when the context is insufficient." A smaller group of papers describes it as source material for other resources or tasks, including a True-False dataset, the UQA corpus, and a document retrieval task sampled from SQuAD v2.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to measure 4 behavioral indicators and no constructs. The prevailing measurement claim is Machine reading comprehension, and several papers also report it as measuring Question answering; smaller lines of work report it as measuring Document question answering and Information retrieval. Overall, the reported uses cluster around reading comprehension and QA behaviors rather than around constructs.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked t

nodes.name: SQuAD v1.1
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the dominant framing is a reading comprehension benchmark for extractive question answering, where a model answers a question from a context passage or Wikipedia article by selecting a text span. Definitions usually refer to the Stanford Question Answering Dataset version 1.1, sometimes contrasted with v2.0, and one paper notes that v1.1 contains no unanswerable questions; a few papers describe it more broadly as an open-book question answering dataset or emphasize its context, question, answer format.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to measure 8 behavioral indicators and 5 constructs. The most frequently linked behavioral indicators are question answering, machine reading comprehension, extractive question answering, open-domain question answering, and downstream task performance; papers also link it to additional behavioral indicators and to 5 constructs, so the reported scope is spread across multiple targets rather than one construct.

Space of uses. Most papers position it as one benchmark within broader evaluation suites rather than a standalone protocol, often alongside GLUE, CoQA, Natural Questions, TriviaQA, and HotpotQA.

nodes.name: SRDD
nodes.definition: A benchmark for evaluating the generation of entire software projects.

nodes.name: SROIE
nodes.definition: A dataset for Scanned Receipt OCR and Information Extraction, used to evaluate a model's ability to perform key information extraction from receipts.

nodes.name: SST
nodes.definition: The Stanford Sentiment Treebank dataset used as a source of prompts for extracting internal representations.

nodes.name: SST-2
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the dominant framing is a binary sentiment classification dataset or benchmark, usually described as Stanford Sentiment Treebank v2 for positive versus negative judgments on movie-review text. Definitions vary slightly on the unit of text, with papers calling it movie reviews, sentences, or, in one description, "872 single sentences extracted from movie reviews"; several also place it within GLUE. A smaller line of work refers to an out-of-distribution version of SST-2 or uses SST2 as a source of out-of-domain samples for another task.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link SST-2 to 5 behavioral indicators and 5 constructs. The prevailing use is to measure sentiment analysis and, more broadly, text classification; smaller lines of work use it for downstream task performance and 2 other behavioral indicators. At the construct level, papers also use it to measure adversarial robustness and calibration, with 3 other constructs also linked, so the construct-level claims are spread across several targets rather than centered on one.

Space of uses. Papers relate SST-2 to 2 other instruments, most commonly GLUE, where it is positioned as one dataset in bro

nodes.name: SST-5
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the dominant framing treats SST-5, also written SST5, as the Stanford Sentiment Treebank for fine-grained sentiment classification with five labels. Definitions usually describe the labels as ranging from very negative to very positive, and one source spells out the five classes as "very positive", "positive", "neutral", "negative", and "very negative"; some papers also specify that the texts are movie reviews. Papers alternate between calling it a benchmark, a dataset, and a task, and one definition describes it as a five-class sentiment classification benchmark used to evaluate fine-tuned model performance.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link SST-5 to 3 behavioral indicators and 2 constructs. The prevailing use is to measure Sentiment analysis, with several papers labeling it as a sentiment analysis or sentiment classification dataset. Smaller lines of work report Controlled sentiment generation and Multiple-choice question answering as measured by SST-5, and single papers also use it to measure In-context learning and Reasoning, so the recorded claims spread across several targets rather than centering on only one construct.

Space o

nodes.name: ST-VQA
nodes.definition: ST-VQA (Biten et al., 2019) is a benchmark for visual question answering focused on scene text, requiring models to understand text in its visual context.

nodes.name: StableToolBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing description treats StableToolBench as a benchmark for evaluating LLM tool invocation or tool use, especially the accuracy of generated function calls. Definitions also describe it as derived from, or evolving from, ToolBench, with a stable API access setup: one paper describes an API caching mechanism, while another mentions a virtual API server and stable evaluation system. The descriptions converge on its scale, reporting 765 solvable tasks or questions organized into six subsets or subtasks, with variation in tool category and instruction complexity from single-tool to multi-tool instructions.

What it is claimed to measure. The available relationship evidence uses StableToolBench to measure tool use. Across the reported relationships, it is linked to one behavioral indicator, Tool use, and no constructs. In one reported use, papers measure tool use by comparing the accuracy of function calls on StableToolBench against baselines, so the measurement claims are concentrated on a single behavioral indicator rather than spread across multiple linked constructs.

Space of uses. Papers place StableToolBench within broader evaluation suites and

nodes.name: Standard CL Benchmark
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most commonly, papers treat it as a continual learning benchmark built from classification datasets. One description presents the standard CL benchmarks as having 4 tasks and 5 categories for assessing performance across task sequences, while another presents a benchmark for language models made up of five text classification datasets: AG News, Amazon Reviews, Yelp Reviews, DBpedia, and Yahoo Answers.

What it is claimed to measure. The recorded measurement use is concentrated on text classification. Papers link it to one behavioral indicator, text classification, describing it as five text classification datasets or five text classification tasks, and no constructs are linked to it.

Space of uses. Papers use it as an evaluation benchmark in continual learning, including for assessing model performance across task sequences and for evaluation setups described as designed for language models. No other measurement instrument is linked to it.

nodes.name: Stanford Cars
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, Stanford Cars is most commonly described as a fine-grained image classification benchmark or dataset for car models. Several definitions specify that it contains 196 classes or categories of cars, and some frame it as assessing fine-grained visual discrimination, while a smaller framing presents it more generally as an image classification benchmark used to test downstream performance. Papers also place it within broader image recognition and fine-grained visual classification benchmark suites.

What it is claimed to measure. In the recorded relationships, papers use Stanford Cars to measure the behavioral indicator Image classification. It is linked to 1 behavioral indicator and no constructs, so the recorded measurement use centers on a single target rather than being spread across multiple constructs. The relationship evidence describes this use in image recognition, zero-shot classification, downstream performance, and broader classification-domain evaluations.

Space of uses. Usage is usually as one dataset among several benchmarks, rather than as a standalone protocol. Quoted passages place it in zero-shot and linear-probe image classification, down

nodes.name: Stanford Dogs
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, Stanford Dogs is treated as a fine-grained visual classification or recognition resource centered on 120 breeds of dogs. The prevailing description places it within the FGVC benchmark, with one paper stating that FGVC includes Stanford Dogs among five Fine-Grained Visual Classification datasets. A smaller usage describes the same benchmark after task reformulation, where it is used as a 4-way multiple-choice question task.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link Stanford Dogs to one construct and one behavioral indicator. It is used to measure fine-grained perception in work that lists it among fine-grained benchmarks for ablation studies, and it is also used to measure image classification in work that includes it among image recognition datasets. The reported measurement claims therefore converge on these two targets rather than spreading across many constructs or indicators.

Space of uses. Papers position Stanford Dogs alongside one linked instrument, FGVC, by treating it as part of that benchmark collection. In use, it appears within broader evaluation suites rather than in isolation, for example among image recognition datasets in one study

nodes.name: STAR
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats STAR as a video question answering benchmark for situated or situational reasoning in real-world videos. Definitions commonly describe it as targeting reasoning about social interactions and events, and one description further says it contains questions about interaction, sequence, prediction, and feasibility. A smaller line of work also places it among multi-choice QA benchmarks and uses it as a source for referred video question answering.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use STAR to measure 3 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator. The most common reported use is measuring video question answering, while individual papers also use it to measure causal reasoning, temporal reasoning, and visual reasoning. In those papers, STAR is described as part of datasets that demand both causal and temporal reasoning abilities, and as one of the datasets used for visual reasoning tasks, so construct claims are spread across several reasoning targets rather than concentrated on one construct.

Space of uses. Papers usually use STAR alongside other video question answering instruments, most often NExT-QA and IntentQA, and sometimes Ego

nodes.name: Star Graph Task
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage treats the Star Graph Task as a synthetic path-finding or planning benchmark on a star-shaped graph. Most descriptions say the model must output or predict the path between nodes, either as the full sequence from a start node to a specified final node or, in another formulation, as next-node prediction conditioned on an edge list, start, goal, and current path. A smaller descriptive variant focuses on the graph-generation setup itself: the start vertex sits at the center, multiple spokes radiate outward, and the goal lies at the end of one spoke.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link this instrument to one construct and one behavioral indicator. The dominant measurement claim is that it measures Planning: papers describe it as a simple path-finding task that requires basic planning, and Planning is recorded as measured by the Star Graph Task in the most common linkage. A narrower usage links it to Pathfinding, so the reported measurement claims are concentrated on these two closely related targets rather than spread across many constructs or indicators.

Space of uses. In use, papers position it mainly as a didactic or

nodes.name: STaRK-Amazon
nodes.definition: A product search dataset from the STaRK benchmark, where documents are derived from product reviews and Q&A records, and a knowledge graph contains relations like 'products viewed together'.

nodes.name: STEER-BENCH
nodes.definition: A benchmark for evaluating community-specific steerability in LLMs using contrasting Reddit communities, comprising over 10,000 instruction-response pairs and 5,500 multiple-choice questions across 30 subreddit pairs and 19 domains.

nodes.name: StereoSet
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, StereoSet is most commonly described as a benchmark or dataset for measuring stereotypical bias in language models with sentence-completion or fill-in-the-blank items that contrast stereotypical, anti-stereotypical, and meaningless or unrelated options. Several descriptions emphasize intrasentence examples, including one account that says the task contains 765 sentences with a gap and three completions, while another describes each sample as a sentence triplet. Some papers describe it more broadly as covering intrasentence and intersentence contexts, and a smaller description frames it as crowdsourced "Context Association Tests".

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link StereoSet to five constructs and two behavioral indicators. The prevailing use is to measure stereotyping, with papers saying it measures stereotypical biases or tests stereotypical associations, including in gender, profession, race, and religion; a recurring but smaller use treats it as measuring fairness and social bias, and individual papers also use it for gender bias and language modeling ability. At the behavioral level, it is reported as measuring sentence completion

nodes.name: StoryCloze
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly describe StoryCloze as a benchmark for story understanding and commonsense reasoning, usually framed as choosing the correct ending to a short story. Most definitions specify a four-sentence story and connect the task to script knowledge, narrative understanding, or coherence, while some instead describe five-sentence stories, cloze-style story completion, or sentence completion. One paper further describes it as a dataset of short stories with a valid and an invalid ending, originally used for story understanding and adapted there for open-ended generation.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link StoryCloze to 1 construct and 2 behavioral indicators. The prevailing measurement claim is that it measures Commonsense reasoning: papers place it among common sense reasoning tasks and describe the final sentence as being selected based on commonsense knowledge. Smaller uses treat it as measuring Multiple-choice question answering and Story generation, with one paper listing it among multiple-choice tasks and another using it for a story generation task while noting its original use for story understanding.

Space of uses. In use, papers most often po

nodes.name: StrategyQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across these papers, StrategyQA is most commonly described as a commonsense question-answering benchmark or dataset built around yes/no, true-or-false, or binary questions that require implicit multi-step or multi-hop reasoning. Definitions repeatedly emphasize inferring a strategy, decomposition, or reasoning path from world knowledge or open-domain questions, and some papers explicitly frame it as an implicit multi-hop benchmark or place it in BigBench. A smaller line of work describes added structure around the questions, including supporting evidence, rationales or explanations, Wikipedia evidence, or, in an agent setting, a curated knowledge base of 10k Wikipedia passages.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use StrategyQA to measure 10 constructs and 6 behavioral indicators. The prevailing usage is for commonsense reasoning, followed by multi-hop reasoning, reasoning, calibration, and factuality. Taken together, the claims spread across many framings rather than staying within one target, with the remaining links covering 5 other constructs and 6 behavioral-indicator uses.

Space of uses. Many papers use StrategyQA alongside other benchmarks rather than on its

nodes.name: StrongREJECT
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, StrongREJECT is most commonly treated as a safety or jailbreak evaluation benchmark built around harmful or forbidden prompts and a way to score model responses. Descriptions vary: some papers present an open-source dataset of manually constructed, realistic malicious instructions, sometimes tied to prohibited-use policies and sometimes used as a 60-prompt, six-category subset or small dataset; others describe a dataset plus scoring system, or a judge model, including a Gemma-2B safety classifier and a GPT-4o-mini based evaluator that score refusal, effectiveness, or harmfulness. A smaller line of work frames it specifically as text-generation evaluation for whether models reject unsafe requests under adversarial or jailbreak conditions.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link StrongREJECT to 3 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators. The prevailing use is to measure harmlessness and safety: papers use StrongREJECT scores or harmful-prompt evaluation to quantify response harmfulness, safety violation, or refusal of harmful requests. One paper also says the evaluator measures both willingness and capabilities, linking it to general ability. On behaviora

nodes.name: StrongREJECT evaluator
nodes.definition: An existing rubric-based evaluation method for LLM safety, adapted here for comparison, which scores responses based on refusal, specificity, and convincingness without a toxicity component.

nodes.name: STS12
nodes.definition: A dataset from the SemEval-2012 workshop on Semantic Textual Similarity, used for evaluating sentence similarity prediction.

nodes.name: STS-B
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing description is a Semantic Textual Similarity Benchmark for sentence-pair evaluation, usually framed as a downstream sentence similarity task or a GLUE task. Several definitions add that it provides sentence pairs with human-annotated similarity scores on a 0 to 5 scale, and papers report correlation-based metrics on it, including Spearman and Pearson correlation. A smaller line of work uses different task framings, treating it as a classification dataset with a modest number of labels or as a scoring task where the model outputs a string form of a numerical prediction.

What it is claimed to measure. Its reported measurement role is concentrated rather than spread across many targets. Papers link it to one behavioral indicator, Semantic textual similarity, and to no constructs; one paper describes STSB as directly measuring the ability of embeddings to capture fine-grained semantic similarity, which matches the broader pattern of using it for sentence similarity evaluation.

Space of uses. Most commonly, papers use it as one item in larger evaluation suites rather than in isolation, for example within GLUE development or fine-tuning task co

nodes.name: STS tasks
nodes.definition: A collection of datasets computed by the SentEval toolkit to evaluate sentence embeddings on the task of semantic textual similarity. It includes datasets like STS 2012-2016, SICK-R, and STS-B.

nodes.name: Student Essay corpus
nodes.definition: A domain-specific dataset of student essays used to evaluate LLM text detection in academic writing contexts.

nodes.name: Subj
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats Subj or SUBJ as a subjectivity classification dataset or benchmark for distinguishing subjective from objective text. Most definitions describe a binary text classification task, often at the sentence level, and some papers place it under general natural language understanding or text classification evaluation. A smaller line describes it as a binary classification dataset of movie reviews labeled objective or subjective, and definitions also situate it in in-context evaluation of fine-tuned models or in low-data evaluation.

What it is claimed to measure. Recorded links focus on behavioral indicators rather than constructs: papers use Subj to measure 2 behavioral indicators, Text classification and Subjectivity classification, and no constructs are linked to it. The dominant linkage is to Text classification, where papers place Subj among datasets that admit classification tasks or use it in text classification evaluation suites. A narrower linkage reports it as measuring Subjectivity classification through the objective versus subjective decision task.

Space of uses. Papers typically use Subj alongside other text

nodes.name: SugarCrepe
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, SugarCrepe is most commonly described as a large-scale benchmark for evaluating the compositional reasoning capabilities of vision-language models, specifically through swaps, replacements, and additions of objects, attributes, and relations. Another description presents it as a compositionality benchmark with fine-grained attribute and semantic relationship distinctions, evaluated primarily with a single image and a caption choice.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use SugarCrepe to measure 2 constructs, and no behavioral indicators are linked to it. The prevailing use is to measure compositional reasoning, with TripletCLIP describing analysis of models' compositional understanding on SugarCrepe, while some work also reports it as measuring relation understanding by evaluating the ability to understand and represent relationships between objects within an image.

Space of uses. Papers typically position SugarCrepe as a challenging benchmark for model evaluation, and no measurement instrument is linked to it. In reported uses, authors mainly evaluate models on it as a composition benchmark, and COCO-Tree notes that, because only a single image is

nodes.name: SummEval
SUN
nodes.definition: An out-of-distribution scene dataset used to evaluate detection of semantically different or near-OOD inputs.

nodes.name: SUN397
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing description treats SUN397 as a scene dataset. One line of work describes it as a scene recognition dataset used for zero-shot transfer evaluation, while another describes it as a dataset for scene classification used to evaluate few-shot learning performance; one source also places it among publicly available image recognition datasets.

What it is claimed to measure. The reported measurement use is concentrated rather than spread across many targets. Papers link SUN397 to one behavioral indicator, Image classification, and to no constructs, using it to measure image classification in finetuning and broader benchmark evaluations.

Space of uses. Papers typically position SUN397 as one member of a larger evaluation suite rather than as a standalone protocol. It appears alongside Oxford Flowers, Food101, FGVC-Aircraft, and Sports100 in zero-shot reporting, and other papers include it among datasets used for finetuning and standard benchmark evaluation; no other measurement instrument is linked to it.

nodes.name: Super-NaturalInstructions
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most papers describe Super-NaturalInstructions as a large instruction-following benchmark or collection of diverse NLP tasks with expert-written or human-written instructions, usually covering both classification and generation formats. Definitions commonly describe it as having over 1600 tasks or 1,616 tasks, while a smaller line of work uses SuperNI Benchmark for a continual learning setup of 15 tasks spanning dialogue generation, information extraction, question answering, summarization, and sentiment analysis. One paper also uses a subset of 53 tasks, described as 19 multiple-choice and 34 classification tasks, and separately tests formatting generation against 100+ tasks from the benchmark.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, it is linked to 4 constructs and 3 behavioral indicators. Among the named targets, instruction following, task generalization, and text generation recur most often: papers use it to measure instruction following, report it as evaluating cross-task or unseen-task generalization, and use it for text generation benchmarks. Smaller uses treat it as measuring text classification, continual learning, multi-task ability, and translation ab

nodes.name: SUPERB
nodes.definition:
What it is. The descriptions treat SUPERB as a benchmark for spoken language understanding, with the prevailing characterization emphasizing coarse-grained semantic understanding tasks. One paper further describes it as the first benchmark specifically designed for spoken language.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use SUPERB to measure speech understanding, and the reported measurement claims converge on that single construct rather than spreading across several constructs. It is also linked to one behavioral indicator, speech recognition, but that connection is described as a related use rather than as a direct measurement claim.

Space of uses. The recorded relationships do not link SUPERB directly to any other measurement instrument. In one use, a paper evaluates ASR with TED-LIUMv3, intent classification with SLURP, and speaker ID with VoxCeleb1, while stating that these evaluations follow the SUPERB configuration.

Concerns raised. A concern raised in the discussion is that SUPERB primarily focuses on coarse-grained semantic understanding tasks and, in that account, overlooks various acoustic features.

nodes.name: SuperGLUE
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, SuperGLUE is most commonly described as a benchmark suite or collection of diverse, challenging language understanding tasks, usually framed as more difficult than GLUE and aimed at reasoning, inference, and comprehension. Definitions differ on its size and composition, with some papers describing 6 tasks, others 7 or 8, and several naming subsets such as MultiRC, BoolQ, WiC, WSC, CB, COPA, RTE, and ReCoRD; some also characterize it through task families such as question answering, textual entailment, coreference resolution, logical reasoning, and classification-style tasks.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use SuperGLUE to measure 2 constructs and 4 behavioral indicators. Most often, they use it to measure Natural language understanding, with a smaller line of work also using it to measure Multi-task ability; one paper says it allows evaluation of "different aspects of natural language understanding" (BERTs are Generative In-Context Learners). At the behavioral level, it is reported as measuring Classification, Coreference resolution, Language understanding task performance, and Word sense disambiguation, so the construct-level claims converge most

nodes.name: SuperGPQA
nodes.definition: Scientific reasoning benchmark with 1500 sampled questions at varying difficulty levels, used to assess broad scientific knowledge and reasoning.

nodes.name: SVAMP
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing description is of SVAMP as a benchmark or dataset of arithmetic, grade-school, or simple math word problems built from simple, controlled, or novel variations of existing problems. Most definitions emphasize linguistic, semantic, structural, or numerical variation and present the dataset as testing compositional generalization, robustness, question sensitivity, structural invariance, or spurious correlations in mathematical reasoning. Some authors also frame it as out-of-domain or out-of-distribution, one paper presents it as a one-step math reasoning set, and individual descriptions note English problems up to grade 4 and a collection of 1,000 problems used only for evaluation.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers most commonly use SVAMP to measure Mathematical reasoning, and the overall measurement pattern centers on math-related reasoning rather than a single narrow target.
