It is linked to five constructs and two behavioral indicators: beyond Mathematical reasoning, papers also use it for Mathematical problem solving, Reasoning, Robustness, and Generalization, with two additional, less common links. In the relationship evidence, papers

nodes.name: SVHN
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly describe SVHN as the Street View House Numbers dataset, containing images of house numbers. In the one definition, it is used for in-distribution image generation and completion tasks, and one quoted passage states, "For imaging ICL experiments, we use SVHN for in-distribution data." Other papers refer to it as a benchmark dataset in broader evaluations and as an external OOD dataset.

What it is claimed to measure. Overall, papers link SVHN to one construct and two behavioral indicators. The most common use in these papers is to measure image classification, with SVHN included in broader classification benchmark evaluations. A smaller line of work uses it to measure out-of-distribution detection, where it is described as an external OOD dataset, and one paper reports it as measuring optical character recognition ability. The measurement claims therefore span several targets rather than converging on a single construct.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to SVHN. Instead, papers usually position it as one component of larger evaluation suites: it appears in classification runs alongside several other benchmark datasets, in one paper

nodes.name: SWAG
nodes.definition: A dataset for evaluating commonsense inference through sentence completion tasks.

nodes.name: SWDE
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, SWDE is described either as an information extraction benchmark used as a recall-intensive evaluation of long-sequence retrieval, or as an information-retrieval benchmark designed to evaluate retrieval from in-context passages scraped from HTML/PDFs. Papers therefore use overlapping but not identical labels for it.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use SWDE to measure 2 behavioral indicators and 1 construct. The behavioral-indicator links are to Information extraction and Synthetic recall, and the construct link is to Associative recall ability; one paper reports that "Recall" represents the average performance across FDA, SWDE, and SQuAD.

Space of uses. Papers do not link SWDE to any other measurement instrument. Instead, they present it within broader evaluation setups: one paper places it among "six recall-intensive tasks," another assesses retrieval on FDA and SWDE, and another includes it in a "Recall" average with FDA and SQuAD.

nodes.name: SWE-bench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, SWE-bench is most commonly described as a benchmark of real-world software engineering tasks built from 2,294 GitHub issues, pull requests, or Issue-Pull Request pairs drawn from 12 Python repositories. Definitions converge on repository-level issue solving, with some papers framing it as testing code editing or code generation capabilities and others as assessing agents' ability to resolve GitHub issues; some also specify evaluation by whether generated patches pass provided unit tests. A related variant, SWE-bench Lite, is described as a 300-instance subset sampled from the full benchmark for a more self-contained evaluation of functional bug fixes.

What it is claimed to measure. The prevailing measurement claim is GitHub issue resolution: papers use SWE-bench to evaluate systems' ability to solve software issues from GitHub repositories, and some descriptions add that models must modify the repository to fix a bug or introduce a feature. The reported measurement claims are concentrated rather than spread across many targets, with links to one behavioral indicator, GitHub issue resolution, and one construct, software engineering ability. A smaller line

nodes.name: SWE-bench Lite
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most papers treat SWE-bench Lite as the lite subset of SWE-bench, and some explicitly call it the most commonly used subset, sampled from the full benchmark for a more self-contained evaluation of functional bug fixes. Some descriptions broaden this to a repository-level evaluation suite for automated software engineering, built from real GitHub issues, code patches, and repository-level code changes; some also specify Python codebases or repositories, and a minority mention hidden unit tests.

What it is claimed to measure. Claims about what it measures are concentrated rather than spread across many targets: papers link it to two behavioral indicators and no constructs. It is used to measure software issue resolution and GitHub issue resolution, with relationship evidence referring to issue resolution rate on SWE-bench Lite and to comparing systems on the same issues' resolution.

Space of uses. Papers commonly use it as a main evaluation benchmark for autonomous or automated software engineering systems, including comparisons of state-of-the-art performance and agentic issue resolution. The only linked instrument is SWE-bench, and papers position SWE-bench Lite in re

nodes.name: SWE-bench Verified
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most commonly described as a vetted subset of SWE-Bench, it contains 500 instances or samples that were further checked by human annotators. One definition emphasizes manual verification by professional software developers for appropriately scoped unit tests and well-specified issue descriptions, while another describes it more broadly as a benchmark dataset for automatically resolving software engineering issues; a quoted passage also says the vetted samples were verified to be non-problematic.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the linked claims, papers use it to measure Software issue resolution, for example by reporting an issue resolution rate on SWE-bench Verified. The claims converge on a single behavioral indicator: it is linked to one behavioral indicator, Software issue resolution, and no constructs.

Space of uses. Papers position it as a benchmark for automatically resolving software engineering issues. No measurement instruments are linked to it, and one source explicitly calls it "the most popular benchmark" for that task while another says it was introduced to improve the robustness and reliability of evaluation.

Concerns raised. The recurring concer

nodes.name: sWUGGY
nodes.definition: A benchmark from the ZeroSpeech challenge that objectively measures a model's language capability by testing its ability to score a real word higher than a phonetically similar non-word.

nodes.name: SyGuS
nodes.definition: A dataset of text editing problems originating from the Syntax-Guided Synthesis (SyGuS) competition, generally considered easier than other benchmarks.

nodes.name: SYNC
nodes.definition: SYNC (SYNthetic Contexts) is a synthetic long-context evaluation suite with graph understanding and unseen-language translation tasks designed for controlled comparisons of LLM capabilities.

nodes.name: Synonym substitution attack
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across definitions, the prevailing framing is a robustness evaluation in which words in generated or test text are replaced with synonyms. Papers variously describe it as an evaluation procedure, an observable attack, or an adversarial evaluation procedure; one definition specifies using BERT and WordNet, and another places it within semantically invariant perturbations alongside text paraphrasing.

What it is claimed to measure. In the papers' own descriptions, it is used to test the robustness or resilience of a watermark or detector, and one quoted passage says papers compare detection F1 scores under different synonymous word substitution scenarios. No constructs and no behavioral indicators are linked to it.

Space of uses. Papers use it as an attack condition for evaluation, not alongside any linked measurement instrument. Reported uses include evaluating resilience with BERT and WordNet, comparing detection F1 across synonym substitution scenarios, and applying synonym replacement with a replacement ratio of 0.2 alongside paraphrase attacks on test data from an unknown target domain.

nodes.name: SyntaxGym
nodes.definition: A suite of diagnostic tests evaluating six distinct syntactic phenomena through surprisal-based metrics, where models are assessed on their ability to assign appropriate surprisal to sentence continuations based on syntactic constraints.

nodes.name: T2R-bench
nodes.definition: A bilingual benchmark for evaluating table-to-report generation, comprising 457 real-world industrial tables across 19 domains, with 910 questions and annotated report keypoints to assess numerical accuracy, information coverage, and general quality.

nodes.name: T-Eval
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats T-Eval as an out-of-distribution benchmark for LLMs. Definitions describe it as evaluating multi-step decision-making and API utilization, sometimes as an OOD task planning dataset, while a smaller framing presents it as a tool-use benchmark that measures the ability to interact with external tools and APIs to complete tasks. One paper also describes it as widely used.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use T-Eval to measure three constructs and two behavioral indicators. The linked constructs are Decision-making, Planning, and Reasoning, and the linked behavioral indicators are Action execution and Instruction following. One paper further says that T-Eval assesses six core competencies: planning, reasoning, retrieval, understanding, instruction following, and reviewing.

Space of uses. In usage descriptions, papers position T-Eval as an OOD evaluation for generalization. One paper uses it for zero-shot generalization experiments, and another places it with ToolBench and ToolAlpaca in an Action Execution category.

nodes.name: T-REx
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the definitions, T-REx is most commonly described as a slot-filling or relation-extraction benchmark. Papers describe it as a slot filling dataset for factual relation extraction-style prediction, sometimes more specifically as a large-scale slot-filling dataset derived from Wikipedia abstracts and aligned with Wikidata triples, and one paper places it in the KILT subset of evaluation tasks; a smaller line of work instead describes it as an open-ended QA dataset derived from knowledge base triples and used to test factual recall on rare relational knowledge.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link T-REx to one behavioral indicator, Information extraction, and to no constructs. The prevailing usage is to measure Information extraction, with the evidence framed as slot filling, including table labels such as "Slot Filling" and descriptions of T-REx as a slot-filling task, so the reported measurement claims converge on a single indicator rather than spreading across several targets.

Space of uses. Papers use T-REx as a task within broader evaluation suites rather than as a standalone protocol paired with other linked instruments. It is described as part of a KI

nodes.name: TabFact
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, TabFact is most commonly described as a benchmark or dataset for table-based fact verification over Wikipedia tables, pairing tables with textual statements and asking whether each statement is supported, entailed or true, or instead refuted or false, by the table. Several papers also call it a large-scale dataset, and some describe a specific evaluation subset, the test-small set with 2,024 statements or test samples from 298 tables. A smaller line of work presents it as a public TableQA resource, describing pairs of content-related question and answer or yes or no answers for TQA evaluation.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use TabFact to measure 2 behavioral indicators and 1 construct. The prevailing measurement claim is fact checking, with papers explicitly using it for fact verification or TFV; a smaller but recurring usage treats it as measuring table question answering, including TableQA settings where the answer is yes or no. At the construct level, it is also reported as measuring table reasoning, so papers connect it both to specific behaviors and to a broader table reasoning construct.

Space of uses. Papers commonly use TabFac

nodes.name: TableBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. In surveyed usage, TableBench is presented as a benchmark for table reasoning, described as covering diverse question types and topics across a wide range of scenarios. As one study puts it, "TableBench presents a challenging benchmark covering diverse question types and topics" (RoT: Enhancing Table Reasoning with Iterative Row-Wise Traversals).

What it is claimed to measure. The recorded claims converge on a single construct: papers use TableBench to measure table reasoning. It is linked to 1 construct, Table reasoning, and to no behavioral indicators.

Space of uses. Papers position it as part of an experimental set of table reasoning datasets. In the reported experiments, it is used alongside WikiTableQuestions and HiTab, and no measurement instrument is linked to it through the recorded relationships.

nodes.name: TableEval
nodes.definition: A real-world benchmark for table question answering featuring complex table structures (hierarchical, nested, concise), multilingual content (Simplified Chinese, Traditional Chinese, English), and cross-domain data from finance, government, academia, and industry reports.

nodes.name: TabMWP
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most papers describe TabMWP as a benchmark or dataset for mathematical reasoning over tables, usually framed as table-based or tabular math word problems. The prevailing description is that each sample contains one table and one natural-language problem, and solving it requires understanding the problem text, extracting relevant information from the table, and performing calculations; several papers also describe the tables as semi-structured contextual input. A smaller line of work places it under structured data question answering, tabular question answering, or tabular data reasoning, and one paper describes it as an open-domain math word problem dataset containing tabular data.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the papers, TabMWP is linked to one construct and one behavioral indicator. The prevailing use is to measure mathematical reasoning, with papers listing it among math reasoning benchmarks or saying that it requires mathematical reasoning; a smaller usage treats it as measuring table question answering, specifically a tabular question-answering setting that requires reasoning over tabular contexts. Overall, the named measurement claims are concentrated ma

nodes.name: TACO
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, TACO is described as a competitive programming benchmark made up of problems sourced from CodeContests, APPS, and various programming contest platforms, and used to evaluate code generation. The prevailing description emphasizes difficulty stratification: one account says the test set is split into easy, medium, medium-hard, hard, and very-hard levels, while another reports using the easy and hard split; one paper also notes that it adopts a subset of TACO.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use TACO to measure code generation. It is linked to one behavioral indicator, Code generation, and to no constructs, so the reported use centers on a single behavioral target rather than a broader set of constructs. The relationship evidence describes it as focused on algorithmic code generation and as a benchmark on which authors report code-generation performance.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it. In the papers, TACO is used in coding experiments either by adopting a subset of it for evaluation or by reporting performance on it as "another competitive programming benchmark," including results on easy and hard splits.

Concerns raise

nodes.name: TACRED
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most papers describe TACRED as a large-scale benchmark dataset for relation extraction. Definitions commonly trace it to the TAC Knowledge Base Population challenges, and one paper specifies it as a large-scale English dataset from the TACKBP4 challenge with 42 distinct relations. One definition adds that it contains annotated entity pairs and relations from news and web text, and one paper refers to TACRED together with variants such as TACRED-Revisit and Re-TACRED.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the papers, the use claims converge on a single target: TACRED is used to measure relation extraction. Papers link it to one behavioral indicator, Relation extraction, and to no constructs, describing it as one of the "widely used RE benchmark datasets" and as part of "standard relation extraction benchmarks" for evaluating relation extraction performance.

Space of uses. Papers most often position TACRED as an evaluation benchmark used alongside other relation extraction datasets, especially SemEval, FewRel, TACREV, TACRED-Revisit, and Re-TACRED. Several papers describe experiments on benchmark sets that include TACRED, and some report few-shot settings on it, such as

nodes.name: TACT
nodes.definition: The TOD-And-Chitchat Transition dataset, designed for training and evaluating agents on their ability to handle fluid transitions between task-oriented and chitchat dialogue modes.

nodes.name: TactfulToM
nodes.definition: An English benchmark consisting of 100 multi-party conversations and 6.7K questions designed to evaluate LLMs’ understanding of white lies, including mental state tracking, justification, and reasoning about prosocial deception.

nodes.name: Talk2Car
nodes.definition: A 3D referring expression comprehension dataset for driving scenarios that evaluates a model's ability to ground a textual command to a specific object in 3D space.

nodes.name: TaskBench
nodes.definition: A comprehensive benchmark framework designed to evaluate the capability of LLMs in task automation across three stages: task decomposition, tool selection, and parameter prediction.

nodes.name: Tatoeba
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the definitions, Tatoeba is described as the validation split of a dataset for cross-lingual sentence retrieval. The only characterization is that papers use this split for independent validation of cross-lingual retrieval findings.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers do not link Tatoeba to any constructs or behavioral indicators as a measurement instrument. Instead, it is described only in relation to validating cross-lingual sentence retrieval results.

Space of uses. The paper uses Tatoeba alongside the test split of BUCC-18, and positions it as an auxiliary validation check rather than describing any broader role. In the quoted usage, authors report that they present results on the validation split of Tatoeba "for an independent validation of our findings."

nodes.name: TDIUC
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the cited work, TDIUC is most commonly treated as a visual question answering dataset and benchmark built around simple visual understanding questions with clear answers. Some authors describe it more specifically as featuring 1.6 million questions across 170,000 images, organized into 12 question types ranging from object identification to positional reasoning. Papers also describe drawing subsets from it, such as selecting ten categories of questions.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use TDIUC to measure one behavioral indicator, Abstention, and no constructs are linked to it. The reported measurement claim is that TDIUC contains absurd questions, about 22% of the total, that are not related to the image and thus should not be answered, so authors evaluate abstention on it. In the linked uses, its measurement role is concentrated on this single behavioral indicator rather than spread across multiple constructs or behaviors.

Space of uses. Papers position TDIUC as a representative benchmark for examining specific topics and question types, and as a source for benchmark tasks in visual question answering. One line of use selects ten categories of questions

nodes.name: TempCompass
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, TempCompass is most commonly described as a benchmark for visual temporal reasoning or temporal understanding in video-language models. Definitions consistently place it on videos, often specifically short videos, and describe task formats that include multiple-choice QA, yes/no QA, caption matching, and caption generation; some papers describe its focus through event ordering, duration inference, temporal order information, or temporal aspects such as speed, direction, and attribute changes. One description also specifies that it contains 410 videos and 7,540 instructions, and one paper explicitly uses a Multiple-Choice subset.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, the most common measurement claim is that TempCompass measures Temporal understanding, followed by Temporal reasoning and Video understanding; papers also link it to one behavioral indicator, Video question answering. These measurement claims are concentrated in three constructs rather than spread across many others, and the evidence describes the benchmark as assessing temporal understanding capabilities across five dimensions, diagnosing multi-facet basic video temporal understandin

nodes.name: TempReason
nodes.definition: A benchmark that evaluates both event-time and event-event temporal relations in time-sensitive question answering using real-world facts.

nodes.name: Text2Cypher
nodes.definition: A large-scale dataset released by Neo4j for evaluating the task of translating natural language to Cypher queries.

nodes.name: Text8
nodes.definition: A character-level text modeling benchmark extracted from English Wikipedia and used to evaluate language model likelihood on short text chunks.

nodes.name: TextEE
nodes.definition: A standardized event extraction framework used to compare models under uniform preprocessing, splits, and implementations.

nodes.name: TextVQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage is as a visual question answering benchmark or dataset built around questions that require reading text within images and reasoning over it. Many descriptions add that the images are natural or real-world, text-rich, and tied to OCR or text comprehension, while a smaller line of work frames it more broadly as a document task or as a benchmark for general VLM capabilities. Papers sometimes refer to it as TextQA, VQAT, or VQAText, and some explicitly mention using the validation split.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use TextVQA to measure 9 constructs and 4 behavioral indicators. The most frequent links treat it as measuring Visual understanding, Fine-grained visual understanding, and General ability, and at the behavioral level Visual question answering and Optical character recognition. Overall, the recorded uses are spread across several capabilities rather than tied to a single construct.

Space of uses. Across evaluations, papers usually include TextVQA in broader benchmark suites, commonly alongside VQAv2, GQA, DocVQA, ScienceQA, and VizWiz. It is often presented as one component of general multimodal or VQA eva

nodes.name: TextWorld
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, TextWorld is most commonly described as a text-based agent benchmark centered on interactive fiction or other text-based games. Definitions frame it either as an evaluation benchmark for capabilities like planning, commonsense reasoning, and exploration, or as a benchmark sandbox for training and evaluating reinforcement learning agents. One paper also describes it as entirely text-based, with no visual component, where the agent explores mazes and interacts with everyday objects through natural language.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the papers, TextWorld is linked as measuring 3 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator. The named construct links are Planning, Commonsense reasoning, and Memory, and one study describes its tasks as requiring commonsense reasoning, long-term planning, and memory. Navigation is the linked behavioral indicator, with a paper connecting it to maze exploration and natural-language interaction with objects, so the measurement claims spread across several capabilities rather than a single construct.

Space of uses. Papers use TextWorld as a text environment for evaluating agents on long-horizon memory and planning, expl

nodes.name: TFDP
nodes.definition: Token-Focused Disparity Probing, a methodology for auditing autoregressive LLMs using single-token masked prediction on minimally contrastive sentence pairs, integrating multi-scale semantic alignment and disparity metrics (PS, PSD, WFS).

nodes.name: TGIF
nodes.definition: The Tumblr GIF dataset, used for evaluating video understanding tasks such as action recognition and description generation.

nodes.name: TGIF-QA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the dominant framing is a video question answering benchmark built from the TGIF, or Tumblr GIF, dataset, with animated GIFs as the video source. Definitions commonly describe it as targeting short video clips or sequences and assessing temporal, causal, or spatio-temporal reasoning, and one recurring description highlights tasks such as repetition counting and state transition recognition. A smaller line of work describes it more broadly as a visual question answering dataset, and one paper uses it as a source of evaluation data for count and reasoning tasks.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link TGIF-QA to 1 behavioral indicator and 1 construct. The prevailing usage is to measure Video question answering: papers describe it as one of the common, open-ended, or zero-shot VideoQA benchmarks. A smaller usage treats it as measuring Video understanding, with one paper placing it in a broader suite of video understanding benchmarks. Overall, the measurement claims are concentrated on these two targets rather than spread across many constructs or behavioral indicators.

Space of uses. Across papers, TGIF-QA is usually used as one item in a larger evaluat

nodes.name: The Pile
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats The Pile as a large, diverse text corpus for language model pre-training. Definitions also describe it as an open-source English corpus for training and evaluation, as a validation or test corpus for next-token prediction, perplexity, and recall-related analyses, and as a source of subsets or splits for domain-specific studies. Some authors further specify coverage such as encyclopedic text, books, social media, code, reviews, and domains like arXiv, GitHub, and PubMed, while others refer to particular variants such as a deduplicated version or selected subsets.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link The Pile to 3 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator. The construct links are to General ability, Long-context understanding, and Specialization, and the behavioral-indicator link is to Pre-training data detection. These claims are spread across several targets rather than centered on one: papers use losses on the Pile to measure general ability, refer to long-context understanding on Pile, treat Pile subsets as target specialization sets, and list Pile among benchmark datasets for detecting pre-training data.

Space of use

nodes.name: The Pile (deduplicated)
nodes.definition: The deduplicated version of The PILE dataset, a large and diverse text corpus used for pretraining and evaluating language models.

nodes.name: The Stack
nodes.definition: A code dataset used here as an additional long-context test bed via a single Python file sample to compare long-context language modeling behavior on code.

nodes.name: TheoremQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, TheoremQA is most commonly described as a benchmark or question answering dataset of university-level or advanced STEM problems that require applying mathematical theorems. Several definitions specify 800 questions or problems spanning mathematics, physics, and engineering. A smaller line of work describes it more narrowly through abstract algebra and formal logic, and one paper reports using only a mathematics subset with logical-reasoning questions and definite answers.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link TheoremQA to one behavioral indicator and three constructs. The prevailing use is to measure mathematical problem solving, and several papers also use it to measure reasoning, describing it as part of evaluations of reasoning across domains or as a representative reasoning benchmark. More narrowly, one paper uses it to measure generalization on theoretical reasoning in STEM, and another uses it for out-of-domain evaluation of mathematical reasoning, so papers connect it to several related targets rather than only one construct.

Space of uses. No paper directly links it to another measurement instrument, though many use it inside broader evalua

nodes.name: Ti-MMLU
nodes.definition: Tibetan adaptation of CMMLU, a multi-task understanding benchmark with 11,528 multiple-choice questions across 67 knowledge-based subdomains in Tibetan.

nodes.name: Ti-SafetyBench
nodes.definition: Tibetan adaptation of SafetyBench, a safety evaluation benchmark with 11,435 questions across 7 safety-critical categories including ethics, bias, health, and privacy.

nodes.name: TibetanQA
nodes.definition: A Tibetan question-answering dataset used for zero-shot evaluation of a model's cross-lingual transfer capabilities in machine reading comprehension.

nodes.name: TIDE
nodes.definition: The Trauma-Informed Dialogue for Empathy (TIDE) dataset, a resource of 10,000 two-turn dialogues based on 500 diverse, clinically-grounded PTSD personas, used for training and evaluating empathetic response generation.

nodes.name: TimeQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, TimeQA is most commonly described as a time-sensitive or temporal question-answering benchmark dataset. Definitions characterize it as derived from natural language and Wikidata, focusing on real-world factual questions about event-time relationships and, more broadly, on time-evolving factual questions grounded in the real world. A smaller description emphasizes its reuse as a source dataset for the context-based task in DATEAUGBENCH.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use TimeQA to measure two constructs and no behavioral indicators. The prevailing usage is temporal reasoning: papers describe it as a benchmark used for temporal reasoning performance and as containing question-answer pairs requiring temporal reasoning. Less often, papers use it to measure factual knowledge, specifically through complex queries that require time-sensitive knowledge, so the measurement claims are concentrated on temporal reasoning rather than spread broadly across constructs.

Space of uses. In use, papers often place TimeQA alongside other temporal QA benchmarks, including TempReason, TGQA, MenatQA, and TimeBench, either in multi-benchmark temporal reasonin

nodes.name: Tiny ImageNet
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across definitions, the common framing is an image classification dataset or benchmark. Papers variously describe it as a smaller version of ImageNet used for faster experimentation, as a benchmark for evaluating automated accuracy prediction across shifted test sets, and as a dataset used both as an adversarial fine-tuning source and as a primary evaluation dataset.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to one behavioral indicator, image classification, and no constructs are linked to it. In the recorded relationships, the measurement claims therefore concentrate on image classification rather than spreading across multiple constructs or behaviors.

Space of uses. Papers use it in several experimental roles rather than one fixed protocol. It appears alongside CIFAR10, CIFAR100, and Food-101 in image classification evaluations, is used "for computational reasons" in one study, is used on "synthetic shifted datasets of TinyImageNet" for correlation comparison, and is also used as the source of adversarial samples for fine-tuning before evaluation across multiple datasets, including Tiny-ImageNet itself. No other measurement instrument is linked to it.

nodes.name: tinyBenchmarks
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, tinyBenchmarks is most commonly described as a smaller, more efficient evaluation resource for language models, variously framed as a suite of few-shot tasks, a collection of small-scale datasets for low-cost evaluation, or smaller versions of popular benchmarks for rapid evaluation. One use description specifies few-shot components including 25-shot tinyARC, 5-shot GSM8K, 10-shot tinyHellaswag, and 5-shot tinyWinoGrande.

What it is claimed to measure. The papers describe it as assessing model performance and enabling efficient evaluation of language models, but they do not explicitly link it to any named constructs or behavioral indicators. No measured_by relationships are recorded for the instrument, so its measurement use is stated in general terms rather than tied to a particular construct.

Space of uses. Papers use tinyBenchmarks as an efficiency-oriented evaluation option. One paper reports scoring models on its few-shot tasks, another says it chose the small-scale datasets "for other tasks," and another states, "We use tinyBenchmarks (Polo et al., 2024) for all the benchmarks except HumanEval to further increase the efficiency of experiments"

nodes.name: TinyStories
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, TinyStories is most commonly described as a synthetic dataset of short, simple stories, often children's stories, generated by large language models. The prevailing framing is as a small, tractable corpus for training and evaluating small or medium-scale models, while still posing text-generation challenges such as coherence and narrative structure.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link TinyStories to 2 behavioral indicators and no constructs. The prevailing use is to measure text generation, with papers using it to train or evaluate models that generate text, while a smaller line of work uses it to measure story generation through story continuation.

Space of uses. Most papers position TinyStories as a practical training and evaluation corpus, including uses in next-token prediction, story continuation, and generation from unseen story prefixes and suffixes; some descriptions also emphasize that its small size makes training and aggregating N-gram statistics computationally efficient. A smaller line of work uses it alongside Children Stories or ROCStories, and another use is to probe character choices as a content planning attribute.

nodes.name: TLUE
nodes.definition: Tibetan Language Understanding Evaluation benchmark, a large-scale evaluation suite for LLMs in Tibetan, comprising Ti-MMLU for knowledge assessment and Ti-SafetyBench for safety evaluation.

nodes.name: TOEFL11
nodes.definition:
What it is. In the one definition, TOEFL11 is treated as the ETS Corpus of Non-Native Written English, and it is described as a benchmark dataset used for Native Language Identification research. The quoted passage also places it among two benchmark datasets for NLI experiments, alongside Write & Improve Corpus 2024.

What it is claimed to measure. The recorded measurement claim is narrow: TOEFL11 is linked to one behavioral indicator and no constructs. Specifically, Native language identification is measured by TOEFL11, so the instrument is reported as evaluating native language identification rather than a broader spread of targets.

Space of uses. One paper uses TOEFL11 together with Write & Improve Corpus 2024 in experiments, positioning it as one of two benchmark datasets for NLI.

nodes.name: TOFU
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, TOFU is most commonly described as a synthetic question-answering benchmark or dataset built from fictitious author biographies or synthetic author profiles. Most descriptions frame it as an unlearning benchmark for author-related knowledge, though some instead describe fictional characters' personal information or personally identifiable information. Papers also refer to splits such as forget05, forget10, and retain90, and they report scales from 200 QA pairs for 10 fictitious authors in forget05 to 4,000 QA pairs from 200 fictitious authors overall, while one paper describes it as 20 question-answer pairs generated by GPT-4.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use TOFU to measure three constructs and one behavioral indicator. The most often named construct-level uses are Forget quality, General ability, and Verbatim memorization, and the linked behavioral indicator is Knowledge generation. Definitions and quoted passages also describe TOFU as assessing forget quality and model utility, and as evaluating recovery of unlearned author-related knowledge and keywords from fictitious QA pairs.

Space of uses. Papers commonly position TOFU as one of sev

nodes.name: TofuEval
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, TofuEval is most commonly described as a dataset or benchmark for evaluating factual consistency in dialogue summarization. Several descriptions make this more specific, calling it a topic-focused dialogue summarization benchmark or dataset that emphasizes marginal or secondary topics, including factual alignment under topic shifts, and one paper describes it as a more challenging benchmark on topic-focused dialogue summarization. Some papers also specify its contents as an annotated subset of MediaSum and MeetingBank with human-annotated sentence-level faithfulness judgments and critiques, though one description presents those subsets as spanning a mix of news and dialogue domains.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link TofuEval to one construct and two behavioral indicators. The prevailing construct-level use is to measure Faithfulness, with one paper using its sentence-level faithfulness judgments and critiques to design intrinsic evaluation tasks for DETECT, CRITIQUE, and REFINE. It is also reported as measuring Meeting summarization and Text summarization, so the construct claims converge on Faithfulness while the behavioral-indicator links

nodes.name: ToM-SSI
nodes.definition: A multimodal benchmark designed to evaluate Theory of Mind capabilities in situated social interactions involving up to four agents in a grid world, covering cooperative, obstructive, and mixed settings.

nodes.name: TOMATO
nodes.definition: TempOral Reasoning MultimodAl EvaluaTiOn, a benchmark designed to rigorously assess Multimodal Foundation Models' temporal reasoning capabilities in video understanding across six tasks.

nodes.name: ToMBench
nodes.definition: A benchmark for evaluating social intelligence, specifically testing a model's theory-of-mind reasoning capabilities.

nodes.name: ToolACE
nodes.definition:
What it is. The description treats ToolACE as a dataset with 11,300 rows, used as a supplementary evaluation set in function-calling safety tasks. The same usage also describes it as a complementary part of MCIP-Bench, used to further validate generalization capability.

What it is claimed to measure. The paper reports ToolACE as being used to further validate generalization capability in function-calling safety tasks. Papers do not explicitly link it to any construct or behavioral indicator.

Space of uses. The observed usage positions ToolACE alongside MCIP-Bench as a supplementary or complementary evaluation resource rather than as a standalone benchmark. In that role, papers use its 11,300 rows to provide an additional generalization check.

nodes.name: ToolAlpaca
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the definitions, the prevailing description is of an agent-generated tool learning dataset with 495 tools and 3975 training examples, used to train and evaluate tool-augmented LLMs in controlled settings. The source description also notes that ToolAlpaca 7B is fine-tuned on this dataset using Vicuna-v1.3.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link ToolAlpaca to one construct and one behavioral indicator, and both links concern tool-related performance. It is used to measure tool use ability in work that describes a multi-agent simulator where GPT-4 simulates tool return values, the model can modify and re-call tools based on those returns, and GPT-4 evaluates the accuracy of process and response. It is also used to measure tool use in work that describes 3.9k tool-use instances from a multi-agent simulation environment, augmented into a multiple-choice format.

Space of uses. No other measurement instrument is linked to ToolAlpaca. In use, papers position it both as training data and as an evaluation setting: definitions describe it as being used to train and evaluate tool-augmented LLMs, while relationship evidence shows it being used through a multi-agent simu

nodes.name: ToolBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, ToolBench is most commonly described as a benchmark or benchmark dataset for evaluating LLM agents' tool use, built around real-world REST APIs, user requests or instructions, and interaction traces or expert trajectories. Definitions vary on whether it is primarily an evaluation benchmark, an instruction-tuning dataset, or a serving workload: some papers describe more than 16k APIs from 49 categories, over 10,000 queries with full interactions, or training demonstrations with complex task-solving traces, while one paper characterizes it by prompts that include tool demonstrations and calls. Several papers also refer to specific slices of the resource, including a second release, test tasks, around 1,000 test cases, or four environments such as Home Search, Trip Booking, Google Sheets, and Virtual Home.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link ToolBench to 3 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators. The prevailing claim is that it measures Tool use, with additional use for Information retrieval; at the construct level it is reported as measuring Decision-making, Reasoning, and Sequential decision-making. The recorded claims therefore spread ac

nodes.name: ToolEval
nodes.definition: An evaluation procedure from ToolBench used to compare decision sequences via win rate and rank them with PRP.

nodes.name: ToolQA
nodes.definition: ToolQA is a benchmark of external-tool tasks spanning domains such as flight status, coffee price, Yelp data, and Airbnb data.

nodes.name: ToolQuery
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across these papers, ToolQuery is most commonly described as a tool-using benchmark built around queries to external tools, with Weather, Movie, and Academia recurring as the named domains or subsets. Definitions also frame it as involving APIs in those domains, and one paper further describes it as a held-out task.

What it is claimed to measure. The papers use ToolQuery to evaluate tool use, specifically an agent's skills in using tools to retrieve and process information across domains such as Weather, Movie, and Academia. They do not explicitly link it to any named construct or behavioral indicator.

Space of uses. In use, papers position ToolQuery as part of a broader evaluation setup rather than on its own. One paper groups it with ToolOperation under the heading of tool using and treats it as a held-out task, while another includes it in a wider multi-benchmark evaluation of model performance.

nodes.name: TopDial
nodes.definition: A personalized conversational recommendation dataset containing dialogues on topics like movies, food, and music, where the system's goal is to recommend a specific item.

nodes.name: TopiOCQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Several papers describe TopiOCQA as a conversational search benchmark or dataset built around multi-turn information-seeking dialogues or queries. One definition specifies gold-standard passage retrieval and response generation labels, and other papers emphasize context-dependent questions that require disambiguation from prior turns; a smaller line of work frames it as a conversational question answering dataset or as a benchmark known for challenging topic shifts within conversations, where systems must decide whether to retain earlier context.

What it is claimed to measure. Recorded links tie TopiOCQA to 1 construct and 1 behavioral indicator. The prevailing measured_by claim centers on Generalization: a paper uses TopiOCQA to evaluate generalization ability by training on its training set and testing on QReCC, and vice versa. The only behavioral-indicator link uses different language, reporting TopiOCQA as related to Query rewriting because its context-dependent questions are used for clarifying an original question into a standalone question.

Space of uses. Across the papers, TopiOCQA is positioned as a widely used evaluation setting for conversational search, es

nodes.name: Torrance Tests of Creative Thinking
nodes.definition: A set of psychometric tests used to assess creative abilities, including divergent thinking, across various tasks.

nodes.name: ToTTo
nodes.definition: An English dataset for data-to-text generation, consisting of Wikipedia tables with highlighted cells paired with a sentence describing those cells.

nodes.name: TounsiBench
nodes.definition: A benchmark for evaluating the capabilities of large language models in understanding and generating responses in Tunisian Arabic, comprising a dataset of 744 instructions and an evaluation framework.

nodes.name: ToxicChat
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly treat ToxicChat as a benchmark dataset for query safety classification and safety detection. Definitions vary in emphasis: some describe a prompt dataset covering multiple harmful categories with simple and story-based templates, while others describe a dataset suitable for training safety classifiers, containing conversations with toxic content, or a benchmark for toxicity detection in real-world user-AI conversations. Papers also note that it has separate train and test splits.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, ToxicChat is used to measure harmful content detection, and papers describe it as part of evaluations on harmful prompts used to assess guardrail or safety models. Across the reported uses, it is connected to one behavioral indicator, Harmful content detection, and to no constructs, so the measurement claims converge on that behavioral target rather than spreading across multiple constructs. Papers also describe it as assessing query safety classification and safety detection across diverse toxic content types.

Space of uses. Papers usually position ToxicChat as a standard or public benchmark within broader guardrail and safet

nodes.name: ToxiCloakCN
nodes.definition: A Chinese adversarial toxicity detection benchmark dataset designed to evaluate the vulnerability of large language models to various evasion tactics, including homophonic substitutions.

nodes.name: ToxiGen
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, ToxiGen is most commonly described as a toxicity benchmark or dataset for evaluating toxic versus neutral generation behavior. Definitions vary in emphasis: some frame it as a benchmark for toxic language generation or safety, while others describe a synthetic or machine-generated dataset for adversarial and implicit hate speech detection. Several papers specify content such as benign or neutral and toxic statements or questions about 13 demographic or minority groups, and one description says it comprises approximately 274k statements evenly split between toxic and non-toxic language. A smaller line of work highlights subset use, for example taking only prompts designed to elicit toxic language.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the surveyed work, claims concentrate on safety and toxicity: papers link ToxiGen to 3 constructs in total, most often Safety and Toxicity, with a smaller line using it to measure Harmlessness. Papers also link it to 4 behavioral indicators, most often Harmful content generation, and additionally Harmful content detection, Hate speech detection, and Text generation. The recorded links consistently describe ToxiGen as measuri

nodes.name: TQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, TQA is most commonly described as Textbook Question Answering. One description presents it as a reading-comprehension benchmark used in generative format, and another as a dataset consisting of scientific textbooks for evaluating knowledge-based reasoning. A smaller line of work uses the same label for TriviaQA, described as a challenging reading-comprehension dataset of question-answer pairs authored by trivia enthusiasts and used for closed-book QA.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers do not link TQA to any recorded construct or behavioral indicator through formal relationships. In authors' own descriptions, it is instead used to assess reading comprehension, and one paper also frames it as evaluating knowledge-based reasoning; a smaller line of work uses the label for closed-book QA.

Space of uses. One paper places TQA alongside HumanEval, GSM8k, and NQ in a four-task suite spanning code, math, question answering, and reading comprehension, and reports F1 scores for TQA together with GSM8k and NQ. Elsewhere, one paper treats TQA as a closed-book QA dataset, while another uses the scientific-textbook version of TQA for fine-tuning.

nodes.name: TRACE
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, TRACE is most commonly described as a public benchmark for continual learning or continual instruction tuning, organized around a learning sequence or multiple sequential fine-tuning tasks. Definitions and quoted passages describe task content such as multi-choice QA, code generation, mathematical reasoning, and summarization, and one paper also describes 8 diverse tasks including domain-specific QA, code completion, and mathematical reasoning. A smaller line of work describes TRACE as a benchmark for improving and evaluating complex instruction-following ability, with 120K training data and 1K evaluation data, while another description says it is designed to evaluate general ability, instruction following, and safety.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link TRACE to 3 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators. The most frequently linked constructs are Complex instruction following ability, Mathematical reasoning, and Safety, and the most frequently linked behavioral indicators are Code completion and Instruction following. Taken together, papers use TRACE to measure several different targets rather than centering it on a single reported construct, a

nodes.name: Traffic
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats Traffic as a time series benchmark dataset for evaluating forecasting models. Most definitions describe road traffic data, often as hourly traffic volume in California, while some instead describe hourly road occupancy rates from the California transportation department on San Francisco Bay area freeways; one definition further specifies 862 sensors. Papers also frame it as a standard or real-world benchmark, and some definitions place it in broader cross-domain forecasting evaluation.

What it is claimed to measure. Measurement claims are concentrated rather than spread across many targets: Traffic is linked to 1 construct and no behavioral indicators. The only recorded measurement claim is that papers use it to measure Zero-shot generalization, with the evidence describing a comparison of zero-shot performance of pre-trained models on the Traffic dataset.

Space of uses. Papers most commonly use Traffic alongside other forecasting benchmarks, especially ETTh1, ETTh2, ETTm1, ETTm2, and Electricity or ECL. It is typically presented as one dataset within larger evaluation suites for forecasting, including long-term fo

nodes.name: TravelPlanner
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the dominant framing is a benchmark for evaluating travel planning agents or LLM agents on complex planning tasks. Most descriptions add a sandbox environment with tools for accessing nearly four million data records, plus curated planning intents or queries, reference plans, and user-specified constraints; some narrow this to U.S. domestic travel planning, while others emphasize itinerary generation over flights, accommodations, and other arrangements, with hard and sometimes soft constraints. A smaller line describes it as a dataset or benchmark task rather than simply a benchmark, and one paper reports results on a TravelPlanner validation setting.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link TravelPlanner to 2 constructs and no behavioral indicators. The prevailing usage is to measure Planning, with papers describing it as a benchmark for real-world, complex, or challenging planning; a smaller line of work uses it to measure Long-horizon planning under user-defined constraints. These measurement claims stay concentrated on planning-related constructs rather than spreading across many targets.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it, a

nodes.name: TREC
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, TREC is most commonly described as the Text REtrieval Conference question classification benchmark, usually framed as a 6-way task with coarse question types such as abbreviation, entity, description, human, location, and numeric. Some descriptions add that it has 50 subclasses or that it is used to classify questions into fine-grained answer types, while a few papers describe it more broadly as a general NLU dataset or as used for information retrieval tasks. A smaller usage treats "Trec" as a dataset from LongBench for few-shot evaluation.

What it is claimed to measure. Its reported measurement role is concentrated rather than spread across many targets. Papers most commonly use TREC to measure the behavioral indicator Text classification, typically in the form of 6-way question classification, and papers link it to one behavioral indicator overall and one construct overall. A smaller line of work reports it as measuring Prompt sensitivity, using TREC examples to compare predicted class distributions across prompt rephrasings.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it through explicit relationships. In the paper descriptions, TREC i

nodes.name: TREC-COVID
nodes.definition: An information retrieval dataset focused on biomedical information retrieval.

nodes.name: TREC-DL 2019
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing description is a benchmark dataset from the TREC Deep Learning Track 2019 for information retrieval evaluation, though one definition presents it as a test set. Descriptions variously emphasize passage retrieval, reranking, document relevance tasks, and deep learning-based ad-hoc retrieval, and one paper notes that it is derived from MS-MARCO-V1 while another highlights human-annotated relevance judgments.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers do not explicitly link TREC-DL 2019 to any constructs or behavioral indicators. Instead, they describe it as evaluating passage retrieval systems, information retrieval and reranking tasks, document relevance tasks, and document re-ranking systems, including LLM-based ranking settings.

Space of uses. Papers commonly use it alongside TREC-DL 2020 or DL20, and some descriptions place it beside MS MARCO or the BEIR benchmark. It is positioned as an in-domain benchmark in one paper, as one of several widely used benchmarks in another, and as a benchmark used to test LLM-based ranking systems across pairwise, listwise, and setwise paradigms.

nodes.name: TREC-DL 2020
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across these papers, TREC-DL 2020 is most commonly described as a benchmark dataset or test set from the TREC Deep Learning Track 2020, used to evaluate passage retrieval, reranking, document relevance, and document re-ranking systems. The descriptions vary slightly: some present it as an in-domain dataset, one says it is derived from MS-MARCO-V1, and another describes it as extending TREC DL 2019 with additional queries and relevance annotations. One source also treats it simply as part of the "TREC-DL2019/2020 benchmarks."

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use TREC-DL 2020 to evaluate performance on passage retrieval and reranking style tasks, including document relevance assessment in LLM-based ranking settings. At the same time, papers do not explicitly link it to any construct or behavioral indicator, so its recorded use here is task evaluation rather than measurement of named constructs.

Space of uses. The prevailing usage is as a benchmark in evaluation suites for retrieval and re-ranking systems. Papers frequently use it alongside TREC-DL19, while some descriptions also place it with BEIR or in conjunction with MS MARCO; one paper notes that TREC-DL'19 and

nodes.name: TrialBench
nodes.definition: Benchmark dataset for clinical prediction tasks including trial approval, patient dropout, mortality, and adverse event prediction, used to evaluate model performance in biomedical contexts.

nodes.name: TriviaQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, TriviaQA is most commonly treated as a reading-comprehension or question-answering benchmark built from trivia questions, usually with short or free-form answers. Definitions differ on whether it is framed as open-domain QA, closed-book QA, or answering from evidence documents: some describe question-answer pairs authored by trivia enthusiasts, while others emphasize question-answer-evidence triples or source documents from Wikipedia and the web. Papers also use named variants and subsets such as TQ, the Wikipedia partition, dev and test splits, a 1000-question dev subset, and a synthesized audio version.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use TriviaQA to measure 15 constructs and 15 behavioral indicators. The prevailing behavioral uses are question answering and open-domain question answering, followed by factual question answering, factual recall, and text generation, with 10 other behavioral indicators also linked. On the construct side, papers most often use it for world knowledge and factuality, then generalization, factual knowledge, and calibration, with 10 other constructs also linked, so the measurement claims are spread across many targets r

nodes.name: TriviaQA-unfiltered
nodes.definition: Open-domain question answering benchmark requiring models to answer factual questions using external knowledge; used to evaluate accuracy in knowledge-intensive tasks.

nodes.name: Trojsten Benchmark
nodes.definition: A Slovak-language dataset of 1,108 high-school STEM competition problems in mathematics, physics, and programming, with reference solutions and difficulty ratings, used to evaluate multistep reasoning in a low-resource language setting.

nodes.name: TRUE
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing description treats TRUE as a fine-tuned T5-11B Natural Language Inference model used as an evaluator inside broader evaluation frameworks. Definitions consistently describe it as judging whether a source passage or premise entails a generated claim or hypothesis, and one paper makes this explicit by using it as an evaluator whose output is 1 for entailment and 0 otherwise; another describes it as fine-tuned on a collection of NLI datasets.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link TRUE to two constructs, most commonly Citation quality and also Faithfulness, and to no behavioral indicators. The measurement claims are concentrated around entailment-based evaluation: papers use it to measure Citation quality by judging entailment in citations or verifying whether a claim is fully supported by cited documents, and they report it as measuring Faithfulness through factual consistency evaluation in context.

Space of uses. Papers do not link TRUE to any other measurement instrument. They generally position it as an NLI component or evaluator within larger evaluation pipelines, including citation rewrite and citation quality evaluation, and o

nodes.name: True-False dataset
nodes.definition:
What it is. The paper treats the True-False dataset as a labeled collection of factoid statements marked True or False, covering six disjoint topics: Cities, Inventions, Chemical Elements, Animals, Companies, and Scientific Facts. It is described as a constructed dataset for factuality probes, and no alternative versions, subsets, or competing format descriptions are reported.

What it is claimed to measure. The same paper says the dataset is used to train and evaluate factuality probes. Papers do not link it to any named constructs or behavioral indicators in recorded relationships.

Space of uses. The description positions it as a standalone dataset for training and evaluation, rather than alongside any other named benchmark or instrument. No other measurement instruments are linked to it.

nodes.name: TruthfulQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, TruthfulQA is most commonly treated as a question answering benchmark or dataset built to elicit false answers from common misconceptions and to test whether models answer truthfully instead. Most descriptions say it contains over 800 questions, often specified as 817 questions across 38 categories, while one paper says 818; examples of named categories include health, law, finance, and politics, and one definition says the questions draw on conspiracy theories, folk theories, apocryphal stories, and other repeated falsehoods. Papers also describe multiple formats: several emphasize multiple-choice questions with one best answer, while others note two protocols, multiple-choice and generation, including open-ended, sentence-level, and long-form responses; some specifically use MC1, MC2, the generation portion, or refer to TruthfulQA 1 and 2.

What it is claimed to measure. The prevailing usage is as a measure of Truthfulness: papers say it tests an LLM's truthfulness, ability to identify true claims, or propensity to reproduce or mimic falsehoods. It is also commonly used to measure Factuality. Beyond those dominant uses, papers link it to 18 constructs a

nodes.name: TSPLIB
nodes.definition: A library of real-world benchmark instances for the Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) used to evaluate the performance of optimization algorithms.

nodes.name: TTT-Bench
nodes.definition: A benchmark consisting of four novel Tic-Tac-Toe-style games (oTTT, dTTT, cTTT, sTTT) designed to assess strategic, spatial, and logical reasoning through text-based board game questions asking for the best next move.

nodes.name: TumEmo
nodes.definition: A multimodal sentiment analysis benchmark used for additional experiments on sentiment prediction.

nodes.name: TurBLiMP
nodes.definition: A Turkish Benchmark of Linguistic Minimal Pairs covering 16 grammatical phenomena, designed to evaluate the linguistic abilities of language models.

nodes.name: Turing test
nodes.definition: A binary classification evaluation procedure that tests whether a detector can distinguish human-generated text from machine-generated text.

nodes.name: TurnBack
nodes.definition: A large-scale benchmark for evaluating the route-level geospatial cognition of LLMs, consisting of a dataset of 36,000 routes, a language-to-geometry converter, and a comprehensive evaluation framework for the route reversal task.

nodes.name: TVQA
nodes.definition: Multiple-choice question answering benchmark based on TV shows, requiring multimodal reasoning across video, audio, and subtitles.

nodes.name: TweetEval
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly describe TweetEval as a multi-task benchmark for tweet analysis on social media, organized as six text classification tasks: emotion, hate speech, irony, offensive language, sentiment, and stance detection. One study states that it "consists of 6 text classification tasks about tweet analysis on social media," while another presents it more narrowly as a benchmark of multiple Twitter-based NLP tasks and uses the emotion recognition and irony detection subsets.

What it is claimed to measure. In the recorded relationships, papers use TweetEval to measure 2 behavioral indicators, Emotion analysis and Irony detection, and 1 construct, Natural language understanding. The task-focused uses come from papers that explicitly take its emotion recognition and irony detection components, while another paper reports conducting experiments on TweetEval "for language understanding," so the reported measurement claims span both specific behaviors and a broader construct.

Space of uses. Across the cited work, TweetEval is positioned as a benchmark for multi-task or multi-class evaluation rather than as a standalone single-task test. One paper uses it alongside Aff

nodes.name: TwiBot-22
nodes.definition: Graph-based Twitter dataset containing one million users, nearly one hundred million tweets, and relational data, used for training and evaluating social bot detection and human-like generation.

nodes.name: TwinViews-13k
nodes.definition: A dataset containing ideologically matched political statement pairs used for evaluating political polarity adjustment.

nodes.name: Twitter Financial News Sentiment
nodes.definition: A dataset for sentiment analysis of financial news from Twitter.

nodes.name: Twitter-FMNERG
nodes.definition: Benchmark dataset for Fine-grained Multimodal Named Entity Recognition and Grounding, extending GMNER with 51 fine-grained entity types.

nodes.name: Twitter-GMNER
nodes.definition: A benchmark dataset for Grounded Multimodal Named Entity Recognition that involves extracting four coarse-grained entity types from image-text pairs from Twitter.

nodes.name: TyDi QA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly describe TyDi QA as a multilingual question answering benchmark or dataset. The prevailing description is that it covers 11 typologically diverse languages, though one paper instead says it includes 9 kinds of languages; several papers also describe gold-passage or Wikipedia-based setups, including questions answered from a given article, single-hop evaluation with wiki contexts, answer-span identification in a passage, language-specific subsets such as ID, SW, and FI, and an Indonesian subset that one paper repurposes from reading comprehension to open-domain QA by removing context.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to 2 constructs and 3 behavioral indicators. The prevailing measurement claim is multilingual ability, with papers explicitly saying they use TydiQA for multilingual ability or to assess multilinguality; a smaller line of work reports it as measuring general ability. On the behavioral side, papers use it to measure multilingual question answering most often, and also question answering and machine reading comprehension.

Space of uses. Papers often place it alongside MMLU, BBH, GSM8K, and TruthfulQA in broader evaluation ba

nodes.name: UCF-101
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across definitions, UCF-101 is most commonly described as a video benchmark or action recognition dataset of human action videos, including realistic YouTube videos and videos in the wild. The prevailing descriptions place it in class-conditional video generation and action recognition evaluation, while some papers also mention image-to-video generation, generated video quality, or action classification.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to 2 behavioral indicators, Video generation and Action recognition, and no constructs are linked to it. The prevailing measurement use is for Video generation, with papers reporting class-conditional, class-to-video, and image-to-video evaluation, while a smaller use reports it for Action recognition or action classification.

Space of uses. Papers use UCF-101 alongside other benchmarks, Kinetics-600 and MSR-VTT in video generation experiments, and ActivityNet and Something-Something V2 in action recognition evaluation. They usually position it as a standard or common benchmark, and one paper reports training class-to-video models on the dataset.

nodes.name: UltraChat
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, UltraChat is most commonly described as a diverse conversational instruction-following dataset, with one definition specifying that it is multi-turn and generated by GPT-3.5-Turbo. Some papers frame it more by role than by format, treating it as an interactive dialogue benchmark, as a benign dataset for safety-patching evaluation, or as a held-out, out-of-domain setting used to test whether a method generalizes beyond summarization.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use UltraChat to measure three behavioral indicators, Instruction following, Question answering, and Text generation, and one construct, Instruction following ability. The claims are spread across several targets rather than centered on one alone: the most recurring framing is instruction-following, while other papers report it as evaluating question answering or text generation.

Space of uses. No other measurement instrument is linked to UltraChat. Papers position it in several ways: as supervised fine-tuning data, as a source of prompts for self-training, as a benign dataset for quantization-assisting and safety-patching evaluation, as an interactive dialogue benchmark, and as a he

nodes.name: UltraDomain
nodes.definition: Long-context benchmark focusing on domain-specific complex question answering, such as in financial, legal, and scientific texts, to assess deep understanding of specialized long documents.

nodes.name: UltraFeedback
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats UltraFeedback as a high-quality instruction or preference dataset for alignment work, built from scored candidate responses and used for instruction tuning. Definitions also describe it as a preference learning benchmark with annotated preference labels over instruction-response pairs, sometimes emphasizing fine-grained or multi-aspect evaluation around instruction following, truthfulness, honesty, and helpfulness. A smaller line of work frames it more specifically as a public benchmark for generative judges on preference prediction, and some papers refer to particular variants or subsets such as a development split or an auxiliary text generation setting.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link UltraFeedback to 5 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators, so its reported measurement use is spread across several related targets rather than concentrated on one alone. The most frequent construct links are to helpfulness, honesty, instruction following ability, generalization, and truthfulness, and the recorded behavioral-indicator links are to instruction following and dialogue generation. In these relationships, papers use

nodes.name: UltraFeedback Binarized
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most descriptions treat UltraFeedback Binarized, also written UF-B or UFB, as a widely used dataset for preference alignment or preference fine-tuning, organized as binarized or paired preference data for dialogue tasks. A more specific description says it is built from GPT-4 scored UltraFeedback completions, where the highest-scoring completion is labeled "chosen" and another, in one account a random completion, is labeled "rejected".

What it is claimed to measure. Papers do not explicitly say that UltraFeedback Binarized measures any construct or behavioral indicator. The descriptions instead frame it as a dataset for preference alignment or preference fine-tuning, and as a resource used to train and evaluate alignment methods.

Space of uses. Across the surveyed work, it is commonly used as an evaluation and fine-tuning dataset for alignment methods. Papers place it alongside Alpaca Comparison and TL;DR in multi-dataset experiments, and one line of work specifically groups it with Alpaca Comparison as one of two dialogue datasets; another states, "For fine-tuning on the UltraFeedback Binarized dataset, we use two families of models."

nodes.name: UltraInteract
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the definitions here, UltraInteract is described as multi-turn conversational data built around complex reasoning tasks. Papers differ in how they characterize its format and role: some describe a multi-turn RLHF dataset with dialogues that cover general chat scenarios and are used to evaluate conversational and instruction-following abilities, while another description presents it as a pairwise alignment dataset of multi-turn conversational data designed to evaluate and improve performance on complex reasoning tasks.

What it is claimed to measure. Recorded links do not spread across many named outcomes: UltraInteract is linked to 1 construct, Reasoning, and to no behavioral indicators. That construct link is reported as related rather than as a measured_by claim, while the definitions and quoted passages say papers use UltraInteract to evaluate conversational ability, instruction-following ability, and performance on complex reasoning tasks.

Space of uses. Papers use UltraInteract both as an evaluation benchmark and as training or alignment data. In one usage, a method is evaluated on responses to instructions with complex reasoning tasks that cover general ch

nodes.name: UNCLE
nodes.definition: A benchmark dataset designed to evaluate uncertainty expression in both long- and short-form question answering, covering five domains with over 1,000 entities and paired questions that share key aspects and gold-standard answers.

nodes.name: UNER
nodes.definition:
What it is. In one paper, UNER is described as a multilingual named entity recognition dataset covering 13 languages. The same description presents it as an evaluation resource for cross-lingual transfer on NER tasks, and the usage note in Translation and Fusion Improves Cross-lingual Information Extraction places it among multilingual NER datasets gathered for that purpose.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers describe UNER as used for evaluating cross-lingual transfer performance on named entity recognition tasks. No construct links and no behavioral-indicator links are recorded for it, so the evidence stays at the task-level description rather than tying it to a broader construct.

Space of uses. The usage in the papers description places UNER alongside MasakhaNER2.0, with papers treating both as multilingual NER datasets gathered for evaluation. Beyond that pairing, no other instrument links are recorded.

nodes.name: UniGeo
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the definition, papers treat UniGeo as a dataset for unified geometry problem solving. In G-LLaVA: Solving Geometric Problem with Multi-Modal Large Language Model, it is also described as a subtask within the MathVista benchmark and is mentioned among more recent datasets.

Space of uses. The same paper uses UniGeo as one of the sub-tasks for reporting results on MathVista-GPS multiple-choice questions, which it presents for easier evaluation. In that usage, it appears alongside GeoQA+, Geometry3K, and GEOS.

nodes.name: US8K
nodes.definition: A benchmark for urban sound classification.

nodes.name: User preference study
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats this as a broad human evaluation protocol rather than a single fixed benchmark. Most descriptions involve people comparing model outputs, choosing a preferred response, ranking alternatives, or rating outputs against stated criteria, with setups ranging from pairwise comparisons and win-lose judgments to Likert scales, binary labels, and free-form feedback. A smaller line of work uses the same label for interactive studies, expert review, survey-style polling, or human baseline task completion. Although one definition centers on showing a question and multiple model responses and asking users to choose the most creative and humorous one, other papers apply the protocol to correctness, faithfulness, safety, usefulness, coherence, cultural appropriateness, and similar dimensions.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link this protocol to 2 behavioral indicators, Human reaction motion generation and Humor generation, and no constructs or other measurement instruments are linked to it. The linked claims therefore concentrate on behavioral indicators rather than constructs: one paper uses it to test creativity and humor, and anoth

nodes.name: V-NIAH
nodes.definition: Video Needle in a Haystack, a long-video retrieval benchmark that tests a model's ability to find a specific image inserted at various positions within a long video.

nodes.name: VAL
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, VAL is most commonly described as an automatic plan validator for PDDL plans. Definitions characterize it as checking whether an action sequence correctly transitions from an initial state to a goal state against ground-truth domain and problem files, and as verifying that a generated sequence is executable and reaches the goal state. A smaller framing presents it as a simulation environment for plan validation that calculates state condition changes and returns error messages when actions fail because preconditions are unsatisfied.

What it is claimed to measure. The reported measurement role is narrow rather than spread across many targets: papers link VAL to 1 behavioral indicator, Plan generation, and to no constructs. In that usage, Plan generation is measured by VAL through validation of the produced plan against the domain and problem files.

Space of uses. Papers use VAL as an evaluation step after a plan has been produced or after natural language responses have been converted into PDDL, then checked for executability and goal attainment. One paper also positions it as a simulation environment for computing state changes and obtaining error messa

nodes.name: Value Kaleidoscope
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly treat this entity as an evaluation dataset for moral scenarios and judgments. One definition describes Value Kaleidoscope as a benchmark with 31K human-authored hypothetical scenarios and moral dilemmas paired with ethical perspectives, used to test whether models support, oppose, or remain neutral toward scenarios from specific viewpoints. A second description uses the name ValuePrism (VP) and frames it more briefly as a moral-judgment dataset with three-way choices for evaluating value profile modeling of ethical reasoning.

What it is claimed to measure. Claims about what it measures converge on one construct: Value orientation. Papers link it to one construct, Value orientation, and do not link it to any behavioral indicators; in the linked use, it is used to probe models' views on moral situations, alongside Anthropic's Election Questions for political topics. Papers do not link it to any other measurement instruments.

Space of uses. Papers use it as an evaluation benchmark. One study places Value Kaleidoscope within "trade-off steerability benchmarks" for assessing proposed approaches, while another uses VP as a moral-judgment dataset in valu

nodes.name: VAST
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, VAST is most commonly described as a stance detection dataset or benchmark built around varied targets.
