Definitions say each instance contains a sentence, a target, and a stance label, with labels given as Pro, Con, or Neutral; one paper adds that it covers a wide range of targets and is used to assess generalization in zero-shot and few-shot settings, while another frames it as an inherently zero-shot stance detection dataset and notes use of the original publisher splits.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use VAST to measure stance detection. In the recorded links, it is connected to one behavioral indicator, stance detection, and not linked to any constructs or other measurement instruments, so its reported use is concentrated on that single behavioral indicator rather than spread across multiple constructs.

Space of uses. Across the cited studies, VAST appears as part of experimental evaluations of proposed stance detection methods. Papers report using it alongside SEM16, PStance, and SemEval-2016 to evaluate methods, and one paper describes results on it as part of validations covering zero-shot, few-shot, and challenging scenarios.

nodes.name: VATEX
nodes.definition: A multilingual video captioning dataset used in the paper as an auxiliary validation and training comparison set.

nodes.name: VBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, VBench is usually presented as a benchmark leaderboard, or more broadly a comprehensive benchmark suite, for text-to-video and video generative models. Definitions describe it as evaluating and ranking model performance across quality and semantic dimensions, and one paper reports average scores over 16 metrics drawn from those two dimensions. Some papers also treat it as a source of evaluation content, describing 946 GPT-augmented text prompts from VBench for generating videos.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use VBench to measure video generation, and this is the only behavioral indicator linked to it; no constructs are linked to it. The claims therefore converge on a single target rather than spreading across many different outcomes. In the recorded evidence, papers describe using VBench to evaluate visual generation capability for video generation, while the definitions frame that evaluation through quality and semantic dimensions.

Space of uses. The prevailing use is as a comparison and ranking benchmark: papers report evaluating models with it, comparing results on its leaderboard, and citing outcomes such as topping the leaderboard. A s

nodes.name: Verbalized confidence
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed definitions, the prevailing usage treats verbalized confidence as a direct self-report protocol: the model or LLM judge is prompted to express confidence in its own answer or judgment. Papers variously describe it as a baseline confidence measure, a black-box self-evaluation procedure, or an evaluation protocol. Most descriptions frame the output as a scalar value, while one definition allows a numerical or categorical confidence rating alongside the answer, and one paper refers to a "Verb. 1S top-1" variant.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to 2 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator. The dominant claim is that it measures Confidence, with definitions repeatedly describing it as prompting the model to self-report confidence or subjective belief strength. A smaller usage applies Verbalization to measure Hallucination by replacing a hallucination detection module with it, while Instruction following ability is not measured by it but is reported as related to it.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it. Papers most often position it as a baseline or black-box self-evaluation method that directly asks for confidence throug

nodes.name: Vicuna-Bench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage is a benchmark or evaluation set for instruction-following and conversational response quality, often described as drawing on user-shared conversations or diverse predefined prompts and judged with GPT-4. Several definitions specify 80 questions, while one paper describes an adapted single-rating version with 80 single-turn chat prompts and 320 responses, and another frames it as a scheme where GPT-4 compares two model responses on 80 questions. A smaller set of definitions describes it more broadly as open-ended text generation, short-text conversational tasks, or general LLM performance evaluation.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers mainly use it to measure instruction following: it is linked to five constructs and four behavioral indicators, with instruction following ability and instruction following the most recurrent targets. Other reported uses include text generation, coding ability, and multi-turn dialogue, with several additional linked targets also reported. Overall, the claims center on instruction following but extend to several adjacent capabilities.

Space of uses. Papers usually use it alongside MT-Bench, and they

nodes.name: Video-ChatGPT benchmark
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage is as an evaluation benchmark or test set for video understanding and video-based conversational models, though papers vary in emphasis. It is described as a benchmark for generative performance, a test set for detailed video understanding via large vision and language models, and a long-video question-answering benchmark. Reported evaluation dimensions include Correctness of Information, Contextual Understanding, Temporal Understanding, and Consistency, with one description naming Detail Orientation and another naming Orientation.

What it is claimed to measure. In the reported relationships, papers use it to measure one behavioral indicator and one construct. The most common link is to video question answering, where papers evaluate models on the Video-ChatGPT test set or treat it as an open-ended video question-answering benchmark; a smaller line of use links it to temporal understanding through the benchmark's Temporal Understanding metric. Overall, the measurement claims are concentrated on these few targets rather than spread across many constructs.

Space of uses. In the papers, it appears as part of benchmark suites f

nodes.name: Video-MME
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, Video-MME, often written VideoMME, is most commonly treated as a multimodal benchmark for video understanding and video-language models, frequently described as a multiple-choice or video question answering benchmark. Several papers also frame it as a long-video benchmark, with videos described as spanning 11 seconds to 1 hour or 1 minute to 1 hour, sometimes split into short, medium, and long groups or reported in a long subset such as VideoMME-L; individual definitions mention 900 videos and 2,700 QA pairs, 6 visual domains and 30 subfields, and reporting with or without subtitles. A smaller set of definitions gives it broader task coverage, including captioning, question answering, and retrieval with subtitles, while others emphasize perception, cognition, reasoning, temporal understanding, temporal ordering, event reasoning, and modality alignment.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link Video-MME to 3 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator. The prevailing use is to measure long video understanding, and many papers also use it to measure video understanding; papers also report it as measuring video question answering, often in long-form or comprehe

nodes.name: VideoHallucer
nodes.definition:
What it is. In the usage in the papers, papers treat VideoHallucer as a benchmark for evaluating video hallucination. The only explicit definition frames it as assessing whether model responses are consistent with video content, and it refers to Basic, Hallucinated, and Overall categories.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers describe VideoHallucer as evaluating video hallucination through whether generated responses stay consistent with the video content. Beyond that task description, papers do not explicitly link it to any named construct or behavioral indicator.

Space of uses. The usage in the papers places VideoHallucer alongside EventHallusion rather than on its own. One study says it adopted two video hallucination benchmarks, VideoHallucer and EventHallusion, so in that use it functions as one of a paired set of video hallucination evaluations.

nodes.name: ViDoSeek
nodes.definition: A benchmark dataset designed for evaluating retrieval-augmented generation systems on visually rich documents, where each query has a unique answer within a large corpus of approximately 6k images.

nodes.name: VirtualHome
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, VirtualHome is most commonly described as a simulated or 3D household environment, variously framed as a simulator, simulation platform, or benchmark for household activities, household task execution, and programs for those activities. The prevailing usage is to test whether generated plans or programs are executable in complex, multi-step tasks with object interactions and goal conditions, and some descriptions add partially observable states and macro-actions. A smaller line of description emphasizes long-horizon and multi-agent tasks with procedural generation, and one paper uses it as one component of ExtendaBench, where the VirtualHome portion contains 605 tasks divided into ultra-short, short, medium, and long subsets.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use VirtualHome to measure 4 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators. Among constructs, it is linked most often to Generalization, including unseen-task and crossover tests across Food Preparation and Entertainment, followed by Cross-domain generalization, Robustness, and Sequential decision-making; among behavioral indicators, it is used for Embodied planning and Task completion. Overall, the re

nodes.name: VISBIAS
nodes.definition: A multimodal evaluation framework that assesses both explicit and implicit social biases in Vision-Language Models through four scenarios: multiple-choice questions, yes-no comparisons, image descriptions, and form completion tasks.

nodes.name: VisDial
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most definitions converge on treating VisDial as a Visual Dialog dataset or multi-turn visual dialogue benchmark centered on conversation about an image. Papers describe it as evaluating a model's ability to engage in a multi-turn conversation about an image, or to answer a series of questions about an image. A smaller framing presents it as a benchmark for chat-to-image acquisition, with experiments for image acquisition in multi-turn chat scenarios, and one source also places it within an ablation study across five datasets.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link VisDial to one construct and two behavioral indicators. The construct-level use is to measure multimodal understanding, while the behavioral indicators most often attached to it are cross-modal retrieval and visual question answering. These claims are spread across several targets rather than restricted to a single one: one paper evaluates visual question answering on VisDial, another reports using the Visual Dialog dataset in cross-modal retrieval for comparability to previous work, and another includes VisDial when assessing multimodal vision and language capabilities.

Space of uses. Papers most often

nodes.name: VisEval
nodes.definition: A natural language to visualization (NL2VIS) benchmark containing high-quality datasets manually annotated by human experts, used to test generalization beyond the Kaggle ecosystem.

nodes.name: VIST
nodes.definition: A dataset for the task of visual storytelling, used as a basis for a task within the InterleavedBench evaluation benchmark.

nodes.name: VisText
nodes.definition: A corpus of charts and summaries used to generate chart question-answer pairs for the gaze dataset.

nodes.name: Visual7W
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most commonly, papers treat Visual7W as a visual question answering benchmark or reference dataset. Some descriptions add that it is predominantly designed for VQA but includes a dedicated grounded VQA subset, where models select the correct bounding box for a "which"-type question, while another definition highlights object-level grounding annotations that link answers to specific image regions. One evaluation description also characterizes its samples as multiple-choice questions paired with a related image.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the papers, its measurement claims center on one construct and one behavioral indicator rather than many targets. Papers use Visual7W to measure Visual grounding, including one account that places it among the "typical datasets" for tasks that establish referential links between textual mentions and image regions, and they also use it to measure Multimodal question answering through multimodal multiple-choice question-image evaluation.

Space of uses. Papers position Visual7W as a reference dataset and evaluation benchmark. Papers do not otherwise link it directly to another measurement instrument, but evaluation setups place

nodes.name: Visual Genome
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the dominant framing is of Visual Genome as a vision-language dataset with dense annotations of objects, attributes, and relationships in images, sometimes used through selected object relationships, region captions, or object data. Some papers note that its object data are converted into a Region-in Text-out format, while a smaller framing describes it as a visual question-answering dataset grounded in scene graphs that grounds visual concepts to language. Papers also refer to specific versions or splits, including VG100K with 108,077 images and over 1.7 million question-answer pairs, and a 77,398-image training split used as detection data.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link Visual Genome to 1 construct and 4 behavioral indicators. The most common measurement claim is that papers use it to measure region captioning, including region-level caption ability; smaller lines use it to measure dense captioning and open-vocabulary object detection, and one paper uses it to measure the construct relation understanding by placing it among relational benchmarks. Visual question answering appears differently: one paper reports that Visual Genome

nodes.name: VisualMRC
nodes.definition: A benchmark for multimodal reading comprehension over visual documents or screenshots.

nodes.name: VisualWebArena
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most descriptions treat VisualWebArena as a real benchmark environment for multimodal agents, or more specifically vision-language agents, on realistic visual web and web navigation tasks. The prevailing description places those tasks across classifieds, social media, and shopping platforms, while some authors emphasize GUI interaction and task completion in browser environments; a smaller usage refers to V-WebArena mainly as a comparison benchmark.

What it is claimed to measure. Among reported links, papers connect it to one behavioral indicator and no constructs. The measurement claim is concentrated on Web navigation: papers describe VisualWebArena as designed to evaluate multimodal agent performance across a wide range of web navigation tasks and environments.

Space of uses. Papers commonly use it as an evaluation environment to build on, for example by adding targeted adversarial tasks and evaluation scripts on top of it. It also appears alongside OSWorld as an existing agent testing environment, one paper restricts evaluation to an easy-task subset and only tests SoM agents, and another cites V-WebArena for comparison; no measurement instrument is linked to it.

nodes.name: VizWiz
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, papers most commonly describe VizWiz as a visual question answering benchmark or dataset built from questions asked by blind or visually impaired users about images they have taken. The prevailing description emphasizes real-world or user-generated content, often with uncurated, low-quality, ambiguous, visually degraded, or otherwise challenging images; some papers further frame it as open-ended VQA or natural-image VQA. A smaller set of papers refers to variants or names such as VisWiz, VizWiz-VQA, VizWizQA, and the VizWiz test-dev split, the latter described as containing 8,000 image-question pairs.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers primarily use VizWiz to measure visual question answering, the only linked behavioral indicator. Construct claims are more dispersed: papers also report 8 construct links, with multimodal understanding, visual perception, visual understanding, and fine-grained visual understanding appearing most prominently, and four other construct framings also reported. Overall, use converges on VQA but is also extended to several broader capability labels.

Space of uses. Across papers, VizWiz is usually one part of broad

nodes.name: VL-RewardBench
nodes.definition: A benchmark for evaluating output-level reward modeling in the vision-language domain.

nodes.name: VLGuard
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across these papers, VLGuard is most commonly treated as a multimodal safety alignment resource, alternately described as a dataset and as a safety benchmark for vision-language models. Definitions present it as an original data source and as a baseline for comparison, while another description says it evaluates the ability to detect and respond to multimodal risks across harmful categories, including combinations of safe and unsafe image-text inputs. Some descriptions also frame it as using safe and unsafe training instructions organized by harmful categories.

What it is claimed to measure. Across these papers, the measurement claim converges on one construct: papers link VLGuard to one construct, Safety alignment, and to no behavioral indicators. In DREAM: Disentangling Risks to Enhance Safety Alignment in Multimodal Large Language Models, it is used to evaluate the safe alignment of an approach, so the recorded use is that papers use it to measure Safety alignment rather than a broader spread of constructs.

Space of uses. Papers position VLGuard both as source material and as an evaluation benchmark. In Think in Safety: Unveiling and Mitigating Safety Alignment Col

nodes.name: VLMEvalKit
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most papers describe VLMEvalKit as an evaluation toolkit or standardized platform for assessing vision-language or multimodal models on benchmarks. Recurring details are that it is open-source, serves as a common codebase, and is used to keep settings consistent across methods for fair comparison or unified reproduction of results. A smaller line of work also treats it as a source of benchmark results, with one paper describing it as including diverse benchmarks and performance results from more than 100 MLLMs.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, VLMEvalKit is not linked to any named constructs or behavioral indicators. Instead, it is described in broad performance terms, assessing vision-language, large vision-language, or multimodal models on various benchmarks, including reasoning benchmarks and benchmark-specific evaluations. The prevailing framing is therefore benchmark evaluation rather than measurement of a single named construct.

Space of uses. In use, papers usually position VLMEvalKit as the shared evaluation framework for running experiments under the same configuration, sometimes within OpenCompass, and one paper uses results obtained through it

nodes.name: VLSafe
nodes.definition: A dataset used for training safety-related components (probers, refusal heads) and for evaluating the safety of multimodal models against toxic queries.

nodes.name: VLSBench
nodes.definition: Comprehensive cross-modal safety benchmark with 2,241 image-text pairs designed to prevent safety information leakage, used to evaluate true multimodal safety understanding.

nodes.name: VNBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, VNBench is most commonly described as a benchmark for long video understanding. Definitions and quoted passages tie it especially to Needle-In-the-Haystack-Search, and a smaller framing presents the associated NIAH protocol as testing whether a model can retrieve specific information from long video sequences. One paper further describes VNBench as containing retrieval, ordering, and counting tasks, with retrieval treated as a short-dependency task and ordering and counting as long-dependency tasks.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use VNBench to measure 2 constructs, Temporal perception and Video understanding, and 2 behavioral indicators, Chronological ordering and Counting. The most detailed measurement claim says its retrieval, ordering, and counting tasks evaluate temporal perception, chronological ordering, and spatio-temporal coherence, while another paper lists it among benchmarks used for video understanding. Overall, the reported measurement claims are spread across several aspects rather than concentrated on a single target.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it directly. In practice, papers position VNBench as par

nodes.name: VocalSound
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, VocalSound is treated as a vocal sound classification dataset. Definitions describe it as featuring non-verbal human vocalizations across different acoustic conditions, and as an evaluation set for a model's ability to recognize non-speech audio events; one paper also labels it as "VSC VocalSound" in a benchmark table.

What it is claimed to measure. No constructs or behavioral indicators are linked to VocalSound. Instead, papers describe it more directly as evaluating whether models can recognize non-speech audio events and human vocal sounds beyond speech, so the reported usage converges on vocal sound recognition rather than a named construct.

Space of uses. Papers use VocalSound as an evaluation benchmark within vocal sound classification setups, rather than linking it to other named measurement instruments. In the descriptions it appears as a benchmark entry and as an included dataset for testing recognition of non-verbal human vocalizations under varying acoustic conditions.

nodes.name: VoiceBBQ
nodes.definition: A spoken-language extension of the BBQ benchmark that assesses social bias in spoken language models using synthesized speech contexts with controlled speaker gender and accent, enabling separate evaluation of content and acoustic influences on bias.

nodes.name: VoiceBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the cited papers, VoiceBench is presented as a benchmark dataset for evaluating speech language models on semantic understanding tasks without relying on auxiliary LLMs for scoring. Definitions describe it through multiple subsets, including AdvBench, IFEval, OBQA, MMSU, and sd-qa, and one study reports adopting those five subsets and, after filtering, obtaining 4,947 test samples. A smaller descriptive thread characterizes parts of VoiceBench as speech versions of existing text benchmarks and spoken-query datasets.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link VoiceBench to 3 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator, and the recorded uses cover several targets rather than a single one. It is used to measure Modality gap, with one paper defining the gap through drops in benchmark scores between text and speech inputs; World knowledge, where it is described as a spoken counterpart to text benchmarks across diverse factual domains; Safety, where spoken queries are used to evaluate whether models reject them; and Instruction following, where papers report that a text-based instruction-following benchmark is synthesized into speech.

Space of uses. No measurement instrume

nodes.name: VoxEval
nodes.definition: A benchmark designed for end-to-end speech interaction evaluation that supports the assessment of speech output, unlike benchmarks that require text responses.

nodes.name: VQA-RAD
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, VQA-RAD is most commonly described as a radiology-focused medical visual question answering benchmark: radiology images paired with clinician-authored questions and answers, used to evaluate how models answer questions about medical scans or clinical images. Most descriptions mention open-ended and closed-ended answers, though one definition refers to open-ended and multiple-choice evaluation and one paper uses the name Rad-VQA. Papers do not describe its contents identically: some report 315 images and 2,248 QA pairs, while others report 315 images and 3,515 clinician-authored QA pairs; one paper additionally says imaging reports were generated from the QA pairs.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use VQA-RAD to measure 2 behavioral indicators and link it to no constructs. The prevailing usage is to measure Medical visual question answering, with a smaller line of work using it for Visual question answering. Overall, papers present it as an evaluation benchmark for model performance on medical VQA tasks rather than as a measure of any named construct.

Space of uses. Papers usually use VQA-RAD as one benchmark within multi-dataset medica

nodes.name: VQA-v2
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly describe VQA-v2 as an open-ended visual question answering benchmark or dataset on natural images, where models answer free-form questions about images. Some descriptions add dataset structure, stating that it contains images, associated questions, and ten ground-truth answers per question, and a few papers name specific evaluation splits or subsets such as validation, test-dev, and a 32+50 subset. A smaller line of work also presents it as a more balanced version of the original VQA dataset, and some authors say its questions require understanding of vision, language, and commonsense knowledge.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, VQA-v2 is linked to 11 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators, so measurement claims are distributed across many targets. The most common links treat it as measuring visual understanding, then multimodal understanding and visual perception; it is also used to measure the behavioral indicators visual question answering and answer generation. Other papers link it to several additional constructs.

Space of uses. In use, papers usually place it inside larger multimodal benchmark suites, most often alongside GQA, OK

nodes.name: VQA-X
nodes.definition: VQA-X dataset with human-annotated explanations used to evaluate explanation generation for visual question answering.

nodes.name: VSR
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly treat VSR, or Visual Spatial Reasoning, as a closed-set benchmark for spatial reasoning over images, testing a model's understanding of coarse object spatial relationships. Some definitions also describe it as the Visual Spatial Reasoning dataset, rich in spatial relational information among objects in images, and one paper places it among single-image benchmarks that test alignment between single images and multiple captions.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the papers, VSR is linked to one construct, Spatial reasoning, and no behavioral indicators. The prevailing usage is as a measure of spatial reasoning, with papers referring to it as one of the spatial reasoning benchmarks and reporting results on visual spatial reasoning in VSR.

Space of uses. Papers use VSR for evaluation, commonly alongside other spatial reasoning benchmarks. The cited benchmark suites place it with SPEC, Whatsup, and EmbSpatial, and one paper also includes it in a set of single-image benchmarks used to evaluate fine-grained visual-language understanding; no other measurement instrument is directly linked to it.

nodes.name: VTAB-1k
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most definitions treat VTAB-1k as a vision benchmark or suite of 19 diverse visual tasks, usually described as image classification tasks, spanning Natural, Specialized, and Structured domains. Definitions also describe it as used to evaluate transfer learning methods and the fine-tuning performance of vision models. Some papers make the 1k setting explicit by stating that each dataset has 1000 training examples, and a smaller line of work frames it as assessing generalization capabilities. One quoted passage further specifies 7 Natural, 4 Specialized, and 8 Structured datasets, while another notes structured tasks such as depth and orientation prediction.

What it is claimed to measure. Across the recorded links, papers use VTAB-1k to measure 1 behavioral indicator, Image classification, and it has no linked constructs. The claims therefore converge on a single target rather than spreading across multiple constructs: relationship evidence repeatedly describes VTAB-1k as evaluating image classification or visual classification tasks, and one paper says it is designed to test "image classification and prediction capabilities."

Space of uses. Papers commonly position VTA

nodes.name: WangchanThaiInstruct
nodes.definition: A human-authored Thai instruction-following dataset containing 6,916 test samples across four domains (Medical, Law, Finance, Retail) and seven task types, used for zero-shot evaluation and instruction tuning.

nodes.name: Waste-Bench
nodes.definition: A benchmark dataset containing 9,520 open-ended question-answer pairs across 952 images of cluttered waste scenes, designed to evaluate VLLMs on robustness and reasoning in real-world waste classification tasks.

nodes.name: WE-MATH
nodes.definition: Multimodal math reasoning benchmark focused on Chinese mathematical problems with visual components.

nodes.name: Weather
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats Weather as a benchmark dataset for time series forecasting based on weather or climate data. Definitions differ on its contents and granularity: some describe meteorological variables such as temperature, humidity, and wind speed, some describe local climate data from 1,600 U.S. locations between 2010 and 2013 with 11 climate features, and others describe 21 meteorological factors collected every 10 minutes or, more generally, a Weather Forecasting dataset recorded at a 10-minute frequency. One study describes it as "local climate data from 1,600 U.S. locations, between 2010 and 2013" (Are Language Models Actually Useful for Time Series Forecasting?).

What it is claimed to measure. Its reported measurement role is narrow rather than spread across many targets. Papers link Weather to 1 behavioral indicator, Time series forecasting, and to no constructs or other measurement instruments. In that recorded relationship, papers use it to measure Time series forecasting, describing it as one of the datasets "widely adopted for evaluating time series forecasting performance" and "extensively used to evaluate time-series forecasting ab

nodes.name: WebArena
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the dominant framing is a realistic, web-based interactive environment and benchmark for autonomous or language agents, used to navigate browser interfaces and complete long-horizon tasks from high-level natural language instructions, and some definitions add that agents act through natural language and code. Most descriptions emphasize realistic or functional websites, often naming domains such as e-commerce, forums, development platforms, content management systems, GitLab, Reddit, and Wikipedia; the most detailed account describes 812 tasks or test examples with evaluation based on functional correctness. A smaller line of work describes it more generally as a real web environment with various scenarios, as a benchmark for shopping tasks, or as a source of environments and workflows reused elsewhere.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use WebArena to measure one construct and two behavioral indicators. The prevailing usage is to measure web navigation, with papers describing binary rewards for whether an instruction is achieved by web navigation and using the benchmark for textual or vision-based web navigation; a smaller group reports it as measur

nodes.name: WebMMU
nodes.definition: A multimodal, multilingual, and multi-task benchmark for evaluating MLLMs on visual web understanding and code generation, covering website VQA, mockup-to-code, and code editing in four languages.

nodes.name: WebNLG
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, WebNLG is most commonly described as a dataset or benchmark for generating natural language from structured inputs, especially RDF triples, DBpedia categories, and knowledge graph triplets. Several definitions frame it as data-to-text, struct-to-text, graph-to-text, or knowledge-graph-to-natural-language, and one definition specifies 22,000 examples across 14 categories; a smaller number of descriptions instead call it a table-to-text dataset or, once, a text-to-data dataset. Some papers also refer to specific versions or subsets, including WebNLG17 as the 2017 graph-to-text setting and WebNLG-Test as the publicly released test set of manually aligned knowledge graphs and English textual descriptions.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link WebNLG to 2 behavioral indicators and no constructs. The prevailing usage is to measure Data-to-text generation, with papers explicitly grouping it under E2E and WebNLG (data-to-text generation); some work uses it more broadly to measure Text generation. The measurement claims therefore concentrate on behavioral indicators rather than on constructs.

Space of uses. Papers often use WebNLG as one benchmark within br

nodes.name: WebQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the descriptions, WebQA is treated as a retrieval-augmented question answering dataset used to evaluate long-context retrieval performance. The prevailing characterization specifies 20 documents per question and frames the evaluation around position-dependent accuracy.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers describe WebQA as evaluating long-context retrieval performance and assessing position-dependent accuracy. No constructs or behavioral indicators are linked to it in the recorded relationships, so the usage in the papers does not converge on any separately named construct.

Space of uses. The quoted passage positions WebQA as one dataset in an evaluation suite, used alongside NaturalQuestions, TriviaQA, and KV Retrieval. In that usage, it appears as part of a broader benchmark set rather than with any recorded linked measurement instrument.

nodes.name: WebQSP
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly describe WebQSP as a benchmark dataset for knowledge base or knowledge graph question answering over Freebase or structured knowledge bases. Several definitions add that it is derived from WebQuestions and pairs natural language questions with SPARQL queries; some describe it as containing both single-hop and multi-hop questions, while others frame it more specifically as a multi-hop dataset or as a benchmark used to test I.I.D. generalization. A smaller number of descriptions mention questions from the Google Suggest API, answers from Freebase, or reasoning over a subset of Freebase.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use WebQSP to measure two behavioral indicators and two constructs. The prevailing claim is that it measures Knowledge graph question answering, while a smaller line of work uses it for Multi-hop question answering. On the construct side, papers report it as measuring Multi-hop reasoning most often and Reasoning more generally less often, so the linked claims cluster around KGQA and reasoning-oriented targets.

Space of uses. In use, papers usually treat WebQSP as one of several benchmark KGQA datasets, most often alongside CWQ an

nodes.name: WebQuestions
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, WebQuestions is most commonly described as an open-domain question answering dataset or benchmark. Definitions repeatedly say its questions come from web queries, Google Search, or the Google Suggest API, and several add that answers are entities in Freebase; some papers further describe it as open-ended text QA, factual question answering, or a fact-recall or closed-book benchmark, and one definition says questions focus on a single named entity. A smaller speech-oriented line repurposes it for spoken QA by synthesizing audio versions from the original dataset, while papers also mention using its training split and a test set of 2032 questions.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use WebQuestions to measure 6 behavioral indicators and 3 constructs. The prevailing use is for open-domain question answering, with smaller lines of work using it for spoken question answering, factual recall, world knowledge, and closed-book question answering, and papers also reporting it as measuring other targets. Overall, the claims spread across several behaviors and constructs rather than centering on one construct.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked

nodes.name: WebShop
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most papers describe WebShop as an interactive online shopping or e-commerce simulator benchmark, though a smaller number call it a dataset or task. The recurring setup is that an agent follows a user instruction, navigates web pages with actions such as search and click, and selects product attributes or options to identify and purchase the right item; some definitions emphasize detailed product descriptions and specifications, a large amount of real-world product data, over a million real-world products, or scraped amazon.com pages. Papers differ slightly in format language, calling it a browser environment, network-based simulation environment, interactive web environment, or online shopping dataset, and a few also specify scoring by completion level or dense final rewards from 0 to 1, while one description says performance is based on attribute, option, product type, and price matches within tasks of 30 timesteps.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers that make measurement claims, the usage is concentrated rather than spread across many targets: WebShop is linked to one construct and one behavioral indicator. Several papers use it to measure Decision-making,

nodes.name: WebSRC
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, the prevailing description treats WebSRC as webpage-centered question-answer data used in vision-language or web comprehension settings. Definitions differ in emphasis: some describe it as a dataset for vision-language tasks or for web-based structural reading comprehension, while another paper calls it "a static HTML comprehension benchmark" where answers are extracted from web pages based on a given question.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link WebSRC to two constructs, GUI understanding and HTML understanding, and no behavioral indicators. The explicit measurement claims cover both constructs: one paper lists WebSRC among benchmarks selected "for GUI understanding," while another says it tests WebAgent on WebSRC as "a static HTML comprehension benchmark" for HTML understanding.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is directly linked to WebSRC, though one GUI understanding evaluation uses it alongside VisualWebBench, ScreenQA-Short, and WidgetCap. Papers position it in several ways: as a benchmark that a web agent is tested on, as one of the vision-language tasks in a main results table "illustrating the multi-modal in-context

nodes.name: WebVoyager
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, WebVoyager is most commonly treated as a dynamic, real-world web dataset or benchmark for evaluating long-horizon planning in web navigation, with task completion assessed in realistic environments. A smaller framing presents it as an out-of-distribution benchmark for evaluating web-agent generalization, emphasizing that it covers diverse domains unseen in the WebArena environment.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use WebVoyager to measure one behavioral indicator, Web navigation, and one construct, Generalization. The prevailing usage is to evaluate web navigation in real-world or live settings, while a smaller line of work reports it as measuring generalization by testing agents on the tasks and golden answers proposed in WebVoyager.

Space of uses. In use, papers frequently place WebVoyager alongside WebArena, for example evaluating on the full WebArena dataset as well as WebVoyager, and one study pairs it with Mind2Web-Live as a live web navigation benchmark. It is positioned both as a main evaluation benchmark for real-world websites and as an additional evaluation setting for unseen domains beyond WebArena.

nodes.name: Weibo21
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, Weibo21 is commonly described as a Chinese benchmark drawn from the Weibo platform for fake news or rumor detection. One description presents it as a Chinese-language fake news detection dataset, while another frames it as a Chinese multi-domain rumor detection dataset covering 9 domains, with each news item containing news content and several comments.

What it is claimed to measure. Across papers, Weibo21 is used to measure one behavioral indicator, Misinformation detection, and it is not linked to any constructs. This usage converges on a single target: papers evaluate misinformation detection with Weibo21, and several descriptions place that evaluation within fake news detection tasks.

Space of uses. Papers use Weibo21 alongside GossipCop, AMTCele, Pheme, and LLM-mis in experimental evaluations. In these accounts it is positioned as one of the benchmark datasets in the test setup, for example as the Chinese dataset paired with GossipCop, or as one of the public datasets used in experiments on cross-domain misinformation detection and rumor detection.

nodes.name: WiC
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, WiC is most commonly described as the Word-in-Context dataset or benchmark for word sense disambiguation. The standard task framing is to decide whether a target word has the same meaning in two sentences or contexts, and some papers make this explicit as a binary classification setup; one study also notes that "all WiC datasets are class-balanced," giving a 50% chance baseline. A smaller line of work places WiC within SuperGLUE, and a few definitions describe it as evaluating polysemy disambiguation or context-sensitive word representations.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link WiC to 3 behavioral indicators and no constructs. The prevailing usage is that WiC measures word sense disambiguation, often phrased as contextual word sense disambiguation. Only isolated papers treat it as measuring natural language inference or zero-shot task performance, so the measurement claims mostly converge on disambiguation despite a few alternative framings.

Space of uses. Papers commonly use WiC inside broader evaluation suites rather than describe it on its own. The only explicit instrument-level link relates it to SuperGLUE, and several definitions also place

nodes.name: WiCE
nodes.definition: Textual entailment dataset based on Wikipedia claims, used in this work for connected reasoning evaluation due to its document-claim-evidence triples.

nodes.name: WikiAnn
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, papers refer to it as WikiAnn or WikiANN and most commonly treat it as a multilingual named entity recognition dataset. Definitions differ on scope and framing: some describe 282-language coverage and its use for low-resource Sino-Tibetan languages, with one survey noting that all ST languages other than Chinese amount to 131K name mentions, while other definitions describe a Wikipedia-extracted NER dataset for crosslingual sequence labeling and report 176-language coverage.

What it is claimed to measure. Claims about what it measures converge on a single behavioral indicator rather than spreading across multiple outcomes. Papers link it to 1 behavioral indicator, Named entity recognition, and to no constructs; correspondingly, it is repeatedly described as a dataset used for named entity recognition evaluation.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked alongside it. Papers use it as a direct evaluation set, including crosslingual sequence labeling evaluation and additional experiments on low-resource Sino-Tibetan languages; as one paper states, "We use WikiANN for named entity recognition (NER)" (LangSAMP: Language-Script Aware Mult

nodes.name: WikiBio
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers describe WikiBio as a benchmark dataset for knowledge editing focused on biographical information. The description does not specify versions or subsets, and it appears in a grouping of datasets used to edit different kinds of knowledge.

What it is claimed to measure. The papers link WikiBio to one behavioral indicator, Knowledge editing, through a measured_by relation, and no constructs are linked to it. The measurement claims therefore center on Knowledge editing rather than being spread across multiple constructs or indicators.

Space of uses. In Unlocking Efficient, Scalable, and Continual Knowledge Editing with Basis-Level Representation Fine-Tuning, WikiBio is used alongside WikiDatarecent, WikiDatacounterfact, ConvSent, and ZsRE, in the authors' setup for editing different kinds of knowledge. No measurement instrument is linked to it beyond this co-usage context.

nodes.name: Wikidata
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the definitions, papers treat Wikidata as a schema matching dataset for a general knowledge base, used to test whether schema matching approaches generalize on structured open-domain data. One paper explicitly places it in a cross-domain evaluation setting, stating that authors evaluate on "Magellan (e-commerce) and WikiData (general knowledge base)" to assess generalizability to other domains (Bootstrapping Self-Improvement of Language Model Programs for Zero-Shot Schema Matching).

What it is claimed to measure. In the reported relationships, papers use Wikidata to measure one behavioral indicator, Schema matching, and it is not linked to any constructs. The linked usage converges on that single indicator rather than spreading across multiple targets: papers report schema matching as measured by Wikidata.

Space of uses. Papers use Wikidata as an evaluation benchmark for schema matching, and one explicit usage description positions it as further evaluation for generalizability to other domains rather than as a standalone setting. In that description, it appears alongside Magellan.

nodes.name: WikiData_counterfact
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers treat WikiData_counterfact as a dataset for knowledge editing evaluation, most commonly described as containing counterfactual statements derived from Wikidata. One paper places it within the KnowEdit benchmark and uses it among datasets selected for experiments covering knowledge insertion and knowledge modification.

What it is claimed to measure. Claims about what it measures are concentrated rather than dispersed. Multiple papers use WikiData_counterfact to measure Knowledge editing, and one paper also reports it as measuring Editing locality, with a Locality ↑ result on this dataset; overall, papers link it to one behavioral indicator and one construct.

Space of uses. In the reported uses, it is positioned as one benchmark within broader evaluation suites. It is used alongside WikiDatarecent, WikiBio, ConvSent, and ZsRE when papers evaluate editing different kinds of knowledge, and one paper describes it as one of two additional benchmarks while another reports a pilot quantitative experiment on it within KnowEdit.

nodes.name: WikiData_recent
nodes.definition:
What it is. In the papers, WikiData_recent is described as a dataset for knowledge editing evaluation that focuses on recent, updated facts from Wikidata. Papers place it among experimental datasets for knowledge insertion and knowledge modification.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to measure one behavioral indicator and two constructs. The linked claims report it as measuring Knowledge editing, and as evaluating Editing locality and Fluency, so its reported use covers a small set of targets rather than only one.

Space of uses. Papers use it as one dataset within broader knowledge editing evaluation suites, alongside WikiDatacounterfact, WikiBio, ConvSent, and ZsRE. One paper also places it in experiments that cover both knowledge insertion and knowledge modification.

nodes.name: WikiHop
nodes.definition: A multi-hop question answering dataset used here to evaluate the effectiveness of web-page retrieval.

nodes.name: WikiHow
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly treat WikiHow as source data built from instructional content. Definitions describe it as a dataset of instructional articles, as a multimodal dataset, and in one study as a dataset derived from the WikiHow online knowledge base and modified by grouping related paragraphs into documents and using summaries as subheadings. Across these uses, it appears as the basis for script generation, project-based learning, and procedural step selection from text and images.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link WikiHow to 1 behavioral indicator, How-to question answering, and to no constructs. The recorded claim is focused rather than spread across many outcomes: a paper reports that this dataset is used to evaluate THREAD on linear how-to questions, so WikiHow is used to measure How-to question answering.

Space of uses. No other measurement instrument is linked to WikiHow. Instead, papers use it as source material within broader evaluations: as the basis for a script generation task in InterleavedBench, as extracted data for MMIE's project-based learning category, as a modified dataset for evaluating organizing skill on expository text, and as a dataset

nodes.name: WikiMIA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing description treats WikiMIA as a benchmark or dataset for evaluating training or pretraining data detection on large language models. Definitions commonly describe it as temporal: it uses Wikipedia data or excerpts labeled as seen or unseen, or as training and non-training, based on publication date relative to a model's training cutoff or release timeline. A smaller framing presents the same date-based split as a membership inference benchmark, with member and non-member data separated by publication date.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use WikiMIA to measure one behavioral indicator, Pre-training data detection, and they do not link it to any constructs. The links converge on that single indicator: papers say pre-training data detection is measured by WikiMIA, and describe it as commonly used for evaluating pretraining data detection methods or for verifying the effectiveness of detection methods. One paper also reports that Membership inference attack is related to WikiMIA, rather than presenting it as what WikiMIA measures.

Space of uses. In use, papers often position WikiMIA as a benchmark within evaluation suites, most explici

nodes.name: Wikipedia
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the cited work, Wikipedia is most commonly treated as an evaluation resource, described either as an external knowledge base or as a text corpus. Definitions vary by use: one paper uses it as the source of retrieved documents for RAG evaluation, drawing on a Wikimedia dump provided by Cohere, while others refer to it as a pre-training dataset or as MassiveText Wikipedia used to test whether findings extend to a more complex corpus and larger scales.

What it is claimed to measure. Across these papers, Wikipedia is not linked to any construct or behavioral indicator, so no explicit claim about what it measures is recorded.

Space of uses. Papers use Wikipedia in several evaluation roles: as the retrieval source in RAG experiments, as a corpus considered when computing Diff-eRank and reduced loss, and as a supporting evaluation setting for robustness checks. No other measurement instruments are linked to it in these papers.

nodes.name: WikiQA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing framing is a question-answering benchmark or dataset built from questions paired with Wikipedia sentences or answers. Some definitions narrow this to answer selection, or to open-domain, closed-book question answering, while one calibration study uses it for sentence-level responses because model responses are complete sentences. A smaller usage applies the test set with synthesised speech queries for spoken-query-based question answering.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to three behavioral indicators and no constructs. The dominant claim is that WikiQA measures question answering, and smaller lines of work use it to measure open-ended question answering and spoken question answering. The reported measurement claims therefore stay within closely related question-answering behaviors rather than broader constructs.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it, but papers often use it alongside other benchmarks such as SQuAD, QASC, QuaRTz, TruthfulQA, and HotpotQA. Across studies it is usually one dataset within a larger task suite, including fine-tuning and evaluation setups, sentence-level calibration evaluation,

nodes.name: WikiSQL
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most commonly, papers treat WikiSQL as a standard or benchmark text-to-SQL dataset. Definitions also place it among early benchmarks for Text-to-SQL parsing over relational tables, including one description that narrows this to single relational tables, while another paper uses it as a benchmark in a main evaluation table for structured knowledge grounding. A smaller usage presents it as another corpus to which a methodology can be adapted.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link WikiSQL to two behavioral indicators and no constructs. It is reported as measuring Table question answering and Text-to-SQL: one paper describes it as one of three challenging table QA datasets, and another places it among early benchmarks that focus on Text-to-SQL parsing over relational tables. The reported measurement role is therefore split across these two task framings rather than tied to a linked construct.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it. Papers nevertheless mention or use WikiSQL alongside other benchmarks, including BIRD and Spider as other text-to-SQL datasets, and alongside WikiTQ and FeTaQA when reporting table question answering results. Another pape

nodes.name: WikiText
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, WikiText is most commonly described as a language modeling benchmark or corpus built from Wikipedia text, often evaluated through perplexity on a held-out or validation split. Some definitions make this more specific by calling it high-quality encyclopedic text, in one case limited to articles marked Good or Featured by human editors, while others refer to Wikitext-2 or frame it as a long-context benchmark across different context lengths. A smaller line of work uses the name for training or calibration data rather than only evaluation, including pre-training on the corpus and using random segments from it for calibration or profiling.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link WikiText to 5 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators. The most common measurement claims are for general ability and language modeling ability, followed by zero-shot generalization and confidence; another reported use is to measure long-form text generation, and the remaining recorded links are 1 other behavioral indicator and 1 related construct. Across these uses, the evidence is phrased in terms of perplexity, cross-entropy loss, likelihood, and prediction confidence, so papers

nodes.name: WikiText-103
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers most commonly describe WikiText-103 as a larger WikiText language modeling benchmark or corpus derived from high-quality Wikipedia articles. The prevailing use is evaluation of language modeling performance, especially perplexity, though some papers use it for pre-training, as an evaluation domain for open-ended generation, or as source text for embeddings, character strings, or word-splitting experiments. Definitions and quoted passages also refer to variants and subsets such as Wikitext-103-v1, train, validation, and test splits, development and test sets, and held-out or validation sequences.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link WikiText-103 to 1 construct and 3 behavioral indicators. The dominant claim is that it measures language modeling ability: papers frame it as a benchmark for language modeling, autoregressive modeling, and next-token generation, often through perplexity. Smaller lines of work report it as measuring text continuation, text generation, and text infilling, including use of validation-set sequences for MAUVE-based infilling evaluation and Wikitext-103-v1 for generation tasks.

Space of uses. Most papers position it as a standard or

nodes.name: WikiText-2
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the dominant framing is a language modeling benchmark or dataset, usually described as cleaned, curated, or high-quality Wikipedia text and evaluated with perplexity on validation or test text. Several papers treat it as a held-out benchmark for compressed, quantized, pruned, or fine-tuned models, while some use the training split, train models from scratch on it, or run zero-shot evaluation without fine-tuning. Papers also use several surface forms, including WikiText2, Wikitext2, and WT-2, and a smaller line of work mentions variants such as WikiText2-v1, described as over 100 million tokens and used for hidden-state analysis plus validation-set perplexity, and WikiText-V2.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link WikiText-2 to 7 constructs and 1 behavioral indicator. The prevailing claims use it to measure language modeling ability and the behavioral indicator text generation, usually through perplexity or LM loss; several papers also state that lower perplexity on Wikitext-2 reflects stronger language modeling ability. Less commonly, papers report it as measuring general ability, generative ability, and linguistic quality, with additional construct

nodes.name: WikiTQ
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most papers describe WikiTQ, also written as WikiTableQuestions or WTQ, as a benchmark or dataset of Wikipedia, sometimes semi-structured or HTML, tables paired with natural-language questions for table-based question answering. The prevailing description emphasizes complex operations such as comparison, aggregation, and arithmetic, while some papers further frame it as short-form or short text span answering; one paper describes about 2100 HTML tables and about 22,033 questions, and another refers to a standard test set with 4,344 table-question pairs. A smaller line of work adapts it into training formats for table-language interleaved learning or column-embedding training, and one study uses a filtered hybrid version requiring semantic inference.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link WikiTQ to one behavioral indicator, Table question answering, and one construct, Table reasoning. The prevailing usage is to measure Table question answering, with descriptions such as table QA, table-based question answering, or short-form QA over semi-structured tables. A smaller group of papers uses it to measure Table reasoning, describing it as a benchmark for table-based reas

nodes.name: WildBench
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most papers describe WildBench as an instruction-following benchmark for evaluating LLM responses, usually with diverse task categories and a fine-grained grading scale against a reference answer. A smaller line of work describes it as an LLM-based evaluation framework or public dataset of model comparisons judged by an LLM judge, while other descriptions present it as a challenging instruction-following QA benchmark with long, multi-turn prompts, real-user questions, human preference judgments, and 1024 manually selected questions from the same source as WildChat; one paper also refers to a WildBench WB-Score.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use WildBench to measure 7 constructs and 5 behavioral indicators. These links are spread across several abilities, including complex reasoning, conversational ability, creativity, instruction following ability, and long-context reasoning, plus 2 other construct links; behavioral indicators include creative writing, data analysis, instruction following, question answering, and role-playing. In the quoted descriptions, the tasks are also said to involve higher-order reasoning and multiple constraints.

Space of uses. A recurr

nodes.name: WildChat
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the definitions, WildChat is most commonly described as a dataset of real-world LLM conversations or real-world user interactions. Papers variously frame it as conversations with GPT models performing daily tasks, collected through a free GPT API in exchange for shared logs, and as a source of out-of-distribution prompts; one paper also describes it as a comprehensive multi-turn, multi-lingual dataset of 1 million timestamped conversations, and another says it "more closely reflects real user needs."

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link WildChat to 2 constructs and 2 behavioral indicators. The main measurement uses in these papers are to measure Overrefusal, Harmlessness, and Multilingual ability: papers describe over-refusal evaluations using WildChat, test harmlessness with "highly toxic prompts from WildChat," and assess multilingual capability with MultiAlpaca and WildChat; a separate paper relates it to Multi-turn dialogue rather than treating that link as a measurement claim. In the papers, these claims are spread across several targets rather than centered on one construct.

Space of uses. WildChat is used as evaluation data rather than alongside an

nodes.name: WildChat-1M
nodes.definition: Real-world dataset of 837,989 conversations from 167,062 users interacting with a ChatGPT mirror site over one year, used to analyze conceptual diversity trends before and after GPT version updates.

nodes.name: WildChat-AQA
nodes.definition: Benchmark for aggregative question answering comprising 6,027 multiple-choice questions derived from 182,330 real-world chatbot conversations, assessing models' ability to extract collective insights across temporal, geographic, and demographic dimensions.

nodes.name: WildGuard
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the cited papers, WildGuard is most commonly described as an automated, classifier-based evaluation procedure for model responses to harmful queries. The prevailing description is that it is used to judge whether a response fully complies with a harmful test query. Some papers describe the same tool more specifically as classifying a response as refusal or compliance, including on XSTest, while another paper frames it as an external harmfulness detection model that assigns a harmfulness probability to each response.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers do not explicitly link WildGuard to any constructs or behavioral indicators. Instead, they describe it as evaluating immediate response properties: whether a model response fully complies with harmful test queries, whether it should be classified as a refusal or compliance, and, in one framing, the probability that a response is harmful. Across these descriptions, the usage clusters around automatic safety evaluation rather than a single explicitly named construct.

Space of uses. No other measurement instrument is explicitly linked to WildGuard. Papers position it as an automatic evaluator for safety-focused mod

nodes.name: WildGuardMix
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the dominant framing treats WildGuardMix as a benchmark dataset for safety guard models, especially for instruction-response pair classification and response classification for content safety. Papers also refer to WildGuardMix Test Response and WildGuardTest: the former is described as a public benchmark for response classification, while the latter is presented as an evaluation dataset or prompt safety benchmark. Definitions of WildGuardTest differ, with one paper describing 1725 prompts, 863 harmful persuasion and 862 safe, and another describing 960 vanilla and 796 adversarial prompts. A smaller line of work instead uses WildGuardMix as a preference dataset for synthesized judge training data, or as a dataset containing a broad spectrum of jailbroken prompts and responses.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link WildGuardMix to three behavioral indicators and no constructs. The reported measurement use is spread across Content moderation, Harmful content detection, and Response harmfulness classification, rather than centered on a linked construct. In these uses, papers present it as evaluating safety guard or content safety classificati

nodes.name: WildScore
nodes.definition: An in-the-wild multimodal benchmark for symbolic music reasoning and analysis, consisting of real music scores paired with user-generated multiple-choice questions from online forums.

nodes.name: WildSeek
nodes.definition: WildSeek is an evaluation dataset of 100 topic-and-intent examples across 24 domains used to assess open-domain long-form generation.

nodes.name: WildVision
nodes.definition: A real-world dataset of image-text pairs used for distribution analysis and comparison.

nodes.name: WinoBias
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, WinoBias is most commonly described as a coreference resolution benchmark or dataset for gender bias, built from Winograd-style examples about professions and pronouns. Definitions converge on testing pronoun resolution in stereotypical and anti-stereotypical settings, often around gender-occupation associations. One description says each example contains two gender-neutral profession names and gendered pronouns, and the task is to identify the coreference link to the correct profession, while another describes the items more broadly as gendered sentence pairs.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link WinoBias to two constructs and one behavioral indicator. The prevailing use is to measure gender bias: papers describe it as evaluating whether models assign stereotypical gender pronouns to occupations, and one paper calls it an "ecologically valid probe" for detecting gender biases in pronoun resolution; another formulation says it measures dependency between output words and social groups. Papers also use it to measure coreference resolution, and a smaller line of work uses it to measure social bias.

Space of uses. Most descriptions position it as

nodes.name: Winogender
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, Winogender is most commonly described as a diagnostic or benchmark dataset for gender bias in coreference resolution, especially gender-occupation bias. Definitions describe it as testing whether models resolve pronouns in a gender-stereotyped manner, and one paper specifies sentence templates with gendered pronouns and a Pearson correlation between model probabilities for female pronouns and occupations' female gender statistics. A smaller line of work repurposes the benchmark for non-stereotypical evaluation by filtering out sentences with strong gender co-occurrences, and another paper groups it with WinoGrad Schema based datasets and describes it as similar to WinoBias.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use Winogender to measure 2 constructs and no behavioral indicators: Gender bias and Social bias. The prevailing framing in the definitions is Gender bias in coreference resolution, while one paper also uses it to measure Social bias as an out-of-distribution bias benchmark for testing generalization. Overall, its reported measurement use stays within bias constructs rather than specific behavioral indicators.

Space of uses. No paper directly

nodes.name: WinoGrande
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, WinoGrande is most commonly described as a large-scale commonsense reasoning benchmark or dataset, usually framed as an adversarial Winograd-schema-style pronoun or coreference resolution task. Definitions often say it requires resolving ambiguous pronouns, sometimes as fill-in-the-blank questions with binary or multiple-choice options; one paper says it "asks the model to fill-in-a-blank with binary options given a sentence which requires commonsense reasoning" (ReFT: Representation Finetuning for Language Models). Several papers also describe it as adversarially filtered or bias-reduced, and another says it consists of "44k problems generated through crowdsourcing and systematic bias reduction algorithms" (LLM Circuit Analyses Are Consistent Across Training and Scale); naming varies slightly across papers, including Winogrande, WinoGrade, Winograde, and Wino.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link WinoGrande to 13 constructs and 11 behavioral indicators. The prevailing usage is as a measure of Commonsense reasoning, with smaller lines of work using it for Reasoning and Natural language understanding; among behavioral indicators, Coreference resolut

nodes.name: Winoground
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, Winoground is most commonly described as a compositional image-text matching dataset or benchmark for probing visio-linguistic compositionality, fine-grained alignment, and reasoning. Definitions converge on a setup with carefully constructed minimal pairs, or paired images and captions, and one recurring task description says the model must correctly match two images and captions whose captions use the same words in different orders. A smaller framing describes it more broadly as a dataset of images for evaluating vision-language models, including image captioning and compositional understanding.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to three constructs and two behavioral indicators. The prevailing usage is to measure compositional reasoning, followed by compositionality and relation understanding: papers describe it as testing compositional visual reasoning, as a benchmark for assessing VLM compositionality, and as evaluating the ability to understand relationships between objects within an image. Smaller uses report it as measuring cross-modal retrieval through binary image-text matching, and self-correction, where authors evaluate

nodes.name: Wizard of Wikipedia
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across definitions, papers describe Wizard of Wikipedia, also called WoW or Wizard-of-Wikipedia, as a knowledge-grounded or open-domain dialogue dataset or benchmark in which one conversational partner, the "wizard," has access to Wikipedia or Wikipedia articles to inform the conversation. The prevailing description is this shared setup, while some papers emphasize it as a benchmark for knowledge-grounded dialogue and others as a dialogue dataset used for training models.

What it is claimed to measure. Several papers report that Wizard of Wikipedia measures dialogue generation. It is linked to one behavioral indicator, Dialogue generation, and no constructs, so dialogue generation is the only reported measurement target.

Space of uses. Papers use it in multiple roles: for evaluation, for training dialogue models, and for dialogue analysis. They place it alongside HotpotQA for evaluation, and alongside DailyDialog and DialogSum for controlled response generation, grammar detection, and grammar skill co-occurrence analysis in adjacent speaker turns; no other measurement instrument is linked to it.

nodes.name: WizardLM
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing description treats WizardLM as a benchmark or evaluation dataset for instruction-oriented, open-ended tasks. One recurring definition presents it as containing 218 questions that span more categories and diverse difficulties, used to assess broader question-type generalization. Papers also describe it differently: one frames it as a benchmark for instruction-following and open-ended generation using complex, multi-step prompts, while another describes it as instruction-generation data that leverages the ChatGPT API to generate 250k instructions from Alpaca training data.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use WizardLM to measure 1 behavioral indicator, Text generation, and link it to no constructs. The reported measurement claim converges on that single target: it is presented as part of evaluating "open-ended generation."

Space of uses. In use, papers place WizardLM within broader evaluation suites and as a baseline against prior resources. One paper includes it alongside Vicuna in a "broad array of out-of-distribution benchmarks" for open-ended generation, and another treats it as a previous-work baseline alongside SELF-INSTRUCT

nodes.name: WMDP
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, WMDP is most commonly treated as a popular unlearning benchmark for hazardous or harmful knowledge. Definitions describe it as evaluating a model's capacity to generate and then unlearn such knowledge, especially in biosecurity and cybersecurity, and some descriptions also include chemical security. Papers do not describe it identically: some call it the World Model Development Project benchmark, others the Weapons of Mass Destruction Proxy benchmark, and one definition specifies a multiple-choice dataset with WMDP-bio and WMDP-cyber subsets.

What it is claimed to measure. In the recorded links, papers use WMDP to measure one behavioral indicator, multiple-choice question answering, and no constructs are linked to it. The explicit measurement links therefore converge on a single behavioral indicator rather than several constructs. Beyond that link, definitions frequently say it evaluates unlearning capability, or the unlearning of hazardous or harmful knowledge, in domains such as biosecurity, cybersecurity, and sometimes chemical security.

Space of uses. Papers position WMDP both as a popular unlearning benchmark and as one dataset within broader e

nodes.name: WMT
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most commonly, papers treat WMT as the Workshop on Machine Translation benchmark or shared task for translation evaluation, often using the English-German setting as WMT EnDe or EN→DE. Definitions also refer to collections of yearly WMT tasks. A smaller line of work describes WMT instead as a human-preference dataset used to construct contrastive instruction-response pairs for machine translation.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link WMT to one behavioral indicator, Machine translation, and to two constructs, Translation quality and Text generation quality. The prevailing claim is that WMT measures machine translation, and papers also report it as measuring translation quality. A smaller usage treats it as measuring text generation quality, with one study noting that "Quality is measured in terms of BLEU for WMT" (Faster Cascades via Speculative Decoding).

Space of uses. Papers use WMT as a translation evaluation task and as one task within multi-task setups. One common pattern is to pair WMT EnDe or EN→DE with CNN/DM, and sometimes XSum, when models are supervised fine-tuned on several tasks; another is to place WMT alongside MLQE-PE and FLORES when discussing

nodes.name: WMT14
nodes.definition:
What it is. Papers commonly describe WMT14 as a machine translation benchmark from the 2014 Workshop on Statistical Machine Translation, used to evaluate translation quality on standard translation directions. The descriptions vary in granularity: some refer to WMT14 generally, while others specify WMT14EnDe with training and test sets drawn from it, and relationship evidence also mentions French-English and English-French portions.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use WMT14 to measure Machine translation: it is linked to 1 behavioral indicator and to no constructs. The reported use is concentrated on that single indicator, with papers describing WMT14 as used for machine translation and for evaluating translation capabilities.

Space of uses. In use, papers present it as a direct translation evaluation, and some also place it in broader benchmark collections. No measurement instrument is linked to it, but one paper reports it alongside IWSLT14, afroMT, IWSLT17, WMT18, and WMT19 for machine translation, another includes WMT 2014 in a multilinguality grouping with two other benchmarks, and one relationship quote uses the English-French subset as part of a training set.

nodes.name: WMT14 De-En
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most commonly described as a WMT 2014 German-to-English machine translation benchmark, papers refer to it as a dataset or benchmark of sentence pairs for evaluating translation quality. A smaller variation in wording emphasizes its use for evaluating speculative decoding on translation text distributions, and one quoted passage specifies 3,003 sentence pairs.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to measure Machine translation: it is linked to one behavioral indicator, Machine translation, and to no constructs. The reported measurement claims are concentrated on that single behavioral indicator, with papers selecting WMT14 De-En for the translation part of broader evaluations.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it directly, but papers use it alongside MT-bench, CNN/Daily Mail, Natural Questions, GSM8K, and Alpaca, with other datasets also mentioned. In those settings it is positioned as the translation component within multi-task evaluations, including speculative decoding studies.

nodes.name: WMT14 en-de
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers here, the prevailing usage treats WMT14 en-de as an English-German machine translation benchmark for translating English to German and evaluating translation quality. Definitions in this direction describe it as a benchmark used to evaluate finetuned LLMs on translation, and one study says it considers "the task on translating English to German using WMT14 en-de." A smaller line of work describes it instead as an English-to-German translation dataset used for both training and evaluation in distillation experiments.

What it is claimed to measure. In the recorded relationships, papers use WMT14 en-de to measure Machine translation. It is linked to one behavioral indicator, Machine translation, and to no constructs. The measurement claims are therefore concentrated on a single behavioral indicator rather than spread across multiple linked constructs or behaviors.

Space of uses. Papers use it within broader training and evaluation setups, not only as a standalone translation check. One line of work presents it as a downstream task for finetuning, alongside WMT19 English-Chinese for translation and multilingual summarization tasks, while another uses it

nodes.name: WMT16
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, WMT16 is most commonly described as a machine translation dataset or benchmark from the 2016 WMT workshop. Definitions vary in the slice emphasized: several papers refer to its English and German splits for cross-lingual detection, some use it for English-to-Romanian fine-tuning and evaluation, and another describes it as focusing on English-to-German translation. A smaller usage treats it more broadly as part of a translation benchmark suite, as in the phrasing "WMT 2014 and WMT 2016" or as an item under multilingual evaluation.

What it is claimed to measure. In relationships, papers link WMT16 to one behavioral indicator and one construct.
