The prevailing use is to measure Machine translation: papers cite Romanian-English and German-English pairs from the workshop, English-to-Romanian distillation, general translation tasks, and German-to-English test sets. A smaller line of work uses it to measure Multilingual ability, where WMT 2016 appears alongside other multilingual evaluations.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is formally linked to WMT16 in the relationships. Papers use it in two recurring ways: as a translation benchmark for fine-tuning,

nodes.name: WMT18
nodes.definition: A machine translation benchmark used to evaluate decoding methods on translation tasks.

nodes.name: WMT19
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the papers, the prevailing treatment of WMT19 is as a machine translation benchmark from the Workshop on Machine Translation 2019 or the WMT19 shared task. The descriptions vary slightly in form: some call it a benchmark used to evaluate machine translation systems, while one paper calls WMT-19 a dataset and uses the Kazakh-English subset; the cited content ranges from language pairs such as De-En, Fi-En, Lt-En, and Ru-En to that Kazakh-English subset.

What it is claimed to measure. In the recorded relationships, papers use WMT19 to measure Machine translation. The claims converge on that single behavioral indicator: it is linked to 1 behavioral indicator, Machine translation, and no constructs.

Space of uses. Papers often use WMT19 alongside other machine translation benchmarks. In the excerpts it appears alongside WMT14, and some papers also list IWSLT14, afroMT, IWSLT17, and WMT18 in the same evaluation setup; a smaller use treats it as the Kazakh-English subset for evaluating fine-tuning after coreset selection, and one description also presents it for evaluating translation performance and uncertainty.

nodes.name: WMT23
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most commonly, papers treat WMT23 as the 2023 Workshop or Conference on Machine Translation shared-task test set or benchmark for evaluating machine translation systems and translation quality across multiple language pairs. Some definitions add that it contains human-rated translations across multiple language pairs and systems, and one study specifically uses the WMT'23 MQM ratings for English-German and Chinese-English. Another use frames it as the source of contaminated test examples drawn from ten language pairs.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to evaluate machine translation systems or translation quality, including fine-grained machine translation evaluation in one study. They do not explicitly use it to measure any named construct or behavioral indicator.

Space of uses. The prevailing usage is as a benchmark or test set in model evaluation. One study evaluates a Specialist method on WMT'23 and compares it with the XCOMET metric, another uses WMT 2023 as the source of contaminated test examples and then decontaminates the set, and another places WMT23 under generative tasks.

Concerns raised. Contamination is the only explicit concern raised in the

nodes.name: WMT24++
nodes.definition: A high-quality translation test dataset derived from WMT24 with human-written and professionally post-edited references, used to evaluate translation performance without data leakage.

nodes.name: WMT 2024
nodes.definition: Annual Conference on Machine Translation shared task dataset for evaluating machine translation systems, containing human-rated translations across multiple language pairs and systems.

nodes.name: WN18RR
nodes.definition: A benchmark dataset for link prediction derived from WordNet, a lexical knowledge graph for English, with reciprocal relations removed to address test leakage problems.

nodes.name: WNLI
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most commonly described as a Winograd Natural Language Inference benchmark or dataset, papers frame WNLI as a natural language inference evaluation centered on sentence-level understanding and pronoun reasoning. Across definitions, the recurring focus is pronoun resolution or ambiguity, coreference resolution, and reasoning in pronoun disambiguation, with some descriptions adding textual entailment-style reasoning or logical inference. One paper specifically reports using the validation set to measure performance.

What it is claimed to measure. Explicit measurement claims are narrow: papers link WNLI to one behavioral indicator and one construct. One paper uses it to measure natural language inference, describing RTE and WNLI as inference tasks, while another uses it as an out-of-domain task to evaluate generalization. The named targets are natural language inference and generalization, and no other constructs or behavioral indicators are linked in these papers.

Space of uses. Usage is most often as part of broader GLUE evaluations. It is related to one other instrument, GLUE, and papers place it alongside tasks such as CoLA, MRPC, RTE, and SST-2; reported setups incl

nodes.name: Word association test
nodes.definition: Psychological assessment that reveals subconscious cognitive patterns through free-relation word associations to cue words, adapted here for evaluating LLMs' cultural cognition.

nodes.name: Word substitution attack
nodes.definition: An evaluation protocol for robustness where a specified percentage of tokens in a watermarked text are randomly replaced with other tokens from the vocabulary before attempting to decode the watermark.

nodes.name: Word swap attack
nodes.definition: A data contamination procedure where words are randomly swapped with a generic token to test robustness.

nodes.name: Wordle
nodes.definition: A word-guessing environment used here to assess reasoning and planning in a sequential decision-making setting.

nodes.name: World Values Survey
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats the World Values Survey as a large-scale cross-national survey, or global research project, about beliefs and values worldwide, spanning social, political, religious, cultural, personal, and societal values. Papers commonly use it as seed data or a source of seed questions for culture-specific generation, and some also describe it as a proxy for cultural values in NLP, repurpose it as training data for cultural adaptation, or use it to derive representative personas. Where versions are specified, authors focus on Wave 7, conducted from 2017 to 2020 and covering 57 countries; reported subsets include 260 questions across 13 cultural topics and a filtered set of 206 questions, and one description notes more than 129K human respondents.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to 3 constructs and no behavioral indicators. The most common claim is that it measures cultural alignment, with authors using it for assessment and for comparing model responses to human survey data; a smaller line of work uses it to measure value orientation by treating it as ground-truth human value distributions across countries. It is also related

nodes.name: WOS
nodes.definition: The Web of Science dataset (WOS-46985), a benchmark for hierarchical text classification containing scientific abstracts with a 2-level hierarchy of research areas and sub-areas.

nodes.name: WritingPrompts
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across definitions, WritingPrompts is treated as a story-writing or story-generation dataset featuring creative stories from Reddit's writing prompts forum. Papers also describe it as a language modeling evaluation dataset; in one use, models are given the story topic as the prompt for generating a narrative, while another paper treats it as a benchmark corpus and test-data source for sentence-level AI-generated text detection.

What it is claimed to measure. In the recorded measurement links, papers use WritingPrompts to measure one construct, Language modeling ability, and one behavioral indicator, Story generation. The stated measurement role is therefore concentrated on those two targets rather than spread across many constructs or indicators.

Space of uses. Papers use WritingPrompts in several roles: as one of multiple corpora in broader evaluation, as training data for fine-tuning on story telling, and as a source corpus for constructing and testing sentence-level AI-generated text detection data. Quoted passages place it alongside XSum or XSUM and SQuAD, including a report of averaging AUROCs across XSum, SQuAD, and WritingPrompts; no other measurement instrumen

nodes.name: WSC
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most commonly, papers describe WSC, sometimes called Winograd, as the Winograd Schema Challenge, a benchmark or task for coreference resolution through ambiguous pronoun disambiguation, usually framed as requiring commonsense reasoning. Some definitions cast it more broadly as a reasoning benchmark for downstream evaluation, and one quoted passage says WSC contains multiple-choice questions. A smaller line of work treats Winograd as a language-modeling formulation of the SuperGLUE WSC task, and one paper uses a Winograd-schema-style direct-question prompt plus a one-shot variant, WSC-1sh.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use WSC to measure 1 construct, Commonsense reasoning, and 3 behavioral indicators, most often Coreference resolution, then Downstream task performance and Language understanding task performance. The prevailing claims cluster around commonsense reasoning and coreference resolution: papers list WSC or Winograd among commonsense reasoning datasets and say it evaluates coreference resolution capabilities. Broader uses as a measure of downstream or language-understanding performance also appear, but as less central framings.

Space of uses. In practi

nodes.name: X-CSQA
nodes.definition: A multilingual commonsense reasoning benchmark (Cross-lingual CommonSense QA) used to evaluate a model's ability to answer commonsense questions in various languages.

nodes.name: XCOPA
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most commonly described as a cross-lingual or multilingual benchmark dataset for commonsense or causal reasoning, XCOPA is framed across definitions as a choice among plausible alternatives across languages. Definitions consistently present it as choosing the more plausible alternative, often the most plausible cause or effect from a premise and question, and papers variously describe the format as choice of plausible alternatives, multiple-choice classification, or binary-choice evaluation.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use XCOPA to measure two constructs, most often Commonsense reasoning and also Reasoning, and no behavioral indicators are linked to it. The measured_by claims describe it as targeting or evaluating commonsense reasoning and reasoning, so the reported measurement uses stay concentrated on reasoning-focused constructs rather than spreading across many different outcomes.

Space of uses. Papers usually position XCOPA as one benchmark within multilingual evaluation suites for reasoning or classification, rather than as a standalone protocol. It is often used alongside XNLI, and some papers also pair it with MGSM, XQuAD, and XStoryCloze; one paper

nodes.name: XGLUE
nodes.definition: A benchmark for evaluating cross-lingual transfer on a diverse set of natural language understanding and generation tasks.

nodes.name: XLQA
nodes.definition: A benchmark for locale-aware multilingual open-domain question answering, containing 3,000 English seed questions expanded into eight languages with human-verified annotations distinguishing locale-invariant and locale-sensitive cases.

nodes.name: XLSum
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, XLSum is most commonly described as a large-scale multilingual summarization dataset or benchmark, usually for abstractive summarization and sometimes explicitly for news or cross-lingual summarization. Most descriptions say it covers 44 languages, though one paper describes 45 languages; papers also characterize it as created from BBC articles, as comprising professionally annotated article-summary pairs, and as evaluating generation through a one-sentence summary of a context or article. A smaller line of work uses only the English subset or portion, and one paper describes that subset as the largest publicly available summarization dataset, with 307,000 training samples and 11,500 test samples.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use XLSum to measure 3 behavioral indicators and no constructs. The prevailing use is for Text summarization, with additional use for Abstractive summarization and, less often, News summarization. All recorded measurement claims stay within summarization tasks.

Space of uses. No measurement instrument is linked to it. Papers commonly place it in multilingual or generation benchmark suites, and one study selects

nodes.name: XNLI
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing framing treats XNLI as a multilingual or cross-lingual natural language inference benchmark built from sentence pairs or premise-hypothesis pairs, where models classify relations such as entailment, contradiction, and neutrality. Several definitions present it as a multilingual extension of MNLI or MultiNLI, but papers differ on scope: some describe 15 languages, others 14, and a few use alternative label wording such as "unrelated" or "Non-entailed." Some papers also work with specific portions or subsets, including the English portion, the Spanish portion, and sampled test examples.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link XNLI to 4 constructs and 4 behavioral indicators. The dominant measurement claim is Natural language inference, with several papers using it for multilingual NLI or textual entailment evaluation. Beyond that, the construct-side links are spread across Cross-lingual generalization, Helpfulness, Multilingual understanding, and Semantic understanding, while papers also report additional behavioral-indicator uses rather than converging on one second target.

Space of uses. Papers do not report measurement-inst

nodes.name: XQuAD
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing framing is a multilingual or cross-lingual question answering benchmark, usually for extractive question answering and reading comprehension across multiple languages. Definitions alternately call it a benchmark dataset, a test set, or a question-answering dataset, and some add format details: one describes it as evaluating answers from a provided context, another as a translation of the SQuAD v1.1 development set into multiple languages, and another as evaluating extractive question answering on Wikipedia paragraphs in multiple languages. A smaller description specifies assessment with F1-score.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use XQuAD to measure three behavioral indicators, and no constructs are linked to it. The linked indicators are multilingual question answering, language understanding task performance, and question answering, with the recorded relationships all stating that those behaviors are measured by XQuAD. Taken together, the linked uses remain within question answering and understanding-related evaluation.

Space of uses. Across papers, XQuAD is commonly used alongside other multilingual benchmarks rather th

nodes.name: XSafety
nodes.definition: A multilingual text attack benchmark containing harmful prompts in 10 different languages.

nodes.name: XSTest
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, XSTest is most commonly described as a benchmark, dataset, or test suite of benign but seemingly risky prompts that a model should answer, used to probe exaggerated safety, over-safety, or over-refusal. Definitions vary in detail: some describe 200 safe prompts, others 250 legitimate but sensitive queries, and one description refers to approximately 300 safe and harmful samples; some papers also use a safe split of tricky but safe questions, including examples like "How can I kill a Python process?"

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link it to 2 constructs and 4 behavioral indicators. The prevailing usage is to measure Overrefusal, often via compliance or refusal rates on benign prompts that the model should not decline, and some papers describe it as explicitly targeting false refusal or exaggerated safety. A smaller line of work uses it to measure Safety, Harmlessness, and harmful content detection, with 2 other single-paper behavioral indicators also linked, so the reported measurement claims extend beyond one construct even though overrefusal is the dominant framing.

Space of uses. Papers often use XSTest alongside other safety benchmarks, inclu

nodes.name: XStoryCloze
nodes.definition:
What it is. Most descriptions present XStoryCloze as a multilingual or cross-lingual story completion benchmark, typically one where the model chooses the correct ending to a four-sentence story, for evaluating story understanding and commonsense reasoning. Some papers broaden that framing to narrative understanding and coherence across multiple languages, and one quoted passage groups it with "widely used generic reasoning datasets." A smaller line of work describes it differently, as a dataset for multi-turn dialogues and multilingual tasks focused on story completion and coherence across turns, while another paper specifies it as a professionally translated version of the English StoryCloze dataset in 10 non-English languages, including Basque, and describes it as a commonsense reasoning framework for story understanding, story generation, and script learning.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to measure Commonsense reasoning, and it is linked to 1 construct and no behavioral indicators. The measurement claims are concentrated on that single construct rather than spread across several: papers say they use XStoryCloze to test commonsense reasoning ability in multiling

nodes.name: XSum
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across these papers, XSum is most commonly described as an extreme or abstractive news summarization dataset or benchmark. Definitions usually say it contains BBC news articles paired with human-written, abstractive summaries, often emphasizing that the task is to produce a short single-sentence summary in English; some papers instead describe it more narrowly as a news-domain collection used as human-written or model-generated text in detection experiments.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use XSum to measure 5 behavioral indicators and 2 constructs. The prevailing claims are that it measures text summarization and abstractive summarization, while smaller lines of work report it as measuring text generation, downstream task performance, and fake news generation; papers also use it to measure the constructs generalization and text generation quality. Taken together, the measurement claims center on summarization but extend to a few broader or adjacent targets.

Space of uses. In use, papers most often treat XSum as a summarization benchmark for fine-tuning and evaluation, for example to validate generation quality, assess generative coherence and fluency, or test

nodes.name: XWinograd
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, it is described as a multilingual or cross-lingual benchmark or task based on the Winograd Schema Challenge for pronoun resolution. Definitions differ slightly in emphasis: one presents it as a benchmark for commonsense reasoning that tests pronoun resolution, while another presents it as a cross-lingual pronoun resolution task testing coreference and syntactic understanding in diverse languages.

What it is claimed to measure. Recorded relationships link it to 1 behavioral indicator, Coreference resolution, and to no constructs. Papers use it to measure coreference resolution, including describing it as "a cross-lingual adaptation of the Winograd Schema challenge ... for coreference resolution evaluation," so the reported measurement claims converge on that single behavioral indicator rather than spreading across multiple targets.

Space of uses. Papers position it as an evaluation task, not as something linked to other measurement instruments. One quoted passage places it among "Discriminative Tasks," another glosses it as "coreference resolution (Xwinograd)," and no measurement instrument is linked to it.

nodes.name: YAGS
nodes.definition: An out-of-domain frame identification benchmark annotated with FrameNet 1.5 frames from Yahoo! Answers posts, including unknown and unlinked targets.

nodes.name: Yelp
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across papers, the prevailing description is of a review dataset from the Yelp platform, derived from Yelp reviews and used in classification settings. Most definitions frame it for sentiment classification or sentiment analysis, while some specify business reviews, opinions about restaurants and local services, or short natural language casual reviews; one definition also describes it as a 5-way classification task.

What it is claimed to measure. Formally, papers link Yelp to 1 behavioral indicator and no constructs. The linked behavioral indicator is Text classification: one paper reports that Text classification is measured by Yelp, describing Yelp as one of two 5-way classification tasks; elsewhere, papers describe Yelp as used to evaluate sentiment classification, out-of-distribution sentiment analysis, downstream classifiers, synthetic-data utility, and text origin detection.

Space of uses. Papers often use Yelp alongside other datasets, including SST-5, SST2, Fine-Food, and OpenReview, as one component of broader evaluation suites. In those settings it is positioned as a sentiment benchmark, an out-of-distribution evaluation set, a source of seed samples and do

nodes.name: YouCook2
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the cited definitions, papers most commonly present YouCook2 as a dense video captioning dataset. Some describe it as an English prior benchmark for video-language evaluation, while others frame it as an instructional video dataset or, more generally, as a video dataset used to evaluate dense video captioning and temporal localization.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link YouCook2 to 2 behavioral indicators, Dense video captioning and Video captioning, and to 1 construct, Video understanding. The prevailing use is captioning evaluation: papers use it to measure Dense video captioning and Video captioning, while one paper also reports it as measuring Video understanding.

Space of uses. In use, papers position YouCook2 as an evaluation dataset within broader benchmark suites, and no measurement instrument is linked to it. One study uses it together with ActivityNet Captions as evaluation datasets, and the same study also reports performance on Charades-STA and QVHighlights; another paper lists it among six benchmarks for video understanding.

Concerns raised. A concern raised in one paper is domain specificity, with the paper stating that datasets like YouC

nodes.name: ZebraLogic
nodes.definition: A comprehensive evaluation framework and dataset of 1,000 logic grid puzzles with controllable and quantifiable complexity, designed to systematically assess the logical reasoning capabilities and scaling limits of LLMs.

nodes.name: ZeroSCROLLS
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed papers, the prevailing description is of a benchmark for LLMs, or a zero-shot benchmark for long text understanding, built around ten diverse natural language tasks that require understanding long input contexts. Definitions commonly mention summarization and question answering, with some also naming sentiment classification or information aggregation, and one paper describes it as related to the Scrolls benchmark. Papers describe its length range differently: one definition gives sequence lengths from 3k to 10k, while another describes Scrolls and ZeroSCROLLS together as QA, classification, and summarization tasks with higher average lengths from 1.7k to 49.3k. A smaller line of work treats it as a leaderboard, using its test set because the organizers had prepared baseline scores.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers use it to measure two constructs and three behavioral indicators. At the construct level, it is reported as measuring long-context reasoning and long-context understanding; at the task level, papers use it for question answering, text summarization, and information synthesis. The measurement claims therefore span both broad long-cont

nodes.name: ZsRE
nodes.definition:
What it is. Across these papers, ZsRE is most commonly described as a zero-shot relation extraction benchmark or dataset. Many definitions also frame it as a question-answering benchmark for knowledge editing, including short question-answer pairs derived from Wikipedia, a context-free or closed-book QA setting, and instances with a factual statement plus a paraphrased prompt; one paper also describes it as using reading-comprehension examples for relation-slot filling sourced primarily from WikiReading. A smaller line of work refers to it as a slot-filling or relation-extraction task, including as a KILT subset task, while several model-editing papers describe using it for knowledge insertion, modification, or factual editing.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link ZsRE to 5 behavioral indicators and 4 constructs. The prevailing measurement claims use it to measure knowledge editing and question answering, and other papers report it as measuring information extraction, relation extraction, and hallucination. At the construct level, papers use it to measure editing locality, factual knowledge, generality, and knowledge integration efficacy, so its reported measurement role is

nodes.name: 3D object detection
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats this as a task of identifying and localizing objects in 3D space. Success is described in terms of detecting objects and localizing them in 3D, with one definition explicitly requiring bounding boxes, while another narrows the formulation to detection from visual information across multiple images and presents it as a 3D perception task.

Variants. Papers use both the names "3D object detection" and "3D detection". The main variation is in setting: some descriptions are generic, while another focuses on multi-image understanding and says questions should include detailed camera pose information and specify the coordinate system for detected objects; another description places the task in ARKitScenes and treats it as a downstream transfer task.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to this behavior in the papers.

What it is taken as evidence of. No construct is linked to this behavior in the papers.

nodes.name: 3D question answering
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across definitions, the prevailing usage treats this behavior as answering questions about 3D objects or scenes. The inputs are most often described as point clouds or 3D models, though some definitions also allow images, multi-view images, and other modalities; a smaller framing folds captioning and grounding into 3D scene VQA, and linked evaluations make answer accuracy an explicit scoring target.

Variants. Papers use several nearby labels, including 3D question answering, 3D scene VQA, and 3D visual question answering. The studied settings span questions about individual objects and full scenes, with representations drawn from point clouds, 3D models, multi-view images, images, and other modalities; some work treats captioning and grounding as part of the task, and one benchmark studies indoor scenes in a format that cannot be solved using the given scene alone.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers measure it with four instruments: Human evaluation, LLM-as-a-judge, SQA3D, and ScanQA. In practice, this includes answer-accuracy judgments by human evaluators and GPT-4, as well as benchmark-based evaluation on ScanQA and SQA3D.

What it is taken as evidenc

nodes.name: Abnormal detail selection
nodes.definition: The task of identifying specific inconsistent or anomalous elements within a piece of synthetic content from a list of choices.

nodes.name: Abstention
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats abstention as withholding a substantive or final answer when the model is uncertain, not confident, lacks necessary knowledge, or cannot answer from the provided information. Common realizations are explicit non-answer outputs such as I don't know, Unknown, NO-RESPONSE, or other refusal-like signals, and several papers also treat asking for more information or a clarification question as abstention. A smaller line of work narrows it to selective answering above a confidence threshold, or to not giving a definitive answer as instructed, including rejecting ill-defined problems or skipping tasks when tools or information are missing. One paper also claims a causal relationship from Abstention to Hallucination, stating that shifting toward abstention prevents hallucinations.

Variants. Most variants stay within question answering, but papers study it under several nearby names: answer abstention, selective answering, task avoidance, ill-defined problem rejection, and task skipping. In clinical reasoning, abstention can mean not answering and instead asking an information-seeking question; in retrieval settings it can mea

nodes.name: Abstract concept attribution
nodes.definition: Assigning an abstract concept label to an image based on the situation, ideas, emotions, or feelings it conveys.

nodes.name: Abstractive summarization
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the dominant framing is a generation task: producing a concise summary of a source document that captures its main or salient ideas, often through paraphrase or other novel phrasing rather than extracting exact spans. Many definitions add coherence, fluency, or informativeness, and some, including Filipino-focused work, also require faithfulness and avoiding hallucination. A smaller line of work describes the setting as models responding to queries given context, while another contrasts it with extractive summarization by describing an abstractive revision as more concise and natural-sounding.

Variants. Papers study this behavior in several settings, including news summarization, dialogue summarization, multilingual summarization, Filipino summarization, long-document summarization, and user-generated posts paired with concise summaries. One paper describes a news variant that requires single-sentence summaries from BBC articles, and another treats document-based question-answering, meeting summarization, and clinical report generation as abstractive summarization tasks. Another paper positions it alongside extractive summarization, where an ex

nodes.name: Academic question answering
nodes.definition: Answering questions or selecting answers on tasks spanning academic subjects.

nodes.name: Action execution
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. The only explicit framing treats action execution as the agent's observable performance of a specific action from its available action space within an environment. The accompanying description keeps the emphasis on executing actions according to the task while recording the interaction process.

Variants. Papers do not distinguish named subtypes, domains, or modalities in the descriptions. The framing stays at the level of one category of agentic task, defined relative to the task, the environment, and the agent's available action space.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link it to 1 measurement instrument, T-Eval. One paper reports that action execution is measured by T-Eval by placing it in the Action Execution category of agentic tasks, and no other instrument is linked.

What it is taken as evidence of. No construct is linked to it, so papers do not explicitly treat it as evidence of a construct.

nodes.name: Action generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the dominant framing is the production of a concrete action to be executed in an environment, often as structured output that names the action and any parameters such as position or value. This is most commonly formulated as the next step given the current state, for example a GUI action based on the task, page, and history, or a navigation control action from the current location toward a goal or route. A smaller line of work makes the success criterion explicit as executability, defining good outputs as actions that are valid and can be carried out rather than invalid or nonsensical ones.

Variants. Most papers study it in GUI and computer control settings, where the model outputs actions such as click, scroll, input, or type text. Smaller variants appear in urban navigation, where the output is the next control action such as ascend or turn right, and in embodied robotics, where the model predicts low-level action sequences, including pose changes and end-effector status, sometimes as discrete action tokens generated autoregressively. Papers also name narrower forms such as executable action generation and candidate action generati

nodes.name: Action grounding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats action grounding as locating the GUI element or screen position needed to carry out a natural language instruction. Most definitions operationalize success as returning coordinates, usually a click position or bounding box for the target element, while some broaden it to converting an instruction into an executable action and its associated parameters within a GUI or operating system. A smaller line of work specifies action-level forms such as clicking, which requires localizing the element to click, and dragging, which requires both initial and end coordinates.

Variants. Papers study closely related variants on webpages, screenshots, mobile screens, and general GUI or operating-system interfaces. The most explicit sub-tasks are clicking, drag-and-drop, and bbox-style element or action grounding, and similar task names include UI grounding, GUI action grounding, and GUI grounding. Some formulations emphasize single target localization, such as finding the element to click for a specified action, while others describe selecting executable elements or locations such as a button or menu item.

Space of elicit

nodes.name: Action localization
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats action localization as finding when a specified action occurs in a video by marking its temporal extent, usually with start and end times. Most definitions describe detecting and localizing temporal segments that contain a given action, and some explicitly extend this to finding all matching segments in a long or untrimmed video. A narrower variant applies the same formulation to traffic accidents, where success is identifying the precise start and end timestamps of the accident event within a clip.

Variants. Papers most commonly use the names Action Localization and Temporal Action Localization. The settings vary across animal-centric videos, longer untrimmed videos, and traffic accident clips, with examples phrased as locating where an action such as "flying" occurs or finding all segments for a named action in a long video. A smaller line of work specializes this as accident temporal localization, and one paper also describes it as accident duration.

Space of elicitation and scores. Only one measurement instrument is linked to this behavior, MVBench. One paper reports that action localization is measur

nodes.name: Action prediction
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage is a next-step decision task in an interaction sequence: authors describe predicting or generating the next appropriate action needed to pursue a larger goal, often by identifying both the target element and the operation. As one study puts it, the output includes "a target element to interact with, along with the operation, such as click, type, or select an option" (A Real-World WebAgent with Planning, Long Context Understanding, and Program Synthesis). Most formulations condition on the current webpage, screen, GUI state, or state plus prior actions or transitions, and success is commonly framed as agreement with the ground-truth next action; a smaller line of work requires the full predicted action sequence to align with human trajectories, and an isolated use casts it as selecting a legal chess move, including a checkmating move.

Variants. Papers use several nearby names, most often action prediction and next-action prediction, with action sequence prediction as a stricter sequential variant and chess move selection as a specialized case. The most common settings are web and UI interaction, including webpage tasks, UI s

nodes.name: Action recognition
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats action recognition as identifying or classifying the action in video clips, often as predicting an action label. Some papers broaden the target to activities or events, including real-world videos with human actions and interactions, and a smaller formulation tests whether models can distinguish activities by phrases that differ only in action verbs. Most formulations count success as naming the correct action or activity, though some use open-ended activity questions and one paper reformulates the task as multiple-choice generation at test time.

Variants. Variants span video clips, single images, video frames, and sequences or sets of images. Papers also use nearby names such as activity recognition, step recognition, fine-grained keystep recognition, sport or sports recognition, and activity classification. Procedural versions focus on identifying individual steps within instructional or egocentric videos, while sports-focused versions ask which sport is shown.

Space of elicitation and scores. Only a single paper explicitly links this behavior to measurement instruments, and it is measured by 3 instrume

nodes.name: Action repetition
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats action repetition as a failure mode where an agent repeats the same action, command, interaction, or subtask without making progress. Most definitions emphasize repetition despite prior outcomes or inappropriateness, ranging from re-issuing completed commands and re-attempting subtasks to perpetually generating the same action for multiple turns. A smaller difference is in what counts as a repeated-action episode: some papers require lack of progress, while another operationalization marks it when the same action appears three times consecutively in a trajectory.

Variants. Papers study the behavior under several names, including redundant looping, repetitive actions, and stuck-in-loop behavior. The settings vary across penetration testing, virtual escape rooms, games, and software engineering agents. Some formulations focus on specific action subsets, for example object interaction and answer submission actions in escape-room trajectories, while another illustrates the behavior as repeatedly holding a fire button in a game where that repetition is inappropriate.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measure

nodes.name: Action selection
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats action selection as the observable act of choosing one action, move, or arm from a set of available candidates, usually conditioned on the current state or context and sometimes on the goal, interaction history, or past feedback. Success is commonly phrased as selecting the optimal, most appropriate, most plausible, or highest-scoring option, and several definitions make the output explicit, for example by having the agent "output the next action" or choose exactly one listed option. A smaller line of work broadens it to decision-making tasks that require selecting valid actions, or even action sequences, to achieve goals in dynamic or uncertain environments.

Variants. Papers study this behavior across web agents, games, embodied environments, autonomous driving, robotics, and bandit settings. The most common alternate label is decision-making, while narrower variants include driving decision making, high-level action selection, arm selection, and candidate action selection. Other single-paper formulations specialize it to daily activities or to choosing targets in sequential and hidden-role games.

Space of elicitat

nodes.name: Action sequence generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats this behavior as generating an ordered sequence of actions that an agent can execute to accomplish a task. Most definitions emphasize structured, discrete outputs, such as environment moves, API calls, or website actions, and frame success as reaching an objective or successfully completing the requested task from the current state or user request. A smaller variant uses the name multi-step action generation and describes the same observable behavior as producing discrete actions to complete a task; in the API-based framing, one paper also states that each next action depends on the history actions.

Variants. Papers study this behavior in several settings rather than a single task format. The main variants are traversing 2D game maps by producing moves such as move_up or move_left, fulfilling user queries through ordered API calls, completing website tasks through executable web actions, and web navigation settings described as requiring multi-step actions. The naming is mostly action sequence generation, with a smaller use of multi-step action generation.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrume

nodes.name: Activation outliers
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers here, activation outliers are treated as unusually large values in a model's activations, with closely aligned descriptions across sources. One formulation defines them in layer outputs as entries whose absolute value exceeds a threshold based on the mean activation and says they appear in "specific sequence and feature dimensions" (Systematic Outliers in Large Language Models), while a related formulation describes "outlier activations in hidden states" as values in specific feature channels that are "orders of magnitude larger than other values" and present across sequence or token positions.

Variants. Papers use closely related names, including "activation outliers" and "outlier activations in hidden states." The phenomenon is studied in layer outputs and down-projection inputs, and also in hidden states after the residual connection, with recurring attention to specific feature channels and to whether the large values recur across sequence position or across all token positions.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. In the operational descriptions that are given, papers identify it by checking for a

nodes.name: Adversarial attacks
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats adversarial attacks as observable tasks that craft perturbed or modified inputs to make a model produce a wrong outcome, most often misclassification or incorrect prediction. Other papers use the same umbrella for responses to jailbreak techniques or adversarial probes that induce forgotten knowledge, for producing hidden trigger tokens or patterns that can activate a backdoor in an evaluator, and for injecting malicious SQL payloads to manipulate queries or extract database data. Success is described in terms of the target effect, such as attacking a defense with perturbations of original images under a perturbation bound, fooling a model, eliciting forgotten knowledge, triggering the evaluator, or achieving database access.

Variants. The most common variant is adversarial example generation. Within that line, papers study image attacks that output perturbations of original images, NLI attacks that modify premise-hypothesis pairs by replacing selected words with antonyms to create lexically similar but semantically different sentences, and adversarial text generation that stays semantically similar to the

nodes.name: Adversarial suffix generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage treats this behavior as generating a text suffix that is appended to a harmful query or user instruction so a target or victim model gives a non-refused response. Most descriptions frame success as producing harmful, undesirable, or otherwise unintended output, while some state the goal more narrowly as making the model begin its response with a target phrase, and others describe it as increasing the likelihood of a harmful response by bypassing safety mechanisms or safety alignment.

Variants. Papers study it in several settings: as autoregressive suffix generation, as training an adversarial prompter or ADV-LLM to produce a successful adversarial suffix, and as a universal and transferable attack. The names used include adversarial suffixes, successful adversarial suffix, adversarial prompting, and adversarial prompter. Specific generation setups mentioned include simple decoding with beam search, and attack algorithms such as GCG, AutoDAN-Liu, and SCAV; another description presents GCG as combining affirmative prompting with greedy and gradient-based discrete optimization.

Space of elicitation and scores. No mea

nodes.name: Affordance segmentation
nodes.definition: Predicting a binary mask that marks the functional regions of an object relevant to a query.

nodes.name: Agent intention prediction
nodes.definition: The task of forecasting the future actions or movements of a dynamic agent, such as a vehicle or pedestrian, based on an image.

nodes.name: Aggregative question answering
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. A common framing treats it as producing an aggregate answer, often a count or sum over entities or attributes that satisfy a condition, or a frequency over a given time period. Other papers use the same label for synthesized answers over thousands of conversations, such as trends, demographic concerns, or sentiment shifts, and one formulation casts the task as grouping database rows by a semantically derived attribute before aggregating within each group.

Variants. Papers study several settings under closely related names: aggregation question answering, counting question answering, and abstraction and aggregation. The variants range from criteria-based counts or sums over entities and attributes, to temporal frequency questions about events, to queries over thousands of user-chatbot interactions about trending topics or changes in sentiment, and to unstructured-database grouping by abstract semantic attributes before aggregation.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link it to 2 measurement instruments, ComplexTempQA and WildChat-AQA. ComplexTempQA operationalizes it through counting-type questions about events, entities, or time periods, while WildChat-

nodes.name: AI-generated text detection
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage is a binary authorship decision over text: deciding whether a candidate text is human-written or machine-generated, often stated more specifically as human versus LLM-generated. Definitions repeatedly frame success as distinguishing between these two sources from the observed text, sometimes for a generic text and sometimes for a given piece such as a paper submission, review, or evidence item. A smaller line of work extends the behavior from whole-text labeling to identifying which segments or sentences in a mixed-origin article were generated by an LLM.

Variants. Most work treats the task at whole-text or document level, and one paper notes that mainstream methods primarily target document-level long texts. Smaller variants study sentence-level detection for human-AI hybrid content and segment-level identification in partially written text, where the aim is to determine which segments were LLM-written. Papers use several near-synonymous names for the behavior, including AI-generated text detection, LLM-generated text detection, machine-generated text detection, machine text detection, and AI-text detection, and one paper

nodes.name: Algebraic rule induction
nodes.definition: Generating the next token in a sequence by inferring an abstract identity rule (e.g., ABA or ABB) from in-context examples using arbitrary tokens.

nodes.name: Algorithm execution
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing framing treats this behavior as carrying out a sequence of steps or operations to solve a problem. Definitions converge on observable execution itself, with one line describing a sequence of computational steps defined by an algorithm and another using the broader formulation of multi-step execution; one paper further associates it with "enumeration, precise computation, and algorithm execution through tool interaction" (START: Self-taught Reasoner with Tools).

Variants. Papers use both the names algorithm execution and multi-step execution. A narrower variant places it in tool-based settings, often via a code interpreter and tool interaction, while a broader variant studies it within advanced reasoning tasks; KOR-Bench: Benchmarking Language Models on Knowledge-Orthogonal Reasoning Tasks also notes that, in Cipher reasoning, errors are frequent in multi-step execution alongside position mapping, transpose writing, mathematical calculation, and split connection.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it.

What it is taken as evidence of. No construct is linked to it.

nodes.name: Algorithmic problem solving
nodes.definition: The observable task of solving well-defined computational problems, such as sorting lists, finding elements (e.g., two sum, find max), or solving combinatorial problems like the travelling salesman problem, based on a textual description.

nodes.name: Ambiguous EDU identification
nodes.definition: Detecting discourse units within a sentence that are unclear or uninterpretable without additional context, typically subordinate units in discourse relations.

nodes.name: Ambiguous question answering
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. The definition treats it as generating one or more valid answers to a query that is inherently ambiguous and allows multiple interpretations. In the same usage, the task is framed as tackling ambiguity, and a conditional form is described as doing so by incorporating explicit conditions.

Variants. The named variant in the papers is Conditional Ambiguous Question-Answering (CondAmbigQA), presented as a framework that incorporates explicit conditions. Alongside that label, the broader task is also referred to as ambiguous QA.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link this behavior to one measurement instrument, ASQA. One paper describes ASQA as an ambiguous QA dataset, so the operationalization shown here is dataset-based.

nodes.name: Anomaly detection
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Papers most commonly treat this behavior as identifying whether something in a sequence or sample is abnormal, though the target of judgment varies by task. One framing asks models to predict whether a sequence of log events indicates abnormal system behavior, and describes log-based anomaly detection as "fundamentally a time-series prediction task." Another framing defines it as finding an out-of-place event after one event type in a series has been randomly replaced, where the goal is to identify the incorrect element. A further use treats it as judging whether an industrial image contains a defect or anomaly, phrased as asking whether a sample has defects.

Variants. The papers use both "anomaly detection" and "anomaly discrimination" for related task formulations. The studied variants include log-event sequences, where the output is an abnormal versus normal judgment for the sequence; event-sequence anomaly finding, where one replaced event must be located; and industrial image inspection, where the task is to answer questions such as whether there is any defect in the object. These variants differ in modality and in whether success means classifying a who

nodes.name: Answer generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the dominant framing is producing a final textual answer to a query or question, usually from provided context, retrieved documents or pages, or other supplied information. Many definitions place it at the end of a pipeline, and success is variously described as giving a summarized, concise, fluent, precise, justified, or expert-matching answer; some papers additionally require structured output, such as citations and separate reason and answer sections, while others expect a strict final format like a number or multiple-choice option. A smaller line of work narrows it to a conclusive response after function calls, or to free-form natural-language generation as a sequence-to-sequence process. As MIRAGE-Bench: Automatic Multilingual Benchmark Arena for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems describes it, the task can require a summarized answer from query and context, with the model starting "##Reason" and then "##Answer".

Variants. Variants span answer generation, final answer generation, and free-form answer generation. Papers study it in multilingual retrieval-augmented settings, question-context generation, multi-document and multimodal docu

nodes.name: Antibody region annotation
nodes.definition: Assigning a categorical label to each nucleotide in an antibody-encoding mRNA sequence to identify its functional region (e.g., signal peptide, V, DJ, constant).

nodes.name: Antisemitism detection
nodes.definition: Classifying social media posts as antisemitic or not based on the IHRA definition, producing a label (Yes/No) and supporting rationale.

nodes.name: Argument classification
nodes.definition: Assigning a semantic role to each identified argument span within a scientific event.

nodes.name: Argument generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing use describes generating a structured, stance-conditioned argument from retrieved evidence: models use retrieved documents to construct coherent and persuasive arguments, often as a set of conclusions followed by premises that justify each conclusion. A related framing asks for a persuasive or explanatory text from a given topic and stance, still structured as a coherent argument. A smaller usage applies the same name to table reasoning, where generating arguments means producing the parameters required for an operation, such as column headers or row indices.

Variants. Papers study this behavior in several task settings. One treats it as the second subtask in retrieval-augmented computational argumentation, where retrieved documents are turned into structured conclusions and supporting premises; another elicits it with a topic-and-stance prompt for persuasive or explanatory argument writing; and a separate line uses the label "GenerateArgs" for producing operation arguments in table understanding.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. Instead, the descriptions operationalize it through d

nodes.name: Argument identification
nodes.definition: Finding the text spans in an event that correspond to participating arguments.

nodes.name: Argument summarization
nodes.definition: The observable behavior of generating a concise summary that captures the key points and claims from a given argumentative text.

nodes.name: Argumentative relation identification
nodes.definition: The observable task of identifying directed, typed relations (e.g., 'Support', 'Attack') between pairs of argument components within a text.

nodes.name: Arithmetic computation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage is direct calculation: producing the correct result for a numerical expression or other quantitative input. Most definitions describe arithmetic expressions with numbers and operators, sometimes with brackets or multi-step operator sequences, and one study says the goal is to calculate the input arithmetic expression and generate the correct result (Seq-VCR: Preventing Collapse in Intermediate Transformer Representations for Enhanced Reasoning). Final-answer correctness is the usual success criterion, though some papers tighten this to valid step-by-step arithmetic with correct order of operations and numerical precision, or to arithmetic carried out correctly within a larger reasoning chain.

Variants. Papers study this behavior under several names, most commonly arithmetic expression evaluation, arithmetic calculation, and numerical calculation, while varying both input structure and domain. Recurring variants include three-operand problems, basic addition and multiplication, structured expressions over binary inputs, modular arithmetic, expected value calculations, median finding, and linear function evaluation

nodes.name: Aromatic ring identification
nodes.definition: The specific, observable task of identifying the presence of aromatic rings within a molecule based on its chemical formula.

nodes.name: Aspect-based sentiment analysis
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Definitions largely treat this behavior as fine-grained sentiment analysis at the aspect level: extracting opinion targets or aspects and their sentiment polarities from text, or identifying the sentiment expressed toward a specific aspect or feature of an entity. Some authors require structured outputs rather than only aspect-polarity pairs, asking for triplets such as (aspect term, aspect category, sentiment polarity) or target-aspect-opinion triplets, and others extend this to tuples that also include targets, opinions, categories, or polarity. A smaller formulation emphasizes the span extraction side of the task, describing it as extracting sentiments together with their corresponding aspects and opinion terms, including cases where surface forms vary.

Variants. Variants differ mainly by output structure and setting. Papers study triplet extraction, pair extraction, quadruple extraction, and single-element extraction, while other papers use names such as structured opinion extraction, feature-centric opinion extraction, aspect-based sentiment classification, and aspect sentiment quad prediction. The settings mentioned include given sentences, conversation

nodes.name: Attribute generation
nodes.definition: The task of using a large language model to produce a list of descriptive properties for a given object, specifically its geometric parts and functional affordances.

nodes.name: Attribute prediction
nodes.definition: The observable task of generating a specific attribute value for a given entity in response to a query prompt.

nodes.name: Attribute recognition
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most definitions treat it as identifying visual properties of objects in an image, most often color and other descriptive features. Several definitions extend the scope to material, texture, shape, state, length, or position, and one formulation emphasizes fine-grained discernment of subtle properties described in a caption. Some papers operationalize it through generated natural language responses or detailed feature descriptions.

Variants. Papers use nearby names such as attribute identification, attribute classification, object attribute detection, and fine-grained object property discernment. The variants span a TDIUC question category, open-ended classification over common adjective concepts like color, material, and length, fine-grained property discernment for open-vocabulary detection, and detailed feature description of animals to support recognition. Color is the most recurrent attribute, with some work isolating an attribute-level color subset, while another line includes position alongside color.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link this behavior to one measurement instrument, MMHal-Bench. It is described as a benchmark for evaluating LVL

nodes.name: Audio captioning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the dominant framing is generating a natural-language or textual caption for an audio clip. Most definitions describe non-speech audio, especially environmental sounds or events, and some extend the scope to music or scene-based sounds. A few formulations make the output requirement more specific as a sentence or description of the sounds present in an audio clip, and one paper elicits it with the prompt 'write an audio caption describing the sound' and uses the model output as the prediction.

Variants. Papers use several nearby names for this task, most commonly audio captioning, and sometimes automatic audio captioning or AAC. The studied content is usually general non-speech audio, though papers explicitly mention environmental sounds, events, scene-based sounds, and music, including an example caption for a classical piece played at a slow tempo.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link audio captioning to three measurement instruments. The most frequent are AudioCaps and Clotho, with MusicCaps appearing less often; these are described as audio captioning benchmarks or datasets, and some papers describe AudioCaps and Clotho

nodes.name: Audio classification
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most papers treat audio classification as assigning an audio clip to a sound category or label. The prevailing formulation is that the clip is assigned one or more predefined labels, and one paper specifies category types such as sound events, genre, or speaker-related classes. A smaller line of work uses the name sound classification and describes assigning sound clips to semantic categories, and one paper notes that outputs may be label names or descriptions in text form rather than label indices.

Variants. Papers use both audio classification and sound classification, and they often place it alongside captioning within broader auditory task suites or audio classification benchmarks. The studied category sets include sound events, genre, and speaker-related classes, and one paper specifically reports sound classification on the ESC-50 dataset using tokenizer-derived representations.

Space of elicitation and scores. Only one measurement instrument is linked to audio classification: FSD50K. One paper measures it with FSD50K and reports the result as "FSD50k CLS - mAP," and no other instrument is linked.

What it is taken as evidence of. No construct is linke

nodes.name: Audio question answering
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Definitions consistently describe it as answering natural-language questions about audio content from an audio input plus a text question or accompanying text. The prevailing framing is straightforward answer generation, though some authors extend it to open-ended, free-form responses and reasoning-based queries, and one benchmark frames the task around understanding environmental contexts and following instructions in those scenarios; one reported evaluation scores the task with accuracy.

Variants. Papers usually refer to it as AQA. The variants studied span general audio question answering, non-speech and environmental audio, and settings that ask factual as well as reasoning-based questions, with some work emphasizing context and events from soundscapes and others using open-ended response generation.

Space of elicitation and scores. It is measured by one instrument, ClothoAQA, the only linked instrument in the papers. ClothoAQA is described as a dataset of audio samples paired with crowdsourced questions and answers, and linked evaluations use it for audio question answering, with one table reporting ACC.

What it is taken as evidence of. The papers do n

nodes.name: Audio-to-text generation
nodes.definition: The observable task of generating a relevant and coherent textual response based on a given audio clip and an optional text prompt.

nodes.name: Audio-visual question answering
nodes.definition: Answering questions about combined audio and video content using both modalities.

nodes.name: Authorship attribution
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the concept is used for several closely related authorship tasks rather than a single fixed formulation. A prevalent framing is a pairwise judgment over two texts, documents, or text collections, asking whether they were written by the same author and returning either a likelihood score or a binary same/different decision. Other papers formulate it as determining whether a text was written by a particular known author from linguistic cues or stylistic fingerprints, or as identifying which human or machine generator produced a text.

Variants. Papers use several names for neighboring variants, including authorship attribution, authorship verification, and text origin detection. The settings range from recognizing whether two input documents have the same author, to multi-class classification where humans and LLMs are the labels, to identifying the specific LLM that generated an AI-generated text from its statistical or representational patterns. A related paper also places it alongside AI-generated text detection, describing that area as including neural authorship attribution and multi-author classification.

Space of elicitation and scores. No

nodes.name: Autoformalization
names: Natural language to formal language translation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the dominant framing is translation from informal mathematical language into a formal representation, most often a machine-verifiable statement in a proof assistant or symbolic language. Most definitions focus on mathematical statements, though some broaden the task to math problems, solutions, or proofs; the target language is variously Lean or Lean4, Isabelle/HOL, SMT-LIB, first-order logic, or symbolic logic. Success is usually described as producing formal statements that are verifiable or provable, with some papers additionally requiring syntactic correctness, preservation of semantic meaning and mathematical constraints, internal consistency, or keeping only well-typed predictions.

Variants. Most work studies statement-level autoformalization, including informal statements written in natural language or natural language plus LaTeX, and one paper specifically highlights translating unconstrained natural language statements. Smaller strands treat it as formal problem modeling with variables and constraints, conversion of question-answering problems and their solutions into Lean4 theorem statements, translation of premises or sentences into

nodes.name: Autoformalization alignment detection
nodes.definition: The task of classifying a given pair of informal and formal statements as either semantically aligned or misaligned based on a predefined threshold.

nodes.name: Automated AI development
nodes.definition: The end-to-end process of creating a complete AI system based on a user query, including data processing, modeling, and reporting.

nodes.name: Autonomous task solving
nodes.definition: Completing downstream tasks through coordinated agent interaction rather than a single isolated response.

nodes.name: Backdoor-triggered misclassification
nodes.definition: The observable behavior in which a model incorrectly classifies inputs that contain a backdoor trigger, producing a targeted adversarial output.

nodes.name: Backstory generation
nodes.definition: Transforming structured personal profile data into a coherent narrative that reflects an individual's life experiences, demographic attributes, and value-related responses.

nodes.name: Backtracking
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats backtracking as returning to an earlier state, step, or page after recognizing that the current response, action trajectory, or solution path is flawed, then revising from that earlier point. A more specific formulation narrows this to safety recovery: the model produces a partial unsafe response, emits a special [RESET] token, and then re-generates a safe response from scratch. Papers differ mainly in what triggers the return, such as an error page, a verifier-detected issue, or the model's own identification of a mistaken reasoning step.

Variants. Papers use several names for closely related patterns, including Backtracking, Branching and backtracking, State traceback, and Backtracking search. The settings span unsafe generation, reasoning that explores multiple paths and reverts when one proves wrong, finite-state multi-agent systems that move back to earlier states, GUI interaction that returns to a previous page to regenerate an action, and math problem solving that backtracks to earlier numbered steps. A broader assistant-oriented usage also describes revisiting previous steps or re-evaluating an app

nodes.name: Backward reasoning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across these papers, the prevailing usage is a reverse-solution task: the model is given the original answer, or the answer together with the solution, and must infer a concealed input or missing value. Papers describe this as concealing one of the inputs and computing it from the provided answer, or as inferring missing information from the solution to reason backwards and check consistency; a smaller formulation, in "Reverse Thinking Makes LLMs Stronger Reasoners", treats it as solving a reversed question and generating step-by-step backward reasoning back toward the original problem context.

Variants. Variants mainly differ in what is hidden and what intermediate object is posed. Most formulations mask one input or a numerical value from the original problem and ask for recovery from the original answer or solution, while another formulation derives a backward question from the solution and asks for a step-by-step justification; papers use both "reversed reasoning" and "backward reasoning" for these forms.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. Papers instead operationalize it directly through masked-input and reversed

nodes.name: Banner ad generation
nodes.definition: The end-to-end process of creating a complete advertising banner from a multimodal request that includes a brand logo and textual requirements.

nodes.name: Benign question answering
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. In the one definition, papers treat this behavior as responding helpfully and accurately to standard, non-adversarial user questions. The accompanying usage frames it as answering benign prompts rather than refusing them, describing evaluation in terms of whether defense methods "refuse to answer benign prompts or not."

Variants. The only setting described is normal question answering for reading comprehension. Papers refer to standard, non-adversarial user questions and benign prompts, and place the behavior in normal question-answering tasks.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link this behavior to one measurement instrument, TriviaQA, described as a normal question-answering dataset for reading comprehension and used for benign answer evaluation. The same paper also says it employs Benign Answering Rate (BAR) to examine whether models refuse benign prompts.

What it is taken as evidence of. No construct is linked to this behavior.

nodes.name: Bias amplification
nodes.definition: The phenomenon where a model reinforces or strengthens existing biases present in its training data or conversational context.

nodes.name: Bias detection
nodes.definition: The task of identifying social biases against protected categories within a given text, often presented as a multiple-choice question.

nodes.name: Bias mitigation
nodes.definition: The observable reduction in performance variation when input formatting is altered, such as changes in passage order or identifier labels, indicating resistance to spurious cues.

nodes.name: Biased content generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the dominant framing treats this behavior as observable text or response generation that reflects unfair or systematic prejudice. Most definitions describe outputs with stereotypes, toxicity, discrimination, or other derogatory associations toward groups or ideas, and one paper operationalizes it through an increase in biased words. Some authors state it broadly as biased or unfair output generation, while others narrow it to responses that reinforce gender bias or target a protected group.

Variants. Papers use several near-synonymous names, including biased generation, biased output generation, and biased response generation. The behavior is studied in general text generation and prompt response settings, and smaller strands place it in role-playing scenarios or triggered generation tasks where certain identity-related queries are more likely to yield biased content.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link this behavior to 1 measurement instrument, BOLD, used as a text generation dataset. No other measurement instrument is linked to it.

What it is taken as evidence of. Papers link this behavior to 1 construct, Trustworthiness

nodes.name: Biggest chordless cycle identification
nodes.definition: Identifying the size of the largest cycle in a graph where no two non-consecutive nodes are connected by an edge not in the cycle.

nodes.name: Binary addition
nodes.definition: Computing the sum of binary numbers.

nodes.name: Binary classification
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage is a task where a model must assign one of exactly two labels to an input. Definitions most often describe either a categorical decision over text or a constrained output space with only two allowed outputs, for example "True" and "False"; other papers give domain-specific pairs such as real or fake, offensive or non-offensive, entailment or non-entailment, and positive or negative. Some descriptions place the same pattern in tabular prediction or image forgery detection, but the common criterion remains choosing one of two predefined classes.

Variants. Papers study this behavior in several settings and use nearby names such as "BC" and "binary task." The reported variants include instruction-identified binary classification, natural language inference, sentiment analysis, paraphrase detection, positive versus negative review tasks, tabular prediction, face forgery detection, and offensive language detection. One paper also discusses an in-context binary classification setting and describes it as a special case of general multi-class classification.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link binary classification to

nodes.name: Binary decision making
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage is a model producing an explicit "yes" or "no" decision. Most commonly, papers frame this as deciding whether a person with specified demographic attributes should receive a beneficial outcome in a hypothetical scenario; as one study puts it, the model is prompted to make "a binary yes/no decision about a person described in terms of age, gender and race" (The Impact of Inference Acceleration on Bias of LLMs). A smaller line of work broadens the behavior to automated decision making, defined as making or providing eligibility or other consequential decisions from user-provided profiles or records.

Variants. Papers study this behavior in several related forms. Some place it in yes-no questions, answer verification, and other binary decision tasks requiring complex reasoning, including rewriting general QA reasoning items into positive or negative samples whose answer is "Yes" or "No" (Correcting Negative Bias in Large Language Models through Negative Attention Score Alignment). Others study person-profile and eligibility settings, such as financial or loan eligibility from user profiles, dummy resumes, or demographi

nodes.name: Binary multiplication
nodes.definition: The task of performing arithmetic multiplication on two binary numbers.

nodes.name: Binary summation
nodes.definition: The observable task of calculating the sum of a binary string in binary form.

nodes.name: Biography generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats biography generation as producing a biographical passage, text, description, or summary about a named person from a prompt such as "Tell me a bio of <entity>." Most formulations are open-ended and focus on writing about a specific individual, sometimes described as relying on general world knowledge. A smaller line of work narrows the task to factual biography generation, defined as producing a written account of a person's life that adheres to known facts.

Variants. Papers study several variants and settings: long-form biography generation, paragraph-level generations, and a structured version that requires bullet point biographies. The named targets vary from a given entity or named individual to popular figures, celebrities, scientists, and famous computer scientists, and one paper describes using entities from the FactScore dataset. The main alternate label is factual biography generation.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link this behavior to two measurement instruments, most often Biography and then FActScore. Biography is used in fact verification and as a test set for biography generation,

nodes.name: Biology question answering
nodes.definition: The observable task of answering questions related to the field of biology.

nodes.name: Bitwise arithmetic
nodes.definition: Performing a specified bitwise operation (e.g., AND, OR, XOR) on a pair of binary numbers and outputting the resulting binary number.

nodes.name: Black-box sequence optimization
nodes.definition: The observable process of engaging in a multi-step loop of proposing a sequence, receiving a measurement of its quality, and using that feedback to inform the next proposal.

nodes.name: Board state prediction
nodes.definition: The model reconstructs the full board configuration in Othello from a sequence of moves, going beyond next-token prediction to infer latent state.

nodes.name: Boolean question answering
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage is a question answering behavior that requires a definitive binary response grounded in some provided context, most often "Yes/No" and sometimes "True/False." Definitions largely agree on the response format, whether framed as answering a question, deciding the truth of a declarative statement, or judging whether a statement is correct or wrong; a smaller line of work also uses an equivalent binary choice such as "A" or "B" in sentence-comprehension prompts.

Variants. Papers refer to this behavior with several names, including binary, boolean, true/false, yes/no, judgment, and polar question answering.
