Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats factual recall as retrieving or generating the correct fact from a subject-relation prompt or direct question, often as completing a subject-relation-object triple or next-token continuation such as 'The Eiffel Tower is in' with the correct object. Many papers frame the fact as stored in model parameters or pretraining data and not supplied by the current context, for example recalling capitals, birth years, birthdays, GDP, or other attribute values. Success is usually the correct object, tail entity, answer token, or short answer against a gold answer, though some papers count a predicted prefix of the object as correct, and one long-form usage defines recall as the percentage of provided facts among all relevant supported facts in a response.

Variants. Papers study nearby variants under names including knowledge recall, fact retrieval, factual knowledge retrieval, long-term knowledge recall, relation prediction, knowledge retrieval, and factual probing. The most common variants remain single-hop factual questions or templated triple completion, but authors also examine paraphrased prompts for edited fact

nodes.name: Fake news generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats this behavior as generating fabricated news articles or deceptive narratives, often with LLMs, in forms that mimic legitimate journalism. Outputs are commonly described as intentionally false or deceitful, and some definitions explicitly add an intent to deceive readers or evade automated detection systems. A smaller line of work states the task more procedurally, as generating news articles from fake headlines or producing the "next version of fake news" through iterative prompt refinement.

Variants. Papers study several variants that differ in how the article is sourced or transformed. Reported settings include generation from fake news headlines, rewriting, expanding, or disguising given fake news, and modifying true news articles to introduce believable factual errors. Some work uses multi-perspective generation in three different styles, including chain-of-thought prompting, while another allows fake news stories to include visual elements and strategic content manipulation.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link this behavior to 1 measurement instrument, XSum. In the linked use, one paper says generated

nodes.name: Fault localization
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats it as locating the source of a software problem in code, whether described as the source of a bug or failure within code or a repository, or as the files, functions, or lines responsible for a reported issue. Most descriptions agree that the task is to identify the responsible code location, though they differ in scope, from general bug or failure localization to inferring which files or functions caused a reported crash from limited diagnostic information. A narrower formulation also stresses speed, describing agents that "pinpoint the source of an issue remarkably quickly."

Variants. Papers use the names fault localization, bug localization, and issue localization. The studied settings range from repository-level debugging to kernel crash reports and reported software issues, with outputs framed as relevant files, functions, or lines of code. A smaller line of usage highlights specific approaches or neighboring distinctions, including "spectrum-based fault localization" to guide context retrieval and a contrast between localizing an issue and "root cause" analysis.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measureme

nodes.name: Feature activation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the cited papers, the prevailing usage treats feature activation, also called feature firing, as the observable case where an internal feature becomes active on particular input tokens or contexts. Papers describe it as identifying which tokens activate a feature and in which contexts, as well as observing non-zero activation, and one recurring formulation is whether a feature fires at all on a given context.

Variants. The main variation is in granularity. Some descriptions focus on very simple features that activate exclusively on individual tokens, while others frame activation more generally over tokens and broader contexts, including analyses that group activating datapoints by activation range and count the tokens that appear there.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. In practice, papers operationalize it by saving the activation of each sparse autoencoder feature over sampled tokens, identifying which tokens activate a feature and in which contexts, counting tokens among datapoints that activate the feature across activation ranges, and testing whether a description lets a model predict on which tokens a f

nodes.name: Feedback generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats feedback generation as producing natural-language rationales that explain an evaluation or diagnose a failure. Most commonly, it is described as explaining why a response received a particular score, sometimes explicitly as analogous to chain-of-thought in evaluation; smaller lines of work use the same label for short explanations of why code failed, richer reflections on how a model can be improved, qualitative essay comments, or personalized formative feedback on quizzes and exercises. What counts as success is usually that the text explains why a score was assigned or what went wrong, and in some papers that it also offers specific suggestions, pinpoints strengths and weaknesses, or guides improvement.

Variants. Papers study several variants under closely related names: general feedback generation, verbal feedback generation, and feedback comment generation. The settings range from model evaluation and socially aligned interaction, where the model provides feedback as rationales, to code self-repair, exemplar-guided reflection for prompt optimization, tutoring, and automated writing evaluation, where co

nodes.name: Few-shot image classification
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most commonly, papers describe it as classifying images into categories when only a small number of examples, or support samples, are available for each category. A more specific formulation casts it as N-way K-shot classification, with N classes, K support samples, and Q query samples per class, where the goal is to classify query samples based on the support samples. Success is described through classification performance, including Top-1 accuracy.

Variants. The main setting that papers spell out is N-way K-shot, organized around support and query samples per class. Papers also refer to the task as few-shot recognition and, in one case, describe doing it with a fixed number of prompts. Evaluations are reported across downstream datasets.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. When papers report results, they do so as classification performance, including Top-1 accuracy across downstream datasets and tabulated few-shot image classification results.

What it is taken as evidence of. No construct is linked to it as evidence of. One paper reports a positive correlation between few-shot classification performance and the cap

nodes.name: Few-shot task performance
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats this as observable downstream or benchmark performance when only a small number of examples are available, most often as in-context demonstrations in the prompt. Success is usually framed as answering, completing, or predicting correctly on those tasks, and papers commonly report it as accuracy or downstream performance. Some descriptions instead speak of an ability or capacity to learn or generalize from few examples, and a smaller line uses the label for settings with only a few labeled examples per class or very limited training data, including adaptation and forecasting setups.

Variants. A common variant appears in long-context evaluations, where few-shot learning is treated as one task category alongside question-answering, summarization, and code completion. Another recurring variant is time series forecasting with only 10% or the first 5 to 10% of time steps available for training. Other papers cast it as N-way-K-shot relation extraction or as tasks with only k labeled examples per class, and some descriptions emphasize using the provided examples to guide output generation or retrieve relevant QA p

nodes.name: Figure-to-text generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats this behavior as converting structured or visual information in a figure into natural-language text. Most formulations differ by the intended output: concise figure summaries, suitable descriptive captions, detailed descriptions, or analytical text about scientific figures. The recurring success criterion is that the text capture the figure’s information in a meaningful, descriptive, or concise way, depending on the task label.

Variants. Papers use several neighboring labels for this behavior, including figure summarization, figure captioning or caption generation, figure description, and scientific figure analysis. Some variants are explicitly framed around scientific figures, and one paper places captioning, summarization, and description alongside figure question answering and scientific reasoning tasks.

Space of elicitation and scores. In the linked operationalization, this behavior is measured by one instrument, ChartX. One paper cites ChartX under the label Figure Des., so the supporting measurement evidence is stated in figure-description terms.

What it is taken as evidence of. The papers do not link thi

nodes.name: Financial distress identification
nodes.definition: Predicting whether a company will face bankruptcy or financial distress.

nodes.name: Financial question answering
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage is finance-domain question answering. Papers agree on the domain, but differ in formulation: the more common description is answering financial questions using retrieved evidence, while another description narrows the behavior to answering multiple-choice questions related to finance.

Variants. The task appears in two named settings. One is presented as "Financial QA" or "FiQA," including a formulation where answers are produced with retrieved evidence; the other is a finance-specific MMLU setting framed as multiple-choice questions related to finance.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers measure this behavior with 2 instruments. The more common instrument is FiQA, described in the papers as a Financial QA task, and another instrument is MMLU, used for finance-related multiple-choice questions; both are benchmark-style instruments in the way the papers describe them.

What it is taken as evidence of. No construct is linked to this behavior, so the papers do not explicitly relate it to any construct.

nodes.name: Fine-grained action recognition
nodes.definition: The task of distinguishing between highly similar actions within a specific domain, requiring attention to subtle differences in movement, posture, and interaction with the environment.

nodes.name: Fine-grained visual recognition
nodes.definition: The observable task of identifying and outputting the specific, subordinate-level category of an object presented in an image.

nodes.name: Flowchart question answering
nodes.definition: Generating natural language answers to questions about the content, logic, or process flow of a given flowchart image.

nodes.name: Forecasting
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, forecasting is treated as producing predictions about future events or outcomes. The prevailing formulations describe using available information, past data, and current trends to answer what will likely happen, including in finance, sports, business, and politics. A narrower task framing presents the prediction as a future-event answer that is often given in multiple-choice or range-based form, and one definition notes that such predictions may influence user decisions and market behaviors.

Variants. Papers use several nearby names for the behavior, including forecasting, predictive analytics, and future event prediction. The settings mentioned include sports projections, financial forecasting, business analytics, and political outcome questions; examples ask what the 10yr treasury yield will be in 2024 and what a president's approval rating will be on a future date. In the business analytics framing, this appears as the predictive class of insights, summarized as "what will likely happen."

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. In the descriptions, elicitation is task-based: papers ask for a predictio

nodes.name: Form filling
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage is entering or selecting values in web form elements according to task instructions. The behavior is described both as entering information into fields and as interacting with inputs such as text boxes, checkboxes, radio buttons, and dropdown menus. One definition also includes tracking which fields have been completed, and one paper describes repeated input of the same words into the same field as a common error in this behavior.

Variants. The papers describe this behavior across several web input types rather than as a single uniform action. Related formulations include labeling or filling in inputs, and the named action types include "modify_text", "modify_checkbox", "modify_radio", and "modify_select".

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. In the descriptions, the behavior is operationalized through web interaction actions such as filling or labeling inputs and modifying text, checkbox, radio, and select elements.

What it is taken as evidence of. No construct is linked to it as evidence of.

nodes.name: Formal language recognition
nodes.definition: The observable action of receiving a string as input and producing a decision to accept or reject it as a member of a language.

nodes.name: Formal theorem proving
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the dominant framing is producing a correct formal proof for a theorem in an interactive theorem prover such as Lean. One recurring task formulation asks models to prove a theorem with access to code from the theorem's repository, and the stated success criterion is a correct formal proof.

Variants. Papers study this behavior across several theorem settings and labels. miniF2F is described as covering high-school level exercises and competition problems, ProofNet as undergraduate-level theorems, and another description groups miniF2F and ProofNet among popular benchmarks focused on isolated competition problems; papers also refer to the behavior as theorem-proving capabilities, formal proof writing, and automated theorem proving with formal languages. A smaller line of work also relates formal theorem proving to premise selection and conjecture generation.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link formal theorem proving to four instruments overall. The most commonly linked are ProofNet and miniF2F, both described as benchmarks, with PutnamBench also used to evaluate theorem-provers; LeanDojo appears as a related tool for extracting training

nodes.name: Format following
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage treats format following as producing outputs that match a requested layout, template, or explicit formatting rule. Papers describe it as arranging text into a specific structure, obeying instruction-specified formatting or style constraints, and applying required section headers, organ labels, and numbering rules, with deviations penalized during evaluation. A smaller formulation treats it as staying consistent with the format shown in in-context examples, and one study notes outputs are "often generated in an inconsistent format" when that example format is disrupted.

Variants. Papers study this behavior in several settings: general text formatting for content creation, rule following under explicit instructions, template adherence in clinical reporting, and format-consistent output generation in arithmetic in-context learning. The named variants are text formatting, rule following, template adherence, and format-consistent output generation. In the structured-report variant, success includes correctly using Findings and Impression section headers and other template rules, while in the arithmetic variant success i

nodes.name: Forward reaction prediction
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. The paper treats this behavior as determining the potential products of a chemical reaction from given reactants and reagents. In LLaMo: Large Language Model-based Molecular Graph Assistant, it is also described as the "proactive determination" of potential products, so the task formulation centers on producing reaction products from the supplied reactants and reagents.

Space of elicitation and scores. It appears as one of several instruction types in the reported dataset collection, but no measurement instrument is linked to it.

What it is taken as evidence of. No construct is linked to it as evidence of.

nodes.name: Frame identification
nodes.definition: The task of selecting the correct semantic frame for a given target word within a specific sentence or context.

nodes.name: Fraud detection
nodes.definition: Classifying transactions or profiles as fraudulent or non-fraudulent.

nodes.name: Free recall
nodes.definition: An experimental task where a subject studies a list of items and is then asked to recall as many items as possible in any order.

nodes.name: Freezing of gait detection
nodes.definition: Detecting episodes where Parkinson’s disease patients experience sudden inability to move while walking, using multimodal physiological and motion signals.

nodes.name: Function composition
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, it is described as solving tasks that require sequentially applying functions or relations to an input and producing the resulting output. One formulation says models "apply them sequentially to a given input" and, when prompted with the non-highlighted part, need to return the highlighted part; another frames success as answering a query for "the value of f(g(x))" after composing relations such as "birthday-of" and "father-of".

Variants. Variation appears mainly in how the task is posed. Some papers study composed mappings built from simple functions with specified inputs and outputs, while others study relation-composition queries in which one named relation is applied and then another; the labels used are "Function composition" and "Function composition solving".

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to this behavior. In the papers, it is elicited directly through the task setup itself, either by giving part of a composed mapping and asking for the missing output or by asking for the result of a composed query.

What it is taken as evidence of. No construct is linked to this behavior. The papers therefore

nodes.name: Function regression
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the dominant framing is a prediction task: the model is given example input-output pairs for a mathematical function in context and must predict the output for a queried input. Most descriptions treat this generally as function fitting or mathematical function learning. A narrower formulation casts it as non-linear function regression with inputs x and y, where the target is the integer part of f(x, y) = √x√y; one paper also presents this task as a way to evaluate reasoning with continuous vector representations.

Variants. Papers use several near-synonymous names, including function regression, function fitting, and mathematical function learning. The main variation is between broad mathematical-function prediction from in-context examples and a specific arithmetic setting built around a non-linear function. One paper specifically studies learning out-of-distribution mathematical functions through in-context learning.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. The operationalizations are direct task formulations, with success described as predicting the function output for a given input and, in the more spe

nodes.name: Functional group identification
nodes.definition: The specific, observable task of identifying potential functional groups within a molecule based on its chemical formula and spectral data.

nodes.name: Future prediction
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the common framing treats future prediction as producing the next observation or state from current context, usually a current observation or state together with an action. Definitions differ mainly in output form: some papers ask the model to choose among candidate next observations, others ask it to predict the next observation at each time point in a stochastic sequence, and others frame it as autoregressively predicting the next state and reward. A smaller line of work casts it as either a probabilistic forecast over unknown state values given context or a text description of the next observation after a single-step action.

Variants. Papers study several closely related variants under the names observation prediction, next-state prediction, state transition prediction, state forecasting, and future prediction. The settings range from sequential decision making with candidate observations, to stochastic processes such as random walks on a graph, to autoregressive state-and-reward prediction, to uncertainty settings where the output is a probability distribution over state values, and to robot learning where the output is a textual next-obser

nodes.name: Game playing
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, it is most commonly framed as interaction with a game environment through repeated moves under the game's rules and state updates in order to achieve objectives or win. One recurring formulation emphasizes end-to-end play, where the model is assessed on managing a game from start to finish and must "independently navigate the game." A narrower formulation treats the behavior as accomplishing specific in-game goals, with examples such as collecting resources, crafting tools, or placing objects, and with success described in terms of unlocking achievements while ensuring survival.

Variants. Papers use several task names for this behavior, including end-to-end gameplay, game playing, and achievement unlocking. The studied settings range from full-run gameplay, where the agent manages the game from start to finish, to open-world goal completion, where the agent continuously interacts with the environment to accomplish tasks. Some formulations target general objectives or winning, while another focuses specifically on unlocking achievements such as collecting resources, crafting tools, and placing objects.

Space of elicitation and scores. No me

nodes.name: Generative error correction
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the cited papers, the prevailing usage treats generative error correction as an ASR task where an LLM maps an N-best list of hypotheses to a corrected transcription. The papers align on the input, ASR N-best hypotheses, and the target, a final or ground-truth transcription; one definition further specifies that this is done in an auto-regressive manner, and one quoted passage describes it as "a direct mapping from the N-best hypotheses list generated by an ASR system to the predicted output transcription" (It's Never Too Late: Fusing Acoustic Information into Large Language Models for Automatic Speech Recognition).

Variants. The formulations that appear are all within automatic speech recognition settings. A recurring name for the core setup is a hypotheses-to-transcription, H2T, mapping from an N-best hypotheses list to a predicted or ground-truth transcription, alongside the shorthand GER.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link it to 1 measurement instrument, HyPoradise. In the recorded relationship language, generative error correction is measured by HyPoradise, which is described as a generative error correction benchmark for LLM-enhanced AS

nodes.name: Generic caption generation
nodes.definition: An observable behavior where the model produces a vague or non-specific description of an image that does not identify the primary objects.

nodes.name: Genetic perturbation experiment design
nodes.definition: The observable task of selecting a set of genes to perturb in an experimental round to maximize the discovery of 'hit' genes with a desired phenotype.

nodes.name: Gibberish generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage describes it as the model producing incoherent, meaningless, irrelevant, unreadable, or otherwise un-useful text. Definitions largely agree on observable forms such as jumbled or repetitive phrases, random characters, mixed languages, garbled characters, and semantically irregular text; one paper describes single phrases or words repeated 'ad nauseum.' In the trigger-based framing, success is defined as eliciting gibberish outputs from the model when the trigger appears.

Variants. Papers use several near-synonymous names for the behavior, including incoherent output, nonsensical response generation, and garbage text generation. The studied settings differ: some elicit it when a specific trigger string is present in context, some when the model is asked to operate in a difficult bijection language, and some after extensive optimization on a proxy reward or under KL-divergence training. A narrower variant emphasizes garbage text specifically as mixed languages or garbled characters.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. Papers instead describe elicitation through context conditions,

nodes.name: GitHub issue resolution
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the descriptions, the prevailing usage treats it as an end-to-end repository task: understanding a problem description from a GitHub issue and generating a code patch that successfully resolves it within the software repository. The success criterion is resolution of the issue through the produced patch, and no alternative task formulation appears in the definitions.

Variants. The quoted passages place the task at the repository level, with one paper noting difficulties in resolving GitHub issues particularly at that level. Benchmark descriptions also frame the behavior as patch-level fixing rather than broader development capabilities. No additional named sub-tasks, domains, or modalities appear in the cited papers.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers describe it as measured by 2 instruments, most often SWE-bench and also SWE-bench Lite. SWE-bench is presented as an evaluation benchmark or dataset specifically designed for evaluating GitHub issue resolution, and one description says it emphasizes patch-level fixes rather than broader development capabilities. SWE-bench Lite is used to compare systems on the same issues' resolution under budget co

nodes.name: Grammatical acceptability judgment
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most papers describe this behavior as judging whether a sentence is grammatically correct, acceptable, or well formed. Many operationalizations use a direct acceptable versus unacceptable decision, often as single-sentence classification, while others use minimal pairs and count the model as correct when it picks the more acceptable sentence or assigns higher probability, likelihood, or MLM score to the acceptable member of the pair. A minority of definitions broaden the target from grammaticality alone to grammatical or semantic acceptability, or to whether a sentence would be acceptable to a native speaker.

Variants. Papers use several near-synonymous labels for this behavior, including linguistic acceptability judgment, grammaticality judgment, grammatical judgment, linguistic acceptability, acceptability judgment, and syntactic well-formedness detection. The main variants are CoLA-style single-sentence judgments and BLiMP or TurBLiMP style minimal-pair comparisons, alongside benchmark-specific formulations such as Bigram Shift and discriminative grammar judgment experiments. The behavior is also studied in different language settings, including English, T

nodes.name: Grammatical error correction
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage is a correction task: taking text or a sentence with grammatical errors and producing a corrected, more grammatically accurate, often error-free version. Most formulations stress both detection and correction, and some explicitly describe the output as rewriting erroneous text into corrected text; one paper states that systems should "detect and correct all grammatical errors in the sentence and produce an error-free sentence as the output," and some descriptions make the edits explicit as insertion, deletion, re-ordering, or substitution. A smaller set broadens the target beyond grammar to spelling, punctuation, awkward phrases, typos, and certain semantic errors, while one proofreading formulation specifies correction without explanations or analysis and one grammar-checking formulation emphasizes outputs that preserve most of the input.

Variants. Papers use several nearby names for this behavior, most often grammatical error correction or grammar correction, with smaller variants such as grammar error correction, grammar checking, proofreading, and text correction. The settings span multilingual GEC, Chinese GEC, English

nodes.name: Graph classification
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats graph classification as a graph-level labeling task. Definitions describe it as assigning class labels to graph inputs represented as projected embeddings, or more generally assigning a categorical label to an entire graph. Papers agree on the core success criterion, producing the graph's class label.

Variants. The variations shown here are in representation and task framing. One paper describes graph inputs as projected embeddings and notes training non-linear projectors on a graph classification dataset, while another reformulates graph classification, alongside node classification and link prediction, as a textual reasoning problem. The linked measurement settings are described as molecular graph classification datasets.

Space of elicitation and scores. It is measured by three instruments: BACE, BBBP, and ClinTox. One paper presents these as three molecular graph classification datasets, so the linked operationalizations all come from a molecular graph classification setting.

What it is taken as evidence of. No construct is linked to it as evidence of.

nodes.name: Graph connectivity
nodes.definition: The observable behavior of determining whether a path exists between nodes in a graph structure, given a textual description of connections.

nodes.name: Graph isomorphism detection
nodes.definition: The task of determining whether two visually distinct graph representations share the same underlying structure, including the same number of vertices, edges, and connectivity patterns.

nodes.name: Graph partitioning
nodes.definition: Dividing a graph into disjoint subgraphs such that nodes within each subgraph are strongly connected internally while minimizing connections between subgraphs, under size or balance constraints.

nodes.name: Graph query generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage is translating natural language questions into complete, executable graph queries, often in openCypher or Cypher, so they can be run against a graph database or knowledge graph to retrieve an answer or structured data. A smaller line of work describes the behavior as generating a structured or pseudo query graph from the question rather than the final executable query, and one paper also describes LLM agents formulating multiple queries from the user's question and previously gathered information.

Variants. Papers use several closely related names for this behavior, including query graph generation, graph query generation, text-to-Cypher generation, and text-to-nGQL generation. The main variants differ by target language and output form: openCypher or Cypher, nGQL, or a query graph or pseudo query graph, and the retrieval setting ranges from knowledge graphs to code graph databases that return relevant code fragments or code structures.

Space of elicitation and scores. Only one measurement instrument is linked to this behavior in the papers: Text2Cypher, described as a large-scale dataset used to evaluate the Text-to-C

nodes.name: Graph question answering
nodes.definition: The task of generating a natural language answer to a question based on the information contained within a provided textual graph.

nodes.name: Grounded multimodal named entity recognition
nodes.definition: The task of identifying named entities in text and linking them to their corresponding visual regions within an associated image.

nodes.name: Grounded response generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats this behavior as generating answers or other text that is explicitly backed by documents, source texts, or other verifiable facts. Most definitions emphasize support from provided or retrieved sources, and the strictest formulation requires showing how an answer is systematically entailed by corpus texts, with some answers counted as fully grounded only when that entailment can be shown. A smaller framing describes it as incorporating external facts, references, or constraints into response generation during inference.

Variants. Papers study closely related variants under the names grounded question answering, source-supported response generation, and knowledge injection. The settings differ in whether the output is an answer to a question, more general generated text backed by provided source documents, or a response generation process that integrates new knowledge or constraints at inference time. One line centers grounding in a corpus of texts, while another explicitly mentions retrieval giving the model in-context access to large corpora for source-supported responses.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers

nodes.name: Group word problem solving
nodes.definition: Given a sequence of elements from a mathematical group, the task is to compute their cumulative product according to the group's operation.

nodes.name: GUI action labeling
nodes.definition: The observable task of producing a sequence of discrete action labels (e.g., 'click', 'type') that corresponds to the user interactions shown in a screen recording video.

nodes.name: GUI automation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats GUI automation as end-to-end task completion through direct interaction with a graphical or computer interface: agents navigate pages or applications and execute actions such as clicking, typing, scrolling, tapping, swiping, or keyboard and mouse input to accomplish a user goal or reach a goal state. Definitions mostly agree that success is completing the requested task through a sequence of UI actions, sometimes explicitly from natural-language instructions or from screenshots and instructions. A smaller line of work narrows this to pixel-level operation, describing direct clicks or typing at screen coordinates without relying on underlying code structures.

Variants. Papers study this behavior under several names, including GUI control, GUI interaction, UI control, GUI navigation, computer control, mobile device control, and interface manipulation. Common variants differ by platform and task scope: web and mobile tasks from screenshots and instructions, desktop or enterprise software operation, and on-device smartphone control. Some papers separate single-app task execution from cross-app or cross-applica

nodes.name: Hallucination
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats hallucination as output that is factually incorrect, fabricated, nonsensical, or otherwise ungrounded in the provided input, source text, image, video, table, tool set, or established world knowledge. Many definitions also include content that is merely unsupported or irrelevant, and some stress that the output may still sound plausible or confident. A smaller line of work gives task-specific criteria, for example any ungrounded span in a response, answers to unanswerable questions, contradictions with a source document, or fabricated numbers, tools, citations, code assets, or observations.

Variants. Variants are most common in multimodal settings, where papers study visual or cross-modal hallucination as object, action, attribute, relation, counting, or spatial errors, such as mentioning entities absent from an image or video or hearing imaginary sounds from visual cues. Text-centered work often treats it as factual inconsistency or grounding error in summarization, question answering, simplification, translation, table or graph generation, and reference generation. More specialized variants include hallucinated rea

nodes.name: Hallucination detection
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage is a judgment task over model outputs: deciding whether an answer, statement, response, or generated content is hallucinated, meaning factually incorrect, fabricated, unsupported, or not grounded in the available context. Most descriptions treat success as labeling content as hallucinated versus non-hallucinated, though some narrow it to tagging object phrases in a description that do not correspond to an image, or marking explanation sentences with a deletion tag when they show knowledge conflict. A smaller formulation treats success as refusing to answer when the needed information is absent, sometimes with the explicit response that the item is not mentioned in the provided context.

Variants. Papers use the label for several variants. A recurring line studies multimodal and visual settings, including concrete inconsistencies in rendered 2D images, responses or captions that are inaccurate relative to an image, and discourse-level hallucination detection over entities or relations in captions. Other variants focus on medical question answering, unsupported claims in data-analysis insights, token-level hallucination degree

nodes.name: Hamiltonian cycle detection
nodes.definition: Determining whether a graph contains a cycle that visits each node exactly once, based on visual input.

nodes.name: Hamiltonian path detection
nodes.definition: Identifying whether a graph contains a path that visits each node exactly once, based on visual input.

nodes.name: Hamiltonian path finding
nodes.definition: Finding a path in an undirected graph that visits every node exactly once.

nodes.name: Harmful content detection
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the dominant framing is a classification task over text or prompts: models label inputs as harmful versus benign, safe, or unsafe, or as toxic, offensive, abusive, or threatening versus not. Success is usually a binary decision, sometimes with constrained outputs such as "OFF" or "NOT_OFF" and "1" or "0", and some papers explicitly use the result to reject or block unsafe prompts before generation. Smaller variants extend the same behavior to instruction-response pairs, multimodal memes or other multimodal inputs, conversational turns judged as problematic, or probability estimates of unsafety instead of a hard label.

Variants. Common variants focus on toxicity detection or classification, offensive language detection, and harmful prompt detection or prompt safety classification. Other papers narrow the target to threats or abusive language, distinguish instruction-only classification from instruction-response pair classification, or ask the model for an explicit harmful request, unsafe intent, or risk judgment, sometimes with finer-grained labels such as hate speech, offensive language, abuse, specific risk categories, sentence or token level

nodes.name: Harmful content generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the dominant framing treats this behavior as an LLM producing harmful, unsafe, toxic, offensive, biased, illegal, or otherwise policy-violating output, usually in response to harmful, adversarial, or jailbroken prompts. The prevailing success criterion is non-refusal: papers count outputs as harmful when the model answers or complies with a malicious request, offers actionable guidance, or directly assists unsafe intent. As one paper puts it, harmful answers are those that “provide concrete and helpful suggestions for malicious instructions” (Catastrophic Jailbreak of Open-source LLMs via Exploiting Generation), while another says fulfillment occurs when a response “provides substantial content that directly assists with the given unsafe instruction” (SORRY-Bench: Systematically Evaluating Large Language Model Safety Refusal). Some papers count even an attempted answer or stated willingness to answer as unsafe, while a smaller line of work narrows the behavior to particular forms such as toxic or aggressive wording, deceptive or false content, or replies that manipulate a user’s beliefs or self-perception.

Variants. Most variant labels narrow t

nodes.name: Harmful request refusal
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats this as an observable model behavior: declining, explicitly rejecting, or abstaining from a substantive answer when a prompt is judged harmful, unsafe, unethical, illegal, malicious, or against safety policies or guidelines. Definitions vary in what counts as the refusal signal, from polite non-compliance and explicit refusal answers to common refusal messages such as “I’m sorry, but I can’t...”; one paper also notes that a completion can begin with “I can’t” and still continue with harmful content.

Variants. Papers use several near-equivalent names, including harmful content refusal, refusal of harmful requests, harmful query refusal, harmful instruction refusal, harmful prompt refusal, and, in a smaller line, safety refusal. The requests studied range from broad harmful or toxic instructions to examples involving cryptocurrency scams, fraud, malware creation, dangerous activities, and malicious requests, and one paper examines whether such refusals generalize to downstream browser agents.

Space of elicitation and scores. Four measurement instruments are linked to this behavior. Papers most often measure it with Ad

nodes.name: Hate speech detection
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the dominant framing is automatic classification of whether a text contains hate speech, hateful content, or content that promotes violence toward individuals or groups, often with reference to protected or other group characteristics. Most definitions treat success as assigning a hate versus non-hate label to a text or tweet, sometimes with fixed outputs such as "HS" and "NOT_HS." Smaller lines of work use broader label sets, including hate, offensive, and safe, or predefined hate types such as dehumanization, derogation, animosity, threatening, and support; another subset targets implicit hate by asking for the implied hateful statement or target context.

Variants. Variants center on different forms and settings of the task. Papers study implicit hate speech, including classification of subtle or indirect cues and tasks where a tweet is mapped to its implied statement, and one line of work discusses dog whistles as a form of hate speech that detectors try to identify. Other variants add source or subject context, or shift from text-only inputs to multimodal meme-style inputs built from an image and optional caption, where the model select

nodes.name: Headline generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage treats headline generation as producing a short title from a source text, commonly described as concise and relevant, and sometimes as engaging. Some authors narrow the task to news articles, and one ablation uses it as an alternate content choice by instructing the model to produce a news headline rather than a tweet. Success is described in terms such as generating concise, contextually accurate headlines and assessing performance on annotated data.

Variants. Papers use both the broader label headline generation and the narrower news headline generation. Studied settings include minority-language headline generation in Tibetan, Uyghur, and Mongolian, and some work examines it alongside summarization across four configurations.

Space of elicitation and scores. One measurement instrument is linked to this behavior: LaMP, which includes LaMP-4, news headline generation, and is used to measure it. Beyond that linked instrument, some evaluations use high-quality annotated data and report ROUGE-L scores for generated headlines.

What it is taken as evidence of. No constructs are linked to headline generation, and pape

nodes.name: Hedging
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, hedging is treated as observable non-commitment in outputs, but the concrete behavior varies by task. One framing describes it as predictions pulled toward the midpoint, such as 0.5, and avoidance of high-confidence estimates, especially when the correct outcome is certain; one study says a model can "underperform when the crowd is highly certain" because it tends to hedge its predictions. Other papers use the same label for cautious or non-committal language that minimizes imposition, or for annotator behavior that assigns "equal" preferences or intermediate ratings when responses seem similar or uncertain.

Variants. Papers study hedging in several settings rather than as a single task. The recorded variants are probability forecasting, politeness strategy production, and feedback acquisition through both ranking and rating tasks; in the politeness work it appears alongside indirectness and other distancing strategies, including when giving positive feedback, and in preference annotation it includes tie situations marked as "equal" feedback.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. In the descript

nodes.name: Helpful response generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, this behavior is described as producing responses that stay relevant and useful to the input, rather than generic refusals or disconnected content. Another formulation emphasizes responses that are informative, accurate, and useful in assisting users with their queries or tasks, and one source characterizes failure as "failing to offer helpful suggestions or relevant content based on the input."

Variants. The papers place this behavior in more than one setting. One treats it as generating "the most harmless and helpful responses tailored to multimodal inputs," while another names a "Helpful Assistant task" and situates it alongside "helpful," "harmless," and "humorous" objectives.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to this behavior. The papers named here therefore do not identify a specific instrument used to elicit or score it.

What it is taken as evidence of. Across the papers that relate this behavior to broader constructs, the only construct named is Helpfulness, and those links are recorded as related. These papers describe the behavior with phrases such as generating "helpful outputs" or learning to

nodes.name: Heuristic generation
nodes.definition: The observable process of producing algorithmic strategies for solving optimization problems, expressed as both natural language thoughts and executable code.

nodes.name: Hierarchical text classification
nodes.definition: The observable task of assigning a document to one or more labels that are organized within a multi-level taxonomy.

nodes.name: Hint generation
nodes.definition: Producing a natural language hint as feedback to aid a learner in resolving programming errors without directly revealing the solution.

nodes.name: Historical narrative generation
nodes.definition: Producing a narrative account of a past event conditioned on a specific persona, reflecting either direct or indirect experiential involvement.

nodes.name: Honest response generation
nodes.definition: Producing a model output that truthfully communicates facts or admits to prior misdeeds without intent to mislead.

nodes.name: Hospital readmission prediction
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. In the paper, the task is described as predicting whether a patient will be readmitted to the hospital within a specific timeframe from historical electronic health records. The formulation is explicitly binary, written as predicting whether the patient will be readmitted within σ days from prior records, with output y ∈ {0,1}.

Variants. The only explicit variation is the prediction horizon, expressed as readmission within σ days. The task is studied in two dataset settings, MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV, and the paper does not name additional sub-tasks or modalities beyond that timeframe-based formulation.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers measure this behavior with 2 instruments, MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV. Both are used as datasets for experiments on hospital readmission prediction.

What it is taken as evidence of. The papers summarized here do not link hospital readmission prediction to any construct, so they do not specify a broader construct that this behavior is taken to indicate.

nodes.name: How-to question answering
nodes.definition: The task of providing step-by-step, procedural responses to questions that ask 'how' to accomplish a goal.

nodes.name: Human reaction motion generation
nodes.definition: The observable task of generating a sequence of human reaction motions in response to an input sequence of human action motions without explicit text prompts.

nodes.name: Humor generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, humor generation is consistently treated as a text generation task in which the model produces a humorous or witty response to a prompt or question, and one definition also makes unexpectedness part of the target output. A narrower, alignment-oriented use treats it as producing outputs that incorporate humor or wit and are evaluated under a humor reward model as a secondary objective, with responses described as optimizing helpfulness while adhering to a humor threshold.

Variants. Named variants are limited and remain within textual response generation. Papers refer to witty response generation and humorous response generation, and one study places the task alongside broader humor-oriented work that also includes humor discrimination.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link humor generation to a single measurement instrument, User preference study, used as a user-preference evaluation to test "the creativity and humor of LLMs." A separate operationalization scores it with a humor reward model: one paper states, "we set humor as the target reward," and describes generated responses as needing to satisfy a humor threshold while optimizi

nodes.name: Hypothesis generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage is producing candidate explanations or rules, usually in natural language, from observations, examples, or other available information. In this framing, models are asked to generate one or more plausible, valid, or accurate hypotheses that explain input-output pairs, transformations, or observed patterns, sometimes as multiple alternatives to be evaluated or refined. Smaller lines of work use the same behavior for scientific inquiry, where hypotheses are designed to be testable and grounded in evidence, constraints, or anomalies, and for agent settings, where the hypotheses explain another agent's latent strategy or goal, or propose a strategy before execution.

Variants. A common variant studies inductive reasoning from examples, with free-form or constrained textual rules, multiple abstract hypotheses, and sometimes a paired Python implementation. Papers also use names such as scientific hypothesis generation, zero-shot hypothesis generation, and hypothesis formulation, covering cases where models generate scientific hypotheses from evidence, constraints, anomalies, or data patterns, sometimes without demonstrations and so

nodes.name: Hypothesis testing
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the behavior is treated as an observable cycle of proposing a hypothesis and then taking actions or running experiments to decide whether evidence supports it. One formulation centers on puzzle solving: agents execute actions, assess the consequences using observations made immediately before and after those actions, and use the outcome to validate or invalidate candidate puzzle solutions while refining later attempts. Another formulation treats it as hypothesis validation for free-form hypotheses, defined as designing and executing experiments to determine whether a hypothesis should be accepted or rejected based on evidence.

Variants. The papers use both the names hypothesis testing and hypothesis validation. One setting studies it in virtual escape rooms, where the hypotheses concern puzzle solutions and evaluation happens through post-action reasoning; another studies automated validation of free-form hypotheses in an agentic framework. The variation is therefore mainly in domain and task object, puzzle-solution hypotheses in one case and free-form hypotheses in the other.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is l

nodes.name: Idea generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the dominant framing is producing a set of ideas in response to a prompt or other provided context, often with novelty or diversity in view. Common formulations include generating ideas or suggestions for brainstorming, generating new topics related to given examples, and listing novel and appropriate uses for everyday objects; one definition also specifies fluency and relevance as the evaluation criteria. A smaller line of work uses the same behavior for more structured outputs, such as generating conceptual predictive features or full research proposals with elements like a title, motivation, proposed method, and experiment plan.

Variants. Papers study this behavior in several task forms: brainstorming within instruction-following, rapid collaborative brainstorming in multi-agent settings, topic brainstorming for argument mining, alternative uses generation in divergent thinking tasks, feature proposal for clinical trial prediction, and research proposal generation. Some variants are explicitly interdisciplinary, combining concepts and methods from distinct fields, and some are situated in closed-loop auto-research, where ideas are generated

nodes.name: Idiom identification
nodes.definition: The task of locating and extracting multi-word expressions that are used idiomatically within a given text, without being provided with a candidate expression in advance.

nodes.name: Illegal action generation
nodes.definition: An observable failure mode where the model produces an action that is not valid in the current state of the environment or does not conform to the required format.

nodes.name: Image blending
nodes.definition: Combining visual elements from multiple images into a single coherent image, such as merging a cat and a tiger into a tiger-cat.

nodes.name: Image captioning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats image captioning as generating textual descriptions of visual input, most often entire images. Most definitions frame success as a caption that reflects the image's content, and several make this explicit by requiring accurate mention of present objects, attributes, and spatial relations, or by asking for an objective description that avoids conjecture. A smaller line of work asks for brief, single-sentence, or concise captions, while others ask for rich or very detailed descriptions, including style, narrative, or text detailed enough to replace the visual input in downstream problem solving.

Variants. Papers use nearby labels such as image description, caption generation, scene description, diagram captioning, and situated captioning. The task is studied at whole-image, region, and crop level, and in both free-form open-ended and structured JSON settings. Domain-specific variants cover comics, medical or pathology images, earth-observation images, driving scenes, and UI elements or 3D surroundings, and some work uses captions as an intermediate step before question answering or as per-image inputs inside summarizat

nodes.name: Image classification
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage is assigning a class or category label to an input or entire image from a predefined set of categories, with success framed as producing the correct label. Many papers cast this in vision-language or prompt-conditioned terms, often in zero-shot form by comparing the image to text prompts or class descriptions, as one paper describes 'image classification via pretrained vision-language models' (Understanding prompt engineering may not require rethinking generalization). A smaller line of work formulates the same behavior through labeled in-context examples, or narrows the required label to a scientific species name or a cell type.

Variants. Papers use several nearby names for the behavior, including object classification, visual classification, image recognition, few-shot classification, zero-shot image classification, and zero-shot object recognition. The studied settings range from whole-image classification to identifying individual cropped objects, industrial products, organisms, and microscopy cell types, and from general image classification to fine-grained visual classification and adaptation tasks. Some work also stu

nodes.name: Image colorization
nodes.definition: The task of adding color to a grayscale image based on a textual instruction.

nodes.name: Image dehazing
nodes.definition: The task of removing haze or fog from an image to improve visibility, guided by a textual instruction.

nodes.name: Image denoising
nodes.definition: The observable task of reducing or eliminating unwanted visual noise from an image.

nodes.name: Image editing
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats image editing as modifying an existing image in response to a natural-language instruction. Definitions largely agree on instruction-guided changes such as replacing, hiding, recoloring, adding, removing, or otherwise changing elements, and one paper also frames it as changing attributes or adding accessories; a smaller line explicitly describes instruction-based editing as following a natural-language command without regional masks or elaborate descriptions. Some papers narrow the task further with extra success conditions, such as plausibly filling the background after removing an object, preserving an object's visual identity while changing pose or view, or inserting a reference object into a background at a specified location and spatial relation.

Variants. Papers study several recurring variants, especially object removal, object replacement, background replacement, style alteration, and drag-based editing. Other papers introduce single-paper variants such as object creation, color alteration, content dragging, object moving, and reference-object editing setups that include compositing, identity-prese

nodes.name: Image generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the dominant framing is creating or synthesizing novel images from text prompts or textual descriptions. A smaller but recurring framing broadens this to conditional generation from class labels or other conditioning signals, including the standard ImageNet class-conditional setting, and some definitions also allow visual or multimodal prompts. Success is usually described in terms of realistic or high-quality outputs, with some papers additionally emphasizing fidelity or faithfulness to the described content.

Variants. Most named variants specialize the behavior by input or domain: papers use text-to-image generation or text-to-image synthesis for purely textual prompts, conditional image generation for class labels or multimodal context, and controllable generation when text is paired with edges, landmarks, or segmentation maps. Smaller lines of work study image synthesis from visual and spatial clues with an external toolkit, chest X-ray generation from anatomical and pathology descriptions, multilingual prompting in Chinese and English, and subtasks such as style generation, subject generation, or multi-image outputs like visual stories

nodes.name: Image inpainting
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across definitions, the common core is filling missing, masked, or corrupted parts of an image. Authors differ in how the fill is conditioned: some describe using the visible parts of the image, others specify a textual instruction or in-context visual examples, and one definition makes success explicit as producing plausible, contextually appropriate content.

Variants. Papers use several nearby names, most commonly image inpainting or image in-painting, with smaller variants such as image infilling and generative fill. The behavior appears in both low-level and downstream settings, including zero-shot control settings, filling different pixel-space masks, and completing the missing half of an example; examples are shown on CelebA-HQ, SVHN, MNIST, and CIFAR-10.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. Elicitation is described procedurally by masking part of an image and having the model generate within that region, in one paper by teacher-forcing ground-truth tokens outside the mask and generating only inside it, and in another by asking for the missing half of an example; no separate scoring instrument is named.

What it i

nodes.name: Image manipulation localization
nodes.definition: The task of identifying specific, localized areas of manipulation within a forged image, rather than just making a binary real/fake judgment.

nodes.name: Image outpainting
nodes.definition: The task of extending an image beyond its original boundaries by generating new content that is consistent with the existing visual context.

nodes.name: Image patch relation prediction
nodes.definition: The task of determining the spatial relationship (e.g., above-below, left-right, or non-adjacent) between two randomly selected patches from an original image.

nodes.name: Image quality assessment
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. The definition treats image quality assessment as a vision-language model's ability to understand, recognize, and assess image quality, including identifying specific types of degradation. In "An Intelligent Agentic System for Complex Image Restoration Problems," this behavior is also framed as the ability to analyze the quality of images generated at each stage of a processing pipeline.

Variants. The paper uses closely related formulations that expand the behavior into recognizing complex image degradations, quality assessment, quality comparison, and reasoning about image quality. It also situates the task in a staged image-processing setting, where images are assessed throughout the pipeline.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to this behavior in the papers.

What it is taken as evidence of. No construct is linked to this behavior in the papers, so the papers does not explicitly present it as evidence of another construct.

nodes.name: Image reconstruction
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed papers, the prevailing usage is a fidelity-oriented task in which an image, or a compressed or latent form of it, is reconstructed so the output can be compared with the original. Most definitions describe encoding and decoding back to the original image, while some frame it as generating an output image that accurately matches a training example, recovering clean fine-grained tokens from noisy tokens, or re-rendering decomposed layers so they yield the original picture. One paper, Reconstructive Visual Instruction Tuning, also describes it as supervising visual outputs by reconstructing the input image. Success is usually expressed as fidelity to the original, through reconstruction quality, reconstruction loss, or a reconstruction error threshold.

Variants. Papers study several variants rather than a single fixed setup. These include reconstruction from compressed representations, from visual outputs or latent visual representations, from noisy tokens back to clean fine-grained tokens, from noise conditioned on visual and textual features, and by re-rendering decomposed layers while recovering occluded regions. One paper also instantiate

nodes.name: Image restoration
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, one common framing treats image restoration as recovering high-quality images from degraded observations through restoration algorithms. Another, narrower framing presents it as blind restoration, where a degraded image is restored without explicit instructions about the degradation type and instead relies on automatically generated analysis or auxiliary prompts; one description says users can input an image "without the need to provide instructions for its restoration."

Variants. The named variants are centered on blind restoration under different degradations. Papers explicitly study low-light enhancement, desnowing, and dehazing, and also mention blind restoration alongside combination tasks; separate work discusses image restoration for diverse degradations in real-world applications and relates it to downstream high-level vision tasks.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. In the papers, it is elicited through restoration tasks themselves, either by recovering degraded images in general or by blind restoration setups where auxiliary prompts are generated automatically and users do not provide expl

nodes.name: Image segmentation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats image segmentation as partitioning a digital image into multiple segments, sets of pixels, masks, or regions, usually to locate objects or boundaries. A smaller line of work defines success more narrowly through what must be delineated, such as a culturally significant object used to justify reasoning, flowchart components, or biological structures in microscopy images. As Seeing Culture: A Benchmark for Visual Reasoning and Grounding puts it, the objective can be to generate a mask that "delineates the area in I relevant to q," with polygons rather than bounding boxes used to capture intricate details.

Variants. Papers use several names for related variants, including cultural artifact segmentation, visual segmentation, and generic segmentation. The settings span instance segmentation, semantic segmentation, object masks for specific objects, and text-query-based mask generation for flowchart components; one tool-use formulation simply asks a model to "Do instance segmentation on the given image." Text4Seg: Reimagining Image Segmentation as Text Generation presents a smaller formulation that casts the task as te

nodes.name: Image-to-text generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats this behavior as generating text from an input image, most commonly as a description or response based on that image. Definitions range from generating descriptions for input images to broader formulations that include conversation, detailed description, and complex reasoning. A smaller line of work makes the text input explicit, defining the task as producing a relevant and coherent response from an image plus an optional prompt, or as a response conditioned on and consistent with both an input image and a textual query.

Variants. Papers use several closely related names, including image-to-text generation, Image2Text, image-to-text (I2T) generation, and image-grounded text generation. The studied forms span plain image description, instruction-following or conversational responses, and broader responses involving detailed description or complex reasoning; one paper instantiates this as a Chinese-English bilingual multimodal chatbot responding to user instructions based on the input image. Some settings also pair the image with user-provided text or a textual query, and one paper treats it as a practical multimodal

nodes.name: Image watermark removal
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats this behavior as an image editing task in which a model removes a watermark from an image, often in response to a textual instruction. Definitions differ slightly between a "visible watermark" and "embedded watermarks," but they agree that success means the watermark is gone and the image's original appearance is restored; one description adds that it should do so "without introducing artifacts" (PromptFix: You Prompt and We Fix the Photo).

Variants. Papers mainly present it as a single low-level image editing task rather than a family of named sub-tasks. The observed variation is mostly in wording and setup: some descriptions emphasize instruction-guided removal, while others describe the removal or elimination of embedded watermarks from images.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it by the papers.

What it is taken as evidence of. No construct is linked to it by the papers.

nodes.name: In-context classification
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats this as predicting the correct label for a target item from exemplars given in context as item-label pairs. The setup is described as an alternating sequence of N items and N labels followed by a query item, x1, l1, x2, l2, ..., xN, lN, xq, ?, and one description calls it a common in-context learning paradigm in which the network’s response to a target item is measured. Success is framed as predicting the target item’s label, and one formulation specifies the prediction objective with binary cross-entropy loss.

Variants. Most descriptions keep the same target-label prediction task but vary the classification regime. Papers discuss both binary and multi-class versions, and one paper explicitly treats in-context binary classification as a special case of the general multi-class setting. One line of work studies the task on Gaussian mixtures, and a related setting examines distribution shift through a different norms condition.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to this behavior. In the task descriptions themselves, elicitation comes from providing a sequence of item-label pairs in

nodes.name: In-context copying
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage treats it as exact reproduction of a token sequence from earlier in the input when prompted. Success is framed as returning the requested segment accurately, for example, one paper states that the objective can be to "output the suffix of the queried prefix" (HoPE: A Novel Positional Encoding Without Long-Term Decay for Enhanced Context Awareness and Extrapolation). Related formulations describe copying the correct token sequence from an input segment into the response, and in some work the target is narrowed to specific code elements such as function names and parameters.

Variants. Papers use several nearby labels, including in-context copying, contextual copying, and precise copying. One line studies retrieval from long contexts, while another studies a code "Copy" subtask centered on predefined parameters, functions, and imported APIs, with the explicit note that "reordering the functions in the input does not affect the output" (Beyond Sequences: Two-dimensional Representation and Dependency Encoding for Code Generation). Another formulation appears in rule-based chatbot settings, where the model may need to ge

nodes.name: In-context linear regression
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage is a prompt-based linear regression task: the model is given labeled input-output examples, infers the linear function they instantiate, and predicts a continuous output for a new input. Definitions agree on the continuous-output setting and on success as producing the held-out response implied by a linear relation, sometimes illustrated as "x1, y1, x2, y2, x3, y3, x4 → y4" with some w such that yi = xi · w. Some authors phrase this more generally as predicting a continuous response variable from one or more explanatory variables, while others describe it as "linear regression solving" from labeled examples.

Variants. Papers use the names "linear regression" and "linear regression solving" for the behavior. The studied settings are described as simple cases or among the simplest setups: linear-regression prompts built from labeled pairs, sometimes with one or more explanatory variables, and sometimes as pretraining of single-layer linear attention models on linear regression with a Gaussian prior.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. Papers instead operationalize it directly throu

nodes.name: In-context prediction
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across definitions, the prevailing usage treats this behavior as making a prediction for a new test example or query from examples supplied in the prompt or support set. Most formulations describe the model as taking context examples together with the new input and then predicting the target output, sometimes in a formal sequence such as (x1, g(x1), ..., xn, g(xn), xt) to predict g(xt). Some authors frame the same behavior more explicitly as producing the correct output by using labels or other information present in the surrounding context, rather than stored associations, and as learning and generalizing from new information given in the input.

Variants. Papers study several named variants, most commonly few-shot prediction, many-shot in-context learning, context-based prediction, and one-shot adaptation. These variants differ mainly in how much support is provided and what is being predicted: a small support set for text or fitness prediction, a large in-context example set before a new query, or a single context trajectory from which the model infers dynamics and then predicts from a new initial condition. Some work also contrasts few-shot settings with z

nodes.name: Inconsistent response generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the shared framing is output-level inconsistency about the same case. Papers describe it as giving different answers to the same problem across repeated attempts under identical conditions, producing logically inconsistent outputs for semantically opposite instructions about one user-item pair, or including mutually inconsistent statements within a single report. One study further notes that, in some number-puzzle cases, "all five responses were distinct and incorrect" (Investigating the interaction of linguistic and mathematical reasoning in language models using multilingual number puzzles).

Variants. The papers study this behavior in several settings and under several names. One line uses inconsistent response generation for repeated-trial variation on multilingual number puzzles, another uses contradictory response generation for paired like or dislike judgments in recommender prompts, and another treats internal contradiction or logical contradiction as contradictions inside medical reports, for example combining "clear lungs" with "left lung infiltrate".

Space of elicitation and scores. No paper links this behavior to a named me

nodes.name: Indirect object identification
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage is a sentence completion or final-token prediction behavior in which the model must output the indirect object from syntactic and semantic context. Most descriptions use prompts with two names where one name is repeated, and success means producing the non-repeated recipient name rather than the repeated subject name, as in prompts like “When Mary and John went to the store, John gave a book to” with intended completion “Mary.” One paper states this directly: “The IOI task is to predict the final token in the sentence to be the IO” (Towards Best Practices of Activation Patching in Language Models: Metrics and Methods).

Variants. The main setting is the IOI task with sentence prompts built around paired names and a transfer event, sometimes described as a name-swapping sentence. Papers vary the surface examples, such as giving a snack, a book, or a bottle of milk, but the recurring pattern is the same: two names appear, one is repeated, and the model should produce the other name, called “the IO name” in one paper.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link this behavior to 1 measurement instrument, the IOI task. In t

nodes.name: Induction copying
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, it is usually framed as a synthetic copying or pattern-matching behavior in which the model must use a pattern established within the current sequence to predict the missing continuation. The recurring formulations require identifying a repeated subsequence or abstract pattern and then outputting either the next item after that subsequence or the associated token, as in a prompt of the form "...x, ℓ...x, ?" where predicting ℓ is the target behavior. One paper states this explicitly as presenting a sequence of words, then a randomly selected subsequence from within it, and asking for the next word.

Variants. Papers use several closely related names for this behavior, including induction copying, induction pattern matching, and zero-shot copying. The variants differ mainly in presentation: one uses word sequences and an in-sequence subsequence, another describes a more general abstract pattern-matching task that includes copying previous tokens, and another focuses on current-context token associations where x and ℓ need not have appeared together during training.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to

nodes.name: Inequality proving
nodes.definition: The observable task of generating a valid proof for a given algebraic inequality problem, typically at the Olympiad level.

nodes.name: Informalization
nodes.definition:
