nodes.definition: The task of assessing and assigning a level of intensity (e.g., low, moderate, high) to the misogynistic content within a meme.

nodes.name: Mistake remediation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats mistake remediation as a response task in which the model gives feedback, guidance, or another response that helps a student fix an error. Definitions largely agree on that goal, though some wording focuses on an identified error in the student's work, while another framing centers on a student's utterance that contains a mistake or confusion and counts success as helping the student correct it.

Variants. Papers use closely related names for this behavior, especially "Mistake correction" and "Student mistake remediation." The narrower wording centers on correcting an identified error, while the broader wording also includes confusion in a student's utterance and says the tutor responds in order to remediate such mistakes or confusions. One paper also describes students' mistake and confusion remediation as "one of the most popular" tasks, and another discusses mistake correction alongside mistake location.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to this behavior, so papers do not identify a recurring instrument for eliciting or scoring it.

What it is taken as evidence of. Pap

nodes.name: ML library development
nodes.definition: The process of creating a collection of machine learning operators written in a specific programming language, often an ASPL, for a particular hardware architecture.

nodes.name: Mnemonic keyword generation
nodes.definition: The process of identifying a sequence of L1 words whose pronunciation approximates segments of an L2 target word, based on phonological and syllabic alignment.

nodes.name: Mode collapse
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. In the one definition, mode collapse is treated as an observable failure mode in knowledge distillation, where a student model's output distribution becomes overly focused on the teacher's dominant modes and ignores less frequent, potentially important information. The accompanying quoted passage uses the same framing, saying the student focuses only on the dominant modes of the teacher distribution, so the behavior is identified by this narrowed output distribution.

Variants. Most of the direct definitional detail comes from distillation, but some papers use the same label in broader generation settings. There it is described as LLMs repeatedly generating the same few completions, reduced across-input diversity under RLHF fine-tuning, or a learned model focusing on only a limited subset of the true data distribution.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. The papers describe the behavior through concentration on dominant modes and reduced diversity, rather than through a named instrument that elicits or scores it.

What it is taken as evidence of. Papers connect mode collapse only to generation diversity. One paper claim

nodes.name: Model provenance identification
nodes.definition: Querying a model via API with predefined watermark inputs and analyzing outputs to detect the presence of embedded identifiers for tracing purposes.

nodes.name: Model search
nodes.definition: The observable process of an LLM agent identifying and selecting candidate machine learning models suitable for a given task.

nodes.name: Model training
nodes.definition: Fitting predictive models on competition data as part of solving an ML task.

nodes.name: Modular arithmetic
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats modular arithmetic as performing arithmetic in a system where values wrap around at a modulus. Definitions usually describe arithmetic operations in general, and one paper makes that scope explicit as addition or counting within the wrap-around system. A narrower formulation appears as modular addition, described as computing the remainder of a sum when divided by a modulus, with outputs also characterized in terms of numbers congruent to a + b mod c, for example whether the answer is even or odd.

Variants. Papers mainly study wrap-around arithmetic through addition and counting. The named variants are modular addition and modular counting, and one source also refers more generally to "both modular arithmetic tasks" without further separating them.

Space of elicitation and scores. No paper links modular arithmetic to a measurement instrument. Accordingly, no named instrument recurs as a way to elicit or score it.

What it is taken as evidence of. Only one construct is linked to modular arithmetic. The recorded relationship is to State tracking ability, and it is framed as related rather than as a measurem

nodes.name: Molecular graph extension
nodes.definition: Generating a single-atom extension of an incomplete molecular graph so that it matches the target molecule.

nodes.name: Molecular property prediction
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage is a prediction task on a given molecule: models take molecular inputs such as structure, graph, description, or string representations like SMILES and produce a chemical, physical, or biological property of that molecule. Most formulations use regression or classification outputs, for example continuous physical properties, toxicity, blood-brain barrier penetration, or assay labels, while some also treat a textual property description as a valid output. One line of work explicitly separates computed property prediction, scored by extracting a numerical value from generated text, from descriptive property prediction, scored with text similarity against ground truth; a narrower formulation recasts the behavior as yes or no functional group detection.

Variants. Variants span regression for continuous physical properties, classification for molecule labels, ADMET-style pharmaceutical prediction, quantum-property tasks around orbital energies and the HOMO-LUMO gap, and yes or no functional group detection. Some authors also distinguish 3D-dependent from 3D-independent settings, and papers sometimes use broader names such as

nodes.name: Molecular structure elucidation
nodes.definition: The overarching task of deducing a molecule's complete chemical structure by integrating clues from various types of spectral data and a molecular formula.

nodes.name: Molecule captioning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats molecule captioning as generating a natural language description or caption from a molecular input, often a molecular structure. One paper states that "the input is a molecular structure and the model is expected to generate a corresponding description or annotation in natural language" (On LLM-Based Scientific Inductive Reasoning Beyond Equations). A smaller line of work broadens the target text to include names, or emphasizes that the generated text should accurately describe the molecule's properties, structure, and function.

Variants. Papers use several near-synonymous names for the same behavior, including molecule captioning, molecular captioning, molecule description generation, molecular description generation, and molecule caption generation. The task is studied with molecular structures or other molecular inputs, and some authors frame it as the inverse of another task, as a crossmodal alignment task, or as part of a context-aware model that integrates captioning with context embeddings.

Space of elicitation and scores. One measurement instrument is linked to this behavior: ChEBI-20. Papers use it to r

nodes.name: Molecule generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats molecule generation as producing a molecular structure or representation from a prompt, objective, natural-language description, or chemical context. Outputs are most often described as SMILES or SELFIES strings, though some papers use molecular graphs, and some papers make novelty explicit. Success is sometimes framed more narrowly as generating valid or drug-like molecules, chemically valid and structurally coherent SELFIES, molecules with target properties, or graphs that satisfy multiple constraints such as property values and structural features.

Variants. Variants appear under several names, most often molecular generation or molecule generation, with smaller strands calling it molecule synthesis or multi-conditional molecular generation. Papers study text-based generation from an input description, generation from natural-language descriptions, protein-target-based generation for criteria such as binding affinity and drug-likeness, and autoregressive SMILES generation by sampling token sequences. Other settings emphasize SELFIES generation and the production of synthetic, natural product, or drug-like molecule

nodes.name: Molecule optimization
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats molecule optimization as searching, generating, or modifying molecules so that a target property is maximized. Most definitions center on molecules or chemical structures, sometimes specifically SMILES, and on success as obtaining molecules with better values on properties such as druglikeness, bioactivity, binding affinity, penalized logP, or QED; one formulation also describes the goal as to "design new molecules with desired properties such as high chemical stability, low toxicity, or selective inhibition against a target disease" (LICO: Large Language Models for In-Context Molecular Optimization). A smaller difference in wording is whether papers emphasize iterative search through chemical space or direct generation of new structures.

Variants. Papers use several nearby names for this behavior, including molecular optimization, property optimization, and targeted molecule discovery. The studied settings include SMILES generation, generating or modifying molecules, and searching the proximate chemical space for molecules with higher property scores; some work also reports evaluation under similarity con

nodes.name: Monitor evasion
nodes.definition: Producing outputs that avoid triggering a monitor or penalty while still influencing the downstream decision.

nodes.name: Moral dilemma response
nodes.definition: The model's generation of a decision and justification when presented with an open-ended moral dilemma in an educational context.

nodes.name: Moral foundation classification
nodes.definition: The task of identifying moral values or foundations (e.g., care/harm, fairness/cheating) expressed in a given text.

nodes.name: Moral judgment
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats moral judgment as scenario-based evaluation of whether an action is morally acceptable, or as assigning blame and judging right and wrong in morally ambiguous interpersonal situations. One example asks models to judge "whether stealing the bread would be morally acceptable" (Eliciting Human Preferences with Language Models). Some authors also describe it as a latent tendency that reflects underlying value systems and sensitivity to moral principles, while a smaller framing casts it as ethical judgment, the observable task of evaluating text under principles such as deontology or justice.

Variants. Papers study it in several formulations: morally ambiguous interpersonal scenarios, direct acceptability judgments about described actions, and ethical judgment tasks labeled deontology and justice. One paper also examines persona-conditioned moral decision making, asking how personas prioritize authority, loyalty, fairness, care, liberty, and sanctity, and reporting that assigned personas affect blaming tendencies (Synthetic Socratic Debates: Examining Persona Effects on Moral Decision and Persuasion Dynamics).

Space

nodes.name: Morphological tag counting
nodes.definition: The task of predicting the total number of morphological tags for a given word.

nodes.name: Mortality prediction
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage is an observable binary clinical prediction task: predicting whether a patient survives or dies from clinical features or historical electronic health records. Most formulations place the outcome during an ICU stay or hospital admission, while one paper defines the target as the patient’s survival status at the next visit, and another uses a narrower timeframe, 48-hour in-hospital mortality.

Variants. Papers use several closely related labels and settings for this behavior. The main names are "mortality prediction" and "in-hospital mortality prediction," with narrower variants including ICU-stay mortality, next-visit mortality from historical electronic health records, and 48-hour in-hospital mortality, also written as "48 IHM."

Space of elicitation and scores. Operationalization centers on two linked measurement instruments: MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV, with MIMIC-III appearing most often. Papers describe mortality prediction as being measured by these datasets, including ICU-oriented extraction from MIMIC-III and reported evaluations on both MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV.

What it is taken as evidence of. No construct is linked

nodes.name: Motif scaffolding
nodes.definition: Generating scaffold regions around a fixed motif while preserving the motif’s structure and function.

nodes.name: Motion planning
nodes.definition: The task of generating a sequence of 3D movements or paths for an object or robot end-effector to achieve a goal state.

nodes.name: Multi-agent collaboration
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats multi-agent collaboration as observable coordination among multiple agents working toward a collective or task-oriented goal. Most descriptions emphasize collective deliberation, communication, and joint output generation, including cross-examination and debate; some papers add that agents are specialized and that collaboration can reveal emergent abilities and combine specialized expertise. A smaller formulation describes it as generating task-oriented outputs from interaction among agents and external knowledge sources.

Variants. Papers study it in several settings. The most explicit variants are collaboration through cross-examination and debate, collaboration among specialized agents, and graph-level tasks where agents communicate with one another and with external knowledge sources to produce task-oriented outputs. One paper narrows this further to answering medical questions through agent interaction with external knowledge, and another relates multi-agent collaboration to iterative response improvement in reasoning tasks with self-generated data.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument

nodes.name: Multi-branch story generation
nodes.definition: Producing multiple coherent and fluent story continuations in parallel from a single prompt, where each branch diverges in narrative trajectory and conceptual content.

nodes.name: Multi-digit multiplication
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats this behavior as multiplying two multi-digit integers in base 10 and outputting the product. Most formulations describe either an explicit output-producing task or the task of calculating the product and generating the correct numerical result; as one paper puts it, "The Multiplication (MUL) task [16] involves multiplying two multi-digit numbers in base 10" (Limits of Transformer Language Models on Learning to Compose Algorithms).

Variants. Papers use closely related names, most often "multi-digit multiplication" or "integer multiplication", and sometimes the abbreviation "MUL". The main variants differ by operand length and setting, including 4-by-3-digit, 4 × 4, and 5 × 5 problems, and one line of work describes multiplication where both multiplier and multiplicand can vary in length, framed as generalization over both operand lengths.

Space of elicitation and scores. Only one linked measurement instrument appears, BIG-bench, which a paper describes as the benchmark containing the multi-digit multiplication task. Scoring is reported with accuracy, and one paper specifically reports exact match accuracy on 5 × 5 in

nodes.name: Multi-document question answering
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most commonly, papers frame multi-document question answering as answering a question from a set of provided documents where only one document, the gold document, contains the answer and the remaining documents are distractors. A smaller line of work uses broader language, describing the task as retrieving, identifying, integrating, or synthesizing relevant information from multiple documents in long-context or retrieval-augmented settings. Across these formulations, success is producing an answer from the supplied context while ignoring irrelevant material, and some papers explicitly use the setup to place a single relevant document among distractors.

Variants. Papers use the names multi-document question answering, multi-document QA, and MDQA. The task appears in long-context settings, including extremely long contexts, with contexts of k documents, often 10 or 30, and in retrieval setups that evaluate top-5, top-10, or top-20 retrieved documents. A smaller variant is visually rich and multimodal, where the system must localize evidence across a large corpus of unstructured documents.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link this behavior to 2 measurem

nodes.name: Multi-document summarization
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage treats this as producing a coherent or concise summary from multiple input documents that synthesizes salient or key information into one output. Some authors explicitly allow either general or query-focused summaries, while one paper instead uses the name document merging for combining multiple document inputs into a single coherent, non-redundant output.

Variants. Variants mainly differ by task scope and source setting: papers distinguish general multi-document summarization from query-focused multi-document summarization, and one line uses the alternate label document merging. The source documents are sometimes described as materials about a single topic or entity, with examples such as news articles about an event or reviews of a product.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers do not link this behavior to a named measurement instrument. The only operational detail reported alongside the task is that one study used "the dataset and the evaluation prompt provided by GoT for document merging."

What it is taken as evidence of. No construct is linked to it.

nodes.name: Multi-hop question answering
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats multi-hop question answering as answering complex questions by finding, retrieving, and combining multiple pieces of information, usually across multiple documents, passages, or other sources, and then producing a final answer. Most definitions emphasize reasoning over distributed evidence, sometimes described as logically connecting relevant information from multiple documents or integrating multiple passages or facts through relational reasoning. A smaller line of work makes the intermediate process explicit: models generate sub-questions or intermediate question-answer pairs until the final answer, or compose a fixed chain such as two relational facts from a provided context.

Variants. Papers study several variants of this behavior. Common settings include open-domain multi-hop QA across different documents, long-context versions that require combining information from multiple parts of a long context or multiple pages, and decomposition-based or compositional settings built from interdependent sub-questions. Smaller variants are named multi-hop tracing, multi-hop factual recall after knowledge edits, t

nodes.name: Multi-image visual question answering
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats this behavior as answering a user's or textual question from information distributed across multiple provided images, often by reasoning over their content and, in some definitions, their relationships. Most definitions say only that the images are multiple, while one benchmark specifies questions involving 2 to 20 images. A smaller variation makes the output explicit as a textual answer.

Variants. Papers use several nearby names, including multi-image question answering, multi-image visual question answering, multi-image VQA, and MIQA. Most descriptions present it simply as question answering over a set of images, though one line of work places it in multi-turn dialogue and combines multi-image Q&A with Q&A for each individual image, so dialogues can mix single-image and multi-image questions. Another paper describes complex MIQA scenarios that involve retrieval and reasoning.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link this behavior to two measurement instruments, most often Mantis-Eval and also MMMU. In evaluation use, papers report that it is measured by Mantis-Eval, described as containing "all multi-image que

nodes.name: Multi-object navigation
nodes.definition: A navigation task where the agent must find a list of specified object categories.

nodes.name: Multi-operand addition
nodes.definition: Computing the sum of multiple numbers with a specific digit length.

nodes.name: Multi-party dialogue understanding
nodes.definition: Tracking and interpreting conversations involving more than two participants, including attributing utterances to correct speakers and maintaining coherent context.

nodes.name: Multi-turn dialogue
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the dominant framing is coherent, context-aware conversation over multiple exchanges, where each response depends on the dialogue history and remains relevant across turns. Many papers cast it as back-and-forth user-assistant interaction, sometimes to resolve a request or accomplish a goal, and some extend this to agent-agent or agent-environment episodes with explicit turn taking. A smaller line of work narrows success to higher-quality, guideline-compliant, or progressively clarifying responses over time.

Variants. Papers use several near-synonyms, most often multi-turn conversation or multi-round dialogue, alongside multi-turn chat, dialogue, conversational interaction, open-ended conversation, and extended conversation. The studied settings range from open-domain and casual chat to task-oriented dialogue, tool-calling, tutoring, doctor-patient consultation, and collaborative agent communication. Others examine grounded or memory-heavy variants, including GUI, graph, image, and video conversations, code-editing chat, and dialogue understanding where the model retrieves relevant material from prior turns.

Space of elicitation and

nodes.name: Multi-turn interaction
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats multi-turn interaction as carrying out a task through repeated action-observation cycles over multiple steps, often with an environment. Definitions agree on the iterative pattern: papers describe a loop that continues across turns, sometimes until a termination action or a final answer, with turns involving new observations and a response such as a thought, action, or revised solution. A smaller line of work uses the same label for interaction with critique or with a guiding model, where several rounds of prompts and responses are used to refine a solution, and one definition also emphasizes maintaining context and updating state across user-agent exchanges to achieve a goal.

Variants. Papers study this behavior in several settings: real-time interaction with an executable computer environment, back-and-forth exchange with a text-based environment, interaction trajectories that involve both an environment and critique, and guided rounds between a task-solving model and a separate guiding model. Across these variants, the main difference is what the model interacts with, an environment, a critique process,

nodes.name: Multi-turn jailbreaking
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, it is most commonly described as a sequence of conversational turns that gradually moves from benign or less harmful prompts toward harmful or policy-violating content. Definitions agree on the multi-turn, stepwise character of the behavior: one description says it "starts with a benign query and gradually escalates to more harmful content by inserting intermediate prompts," while others stress exchanges in which each turn builds on earlier responses. A narrower formulation treats success not just as eliciting harmful content once, but as continuing and refining a successful jailbreak over later turns as new contextual information appears.

Variants. The papers use several near names for related versions of the behavior: "multi-turn jailbreak," "multi-turn jailbreak persistence," and "multi-turn adversarial conversation." Common variants differ in where the sequence places emphasis, either on escalation through intermediate prompts, on second-turn refinement and enhancement of an already successful strategy, or on automated red-teaming style exchanges in which an attacker model dynamically uses a wide set of prompting techniques. One descrip

nodes.name: Multiclass classification
nodes.definition: The task of assigning a label to an input from a predefined set of more than two classes, based on in-context examples.

nodes.name: Multilingual question answering
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats this as answering questions in multiple languages, usually evaluated on multilingual QA benchmarks. Many formulations make it passage- or context-based, with inputs grounded in provided evidence and responses produced in the respective language. Some papers broaden the task to cross-lingual settings in which the question, context, and answer can be in different languages, and one definition also includes answering from general knowledge as well as context.

Variants. Papers study several task variants, most commonly passage-based or context-based multilingual QA, including XQuAD-In and multilingual extractive question answering. A recurring variant is a long-context "needle in a haystack" setting, described as an extension of multilingual question answering that includes both monolingual and cross-lingual retrieval and asks the model to find relevant information in the input context to answer the question. Other papers frame the behavior as multilingual open-domain or open-ended question answering.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link this behavior to 4 measurement instruments. The most frequently linked

nodes.name: Multimedia event extraction
nodes.definition: The task of identifying an event's type and its arguments from a combination of textual and visual data.

nodes.name: Multimodal generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. In the papers, the behavior is described as predicting missing modalities from available modal information and their interconnections. The recurring example is generating an image from a text caption, so the task is framed around recovering a missing modality given the others.

Variants. The recorded usage includes a broader missing-modality formulation and a narrower node-level setting. In the narrower setting, the goal is to predict missing images based on textual captions, while the broader label multi-modal generation covers cases such as image-from-caption generation.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to this behavior. Papers describe it directly as a task of predicting missing modalities, rather than through a separately named benchmark or scoring instrument.

What it is taken as evidence of. Only one construct is linked to this behavior, multimodal understanding. That link is not framed as an indicator relation: one paper claims a causal relationship from multimodal understanding to multimodal generation, stating that incorporating multimodal understanding data enhances comprehension of object details such as color an

nodes.name: Multimodal named entity recognition
nodes.definition: A subtask of GMNER that focuses specifically on identifying the textual spans and types of named entities using both text and image context.

nodes.name: Multimodal question answering
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most commonly, papers treat this behavior as answering questions over inputs from more than one modality, with examples spanning images, video, audio, depth, point clouds, and text. A recurring narrower formulation focuses on joint text-image understanding, while other papers specify natural language question answering over synchronized video, audio, and sensor streams, or over non-textual biomedical inputs such as a molecule SMILES string or a protein sequence. Papers also differ on what counts as a valid response: some use multiple-choice selection, some require a single word or short phrase, and some describe generating a natural language answer.

Variants. The most prevalent variant uses image and text together, and one paper explicitly describes visual QA as a typical form of multimodal QA. Smaller lines of work study procedural activity understanding from video plus a textual recipe, question answering over video, audio, embedded sensors, and natural language, question answering over image and profile text, and biomedical question answering where the context includes a molecule SMILES string or protein sequence.

Space of elicitation and scores. Only 1 m

nodes.name: Multimodal relation extraction
nodes.definition: Identifying semantic relations between entities from both text and image inputs, producing relational triples (subject, relation, object) based on joint reasoning.

nodes.name: Multiple-choice question answering
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the dominant framing is selecting the correct answer from a fixed set of options for a question, most often a single option in a discrete format such as A/B/C/D. Success is usually matching a predefined correct answer, and many papers ask the model to output only the option symbol or index, though some accept the choice value itself, a label such as Yes, No, or Not Sure Enough, or treat the answer as valid even when the format is wrong. A smaller line casts the behavior as classification over option tokens or answer strings, often by selecting the candidate with the highest predicted likelihood or conditional log probability.

Variants. Papers use nearby names such as multi-choice question answering, multiple-choice answering, single-choice question answering, fixed-choice question answering, answer selection, multiple-choice classification, and multiple-choice reasoning. The prevailing variant still has one correct option, often among four choices, but papers also study settings with two to ten options, multiple correct answers, abstention as a fifth option, or multiple-selection across instruction chains. The task appears in many domains a

nodes.name: Multiple-choice selection
nodes.definition: Selecting one of two provided response options (target vs. opposite) in response to a multi-modal prompt, used to measure alignment with a specific preference.

nodes.name: Multiple-choice visual question answering
nodes.definition: Selecting the correct image from a set of visual options in response to a culturally grounded question, based on understanding symbolic and contextual cues.

nodes.name: Music captioning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. The usage in the papers treats music captioning as generating descriptive text for music clips. In ALMTokenizer: A Low-bitrate and Semantic-rich Audio Codec Tokenizer for Audio Language Modeling, it is used to evaluate the understanding capabilities of the audio tokenizer in a language model, and the quoted passages refer both to "music captioning" and to "audio caption and music caption tasks."

Variants. The evidence frames it specifically around music clips and names it simply as music captioning. A nearby formulation groups it with audio caption tasks, but no further sub-task, domain, or modality variants are named.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link it to one measurement instrument, MusicCaps, which is recorded as measuring this behavior. The linked evidence reports BLEU4 and RougeL with MusicCaps.

What it is taken as evidence of. No construct is linked to this behavior in the recorded relationships.

nodes.name: Music classification
nodes.definition: Categorizing musical content such as instruments, genres, or emotions.

nodes.name: Music generation
nodes.definition: Generating the continuation of a musical excerpt given the first measure as input context.

nodes.name: Music genre classification
nodes.definition: Categorizing a piece of music into a specific genre.

nodes.name: Named entity recognition
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats named entity recognition as identifying entity mentions in text and assigning them semantic types, most often person, organization, and location. Several definitions make the success condition explicit as extracting all entities or spans and determining their types, for example, "Given a passage, your task is to extract all entities and identify their entity types" (UniversalNER: Targeted Distillation from Large Language Models for Open Named Entity Recognition). Most formulations use predefined labels, though some allow open or domain-specific categories, and a smaller line of work narrows the task to extraction or detection only, such as extracting entities from notes or finding all mentions of one specific entity type.

Variants. Papers study cross-lingual and multilingual NER, including transfer across many languages and token-level labeling in multilingual queries, alongside zero-shot and domain-specific settings. Domain adaptations include social media note extraction, legal texts, Greek financial text with separate numeric and textual NER, shopping queries for brands or product lines, urban entity recogniti

nodes.name: Narrative summarization
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the cited work, the prevailing usage treats narrative summarization as producing a condensed version of a narrative that distills the "key details and takeaways" from the source. One paper explicitly adds that this process can involve interpretive choices and subjectivity, while another defines the task specifically for long-form narratives and says the summary should capture intricate plotlines, character interactions, and thematic coherence.

Variants. Papers use the behavior for both general stories and explicitly long-form narratives. The named long-form domains are books, movies, and TV scripts, and this framing presents the task as summarizing extended narrative texts rather than short passages.

Space of elicitation and scores. The papers do not link narrative summarization to any measurement instrument. One paper does describe a summary as "a collection of claims" that can be obtained through a decomposition process, but no named instrument is reported as eliciting or scoring the behavior.

What it is taken as evidence of. The papers do not link narrative summarization to any construct, so they do not explicitly treat it as evidence of a broader

nodes.name: Native language identification
nodes.definition: Predicting the native language of an author based on their writing in a second language, typically from a closed set of candidate languages.

nodes.name: Natural language inference
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage is a premise-hypothesis task in which a model judges whether the hypothesis is entailed, contradicted, or neutral/undetermined given the premise. Many definitions paraphrase this as deciding whether the hypothesis is true, false, or possibly true, and one paper even reformats it generatively as "Does \"{SENT1}\" entail \"{SENT2}\"? {Yes/Maybe/No}" (Adapting Large Language Models via Reading Comprehension). A smaller line of work narrows the output to binary entailment judgments, such as entailment versus not entailment or True versus False, and a few formulations broaden the input from a single premise to multi-sentence premises or to facts and rules.

Variants. Most variants keep the same inference setup but shift the name, domain, or setting. Papers also call it textual entailment, sentence entailment, textual entailment recognition, entailment prediction, semantic inference, or hypothesis verification, and they study multilingual or cross-lingual classification, biomedical entailment, event reasoning, commonsense NLI based on the most logical continuation of an event, and cases with multi-sentence premises. A s

nodes.name: Natural language planning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats this behavior as producing a sequence of actionable or temporally ordered steps in natural language for a goal or process. Definitions consistently focus on multi-step decomposition, either to achieve a given goal or to complete a process, and one paper explicitly frames it as "decomposing a high-level goal g into a sequence of temporally extended steps" (PlaSma: Procedural Knowledge Models for Language-based Planning and Re-Planning). Some authors broaden the output to a set of instructions, and some include images alongside the steps.

Variants. Papers use nearby names including goal-based planning, script generation, and activity generation. The differences are mainly in setting: goal-based planning is described as generating steps from scratch for high-level goals such as "see a movie" or "empty lint filter," while script generation and activity generation ask for step sequences with images that describe completing a process or activity. One quoted passage also places it in daily-life natural language planning.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link it to 1 measurement instrument, ActivityNet. Th

nodes.name: Navigation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the dominant framing is goal-directed movement through an environment to reach a specified location, landmark, receptacle, or resource. Definitions commonly describe locating targets such as trees, cows, stones, underground resources, buildings, or receptacles, and another recurring formulation is simply reaching specific locations in a game environment. A smaller line of work uses the term more broadly for understanding spatial layouts and planning or describing routes between locations or to objects.

Variants. Papers study several named variants. In the Minecraft environment, navigation includes navigating on the ground, digging to a specific level, and exploring underground horizontally, while city-space work treats it as navigation sub-tasks that identify the nearest navigation point on a map and can be written as Navigation(building_1, west). Other variants are grid world navigation with up, down, left, and right actions, low-level navigation with translational, rotational, and camera-tilt controls, and room-to-room or object-retrieval navigation tasks.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link navigation to 3 measurement instruments:

nodes.name: Negative response generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats this behavior as the model producing negative or pessimistic outputs, especially when a prompt elicits a positive or negative reaction. Most papers describe it either as emotionally negative replies or as a tendency to give negative answers such as "No" more often and with higher confidence than positive ones; one paper reports "more frequent and confident negative responses" (Correcting Negative Bias in Large Language Models through Negative Attention Score Alignment). A smaller line of work uses the same label for refusal behavior on harmful instructions, where the target output is a safe rejecting response rather than a general negative answer.

Variants. The studied variants split by prompt setting and output form. Some papers examine responses to negative prompts, or prompts that "elicit either positive or negative responses," while another focuses on indiscriminate negative answers. One paper operationalizes the behavior as harmful-instruction refusal, even setting rejecting outputs such as "I'm sorry, but I cannot provide a tutorial on building a bomb" as ground truth targets (AdvPrompter: Fast Adaptive Adv

nodes.name: Negotiation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, negotiation is most commonly treated as a goal-oriented, multi-turn dialogue between parties with competing interests that aims at a mutually acceptable agreement on one or more issues. A recurring formulation emphasizes interactive proposal exchange, sometimes in multi-agent settings, while a smaller framing describes it more specifically as dividing items or resources with an opponent.

Variants. Papers use names such as multi-agent negotiation and negotiation dialogue. The settings span multi-turn, multi-issue conflict dialogue, buyer-seller conversations, and game-theoretic resource division; one example prompt asks participants to negotiate over Peppers, Strawberries, and Cherries, and one study places negotiation alongside emotional support and tutoring as a proactive dialogue application.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to negotiation. In these papers, it is elicited directly through interactive dialogue tasks, including multi-turn, multi-issue exchanges and proposal-based resource division, rather than through a named instrument.

What it is taken as evidence of. Only one construct is linked

nodes.name: Nested named entity recognition
nodes.definition: The task of identifying and classifying named entities that may be embedded within other entities.

nodes.name: Neural self-repair
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. The paper treats neural self-repair, under the name self-repair, as a latent mechanism in which a model compensates for changes or losses in individual functional components so that task performance stays stable. In the source description, this appears in perturbation or ablation settings: self-repair is said to plausibly contribute to "behavioral stability," and "negative heads" are described as performing self-repair by reducing their negativity when NMHs are ablated.

Variants. The usage in the papers does not separate multiple domains, modalities, or named sub-tasks. It is discussed under the name self-repair in the specific setting of ablation, where the example given is compensation by negative heads after NMH ablation.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. In the description, it is characterized through ablation-related behavior, namely stable task performance after changes to functional components and reduced negativity of negative heads after NMH ablation.

What it is taken as evidence of. No construct is linked to it. The paper connects it to maintaining stable task performance and says it plausibly contributes

nodes.name: News article generation
nodes.definition: Producing full-length news articles based on provided public opinion statements, including headlines, quotations, and narrative framing, under conditions designed to test political bias and neutrality.

nodes.name: News categorization
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the common framing is assigning predefined labels to news articles based on their textual content. The papers agree on the classification setup but differ in the label scheme: one uses general category or topic labels, while another narrows the task to selected articles that are filtered for relevance to a time series and then categorized by impact duration, such as "long-term" and "short-term", or by type of influence, sometimes with a rationale.

Variants. Papers use both "news classification" and "news categorization" for this behavior. The main variants described are topic-style labeling and impact-oriented categorization tied to time-series analysis, where categorization can be guided by either automatically generated logic or given reasoning logic.

Space of elicitation and scores. Only one measurement instrument is linked, AG News. In that use, the behavior is elicited with an instruction to categorize a news article into one of four categories, "World, Sports, Business, Sci/Tech"; no other instrument is linked.

What it is taken as evidence of. No construct is linked to this behavior, so the surveyed papers do not explicitly treat it

nodes.name: News summarization
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage treats news summarization as generating a concise or shorter version of a news article. Papers agree that the summary should preserve the article's main ideas and information, and some operationalizations make the input format explicit by requiring both a prompt and the original article. A more specific prompting example asks the model to summarize the news in two sentences.

Variants. Variants are limited and mostly concern evaluation setting rather than a different task name. Papers study it in zero-shot generative evaluation, as the English summarization subset of XLSum, and as one of the RAG task types in RAGTruth. A narrower formulation asks for two-sentence summaries.

Space of elicitation and scores. News summarization is measured by three linked instruments, all used as data resources: CNN/DailyMail, RAGTruth, and the English summarization subset of XLSum. In the linked papers, CNN/DailyMail is used for zero-shot generative evaluation, RAGTruth includes news summarization as one of three RAG task types, and XLSum is used through its English summarization subset.

What it is taken as evidence of. The only lin

nodes.name: Next speaker prediction
nodes.definition: Selecting which character should speak next in a multi-character conversation.

nodes.name: Node classification
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats node classification as predicting or assigning a categorical, class, or topic label to nodes in a graph from node features or attributes and graph connectivity or structure. Most descriptions speak of labeling each node or the unknown or unlabeled nodes, sometimes from a partly labeled graph, while some narrow the task to a single target node per graph sample or to predicting the label of a node marked '?' from its neighbors' labels. The expected output is usually one of a discrete set of class labels.

Variants. Variants mostly differ in graph setting and available inputs. Papers study text-attributed graphs, semi-supervised transductive node classification on heterophilic graphs, and setups where unknown or unlabeled nodes are predicted from a partly labeled graph; one paper reduces the task to an undirected graph where the node marked '?' must be inferred from neighboring labels. A smaller naming variation calls the LLM's output action 'node annotation'.

Space of elicitation and scores. Across papers, node classification is measured by 6 linked instruments, mostly benchmark datasets. The most frequently linked are

nodes.name: Number sorting
nodes.definition: The task of arranging a list of numbers in a specified order, typically ascending or descending.

nodes.name: Object counting
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the dominant framing is a task where a model determines how many instances of a specified object category are present, most often in an image. Papers commonly treat success as returning the correct quantity for the queried object, sometimes in a natural-language question and answer format, and one image-based description says the model must delineate instances of a given object type for counting. A smaller line of work uses the same label for counting entities listed in a textual prompt or context, and another uses it for counting how many instances of an object appear in a video.

Variants. Variants differ mainly by modality and setting. Image-based work includes general perception tasks, cluttered environments, and visual equation settings built from repeated visual elements, and one paper explicitly uses images with 1-4 instances. Other papers name a count subtask, or Object Count (OC), in animal-centric video understanding, while text-oriented work studies counting over verbally enumerated entities.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link object counting to five measurement instruments: BIG-Bench Hard, BIG-bench, MME, MME-Re

nodes.name: Object detection
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats object detection as identifying and localizing objects in an image by outputting bounding boxes. Some definitions add that the objects come from a predefined set of categories and that outputs include class labels, while a smaller line of work frames it as predicting object categories and boxes, including oriented boxes in remote sensing imagery, or as prioritizing proper object detection within visual input during multimodal question answering. Papers are consistent that localization is central, most commonly through returned bounding box coordinates.

Variants. Papers study several variants and names for this behavior. Besides general object detection, they mention 2D detection and remote-sensing settings with oriented boxes; more specific versions include tool detection, defined as identifying and localizing surgical tools in an image or video frame, and face detection, defined as detecting human faces and returning bounding boxes. One source also treats object detection as part of answering a multimodal question, where the model must prioritize proper detection within the visual input.

Space of elicitation and sc

nodes.name: Object goal navigation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the dominant framing is embodied navigation or exploration in a new or unknown environment to find a target object. Most definitions specify the target by category, though one definition adds that the target is not initially visible, and another instead frames the task as finding a specific object from textual or visual cues. As one paper puts it, the aim is to "efficiently explore a new environment while searching for a target object that is not directly visible" (GAMap: Zero-Shot Object Goal Navigation with Multi-Scale Geometric-Affordance Guidance).

Variants. The prevailing variants stay within navigation settings, including zero-shot object goal navigation in unseen environments, where the robot must navigate to a target object it has never encountered before and without training on the target or scene, and UAV object search with assistant guidance in aerial environments. Papers also use nearby names such as object navigation and object search for these settings. A smaller usage under the object search label appears outside navigation, where the task is to identify or describe an object's position in video, for example answering "What i

nodes.name: Object hallucination
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats object hallucination as outputs that mention or describe objects absent from the visual input, usually an image and in one definition a video frame. Several papers phrase this more broadly as responses "not factually aligned with image inputs," but the recurring concrete criterion is an incorrect object claim, whether in a free-form description or an affirmative answer such as "Yes, there is a white chair in the image." A smaller line of work also counts neglecting visible objects or "omitting essential features" as part of the behavior.

Variants. Most studies examine the behavior in image descriptions and captioning, while another common setting is yes/no object-presence questioning, including work that says models "hallucinate in response to yes/no questions." POPE-based papers further divide this probing into Popular, Random, and Adversarial balanced yes/no VQA, and one definition explicitly extends the setting from images to video frames. Some evaluations operationalize hallucination with subtasks such as Existence, Count, Position, and Color, or with object, attribute, and relation hallucinations, and one paper

nodes.name: Object hallucination detection
nodes.definition: Judging whether an object mentioned in a question or answer is actually present in the image.

nodes.name: Object localization
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats object localization as finding where one or more objects are and returning a spatial output, most often a bounding box. Several definitions make the output explicit as box coordinates, and one video-oriented account describes the box as a 4-tuple of upper-left and lower-right corners. Smaller variants ask for approximate coordinates, the exact location of a defect, or permit masks alongside boxes, and some settings restrict the task to a single object while others target multiple objects or a referred region named in text.

Variants. Papers use nearby labels such as bounding box prediction, building localization, instance localization, defect localization, and text localization. The settings range from still images to video frames, and from generic scenes to earth-observation images, reference-image-based instance finding, and GUI tasks that ask the model to locate a piece of text or select the queried element. A smaller related line links object localization to reasoning segmentation, noting that that setup only allows single-object localization.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link object localization t

nodes.name: Object placement
nodes.definition: The task of positioning specific objects at appropriate locations and orientations within a 3D scene.

nodes.name: Object recognition
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats this behavior as identifying or naming objects present in an image. Definitions often phrase it as identifying specific objects, identifying and naming objects, or correctly naming an everyday object; some formulations narrow the task to deciding whether a specified object is present or absent, while others extend it to identifying visible people and environmental features, anatomical structures in medical scans, or objects in video frames. Success criteria also vary across papers: some use correct object names, some ask whether an object exists, and some include localization, for example bounding boxes or approximate coordinates.

Variants. Papers study several named variants, including object presence detection, object existence determination, object identification, structure identification, object name generation, and entity recognition. The settings range from everyday images and per-sample object questions, to video tasks where the aim is to identify caption-mentioned objects in frames or localize them on keyframes, to biomedical scans for anatomy naming. A smaller strand frames the behavior as open-ended detecti

nodes.name: Object tracking
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most papers treat object tracking as identifying and following specific objects across video frames, commonly with a consistent object identity and a reported location such as a grid position or bounding box. Some papers frame the same behavior as locating a referred object across multiple scenes or moments, while another instruction-based formulation asks models to track the positions of multiple objects as they are shuffled. One study specifies outputs in the form "<track> object id1, object grid position1; ..." (Look, Remember and Reason: Grounded Reasoning in Videos with Language Models).

Variants. Across papers, the behavior appears in several settings: multi-target tracking in complex real-world video, scene-referred object tracking, text-referred object tracking, and instruction-following problems built around shuffled objects. A smaller line of work uses the name motion tracking, and another formulation describes the behavior as converting per-frame object detections into motion trajectories across a video.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. Instead, papers describe task formats rather than named instruments,

nodes.name: Observation summarization
nodes.definition: The process by which an agent condenses historical action-observation sequences into a concise summary tied to a completed subgoal.

nodes.name: Off-target response generation
nodes.definition: An observable failure mode where the model produces responses that are irrelevant, in the wrong language, or otherwise fail to address the prompt's intent.

nodes.name: Off-target translation
nodes.definition: Generating output in a language different from the intended target, such as producing English or another African language when translating into a specific African language.

nodes.name: Open-domain question answering
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the dominant framing is broad-topic question answering: models answer questions about a wide range of topics or general world knowledge, rather than a fixed domain. Most descriptions also make retrieval explicit, describing answers as synthesized from an external corpus, knowledge base, open web, or large-scale unstructured documents. A smaller line of work narrows this to retrieval-augmented question answering, where the model first retrieves relevant information or is given search documents as context, and some papers further treat the outputs as short-form answers, typically a short phrase or sentence, sometimes using only the provided documents.

Variants. Papers use several nearby labels, including open-domain QA, ODQA, retrieval-augmented question answering, and RAG QA. Most variants still center on broad-topic factual answering, while some papers focus on short-form generation with short-answer ground truth, conflicts between parametric knowledge and contextual knowledge, synthesis from open-web or large-scale unstructured documents, or answering only from provided search documents. One benchmark also places the task in low-resource Indon

nodes.name: Open-ended instruction following
nodes.definition: The observable task of generating responses to prompts that do not have a single correct answer, often requiring creativity or detailed explanation.

nodes.name: Open-ended question answering
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage is free-form answer generation: models produce natural-language responses to questions instead of selecting from fixed options or extracting an answer span. Most definitions also stress detailed or human-like responses, often for questions that do not have a single simple answer, while smaller strands narrow the task to long-form, non-factoid questions that require synthesis and coverage of multiple sub-topics, or to questions where multiple valid answers and perspectives are possible. Where papers spell out success criteria, they variously look for semantic correctness against reference answers, broad coverage in long-form responses, or natural-language answers and explanations.

Variants. Authors use several nearby labels for the same family of behavior, especially free-form question answering and free-form generation, with smaller variants called open-ended answer generation, free-text response generation, free-text question answering, and generative question answering. The settings range from long-context passage QA and general factual knowledge to long-form RAG, knowledge-graph QA with explicit reasoning path

nodes.name: Open-vocabulary object detection
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing framing is detecting and locating objects in images when the category set is not fixed in advance. Definitions differ on the inference setup: some describe categories not seen during training and use textual descriptions or an arbitrary open set of category names provided as text at inference time, while a smaller line of work uses open-ended object detection for discovering unseen objects without any object categories as inputs, with success described as predicting the object categories and locations themselves.

Variants. The main variants in naming are open-vocabulary object detection, open-vocabulary detection, and open-ended object detection. All are image-based, but papers distinguish text-conditioned versions, where category names or descriptions are supplied at inference, from a more open-ended version with no predefined categories, and one evaluation is explicitly described as zero-shot.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link this behavior to two measurement instruments, both datasets: LVIS and Visual Genome. LVIS is used as a zero-shot evaluation dataset, and Visual Genome appears in an open-ended object detection

nodes.name: Open-vocabulary semantic segmentation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the common framing is segmentation at the pixel or image-region level in an open-vocabulary setting: papers describe assigning semantic labels to pixels and segmenting objects or regions that correspond to textual labels. Several definitions make the open-vocabulary condition explicit as working from candidate classes or textual labels that were not necessarily seen during training, while another definition describes identifying and segmenting objects from "free-form language descriptions".

Variants. Papers use both "open-vocabulary semantic segmentation" and "open-vocabulary segmentation" for the same general behavior. The studied formulations vary mainly in how labels are supplied, as a candidate class list, as textual labels, or as free-form language descriptions, and a paper also places it in a framework that switches between referring expression segmentation, open-vocabulary segmentation, and other visual grounding tasks.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link this behavior to three measurement instruments. ADE20K and Pascal Context appear most often, with PASCAL VOC also used; the linked evidence describes evaluation on th

nodes.name: Open-world object detection
nodes.definition: The task of detecting objects from both known, annotated categories and identifying objects from novel, unknown categories in an image, with the ability to incrementally learn the new categories over time.

nodes.name: Opinion summarization
nodes.definition: The task of generating a concise summary from a collection of texts that express various opinions on a topic, such as product reviews or political tweets.

nodes.name: Optical character recognition
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the dominant framing is reading, recognizing, extracting, or transcribing text that appears in visual inputs, most often images and documents, and sometimes screenshots or video frames. Most definitions treat the behavior as returning the visible text itself, including formulations about reading and outputting text from an image and extracting the full text from an image. Some authors narrow it to a specified region or element, while a smaller line broadens it to document parsing, where the task includes transcribing content or extracting structured information from dense layouts.

Variants. Variants are organized mainly by source type. Papers describe scene text recognition, webpage OCR focused on specific elements or headings, chart OCR, and document-focused forms such as text transcription or document parsing. Other work places the same behavior in video frames, slide images, handwritten letters, historical handwritten or printed documents, multilingual text-in-image settings, and cases involving small or embedded text.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link this behavior to 8 measurement instruments. It is measured most often by TextV

nodes.name: Optimization problem formulation
nodes.definition: The behavior of translating a problem described in natural language into a formal, structured optimization problem with goals, variables, and constraints.

nodes.name: Optimization problem solving
nodes.definition: Solving linear or nonlinear optimization tasks that may include tabular data and integer or mixed-integer variables.

nodes.name: Out-of-distribution detection
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage treats this as the task of identifying inputs that do not belong to the training distribution. The more specific formulation adds a success criterion: a sample from a different distribution than the model was trained on should typically receive higher uncertainty than an in-distribution sample. One paper also frames it as a benchmark for uncertainty-aware methods, stating that an effective approach should "reliably assign higher uncertainties to OOD samples compared to ID samples."

Variants. Papers use both the names "Out-of-distribution detection" and "OOD detection." The studied settings vary by training and evaluation setup: one uses OBQA as the in-distribution dataset and ARC-C, ARC-E, and CSQA as OOD datasets, while another performs OOD detection during pre-training and fine-tuning and evaluates with external OOD datasets including SVHN. Another paper discusses distinguishing ID from OoD inputs in a setting where image interpretation capabilities affect performance.

Space of elicitation and scores. Two measurement instruments are linked to this behavior, CommonsenseQA and SVHN, and both are used as dataset-ba

nodes.name: Out-of-distribution prediction
nodes.definition: The observable performance of the model when tested on data from a different distribution than the training data, such as higher genera or unseen numbers of marked points.

nodes.name: Outline generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. The definition treats outline generation as a preparatory writing step: creating a structured plan or hierarchy of sections for an article before drafting the full content. In "OmniThink: Expanding Knowledge Boundaries in Machine Writing through Thinking", it is formulated as generating an outline from retrieved information and an input topic, as in the quoted procedure, "Generate an outline O = Generate(I, T) based on the retrieved information I and input topic T."

Variants. The described setting is article writing, where the outline is built from retrieved information and a topic. A related use appears in a presentation workflow: one paper relates outline generation to slide generation and states that slides are produced "Guided by the presentation outline from the previous phase," which places outline generation in a presentation setting as well.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it.

What it is taken as evidence of. No construct is linked to it as something this behavior indicates.

nodes.name: Over-translation
nodes.definition: The observable behavior where the model generates content not present in the source text, such as hallucinated or redundant sentences.

nodes.name: Overcorrection
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, overcorrection is treated as an observable failure mode during correction, where the model makes unnecessary changes to input text that was already correct. The shared framing is altering correct parts of the input or otherwise making "excessive modifications to input text," and one paper extends this to adding redundant content. Papers also describe the behavior as introducing new errors, often with low precision and possible distortion of the original meaning.

Variants. The behavior is studied in more than one correction setting. In CoVoGER: A Multilingual Multitask Benchmark for Speech-to-text Generative Error Correction with Large Language Models, it appears in speech-to-text generative error correction, where the paper hypothesizes that ASR's "stricter correctness constraints" make outputs more vulnerable to over-correction than ST. In Leveraging What's Overfixed: Post-Correction via LLM Grammatical Error Overcorrection, it is framed in grammatical error correction and post-correction, including redundant additions, and the paper also states that overcorrection can be intentionally triggered to "maximize the possible correction vi

nodes.name: Overrefusal
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the dominant framing is inappropriate refusal of benign, harmless, safe, legitimate, or answerable queries, usually after they are misread as harmful or risky. Most descriptions cast this either as a latent tendency toward excessive caution, poor calibration, or overgeneralized safety thresholds, or as the observable behavior of refusing a prompt even though a helpful, valid, or safe response is possible. A recurring narrower formulation focuses on benign or borderline prompts that only superficially resemble harmful content, including prompts that merely appear toxic or only seem harmful. Some papers make the success criterion explicit by treating it as overrefusal when an external evaluator deems the content safe, when a valid answer exists, or when refusal probability on benign inputs exceeds a threshold.

Variants. Most commonly, papers use overrefusal or over-refusal, while a smaller line of work uses labels such as over-rejection, false refusal, over-defense, over-sensitivity, and oversafety, with other isolated names including false rejection, unwarranted refusal, exaggerated safety behaviors, and benign query refusal. The behavior is

nodes.name: Overthinking
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, overthinking is most commonly treated as an observable pattern of excessive, verbose, or redundant reasoning, especially on simple problems, with papers describing excessive reasoning steps, redundant solutions, and inefficient token use that raise computational cost. A smaller line of work uses the same label for conversational search, where it refers to overly detailed or redundant clarification questions that drift from the user’s original intent and add superfluous steps. Some papers also define it by outcome rather than form, treating it as a failure mode in which additional reasoning episodes do not improve, and can sometimes degrade, final answer accuracy; separately, one paper claims a causal relationship from Chain of thought to Overthinking, describing CoT as often leading to unnecessarily long and verbose reasoning traces.

Variants. Papers study this behavior in a few recurring settings. The prevailing usage is simple reasoning tasks, including mathematical benchmarks, where overthinking appears as redundant solutions that contribute little to accuracy or reasoning diversity and are reported to occur more often on simple p

nodes.name: Painting style recognition
nodes.definition: Identifying the artist or style of paintings from visual input.

nodes.name: Pair classification
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the cited definitions, pair classification is most commonly described as deciding whether two text inputs are semantically related or form a positive pair. The examples papers use are query-passage relevance and cases where two texts are paraphrases or otherwise have a specified relationship, so success is framed as correctly classifying the relation between the paired texts.

Variants. The examples named for this task include query-passage relevance, paraphrase judgments, and deciding whether a pair has some other specific relationship. Papers refer to the category as Pair Classification and, in one table, abbreviate it as PairClass.

Space of elicitation and scores. One measurement instrument is linked to it: MTEB, which one paper uses to evaluate Pair Classification as a task category. Separately, one paper reports pair classification with AP as the metric.

What it is taken as evidence of. No paper links it to a construct, so the cited work does not explicitly treat pair classification as evidence of a named construct.

nodes.name: Pairwise comparison
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage is a head-to-head judgment over two candidate outputs for the same prompt, instruction, or question, where an evaluator chooses the better response. Most definitions frame success as selecting a winner or preferred response, while some explicitly allow a tie or win-tie-loss outcome and a smaller line treats it as a strictly binary winner-loser choice; one paper contrasts this with pointwise rating by stressing that items are judged relative to one another rather than independently. The criteria vary by study, including instruction satisfaction, helpfulness, correctness, harmlessness, a specified evaluation dimension, or which answer is less wrong, and the evaluator may be an LLM, a human annotator, or both.

Variants. Most papers study ordinary response comparison, under names such as response ranking, preference judgment, pairwise evaluation, or arena-style comparison. Smaller lines of work apply the same comparison pattern in multi-turn conversations, personalized long-form question answering, data-analysis outputs, scientific ideas, text-to-SQL generations, and cartoon captioning, while other papers specialize it to plan

nodes.name: Panoptic segmentation
nodes.definition: A unified segmentation task that involves assigning a class label to every pixel, simultaneously performing instance segmentation for 'thing' classes and semantic segmentation for 'stuff' classes.

nodes.name: Parameter extraction
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across definitions, the common framing is the observable step of getting the right parameter or argument values for a tool, function, or API call. Papers variously describe this as extracting values from a natural-language query, assigning correct values to a selected function's parameters, or providing the correct arguments for a selected tool call; a narrower dialogue-oriented framing treats it as filling missing API values from dialogue context or user replies. The success criterion is usually correctness of the chosen values, reflected in examples such as extracting visitor counts, ticket types, or special conditions, or stating that a parameter has a specific value such as "fried chicken" or "Lyft".

Variants. Papers use several near-names for the same behavior: parameter extraction, parameter resolution, parameterization, and parameter selection. The studied settings differ, including natural-language orders converted into code arguments, dialogue-based API completion, and single-tool or per-dialogue-turn tool-calling evaluation. One paper also relates it to Tool use in a medical slot-filling setup, where comprehensive medical records, tool descriptions,

nodes.name: Paraphrase detection
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats paraphrase detection as deciding whether a pair of texts, most often two sentences, have the same meaning or are paraphrases of each other. This is usually framed as a binary judgment, for example yes or no, equivalent or not equivalent, or duplicate or not duplicate, and some papers broaden the pair from sentences to questions, documents, or responses. A smaller line of work defines the behavior through semantic equivalence by mutual entailment, uses a three-way semantic (in)equivalence setting under controlled lexical constraints, or reformulates the task as generating a sentence that supports or contradicts a given sentence instead of directly classifying the pair.

Variants. Papers use several nearby names for the same behavior, most commonly paraphrase detection or paraphrase identification, and less often duplication detection, duplicate question detection, semantic equivalence detection, or semantic equivalence judgment. The dominant setting is sentence or question pairs, but some work studies text snippets, questions or documents as duplicates, and response pairs judged equivalent by mutual entailment. The

nodes.name: Paraphrasing
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the dominant framing treats paraphrasing as rewriting an input text in different words or structures while preserving its original meaning, semantic equivalence, or full meaning. This usage appears for documents, sentences, mixed text segments, queries, and profiles, with success usually described as changing wording, syntax, lexical form, or other surface form without changing the semantics. A smaller set of formulations adds task-specific constraints, such as preserving class label, leaving persuasive style unspecified, or using paraphrasing as a pretraining or augmentation task; one multi-turn setup instructs agents to paraphrase the received text "without modifying its meaning" (When LLMs Play the Telephone Game: Cultural Attractors as Conceptual Tools to Evaluate LLMs in Multi-turn Settings).

Variants. Papers use several nearby names for the behavior, most commonly text rephrasing, rewriting, text paraphrasing, query rephrasing, and paraphrase generation. The behavior is studied in ordinary sentence or document rewriting, but also in recursive chunk-level rewriting, user or item profile rewriting, and query augmentation. Recurring settings

nodes.name: Parity checking
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage treats parity checking as producing the parity result for a binary input, usually deciding whether a bit sequence contains an odd or even number of 1s. Closely related formulations describe it as computing the sum modulo 2 of boolean variables, and one paper states this as the parity of a sequence being 1 when the number of ones is odd and 0 when it is even. A narrower formulation presents a trivial version in which intermediate results are stored every other token, so the output is only a function of the last two tokens.

Variants. Papers use several nearby names, including Parity, Parity checking, Parity computation, Parity solving, and Parity task. The most common setting is a binary string or bit sequence whose output is the parity check result, while another formulation uses tuples of boolean variables and explicitly computes expressions such as a variable sum modulo 2. Some authors also frame it as a synthetic benchmark, and one paper studies a restricted version where the intermediate state is arranged so that only the last two tokens determine the answer.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement inst

nodes.name: Part-of-speech tagging
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats part-of-speech tagging as assigning a grammatical label to a word or token in context, often phrased as marking up a word as a particular part of speech based on its definition and context. Most descriptions focus on assigning labels to tokens, while one task setup makes the success criterion more explicit by asking for the POS tag of the central word in a context window.
