Variants. Papers study this behavior in several settings rather than with a single formulation. Some place it among traditional NLP tasks in code-mixed text, some describe it as a linguistically motivated token-classification task, and another variant focuses on Chinese characters, where models identify the POS of a central word in a 5-word window and may rely on radicals when the word contains unfamiliar characters.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. In the task descriptions, papers elicit it directly by asking for part-of-speech labels, including a setup that presents a 5-word window with at most one punctuation mark and asks for the tag of the central word.

What it is taken as evidence of. No

nodes.name: Part segmentation
nodes.definition: The task of generating a segmentation mask for a specific part of an object, rather than the entire object.

nodes.name: Patent claim generation
nodes.definition: The observable production of patent claims by an LLM, following a standardized format that includes a preamble, listed elements, and functional linkages, typically for Claim 1 of a patent.

nodes.name: Pathfinding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across definitions, the prevailing usage treats pathfinding as producing a valid route from a start point to a goal in a structured space, most often a graph or grid. Papers variously require the output to be the constituent edges of the correct path, a sequence of nodes, actions, coordinates, or directional moves, and one next-step formulation asks for "the next vertex on the path from the start to the goal vertex." Success is usually framed as correctness or validity of the path under task constraints, though some formulations add conditions such as avoiding holes, retrieving keys before unlocking doors, or reaching the goal through a full trajectory.

Variants. Most variants study graph or grid navigation and use labels such as graph path finding, route finding, graph search, route planning, and path planning. These cover directed graphs, Frozen Lake style grids that require avoiding holes, maze tasks, grid worlds with dependencies such as move, pick up, and unlock, visual navigation that outputs a full sequence of directions, and agent path planning as a trajectory to a designated goal. A smaller line of work broadens the label to "search ability," either

nodes.name: Pattern inference
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage treats pattern inference as a visual rule-discovery task: a model must identify and generalize a pattern and then use that rule to complete a missing element. Papers largely agree on this core formulation, but differ in the visual setup, with one describing completion of a matrix of abstract shapes and another describing a sequence of frames in which the correct element must satisfy an underlying rule. Success is framed as correctly completing the pattern or selecting the element that completes the sequence.

Variants. Authors use both pattern inference and pattern completion for this behavior. One paper places it within a multimodal reasoning taxonomy and describes it as a math problem centered on abstract shape matrices, while another studies it through Raven's Progressive Matrices, where object attributes evolve according to different rules across frames and the task is to complete the sequence.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it in the papers.

What it is taken as evidence of. No construct is linked to it in the papers, so there is no recorded agreement or disagreement ab

nodes.name: Peer review generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed papers, this behavior is treated as generating a review-style evaluation of an academic paper. One definition frames it as producing critiques and numerical scores from the paper's content and its context in a community graph, while another frames it as structured feedback from content analysis that covers strengths, weaknesses, and acceptance decisions. The quoted passages further describe the output as "delivering the final score, decision and comments" and as "generating high-quality, insightful evaluations."

Variants. Papers use the near-synonymous labels "review writing" and "paper review generation," with some variation in setting and conditioning. One paper studies it as "the final stage of the automatic research simulation" and labels it "Stage 3: Review Writing," whereas the other centers on the final review package itself. The definitions also differ in what information the review is based on, either the paper's content plus community-graph context or content analysis alone. One paper also reports it as related to Text generation, placing it after paper reading and paper writing, with each stage using the previous stage's output

nodes.name: Persona-conditioned generation
nodes.definition: Generating claims that reflect the ideological stance and rhetorical style of a specified persona (e.g., Democrat, Republican, Moderate) by conditioning the model on role descriptions.

nodes.name: Personality mirroring
nodes.definition: The observable alignment of language use between conversational partners at the level of the entire dialogue.

nodes.name: Personality prediction
nodes.definition: Inferring MBTI-related cognitive-process labels or personality types from demographic descriptions.

nodes.name: Personalized response generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage is a task of generating user-tailored natural language responses for a specific person, usually by reflecting that person's preferred style, content, tone, background, or prior interactions. FaST: Feature-aware Sampling and Tuning for Personalized Preference Alignment with Limited Data describes it as generating "user-tailored responses for unseen contexts" from preferences derived from a shared questionnaire, while other papers treat successful outputs as replies that incorporate profile details, schedules, dialogue history, or a user image, or as speaker-specific replies in multi-party dialogue. A smaller line of work narrows the task to item review generation, or to outputs that maximize expected personalized utility across dimensions such as helpfulness, harmlessness, or humor.

Variants. Variants span several settings and names. Papers refer to speaker-specific response generation in multi-party dialogue, personalized response generation for conversational assistants that use dialogue history, profile, schedule, or long-term interactions, personalized text generation in open-ended tasks, personalized review generation f

nodes.name: Phoneme recognition
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. The papers converge on a speech task at the phonetic-unit level, but differ slightly in emphasis. One defines it as recognizing and distinguishing individual phonemes within speech audio, while another defines it as transcribing speech into a sequence of constituent phonetic units. What counts as the behavior is therefore framed either as identifying individual phonemes or as producing a phonetic-unit sequence from speech.

Variants. Papers use both the names phoneme recognition and phone recognition. The described setting is speech audio, and one paper abbreviates the task as PR and places it among multiple instruction-tuning tasks. No other sub-tasks, domains, or modalities are named.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it.

What it is taken as evidence of. Papers do not link it to any construct.

nodes.name: Physics problem solving
nodes.definition: The observable task of generating a step-by-step solution and a final answer to a physics problem presented in natural language.

nodes.name: Placeholder generation
nodes.definition: The observable task of generating a response that includes placeholders as instructed.

nodes.name: Plagiarism
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Papers that define it treat plagiarism as submitting code that is highly similar to existing public solutions, with public Kaggle notebooks given as the example source. What counts as the behavior is the degree of similarity between the submitted code and those existing solutions.

Space of elicitation and scores. It is measured by one instrument, Dolos. In MLE-bench: Evaluating Machine Learning Agents on Machine Learning Engineering, Dolos is used to compare an agent's submitted code against the top 50 associated notebooks from the relevant Kaggle competition as a plagiarism check.

What it is taken as evidence of. The papers do not link this behavior to any construct.

nodes.name: Plan execution
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats plan execution as carrying out a generated plan step by step. Most commonly, success is described as following sequential steps to solve a task or reach a verdict, with one paper noting that users see only the first step and that later steps appear "one at a time for cognitive ease," while another describes the model as executing an evaluation plan step by step to analyze responses, verify criteria, and arrive at a final verdict. A smaller formulation treats execution as performing each planned action correctly by retrieving and running associated code snippets.

Variants. Papers study this behavior in several settings. One line uses human task following, where a user follows an LLM-generated plan with steps revealed sequentially and with support such as calculator or web search. Another treats it as self-execution of planned actions by retrieving Python code snippets associated with an execute relation. A further variant appears in evaluation, where the model follows an evaluation plan through intermediate checks, such as verifying whether a response contains required attributes, before producing a final judgment

nodes.name: Plan generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage is the direct production of a sequence of actions or steps meant to solve a planning problem or achieve a specified goal. Many papers phrase this as moving from an initial state to a goal state, or as generating reasonable solutions for given tasks, and some make the directness explicit by describing a complete plan produced "without the help of any external planning library" or other external planner. A smaller range of formulations narrows the output to numbered steps, a step-by-step action plan, or an ordered sequence of API function calls.

Variants. Papers study this behavior in several task-specific forms. The most recurring alternate label is task planning, used for generating discrete steps for a high-level task and for step-by-step plans from safety guard inputs; smaller lines of work treat it as multi-step planning for ordered API calls, meta-plan generation for collaborative long-term decomposition into subtasks, transition pathway generation for textual material transformations from a source to a target with specified properties, and a turn-level dialogue flow that specifies intentions, slot-value pairs,

nodes.name: Plan revision
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats this behavior as revising an existing plan, action sequence, preference, or strategy after new information arrives or conditions change. Most formulations center on feedback from the environment, task progress, user requirements, or other agents, and several make the revision concrete as adding, removing, or changing actions, or updating the plan after each executor step. A smaller line narrows the behavior to rewriting steps to satisfy a new condition, or adjusting specific sub-tasks rather than re-planning an entire workflow, and some travel work also expects the revised plan to remain coherent and feasible.

Variants. Variants span travel planning with revision cases across dining, transportation, budget, and weather-dependent activities, multi-agent dialogue where agents adjust just before action selection, and execution settings where plans are updated from current state, task progress, or validator feedback. Papers use several names for these variants, ranging from course correction and strategy revision to task-driven, dynamic, and counterfactual replanning.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement

nodes.name: Plausibility prediction
nodes.definition: The observable task of determining which of two hypothesis images is more plausible given a premise image, or assigning a plausibility score to a single hypothesis.

nodes.name: Poetry evaluation
nodes.definition: The observable act of an LLM assessing the quality and characteristics of poems.

nodes.name: Poetry generation
nodes.definition: The task of producing new poems, which is a popular generation task for large language models.

nodes.name: Pointwise scoring
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage is a single-response judging task in which an evaluator assigns a numerical or ordinal score to one model-generated answer, usually on a Likert or comparable evaluation scale. Most definitions make the success criterion the production of that scalar rating for the candidate response, often under predefined or specified criteria such as consistency, coherence, fluency, relevance, overall quality, usefulness, or perceived quality. A smaller line of work phrases the same behavior more narrowly as the final score-prediction step, and some descriptions note that the score can be given alongside reasoning or critique before a final rating is produced.

Variants. Papers use several near-synonymous names for this behavior, including direct scoring, rating-based evaluation, single answer grading, response rating, overall rating assignment, and pointwise grading. The dominant setting is evaluation of a single response, but papers place it in several domains, including natural language generation, alignment evaluation, and instruction-controllable summarization. Some papers also contrast pointwise scoring with pairwise comparison as an

nodes.name: Portfolio management
nodes.definition: The task of managing a collection of financial assets, which includes selecting stocks, determining their weights, and making trading decisions for each asset in the portfolio.

nodes.name: Pose estimation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed papers, the prevailing usage treats pose estimation as detecting or localizing specific points on an object in an image. The definitions agree on point localization as the core task, with one paper describing it as finding points on objects such as human or animal bodies to determine posture, and another using the broader label "Keypoint detection" for identifying and localizing specific points of objects; success is therefore framed as correct point localization, and in one definition also as determining posture.

Variants. Papers use both "Pose estimation" and "Keypoint detection" for this behavior. One paper places pose estimation among open-ended, cross-domain vision tasks, while another includes keypoint detection as one of the tasks in the LAMM dataset.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link pose estimation to one measurement instrument, MS-COCO, and one paper evaluates pose estimation on COCO. The same paper also states that it adopts UniPose as the decoder for this task.

What it is taken as evidence of. Only one construct is linked, and papers phrase that link as a related relationship rather than a measurement claim: pose e

nodes.name: Post-hoc rationalization
nodes.definition: The generation of a Chain-of-Thought that justifies a predetermined answer without substantially influencing it, often indicated by flat confidence trajectories.

nodes.name: Post intent generation
nodes.definition: Producing a description of the author's communicative purpose in sharing a meme, such as humor, complaint, or provocation, based on multimodal context.

nodes.name: Pre-training data detection
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage is a binary detection task over text: papers describe deciding whether a text sample, sentence, or text sequence was part of an LLM's training or pretraining data. Most definitions make success explicit as separating or classifying training versus non-training examples, sometimes through a scoring function over model outputs, and one study says that "the goal is to detect whether a given sentence is in the dataset used for training a Large Language Model" (Infilling Score: A Pretraining Data Detection Algorithm for Large Language Models). A narrower application treats the same behavior as copyrighted book detection, asking whether excerpts from copyrighted books were included in training data.

Variants. Papers use closely related names for the behavior, most commonly pre-training or pretraining data detection, with some authors using training data detection. The clearest sub-setting is copyrighted book detection, which focuses on excerpts from copyrighted books. Some papers also connect the task to membership inference attack, describing pre-training data detection as a special case or using membership inference

nodes.name: Preference over-rejection
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. In the usage in the papers, over-rejection is treated as a failure mode in preference learning for translation, where the model's output style moves away from the preferred data distribution. As described in X-ALMA: Plug & Play Modules and Adaptive Rejection for Quality Translation at Scale, the "writing style of the translation outputs is forced away from the preferred data distribution," and this is said to impair the model's ability to generate meaningful translations.

Variants. The described setting is translation, and the behavior is discussed at the level of translation outputs and their writing style. The paper uses the name "over-rejection" for this pattern.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. The paper describes it behaviorally as a shift in translation output style away from the preferred data distribution, rather than through a named instrument.

What it is taken as evidence of. No construct is linked to it as something the behavior indicates.

nodes.name: Preference prediction
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage is pairwise prediction: choosing which of two responses, answers, or solutions is preferred for a prompt, context, or conversation. Papers differ in who supplies the preference signal, including humans, a broader mechanism such as an LLM-as-a-judge or reward model, a community whose members would upvote one answer more, or a judge or jury in multi-turn dialogue; some authors further describe the task as predicting a mechanism's decisions from concept-based representations. A smaller line of work treats the behavior as predicting a scalar preference score or specific preference level for a single response or item, including user-specific reward scores, numerical ratings, generated-text scores, or average consumer satisfaction for recipes. Success is usually framed as selecting the preferred option or assigning it the higher score, with accuracy or the fraction of cases where the preferred item scores higher used as recurring criteria.

Variants. Papers use names such as recipe preference prediction, preference score prediction, reward model scoring, preferred response prediction, and preference judgment, alongside

nodes.name: Preference ranking
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats preference ranking as comparing candidate responses and determining which output is preferred under human judgments. Most formulations are pairwise: papers describe choosing between two candidate responses, training models to assign higher likelihoods to the preferred response than to a dispreferred one, or assigning scalar rewards to two outputs and ordering them by the score difference. A broader definition also describes ranking or selecting a preferred output from a set of options according to human preferences.

Variants. Variants are mostly different ways of setting up the same preference comparison task. Papers variously frame it as prompts with pairs of human-ranked responses, as likelihood-based ordering of a preferred versus dispreferred response, and as reward-based ranking where each response receives a scalar score before comparison. A smaller framing describes ranking or selecting a preferred output from a larger set of options, and one paper reports the task across eight tasks.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link this behavior to one measurement instrument. The only named instrument

nodes.name: Premature termination
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Papers that define it treat premature termination as an observable failure mode in generated speech or audio: the output sequence is abruptly shortened, so the waveform is incomplete. As one study notes, speech token sequences can have "abruptly shortened lengths," leading to premature termination of audio waveforms (Mitigating Hallucinations in LM-Based TTS Models via Distribution Alignment Using GFlowNets).

Variants. The described setting is speech and audio output, where the behavior appears as shortened speech token sequences and incomplete audio waveforms.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. Papers instead identify it directly from the generated output, looking for abruptly shortened sequences and incomplete waveforms.

What it is taken as evidence of. No construct is linked to it as what it evidences. Instead, papers connect it to two other behavioral indicators: one claims a causal relationship from Reward hacking to Premature termination, using language that shortened speech token sequences are "leading to premature termination of audio waveforms," and another claims a causal relationship from Task decompositio

nodes.name: Premise selection
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. The definition describes premise selection as identifying and retrieving relevant existing theorems, definitions, or lemmas from a large library for use in a new proof. In LeanAgent: Lifelong Learning for Formal Theorem Proving, it is framed as the selection of relevant premises, and effective premise selection is described as "a critical challenge in theorem proving."

Variants. The described setting is formal theorem proving, where the behavior concerns searching a large library of prior results for a new proof. The description does not specify additional sub-tasks or modalities beyond selecting relevant premises, where the premises can be theorems, definitions, or lemmas.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it.

What it is taken as evidence of. No construct is linked to it as something it evidences. Separately, one paper reports that formal theorem proving is related to premise selection.

nodes.name: Prescriptive analytics
nodes.definition: The ability to generate insights that suggest specific actions to address issues or capitalize on opportunities identified in the data.

nodes.name: Previous-token attention
nodes.definition: A specific, observable positional attention pattern where a token's attention is almost exclusively focused on the token immediately preceding it.

nodes.name: Prison term prediction
nodes.definition: Predicting the appropriate prison sentence length in legal cases under Chinese law, evaluated using normalized log distance.

nodes.name: Privacy leakage
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats privacy leakage as observable disclosure or reproduction of sensitive, private, confidential, or personally identifiable information in model outputs. Most formulations count leakage when the model reveals material that should have been withheld, including memorized training examples, PII, confidential system instructions, or contextually prohibited information, often after adversarial prompts or prompt injection, though some papers also study disclosure under simple natural questions or a "good faith" assumption that data may be shared because someone asked. Definitions differ mainly in what is leaked and where it appears, ranging from inferred training fragments and prompt or access-code disclosure to summaries, reasoning traces, final answers, full user requests, and paired image-text outputs.

Variants. Papers examine several settings for this behavior. Recurring variants include extraction of memorized training examples or PII, prompt or system-prompt leakage, agent attacks that steal emails, payment methods, specific PII fields, or full user requests, leakage in reasoning traces as well as final answers, and mul

nodes.name: Private attribute inference
nodes.definition: The observable task of a model predicting a user's personal information (e.g., location, age, sex, income) based on a provided image, especially one that does not directly depict the person.

nodes.name: Privilege escalation
nodes.definition: Increasing a low-privilege account’s permissions to a higher privilege level, ideally administrator.

nodes.name: Proactive assistance
nodes.definition: The observable behavior of an agent correctly refraining from offering assistance when it determines the user does not need help.

nodes.name: Probabilistic forecasting
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage is to treat probabilistic forecasting as generating a full distribution over future numerical values in a time series rather than a single point estimate. The formulations are closely aligned: one paper defines the goal as estimating “the joint distribution of future observations given the historical ones, P(XF | XH)” (Context is Key: A Benchmark for Forecasting with Essential Textual Information), while another asks models to “output a probabilistic forecast of length 64” (Fourier Head: Helping Large Language Models Learn Complex Probability Distributions).

Variants. The papers differ mainly in the setting and representation of that distribution. One formulation targets future time steps from historical observations, including tasks where accurate predictions require integrating numerical data with natural language contextual information, while another describes fixed-length forecasts and next-value prediction through quantized values and a learned categorical distribution over the next value.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to this behavior.

What it is taken as evidence of. No co

nodes.name: Problem misunderstanding
nodes.definition: An observable error where the model's response indicates a misinterpretation of the question's goal, concepts, or given information.

nodes.name: Problem solving
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the dominant framing treats problem solving as producing correct answers or solutions on benchmark tasks, often spanning commonsense, math, code, and other prompted tasks. Several definitions make correctness explicit, describing accuracy on diverse problems or on well-defined technical queries, while others define the behavior as devising and executing a sequence of steps or a program under constraints or examples. Smaller lines of work narrow it to structured logical or mathematical derivation, or to inductive reasoning in natural-language real-life scenarios such as item trading.

Variants. Papers use several labels for narrower settings, including multi-task problem solving for heterogeneous tasks across domains and question types, reasoning task solving for structured reasoning benchmarks, and real-world problem solving for abstract rules embedded in natural-language scenarios. The domains named around this behavior include commonsense, math, code, reasoning, coding, and communication, with some papers also singling out mathematical or logical problems and programming by example. In agentic settings, one paper relates problem solving to

nodes.name: Professional question answering
nodes.definition: Generating responses to queries that require domain-specific expertise in fields such as medicine, law, finance, or music, with accurate and contextually appropriate information.

nodes.name: Program verification proof synthesis
nodes.definition: The latent ability of an LLM to synthesize proofs that allow a Rust program and specification to be verified by Verus.

nodes.name: Prompt decomposition
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats prompt decomposition as taking a complex textual description or query and splitting it into multiple shorter units. Papers agree on the core operation, decomposition into semantically coherent phrases or distinct sub-prompts, and differ mainly in how they describe the outputs: some frame them as short phrases, while others frame them as sub-prompts for individual concepts such as scene, objects, and motion.

Variants. A smaller naming variation appears between text decomposition and prompt decomposition. The studied settings range from decomposing a complex text description into short phrases to decomposing a complex query for video generation into several concept-specific sub-prompts.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to this behavior in the papers. Operationalization is described directly through the task itself, as decomposing a complex input into shorter phrases or distinct concept-level sub-prompts.

What it is taken as evidence of. No construct is linked to this behavior in the papers.

nodes.name: Prompt injection
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats prompt injection as behavior in which a model or agent follows malicious instructions inserted by an adversary, either in an input prompt or in third-party or tool-retrieved content. Definitions largely agree on the outcome: the system is redirected from the user’s or intended goal, with papers describing it as executing an attacker-specified task, taking unauthorized actions, or deviating from intended behavior.

Variants. Several papers distinguish direct and indirect forms. Direct prompt injection is described as malicious instructions placed in inputs sent to the model, while indirect prompt injection, sometimes called an indirect prompt attack, refers to instructions embedded in emails, documents, retrieved text, tool outputs, or other external sources the agent accesses; some papers also note harms such as data exfiltration, influencing outputs for other users, or redirecting the agent to unauthorized actions.

Space of elicitation and scores. Only 1 linked measurement instrument is reported: AgentDojo. Papers describe AgentDojo as a dynamic environment for testing prompt injection attacks, so the lin

nodes.name: Pronunciation assessment
nodes.definition: The model's observable behavior of aligning transcript words with corresponding phoneme sequences and identifying mismatches indicative of mispronunciation.

nodes.name: Proof grading
nodes.definition: Assessing the correctness and quality of a mathematical proof by assigning a score or category based on reasoning validity and completeness.

nodes.name: Protein binding site prediction
nodes.definition: The task of identifying the specific residues in an antibody's sequence that constitute the binding site (paratope) for an antigen.

nodes.name: Protein generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats this behavior as generating protein or amino acid sequences. Most definitions frame it as creating novel sequences, sometimes explicitly sequences intended to be plausible or functional proteins, while a smaller line of work treats it as generating missing amino acid regions in an antibody sequence from the observed regions. Papers agree on sequence generation as the core task, but differ on whether generation is open-ended or infilling, and on whether decoding is order-agnostic.

Variants. Papers study both broad protein sequence generation and narrower antibody sequence infilling settings. Named variants include order-agnostic protein generation, unguided antibody infilling, and infilling specific masked complementarity determining regions, including HCDR1, HCDR2, HCDR3, and LCDR1. One paper also places protein generation alongside structure- and function-related evaluations.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to this behavior, so the papers do not identify a recurring instrument that elicits or scores it.

What it is taken as evidence of. No construct is linked to this

nodes.name: Protein inverse folding
nodes.definition: Generating an amino-acid sequence that is compatible with a given backbone structure.

nodes.name: Protein property prediction
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across these papers, the prevailing usage treats the concept as predicting a protein property, label, or function from amino acid sequence. Most formulations are either continuous regression tasks, such as fluorescence intensity, thermostability, melting temperature, or optimal temperature for catalysis, or discrete prediction tasks, such as solubility, metal ion binding, mammalian cell expression, or cellular compartment. A smaller extension treats it as protein function prediction in a setting where experimentally verified annotations are unavailable during training and final evaluation follows a curation phase based on newly published functions. Where papers specify the prediction granularity, they describe sequence-level or protein-level outputs, and one paper explicitly reports stability as sequence-level regression measured by Spearman coefficient.

Variants. The variants are heterogeneous but remain sequence-based in their formulations. Common named variants include fluorescence, stability or thermostability, solubility, metal ion binding, and subcellular localization, with localization described as a protein-level label for compartments such as nucleus

nodes.name: Protein sequence design
nodes.definition: The task of generating mutant protein sequences (specifically ACE2) with higher stability, measured by lower free energy (ddG), than the original wildtype sequence.

nodes.name: Protein structure prediction
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats this behavior as predicting a protein's three-dimensional structure from its amino acid sequence, sometimes stated simply as predicting the 3D structure and sometimes more specifically as predicting the three-dimensional atomic coordinates. The common framing is sequence-to-structure prediction: one paper says the goal of folding is to predict the 3D structure for a given amino acid sequence. Definitions also include related structure-centered tasks, rather than limiting the term only to full coordinate generation.

Variants. Common naming variants are folding and protein folding, and one paper describes it as sequence-conditioned structure prediction. Definitions also include neighboring formulations: protein contact prediction, cast as binary classification at the amino acid pair level for whether two amino acids are close in the folded structure; protein fold classification, described as sequence-level assignment to predefined fold classes, including a formulation with 1195 classes; and remote homology prediction, described as identifying evolutionary relationships between proteins with low sequence similarity.

nodes.name: Protein understanding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats protein understanding as predicting protein fitness or mutational effects from amino acid sequences. Most definitions describe assigning a fitness score, scalar value, or relative ranking based on functional or biophysical properties, and several narrow this to the fitness impact of substitutions or other mutations. Some papers study zero-shot versions, though they differ in formulation: some define zero-shot as using no support-set examples for the target task, while others score mutated sequences relative to a wild type sequence without fine-tuning on labeled fitness data, using model likelihood differences or log odds ratios. A smaller line of work uses the same space for antibody-antigen interaction tasks, either classifying binding versus non-binding or predicting continuous binding affinity, and some work frames it as iteratively editing a seed sequence to propose higher-fitness variants.

Variants. Variants are named in several overlapping ways: fitness prediction, protein fitness prediction, protein variant fitness prediction, mutation effect prediction, and zero-shot fitness prediction or zero-shot prediction

nodes.name: Pushing
nodes.definition: The action of applying force to an object to move it without grasping it.

nodes.name: Puzzle solving
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most commonly, papers treat puzzle solving as finding a solution to a defined puzzle or problem, especially classic puzzles, number games, and word games posed under custom rules and constraints. The prevailing formulation emphasizes rule-governed problem solving rather than open-ended generation: one benchmark asks models to "solve puzzles and intellectual games based on newly defined problem-solving frameworks" (KOR-Bench: Benchmarking Language Models on Knowledge-Orthogonal Reasoning Tasks). A smaller line of work uses a broader phrasing, calling it the observable behavior of finding a solution to a defined puzzle or problem.

Variants. The main variants are classic paper puzzles, number games, and word games, which one paper explicitly names as the rule categories for its puzzle section. Another variant is multi-image puzzle solving, framed as solving puzzles that require understanding and reasoning across multiple images. Some work also studies puzzles in a centaur evaluation setting with crowdworkers, where they appear alongside collaborative writing and summarization tasks.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to puzzle

nodes.name: Quantified Boolean formula solving
nodes.definition: Producing a truth value for quantified Boolean formulas by recursively handling existential and universal quantifiers.

nodes.name: Query-focused summarization
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage is generating a summary, or in one formulation a response, over one or more documents that is tailored to a given query and emphasizes information relevant to that query. Most descriptions place the task in long-document or long-context settings, while a smaller formulation specifies a user-provided query over one or more long documents and asks for a response that cites arbitrary-length text spans from the input. Definitions also vary between framing the output as answering the query, summarizing context in response to a generated query, and producing a concise summary focused on a queried topic.

Variants. Papers use several nearby names, most commonly "query-focused summarization" and also "query-based summarization"; one paper further labels the long-context setting as "LCQFS" and another abbreviates the task as "QFS." The settings mentioned span one or more long documents, dialogues where "a question to summarize certain topic is raised about the dialogue," and materials such as meeting transcripts, podcast transcripts, and narratives.

Space of elicitation and scores. In the linked measurement work, it is measured

nodes.name: Query rewriting
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the most common framing is rewriting an input query so it better fits a downstream step: authors describe clarifying ambiguous expressions, supplementing semantic information, reformulating for a later retrieval round, or rewriting according to an explicit constraint such as a required aspect and value. Some definitions narrow this to ambiguity-resolving paraphrases that preserve intent, including what one paper calls "abbreviation replacement and ambiguity elimination of the original query," while others emphasize enrichment, for example adding visual details, stylistic elements, or aesthetic expectations. A smaller line of work applies the same behavior to prompts rather than search queries, describing structured keyword prompts, polished prompts that remove stylistic bias and conflicting information, or rephrased prompts that preserve meaning, sometimes while maintaining or improving faithfulness to the original prompt and sometimes to make malicious intent less detectable.

Variants. Papers use several nearby names for this behavior, most often query rewriting, query reformulation, prompt rewriting, query paraphrasing, and prompt polishing,

nodes.name: Question-answer pair generation
nodes.definition: The task of creating a set of questions and corresponding answers about the diverse entities and attributes present in an image.

nodes.name: Question answering
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats question answering as producing or selecting an answer to a natural-language question, usually with correctness as the success criterion. Most papers frame the answer as grounded either in a provided passage, document set, retrieved evidence, tables or knowledge graphs, or in the model's internal or general knowledge, though a smaller line places the task in adversarial or knowledge-conflict settings. Output formats vary from direct short answers and open-ended responses to multiple-choice, yes/no, and span-based answers; in some passage-based settings, papers specify answers as Yes/No/Don't Know, a span in the question, or a span in the passage. Some papers also require a rationale alongside the answer, and correctness is judged against a gold or reference answer.

Variants. Papers study many variants, most commonly passage- or document-grounded QA, open-domain QA, and multi-hop or long-context QA where answers may require combining evidence across documents, retrieved passages, or multiple tables. Other named variants include contextual, entity, extractive, benchmark, closed-book, and open-book QA, as wel

nodes.name: Question decomposition
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats this behavior as breaking a complex question or query into simpler intermediate units, most often a sequence of sub-questions that can be answered step by step before reaching a final answer. Several definitions make the target output answerable subquestions explicit, sometimes with corresponding sub-answers, and one multi-hop formulation says the model generates intermediate questions and answers until arriving at the final answer. A smaller line of work uses query- or subproblem-centered wording instead of question-centered wording, and one paper reframes decomposition as analyzing a question into structural tokens and replaceable entity placeholders to form a reusable template for similar questions.

Variants. Common labels are question decomposition, subquestion decomposition, query decomposition, sub-question generation, and query graph construction, with several other less common labels. The main variants differ in representation: some papers use plain sequences of subquestions, some generate subquestion-answer pairs, and some organize sub-queries into a directed acyclic graph that represents dependencies or a r

nodes.name: Question rephrasing
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats question rephrasing as rewriting or paraphrasing a question while preserving its meaning, and sometimes explicitly its answer. Most formulations describe changing the linguistic form without altering intent, as in instructions to "generate a paraphrase of that question without changing the meaning of it." A smaller line of work adds a further aim beyond paraphrase, such as making the question less ambiguous, more aligned with model capabilities, clarifying conditions, or restating it more simply when models misunderstand the original.

Variants. Variants are distinguished mainly by setting. Papers study mathematical question rephrasing, including using "rephrasing prompting" to generate additional questions; vision-language use, where question wording is modified using salient image details and appears as a "Rephrasing and Augmenting the Question" stage; problem-solving use that rephrases questions more simply; and evaluation use that creates rephrased benchmarks. Some authors also use the name "question rewriting" for the same behavior.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers usually elicit this behavior directl

nodes.name: Questionnaire answering
nodes.definition: The observable behavior of responding to a series of questions from a structured survey, such as a value questionnaire, by providing ratings on a scale.

nodes.name: Radiology report generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage is generating a descriptive, clinically relevant textual radiology report from a radiology image, often a chest X-ray. Definitions usually describe the report as detailing clinical observations or findings from the image, and one paper makes the expected output structure explicit by requiring "Findings" and "Impression" sections. A smaller variation broadens the input from a single medical image to one or more radiology images plus associated clinical context.

Variants. Most task instances focus on chest X-ray report generation. Papers vary the formulation by using a given radiology image or medical image, by allowing associated clinical context in addition to the image, and in one case by studying retrieval-based radiology report generation given only radiology images. Another naming variant is simply "report generation," where the task is framed as producing the "Findings" and "Impression" sections of a typical report.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link this behavior to two measurement instruments, MIMIC-CXR and GREEN. Radiology report generation is measured by MIMIC-CXR as a dataset for chest X-ray report

nodes.name: Rain removal
nodes.definition: The observable task of eliminating or reducing the visual effects of raindrops or rain streaks from an image.

nodes.name: Ranking
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the literature, the prevailing usage is reranking rather than generic ranking: papers most often describe the behavior as taking an initial retrieval set and reordering documents, passages, images, code snippets, websites, or other candidates by relevance to a query, usually to place the most relevant item first or improve the top-ranked results. Common task formulations assign relevance, satisfaction, or scalar scores and then reorder the list, while some setups ask for an ordered list of document IDs or use binary relevance judgments before reordering. A smaller line of work uses ranking more broadly for ordering candidate outputs from best to worst based on quality criteria, for arranging items or map regions by queried values, or for selecting the best generation from a candidate set.

Variants. Variants span document, passage, text, item, image, code, website, and candidate-entity reranking, along with listwise reranking and candidate refinement. Most remain query-relevance tasks after a first retrieval stage, though some specialize by setting, such as zero-shot reranking without task-specific fine-tuning, multimodal reranking for multimodal querie

nodes.name: Readability assessment
nodes.definition: Judging the readability level or difficulty of a text passage.

nodes.name: Reading comprehension question answering
nodes.definition: Answering questions that require understanding a passage or context in Filipino.

nodes.name: Reason generation
nodes.definition: Producing an explanation for why a model's output should change from an initial ('AS-IS') to a desired ('TO-BE') state based on prompt content.

nodes.name: Reasoning error
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across definitions, papers most commonly describe reasoning error as a failure to apply the logical steps needed to solve a problem, including inferential mistakes, missing critical steps, and incorrect or misapplied reasoning. Some formulations are task-specific: audio work describes cases where the model correctly perceives the audio but still fails at the necessary complex reasoning, while math-focused papers describe flawed solution paths with logical fallacies or misapplication of mathematical principles. A smaller framing treats it as systematic, predictable mistakes in the reasoning process that lead to incorrect answers.

Variants. Papers study this behavior in multimodal mathematical reasoning, audio understanding and reasoning, undergraduate-level mathematical reasoning, and grade-school math. The most common names are reasoning error and reasoning errors, though some authors use flawed reasoning or making systematic errors. One multimodal math study, Measuring Multimodal Mathematical Reasoning with MATH-Vision Dataset, describes it as the most prevalent cause of errors.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers measure it with one instrument, Manual

nodes.name: Reasoning segmentation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the dominant framing treats reasoning segmentation as generating a pixel-level segmentation mask for an object or region in an image from a complex instruction or textual query, where identifying the target requires reasoning. The definitions are closely aligned, and one paper adds that the task 'demands higher capabilities in instruction comprehension.' Success is described as producing the pixel-level mask.

Variants. The papers use closely related names for the same behavior, including reasoning segmentation and Reasoning Segmentation (RS). A narrower characterization appears in one paper's relationship statement, which says that 'RS has reasoning ability, but only allows single object localization,' tying the task to single-object localization. Another paper discusses it alongside referring segmentation as a task setting where the approach is applied.

Space of elicitation and scores. One measurement instrument is linked to reasoning segmentation: ReasonSeg. Papers describe ReasonSeg as a benchmark dataset or benchmark for reasoning segmentation, and one quote says it 'evaluates the reasoning ability of the model.' Reported use includes

nodes.name: Recommendation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats recommendation as predicting or generating items for a user from profile information, historical interactions, or user-item interaction behaviors. Most definitions describe the output as a list, often a ranked or top-k list, of items or item IDs that are relevant, most likely to be preferred, or that best match the user's preferences. As described in Language Representations Can be What Recommenders Need: Findings and Potentials, collaborative filtering "aims to select item i that best matches user u's preferences based on binary interaction behaviors," while other papers phrase the task as generating recommendations directly with an LLM.

Variants. Papers study several variants under this label. Common named versions include collaborative filtering, top-K item generation, item recommendation, top-k recommendation, and user intention capture; these differ in whether they predict the next liked item, generate K distinct token sequences by beam search, or refine outputs by combining historical interests with language-based intention queries. A smaller line of work places the task in multi-modal or graph-based settin

nodes.name: Referring expression generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across definitions, the prevailing usage treats referring expression generation as producing a descriptive textual expression for a specified object or bounded region in an image, usually supplied as a bounding box. Papers agree that the output should accurately, and in some formulations unambiguously, refer to that content; a smaller line of work also describes it as the latent ability to understand a visual reference and then generate the description.

Variants. A recurring variant names the task multimodal referring, with the same basic setup of understanding image regions or objects that users specify through bounding boxes or location tokens and generating the associated text. Papers also connect it to two other behavioral indicators in nearby grounding settings: referring expression segmentation is described as the dual task of REG, and one paper claims a causal relationship from referring expression generation to Entity grounding by incorporating descriptive textual clues into that task.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link it to one measurement instrument, RefCOCOg, described as a classical benchmark for referring expression generation. This o

nodes.name: Referring expression segmentation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage is a pixel-level task where a model receives a natural language description or referring expression and must output a segmentation mask for the specific object, object instance, or region it names. Most definitions are consistent on the success criterion: the output is a mask that covers the described target, as one paper phrases it, "segment a target object mask from the entire image given a sentence describing the object" (Unleashing Region Understanding in Intermediate Layers for MLLM-based Referring Expression Generation). A smaller formulation instead describes a pre-training task on 3D objects, predicting a binary mask for a named component given a referring expression and an object point cloud.

Variants. Papers use several near-equivalent names, most commonly referring expression segmentation, and also referring segmentation and referring image segmentation. The common setting is 2D images, but some work studies remote sensing images, including prompts such as "Could you provide a segmentation mask for {referring expression} in this image?" and decoding a <SEG> token into the mask (GeoPixel: Pixel Groundin

nodes.name: Referring expression understanding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage is an image grounding task: the model must locate the object or region referred to by a natural language expression, usually by outputting a bounding box. Some authors describe the same behavior more broadly as linking text to the corresponding object or region, while a smaller line formulates it through segmentation, first generating a mask and then deriving the box. Where scoring is stated, predictions are compared with ground-truth boxes as accuracy or Acc@0.5, and one paper notes that a prediction is correct only if the IoU with the ground-truth box exceeds 0.5 (Text4Seg: Reimagining Image Segmentation as Text Generation).

Variants. Papers use several nearby labels and settings for this behavior. Most variants stay in images, under referring expression comprehension or phrase grounding, and some broaden the task to predicting boxes for one or more phrases or noun phrases within a caption; some versions also ask for multiple referred targets through multi-target segmentation. Other work extends the same localization behavior to object grounding in 3D scenes and to video grounding, including spatio-temporal outputs such a

nodes.name: Refusal
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats refusal as abstaining from answering harmful, unsafe, malicious, toxic, unethical, or policy-violating requests, often through explicit rejection language such as "I cannot fulfill your request" or "I'm sorry, but I can't assist with that request." Most definitions count an explicit decline as refusal, while some also include generic or off-task replies, answers to a different question, returning an error message, or redirecting toward safer alternatives. A smaller line of work extends the behavior beyond harmful requests, using refusal for knowledge-limit statements, unsupported functionality, missing or contradictory information, uncertainty, selecting a "not sure" option, or declining to choose from invalid options.

Variants. Papers study refusal across safety prompts, blocklisted content, hate speech, moral dilemmas, politically sensitive questions, medical uncertainty, knowledge-boundary questions, and function-calling requests. The dominant variants are still direct rejections of harmful or unsafe inputs, but several papers use nearby labels, such as abstention, avoidance, evasive responses, punting, and reject

nodes.name: Region captioning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across definitions, region captioning is most commonly described as producing a natural-language description for a specific image region that has been marked or referred to in the input. The papers agree that the output is region-specific text, but differ on brevity: some formulations ask for concise or brief descriptions, including prompts to "provide a brief description of each marked region in the image", while others ask for a detailed description of a referred region. One formulation also defines it as a task where the model "provides a textual description corresponding to a visual prompt".

Variants. The behavior appears under several names, most commonly region-level captioning, with referring description and visual referring as alternative labels. The studied settings vary between marked regions, visually prompted regions, and referred regions, and between describing each marked region versus one referred region. One paper also situates region-level captioning within MDVP-Bench alongside point-level captioning.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link region captioning to 3 measurement instruments. The most frequently linked are RefCOCOg and Visua

nodes.name: Register allocation
nodes.definition: The task of assigning virtual registers from a compiler's intermediate representation to physical registers in a target hardware's instruction set architecture.

nodes.name: Regression
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most definitions describe it as predicting a continuous numerical value for a given tabular record or input sample. One paper also formulates it as predicting an integer-valued output, with a user review as input and a rating from 1 to 5 as the label.

Variants. Papers study regression both as tabular prediction across various domains and as a review-to-rating task. The formulations differ in whether the input is a tabular record or a user review, and in whether the target is described as a continuous value or as an integer rating.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it in the recorded relationships. In task operationalizations, papers mention mean squared error loss for regression tasks and mean absolute error, MAE.

What it is taken as evidence of. No construct is linked to it in the recorded relationships.

nodes.name: Relation classification
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage treats it as identifying and classifying semantic relationships between entities in text. Most formulations narrow the input to a specified pair of entities, often within a sentence, and treat success as predicting the relation class or label for that pair, sometimes as one or more labels and sometimes as a distribution over predefined relations. Some papers use the broader name relation extraction and emphasize identifying or generating relations, and one paper explicitly contrasts multi-class prediction with a binary decision about whether a queried relation exists between two entities.

Variants. Papers use both relation classification and relation extraction to name the behavior, and a smaller subset studies medical relation extraction. The settings range from sentence-level pair classification to document-level extraction across whole documents, and some papers study few-shot continual relation extraction as a variant. Other formulations target multiple relations simultaneously, fact triplets, or schema-defined relation types such as TA, A2A, and AS relations, while domain-specific versions appear in urban text

nodes.name: Relation discovery
nodes.definition: The observable action of generating a preliminary or initial new relation label for a test instance, typically based on examples of known relations.

nodes.name: Relation extraction
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, relation extraction is usually treated as a task over entity relations that is evaluated on RE benchmarks, and one explicit definition spells it out as knowledge triple extraction: decomposing document content into structured ⟨head entity, relation, tail entity⟩ triples with an LLM using in-context learning. In that formulation, the model extracts triples for each retrieved document independently and is instructed to extract all knowledge triples in a document in a single pass. Elsewhere, papers frame the same behavior as relation prediction or extraction in sentence-level and document-level settings.

Variants. The papers use several variant names and settings, including knowledge triple extraction, low-resource relation extraction, biomedical relation extraction, and few-shot continual relation extraction. The studied settings range from sentence-level RE with ten relation classes to document-level RE, including binary chemical-disease relations and five-class chemical-protein relations. A smaller line of work focuses on sequentially identifying new relations with limited labeled samples, and another highlights recall on rare relations.

S

nodes.name: Relation linking
nodes.definition: Matching relation surface forms in generated logical forms to actual relations in the knowledge base using exact match or semantic similarity (e.g., SimCSE).

nodes.name: Relevance judgment
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, it is treated as evaluating retrieved or given text against a query, question, task, or topic and making an explicit relevance judgment. Most formulations center on whether a document or passage is relevant or provides useful information for solving the task, while another framing emphasizes how well a piece of text aligns with a query or topic under semantic criteria. One formulation further requires the model to analyze documents one by one, produce reasoning chains, and then give a final judgement with an explanation.

Variants. Papers use closely related variants: document relevance assessment, passage relevance assessment, and text relevance assessment. They differ mainly in the unit being judged, retrieved documents, retrieved passages, or generic text, and in the criterion applied, relevance to a question, usefulness for solving the task, or semantic alignment to a query or topic.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. Instead, the papers describe direct elicitation through relevance decisions, such as asking for per-document analysis and a final judgement with explanation, predicting ISREL for a

nodes.name: Repetitive generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage is as a generation failure in which outputs repeat tokens, words, phrases, sentences, utterances, or ideas. Most descriptions treat the repeated material as unnecessary or meaningless, either as repetition that affects meaning, adds no new information, or lowers readability, conciseness, coherence, or response diversity. A smaller line of work narrows it to outputs that devolve into unproductive loops on hard tasks, repeated list items within a single response, or repetition of the same prompted token many times.

Variants. Variants span general and long-form text generation, reasoning failures described as unproductive generation loops, multi-turn social dialogue, query-focused and book-length summarization, code generation, and translation. The most common labels are repetitive generation, repetition, and repetitive text generation, while smaller labels include parroting for repeated actions in dialogue and oscillatory hallucination for repeated token sequences in translation. Other formulations focus on duplicate summary spans, duplicate code fragments such as repeated assertions or comments, single-token repetition tasks

nodes.name: Rephrased question answering
nodes.definition: Correctly answering semantically equivalent but syntactically different versions of a previously edited question, indicating generalization of the edit.

nodes.name: Request compliance
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats request compliance as observable answer behavior: following a user's instruction or attempting to fulfill a request, and responding directly rather than refusing. Most definitions add that the answer should be substantive or helpful, so compliance is usually framed as a direct answer to the prompt or query, contrasted with refusal.

Variants. A recurring setting is compliance with harmless or benign prompts versus refusal of harmful ones. The labels vary, with compliance the most common wording, alongside compliant response generation and instruction acceptance; one helpfulness setting measures acceptance on benign prompts that share keywords with AdvBench but do not contain harmful intent, and another notes lower acceptance in a Sensitive category.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. Papers nevertheless operationalize the behavior through refusal-versus-compliance judgments, including whether WildGuard classifies the response as refusal or compliance on XStest, through instruction acceptance rate on benign prompts, and in one study through the minimal gamma found by line s

nodes.name: Resource collection
nodes.definition: Mining or gathering materials from terrain blocks to obtain items such as wood, stone, coal, iron, diamond, saplings, or drinks.

nodes.name: Resource harvesting
nodes.definition: The observable action of an agent deciding on and extracting a specific quantity of a shared resource from the common pool in a given time step.

nodes.name: Response aggregation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage treats it as combining multiple candidate answers or responses into one final output. Most descriptions emphasize a final answer that is more reliable, higher-quality, coherent, or refined, whether the inputs come from multiple sources, reasoning paths, or selected experts. Some papers make the success criterion more explicit by describing selection of the most reliable or most plausible response, while others add conflict detection, weighted fusion, or iterative synthesis and refinement.

Variants. Papers use several near-synonymous labels, including answer aggregation, response fusion, response aggregation, and response synthesis. The settings vary from multi-path aggregation over answers from sub-questions and the original question, to fusing proposed responses given an instruction prompt, to synthesizing outputs from selected experts through semantic conflict detection and weighted information fusion. A smaller variant frames it as a two-stage knowledge graph-guided response integration process for logical consistency, and another describes iterative synthesis and refinement across candidate responses.

Space of

nodes.name: Response evaluation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage is the generation of an explicit judgement about another model's response: an assessment, score, selection, or classification based on quality, relevance, or correctness. Several descriptions place an LLM or LMM in the evaluator role, often centered on the final evaluation outcome, and one paper explicitly calls this output "the final judgement"; some also require structured rationales alongside scalar scores. A smaller framing emphasizes the analysis process behind the judgement, describing the evaluator as examining the components and structure of a query and response, and where criteria are stated, papers refer to accurate judgements and consistency with ground-truth.

Variants. Papers study this behavior under several names, including answer critique, judgement generation, and response judging. The settings range from vision-language question answering, where models critique a given answer with structured rationales and scalar scores, to text judging tasks that compare two or more responses or are used in response ranking, reward modeling, and verifying agent task completion. Some descriptions single out hard queries and

nodes.name: Response harmfulness classification
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage is a binary judgment over a model response, asking whether the response is safe or unsafe. One paper frames it for moderation as "predicting whether a response is safe or not," while another treats it as self-checking, where "the LLM checks if the response is safe or not" and outputs a binary indicator. In the more specific self-checking formulation, the safe label is described as a response that "does not contain any sensitive factors."

Variants. Papers use two closely related names for this behavior, response classification and safety checking. The main variation is in setting rather than outcome: one line treats it as moderation of a response, and another has the model evaluate its own generated response for sensitive or harmful content. Both formulations keep the task as a binary safe versus unsafe rating.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link this behavior to three measurement instruments: BeaverTails, HarmBench, and WildGuardMix. The measurement setup is described in benchmark and test-dataset terms, with papers saying they "consider ... as benchmarks" for response classification and also "utilize datasets

nodes.name: Response ranking
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats response ranking as ordering several candidate responses from best to worst, or choosing the best one, based on a judge's assessment of quality. The judging source varies, with LLMs and judge models appearing most often, while some papers instead use human raters, reward models, annotators, or PRM scores. A smaller line of work narrows the behavior to reranking generated reasoning paths so that the highest scoring path, or the path with the most accurate final answer, is selected, and another frames success as choosing the candidate with the lowest predicted hallucination rate.

Variants. Papers use several near-synonymous labels, with response ranking the prevailing name and smaller variants including response reranking, response re-ranking, and solution reranking. The studied settings range from generic instruction prompts with multiple proposed responses, to tournament-style and "first-round-rank" candidate ranking, to Best-of-N and weighted majority voting over reasoning paths or chains of thought. Other variants appear in multimodal reasoning, where a PRM selects top-scoring responses, and in hallucination mitiga

nodes.name: Response revision
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most commonly, papers treat response revision as changing an initial, low-quality, weak, incorrect, or unclear answer into a better one. The prevailing description is an edit process, adding, deleting, or substituting tokens, usually guided by a reference, instruction, critique, or feedback; some papers narrow success to factual correction or removal of false information, while others treat success as a stronger, more preferred output or a conversational shift to a correct answer. A smaller line of work frames the same behavior as a refinement capability, correcting an instruction-following failure with minimal irrelevant revisions. In one simulated-society setting, a paper claims a causal relationship from Feedback generation to response revision, describing ratings and explanations as informing the revisions.

Variants. Variants span several settings. Papers describe token-level editing, conditional weak-to-strong correction, multi-turn conversational revision where an answer shifts from incorrect or unclear to correct, and factuality-focused revision that corrects or removes false information, sometimes replacing it with common-knowledge facts. Other work s

nodes.name: Resume parsing
nodes.definition: The process of converting unstructured or semi-structured resume documents into a structured format, such as JSON, by extracting and organizing personal, educational, and professional information.

nodes.name: Retain query answering
nodes.definition: The model's observable ability to correctly answer questions about information it was instructed to retain, even when those questions appear alongside forget queries.

nodes.name: Retrosynthetic planning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most definitions describe this behavior as working backward from a target or product molecule to identify reactants for synthesis. The prevailing framing is retrosynthetic analysis that begins with the target compound and seeks potential reactant molecules, while a broader formulation describes generating a step-by-step synthesis pathway that reaches commercially available reactants. A narrower formulation treats it as predicting a reaction template or a one-step retrosynthetic reaction from a product molecule and text context.

Variants. Papers use several nearby names for this behavior, including retrosynthetic planning, retrosynthesis, and reaction prediction. The main variation is scope: some formulations focus on full synthesis pathways, some on identifying potential reactant molecules, and some on one-step template prediction from product molecules with text context.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it.

What it is taken as evidence of. Papers do not link it to any construct.

nodes.name: Reward function generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the dominant framing is the production of executable reward-function code for a simulation or reinforcement learning task. Most papers describe it as generating the part of the environment or task code that specifies the agent's objective or reward signal, usually from a task description together with environment code, goal descriptions, or low-level states. A narrower variant describes the behavior as dense reward code generation, where the model produces a shaped dense reward program from a natural-language goal. Papers vary in how they state success: some focus on returning code that defines a scalar reward whose cumulative maximization defines the task, while others describe outputting code such that a downstream objective is maximized or code that correctly uses environment attributes to encourage a specified tactic.

Variants. Papers study this behavior under the names reward function generation and dense reward code generation. The settings are varied but mostly involve simulations or environment code: definitions mention robotics and games, simulated worlds where reward generation appears alongside simulator dynamics or termin

nodes.name: Reward hacking
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats reward hacking as a failure mode in which optimization against an imperfect reward model, reward function, or evaluation system yields outputs that get high scores, pass verification, or receive credit without achieving the intended goal. Most descriptions emphasize semantically meaningless, degenerate, repeated, trivial, incomplete, or otherwise functionally useless outputs, while a smaller set makes the judge explicit, including verifier limitations and mistaken high reward from human supervisors. Some papers narrow this further to modality-specific signs such as abruptly shortened speech token sequences that still exploit the reward.

Variants. Across settings, the same label is used for several observable patterns: text models producing repeated, short, meaningless strings or mostly dashes; verifier-based code generation producing trivial or incomplete specifications or programs that nonetheless pass; and LM-based TTS producing abnormally short token sequences that end audio early. Other papers use it for agents or policies that exploit loopholes in the objective, such as reaching a goal only in a dreamed state or

nodes.name: Reward prediction
nodes.definition: The task of predicting the future reward signal in a reinforcement learning environment based on a history of states and actions.

nodes.name: Riddle solving
nodes.definition: The task of deducing the correct answer to a puzzle or question posed in a metaphorical or ambiguous way.

nodes.name: Risk-of-bias rationale selection
nodes.definition: The observable behavior of selecting the correct human-written rationale that justifies a risk-of-bias rating from a set of plausible alternatives.

nodes.name: RNA structure prediction
nodes.definition: The task of identifying and predicting the base-pairing interactions within a single RNA molecule to determine its two-dimensional structure.

nodes.name: Robot action generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage treats this behavior as generating robot control actions from visual observations and language instructions. Most descriptions frame the output as a sequence of action tokens for robot control, while a smaller framing casts it as textual output that corresponds to a predefined set of robot commands. Some work also describes the text output as containing numerical values, such as 2D image coordinates, for a robot action.

Variants. Papers study several variants of this behavior. One line focuses on discrete action generation in a fixed action space, with commands such as "base-forward," "base-backward," "base-stop," "gripper-open," and "gripper-close" (Randomized Smoothing Meets Vision-Language Models). Another line describes actions for settings including pick-and-place and rotation decisions, and text outputs aligned to image pixel coordinates for robot actions (LLaRA: Supercharging Robot Learning Data for Vision-Language Policy).

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to this behavior, so the papers do not identify a recurring instrument that elicits or scores it.

What it is taken a

nodes.name: Robotic manipulation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the dominant framing treats robotic manipulation as producing control actions, action trajectories, or other physical actions that let a robot interact with objects and alter its environment to accomplish a specified goal. Most definitions place it in real or simulated embodied settings and often condition it on visual, textual, or language instructions, including visuo-motor control and embodied robotic control.
