One paper states, "Given several images of a specific subject and a textual prompt, subject-driven generation aims to generate images of the same subject in a context aligning with the prompt" (Bridging The Gap between Low-rank and Orthogonal Adaptation via Householder Reflection Adaptation). A smaller wording variation describes generating new, customized images from one or more reference images, often placing the subject in new contexts or styles.

Variants. Papers use both "subject-driven generation" and "subject-driven image generation" for closely similar tasks. The variants explicitly named are single-entity subject-driven generation and multi-image subject-driven generation. The multi-image variant is described as requiring that the main subjects across multiple reference images represent the same instance, while other formulations allow one or more reference images.

Space of elicitation and scores. Some papers mention "subject-driven generation

nodes.name: Subject-verb agreement
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, subject-verb agreement is treated as performance on grammar-sensitive outputs: either choosing the appropriate verb inflection from the grammatical number of the subject, or giving correct acceptability judgments for sentences that test agreement. One study says that "the model's task is to choose the appropriate verb inflection" (Sparse Feature Circuits: Discovering and Editing Interpretable Causal Graphs in Language Models), while another frames it through acceptability judgments and includes examples such as "The sisters bake/*bakes."

Variants. Papers use two related formulations. One is a suite of subject-verb agreement tasks, and another is subject-verb agreement judgment, abbreviated as "S-v agr.," with a recurring focus on sentences containing attractor nouns; one paper specifically notes that attractors in a relative clause can hinder acceptability judgments.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. In the papers, it is elicited directly through agreement tasks and acceptability-judgment items rather than through a named instrument.

What it is taken as evidence of. The papers do not link this beh

nodes.name: Subjectivity classification
nodes.definition: The observable task of determining whether a given text is subjective (expressing opinions) or objective (stating facts).

nodes.name: Subtask dependency identification
nodes.definition: Correctly recognizing and acting upon prerequisite relationships between subtasks in a non-linear task structure.

nodes.name: Subtraction
nodes.definition: Performing subtraction operations on numerical operands, including anti-symmetric operations.

nodes.name: Success detection
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, it is consistently used for a judgment about whether a task has been completed successfully. One formulation treats it as determining task or sub-task success from environmental feedback, summarized as "Determine if the task is successful" and as something that "determines sub-task success based on environmental feedback" (MLLM as Retriever: Interactively Learning Multimodal Retrieval for Embodied Agents). Another formulation narrows it to a binary success-versus-mistake decision for a procedural task, made from procedural text plus visual evidence gathered through dialog.

Variants. Papers use both success detection and success classification for closely related versions of the behavior. The main variation is in scope and evidence source: some descriptions target whole-task or sub-task success from environmental feedback, while another studies procedural execution and asks after each iteration whether the procedure was successfully executed from "the video frame and entire dialog history" (Transparent and Coherent Procedural Mistake Detection).

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to this behavior. In the de

nodes.name: Sudoku solving
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage is completing a partially filled Sudoku grid so that all row, column, and box or subgrid constraints are satisfied. Most descriptions treat success as filling the remaining cells of the whole board, with one formulation stating that the board should contain numbers 1 to 9 without duplicates in each row, column, and box. Some task setups add procedural or output requirements, such as first searching over empty cells to decide which cell to fill, or returning the solved puzzle without extraneous text.

Variants. The variants mentioned are mostly about setting and format rather than different success criteria. Papers describe Sudoku solving both as puzzles presented in a textual format and as 9 × 9 Sudoku problems; a smaller variation requires an answer-only output, while another frames solving as an iterative process that searches over empty cells before filling a chosen cell. The name also appears as "Sudoku-solving" in one task description.

Space of elicitation and scores. The papers do not link Sudoku solving to any measurement instrument.

What it is taken as evidence of. The recorded relationships do not present Sudoku s

nodes.name: Suicide risk detection
nodes.definition: The task of identifying language or patterns in user input that indicate a risk of suicide.

nodes.name: Super-resolution
nodes.definition: The task of increasing the resolution and detail of a low-resolution image, guided by a textual instruction.

nodes.name: Support strategy selection
nodes.definition: The observable process of choosing one or more conversational strategies (e.g., Question, Reflection of feelings) to use in a response.

nodes.name: Supportiveness judgment
nodes.definition: The observable task of assigning a discrete label (e.g., true/false) to a claim indicating whether it is supported by provided evidence.

nodes.name: Surgical phase recognition
nodes.definition: The task of classifying individual frames from a surgical video into a set of predefined procedural phases, such as 'Preparation' or 'ClippingCutting'.

nodes.name: Survival prediction
nodes.definition: The model's output of a probability distribution over discrete time intervals, representing the individual incidence function from which survival probabilities are derived.

nodes.name: Sycophantic response generation
nodes.definition: Producing answers that conform to user suggestions or doubts even when they are factually incorrect, such as changing a correct answer after an 'Are you sure?' prompt.

nodes.name: Symbolic manipulation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across definitions, the prevailing usage treats symbolic manipulation as rule-based operations over symbolic inputs, especially mathematical or logical symbols. Papers describe it as the observable act of manipulating symbols according to a set of rules, and as performing operations such as identifying syntactic roles or evaluating logical conditions over structured values.

Variants. The behavior appears both as a broad task category and as named task instances. Papers mention tasks requiring symbolic manipulation in general, and one paper instantiates the category with Indirect Object Identification (IOI) and PriceTag within a broader set of language modeling tasks.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. The evidence names task examples, but does not specify a separate elicitation or scoring instrument for this behavior.

What it is taken as evidence of. No construct is linked to it. The papers do not state what symbolic manipulation is taken to indicate.

nodes.name: Symbolic regression
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. In the usage in the papers, symbolic regression is treated as a search task over compact or succinct programmatic mathematical expressions that explain a dataset of input-output examples. The formulations in the same paper make success depend on producing a programmatic hypothesis that is compact and that best explains the dataset, including hypotheses written in a flexible, domain-specific programming language. As one study puts it, the task is to find "succinct programmatic hypotheses" that "best explain a dataset" (Symbolic Regression with a Learned Concept Library).

Variants. The papers mostly keep a single task name, symbolic regression, often abbreviated as SR, rather than splitting it into named sub-tasks. One paper frames the hypothesis space as a flexible, domain-specific programming language, and another paper relates symbolic regression to code generation by formulating SR as a program synthesis problem. A separate discussion also places SR in settings that seek transparent models in fields such as physics, biology, and finance.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to symbolic regression. In the papers, it is operat

nodes.name: Syntactic parsing
nodes.definition: Generating syntactic constituents such as noun phrase subjects (NP-SBJ) from text, based on Penn Treebank annotation schemes.

nodes.name: Synthetic data detection
nodes.definition: The task of making a binary determination of whether a given piece of data is synthetic or real.

nodes.name: Synthetic recall
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage is a family of long-context retrieval tasks in which a model must reproduce or extract specific inserted information, the "needle", from a long context or haystack that is often synthetic, irrelevant, or repetitive. A common formulation is passkey retrieval, where the model finds a short five-digit number embedded at some depth in otherwise meaningless text, but other papers frame the target as a statement, fact, string, or other inserted item at varying positions. Success is usually exact recovery of the inserted content, though some settings require all inserted items to be retrieved, and multimodal or audio versions require the response to stay explicitly tied to the located needle.

Variants. Most variants stay within text-only needle-in-a-haystack and long-context retrieval, including single-needle and multi-needle versions, with passkey retrieval the most recurring named subtype. Smaller variants add multi-needle reasoning, prefix-suffix dictionary matching, and retrieval of a target item far back in context. Another smaller line extends the setup to multilingual text, mixed text-image documents, and audio Needle QA, w

nodes.name: Table detection
nodes.definition: The task of identifying and outputting the bounding box coordinates of all tables within a document image.

nodes.name: Table question answering
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across definitions, the prevailing usage is answering a natural language question from table content and producing a natural language answer. Most descriptions ground the answer in a given table or in one or more provided tables, while smaller lines extend the task to multiple tables that must be retrieved and synthesized, or to mixed tabular-text data. Papers vary in the expected output: some emphasize concise, brief, or precise answers, others stress correct, accurate, or coherent answers, and one variant allows open-ended paragraph-length responses. Several definitions also note that the questions can require interpreting numerical or textual information, extracting and comparing table entries, or providing an arithmetic expression.

Variants. Papers use several names for variants. One paper explicitly distinguishes short-form table QA, with brief precise answers often involving extraction or aggregation of specific cell values, from free-form table QA, with open-ended answers grounded in tabular information. Other definitions introduce multi-table and multi-hop question answering, mixed tabular-text question answering in a financial conversational setting,

nodes.name: Table structure recognition
nodes.definition: The task of parsing the internal structure of a given table image into its constituent elements, such as rows, columns, and cells, and their relationships.

nodes.name: Table-to-report generation
nodes.definition: The task of converting structured tabular data into a comprehensive, coherent, and accurate natural language report that includes descriptions, analysis, and conclusions.

nodes.name: Tabular classification
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing use is as a supervised prediction task over structured tables: predicting a categorical label for a data point represented by tabular features. The definitions do not introduce alternative success criteria or judging schemes, and one paper discusses the task in sample-efficiency terms, noting that test-time training reduces the number of required samples for tabular classification by about 3 to 5 times.

Variants. The only explicit setting attached to the behavior is its use with in-context learning, described as leveraging the in-context learning capability of large language models for tabular classification with training-free adaptability across diverse datasets. Beyond that framing, the papers do not name additional subtasks, domains, or modalities.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. The papers therefore do not identify a recurring elicitation or scoring tool for this behavior, although one study operationalizes progress through required sample size and reports fewer samples under test-time training.

What it is taken as evidence of. Papers do not converge on tabular classification

nodes.name: Target identification
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Papers use this label for target-finding tasks, but not with a single uniform meaning. In AmpleHate: Amplifying the Attention for Versatile Implicit Hate Detection, it is framed as detecting and isolating entities in text that may be the focus of hate, including groups, organizations, nationalities, religions, and locations, and the paper notes that it "first identifies explicit targets" before hatefulness becomes clear. In Superlatives in Context: Modeling the Implicit Semantics of Superlatives, it is framed as recognizing the entity or event that has the maximal or minimal value in a comparison, where the target is one of the entities or events in the comparison set.

Variants. The observed variants split by setting. In the hate-related usage, papers treat it as explicit target extraction, with retained labels such as ORG, NORP, GPE, LOC, and EVENT. In the superlative usage, papers speak of "the target of the comparison," allow either an entity or an event as the target, require the target to stand in an IS-A relation with the comparison set, and illustrate it with cases where a named item such as "Nemo" is the max or min element.

Space of elicitation and s

nodes.name: Task completion
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats task completion as reaching the intended end state or user goal of a task, usually under task-specific evaluation criteria. Definitions commonly ask whether "the goal of each task is accomplished", sometimes with a binary "success flag (0/1)", and other papers describe it as fulfilling user requests through sequences of actions, tool calls, or UI interactions. Smaller usages narrow it to accepted predicted task execution, dialogue-game success, satisfaction of specified goal predicates, finishing baseline items in a study procedure, or generated code passing all predefined tests.

Variants. Papers study task completion across several settings. A common cluster is embodied and simulated work: household task execution, indoor task simulation through language interaction, household activities defined by predicates with specific counts, and open-ended embodied tasks specified by text or video. Other variants focus on graph-structured tasks with dependencies, branches, and hierarchical levels, web or application tasks translated from natural-language requests into actions, tool-use tasks with real-world API calls, and smal

nodes.name: Task decomposition
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats task decomposition as breaking a complex, high-level goal, instruction, query, or problem into smaller and more manageable subtasks, sub-actions, or subgoals. Most descriptions make these units concrete and actionable, often as ordered steps or structured plans, and some further require feasibility from current observations and memory or specify dependencies and execution order. A smaller line of work treats it as a latent ability to hierarchically break down problems, rather than only as an overt generated plan.

Variants. Papers use several neighboring names for this behavior, including program, problem, request, and plan decomposition, along with subgoal generation or setting. The settings are varied: code generation and modular functions, tool and web agent planning, multi-agent robot instructions, multimodal queries represented as computation graphs, and math or control problems where the output is intermediate statements or STL constraints. Other papers recast the behavior as sub-instruction prediction, constraint decomposition, action decomposition, requirement analysis, or high-level planning.

Space of elicit

nodes.name: Teaser generation
nodes.definition: The task of crafting intriguing but vague glimpses of a document's content to entice readers without revealing substantive information.

nodes.name: Teaser narration generation
nodes.definition: Producing a short teaser script from a longer documentary narration, including story-like rewriting and an ending question.

nodes.name: Technical problem solving
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats technical problem solving as the behavior of generating answers to well-defined technical queries. The definitions align closely: one describes it as answering well-defined technical queries, while another frames it as answering questions that require specialized technical knowledge and problem-solving skills.

Variants. Variation is limited in the descriptions. Papers alternate between calling the items well-defined technical problem-solving queries and technical problem-solving questions, and one description emphasizes that these questions require specialized technical knowledge and problem-solving skills.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link it to one measurement instrument, Arena-Hard. They describe Arena-Hard as a benchmark or dataset made up of well-defined technical problem-solving queries, including descriptions that it builds on MT-Bench and is designed to test more advanced capabilities.

What it is taken as evidence of. At the construct level, the only linked construct is Error recovery. One paper claims a causal relationship from technical problem solving to Error recovery, stating that

nodes.name: Temporal graph attribute forecasting
nodes.definition: The forecasting of future numerical values associated with nodes in a temporal graph based on historical attribute and structural data.

nodes.name: Temporal grounding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the dominant framing is localizing a moment, span, segment, or timestamps in a video that match a question, answer event, supporting evidence, or a natural-language query. Most definitions converge on finding the video evidence needed for a question, often described as selecting the related clips or localizing the answer event span; some formulations make the required output more explicit by asking for start and end timestamps or the intervals of clues that can accurately answer the question. A smaller strand casts the same behavior as grounding a textual description to a video segment, and one egocentric formulation asks models to find the visual event that can answer the question.

Variants. Papers use several near-synonymous task names, most commonly moment localization, temporal video grounding, clue retrieval, episodic memory, and moment retrieval. The common setting is video, but the prompts vary: some studies use question answering over answer-supporting evidence, some use query sentences or textual descriptions, and some focus on egocentric scenarios. A smaller line of work extends the label beyond video, describing temporal grounding as

nodes.name: Temporal prediction
nodes.definition: The task of generating a sequence of images and text that forecasts future events or reconstructs past events based on an input.

nodes.name: Temporal question answering
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, temporal question answering is most commonly described as answering questions that require understanding and reasoning about temporal knowledge, time-related information, events, and temporal relationships, including questions about when an event occurred or whether one event preceded another. A narrower formulation treats it as context-based date resolution, where the answer depends on resolving a date mentioned in a passage, for example identifying which team a player was associated with on a specific date. Another usage frames it as answering questions about recent events that occurred after a model's primary training cutoff.

Variants. Papers study several settings under this label. One is a context-based split built from question-context pairs that each require resolution of a date mentioned in the passage. Another is temporal question answering generation, abbreviated TQA-G, used through a separate LoRA layer and also in joint fine-tuning with MCMS to inject up-to-date knowledge from recent local news articles; a further variant is MIDTERMQA, a QA benchmark centered on the 2022 U.S. midterm elections for evaluating temporal knowle

nodes.name: Temporal referring
nodes.definition: The observable behavior of formulating or answering questions that refer to particular temporal positions within the content.

nodes.name: Temporal referring expression
nodes.definition: Identifying the specific image or images in a sequence where a described change occurred.

nodes.name: Temporal relation extraction
nodes.definition: The task of identifying and classifying the temporal relationship (e.g., before, after, includes) between a given pair of event mentions in a text.

nodes.name: Test output prediction
nodes.definition: The observable task of generating the expected output for a given test case input, based solely on a natural language problem statement.

nodes.name: Text chunking
nodes.definition: The process of segmenting a long document into smaller, semantically coherent, and self-contained pieces of text.

nodes.name: Text classification
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the dominant framing treats text classification as assigning a predefined, discrete category to a text input, variously described as a sentence, sequence, document, or piece of text. Success is usually framed as producing the target class label, and one paper describes the common setup as inputting a sentence or paired sentences and outputting a categorical label. A smaller line of work broadens the task to multi-label outputs or other binary classification decisions.

Variants. Recurring variants include topic classification, sentiment analysis, question classification, sentence classification, and sequence classification. Other papers adapt the same behavior to specialized domains and alternative settings, including multilingual, long-document, and multi-label formulations.

Space of elicitation and scores. Text classification is measured by 27 linked instruments. The most frequently linked are AG News, TREC, GLUE, SST-2, and DBPedia, and papers use them as datasets or benchmark suites for news or topic classification, question classification, sentiment classification, or broader sequence-classification evaluation. Many other instruments also

nodes.name: Text clustering
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats text clustering, often called just clustering, as grouping a set of texts into groups so that texts in the same group are more similar to one another than to texts in other groups. A smaller variation states the task as grouping similar text inputs into coherent clusters based on embedding proximity and explicitly notes that this is done without prior labels. Papers also consistently present it as one task category alongside other embedding tasks.

Variants. Papers use both the names "Clustering" and "Text clustering" for the same behavior. The named variants are mostly dataset and setting specific: Arxiv, Biorxiv, Medrxiv, Reddit, and StackExchange clustering appear in S2S and P2P forms, and TwentyNewsgroups-Clustering is also listed. Beyond these named datasets, papers mainly discuss it as a general task category within broader evaluations.

Space of elicitation and scores. One measurement instrument is linked to text clustering, MTEB, and papers describe it as a collection of datasets or a benchmark that includes clustering among its task categories. This is the only reported way papers measure the behavior, with m

nodes.name: Text continuation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats text continuation as generating the next portion of text from a given prefix, prompt, sentence, or opening passage. Most definitions describe success as producing a continuation that coherently and contextually follows the input, and some add that it should logically follow the prefix or preserve stylistic consistency with it. Smaller lines of work formulate it as regenerating the remaining part of a truncated passage, continuing from compressed memory slots, or generating continuations under added logical constraints or in red-teaming setups.

Variants. Papers use several nearby names, including text completion, text continuation generation, open-ended text completion, and transcript continuation. The task appears in sentence and article completion, five-token prompt continuation for trial and demonstration settings, continuation from a truncated movie review or other passage prefix, and continuation from speech-derived prompts where paralinguistic cues may shape the preferred completion. Some variants explicitly condition the continuation on style or control requirements, such as continuing in AAE or producing a

nodes.name: Text editing
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the dominant framing is broad text modification: a model either generates insertion or continuation suggestions that must respect contextual and logical constraints, or rewrites an existing passage to correct or improve it. Success is described in task-specific terms, including fixing misspellings and restoring intended content, matching clearly defined correction answers, identifying and correcting errors in a legal text, or editing a response by correcting factual inconsistency, removing hallucinations, and improving style, coherence, and fluency. A smaller line of work treats the behavior as changing review text so that its sentiment moves beyond a given rating range.

Variants. Variants span story writing, proofreading, and controlled rewriting. Papers study insertion and continuation in stories under combinations of logical constraints, text correction for noisy surgical narrations and smartphone-style correction tasks, grammatical error correction framed as explicit insert, delete, and replace operations, legal document proofreading, editing of machine-generated text by human experts or LLMs, and review rewriting that shifts 2 to 4 sta

nodes.name: Text embedding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage describes text embedding as mapping text inputs to dense or fixed-dimensional vector representations that capture semantic content or meaning. Most definitions tie these representations to similarity-based use in downstream methods, and some make the downstream target explicit by referring to classification or retrieval. Some papers also cast LLMs as text embedders, including a formulation in which models take text inputs and output 3072-dimensional vectors.

Variants. Papers study this behavior in several settings. Some treat it broadly as embedding tasks, while others narrow it to text similarity, specifically STS tasks, or to downstream tasks such as classification or retrieval. Several papers compare embeddings from different model or fine-tuning layers, and one paper frames the task through contrastive learning as evaluating the ability to contextually model bidirectional information.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link text embedding to one measurement instrument, MTEB. The linked studies use it either across 32 embedding tasks or on ten text similarity (STS) tasks, so the reported measurement practice center

nodes.name: Text generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the dominant framing is producing coherent, contextually appropriate natural-language sequences or responses from a prompt, instruction, query, prefix, or dialogue history, often through autoregressive, token-by-token decoding. A recurring formulation is continuation, for example taking an initial span of tokens and generating the next segment, or sampling an output string response conditioned on the input. Papers broadly agree on this behavior, but differ on whether they present it as open-ended free-form generation or include constrained cases such as paraphrasing, classification-style outputs, or task-specific completions, and they vary in whether success is tied to reference similarity, fluency and coherence, or usefulness and alignment with preferences.

Variants. The most common variant names are response generation, open-ended generation, natural language generation, language generation, and text completion. Many papers also place it in dialogue settings, especially single-turn interaction, and in multimodal settings where interleaved images and text lead to text completions, captions, answers, or descriptions. Smaller lines of

nodes.name: Text infilling
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage is generating missing text from surrounding context, usually a prefix and suffix, with the output expected to fit coherently between them. Several definitions describe filling masked spans, fragments, or the middle of a document or sequence, and some make this concrete as infilling middle tokens from given initial and final tokens or generating the middle of a story from its beginning and end. A smaller line of work narrows the task to masked-token or cloze prediction, including single scientific terms or entity names, and some fill-in-the-blank setups allow either generating or selecting the missing completion.

Variants. Papers use several narrower names and settings for this behavior, most often story infilling, masked token infilling, cloze completion, fill-in-the-blank completion, and text insertion. The settings range from short stories with masked fragments, to Arabic [MASK] fillings used to compare Arab and Western entity preferences, to climate-science blanks requiring a single scientific word, localized medical prompts with traditional versus allopathic candidates, knowledge probes with a blanked fact, and profile-

nodes.name: Text prompt generation
nodes.definition: The task of automatically creating suitable text prompts, including positive and negative examples, to guide an image generation model.

nodes.name: Text rewriting
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats text rewriting as an LLM taking an existing text and producing a modified version in response to instructions such as "polish," "rewrite," "refine," or "rephrase." Most definitions describe success as changing wording, phrasing, structure, or style while preserving the original meaning or remaining semantically relevant to the input. A smaller line of work adds stricter requirements, asking the model to change one aspect, such as topic, style, or factual content, while preserving others, and some watermark papers frame the same behavior as modifying text to remove a watermark while preserving meaning.

Variants. Papers study several variants of this behavior. Common variants include paraphrasing, rephrasing, synonym substitution, and other structural or stylistic edits that preserve meaning, while another recurring setup rewrites documents so that topic, style, or factual content changes selectively. Some work applies rewriting in a poetry setting, where a parent poem is turned into an "inspired, different poem" or, under the name "LMX-rewrite," into an offspring with different diversity characteristics; a smaller lin

nodes.name: Text simplification
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage is rewriting complex text into a clearer, easier-to-understand version while preserving the original meaning. Definitions repeatedly frame success as reducing complexity to improve readability or comprehension, often by using simpler words, rephrasing complex syntactic structures, and shortening sentences; as one study puts it, the aim is to "enhance the clarity and comprehensibility of a complex text while preserving its original meaning." A smaller line of work narrows the behavior to sentence-level conversion of complex, compound, or compound-complex inputs into one or more simple sentences. One paper also describes simplification as a tendency that may run against a specialized revision task.

Variants. Variants are most commonly distinguished by unit and constraint. Some papers use the names sentence simplification or sentence decomposition for breaking syntactically complex, compound, or compound-complex sentences into simpler forms, sometimes explicitly into one or more simple sentences; one variant additionally requires the output to match a target learner proficiency level while keeping as much level-appr

nodes.name: Text summarization
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the dominant framing is the production of a concise, coherent shorter text from a longer source, usually a document, article, post, or conversation, while preserving the main or salient content. Some definitions make this explicit as extractive or abstractive summarization, and several papers add quality criteria such as coverage, accuracy, coherence, overall quality, faithfulness, or factuality. A smaller group broadens the target from a standard summary to a title, a one-sentence or bullet-point summary, or a structured description of a document's attributes.

Variants. Most work studies document or article summarization, including news and long documents, but dialogue summarization is also recurring, and papers also cover multi-document and query-based meeting summarization. Multilingual settings appear as well, with summaries generated across several languages, and some tasks fix the output form to one sentence, a TL;DR, or key points in bullets. A smaller line of work uses nearby labels such as summary generation, document summarization, document description, text abbreviation, spotlight generation, and paper reading, and extends the behavi

nodes.name: Text-to-3D generation
nodes.definition: The general task of synthesizing a three-dimensional asset from a natural language description.

nodes.name: Text-to-audio generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the dominant framing is generating audio from a textual or natural language prompt. Most definitions describe success as producing a novel audio clip or relevant sound that corresponds to the prompt, and one paper states the output more explicitly as an audio waveform or spectrogram. A narrower formulation limits the target to non-speech audio, such as environmental sounds.

Variants. Papers use several closely related names for the behavior. The prevailing labels are text-to-audio generation and Text2Audio, some authors also call it text-guided audio generation, and a smaller line of work uses text-to-sound when focusing on non-speech outputs such as environmental sounds.

Space of elicitation and scores. Only one measurement instrument is linked to this behavior, AudioCaps. One paper reports evaluating it on the AC evaluation set, following the AudioLDM protocol and using its evaluation toolkit, so the recorded operationalization is through an evaluation set for generated audio outputs.

What it is taken as evidence of. No surveyed paper links this behavior to a construct, so the literature here does not specify what it is evidence

nodes.name: Text-to-CAD generation
nodes.definition: The end-to-end task of converting a natural language textual description into a complete Computer-Aided Design (CAD) model.

nodes.name: Text-to-speech synthesis
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats it as generating human-like or audible speech from text input, a text transcript, or written text. Definitions usually focus on producing spoken audio, and some formulations describe this as translating text into sequences of discrete audio tokens or producing speech from intermediate text responses. A smaller line of work broadens the task to converting textual content plus style instructions into speech, or to generating speech that is contextually appropriate for multi-turn dialogue; in those cases, success is described in terms of fluent, human-like speech with the requested acoustic style, users' needs, or dialogue context.

Variants. Several variants appear under nearby names, including conversational speech synthesis, speech generation, text-to-speech generation, and speech synthesis. Papers study context-aware conversational TTS, prompt-based customization with human-like intonation, style-conditioned generation from open-domain instructions, simple text-to-speech, and zero-shot TTS conditioned on a reference audio prompt or unseen speakers' prompts, sometimes described as generating speech in the voice of a t

nodes.name: Text-to-SQL
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats this behavior as translating a natural language question, query, or prompt into a structured SQL statement or program, usually given a database or table schema and sometimes database content or auxiliary documentation. Most definitions stress that the output should be correct or executable against a database and retrieve the desired information, though some papers frame SQL generation as an intermediate step in broader table question answering or as database querying that can also manipulate data.

Variants. Papers use several nearby labels, most often SQL generation or text-to-SQL generation, with smaller pockets using NL2SQL, text-to-SQL parsing, and database query generation. Beyond standard single-turn retrieval, variants include multi-turn and dialogue settings with schema and context tracking, open-domain or large-table reasoning over retrieved tables, incremental generation via sub-syntax trees, dialect-specific SQL, and database-action forms such as SQL UPDATE and SQL TRIGGER generation. Several papers also study it in decomposed pipelines, claiming a causal relationship from Schema linking to Text-to-SQL, whi

nodes.name: Textual reasoning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across definitions, the dominant framing is solving or answering reasoning problems in natural language. Papers describe it as drawing inferences or making judgments from text-based premises, answering directly in natural language rather than executable code, and handling verbal reasoning problems without relying primarily on mathematical calculation.

Variants. Other names include verbal reasoning and natural language reasoning. Papers study it as direct natural-language answering instead of code execution, and also in multimodal settings. They relate it to natural language inference and other language-task families, while a separate paper claims a causal relationship from textual reasoning to code debugging.

Space of elicitation and scores. Only one measurement instrument is linked to it: AlpacaEval. A paper uses AlpacaEval to assess pure text reasoning ability, and no other instrument is linked to it in the papers.

What it is taken as evidence of. Rather than treating it as evidence of one construct, papers relate this behavior to five constructs: visual understanding, chain-of-thought reasoning, mathematical reasoning, natural language understanding, and

nodes.name: Theorem generation
nodes.definition: The observable behavior of autonomously creating new, non-trivial mathematical theorems and their proofs.

nodes.name: Theorem proving
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the dominant framing treats theorem proving as producing a proof that establishes a given theorem, usually as a complete, formal, and verifiable sequence of proof steps inside a proof assistant. Papers often describe success as generating the full proof from the theorem statement, or searching for tactics and proof trajectories that complete the formal theorem, with correctness checked by a formal verifier or correctness checker. A smaller line of work narrows the behavior to single-step tactic prediction from a current proof state, while a few papers broaden it to human-readable natural language proofs or constructive proofs that establish a result by constructing an object that satisfies specified constraints. Some authors also phrase theorem proving as an ability to construct valid proof sequences, though the prevailing usage remains the observable proof production task.

Variants. Most variants stay in formal settings, especially proof assistants centered on Lean, and papers use labels such as proof generation, formal proof generation, formal-to-formal proving, and formal proof synthesis for producing complete proof terms or scrip

nodes.name: Thought generation
nodes.definition: Producing a compact summary of retrieved information to maintain context across iterations in multi-hop reasoning.

nodes.name: Throwing
nodes.definition: The action of propelling an object through the air.

nodes.name: Time series classification
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across definitions, the prevailing usage treats time series classification as whole-sequence labeling: assigning a class or categorical label to a sequence of time-ordered data points, often phrased as labeling an entire time series. Most descriptions stay at the level of outputting the label for the input sequence, while some further specify univariate or multivariate inputs or say the label is assigned from temporal patterns. A smaller formulation casts it as assigning a class label to a time-series input in response to a textual question or prompt.

Variants. Papers study this task across several settings, including human activity recognition, medical physiological-signal tasks, and datasets spanning biology, healthcare, electricity, physics, and nature. Variants include binary and multi-class classification, fine-grained and coarse-grained classification, and both univariate and multivariate sequences. Some examples are framed around physiological signals, such as diagnosing sepsis from a mean arterial pressure sequence, and papers also describe it as related to Emotion analysis and Sleep stage classification in that application area.

Space of elicitation

nodes.name: Time series forecasting
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage is predicting future data points or values in a sequence from historical observations. Success is usually framed as producing the next value or values at future time steps, often described as forecasting the next H timestamps or the next n values; some formulations specify multivariate or univariate series, and one prompting setup asks for continuing the sequence without any additional text. A smaller line of work narrows the behavior to forecasts that change when relevant textual context accompanies the numerical history.

Variants. Papers study several variants under this label. Common variants include multivariate time-series forecasting, next-value prediction, and long-term versus short-term forecasting; additional settings are few-shot forecasting, where only a small fraction of the available training data is used, and zero-shot forecasting, where forecasting is done on a target dataset or domain without training on its data, often in source-to-target setups. Some work also uses the name context-aided forecasting for cases where accurate forecasts depend on both numerical sequences and accompanying text.

Space of elici

nodes.name: Token classification
nodes.definition: Assigning a label to each token in an input sequence for linguistic analysis tasks.

nodes.name: Token copying
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, token copying is most commonly described as producing a token from the prompt or earlier context, often by identifying a token at a specified position such as the first or last token and reproducing it. The descriptions agree on that core behavior, though one phrasing emphasizes a position-based task while another states it more generally as generating a token that appeared earlier in context. Some authors also broaden the scope from a single token to single or multiple tokens and treat copying and recalling as interchangeable labels for the behavior.

Variants. The variants discussed are mainly positional and span based: copying a token from a designated prompt position, copying elements that occur earlier along an input sequence, and recalling either a single token or multiple tokens from the prompt. The examples given also include copying an earlier name token and copying a color token from context.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. Instead, papers describe it through task prompts that require reproducing the requested token, either from a specified position in the prompt or from earlier in the c

nodes.name: Token-level attribution
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage is an explanation behavior that assigns token- or word-level importance to the input for a model output. Most definitions describe highlighting or scoring the specific input tokens, words, spans, or token pairs that contribute to a prediction, and one study describes these highlights as "faithful cues reflecting the model's reasoning logic toward answer prediction." Some authors make the attribution label-specific and signed, so tokens have positive or negative impact on a particular class, while one paper frames the same behavior as prompt-token influence on the generation of a target output token rather than an alternative.

Variants. Variants appear as per-label attribution, word-level attribution or explanation generation, highlight explanation extraction, input saliency, and prompt influence. The settings differ: papers study words in a tip for relevance or triage predictions, highlight tokens, token pairs, or spans for answer prediction, prompt tokens' effect on each generated token in an output sequence, and explanation signals for intent classification that mark main predicates and their arguments.

Space of elicitat

nodes.name: Tone analysis
nodes.definition: Identifying the rhetorical tone of a text, such as sarcasm or satire, to assess its potential for misleading interpretation.

nodes.name: Tool use
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats tool use as an observable behavior in which a model selects and invokes external tools, APIs, functions, or other systems to solve a sub-problem or complete a user request. Most definitions make success depend on choosing the appropriate tool and supplying the right arguments or parameters, often by generating a structured request such as JSON, an API call, or Python code; some also include executing the call and using returned feedback or tool-provided content in later reasoning and answer formation. A smaller line of work frames it more broadly as a latent ability to know when a tool is needed, use it effectively, and interpret outputs. As one paper puts it, the model may access tools by generating tool calls as code that conforms to the API specification (When2Call: When (not) to Call Tools).

Variants. Papers use several near-neighbor names, especially function calling, tool calling, tool invocation, tool usage, and API call generation or interaction. The most common variants split by call structure: single-API versus multi-API use, dependent or chained calls where one output feeds the next, parallel calls, multi-

nodes.name: Touching
nodes.definition: The action of making physical contact with an object, often with controlled force.

nodes.name: Traffic accident recognition
nodes.definition: The task of classifying a given image or video clip as either containing a traffic accident ('Accident') or not ('Normal').

nodes.name: Training data regurgitation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing use refers to a model outputting exact or near-exact material from its training data, usually when given a prefix or related context from the same example. Most definitions describe word-for-word copying of text, substrings, or subsequent tokens, while some focus on specific payloads such as PII, secrets, canaries, copyrighted passages, or quotations; success is typically the model reproducing the target continuation, exact digits, or another matching sequence. A smaller framing broadens this to training data leakage, where private or copyrighted content is exposed or inferred through outputs or internal signals, and a few papers allow overlap or strong similarity rather than strict exact match.

Variants. Papers use labels such as verbatim memorization, training data extraction, recitation, verbatim quoting, and secret regurgitation. The settings vary across ordinary text, code or configuration quoted passages, quotations from interviews or movies, high-quality pre-training sources such as Wikipedia, and privacy-sensitive content such as PII, credit card numbers, or inserted canaries. Some descriptions emphasize extraction by adv

nodes.name: Trajectory captioning
nodes.definition: Producing a natural language summary of an agent's movement path using visual cues or landmarks observed in a video.

nodes.name: Trajectory generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, trajectory generation is most commonly treated as producing ordered sequences, but the contents of those sequences vary by task: imagined states, actions, and rewards based on retrieved knowledge; future UAV poses or waypoints for navigation; or new plausible state sequences that conform to dynamics supplied in context. When papers elaborate the behavior, they describe it as rehearsing decision-making trajectories, generating an imaginary dataset, or producing trajectories described as relevant and as closely matching the real simulated trajectory distribution.

Variants. Papers study several variants of the behavior. One line uses it for decision-making rehearsal from retrieved knowledge, another for hierarchical trajectory generation in UAV navigation, where a decoder generates the next target pose or waypoint, and another for generating new trajectories from in-context examples alone, without an initial state query. The same papers also use nearby labels such as decision-making trajectories, imaginary dataset generation, and hierarchical trajectory decoding.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. Wher

nodes.name: Transcreation
nodes.definition: The observable task of adapting a persuasive message for a new audience or context while maintaining the original message's core intent and persuasive goal.

nodes.name: Transliteration
nodes.definition: The observable behavior of converting text from one writing system (script) into another, based on phonetic similarity.

nodes.name: Treatment planning
nodes.definition: The observable task of determining a course of medical action, such as selecting appropriate examinations or therapies, based on a patient's clinical scenario.

nodes.name: Trend analysis
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, it is most commonly described as analyzing and describing directional changes in sensor time-series over specified intervals, with outputs marking segments as upward, downward, or stable. Some papers frame the same behavior as generating natural-language trend descriptions from sensor data, while another formulation asks the model to analyze variations across multiple periods to infer a degradation trajectory. Outputs are described either as interval-by-interval directional labels or as free-text trend summaries.

Variants. The prevailing setting is sensor time-series, where prompts ask for trend variations within a stated window and responses can enumerate successive segments as downward, stable, upward, and downward. Papers also use the names trend description generation for free-text sensor descriptions and degradation trend inference for reasoning over signal or semantic variations across consecutive cycles in a system-degradation setting.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link it to 2 measurement instruments: Human evaluation and LLM-as-a-judge. Both are used to score generated trend descriptions, with GPT-4o rating outputs

nodes.name: Trigger identification
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most definitions describe trigger identification as locating the word, phrase, or text span that marks an event occurrence. Across these formulations, success is usually framed as extracting the trigger for a detected event or finding the event-indicating item in a sentence, and one paper makes correctness explicit by counting a prediction as correct only when its offsets and type match a gold trigger. A scientific-event formulation places this within a text segment and describes the event as often represented as an agent-action-object tuple; another example treats "killed" as the trigger word in a sentence.

Variants. Papers use both trigger identification and trigger extraction for closely related formulations. The task appears at different granularities: extracting the trigger for each detected event, identifying a specific word or phrase in a sentence, locating a text span in a sentence or document, and selecting the most appropriate trigger word from an unlabeled sentence for a filtered event type. The settings mentioned include scientific events and target-domain unlabeled data.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it.

nodes.name: Triple classification
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats this behavior as judging whether a knowledge graph triple or triplet is correct. Papers agree on the core success criterion, a correctness judgment for a given triple, while differing in specificity: one defines it as predicting a binary label, correct or incorrect, for a triple based on a context document, and another describes it more broadly as estimating or validating the correctness of a fully formed triplet.

Variants. Papers use both "triple classification" and "triplet classification" for this task. The settings mentioned include classifying triples in generated graphs in a graph judgement setting, and a related knowledge graph completion setting where triple classification assesses the correctness of a given triple (h, r, t) and is discussed alongside link prediction for (h, r, ?).

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. In the task descriptions themselves, elicitation is direct: a knowledge graph triple or triplet is presented, sometimes with a context document, and the response is scored as a correctness judgment, most explicitly a binary correct versus incorrect lab

nodes.name: Triple extraction
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the shared framing treats this behavior as identifying entities and relations together rather than separately. One paper describes it as joint entity and relation extraction in a single step, with correctness requiring both entity spans, subject and object, and the relation label to exactly match the gold annotation. Another frames it as identifying entities and relations in a question or answer and converting them into head-relation-tail triples, and says the fixed triple structure requires the LLM to extract as many entities and relations from the question as possible.

Variants. Authors use both "joint entity and relation extraction" and "triple extraction" for closely related task formulations. The variants differ mainly in setting and output form: one is a few-shot joint extraction setting over named entity spans and semantic relation labels, and the other first identifies entities and relations within a question and then generates triples for the answers.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it in the papers. The only explicit scoring detail is an exact-match rule in the joint extraction setting, whe

nodes.name: Turn-taking
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. In the usage in the papers, turn-taking is treated as managing dialogue turns in a smooth, human-like way during interaction. One paper further describes seamless conversational turn-taking as a high-level cue, and characterizes conversational bots that follow the conversation flow as generally rated as more engaging and trustworthy.

Variants. The only label used here is conversational turn-taking.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it in the papers.

What it is taken as evidence of. No construct is linked to it as evidence of in the papers.

nodes.name: Turn-taking prediction
nodes.definition: The observable generation of speech tokens that align with appropriate conversational transitions, such as when to speak, pause, overlap, or interrupt, based on dual-channel input dynamics.

nodes.name: Tweet generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats tweet generation as producing short-form text in tweet format in response to an instruction or prompt. The common formulation is that the model returns the tweet itself, with one paper stating that in this task the response is "the exact tweet"; another frames it through prompts tailored to "a specific medium (a tweet)" and through creating instructions for a tweet.

Variants. A recurring variant is community-specific tweet generation, where papers describe generating tweet-like text on given topics for a specified community, including creating a synthetic corpus by prompting a community-aligned model to generate tweets. Another formulation has an attacker LLM create instructions for a tweet, with the prompt design adapted to the tweet medium.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to tweet generation.

What it is taken as evidence of. No construct is linked to tweet generation.

nodes.name: Type inference
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage is inferring missing static type information and adding it back into code. One formulation focuses on Python code, where missing type hints are inserted for function parameters, return values, and variables, and phrases the goal as inferring types that could have been written by developers; another describes the task more broadly as assigning static types to variables and functions in a dynamically typed programming language.

Variants. Authors use both type annotation prediction and type prediction for this behavior. The clearest variant is work on untyped Python repositories, illustrated by adding annotations such as `def greet(name):` to `def greet(name: str) -> str:`, while a broader variant is stated at the level of variables and functions in dynamically typed languages without further subtask detail.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to this behavior in the papers.

What it is taken as evidence of. No construct is linked to this behavior, so the papers do not state what broader construct it is taken to indicate.

nodes.name: UI element referring
nodes.definition: The observable task of identifying or describing a specific UI element based on its properties, such as recognizing text within a bounding box or classifying a widget's type.

nodes.name: Unanswerability detection
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Most commonly, papers treat this behavior as a judgment about whether a question can be answered from the available context, often phrased as predicting whether it is answerable or should be marked unanswerable. A smaller line of work narrows the behavior to checking whether a math problem provides sufficient information to solve, or whether the correct answer to a medical question exists within a candidate option set. Across these formulations, success is the correct decision about answerability, sufficiency of information, or existence of an answer.

Variants. Papers study it in several settings under different names: answerability classification for context-based question answering, answerable judging for mathematical reasoning, and answer existence judgment for medical questions with candidate options. The math variant asks the model to analyze the question, identify the conditions needed to solve it, and verify whether those conditions are present, while the medical variant asks whether the correct answer exists in the option set and is described as assessing answer plausibility in open decision spaces.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement ins

nodes.name: Under-translation
nodes.definition: The observable behavior where content from the source text is missing in the model's translation output.

nodes.name: Undercorrection
nodes.definition: Failing to make all needed edits, leaving some grammatical errors uncorrected.

nodes.name: Unit conversion
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the dominant framing is narrow: unit conversion is treated as transforming a clinical measurement from one unit to another within a calculation workflow, such as converting µmol/L to mg/dL. Papers also describe the behavior as testing accuracy in numerical standardization, and a worked example converts serum creatinine from 417 µmol/L to about 4.72 mg/dL.

Variants. Papers provide little subdivision beyond clinical measurement conversion itself. The clearest instantiated case is serum creatinine conversion, and one paper studies the behavior in a tool-mediated setting where parameter unit mismatches trigger nested tool calling so that additional tools can be selected and used to resolve the mismatch across a complex toolchain.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. Instead, papers operationalize it directly through unit-conversion examples and score it in terms of accuracy in numerical standardization.

What it is taken as evidence of. No construct is linked to it as evidence of.

nodes.name: Unit test generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats this behavior as producing unit tests, or an entire unit test suite, for a given piece of code or file under test so that functional correctness can be checked. A smaller line of work uses a broader task framing, describing the behavior as creating executable test cases or logical checks from a problem description, or writing desired input/output pairs before solving the problem; in those formulations, the tests are used to assess response accuracy and relevance or are rewarded for validity and correctness.

Variants. Papers use several nearby names, most often "unit test generation," and less often "test generation" or "test case generation." The main variants are generating a full suite for a file under test, generating diverse tests from a natural language specification in zero-shot prompting, producing 5-10 concise test statements from an instruction prompt, and writing input/output pairs to formalize a programming problem before solving it; one benchmark describes the goal as generating "an entire test suite given a file under test" (TestGenEval: A Real World Unit Test Generation and Test Completion Benchmark

nodes.name: Variable assignment
nodes.definition: A synthetic task where the model must output the latest value for a named variable based on a sequence of repeated assignments.

nodes.name: Variance analysis
nodes.definition: The task of determining if the variances of two different attributes across a population of entities differ significantly.

nodes.name: Velocity comparison
nodes.definition: Comparing the speed or motion state of one object against another in a video scene.

nodes.name: Verbal analogy solving
nodes.definition: Solving analogical reasoning problems involving semantic relations such as synonymy or antonymy (e.g., hot is to cold as up is to down).

nodes.name: Verbatim regurgitation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the behavior is treated as generating exact or near-exact text that matches copyrighted source material, with particular emphasis on long excerpts. The definition in "Certified Mitigation of Worst-Case LLM Copyright Infringement" specifies exact or near-exact sequences, particularly long spans exceeding a defined threshold, and its quoted passages describe this as "generating content that is substantially similar to copyrighted material" and as producing "long verbatim quotes from copyrighted sources."

Variants. The papers uses the label "verbatim quote generation" for this behavior. In that usage, the focus stays on copyrighted sources and especially long verbatim excerpts.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to this behavior. The only operational detail given in the definitions is that the matching text can be exact or near-exact and is particularly noted when it involves long spans exceeding a defined threshold.

What it is taken as evidence of. The only linked construct is Memorization. In "Mitigating Memorization in Language Models," one paper claims a causal relationship from Memorization to Verb

nodes.name: Verbose generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage is outputs that are longer or wordier than needed for the prompt or task. Most definitions treat it as excessive length, often with redundant or irrelevant continuation; some add that it can continue until the maximum generation length and become incoherent, or that an answer may begin correctly but then keep going with unrelated content that lowers evaluation scores. Papers also frame the threshold relative to desired conciseness or task complexity, and one study describes models as producing "longer and more verbose captions than top human ones" (Humor in AI: Massive Scale Crowd-Sourced Preferences and Benchmarks for Cartoon Captioning).

Variants. Papers use several nearby names, most often overgeneration, overly verbose generation, verbose response generation, response length generation, and unnecessarily lengthy output generation. The behavior appears in settings such as captioning, general prompt answering, and cases where a model gives the correct answer first but then adds unrelated material. A smaller line of work treats it more neutrally as response length with measurable word counts that vary by model,

nodes.name: Video captioning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats video captioning as generating a textual or natural-language description of a video's content or events. Most definitions stay broad, covering whole videos or video segments, while some sharpen the target to captions that accurately and comprehensively summarize the video, closely resemble human-written captions, or are refined using video-text similarity feedback.

Variants. Most papers keep the generic captioning framing, but a smaller line of work studies narrower variants. These include video scripting, with structured scene details such as a title, content, shot type, and camera movement; clip summarization for a time-stamped clip inside a longer video; audio description generation as accessibility-oriented narration of key visual elements; video narration as real-time descriptive text for a video stream; and video description generation focused on anomalous events. Some papers also shift from whole-video outputs to segment-level descriptions or emphasize especially detailed descriptions of subjects, environment, motion, camera parameters, and style.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link video caption

nodes.name: Video comparison and trend analysis
nodes.definition: The ability to compare different entities or events and analyze emerging patterns or trends over the course of a video.

nodes.name: Video detailed captioning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage is generating comprehensive and coherent textual descriptions of video content, often as long-form or summary-style outputs. Definitions agree that the description should cover more than primary actions and objects: one paper says it should capture "intricate details, contextual nuances, and temporal dynamics" (AuroraCap: Efficient, Performant Video Detailed Captioning and a New Benchmark), while another describes summaries that capture characters, actions, settings, and narrative elements. Across definitions, the desired output is repeatedly described as comprehensive and coherent.

Variants. Papers use both "video detailed captioning" and "video detailed description" for closely matched task formulations. The emphasized content differs across definitions, with some descriptions foregrounding actions, objects, context, and temporal dynamics, and others foregrounding characters, settings, and narrative elements. One example prompt is simply "Describe the video in detail," and the illustrated response begins, "The video begins with a scene featuring two animated characters..." (LongVU: Spatiotemporal Adaptive Compression

nodes.name: Video editing
nodes.definition: The task of modifying an existing video according to a user's instruction, which can involve changes to content, style, or objects over time.

nodes.name: Video generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats video generation as synthesizing a sequence of coherent video frames or realistic video sequences. Most commonly, papers frame it as generation conditioned on an input such as a text prompt, a class label, previous frames, or, in some work, a static image, though some definitions also allow unconditional generation. Success is described in terms such as coherence and realism, and some papers further emphasize spatial and temporal coherence with the input description, desired attributes and motion patterns, semantic faithfulness to captions, or fidelity to the prompt and visual quality.

Variants. Most papers study text-to-video generation, described as generating a novel video sequence or video clip from a textual description or caption. Smaller lines of work separate image-to-video generation from a static input image, class-conditional generation, and frame prediction with a 5-frame condition. A more specialized variant is impossible video generation, where the prompt asks for scenes that violate physical, biological, geographical, or social laws while the model is still expected to follow the prompt.

Sp

nodes.name: Video object segmentation
nodes.definition: The task of identifying and tracking the pixel masks of one or more objects across the frames of a video sequence, also known as video tracking.

nodes.name: Video question answering
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the dominant framing is answering a natural-language question from a given video, with the answer grounded in the video's content and often in its dynamic, visual, and temporal information. Most definitions treat success as producing a correct or accurate answer, often a textual one. Some papers frame the task as open-ended natural-language generation, while others use multiple-choice or instruction-following settings. One paper calls it a task that "requires understanding complex visual and temporal relationships within videos to answer questions accurately."

Variants. Papers study several variants. A common split is between closed-ended or multiple-choice VideoQA and open-ended, including long-form, answer generation, and one long-video line explicitly separating multiple-choice-based selection from text generation. Smaller strands examine long-video question answering, egocentric question answering on first-person videos, and temporal video reasoning, where questions concern relationships between actions over time such as sequence or frequency; one paper also says typical video-language tasks can be formulated as video question answering

nodes.name: Video scene segmentation
nodes.definition: Dividing a long video into coherent scenes based on shot transitions, visual changes, and narrative logic to support downstream audio generation.

nodes.name: Video summarization
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the task is framed as producing, or supporting the production of, a summary of a video's content from frame-level evidence. The papers agree on the summary goal, but differ in how they describe the input and process: Frame-Voyager: Learning to Query Frames for Video Large Language Models emphasizes selecting evidence from frames and notes that simple frame matching can miss subtle transitions between scenes, while Video2Roleplay: A Multimodal Dataset and Framework for Video-Guided Role-playing Agents describes taking frame descriptions in video order and generating a comprehensive summary with Chain-of-Thought.

Variants. The papers treats it as a video-language task grounded in ordered visual evidence. One formulation centers on selecting evidence from frames, another on aggregating frame descriptions in video order, and one paper also relates video summarization to video question answering by stating that video-language tasks including summarization can be formulated as video question answering tasks.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it in the papers. There is no named elicitation or scoring ins

nodes.name: Video-to-text generation
nodes.definition: The observable task of generating a relevant and coherent textual response based on a given video and an optional text prompt.

nodes.name: Vision-and-language navigation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the framing is consistent: an embodied agent follows natural language instructions to navigate through a visual environment, with success described as reaching a target destination or completing the language-specified goal. One paper also phrases the task as grounding a destination point within a given environment, which matches the same instruction-following navigation setup.

Variants. The named settings are high-level vision-language navigation tasks in ALFRED and a broader range of environments described as both discrete action and continuous robotic control. Papers also use closely aligned names such as vision-language navigation and VLN for the same instruction-guided navigation behavior.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it in these papers, so they do not identify a recurring instrument for eliciting or scoring this behavior.

What it is taken as evidence of. No construct is linked to it as what this behavior indicates, so the papers do not specify a construct that it is taken to reflect.

nodes.name: Visual dialogue
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage is open-ended, multi-turn conversation grounded in images, where a model responds in natural language to image-based prompts, questions, or instructions. Most definitions add that replies should be conditioned on both the visual input and prior turns, and several describe the setting broadly as multimodal dialogue with text and images rather than only a single image-centered exchange. A smaller line of work narrows the expected output to contextually relevant biomedical answers or step-by-step responses for interleaved-image tasks.

Variants. Authors use several near-synonymous names, most commonly multimodal chat, dialogue, or conversation, and visual conversation, visual chat, or visual dialog; less common labels include image-based conversation, image dialogue, and conversational VQA. Studied settings range from one-image chats to multi-image and interleaved multi-image dialogue, and some papers add visual prompt-based conversation in which users refer to regions with points, boxes, or masks. Other variants place the behavior in biomedical, pathology, or broader clinical contexts, or in multilingual and bilingual conversa

nodes.name: Visual editing
nodes.definition: The observable act of modifying an input image through operations such as drawing boxes, highlighting regions, or masking out areas to guide visual attention.

nodes.name: Visual entailment
nodes.definition: The task of determining whether a textual hypothesis is true, false, or neutral based on the content of a given image.

nodes.name: Visual hallucination
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage treats visual hallucination as a failure mode in which an MLLM produces incorrect visual claims or unsupported descriptions while interpreting an image. Most formulations focus on text that mentions objects, attributes, or relationships not present in the image, and a smaller formulation uses the name multimodal hallucination for outputs that contain information inconsistent with or absent from the provided multimodal inputs. Success is correspondingly framed as keeping the response consistent with the image content, or more broadly with the given multimodal inputs.

Variants. Papers most commonly study it when models respond about an image, especially when they describe objects, attributes, or relationships that are not in the input image. A smaller line of work broadens the setting from images to multimodal inputs and uses the label multimodal hallucination. One quoted passage also highlights failures in granular visual recognition, such as identifying small and occluded objects.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers measure it with four linked instruments. The most common is POPE, which papers describe as aimi

nodes.name: Visual information retrieval
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the dominant framing is retrieving specific visual content from long sequences of images or video, often by locating a target image, frame, or other needle embedded deep in the input. Success is commonly described as correctly identifying that target or extracting the requested information in response to a query, including questions like whether an image with an anchor object also contains a target object.
