A smaller usage formulates the behavior as recall from video observations, asking for the next or previous action step, an object near a landmark, scene details at a specific moment, or the start and end positions of an agent's movement.

Variants. A recurring naming pattern is needle retrieval and long video retrieval, studied in long videos, long image sequences, and needle versus haystack settings. These variants insert specifically designed images or a target frame at different depths within background frames, sometimes add distractor frames, and examine retrieval across varying background lengths or total frame counts. In urban video work, related task variants are named sequence recall, object recall, scene recall, and start/end posi

nodes.name: Visual instruction following
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage treats it as producing a textual response to a natural language instruction or question given an accompanying image. The wording is consistent across papers: one definition emphasizes a response based on the combination of a visual image and language input, while another emphasizes that the instruction requires understanding and reasoning over the image. The quoted passages illustrate example responses such as identifying a place from an image or deciding whether to go left or right.

Variants. Papers use both "visual instruction following" and "image-conditioned instruction following" for this behavior, and they also place it in multimodal or visual-language settings. The studied formulations include evaluation on Mixed Visual Instruction Tuning 665k with seven datasets, including VQA-v2, GQA, and VisWiz, and one paper reports it is related to visual question answering in a multitask setup that includes VQA and region-level VQA. It also appears in discussions of instruction tuning for visual-language tasks.

Space of elicitation and scores. It is measured by 6 instruments in the papers. The most commonly linked ins

nodes.name: Visual object categorization
nodes.definition: The task of discriminating between pairs of images, where looking time is used as a measure of perceived similarity or dissimilarity.

nodes.name: Visual object localization
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, this behavior is framed as producing the location of a target within visual input. One formulation asks for the original position of a masked image patch in a partially masked grid, while the UI-focused formulations ask for the location of a described interface element, either as precise screen or mouse click coordinates or as a bounding box. The papers therefore agree on localization as the core behavior, but differ in whether the target is an image patch or a UI widget and in the required output format.

Variants. The named variants are piece localization, UI element localization, and widget localization. Piece localization is posed on a partially masked image and asks for a patch's original position; one paper presents it as a representative single-step spatial reasoning capability. The UI variants use natural language instructions or widget descriptions with screenshots or interfaces and ask the model to find the target element, and one paper describes this as mapping "instructions and screenshots to precise mouse click coordinates" (AgentStudio: A Toolkit for Building General Virtual Agents).

Space of elicitation and scores. No measure

nodes.name: Visual question answering
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage is answering a natural language question about visual content, usually a given image, by producing a textual response from the image and the question. Papers often describe an image and an associated question that the model is expected to answer, sometimes in a short-answer format, and some definitions explicitly cover questions about objects, attributes, relationships, or scene text. A smaller line of work broadens the input to one or more images, 3D scenes, website screenshots, embedded webpage images, or video, and the response format varies across open-ended answers, multiple-choice answers, and yes or no answers.

Variants. Most papers stay with general VQA or image question answering on single images. Smaller lines of work use names such as general visual question answering, simple question answering, single-image question answering, region-text interleaved VQA, and scene text question answering; other settings specialize the same behavior to GUI screenshots, embedded webpage images, medical images, 3D scenes, industrial object analysis, or visually prompted regions. One paper also distinguishes questions th

nodes.name: Visual relation identification
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats this behavior as identifying or describing relationships among visual entities: "connections, interactions, or spatial dynamics" between specified objects or regions, or interactions between objects in an image. A smaller line of work narrows it to dynamic interactions in traffic scenes, including an ego vehicle's reaction to other traffic elements, while another formulation asks models to identify which properties change or stay the same across paired images in a visual analogy. In these formulations, the output is an analysis or identification of the relation, such as analyzing the relationship between marked regions or naming changed and unchanged properties.

Variants. Papers use several nearby names for the behavior, including inter-relationship analysis, object interaction analysis, interaction relation understanding, and relationship identification. The main settings are marked regions or arbitrarily shaped ROIs inside an image, traffic scenes with multiple agents, and cross-image analogy tasks. Some variants emphasize spatial dynamics with surrounding entities and backgrounds, while others emphasize extrac

nodes.name: Visual search
nodes.definition: The task of detecting the presence or absence of a specific target object within a visual array of distractor objects.

nodes.name: Visual storytelling
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats visual storytelling as generating a coherent narrative or story from a sequence of images. Most papers keep this sequence-to-story framing, though some narrow the task to story completion, asking for a concluding narrative sentence from preceding images and captions plus a last image, and another paper describes a narrative story accompanied by relevant images in an interleaved format. One paper instead states it as generating a narrative or story based on the content of an image.

Variants. Papers use the names visual storytelling, visual story telling, and VST. The main variants are full story generation from image sequences, interleaved text-and-image storytelling, and finishing a story from earlier image-caption pairs and a final image. In related usage, one paper claims a causal relationship from interleaved text-and-image generation to visual storytelling, saying it "opens up possibilities" for this application.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link visual storytelling to one measurement instrument, VIST, and no other instrument is linked to it. The paper that links it to VIST refers to "visua

nodes.name: Voice cloning
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing framing treats voice cloning as zero-shot text-to-speech: generating speech in a new or unseen speaker's voice from a short audio prompt, without speaker-specific training or fine-tuning. Definitions also describe it as synthesizing speech that mimics a particular person's voice, often from a brief audio sample. Some formulations make the text input explicit and describe the target as natural speech conditioned on a speech prompt.

Variants. Most papers use the names zero-shot text-to-speech or zero-shot TTS, while some explicitly call it voice-cloning speech synthesis. A smaller line of work places it in multilingual settings or alongside speech editing, and one paper frames zero-shot TTS as a conditional continuation task in which prompting texts, target text, and prompting speech are concatenated as prefix context. One paper also reports it as related to text-to-speech synthesis.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to this behavior. Papers nevertheless describe evaluation in zero-shot TTS setups, including evaluation on the VCTK dataset and comparisons in zero-shot TTS tasks where on

nodes.name: Vulnerability identification
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing framing is an observable task of identifying whether code, a function, or a repository contains bugs, vulnerabilities, or other defects. A common formulation uses a binary decision, for example classifying a target function as vulnerable or benign or deciding whether a quoted passage contains a defect, while other formulations ask for the weakness to be located and specified, including its location, type, or a report of CWE-style flaws. A smaller line of work broadens the target beyond source code to code, configurations, or systems, and one paper breaks the activity into subtasks such as identifying leaked credentials or insecure code.

Variants. Papers use several nearby labels, most commonly vulnerability detection and bug detection, with security vulnerability detection, code defect detection, and vulnerability location as additional names. The behavior is studied in function-level classification with interprocedural repository context, in whole-repository reasoning and repository-level auditing, and in file-level analysis that identifies vulnerability locations and types within source code or decompiled executable code. Some

nodes.name: Watermark decoding
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage treats watermark decoding as recovery of an embedded code or message from watermarked text. The observable outcome is extracting the intended binary or multi-bit content, though the decoding rule varies: one description uses a trained classifier on segmented text, another computes the text likelihood under competing message hypotheses and selects the best one, and another uses a secret key plus token-pattern statistics, choosing the candidate that minimizes red list token counts.

Variants. Papers use several names for this behavior, including watermark decoding, message decoding, and message extraction. The main variants differ by what is recovered and at what unit: binary watermark codes versus multi-bit messages, decoding independently within each segment, or extracting a message chunk at each position. Some descriptions also frame the recovered message as provenance information, such as userID, TimeStamp, and modelID.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to this behavior. Instead, papers operationalize it through the decoding procedure itself, such as a decoder applied to text segments, l

nodes.name: Watermark detection
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage is a binary decision task over a text sequence, suspect text, or generated content: determining whether it contains a watermark signal or was generated by a watermarked model. Success is usually framed as outputting watermarked versus not, often through a thresholded statistic, for example when the average watermark logit is greater than zero, when a z-value exceeds a threshold, or when the text is judged more likely under a marked than an unmarked distribution. Some papers phrase the alternative class specifically as human-generated text.

Variants. Papers study several closely related formulations, including text sequence detection, suspect or candidate text detection, and detection from generated content. Some explicitly describe it as the inverse problem of watermark embedding, some recover a key sequence from the content during detection, and others cast it as a statistical hypothesis test over a model and watermarking key. The decision labels vary slightly, with papers using watermarked versus unwatermarked, generated by the watermarked model versus not, or watermarked versus human-generated.

Space of elicitation

nodes.name: Watermark removal
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats watermark removal as modifying watermarked training data, model outputs, or text so the watermark signal is eliminated, neutralized, or made undetectable. Definitions agree that success means the watermark is no longer detected or retained, though they differ on scope: some place it in unauthorized knowledge distillation, while others describe reverting a watermarked language model or its output to an unwatermarked state, or making rewritten text undetectable to the corresponding detector. A smaller line of work narrows the behavior to watermark evasion or scrubbing, where a paraphrased or semantically similar text avoids verification while maintaining textual quality.

Variants. Papers use several names and intervention points for this behavior. The most explicit split is between pre-distillation removal, through untargeted and targeted training data paraphrasing, and post-distillation removal, through watermark neutralization that applies inverse or inverted watermark rules during the student model's decoding phase. Other variants describe text rewriting or synonym substitution, adaptive and non-adaptive paraphr

nodes.name: Watermark spoofing
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage treats it as an attack behavior in which an attacker generates new text that is falsely detected as watermarked. Both definitions center the success condition on detector acceptance, phrased as text being "detected as watermarked" or "incorrectly identified as containing a valid watermark." One definition adds that the spoofer does this "without knowing the private key ξ," while another discusses forgery when shared key exposure or enough understanding of the watermark generation rule would enable the attacker to forge watermarked text.

Variants. A smaller naming difference appears in whether papers call the behavior watermark spoofing or watermark forgery. The quoted passages also describe targeted attacks on Red-Green watermarks that allow "impersonating (spoofing) the watermark," and they note a learning-based variant in which an attacker queries the watermarked model, builds a watermarked dataset D, and then learns the watermark from that dataset.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. In the definitions and quoted passages, papers operationalize success through the detecto

nodes.name: Watermarked text generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage treats this behavior as generating text that carries an embedded watermark signal, usually described as detectable under standard or specialized decoding. Definitions commonly operationalize it by altering generation itself, for example by modifying token sampling, reweighting candidate tokens with a secret key, perturbing model weights, or changing the model’s output distribution during generation. As one study puts it, models can "learn to generate watermarked text with high detectability" (On the Learnability of Watermarks for Language Models), though a smaller line of work describes probabilistic reweighting that embeds an "undetectable watermark."

Variants. Papers use several nearby names for the behavior, including watermark embedding and watermark generation. The settings described include weights-based watermarking that generates watermarked text directly from the model under standard decoding, structural watermarking that samples from a weight-perturbed model, and message embedding that pseudorandomly encodes a message into balanced bits for multilayer reweighting. Another recurring variant combines logits-base

nodes.name: Waypoint selection
nodes.definition: Choosing the next exploration location or frontier to move toward during navigation.

nodes.name: Web navigation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage is a sequential interaction task in which an agent follows a user instruction or request by taking browser or webpage actions, typically clicking, typing, following links, or filling forms, until the instruction is achieved on a website. Success is most often framed as finding information or completing a goal, though some definitions narrow it to reaching a target section of a site, completing online forms or transactions, or purchasing an item. One paper describes it as a class of sequential decision-making problems where agents interact with web interfaces following user instructions, while another makes the sequence explicit as executable actions used to accomplish the task on the website.

Variants. Papers use several near-names for the behavior, most often web browsing alongside web navigation, and a smaller line of work refers to site navigation, web task completion, or webpage interaction. The settings vary from browser use for search and information retrieval to real-website task completion and online shopping, and some benchmarks are described as spanning domains such as travel, shopping, and social media. A more sp

nodes.name: Web search
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage treats web search as invoking a search tool, search engine, or search API with a generated or structured query to retrieve web information for answering a user query. A common formulation is retrieving a list of webpages from a live search engine, while one paper describes a fuller sequence in which the model formulates structured search queries, sends them through web search APIs, then "fetch[es] complete web pages, primarily the HTML content," extracts relevant text, and synthesizes an answer. Papers also describe it as web browsing used to answer a question.

Variants. Papers study several nearby forms of this behavior. Alongside the label "Web search," some authors use "Web content retrieval"; examples include general question answering, "complicated web browsing" to answer a question, searching for time-sensitive or source-specific information, and site-specific searches such as Google search or looking on BBC Good Food for recipes and ingredient lists.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. Instead, papers describe the behavior procedurally through explicit tool use, suc

nodes.name: Web shopping
nodes.definition: Navigating shopping websites to search for products and select items from search results.

nodes.name: Word association
nodes.definition: Generating culturally conditioned associative words in response to a given cue word, reflecting implicit semantic and cultural knowledge.

nodes.name: Word grouping
nodes.definition: The observable behavior of partitioning a set of words into groups of equal size based on shared topics or categories, as required by the GLOBALGROUP task.

nodes.name: Word guessing
nodes.definition: The observable task of iteratively guessing words to find a hidden target word, guided by scalar similarity feedback.

nodes.name: Word puzzle solving
nodes.definition: Sorting words into groups based on shared connections or categories.

nodes.name: Word segmentation
nodes.definition: Splitting continuous character sequences into meaningful words, particularly challenging in character-dense languages like Chinese.

nodes.name: Word sense disambiguation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed work, the prevailing usage is a Word-in-Context style binary judgment: given a word and two sentences, papers ask whether the word is used with the same sense in both, with positive cases defined as the same sense and negative cases as different senses or different homonyms. A recurring alternative treats it as selecting or assigning the correct sense of a target word in context from a predefined inventory or pool of candidate senses. Smaller formulations cast the same behavior as choosing the context-appropriate translation of an ambiguous word, resolving homonyms with context and POS cues, or associating pun words with their intended senses.

Variants. Papers study several named variants. The most common are Word-in-Context and polysemy disambiguation, both using paired sentences and a same-sense versus different-sense decision; Belarusian work uses the same pattern in BeWiC. Other variants include sense labeling, where models assign sense labels to polysemous words in a corpus, homonym disambiguation in Chinese with context similarity and POS conditions, word-sense association or pun interpretation for literal and figurative senses in pu

nodes.name: Word sorting
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the dominant framing treats word sorting as the task of arranging a given list of words in lexicographical, alphabetical order. Some authors state the rule more generally, as arranging words according to a specified criterion or the task's required sorting rule, but they still describe the behavior as producing an ordered list of words.

Variants. Papers usually refer to the behavior simply as Word Sorting, and one source abbreviates it as WS. The main variation is in how the ordering rule is stated: most commonly lexicographical ordering, with a smaller wording that leaves the criterion task-specific. Papers also place the task in BIG-bench reasoning-task settings, and one paper additionally lists it among BIG-Bench Hard tasks.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers measure this behavior with two instruments: most commonly BIG-bench, and also BIG-Bench Hard. In these uses, word sorting is presented as one of the reasoning tasks evaluated in BIG-Bench, while another paper includes it as one of the tasks in BIG-Bench Hard. No other measurement instrument is linked to it.

What it is taken as evidence of. No construct is linked to word sorti

nodes.name: Word unscrambling
nodes.definition: Rearranging the letters of a jumbled word to form a meaningful word.

nodes.name: Wordplay formalization
nodes.definition: The process of translating a natural language wordplay explanation into a structured, executable format, such as Python code with assert statements.

nodes.name: Workflow generation
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, the prevailing usage treats workflow generation as producing a structured, executable workflow in response to a user query, often in code form. A smaller framing narrows the behavior to producing an ordered sequence of subtasks that serves as the topological sequence for a workflow. One paper describes WorkflowBench as "the first dataset explicitly designed for workflow generation" (WorkflowLLM: Enhancing Workflow Orchestration Capability of Large Language Models).

Variants. Papers mainly use the general label workflow generation, though one paper uses node chain generation for the version centered on an ordered subtask sequence. The main variation is whether the target output is a full structured, executable workflow or the ordered chain of subtasks that organizes that workflow.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers do not link workflow generation to any measurement instrument.

What it is taken as evidence of. Papers do not link this behavior to any construct.

nodes.name: Zero-shot classification
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the surveyed papers, the dominant framing treats zero-shot classification as assigning an input to one of several class labels without task-specific training, fine-tuning, or labeled examples, often from a prompt and the model's internal knowledge. Some definitions narrow this to text, where the task is to assign the correct label to a text using semantic alignment between the input and class labels, while others state it more generally as asking for a prediction on any set of classes or, in multimodal form, selecting the most probable label from text descriptions. Reported success is usually phrased as predicting the correct label or achieving zero-shot accuracy.

Variants. The task appears in several settings. Papers study zero-shot text classification, prompting GPT-3.5 with paper titles, abstracts, and questions for classification on ogbn-arxiv, common reasoning zero-shot classification datasets, image settings using ImageNet pretrained features with 1-NN evaluation, and multimodal classification where an image is matched to the highest-scoring text label. One paper also relates zero-shot classification to pathology detection in a medical diagnosis

nodes.name: Zero-shot cross-lingual transfer
nodes.definition: Performing a task in a target language that was not included in the fine-tuning data, relying solely on pretraining and cross-lingual generalization.

nodes.name: Zero-shot inference
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the definitions, zero-shot inference is described in two task formulations. One describes producing segmentation predictions on an unseen dataset with a supplied vocabulary and no dataset-specific retraining, with the model "trained on Ctrain and directly tested on Ctest"; another describes producing predictions from a human-designed instruction without labeled demonstrations, and characterizes the setup as "zero-shot, inference-only". The papers therefore differ mainly in whether the setting is unseen-dataset segmentation or instruction-conditioned prompting.

Variants. Papers study zero-shot inference in at least two settings, open vocabulary semantic segmentation on unseen datasets with customisable vocabulary, and instruction-conditioned prompting. A named related variant is Zero-shot with Chain-of-Thought (CoT), which is described as incorporating reasoning prompts to generate intermediate reasoning steps before the final answer.

Space of elicitation and scores. No measurement instrument is linked to it. In the papers, the behavior is elicited either by conditioning on a human-designed instruction without labeled demonstrations, or by directly tes

nodes.name: Zero-shot question answering
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. The prevailing usage treats zero-shot question answering as answering questions without task-specific examples in the prompt or context, and often without fine-tuning or additional training. Most definitions describe success as producing correct answers, commonly on multiple-choice tasks, and papers usually report it as zero-shot accuracy; some authors broaden it to downstream or reasoning tasks answered from provided context or general knowledge, while one paper frames it as relying only on pre-trained internal knowledge and the prompt.

Variants. Papers use closely related labels such as zero-shot QA, zero-shot evaluation, zero-shot accuracy evaluation, and zero-shot tasks or zero-shot settings. The behavior is most often studied on benchmark tasks like BoolQ, PIQA, WinoGrande, HellaSwag, and ARC, and some papers broaden it to question answering and other natural language understanding tasks across various domains.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers link this behavior to 10 measurement instruments. It is most often measured by benchmark datasets or tasks, especially BoolQ, PIQA, WinoGrande, HellaSwag, and ARC; scoring is typically reported as zero-shot

nodes.name: Zero-shot task performance
nodes.definition:
Space of definitions. Across the papers, the prevailing usage is evaluation of model performance on downstream or language-understanding tasks when no in-context examples are provided, and often when no task-specific fine-tuning is used. Most definitions describe answering benchmark questions or completing tasks such as question answering, commonsense reasoning, reading comprehension, or natural language inference from the prompt alone. Success is usually expressed as accuracy, including zero-shot accuracy or reasoning accuracy across benchmark tasks, though some authors phrase the setting as instruction-only execution without examples.

Variants. Authors also use nearby labels such as zero-shot evaluation, zero-shot reasoning, and zero-shot downstream task performance. The studied settings recur around commonsense and question-answering benchmarks, with some papers narrowing the scope to multiple-choice or yes or no reasoning tasks, others to reading-comprehension datasets, and others to broader prompt-based downstream suites.
